Beneficiaries are approved by a specific Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation act conditioned on tax compliance. Benefits include zero rates on PIS/Pasep, Cofins, IPI and import duty for qualifying purchases and imports, a 100% income-tax reduction on profits from device sales, and a financial tax credit tied to prior-quarter R&D spending. Beneficiaries must invest at least 5% of gross revenue in R&D, file annual reports with audit opinions, and face suspension or cancellation for breaches, plus a 20% fine and SELIC interest on unspent residual investment. PATVD (Chapter II) concerned digital-TV transmitters and is revoked by Lei 14.968/2024. Chapter III protects integrated-circuit layout topographies: INPI registration, ten-year protection, exclusive rights, compulsory licensing conditions, and a criminal offence of infringement. Chapter IV amends Lei 8.666/1993 to add a direct-procurement ground for high-complexity defence supplies. The text is a compiled version with many amendments; the operative provisions above reflect the amended wording shown.

title: Projeto de Lei nº 2338, de 2023 - Dispõe sobre o desenvolvimento, o fomento e o uso ético e responsável da inteligência artificial com base na centralidade da pessoa humana
summary_short: Brazilian bill (Senate-passed text) setting national rules for AI: bans excessive-risk uses, imposes rights, governance and impact-assessment duties for high-risk and general-purpose AI, requires remuneration for copyrighted training content, and creates an ANPD-coordinated supervisory system. Most provisions would apply 730 days after publication.
summary_long: PL 2338/2023, approved by the Senate on 10 December 2024 and pending in the Chamber of Deputies, would set national general rules for developing, deploying and using AI systems. It excludes private non-economic use, national defence, pre-market research and testing, and pure data infrastructure. It prohibits excessive-risk systems: harmful behavioural manipulation, crime-risk profiling, child sexual abuse material, public-authority social scoring, autonomous weapons, and real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces outside listed law-enforcement exceptions. For listed high-risk uses (critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, justice, health, emotion recognition, migration and others), developers and deployers must document, test, mitigate bias, ensure human oversight and carry out algorithmic impact assessments with public conclusions; affected persons gain rights to explanation, contestation and human review. General-purpose and generative AI developers must make preliminary risk assessments; those with systemic risk must document testing and publish training-data summaries. Developers must disclose and remunerate copyrighted content used, subject to a research mining exception and rightholder opt-out. The ANPD would coordinate a national system (SIA) of sectoral regulators. Fines reach R$50 million or 2% of group revenue in Brazil per infraction. Most rules apply 730 days after publication; prohibitions, general-purpose AI and copyright rules after 180 days.
text_version: Senate-passed text (approved by the Federal Senate plenary 2024-12-10 as Substitutivo, Emenda nº 199; autógrafo dated 2025-01-31, sent to the Chamber of Deputies 2025-03-17). No later official Chamber version: the Chamber special committee (PL233823) had not reported as of 2026-10-11.

title: Projeto de Lei nº 2630, de 2020 - Institui a Lei Brasileira de Liberdade, Responsabilidade e Transparência na Internet
summary_short: Bill (PL 2630/2020) setting transparency, moderation and anti-inauthentic-account duties for social-network and private-messaging providers in Brazil, and creating a Transparency and Responsibility Council; most articles would apply 90 days after publication.
summary_long: Bill PL 2630/2020, the proposed Lei Brasileira de Liberdade, Responsabilidade e Transparência na Internet, applies to providers of social networks and private messaging services. Providers offering services to fewer than 2,000,000 registered Brazilian users are subject only to good-practice guidance. Foreign-seated providers are covered if they offer services to the Brazilian public or a group company has an establishment in Brazil. Providers must prohibit inauthentic accounts and unidentified automated accounts, label paid content, and disable group-inclusion by default in messaging services. Messaging services must keep mass-forwarding records for three months and must not allow external mass-messaging tools. Moderation requires notice, reasons and appeal, and providers must repair harm from wrongful content classification. Social networks must publish quarterly transparency reports within 30 days after each quarter and facilitate data sharing with academic researchers. Election-related advertising must be publicly available, and advertisers must confirm their identity. The bill creates a 21-member Council for Transparency and Responsibility on the Internet, which certifies self-regulatory bodies. Sanctions are a warning or a fine of up to 10% of the Brazilian economic group's revenue in its last fiscal year, with fines directed to Fundeb. The bill also amends the Marco Civil da Internet on six-month access-log retention. Council provisions take effect on publication; most other articles take effect 90 days after publication.

title: Projeto de Lei nº 2768, de 2022 - Dispõe sobre a organização, o funcionamento e a operação das plataformas digitais que oferecem serviços ao público brasileiro
summary_short: Bill PL 2768/2022 would let Anatel regulate digital platforms serving the Brazilian public. Platforms with R$70 million or more in annual operating revenue would be designated as holding essential access-control power and face transparency, non-discrimination, data-use and access duties, plus competition-law limits and a fee-funded oversight fund. Effective on publication.
summary_long: Bill PL 2768/2022 would regulate the organisation, operation and oversight of digital platforms offering services to the Brazilian public, assigning Anatel that role. Anatel would gain powers to issue rules, interpret the law administratively, settle conflicts between operators and professional users, repress user-rights infringements and handle competition matters outside CADE's remit. Covered platform modalities include search, social networks, intermediation, operating systems and cloud computing. Operators with annual Brazilian operating revenue of R$ 70 million or more would be deemed to hold essential access-control power and bear duties on transparency, non-discriminatory treatment, appropriate use of collected data and not refusing platform access to professional users; Anatel may impose separation, data-portability and interoperability measures. Concentrations and certain contract practices are subject to competition control. A Digital Platform Oversight Fund (FisDigi) would be created, financed by an annual fee on essential-access-control operators and other sources. Sanctions include warnings, fines up to 2% of Brazilian group revenue, obligations to do or not do, temporary suspension and prohibition of activities; foreign firms' Brazilian branches are jointly liable for fines. Effective on publication.

title: Projeto de Lei nº 3821, de 2024 - Altera o Código Penal e a Lei das Eleições para tipificar o crime de manipulação digital de imagens por inteligência artificial
summary_short: Bill that would amend the Penal Code and Electoral Code to criminalise producing, disseminating or sharing AI-manipulated images of nudity or sexual acts, including sexual content involving candidates, with prison terms of 2 to 6 and 2 to 8 years and aggravations for certain victims. Effective on publication.
summary_long: Bill (PL 3821/2024) that would amend two codes. New Penal Code Art. 216-C criminalises manipulating, producing or disseminating, by any means, false nudity or sexual-act content generated by artificial intelligence or other technological means, punishable by reclusão of 2 to 6 years and a fine, unless a more serious crime applies. The penalty rises by one third to one half where the victim is a woman, child, adolescent, elderly or disabled person, and by one third to double where the content is disseminated en masse through social networks or digital platforms. New Electoral Code Art. 326-C criminalises creating, disseminating or sharing images manipulated by artificial intelligence or similar technology with explicit or simulated sexual content involving candidates, punishable by reclusão of 2 to 8 years and a fine. The penalty rises by one third to one half where the victim is a woman, elderly or disabled person. If the conduct is committed by a candidate, cassation of the candidacy registration or diploma is also imposed. The law would enter into force on the date of its publication (Art. 4). The document is the bill text, and its status is pending.

title: Projeto de Lei nº 3982, de 2026 - Altera a Lei nº 9.610, de 19 de fevereiro de 1998 (Lei de Direitos Autorais), para regular a exploração econômica de obras intelectuais no âmbito do treinamento de sistemas de inteligência artificial, instituir o direito de remuneração proporcional e aperfeiçoar os direitos morais de atribuição.
summary_short: Bill PL 3982/2026, presented 17 July 2026, would amend Brazil's Copyright Law (Lei 9.610/1998) to regulate the economic exploitation of intellectual works used in training AI systems, create a proportional remuneration right and refine moral attribution rights.
summary_long: Proposed federal bill by deputy Amom Mandel, presented to the Câmara dos Deputados on 17/07/2026. According to its ementa (summary of purpose), it would amend Law 9.610 of 19 February 1998 (Brazil's Copyright Law) to regulate the economic use of intellectual works within the training of artificial intelligence systems, establish a right to proportional remuneration, and improve moral rights of attribution. The fetched Câmara page contains only the ementa and the procedural record; the articles of the bill (inteiro teor) are not in the document, so specific obligations, thresholds, exceptions and enforcement cannot be described. As of retrieval the bill is listed as awaiting dispatch by the Chamber president.

title: Projeto de Lei nº 4025, de 2023 - Esta lei altera a Lei nº 10.406, de 10 de janeiro de 2002 - Código Civil, e a Lei nº 9.610, de 19 de fevereiro de 1998, dispondo sobre a utilização da imagem de uma pessoa, viva ou falecida, e dos direitos autorais, decorrentes da utilização de inteligência artificial.
summary_short: Brazilian bill PL 4025/2023 would amend the Civil Code and the Copyright Law (Lei 9.610/1998) on use of a living or deceased person's image and copyright arising from artificial intelligence. Presented 21/08/2023; awaiting rapporteur in the CCJC.
summary_long: The document is the Câmara dos Deputados portal page for PL 4025/2023, not the bill's operative text. According to its ementa, the bill amends the Civil Code (Lei 10.406/2002) and the Copyright Law (Lei 9.610/1998) on use of a person's image, living or deceased, and on copyright arising from use of artificial intelligence. The indexing terms refer to manipulation of images, authorisation for use, works generated by AI systems, copyright protection, and training of AI systems. Mechanisms, addressees, thresholds, obligations and penalties cannot be verified from this document and are not coded. Procedural record: presented 21/08/2023 by Dep. Marx Beltrão (PP/AL) under conclusive committee review. The Comissão de Cultura approved its rapporteur's opinion with a substitute on 17/12/2025. The CCJC designated a rapporteur on 28/05/2026, and three amendments to the project were presented by 16/06/2026. Status: awaiting the rapporteur's opinion in the CCJC.

title: Projeto de Lei nº 4675, de 2025 - Altera a Lei nº 12.529/2011, dispõe sobre a designação de agentes econômicos de relevância sistêmica em mercados digitais e cria a Superintendência de Mercados Digitais no CADE
summary_short: Bill amending Brazil's competition law (Lei 12.529/2011) to let CADE designate systemically relevant digital-market firms, create a Digital Markets Superintendency within CADE, and impose special obligations on designated firms. Takes effect 60 days after publication.
summary_long: The bill amends Law 12.529/2011 to create a designation process for economic agents of systemic relevance in digital markets, decided by CADE's Tribunal on proposal of a new Digital Markets Superintendency within CADE. Designation criteria (Art. 47-C) include multi-sided markets, network effects, vertical integration, access to personal and commercial data, and number of users. Eligibility depends on group gross annual revenue above R$ 50 billion worldwide or above R$ 5 billion in Brazil (Art. 47-C §1), adjustable by joint ministerial act. A designation lasts up to ten years and covers the whole economic group (Art. 87-A). Designated agents must keep an office in Brazil and updated notification addresses (Art. 47-D); a daily fine of R$ 20,000, raisable up to fifty times, applies to failing to set up the office within the deadline (Art. 44-A). Special obligations (Art. 47-E) may include merger submission, transparency duties toward business and end users, bans on self-preferencing and tying, free data-transfer tools and interoperability, each set through a separate administrative process; they start sixty days after publication of the decision (Art. 87-B §2). Designated agents must file compliance reports (Art. 87-H). Non-compliance triggers the sanctions for economic-order infractions (Art. 47-G). The Act enters into force sixty days after publication.

title: Projeto de Lei Complementar nº 112, de 2021 - Dispõe sobre as normas eleitorais e as normas processuais eleitorais brasileiras (Novo Código Eleitoral)
summary_short: Bill PLP 112/2021 (Brazil, presented 3 August 2021, pending) would enact a new Electoral Code setting norms for parties, party finances, voter registration, candidate eligibility, electoral courts and elections. It is not AI-specific; it includes rules on paid online content boosting and data protection.
summary_long: PLP 112/2021 (text provided as part 1 of 5, Arts. 1–191) would institute a new Electoral Code. Livro I sets electoral principles and application rules. Livro II covers voting rights and duties: voting is compulsory from 18, optional at 16–17 and over 70, with fines for non-voting. Livro III governs political parties: TSE registration, internal autonomy, party finances (Fundo Partidário, donation bans, spending rules including paid online content boosting), and audits with fines for irregular accounts. Livro IV organises the Electoral Justice, electoral prosecutors and electoral defenders. Livro V sets voter registration, transfer and cancellation. Livro VI covers election dates, electoral systems and ineligibility grounds, including conduct by internet agents. Livro VII sets candidate eligibility and resignation requirements. Party processing of member data must follow the LGPD. Obligations address parties, candidates, electoral authorities and voters; the text is not AI-specific.

title: Lei nº 15.504, de 15 de setembro de 2026 - Altera a Lei nº 11.196/2005 para instituir o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), e a Lei nº 15.211/2025
summary_short: Amends Lei 11.196/2005 to create Redata: suspension, then zero-rating, of PIS/Pasep, Cofins, IPI and import duty on ICT equipment for accredited data-center projects in Brazil that commit to domestic-capacity, renewable-electricity, water-efficiency and R&D-investment conditions. Benefits last five years; in force 15 September 2026.
summary_long: Lei 15.504/2026 amends Lei 11.196/2005 to create Redata, a special tax regime for data-center services, and excludes data-center services from the Repes export regime. Firms implementing data-center installation, modernisation or expansion projects in Brazil may be accredited (habilitação) by the Federal Revenue Service; manufacturers supplying ICT products for an accredited firm's fixed assets may be co-accredited. Accreditation requires federal tax regularity and no Cadin record, and excludes Simples firms. Accredited firms commit to offer at least 10% of the capacity installed with Redata benefits to the domestic market (or invest an extra 10% of benefited purchases in R&D), meet sustainability criteria set by regulation, source all electricity from renewable or low-emission supply, keep water usage effectiveness at or below 0.05 L/kWh, and invest 2% of benefited purchases in R&D programmes. The domestic-capacity and R&D commitments fall by 20% in the North, Northeast and Center-West. Suspended taxes become zero-rated once commitments are met. Non-compliance leads to repayment with interest and late-payment fines, ex officio assessment, or suspension and cancellation of accreditation. Benefits last five years; PIS/Cofins/IPI benefits end 31 December 2026. The law also directs ECA Digital fines to the national children's fund for five years.
text_version: original as published (DOU 2026-09-15, edição extra); the Planalto page shows no later amendments or vetoes as of retrieval

title: Lei nº 10.431, de 21 de junho de 2024 - Regime diferenciado de tributação para empresas de CNAE 6311-9/00 (data centers), com adesão à Lei nº 10.550/2016 do Espírito Santo
summary_short: Rio de Janeiro state law granting a differentiated ICMS tax regime to companies whose main activity is CNAE 6311-9/00 (data processing, application and internet hosting services) that install or operate in the state, effective on publication and running to 31 December 2032.
summary_long: Rio de Janeiro state statute of 21 June 2024 creating a differentiated ICMS tax regime for companies whose main economic activity is CNAE 6311-9/00 (data processing, application service providers and internet hosting) that establish or already operate in the state. It partially adopts the benefits of Espírito Santo's Law 10.550/2016 under LC 160/2017 and ICMS Convênio 190/2017. Art. 2 grants ICMS deferral on imports, interstate purchases (rate differential) and internal sales of equipment for fixed assets, and an exemption for goods used for construction or expansion; covered equipment includes servers, switches and optical transceivers identified by Mercosur NCM codes. The deferred tax is payable by the acquirer on disposal. Benefits are conditioned on proof of listed requirements (use of state port and airport infrastructure, customs clearance in the state, capacity expansion, or 12 months of suspended activity for revitalization); the Executive regulates proof. Art. 3 requires at least one of six conditions, such as job creation or use of state inputs, and excludes Simples Nacional opt-ins. Art. 4 refers procedure to Lei Estadual 8.445/2019. Art. 5 removes the regime for irregularities after a 30-day notice to cure, with ordinary ICMS then due. Art. 6 revokes Lei 9.510/2021. Art. 7: in force on publication, effects until 31 December 2032.

title: Decreto nº 64.771, de 3 de fevereiro de 2020 - Dispõe sobre a tributação do ICMS nas operações com os equipamentos que especifica (data centers, CNAE 6311-9/00)
summary_short: São Paulo State decree granting ICMS suspension, deferral and exemption on listed servers, switches and rack equipment acquired for fixed assets by companies whose main activity is CNAE 6311-9/00 (data processing, application hosting). Requires a special regime request; conditions include employment, regional and environmental criteria. Effective 1 January 2021.
summary_long: The decree sets ICMS treatment for listed data-center equipment acquired for fixed assets by companies whose main economic activity is CNAE 6311-9/00 (data processing, application service providers and internet hosting). Covered items are rack-mounted servers with storage, ASIC and hypervisor features, and switches with at least 128 10/40/100 Gbps ports, classified under NCM 8471.49.00 and 8517.62.39. Imports are suspended and domestic sales deferred, with other operations exempt (Art. 1). Suspension applies only to equipment used exclusively in the importer's production process, and the suspended or deferred tax is paid with the recipient's later sale (Art. 1 §§ 2-3). Eligibility requires at least one of six conditions, including job creation, a non-existent activity, local inputs, strategic status, a priority region or logistics infrastructure (Art. 2). Simples Nacional firms and communication services are excluded; the regime is conditioned on use of state port or airport infrastructure, customs clearance in São Paulo, expansion or revitalization projects, and environmental compliance (Art. 3). Firms must request a special regime, which is automatically revoked for non-compliance, unapproved design changes, environmental harm, tax crimes, definitive shutdown or economic-order offences (Art. 4). Takes effect 1 January 2021 (Art. 5).

title: Supremo Tribunal Federal - RE 1.037.396 (Tema 987) e RE 1.057.258 (Tema 533): inconstitucionalidade parcial do art. 19 do Marco Civil da Internet
summary_short: Brazil's Supreme Court partly struck down Marco Civil da Internet art. 19, which required a court order for platform liability for third-party content. Platforms are civilly liable in listed cases, including failure to remove listed serious crimes, and must meet notice, transparency and local-representative duties, from 5 Aug 2025.
summary_long: STF decision on Tema 987 (RE 1.037.396/SP), judged 26 June 2025, with embargos de declaração on 17 June 2026, declaring art. 19 of Marco Civil da Internet (Law 12.965/2014) partially unconstitutional. Internet application providers are civilly liable, jointly and severally under art. 21 of that law, for third-party content in cases of crime or unlawful acts, unless reasonable doubt on unlawfulness is shown after qualified diligence. Art. 19 still governs crimes against honour, email, closed video or voice meetings and private messaging. A relative presumption of fault applies to paid advertising, boosting and artificial inorganic dissemination mechanisms. Providers are liable for systemic failure to promptly remove content of listed serious crimes, such as anti-democratic acts, terrorism, incitement to suicide, violence against women and child sexual abuse material. Marketplaces answer under the Consumer Protection Code. Providers must adopt self-regulation covering notice systems, due process and annual transparency reports, offer user and non-user channels, and keep a legal representative in Brazil. Strict liability is excluded. Effects are ex nunc from publication of the 5 August 2025 minutes; the item 5 structural obligations run 60 days from publication of the 2026 embargos minutes.
text_version: STF judgment decision (certidão/decisão de julgamento) of 26.6.2025 with the Tema 987 thesis, plus the 17.6.2026 ED decision restating the thesis

title: Resolução TSE nº 23.732, de 27 de fevereiro de 2024 - Altera a Res.-TSE nº 23.610/2019 (propaganda eleitoral)
summary_short: Amends TSE Resolution 23.610/2019 on electoral propaganda in Brazil. Requires labelling of AI-generated political content, restricts manipulated content and deepfakes in campaigns, sets platform duties and paid-boosting rules, and imposes data-protection duties on campaigns. Takes effect on official publication (Art. 6).
summary_long: Amends TSE Resolution 23.610/2019 on electoral propaganda, in force on publication (Art. 6). Allows paid boosting (impulsionamento) of political content in pre-campaign only under cumulative conditions and bars its use for negative propaganda (Arts. 3-B, 29 §7-A). Requires explicit labelling of AI-generated or manipulated content (Art. 9-B) and bans manipulated content spreading notoriously false facts and deep fakes used to harm or favour candidacies (Art. 9-C §1); the deep-fake ban is treated as abuse of political power, with possible cassation of registration or mandate (Art. 9-C §2). Platforms must adopt measures against notoriously false content and are jointly liable, civilly and administratively, for not immediately removing content in listed risk cases during the electoral period (Arts. 9-D, 9-E). Boosting providers must keep a public ad repository and API access (Art. 27-A). Campaigns and platforms processing personal data must follow data-protection duties, keep processing records, and may be asked for impact reports in some elections (Arts. 33-B to 33-D). Paid online circulation of propaganda is barred from 48 hours before to 24 hours after elections (Art. 29 §11).
text_version: TSE compiled text of the amending resolution (DJE-TSE nº 29, 4.3.2024, p. 132-145)

title: Resolução TSE nº 23.755, de 2 de março de 2026 - Altera a Resolução nº 23.610/2019, que dispõe sobre propaganda eleitoral
summary_short: Amends TSE Resolution 23.610/2019 on electoral propaganda. Requires disclosure of AI-generated or manipulated campaign content and bans new synthetic content of candidates near polling day. Restricts AI systems from ranking or recommending candidates, requires compliance plans from internet application providers, and takes effect on publication.
summary_long: Resolution of the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) of 2 March 2026 amending TSE Resolution 23.610/2019 on electoral propaganda; it takes effect on publication (Art. 2). AI provisions (Art. 9-B) require whoever uses AI-generated or manipulated multimedia content in electoral propaganda to disclose explicitly and accessibly that the content was manufactured or manipulated and which technology was used, including on each page or face of printed material. Publishing, republishing or paid boosting of new synthetic content using the image, voice or statements of a candidate or public figure is barred from 72 hours before to 24 hours after the end of the election (Art. 9-B §3-A); non-compliance requires immediate removal or service suspension by the application provider or by court order (Art. 9-B §4). Application providers offering AI systems may not rank, recommend or favour candidates, alter sexual or nude imagery of candidates, or create electoral advertising depicting political violence against women (Art. 28 §1-C). Judges may reverse the burden of proof in synthetic-content cases (Art. 9-I). Internet application providers must prepare a compliance plan with measurable indicators, which is a requirement for credentialing and registration (Art. 125-B). The resolution also amends rules on campaign events and live streams (Art. 3), paid boosting with a public repository (Art. 3-B), profile removal (Art. 38-A), coercive fines for breach of Art. 15 (Art. 15 §5), and free-airtime allocation by gender, race and indigenous candidacies (Arts. 53, 77).
text_version: TSE compiled text of the amending resolution (DJE-TSE nº 30, ed. extraordinária, 4.3.2026, p. 93-102)

title: Broadcasting Regulatory Policy CRTC 2024-121: The Path Forward - Working towards a modernized regulatory framework regarding contributions to support Canadian and Indigenous content
summary_short: The CRTC sets base contribution requirements for online undertakings that, alone or with their broadcasting ownership group, have $25 million in annual contributions revenues and are not affiliated with a licensed broadcaster: 5% of those revenues to designated Canadian and Indigenous content funds from the 2024-2025 broadcast year.
summary_long: CRTC Broadcasting Regulatory Policy 2024-121 imposes base contribution requirements on online undertakings through proposed orders under the Broadcasting Act. They cover operators not affiliated with a licensee, where the operator, alone or with its broadcasting ownership group, has $25 million in annual contributions revenues, excluding audiobook, podcast, video game, user-generated content and exempt-undertaking revenue. Covered operators must devote at least 5% of the previous broadcast year's annual contributions revenues to Canadian and Indigenous content from the 2024-2025 broadcast year. Audio-visual operators allocate this among the Canada Media Fund (2%, with up to 1.5% reducible by certified Canadian content expenditures), the Independent Local News Fund (1.5%), the Indigenous Screen Office Fund (0.5%), diversity funds (0.5%) and eligible production funds (0.5%). Audio operators allocate it among FACTOR and Musicaction (2%), a temporary commercial radio news fund (1.5%), the Canadian Starmaker Fund and Fonds RadioStar (0.5%), the Community Radio Fund of Canada (0.5%), flexible initiatives (up to 0.35%) and an Indigenous music fund (0.15%). Operators file reviewed financial statements, and the Commission will publish aggregate contributions per fund.
text_version: CRTC official decision page (Broadcasting Regulatory Policy CRTC 2024-121, 4 June 2024), incl. appendices and footnotes

title: Online News Act, S.C. 2023, c. 23
summary_short: Regulates digital news intermediaries (search engines, social media) with significant bargaining power over news businesses. Requires operator notification, bargaining with eligible news businesses over compensation for news content with final-offer arbitration, anti-discrimination rules, and Commission oversight. Initial provisions in force 19 December 2023.
summary_long: The Online News Act applies to digital news intermediaries (online communications platforms, including search engines and social media services, that make news content produced by news outlets available to persons in Canada) where the operator has a significant bargaining power imbalance with news businesses, assessed by size, strategic market advantage and prominent market position (s. 6). Operators must notify the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (s. 7). Eligible news businesses may start bargaining over compensation for news content: 90 days of negotiation, 120 days of mediation, then final offer arbitration for 45 days limited to monetary disputes (s. 19). Operators may request exemption orders based on agreements meeting listed criteria, and the Commission may issue interim orders (ss. 11-12). Operators must bargain in good faith and must not unjustly discriminate against or give undue preference to eligible businesses, including themselves (ss. 22, 51). A code of conduct is to be made by regulation (s. 49). Sections 45 and 90.1 of the Competition Act do not apply to covered activities (ss. 47-48). Enforcement includes Commission compliance and conditions orders, administrative monetary penalties of up to $25,000 for an individual and $10 million for an entity on a first violation, and civil recovery of agreement payments (ss. 45-46, 50, 59-61). Certain provisions were in force 19 December 2023; others by order in council or 180 days after royal assent (s. 93). The Minister must cause a review before the fifth anniversary of the day section 87 comes into force (s. 87).

title: An Act to amend the Broadcasting Act and to make related and consequential amendments to other Acts (Online Streaming Act), S.C. 2023, c. 8
summary_short: Amends the Broadcasting Act (assented 27 April 2023) to regulate online undertakings that transmit programs over the Internet: it adds them as a broadcasting class, exempts user-uploaded social media programs, and gives the CRTC order-making, expenditure and administrative penalty powers.
summary_long: The Act amends the Broadcasting Act to add online undertakings (transmitting programs over the Internet) as a distinct class of broadcasting undertakings. It excludes programs users upload to social media services, unless the provider uploads them or they are prescribed by regulation. It updates the broadcasting policy, including duties for foreign online undertakings to make the greatest practicable use of Canadian creative resources. The CRTC may make orders imposing conditions on broadcasting undertakings, such as Canadian programming proportions, carriage and information duties, and may require expenditures on Canadian programming. Licences remain required for non-online broadcasting undertakings; online undertakings need none. Offences carry fines, and administrative monetary penalties of up to $25,000 (individuals) or $10 million (other persons) for a first violation may be imposed, with a due diligence defence. Consequential amendments touch the Canada Elections Act, Copyright Act and Accessible Canada Act. Some provisions take effect on a date fixed by order; a parliamentary review follows in the fifth year.

title: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act, S.C. 2000, c. 5
summary_short: Federal privacy statute for private-sector organizations: requires those collecting, using or disclosing personal information in commercial activities to follow Schedule 1 principles, including consent, access and breach reporting, enforced by the Privacy Commissioner and Federal Court. Part 1 in force from 2001-01-01; Part 2 allows electronic alternatives to paper requirements.
summary_long: Part 1 applies to organizations collecting, using or disclosing personal information in commercial activities, and to employee information of federal works, undertakings or businesses (s. 4(1)); it excludes government institutions under the Privacy Act, personal or domestic use, and journalistic, artistic or literary purposes (s. 4(2)). Organizations must comply with the Schedule 1 principles (s. 5(1)), use personal information only for purposes a reasonable person would consider appropriate (s. 5(3)), and obtain valid consent (s. 6.1) subject to exceptions (ss. 7 to 7.4). Access requests must be answered within 30 days, subject to exceptions (ss. 8, 9). Breaches of security safeguards creating a real risk of significant harm must be reported to the Commissioner and affected individuals, and breach records kept (ss. 10.1, 10.3). Individuals may complain to the Commissioner (s. 11); the Federal Court may order corrections of practices and award damages (s. 16). Knowingly contravening listed provisions or obstructing the Commissioner is an offence, with fines up to $10,000 on summary conviction or $100,000 on indictment (s. 28). Employers may not retaliate against employees who report contraventions (s. 27.1). Part 2 provides electronic alternatives where federal laws require paper. Part 1 came into force 1 January 2001 according to a note in the Act.

title: An Act to modernize legislative provisions as regards the protection of personal information, S.Q. 2021, c. 25
summary_short: Quebec statute amending the public-sector access and privacy Act and the private-sector personal information Act (P-39.1). It sets rules for consent, transparency, privacy impact assessments, incident notification, automated decisions, data releases and penalties for public bodies and enterprises. Most provisions apply from 22 September 2023.
summary_long: The Act amends the Act respecting Access to documents held by public bodies and the Protection of personal information and the Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector, and amends several other statutes, including the Election Act. Public bodies and enterprises must appoint a person in charge of personal information, publish governance rules and policies, and conduct privacy impact assessments for information system projects and before releasing personal information outside Québec. Confidentiality incidents with a risk of serious injury must be reported to the Commission d'accès à l'information and to affected persons. Consent must be clear, free and informed, and express for sensitive information; consent for a minor under 14 is given by a parent or tutor. Persons must be informed of profiling technology and of decisions based exclusively on automated processing, with a right to the reasons and to submit observations. Privacy settings of technological products offered to the public must be set to the highest confidentiality by default. Data may be released for study, research or statistics under a privacy impact assessment and a written agreement. Individuals gain rights to computerized data portability and to de-indexing. Monetary administrative penalties, penal fines and punitive damages are provided, with maxima stated in the Act. Effective dates vary, with most provisions coming into force on 22 September 2023.</br>

title: Online News Act Application and Exemption Regulations, SOR/2023-276
summary_short: Sets application rules and exemption criteria under the Online News Act for digital news intermediary operators: an imbalance test with revenue and user thresholds, a 180-day notice duty to the Commission, and conditions for exemption orders. In force 19 December 2023.
summary_long: The Regulations, made under the Online News Act, do three things. First, for section 6 of the Act, they set when a significant bargaining power imbalance exists between an operator and news businesses: the operator's total revenue from all sources in the previous calendar year must exceed $1 billion, and the digital news intermediary must be a search engine with an average of at least 20 million unique visitors in Canada per month or a social media service with an average of at least 20 million active users in Canada per month. Second, an operator that must notify the Commission under subsection 7(1) of the Act must do so within 180 days after the Act begins to apply to the intermediary. Third, they set conditions for an exemption order under paragraph 11(1)(b) of the Act, including an open call process with notice periods of at least 60 days, information to the Commission, and a dollar valuation of non-monetary compensation. They also direct how the Commission interprets the compensation criteria: fair compensation, use of an appropriate portion for local, regional and national news content (a majority of monetary compensation), freedom and independence, and sustainability. For the largest search engine, a formula of $100 million adjusted by CPI applies. Group agreements are allowed, with allocation limits of 30% for non-CBC broadcasters and 7% for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The text sets no penalties. It comes into force on December 19, 2023, or on registration if later.

title: Verordnung ueber den Datenschutz (Datenschutzverordnung, DSV) vom 31. August 2022 (SR 235.11)
summary_short: Swiss federal data protection ordinance under the FADP. It sets data security measures, logging and processing-regulation duties, cross-border disclosure safeguards, data subject access and portability procedures, and rules for federal bodies' registration and pilot projects. Applies from 1 September 2023.
summary_long: The Datenschutzverordnung (DSV) implements the Federal Act on Data Protection and applies to controllers and processors. Articles 1-3 require protection-needs assessments and technical and organisational security measures calibrated to risk. Article 4 requires logging of automated processing of especially sensitive personal data at large scale or high-risk profiling where preventive measures are insufficient, and Articles 5-6 require processing regulations in defined cases. Articles 8-12 govern disclosure abroad: an adequacy list in Annex 1, standard data protection clauses, binding corporate rules, and codes of conduct or certifications, with the EDÖB approving certain instruments. Articles 13-15 set information duties, a two-year retention period for data protection impact assessments, and breach notification to the EDÖB. Articles 16-22 set procedures for access and data portability rights, including a 30-day response period and a fee cap of 300 francs. Articles 23-28 regulate data protection advisers, and Article 24 exempts firms with fewer than 250 employees from keeping processing records unless sensitive data or high-risk profiling is involved. Articles 31-34 regulate notification and pilot trials by federal bodies. Article 44 sets EDÖB fees. The ordinance entered into force on 1 September 2023.
text_version: SR 235.11 consolidated as of 1 December 2025 (Stand am 1. Dezember 2025), German

title: Bundesgesetz ueber den Datenschutz (Datenschutzgesetz, DSG) vom 25. September 2020 (SR 235.1)
summary_short: Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection (revFADP), in force 1 September 2023: sets principles, duties and data-subject rights for private persons and federal bodies processing personal data, including automated individual decisions and cross-border disclosure, supervised by the EDÖB and backed by criminal fines.
summary_long: The Act protects the personality and fundamental rights of natural persons whose personal data is processed (Art. 1). It applies to private persons and federal bodies, and to matters with effects in Switzerland even if initiated abroad (Arts. 2-3). Controllers and processors must observe processing principles, privacy by design and by default, and data security duties (Arts. 6-8). Foreign controllers meeting listed conditions must designate a Swiss representative (Art. 14), and disclosure abroad requires adequate protection or listed safeguards, subject to exceptions (Arts. 16-17). Data subjects receive information duties, notice of automated individual decisions with a right to human review, and access and portability rights (Arts. 19, 21, 25, 28). High-risk processing requires a data protection impact assessment, with EDÖB consultation where residual risk remains (Arts. 22-23); security breaches are reported to the EDÖB (Art. 24). The EDÖB may investigate and order administrative measures against named controllers (Arts. 49-51). Private persons face fines up to CHF 250,000 for listed offences, prosecuted by the cantons (Arts. 60-65).
text_version: SR 235.1 consolidated as of 7 July 2025 (Stand am 7. Juli 2025), German

title: Bundesgesetz über das Urheberrecht und verwandte Schutzrechte (Urheberrechtsgesetz, URG) vom 9. Oktober 1992 (SR 231.1)
summary_short: Swiss federal copyright statute (URG, 9 October 1992; in force 1 July 1993 per enactment note). Sets authors' and related-rights holders' exclusive rights, exceptions, protection terms, collecting society regulation, technical-measure protection, hosting duties and civil and criminal enforcement for works in Switzerland.
summary_long: The Swiss Federal Act on Copyright and Related Rights (URG) of 9 October 1992 sets out authors' exclusive rights in literary and artistic works (Arts. 9–16) and related rights of performers, phonogram producers and broadcasters (Arts. 33–39). It defines protected works (Art. 2), lists exceptions including private use (Art. 19), quotation (Art. 25), reproductions for scientific research (Art. 24d) and works made accessible to persons with disabilities (Art. 24c), and sets protection terms (Arts. 29–31). Collecting societies require authorisation from the Institut für geistiges Eigentum (IGE) (Arts. 41–43), and their tariffs are approved by an arbitration commission (Arts. 46, 55–59). The Act prohibits circumvention of effective technical measures and the making or sale of related devices (Art. 39a), protects rights-management information (Art. 39c), requires hosting operators to prevent repeated infringement under stated conditions (Art. 39d), and provides for civil remedies, criminal penalties and border measures against infringing goods (Arts. 61–77h). The enactment note gives 1 July 1993 as the date of entry into force.
text_version: SR 231.1 consolidated as of 1 July 2025 (Stand am 1. Juli 2025), German

title: Proyecto de ley que regula los sistemas de inteligencia artificial (Boletín N° 16.821-19, refundido con 15.869-19)
summary_short: Bill regulating AI systems by risk: bans unacceptable uses, imposes duties on high-risk systems, requires transparency for limited-risk systems and synthetic content. Applies to providers and deployers in Chile and to foreign providers whose output is used there. Fines in UTM; applies from the twelfth month after publication.
summary_long: Bill (merged with boletín 15.869-19) approved by the Chamber of Deputies and sent to the Senate on 13 October 2025. Applies to providers, deployers, importers, distributors and authorised representatives in Chile, and to foreign providers and deployers whose output is used in Chile. Classifies uses by risk (Art. 6): unacceptable uses are banned (Art. 7, e.g. subliminal manipulation, social scoring, real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces); high-risk uses must meet risk management, data governance, documentation, logging, human oversight, accuracy and cybersecurity rules and post-market monitoring (Arts. 8–10); limited-risk uses must be transparent (Art. 11), and generated synthetic content must be identifiable (Art. 5). Exempt: national defence systems, pre-market research and testing, and free open-source components. Controlled testing spaces create liability for harm (Art. 12); SMEs get priority access (Art. 13); ministries promote ethical development (Art. 14). Infringements are minor, serious or very serious (Art. 16), with fines up to 5,000, 10,000 and 20,000 UTM (Art. 17) and civil claims (Arts. 18–19). Applies from the first business day of the twelfth month after publication in the Diario Oficial.
text_version: Text approved by the Cámara de Diputados (oficio N° 20.843 to the Senate, 2025-10-13), boletines 15.869-19 y 16.821-19 refundidos

title: Proyecto de ley: Sobre protección de los neuroderechos y la integridad mental, y el desarrollo de la investigación y las neurotecnologías (Boletín N° 13828-19)
summary_short: Senate-approved Chilean bill (Boletín 13.828-19) on neurorights. Would require prior registration of neurotechnologies with the Instituto de Salud Pública, consent for interventions on others, and treat neural data as sensitive data; allows health authority to restrict uses; sets producer liability and criminal offences. Takes effect six months after publication.
summary_long: The bill (Boletín N° 13.828-19, Senate-approved text communicated 7 December 2021) sets rules for neurotechnologies and neural data, with stated purpose the protection of life and physical and psychic integrity (Art. 1). Under Art. 7, neurotechnologies must be registered in advance with the Instituto de Salud Pública before use on people. Art. 4 requires free, prior and informed consent, expressed in writing and essentially revocable, to use neurotechnology on another person. Art. 6 requires installation and operation to be essentially reversible, except therapeutic uses. Art. 8 allows the health authority, by reasoned resolution, to restrict or prohibit uses in listed cases, including influencing behaviour without consent, exploiting vulnerabilities, unauthorised data extraction and harm to the neuroplasticity of children and adolescents. Art. 9 makes producers, providers and administrators jointly and objectively liable for damage, with listed exemptions. Art. 10 sets criminal offences with presidio penalties. Art. 11 treats neural data as generally confidential and as sensitive data under Law 19.628. Arts. 13 to 15 amend Laws 20.120 and 19.628 and the electoral law. Art. 12 provides for a Ministry of Health regulation. The law enters into force six months after publication in the Diario Oficial.
text_version: Text approved by the Senate (oficio N° 578/SEC/21 to the Cámara, 2021-12-07)

title: Proyecto de ley: Modifica el Código Penal, con el objeto de tipificar la generación y difusión de imágenes o hechos de carácter privado o íntimo, creados con herramientas de inteligencia artificial (Boletín N° 17307-07)
summary_short: Proposed bill amending Penal Code arts. 161-A and 161-C to criminalise capturing, AI-generating or disseminating private or intimate images or facts without consent, punished with prison and fines. Operative provisions have no stated entry-into-force date.
summary_long: Bill (Boletín 17307-07) amending Penal Code arts. 161-A and 161-C. Art. 161-A covers capturing, intercepting, recording or reproducing private conversations, communications, documents, or images or facts (including those generated with artificial intelligence or editing tools) in private premises without the affected person's consent, and disseminating them. Penalty: minor imprisonment in any degree and a fine of 50 to 500 monthly tax units (UTM); where the same person obtains and disseminates, minor imprisonment in its maximum degree and 100 to 500 UTM. Art. 161-A excludes persons acting under law or judicial authorization. Art. 161-C covers capturing, recording, filming, photographing or generating with artificial intelligence images, videos or audiovisual records of another person's genitals or other intimate body part, for sexual purposes and without consent, in public or freely accessible places. Penalty: minor imprisonment in its minimum degree and 5 to 10 UTM; dissemination 10 to 20 UTM; higher penalties where the same person both obtains and disseminates. The bill imposes no duties on AI providers or platforms. Its statement of reasons cites a deepfake case and says existing Chilean law does not specifically address deepfakes. No entry-into-force date is stated.

title: Proyecto de ley: Regula la creación y difusión de imitaciones digitales realistas de la imagen, cuerpo o voz de las personas, generadas mediante inteligencia artificial (Boletín N° 17795-19)
summary_short: Bill protecting persons' identity and integrity against realistic false digital representations of their image, body or voice made or altered with AI. Prohibits generating or disseminating them, requires social media platforms to label AI content and resolve takedown complaints within 72 hours, and provides civil liability and fines. In force six months after publication.
summary_long: Bill (committee-approved text, Boletín 17795-19) protecting persons' identity and integrity against realistic false digital representations of their image, body or voice made or altered with AI or other technology. Article 6 prohibits generating or disseminating such representations; Article 3 defines them, and Article 5 exempts clearly labelled satire, parody, criticism or artistic expression. Article 2 applies the law to all persons and to social media platforms offering services in Chile, under criteria including a .cl domain or local payment methods. Platforms must appoint a Chilean legal representative (Art. 4), label AI-generated or manipulated audio, image and video (Art. 7), and resolve takedown complaints within 72 hours (Art. 10). Courts may order removal or blocking on request and impose civil liability for damages (Arts. 8-9). The Data Protection Agency imposes fines of 5,000 to 10,000 monthly tax units, weighted by factors including harm to minors and recidivism (Arts. 11-12). The law takes effect six months after publication.
text_version: Text approved by the Cámara committee (Ciencias y Tecnología) in its first report, 2026-04-06; approved in general by the Chamber floor 2026-07-22

title: Proyecto de ley: Prohíbe el acceso a plataformas de redes sociales a menores de dieciséis años y establece exigencias para los proveedores de servicios digitales (Boletín N° 18090-19)
summary_short: Bill (Boletín 18.090-19) that would bar under-16s from social media accounts, require platform operators, including foreign ones serving Chile, to verify ages and mitigate risks to minors, and fine breaches 1,000–5,000 UTM, applying six months after publication.
summary_long: Bill (Boletín 18.090-19), introduced by senators by motion, which would prohibit persons under sixteen from registering for, accessing or using social media platform accounts (Art. 4), and require platform operators to delete active accounts held by such minors. It applies to any provider offering or directing social media services to Chile, whether or not domiciled there (Art. 2). Providers would have to implement effective age verification systems (Art. 5), with verification processed under Law 19.628 (Art. 6), and to prevent registration by under-sixteens and mitigate risks to minors, including harmful content and manipulative attention-maximising design (Art. 7). Breaches would be fined 1,000 to 5,000 monthly tax units (UTM); repeat offences would bring a fine twice the previous amount plus temporary suspension of the service in Chile (Art. 8). Other civil, criminal or legal liabilities are not affected. The stated purpose is protecting the physical, psychological, social and moral wellbeing of children and adolescents (Art. 1). The transitional provision sets entry into force six months after publication in the Diario Oficial.

title: Proyecto de ley: Establece deberes y prohibiciones aplicables al uso de sistemas de inteligencia artificial y cuentas automatizadas en procesos electorales y plebiscitarios (Boletín N° 18669-06)
summary_short: Chilean bill (Boletín 18669-06) that would ban coordinated automated-account networks for electoral propaganda, require labelling of AI-generated electoral content, prohibit deceptive synthetic depictions of persons, require declarations and record-keeping, and impose fines and disqualification.
summary_long: The bill would apply to elections and plebiscites governed by Chilean electoral laws (Art. 2). It defines automated accounts, coordinated non-authentic behaviour and synthetic content (Art. 3). Art. 4 prohibits commissioning, contracting, financing or operating, directly or through third parties, a set of automated accounts to make electoral propaganda, excluding coordinated diffusion by unpaid volunteers. Art. 5 requires digital propaganda providers to file a sworn declaration at contracting, sent with the campaign's accounts to the electoral administrator. Art. 6 requires candidates, parties, electoral pacts and plebiscite sponsors to declare to the Servicio Electoral digital positioning contracts made within twelve months before the election. Art. 7 requires electoral propaganda that is synthetic to carry the label "Contenido generado o alterado con inteligencia artificial" and the sender's name. Art. 8 prohibits commissioning, contracting or disseminating synthetic content that invents or alters the actions, image or voice of a living, deceased or fictional person in a way a reasonable person could take as authentic. Art. 9 requires a public record of synthetic products in electoral expense reports. Art. 10 sets municipal-benefit fines of 30 to 300 monthly tax units for breaches of Arts. 4 and 8, fiscal fines of 10 to 100 monthly tax units for false declarations, without prejudice to criminal liability, and disqualification of providers from the next two electoral processes. The text states no entry-into-force date.},

title: Norma de Carácter General N° 514 - Norma que regula el Sistema de Finanzas Abiertas
summary_short: CMF Norma de Carácter General N° 514 (2024) sets operating rules for Chile's Open Finance System under Title III of Fintec Law 21.521: registration of information and payment initiation providers, mandatory APIs, security, consent, and phased deadlines for financial institutions.
summary_long: CMF Norma de Carácter General N° 514 (3 July 2024) sets rules for the Open Finance System (SFA) under Title III of Fintec Law No. 21.521. It covers financial information providers (IPI), account providers (IPC), information-based service providers (PSBI) and payment initiation providers (PSIP). PSBI registration is voluntary. PSIP registration is mandatory for entities already providing initiation services, within twelve months. PSIP applicants must post a guarantee tied to average daily amounts, with a UF 1.000 base. Temporary fund custody, where permitted, is capped at 72 hours. IPI and IPC must offer APIs meeting listed standards, with availability and response-time minimums, plus an alternative mechanism. The norm sets consent and dashboard requirements, five-year record-keeping, security and incident-reporting duties, and call-volume thresholds for reimbursable costs. The CMF may suspend participants and apply sanctions under Title III of DL 3.538. Deadlines are staged, from 6 to 36 months depending on participant group.

title: Decreto 17 - Aprueba modificación al Decreto Supremo Nº 40, de 2012, del Ministerio del Medio Ambiente, que establece el Reglamento del Sistema de Evaluación de Impacto Ambiental
summary_short: Amends Chile's Decree 40 (2012), the environmental impact assessment regulation, by revising project-type thresholds that determine whether projects must enter the SEIA. Addressed to project proponents; the text states no entry-into-force date. No AI-specific provisions.
summary_long: Amends Supreme Decree No. 40 (2012), which establishes the Regulation of the Environmental Impact Assessment System (SEIA), through a single article with three numbered items. Item 1 amends the entry rule for project modifications in Art. 2 literal g.1. Item 2 amends the project-type list in Art. 3: it defines high-voltage transmission lines (over 23 kV and 2 km), replaces several numeric thresholds with higher values (for example liquid storage from 200,000 L to 850,000 L, and waste treatment population thresholds from 10,000 to 15,000 and from 2,500 to 5,000 inhabitants), revises area, volume, throughput and capacity thresholds for aquaculture, toxic, explosive, flammable, corrosive and reactive substances, land transport, and solid, liquid and hazardous waste systems, adds an exemption for certain mining tailings reprocessing, and deletes the peat reference and literal i.6. Item 3 adds literal d.7 to Art. 60 on the project typologies applicable to project parts, works or actions. Thresholds are expressed in tonnes, cubic metres, kilograms, square metres and inhabitants. The text states no entry-into-force date, contains no penalty provisions, and contains no AI-specific provisions.
text_version: LeyChile (BCN) text as published in Diario Oficial 2026-01-21

title: Decreto 285 - Aprueba reglamento del procedimiento de calificación de los operadores de importancia vital de la Ley N° 21.663
summary_short: Sets the procedure for the ANCI to qualify essential-service providers and other institutions as operators of vital importance under Law 21.663 on cybersecurity: criteria, sectoral reports, preliminary and final lists, public consultation and appeals. Issued by decree dated 6 September 2024.
summary_long: Decree No. 285 (6 September 2024) approves the regulation on the procedure for qualifying operators of vital importance (OIV) under Law 21.663, the Cybersecurity Framework. The ANCI may qualify essential-service providers that depend on computer networks and whose affectation would have a significant impact, assessed by criteria on potential affected persons, redundancy, monoprovision, dependency and institutional relevance. It may also qualify private institutions that have acquired a critical role or are highly exposed to cybersecurity risk. Sectoral bodies must issue reports within 30 days. The ANCI prepares a preliminary list, approved by resolution and published, which is subject to a public consultation of at least 30 days, with notification to listed institutions and an executive summary of the consultation. The final list of private institutions, showing name, RUT and legal domicile, is approved by reasoned resolution and published; appeals under the administrative procedure law and a judicial claim under Law 21.663 Art. 46 are available. Public institutions follow a separate title with a Ministry of Finance report. Qualifications are reviewed at least every three years. Transitional provisions set a 90-day deadline for the first qualification and allow electronic notification under phased rules, otherwise registered mail.
text_version: LeyChile (BCN) text as published in Diario Oficial 2025-03-13

title: Decreto 295 - Aprueba reglamento de reporte de incidentes de ciberseguridad de la Ley N° 21.663
summary_short: Regulation implementing Law 21.663 (Chile) requires essential-service providers and vital operators to report significant cybersecurity incidents to the national CSIRT: an early alert within three hours, a second report after 72 hours, and a final report within 15 days of the alert.
summary_long: Chile's regulation under Law 21.663 sets reporting rules for significant cybersecurity incidents. Essential-service providers and vital operators must report to the national CSIRT. An incident is significant if it can interrupt an essential service, affect physical integrity or health, affect IT assets or networks even without immediate service impact, enter systems without authorisation, or affect systems holding personal data; the number of people affected, duration and geographic extent are also considered (Art. 3). Reports go through the Agency's platform, which operates 24 hours a day (Art. 8). Reporting is staged: an early alert within three hours of becoming aware of the incident (Art. 9), a second report after 72 hours (Art. 10; 24 hours for a vital operator whose essential services are affected), an action plan within seven calendar days for vital operators (Art. 11), and a final report within 15 calendar days of the early alert once the incident has been managed (Art. 12). Partial reports are due every 15 days for prolonged incidents (Art. 13). Reports must omit personal data (Art. 6). Planned maintenance is not an incident (Art. 4). The Director may exempt incident categories and essential-service providers from notification (Art. 3). Heads of state bodies must require IT service providers to share vulnerability and incident information (Art. 15). The regulation takes effect when the Agency starts its activities (first transitional article).
text_version: LeyChile (BCN) text as published in Diario Oficial 2025-03-01

title: Decreto 38 - Establece norma de emisión para grupos electrógenos
summary_short: Chilean decree setting air-pollutant emission limits for new compression-ignition generator sets of 19 kW or more, applying nationwide. Requires pre-import documentary verification, annual owner reporting, sales reporting by manufacturers and importers, and customs data sharing, supervised by the Superintendencia del Medio Ambiente. Takes effect on publication.
summary_long: Decree No. 38 of 2020 sets national exhaust-emission limits (g/kWh) for new generator sets with compression-ignition engines and maximum engine power of 19 kW or more, applicable throughout Chile (Arts. 1, 4-7). Units supplying residential customers in areas without access to the national electrical system are excluded (Art. 2). Limits vary by power band and engine displacement; those for 130 kW and above apply to units imported from 15 September 2028 (Arts. 6-7, as amended in 2025). Manufacturers, representatives, distributors and importers must submit compliance documentation to the Superintendencia del Medio Ambiente before import; the verified documentation supports customs clearance (Art. 8). New units need a sealed, non-resettable hour meter, and owners of units of 19 kW or more report annually through the RETC single-window system (Art. 9). Sales reporting to the Superintendencia starts 36 months after entry into force (Art. 10); Customs reports monthly imports from 24 months (Art. 11). Protocols are due within 6 months (Art. 13). Supervision falls to the Superintendencia under Law 20.417 (Art. 12). The decree takes effect on publication (Art. 14); no penalty amounts appear in the text.
text_version: LeyChile (BCN) current version (vigencia from 2025-09-25, incorporating later modifications)

title: Ley 21.431 - Modifica el Código del Trabajo regulando el contrato de trabajadores de empresas de plataformas digitales de servicios
summary_short: Amends the Chilean Labour Code to regulate digital service platform companies and their workers, treating those working dependently as employees and setting pay floors, working-time, data, non-discrimination and protection rules for dependent and independent platform workers, from the first day of the sixth month after publication.
summary_long: Law 21.431 amends the Labour Code (Art. 38 and a new Chapter X, Arts. 152 quáter P to 152 quinquies I) to regulate work through digital service platforms. It defines platform service companies and platform workers, and treats a platform worker as dependent when the subordination conditions of Art. 7 are met, and as independent otherwise. Dependent workers' contracts must set out terms such as work location, remuneration method and a complaints channel, and their hourly pay may not fall below a proportion of the minimum monthly wage increased by 20%. Independent workers receive a written contract, a minimum hourly fee on the same basis, a minimum daily disconnection period of twelve continuous hours, 30 days' written notice of termination after six months of continuous service, and social security coverage. Common rules cover information on offered services, access to and portability of personal data, a duty to avoid algorithmic discrimination, safety training and protective equipment, and collective bargaining rights. The Dirección del Trabajo supervises compliance, and fines under Art. 506 are doubled for repeat offences. Transitional provisions give existing companies three years to meet the employer requirement in Art. 19(1) of the Labour Code and require an annual report by the Consejo Superior Laboral for three years.](truncated)

title: Ley 21.459 - Establece normas sobre delitos informáticos, deroga la Ley N° 19.223 y modifica otros cuerpos legales con el objeto de adecuarlos al Convenio de Budapest
summary_short: Establishes criminal offences against computer systems, data, fraud and forgery in Chile, repeals Law 19.223, and amends criminal procedure and other laws to align with the Budapest Convention.
summary_long: Law 21.459 creates criminal offences against computer systems and data (Arts. 1-8), with prison terms and, for fraud, fines in monthly tax units. Article 2 exempts certain access to Chilean-domiciled systems that meets listed conditions, including Agency registration and prior reporting. Article 10 sets aggravating circumstances, including abuse of trust, of children, adolescents or older adults, and disruption of public utilities or elections. Title II lets investigations start on complaint of the Minister of Public Security (Art. 11) and lets judges order investigative techniques (Art. 12) and confiscation (Art. 13). Article 18 adds Criminal Procedure Code article 218 bis, letting prosecutors require service providers to preserve data for 90 days, extendable once up to 180, and keep the procedure secret. Article 17 repeals Law 19.223; Articles 19 to 21 amend three other laws. Article 18 takes effect after a Transport Ministry regulation; Articles 19 and 21 six months after publication.

title: Ley 21.521 - Promueve la competencia e inclusión financiera a través de la innovación y tecnología en la prestación de servicios financieros (Ley Fintec)
summary_short: Chile's Fintec Law 21.521 requires crowdfunding, alternative trading, brokerage, order-routing, custody and advisory providers to register with the CMF and obtain authorization, and creates an open finance regime for consent-based data sharing and payment initiation. Titles II and III apply from CMF rules.
summary_long: Law 21.521 (Fintec) is supervised by the CMF. Title II requires providers of crowdfunding platforms, alternative trading systems, brokerage, order routing, custody and credit or investment advice to register and obtain prior authorization for each service, meet guarantee, minimum equity, governance and cybersecurity requirements, and inform clients. Registration is refused to persons with specified prior sanctions and can be cancelled for serious infractions (Art. 14). Title III creates an open finance system in which banks and card issuers must provide consented client data through standardized interfaces, with payment initiation providers able to initiate payments with client consent; data-access fees are limited to incremental costs and clients cannot be charged for these services. Consent is revocable at any time. The CMF may order suspensions and sanction breaches under DL 3.538. Title IV requires product suitability and non-misleading advertising. Title V amends banking, securities, fund management, insurance, anti-money laundering and Law 20.009 fraud rules; algorithms automating certain fund functions must demonstrate suitability. Titles II and III apply from CMF rules; existing providers have 12 months to register and CMF rules are due within 18 months.

title: Ley 21.663 - Ley Marco de Ciberseguridad
summary_short: Ley 21.663, dated 26 March 2024, sets cybersecurity duties for State bodies and for private institutions that provide essential services, and creates the National Cybersecurity Agency (ANCI) with supervisory and sanction powers.
summary_long: Ley 21.663, the Cybersecurity Framework Law dated 26 March 2024, sets institutional rules and cybersecurity duties for State bodies and for private institutions providing essential services. Essential services and vital-importance operators are designated by resolution of the ANCI. Vital operators must maintain a continuous information security management system and certified continuity and cybersecurity plans. All covered institutions must report significant incidents to the national CSIRT: an early alert within three hours, an update within 72 hours (24 hours where a vital operator's services are affected), and a final report within 15 days. The Agency issues binding protocols and standards, supervises compliance, and may order particular audits, inspections and system access, with contested access requiring judicial authorisation. The law also creates a multisectoral council, a defence CSIRT, a secure state network and an interministerial committee. Infringements are minor, serious or very serious, with fines of up to 5,000 to 40,000 UTM depending on tier and vital-operator status; Penal Code sanctions apply to confidentiality breaches. Good-faith vulnerability research is exempted from criminal liability under registration and notification conditions. Sectoral authorities may issue equivalent rules that prevail. Transitional provisions let the President set the Agency's start date by decree within one year of publication.

title: Ley 21.719 - Regula la protección y el tratamiento de los datos personales y crea la Agencia de Protección de Datos Personales
summary_short: Rewrites Chile's personal data law (Ley 19.628). It sets principles, data-subject rights (including rights on automated decisions), controller duties, international transfer rules, and three tiers of infringement with fines up to 20,000 UTM, and it creates the Agencia de Protección de Datos Personales. In force 1 December 2026.
summary_long: Ley 21.719 replaces most of Ley 19.628 and renames it a personal data protection law. It applies to public and private controllers established in Chile, and to foreign controllers that offer goods or services to people in Chile or monitor them. It sets principles, lawful bases and rights of access, rectification, erasure, objection, portability and blocking. It adds a right to object to, and not be subject to, decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, with safeguards: explanation, human intervention and review. Controllers must publish transparency information, apply privacy by design and security measures, report security breaches to the Agency, carry out impact assessments for high-risk processing, and meet stricter rules for sensitive, biometric, health and children's data. International transfers require adequacy, adequate safeguards or listed exceptions. The Agency, led by a three-member council, issues binding instructions and sanctions. Infringements are minor, serious or very serious, with fines of up to 5,000, 10,000 or 20,000 UTM. Repeat offences can bring triple fines, or 2% or 4% of annual revenue for firms that are not SMEs, plus suspension of processing. Heads of public bodies can be fined, and controllers are liable for damages. Most provisions apply from 1 December 2026.
text_version: LeyChile text of Ley 21.719, version dated 2026-02-05 (Artículo cuarto transitorio amended; all other parts as published 2024-12-13); deferred entry into force 2026-12-01

title: 人工智能科技伦理审查与服务办法（试行）
summary_short: Requires ethics review of AI scientific research and technology development in China. Research bodies and enterprises must establish ethics committees or use review centres; activities follow general, simplified or emergency procedures; listed activities need expert re-review; records go to a national platform. Effective from 20 March 2026.
summary_long: The Measures require ethics review of AI scientific research and technology development in China that may affect human dignity, public order, life and health, ecology or sustainable development (Arts 1-2). Universities, research institutes, medical institutions and enterprises must set up ethics committees or apply to an entrusted service centre (Arts 9-12). Applications must include a plan, a risk assessment and a written pledge. Reviews assess human welfare, fairness and bias prevention, robustness, transparency and explainability, traceability and privacy (Art 15). Decisions are due within 30 days of acceptance (Art 16). General, simplified (Art 19) and emergency procedures (72 hours, Art 27) apply by risk level. Listed activities, including human-machine fusion systems, opinion-mobilising algorithms and highly autonomous automated decision systems, require expert re-review (Arts 21-25, Annex). Ongoing activities are tracked at intervals of up to 12 months, or 6 for listed activities (Arts 17, 25). Ministries and local authorities supervise, and records are filed on a national platform (Arts 29-30). Violations are handled under the Cybersecurity, Data Security and Personal Information Protection laws; no penalty amounts are set (Art 32). Standards, services, research and training are encouraged (Arts 4-8). The Measures take effect on issue, 20 March 2026 (Art 37).
text_version: as issued 2026-03-20 (工信部联科〔2026〕75号, published 2026-04-02)

title: 人工智能生成合成内容标识办法 (Measures for Labeling AI-Generated Synthetic Content)
summary_short: Requires Chinese online service providers covered by the algorithm-recommendation, deep-synthesis and generative-AI rules to add visible and metadata labels to AI-generated text, images, audio, video and virtual scenes. Content platforms and app stores must check and display labels, and removing labels is prohibited. Effective 1 September 2025.
summary_long: Issued jointly by the CAC, MIIT, the Ministry of Public Security and the NRTA, the Measures apply to network information service providers covered by the Algorithmic Recommendation Provisions, the Deep Synthesis Provisions and the Generative AI Interim Measures. They distinguish explicit labels, which users can perceive (text, sound or graphics), from implicit labels embedded in file data. Providers of services listed in Article 17(1) of the Deep Synthesis Provisions must place explicit labels in text, audio, images, video and virtual scenes, including in downloaded or exported files. All providers must write implicit labels into file metadata, recording content attributes, the provider's name or code and a content number; digital watermarks are encouraged. Content-dissemination services must check metadata, label confirmed, user-declared and suspected synthetic content, add their own metadata and offer users a labelling function. App distribution platforms must ask apps whether they offer AI generation and check their labelling materials. Providers may supply unlabelled content on request under a user agreement, keeping logs for at least six months. Users must declare synthetic content, and no one may maliciously remove, alter, forge or conceal labels. Violations are handled by the competent authorities under other laws.
text_version: original as issued (notice dated 2025-03-07, released on cac.gov.cn 2025-03-14); the text mentions no amendments

title: 互联网信息服务算法推荐管理规定 (Provisions on the Management of Algorithmic Recommendations in Internet Information Services)
summary_short: Regulates providers of algorithmic recommendation services in mainland China, setting duties on content governance, algorithm security, user rights, minors, workers and consumers, plus filing for services with public-opinion or social-mobilization capability and administrative penalties. Takes effect 1 March 2022.
summary_long: The instrument regulates the use of algorithmic recommendation technology to provide Internet information services within mainland China. Chapter II sets norms for providers: mainstream value orientation, primary responsibility for algorithmic security, regular examination of algorithms, models and data, feature databases for unlawful information, marking of algorithmically generated or synthetic information before further dissemination, limits on user tagging, display management, a news information permit requirement, and bans on manipulating users, content rankings and competition. Chapter III requires clear notice to users, an option not to be targeted or to switch off recommendation services, functions to delete user tags, explanations where algorithms have a major influence on rights, protections for minors, the elderly and dispatch workers, a ban on unreasonably differentiated trading prices for consumers, and complaint channels. Chapter IV provides graded and categorized management based on public-opinion properties, social-mobilization capability, content, user scale and other criteria; filing within 10 working days for services with such properties; security assessment; and confidentiality duties for officials. Chapter V provides for warnings, rectification orders, provisional suspension of information updates and fines of 10,000 to 100,000 yuan, with criminal liability where a crime is constituted. Takes effect 1 March 2022.

title: 人工智能拟人化互动服务管理暂行办法 (Interim Measures for the Administration of AI Anthropomorphic (Human-like) Interactive Services)
summary_short: Interim measures issued under China's cybersecurity, data and personal information laws governing human-like interactive AI services that provide sustained emotional interaction to the public within mainland China. Sets provider duties on safety, minors, data, labelling and security assessments, with fines and warnings for violations; effective from 7/15/2026.
summary_long: The Measures apply in mainland China to AI services providing the public with sustained emotional interaction simulating personality, thinking and communication styles, excluding customer service, Q&A, work, education and research uses without sustained emotional interaction (Art. 2). Providers must run safety and ethics management systems and lifecycle security duties (Arts. 9–10), avoid listed prohibited content (Art. 8), and manage training data (Art. 11). For minors, they must not offer virtual close relationships, must obtain guardian consent under 14, and must provide minors modes (Art. 14). Users must be told they are interacting with AI, with a reminder after two hours of continuous use (Art. 18); exit channels and advance notice of service termination are required (Arts. 19–20). Interaction data may not go to third parties without consent or legal basis (Art. 16). Security assessments are required on listed triggers, such as 1,000,000 registered or 100,000 monthly active users (Art. 22); algorithms must be filed (Art. 26), and app stores must check these (Art. 25).
