summary_long: The Measures apply to S&T activities involving human research participants, laboratory animals, or other activities that may pose ethical risks to life, health, the environment, public order or sustainable development (Art. 2). Work units in life sciences, medicine and artificial intelligence whose research involves sensitive ethics areas must establish S&T ethics (review) committees, which must have at least seven members and must be independent (Arts. 4, 7). Applicants submit materials including risk assessments and informed consent forms (Art. 9). Committees decide to approve, approve with modifications, re-review or disapprove, with a two-thirds majority of members present (Art. 16), generally within 30 days (Art. 17). Simplified procedures apply to minimal-risk activities (Art. 22). Activities on a checklist published by MOST require a preliminary committee review and then expert reconsideration by an oversight department panel (Arts. 25-30). Follow-up reviews occur at intervals of 12 months, or six months for checklist activities (Arts. 19, 33). Committees and work units must register with a national platform within 30 days and file annual reports by 31 March (Arts. 43-45). Penalties for violations are imposed by the competent agency, with civil and criminal liability where applicable, without fixed amounts in this text (Arts. 47-48). The appendix lists checklist activities including algorithmic models that can mobilize public opinion and highly autonomous automated decision-making systems (Appendix).

title: 杭州市人民政府办公厅关于印发支持人工智能全产业链高质量发展若干措施的通知
summary_short: Hangzhou municipal measures, in force 19 August 2024 to 31 December 2027, that subsidise and reward AI enterprises, research bodies and computing infrastructure projects across the AI industry chain: R&D grants, interest subsidies, compute vouchers, model-filing and open-source rewards, and talent support.
summary_long: A Hangzhou municipal government office notice issues fourteen measures in five parts to support the AI industry chain. Part 1 (compute infrastructure) provides R&D funding of 25% of state or provincial grants actually received, capped at 5 million yuan; interest subsidies of up to 1.5 percentage points on loans for approved computing infrastructure projects (total investment at least 50 million yuan), capped at 10 million yuan per enterprise per year; and a compute voucher pool raised to 250 million yuan per year, covering up to 30% or 20% of compute contract fees depending on the compute used, capped at 8 million yuan per enterprise per year. Part 2 (model ecosystem) offers a one-off reward of up to 500,000 yuan to enterprises obtaining central generative AI model filing, and tiered rewards of 200,000 to 1 million yuan for up to 10 enterprises contributing to open-source models, alongside competitions and talent recognition. Parts 3 to 5 cover public innovation platforms and manufacturing AI demonstrations, industrial clusters, enterprise attraction, rent reductions and industrial parks, and talent recruitment, training and an AI track in an existing talent programme. The measures apply from 19 August 2024 to 31 December 2027, are led by the Municipal Economy and Information Technology Bureau, and are funded jointly by the city and districts. Overlapping city policies are applied at the highest standard without double counting, and stated amounts are maximum standards.

title: 杭州市促进具身智能机器人产业发展条例
summary_short: Hangzhou municipal regulation in force from 1 May 2026 promoting the embodied intelligent robot industry. It sets government support for R&D, infrastructure, data, industry and public-sector use, and binds developers, providers and deployers to safety, ethics, data-security and standards duties and prohibitions on harmful products.
summary_long: Regulation adopted by the Hangzhou Municipal People's Congress Standing Committee on 29 December 2025, approved by the Zhejiang Provincial People's Congress Standing Committee on 26 March 2026, effective 1 May 2026 (Art. 50). It applies to activities promoting the embodied intelligent robot industry within the Hangzhou administrative area (Art. 2). Chapters 2 to 6 cover technology innovation (basic research, core components, open-source ecosystems, intellectual property), infrastructure (networks, computing power, public and training datasets, pilot bases, testing platforms), industry development (financial, talent, land and fund support, standards, statistics), application in public and industrial sectors (including government procurement and open scenarios), and safety management. Article 43 prohibits products or services that endanger national security, public safety, user safety or privacy, and monopolistic or unfair conduct; violations are pursued under other laws cited by reference, and no separate penalty is set out. Articles 44 and 45 require ethics principles and full-process data security and personal information protection systems. Article 47 requires assessment before new market-access measures. Article 48 calls for study of registration, certification and traceability, and provides for graded supervision and sandbox regulation.
text_version: as promulgated 2026-04-02 (Hangzhou PC Standing Committee announcement No. 55), adopted 2025-12-29, approved by Zhejiang PC SC 2026-03-26, in force 2026-05-01

title: Decreto 0769 de 2026 - Por el cual se adiciona el Título 31 a la Parte 2 del Libro 2 del Decreto 1078 de 2015, para reglamentar la Ley 2489 de 2025 (entornos digitales sanos y seguros para niños, niñas y adolescentes)
summary_short: Decree adding Title 31 to Decree 1078 of 2015 to regulate Law 2489 of 2025 on safe digital environments for children and adolescents. Imposes risk-mitigation, age-verification, parental-control, privacy-by-design and reporting duties on digital service providers and the software industry, and creates coordination bodies. Effective 18 July 2026.
summary_long: Decree 769 of 16 July 2026 adds Title 31 to Decree 1078 of 2015 to regulate Law 2489 of 2025 on safe digital environments for children and adolescents. Private duties fall on telecommunications network providers, digital platforms and service providers, and the software industry, including AI system developers (Arts. 2.2.31.1.2, 2.2.31.3.4). Measures against harmful content include mandatory blocking and immediate reporting of child sexual exploitation material, parental control tools and risk-based age verification (Art. 2.2.31.2.6). Providers must implement privacy and security by design and by default (Art. 2.2.31.2.8). Algorithm guidelines cover child-rights impact assessment, bias mitigation and data protection, framed as self-regulation (Art. 2.2.31.3.2). The state monitoring system is barred from collecting biometric data or commercially profiling children (Art. 2.2.31.6.2). Covered providers file semi-annual reports with MinTIC (Art. 2.2.31.3.5), and MinTIC issues technical definitions and policy within twelve months (Arts. 2.2.31.1.3, 2.2.31.2.1). The decree regulates coordination bodies, a monitoring system, a good-practice repository and school guidelines (Chapters 2-6). The decree sets no penalties; MinTIC supervision follows the sanctions regime of Law 1341 of 2009 (Art. 2.2.31.3.3).

title: Ley 1266 de 2008 - Por la cual se dictan las disposiciones generales del hábeas data y se regula el manejo de la información contenida en bases de datos personales, en especial la financiera, crediticia, comercial, de servicios y la proveniente de terceros países
summary_short: Colombian statute on habeas data governing personal data in databases, especially financial, credit, commercial and service data. It sets data subjects' rights, duties of data sources, operators and users, retention limits for negative credit records, and supervisory sanctions. Applies from publication in December 2008.
summary_long: Colombian statute on habeas data regulating personal data in databases, particularly financial, credit, commercial, service and third-country information. It covers public and private database administrators, excluding certain intelligence databases, purely personal data and internal flows (Art. 2). Art. 4 sets principles of accuracy, purpose, restricted circulation, temporality, security and confidentiality. Art. 6 gives data subjects rights to consult, seek correction and request proof of authorization. Arts. 7 to 9 impose duties on operators, sources and users, including prior notice before reporting negative data (Art. 12). Art. 13 limits retention of negative data to double the delinquency period, up to four years after payment. Art. 15 restricts user access to listed purposes. Art. 16 sets procedures and deadlines for consultations and claims. Art. 17 empowers the Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio and the Superintendencia Financiera to supervise, order audits and correct data. Art. 18 provides fines up to 2,000 monthly minimum wages, suspension up to six months and closure. Amended by Ley 2157 de 2021 and Ley 2573 de 2026 as compiled. It contains no provisions specific to AI systems.

title: Ley 1273 de 2009 - Por medio de la cual se modifica el Código Penal, se crea un nuevo bien jurídico tutelado denominado "de la protección de la información y de los datos"
summary_short: Colombian Law 1273 of 2009 adds Title VII BIS to the Penal Code, criminalising computer-related offences against information systems and personal data, plus a computer-means aggravating circumstance; it applies to any person and takes effect on promulgation.
summary_long: Law 1273 of 2009 inserts Title VII BIS, 'Protection of information and data', into the Colombian Penal Code (Art. 1). Articles 269A-269H criminalise unauthorised access to computer systems, obstruction of systems or telecommunications networks, interception of computer data without judicial order, data damage, use of malicious software, violation of personal data, and website or DNS spoofing to capture personal data. Articles 269I-269J criminalise computer-assisted theft and non-consented transfer of assets, and penalise making or possessing programs for these offences. Article 269H raises penalties by half to three-quarters for aggravating circumstances, including attacks on state or financial-sector networks, conduct by public servants, and disclosure or gain. Article 2 adds use of computer, electronic or telematic means as an aggravating circumstance to Penal Code Art. 58; Article 3 assigns these offences to municipal criminal judges. The law applies from promulgation and repeals contrary provisions, notably Art. 195 of the Penal Code. Prison terms and fines in minimum monthly legal wages are stated for each offence.

title: Ley Estatutaria 1581 de 2012 - Por la cual se dictan disposiciones generales para la protección de datos personales
summary_short: Statutory Law 1581 of 2012 sets general personal-data rules for public and private entities: principles, consent, data subject rights, controller and processor duties, enforcement by the Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio (fines, suspension, closure), a national database register, and limits on cross-border transfers. In force from promulgation.
summary_long: Statutory Law 1581 of 2012 sets general rules for processing personal data in any database held by public or private entities, applying in Colombia and to controllers or processors abroad where Colombian law applies under international norms (Art. 2). Definitions are in Art. 3, and principles of legality, purpose, consent, accuracy, transparency, restricted access, security and confidentiality are in Art. 4. Sensitive data processing is prohibited except in listed cases, and children's and adolescents' data may not be processed except public data (Arts. 5-7). Data subjects may access, update and rectify their data and, in stated cases, revoke authorization or request deletion (Art. 8). Prior, informed authorization is required unless an exception applies (Arts. 9-10). Consultations must be answered within ten business days and complaints within fifteen business days (Arts. 14-15). Controllers and processors have listed duties, including internal policy manuals (Arts. 17-18). The Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio supervises compliance and may impose fines up to 2,000 legal monthly minimum wages, suspend processing for up to six months, or order temporary or definitive closure (Arts. 19-24). A public National Register of Databases is created (Art. 25). Transfers of personal data to countries without adequate protection are prohibited, subject to listed exceptions (Art. 26). Existing actors have six months to comply (Art. 28), and the law takes effect on promulgation (Art. 30).

title: Ley 1928 de 2018 - Por medio de la cual se aprueba el "Convenio sobre la Ciberdelincuencia", adoptado el 23 de noviembre de 2001, en Budapest
summary_short: Approves the Council of Europe Convention on Cybercrime (Budapest, 23 November 2001). The Convention requires Parties to criminalise computer-related offences, to create investigative powers over electronic evidence, and to cooperate internationally.
summary_long: Law 1928 of 2018 approves the Council of Europe Convention on Cybercrime, adopted in Budapest on 23 November 2001, and reproduces its Spanish text. The Convention requires each Party to make specified conduct criminal under domestic law: illegal access, interception, data and system interference, misuse of devices, computer forgery and computer fraud (Arts. 2-8), child pornography (Art. 9) and intellectual-property infringements committed on a commercial scale through a computer system (Art. 10), with attempt and complicity (Art. 11). Legal persons may be held liable (Art. 12), subject to effective, proportionate and dissuasive sanctions including custodial penalties (Art. 13). Procedural powers cover expedited preservation of stored data for up to ninety days (Art. 16), production orders to persons and service providers (Art. 18), search and seizure (Art. 19), and real-time collection of traffic and content data (Arts. 20-21), subject to safeguards (Art. 15). Parties must establish jurisdiction (Art. 22) and cooperate on extradition, mutual assistance and spontaneous information (Arts. 23-28). Several reservations are permitted. The fetched text reproduces the Convention, with the law's title and headers; it does not contain separate operative articles of the approving law, and it gives 24 July 2018 as the law's date.

title: Ley 2466 de 2025 - Por medio de la cual se modifica parcialmente normas laborales y se adopta una Reforma Laboral para el trabajo decente y digno en Colombia
summary_short: Colombia's Law 2466 of 2025 amends the Labor Code on contracts, working hours, discipline, discrimination, apprenticeships, telework and subcontracting, and creates a hiring subsidy. Rules for digital delivery-platform workers, including automated-system transparency and human review, apply only after a later regulatory trigger (Art. 67).
summary_long: Law 2466 of 2025, dated 25 June 2025, amends the Substantive Labour Code and other labour norms. It covers fixed-term and indefinite contracts, disciplinary due process, working hours and overtime limits, surcharges for rest-day work, employer duties including disability hiring quotas (two workers per 100 for firms up to 500 staff), bans on discrimination and workplace violence and harassment, apprenticeship and internship rules, joint liability in subcontracting and limits on temporary staffing, telework including transnational telework, and the CREA EMPLEO hiring benefit funded from the national budget. Articles 24 to 30 regulate digital delivery (reparto) platforms: worker categories, a platform company contribution of 60% to health and pension contributions for independent workers, registration of platform companies with the Labour Ministry, information to workers on automated supervision and decision systems, personal-data processing limited to authorised purposes, periodic impact evaluation, and a right to request human review. Those articles take effect 12 months after the government completes their regulation and implementation (Art. 67). The Labour Ministry supervises compliance, the UGPP oversees contributions, and Art. 48 sets a daily wage indemnity for fraudulent use of sector or microenterprise privileges, capped at 24 months.

title: Ley 2489 de 2025 - Por medio de la cual se establecen disposiciones para el desarrollo de entornos digitales sanos y seguros para los niños, niñas y adolescentes del país
summary_short: Colombian statute (Law 2489 of 2025) that sets duties for the government, digital service and software providers, telecom industry, schools and parents to promote healthy and safe digital environments for children and adolescents. In force from publication; regulation due within six months.
summary_long: Law 2489 of 2025 sets principles and duties to promote healthy and safe digital environments for children and adolescents in Colombia (Arts. 1-3). The national government must adopt measures against online violence, exploitation, discrimination and harmful content, require digital service providers to cooperate, and recognise parental control tools, age-classification notices and age-verification mechanisms (Art. 4). The Ministry of ICT must set policies on safe use of ICT in coordination with the Communications Regulation Commission and run awareness programmes (Art. 5). The Ministry of Education must set curriculum guidelines on digital citizenship and privacy (Art. 6), and schools must run workshops for parents (Art. 7, par. 2). The law creates a National Committee on Technology, Childhood and Adolescence that meets at least once a year (Art. 7). Parents and caregivers receive responsibilities (Art. 8), the software industry must protect children and design software ethically (Art. 9), and the ICT Law gains a funding function (Art. 10). Ministries must submit annual reports (Art. 11), consolidate an open-resource repository (Art. 12), and establish an integrated monitoring and evaluation system that must respect children's privacy and oversee telecom industry use of secure-design guidelines (Art. 13). Regulation is due within six months of entry into force (Art. 14). The law takes effect on publication (Art. 15) and contains no sanction provisions.

title: Ley 2502 de 2025 - Por medio de la cual se modifica y establece un agravante al artículo 296 de la Ley 599 del 2000, Código Penal colombiano y se dictan otras disposiciones
summary_short: Amends Article 296 of Colombia's Penal Code: personal impersonation (falsedad personal) committed with artificial intelligence incurs a fine increased by up to one third. Also defines deepfake and directs public policy and AI case traceability. Amended provision effective one year after sanction.
summary_long: Law 2502 of 2025 amends Article 296 of Colombia's Penal Code (Law 599 of 2000), which penalises personal impersonation (falsedad personal) carried out to obtain a benefit or cause harm. The amendment adds that when the impersonation is carried out using artificial intelligence, the fine is increased by up to one third, provided the conduct does not constitute another crime. Article 2 defines DeepFake, identity, image and individuality. Article 4 requires the national government, the Fiscalía, the Police and the Ministry of Justice, with the ICT Ministry, to formulate within two years a public policy on harmful AI use, with minimum guidelines on ethics, inter-sector collaboration, education, R&D, algorithm transparency and governance including audits, international cooperation and rapid response. Article 5 requires the Fiscalía to keep traceable records of AI-enabled impersonation cases and to report annually to Congress. The Article 296 amendment takes effect one year after sanction; the rest of the law takes effect on sanction, promulgation and publication.

title: Proyecto de Ley 247 de 2024 Senado - 359 de 2025 Cámara: por medio de la cual se adoptan medidas de sensibilización, prevención, protección, reparación y penalización de la violencia de género digital - ley de protección integral de violencia de género digital
summary_short: Colombian bill (Senate 247/2024S, House 359/2025C; Ley Ordinaria) with the stated object of adopting awareness, prevention, protection, reparation and penalisation measures against digital gender-based violence in public and private digital environments. Still in House committee; the document contains no operative articles.
summary_long: The document is the Congress of Colombia's bill record page for Proyecto de Ley 247 de 2024 Senado / 359 de 2025 Cámara, a Ley Ordinaria titled as a law on comprehensive protection against digital gender-based violence. Its stated object is to adopt measures of awareness, prevention, protection and reparation, and to penalise conduct of digital gender-based violence carried out through ICT, so as to secure human dignity, privacy and a life free of violence in digital environments, in both public and private settings. The record shows Senate filing on 24/9/2024, House filing on 23/9/2025, a Senate-approved text (Gaceta 1732/25), and that the bill is in the Comisión Primera Constitucional Permanente, with a public hearing on 24 November 2025 and a positive first-debate report (Gaceta 432/2026). The page reproduces no articles, so the mechanisms, obligations, thresholds, sanctions and entry-into-force date cannot be coded from it and are not stated in this record. Classification is limited to the stated object and the bill type.

title: Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio, Circular Externa 005 de 10 de agosto de 2017 - Adiciona el Capítulo Tercero al Título V de la Circular Única (transferencia de datos personales a terceros países)
summary_short: SIC Circular Externa 005 of 2017 adds Chapter Three to Title V of the Circular Única on international transfers of personal data. It sets the standards for an adequate level of protection in recipient countries, lists countries considered adequate, and sets a declaration-of-conformity procedure for other transfers.
summary_long: Colombia's Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio (SIC) issued Circular Externa 005 of 10 August 2017, adding Chapter Three to Title V of the Circular Única. It applies to controllers (Responsables) and processors (Encargados) that transfer personal data to other countries, and it builds on Article 26 of Statutory Law 1581 of 2012, which prohibits transfers to countries without an adequate level of protection, subject to listed exceptions (express authorisation, medical data, banking transfers, treaties, contract performance, public interest or judicial claims). The Circular sets six standards for adequate protection (rules, principles, data subject rights, duties, judicial and administrative remedies, and a supervisory authority). It gives a non-exhaustive list of countries the SIC considers adequate, which the SIC may revise at any time. Controllers must still demonstrate accountability measures when transferring to listed countries. For other transfers, controllers may request a declaration of conformity under the procedure in Section 3.3. A contract or other instrument guaranteeing compliance creates a presumption of viability, with prior communication to the SIC. Mere transit of data through other territories is not a transfer. Breaches may be investigated and sanctioned. The Circular takes effect on publication in the Diario Oficial.
text_version: Diario Oficial 50.321 (2017-08-10) text as originally issued

title: Bundesdatenschutzgesetz (BDSG) vom 30. Juni 2017
summary_short: German Federal Data Protection Act (BDSG), described only by its table of contents. It sets rules for personal data processing by public and private bodies under the GDPR and for law enforcement under Directive (EU) 2016/680, and creates a Federal Data Protection Commissioner.
summary_long: The Bundesdatenschutzgesetz (BDSG) is known here only from its unofficial table of contents; no operative provision text is in the document, and the outline gives no date of entry into force. Part 1 (common provisions) covers scope and definitions, processing by public bodies, video surveillance of publicly accessible spaces, data protection officers of public bodies, and the Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information with its powers, reports and cooperation, plus judicial remedies. Part 2 implements processing rules for the purposes of Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, covering special categories and further processing, employment, research, archiving, consumer credit, scoring, data subject rights including automated individual decisions, controller and processor duties, state supervisory authorities, fines, criminal provisions and court remedies. Part 3 implements Directive (EU) 2016/680 for law enforcement, with principles, legal bases, data subject rights, duties of controllers and processors, breach notification, impact assessments, third-country transfers, liability and penalties. Part 4 covers processing outside the scope of EU law and processing for state honours.

title: Betriebsverfassungsgesetz - §§ 80(3), 90, 95(2a) as amended by the Betriebsraetemodernisierungsgesetz (2021) - KI in Auswahlrichtlinien
summary_short: Requires works council consent for guidelines on personnel selection for hiring, transfers, regrouping and dismissals. In firms with more than 500 employees the works council may demand such guidelines. Both rules apply when AI is used to draft them.
summary_long: Section 95 of the German Works Constitution Act makes guidelines on personnel selection for hiring, transfers, regrouping and dismissals subject to works council consent (Abs. 1). If no agreement is reached, the conciliation committee (Einigungsstelle) decides on the employer's application, and its award replaces the agreement. In firms with more than 500 employees, the works council may demand guidelines on the professional and personal requirements and social criteria to be observed in such measures, with the same conciliation procedure (Abs. 2). Abs. 2a states that paragraphs 1 and 2 apply even where artificial intelligence is used in drafting the guidelines. Abs. 3 defines a transfer as the assignment of another work area expected to exceed one month or involving a significant change in working conditions, and excludes the determination of a workplace for employees who usually do not work at a fixed workplace. The reproduced text contains no fines or other sanctions.

title: Gesetz ueber das Bundesamt fuer Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik und ueber die Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik von Einrichtungen (BSIG), as enacted by the NIS-2-Umsetzungs- und Cybersicherheitsstaerkungsgesetz (2025)
summary_short: German federal statute creating the Federal Office for Information Security and setting IT-security duties for essential and important entities, domain-name registries and federal agencies, with supervision and fines. Only the table of contents was supplied, so dates and operative text are not verified.
summary_long: The statute (BSIG) is outlined in nine parts. Parts 1 and 2 establish the Federal Office for Information Security with tasks and powers: reporting offices, detection, warnings, information requests, individual orders to telecommunications and digital service providers and ICT product manufacturers, and provision of IT-security products. They also set data-processing and data-subject rights rules. Part 3 sets duties for essential and important entities (sector annexes 1 and 2): risk-management measures, incident reporting, registration, notification, management training, proof duties for critical installations, a prohibition on the use of critical components, and duties for federal administration bodies. Part 4 concerns domain-name registration databases and access. Part 5 covers certification, conformity assessment and a voluntary IT-security label. Part 6 contains ordinance powers, restrictions of fundamental rights and the Office's reporting duties. Part 7 sets supervision and enforcement measures. Part 8 contains fines. Part 9 contains application and transitional rules. The supplied document is a table of contents only. Obligation content, thresholds, dates and penalty amounts are not in the text and are not coded. The start date is not stated in the outline; section 66 holds the application rule.

title: Digitale-Dienste-Gesetz (DDG)
summary_short: German Digital Services Act implementation statute (DDG). Implements Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (DSA) for digital intermediary services: designates competent authorities, creates a Digital Services Coordinator, sets liability, blocking and information rules, enforcement powers and fines. From the table of contents only; operative text not in the fetched document.
summary_long: The DDG is a German statute that implements Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (DSA) for digital services. Part 1 sets general rules: scope and definitions, the European seat of providers, a country-of-origin principle and freedom of admission. Part 2 sets general information duties and special duties for commercial communications. Part 3 covers users' infringements: limited liability of providers and a claim to blocking. Part 4 covers audiovisual media service and video-sharing platform providers, including provider lists, information requests and contractual use bans. Part 5 designates competent authorities and sets up a Digital Services Coordinator with a central complaints office and advisory board; it also covers reporting suspected offences to the Federal Criminal Police Office. Part 6 assigns further authorities under Regulations (EU) 2019/1150, 2024/1028 and 2018/302 and a liaison point under Directive 2000/31/EC. Part 7 sets investigation, information, search and seizure powers, enforcement, public information, Federal Network Agency powers, legal remedies and procedure. Part 8 contains fine provisions. Part 9 contains transitional and final provisions and an evaluation clause. Only the table of contents was fetched: provision texts, entry-into-force dates and penalty amounts are not stated in this document.

title: Gesetz zur Steigerung der Energieeffizienz in Deutschland (Energieeffizienzgesetz - EnEfG) vom 13. November 2023 (BGBl. 2023 I Nr. 309)
summary_short: Germany's Energy Efficiency Act sets national energy-saving targets and duties for federal and Länder governments, public bodies and energy-intensive firms, and imposes PUE limits, renewable-electricity, waste-heat reuse, energy-management and annual reporting duties on data centres of 300 kW or more. In force 18 November 2023, with phased dates to 2030.
summary_long: The EnEfG sets 2030 targets for final and primary energy consumption, annual savings duties for the Federation (45 TWh) and the Länder (3 TWh) from 2024 to 2030, and 2% annual savings for public bodies using 1 GWh or more. Firms averaging more than 7.5 GWh must set up an energy or environmental management system; firms above 2.5 GWh must publish certified implementation plans for economic savings measures, avoid and reuse waste heat, and report waste-heat data for a public platform. Data centres (non-redundant connected load of 300 kW or more, network nodes excluded) must reach a PUE of 1.5 from July 2027 and 1.3 from July 2030 if operating before 1 July 2026; later centres must reach PUE 1.2 and a reused-energy share of 10%, rising to 15% and 20% for centres opening from July 2027 and July 2028, with exemptions tied to heat-network agreements. Operators must cover electricity 50% from renewables from 2024 and 100% from 2027, set up management systems by July 2025 (certified from 2026 above 1 MW), report Anlage 3 data annually to a federal register, and show customers their energy use. Administrative fines reach EUR 100,000.

title: Entwurf eines Gesetzes zur Beschleunigung der Umsetzung der Energieeffizienzrichtlinie
summary_short: Bill amending the Energy Efficiency Act (EnEfG), Energy Services Act (EDL-G) and procurement regulations VgV, SektVO, KonzVgV to implement EU Directive 2023/1791. Sets efficiency duties for public bodies, energy audits, management systems, data-centre efficiency and waste-heat rules, and procurement criteria; in force the day after promulgation.
summary_long: The Federal Government's bill (Drucksache 21/8027, dated 16 September 2026) amends the Energy Efficiency Act (EnEfG), the Energy Services Act (EDL-G), the Vergabeverordnung (VgV), the Sektorenverordnung (SektVO) and the Konzessionsvergabeverordnung (KonzVgV) to complete the transposition of EU Energy Efficiency Directive 2023/1791. For public institutions, it sets an annual 1.9% final-energy saving target from a 2021 base (§ 6), energy or environmental management system duties, and annual consumption reporting to a federal energy register (§ 6a). For firms, it requires cost-benefit assessment of energy-efficiency solutions for planning or investment decisions above EUR 100 million (§ 5), energy audits for enterprises above 23.6 GWh of annual consumption (§ 8), and implementation plans for those between 2.77 and 23.6 GWh (§ 9). Data-centre operators face power usage effectiveness limits of 1.6 from 1 July 2027 and 1.4 from 1 July 2030 for facilities commissioned before 1 July 2026, reuse-energy shares, a renewable electricity share rising to 100% from 2030, and waste-heat cost-benefit analyses (§§ 11, 16). Procurement rules require energy-efficiency classes and reference values in tenders and concessions (VgV § 67, SektVO § 58, KonzVgV § 33a). The BAFA conducts random checks, and violations may be fined up to EUR 100,000 or EUR 50,000 (§§ 18, 19). The Act enters into force the day after promulgation (Art. 6).

title: Gesetz gegen Wettbewerbsbeschraenkungen - § 19a (Missbraeuchliches Verhalten von Unternehmen mit ueberragender marktuebergreifender Bedeutung fuer den Wettbewerb), eingefuehrt durch GWB-Digitalisierungsgesetz
summary_short: Empowers the Bundeskartellamt to designate, by order, an undertaking of overriding cross-market significance for competition, and then to prohibit listed conduct toward other firms. Designations are limited to five years; applies to firms active to a considerable extent in § 18(3a) GWB markets.
summary_long: Section 19a GWB lets the Bundeskartellamt, by order, find that an undertaking active to a considerable extent in § 18(3a) markets has overriding cross-market significance for competition, weighing market dominance, financial strength, vertical integration, access to competition-relevant data and its role in third parties' market access. The finding is limited to five years after it becomes final. Once made, the authority may prohibit the undertaking from favouring its own offers (including by pre-installation), hindering rivals, tying services, creating entry barriers through data processing, refusing interoperability or data portability, inadequately informing business partners, or demanding disproportionate advantages. Objectively justified conduct is excluded, the burden of proof lying with the undertaking. Sections 32(2)-(3), 32a and 32b apply accordingly, and a prohibition may be combined with the finding. Sections 19 and 20 are unaffected. The Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy must report to the legislature on experience four years after the provisions enter into force. The text gives no entry-into-force date.

title: Gesetz zur Marktüberwachung und Innovationsförderung von künstlicher Intelligenz (KI-Marktüberwachungs-und-Innovationsförderungs-Gesetz - KI-MIG) vom 22. Juli 2026 (BGBl. 2026 I Nr. 223)
summary_short: German law implementing the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689): names the Bundesnetzagentur as default market surveillance authority, single point of contact and complaints office, assigns sectoral authorities, sets up AI sandboxes, a register and real-world-testing approvals, and sets fines. In force 29 July 2026.
summary_long: The KI-MIG carries out Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 in Germany. The Bundesnetzagentur is the default market surveillance authority; product-safety authorities under Annex I Section A legislation keep AI systems linked to their products; BaFin supervises AI systems directly linked to regulated financial activity of listed supervised firms; Länder authorities cover Länder public bodies and media service providers; an independent KI-Marktüberwachungskammer at the Bundesnetzagentur supervises certain law-enforcement, migration, justice and democracy high-risk systems. Notifying authorities follow existing harmonisation law, with the BSI acting for biometric systems until the Cyber Resilience Act authority is named. The Bundesnetzagentur hosts a coordination and competence centre, the single point of contact, a central complaints office, at least one AI regulatory sandbox, innovation support and a non-public register of critical-infrastructure high-risk systems. Providers must have real-world tests outside sandboxes approved, with tacit approval after 30 days. Market surveillance authorities use the powers of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020. Listed breaches of the AI Act (Art. 21, 27, 45, 86) carry fines up to EUR 50,000; fines under AI Act Art. 99(3)-(5) follow the Administrative Offences Act; public bodies are not fined. The Federal Government evaluates the structure after 18 months and three years.
text_version: original as promulgated (Ausfertigungsdatum 22.07.2026, BGBl. 2026 I Nr. 223); the portal marks the text as not yet documentarily processed ('dokumentarisch noch nicht bearbeitet'), no later amendments shown

title: Gesetz zur Verbesserung der Rechtsdurchsetzung in sozialen Netzwerken (Netzwerkdurchsetzungsgesetz - NetzDG)
summary_short: For-profit operators of social networks (§ 1) that lack another EU member-state seat must appoint and publish a domestic service agent (§ 5). Failure is an administrative offence fined up to €500,000 (§ 4). The Bundesamt für Justiz supervises compliance (§ 4a). Enacted 1 September 2017, in force 1 October 2017.
summary_long: The Network Enforcement Act (NetzDG) applies to providers that operate platforms for profit where users share or make content publicly available (social networks). Journalistic-editorial offerings and platforms for individual communication or specific content are excluded (§ 1(1)). Unlawful content is defined by reference to listed Criminal Code offences (§ 1(3)). In this consolidated text, last amended by Art. 29 of the Act of 6 May 2024, §§ 2 to 3f are marked as removed (weggefallen). Providers without another EU member-state seat under the Digital Services Act must appoint and publicly identify a domestic service agent for court service (§ 5). Failure to do so is an administrative offence fined up to €500,000, and it may be sanctioned even if committed abroad (§ 4). The Bundesamt für Justiz is the administrative authority (§ 4). It monitors compliance and may take necessary measures, including ordering a provider to end a violation (§ 4a(1)–(2)). On request, providers must disclose measures taken, registered domestic users and complaints about unlawful content in the previous calendar year (§ 4a(3)). Transitional rules keep the Bundesamt für Justiz competent for certain pending fine proceedings (§ 6).

title: Gesetz über Urheberrecht und verwandte Schutzrechte (Urheberrechtsgesetz) - § 44b Text und Data Mining
summary_short: Section 44b of Germany's Copyright Act defines text and data mining and permits reproductions of lawfully accessible works for that purpose, to be deleted once no longer needed. Uses are excluded where rights holders have reserved them; online reservations count only if machine-readable.
summary_long: This document is § 44b of the German Copyright Act (Urheberrechtsgesetz), a partial text covering only that section. Paragraph 1 defines text and data mining (TDM) as the automated analysis of one or more digital or digitised works to obtain information, in particular about patterns, trends and correlations. Paragraph 2 permits reproductions of lawfully accessible works for TDM and requires that they be deleted once they are no longer necessary for that purpose. Paragraph 3 makes these uses permitted only where the rights holder has not reserved them; for works accessible online, a reservation is effective only if made in machine-readable form. The section does not name a specific addressee role, sets no thresholds, penalties or dates, and does not mention artificial intelligence.
text_version: current text of § 44b UrhG as published on gesetze-im-internet.de (retrieved 14 Oct 2026)

title: Bekendtgørelse om indberetning og offentliggørelse af oplysninger vedrørende datacentres energimæssige ydeevne (BEK nr. 926 af 09/07/2024)
summary_short: Danish executive order (BEK nr. 926 of 2024) requiring operators of data centres with at least 500 kW installed IT power to report energy, water and related indicators to the European data centre database, supervised by the Danish Energy Agency; in force from 1 September 2024.
summary_long: Danish executive order (BEK nr. 926 of 9 July 2024), issued under the Energy Efficiency Act and in force from 1 September 2024 (§ 12). Operators of data centres with installed IT power of 500 kW or more must report to the European data centre database (§§ 3-4), first by 15 September 2024 and then by 15 May each year. Reported data covers name, owner, commissioning date, location, floor area, installed power, data traffic, stored data and the indicators in Annexes I and II, including energy, water, renewable energy, heat reuse and IT capacity. Facilities used solely for defence and civil protection are exempt (§ 3(2)). Information protected by trade-secret or confidentiality rules may be exempted from publication (§ 5(2)), and exemption documentation may be submitted to the Danish Energy Agency for approval (§ 6(2)). The agency supervises compliance and may issue orders with a deadline (§§ 8-9). Non-compliance, false reporting or failure to obey an order is punishable by fines, and companies may face criminal liability (§ 10). Decisions may be appealed to the Energy Appeals Board within four weeks, and to courts only after the final administrative decision (§ 11). The order implements parts of Directive (EU) 2023/1791 and reproduces Annexes I-IV of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364, which the text says applies directly in each Member State.
text_version: BEK nr 926 af 09/07/2024 as published in Lovtidende A (status 'Valid' on retsinformation, retrieved 14 Oct 2026)

title: Forslag til lov om supplerende bestemmelser til forordningen om kunstig intelligens. (AI-loven)
summary_short: Danish bill supplementing the EU AI Regulation (2024/1689). It designates national competent and market-surveillance authorities, gives them inspection, order, blocking and disclosure powers, requires registration of certain AI systems, and sets fines and criminal liability. Proposed entry into force 2 August 2026.
summary_long: The bill supplements Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on AI. It has the Minister for Digitalisation set rules designating competent and market-surveillance authorities, makes the Digitaliseringsstyrelsen the central contact point and coordinator, and gives the Domstolsstyrelsen market-surveillance tasks over courts' use of AI systems. Market-surveillance authorities may request information, order warnings, remedies, withdrawal or recall of non-compliant AI systems, impose temporary bans on supply or marketing, sample systems, access premises without a court order, and publish information on non-compliant systems. Orders to owners of online interfaces may be enforced by court-ordered blocking. AI systems used as safety components in critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or water, gas, heat and electricity supply must be registered with the Digitaliseringsstyrelsen. Fines apply to listed violations of the AI Regulation's provisions, and legal persons may face criminal liability; the limitation period is 5 years. Fines may be settled by summary penalty notice. The bill would enter into force on 2 August 2026 and does not apply to the Faroe Islands and Greenland.
text_version: Lovforslag L 111 (Folketingsår 2025-26, 1. samling) as fremsat 18 Feb 2026 (retsinformation LSF 2025/1 111)

title: Forslag til lov om supplerende bestemmelser til forordningen om kunstig intelligens (AI-loven)
summary_short: Proposed Danish act supplementing EU AI Regulation 2024/1689. Designates market-surveillance and contact authorities, gives them inspection, order, temporary-ban and online-blocking powers over AI providers, deployers, distributors and online-interface owners, requires registration of certain AI safety components, and sets fines. Effective the day after promulgation.
summary_long: The bill, introduced on 7 October 2026 by the Danish research, education and digitalisation minister, supplements Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the AI Act) for Denmark. It designates the Agency for Digitalisation as central contact point and coordinator of market-surveillance authorities, and makes the Danish Courts Administration a market-surveillance authority for courts' own use of AI systems. The minister may set by regulation which authorities act as national competent or market-surveillance authorities. Market-surveillance authorities may require information, sample AI systems, enter premises and issue orders requiring warnings, halting marketing, corrective action, withdrawal or recall. They may impose temporary bans on supplying an AI system that poses a risk. Owners of online interfaces may be ordered to change, remove or warn against content referring to non-compliant AI systems; blocking requires a court ruling. AI systems intended as safety components in critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or water, gas, heating and electricity supply must be registered with the Agency. Providers must keep certain information for five years after their AI system is placed on the market or put into service. Listed violations of AI Act provisions and of this act are punishable by fines, with legal persons liable under the Criminal Code; the limitation period is five years. Fines may be settled by summary penalty notice. The act enters into force the day after publication and repeals Act No. 467 of 14 May 2025. It does not apply to the Faroe Islands or Greenland.
text_version: Lovforslag L 3 (Folketingsår 2026-27, 1. samling) as fremsat 7 Oct 2026 (retsinformation LSF 2026/1 3)

title: Lov nr. 467 af 14. maj 2025 om supplerende bestemmelser til forordningen om kunstig intelligens
summary_short: Danish supplementary act to the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). Designates Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, Datatilsynet and Domstolsstyrelsen as national competent and market surveillance authorities, gives them inspection and order powers, and sets fines and criminal liability for listed breaches. In force 2 August 2025.
summary_long: Supplements the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), reproduced as Annex 1. Designates Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, Datatilsynet and Domstolsstyrelsen as national competent and market surveillance authorities, with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen also acting as authorising authority and single point of contact. Market surveillance authorities may demand information, enter business premises without a court order, carry out technical inspections, publish decisions on prohibited AI practices, issue compliance orders, and impose temporary bans on supplying an AI system that poses a risk. The minister may, after negotiation, set rules for notified conformity assessment bodies. Breaches of the Article 5 prohibitions, false or misleading information, non-compliance with information demands, orders or temporary bans, and obstruction of access are punishable by fines; legal persons may be criminally liable under the Criminal Code; the limitation period is five years. Fine orders may be issued without trial where the offender admits guilt and agrees to pay. The act enters into force on 2 August 2025 and does not apply to the Faroe Islands or Greenland.

title: Anteproyecto de Ley para el buen uso y la gobernanza de la Inteligencia Artificial
summary_short: Draft Spanish organic law that would designate national AI authorities (notifying authority and market surveillance authorities, led by AESIA), create an AI regulatory sandbox, impose public-sector AI inventory and officer duties, and set a sanctions regime with fines for breaches of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 by AI systems used in Spain.
summary_long: Draft organic law for the good use and governance of AI, adapting Spanish law to Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act). Chapter I sets the object, definitions and scope for providers, deployers, manufacturers, importers, distributors and notified bodies, covering AI systems placed on the market or used in Spanish territory. Chapter II designates the notifying authority (Dirección General de Inteligencia Artificial) and market surveillance authorities (AESIA by default, plus data protection, financial, judicial and electoral-process designations), a single point of contact, a complaints channel and whistleblower protection. Chapter III requires AESIA to set up an AI regulatory sandbox. Chapter IV imposes duties on the Spanish state public sector: information on AI use, a national AI systems inventory and an AI delegate. Chapter V classifies infringements as very serious, serious or minor, with maximum fines of EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide turnover (prohibited practices), EUR 15 million or 3%, EUR 7.5 million or 1%, and EUR 500,000 or 0.5% (minor), plus limitation periods, provisional measures and coercive fines. Final provisions amend tax, social security and electoral laws. Enters into force the day after BOE publication.
text_version: BOCG Congreso, Serie A, núm. 97-1, 12 June 2026: Proyecto de Ley Orgánica para el buen uso y la gobernanza de la inteligencia artificial (121/000096)

title: Ley 12/2021, de 28 de septiembre, por la que se modifica el texto refundido de la Ley del Estatuto de los Trabajadores para garantizar los derechos laborales de las personas dedicadas al reparto en el ambito de plataformas digitales
summary_short: Amends Spain's Workers' Statute to give works councils information on parameters, rules and instructions of algorithms or AI systems affecting working conditions and employment; creates a presumption that delivery work organised via algorithmic management on digital platforms falls within the Statute. Enters into force the day after BOE publication.
summary_long: Law 12/2021 amends the consolidated Workers' Statute (Real Decreto Legislativo 2/2015) in two respects. First, it adds letter d) to Article 64(4), giving the works council the right to be informed by the company of the parameters, rules and instructions on which algorithms or AI systems are based where they affect decisions that may bear on working conditions, access to and maintenance of employment, including profiling. Second, it adds Additional Provision 23, which creates a presumption that the activity of persons performing paid delivery or distribution of consumer products or goods is included in the Statute's scope where the employer exercises organisational, direction and control powers, directly, indirectly or implicitly, through algorithmic management of the service or working conditions via a digital platform. The presumption does not affect Article 1.3 of the Statute. The law is enacted under the state's exclusive competence over labour legislation (Article 149.1.7.ª of the Constitution) and enters into force the day after its publication in the BOE. The text contains no separate sanctions provisions.

title: Ley 15/2022, de 12 de julio, integral para la igualdad de trato y la no discriminacion
summary_short: Spanish statute, in force the day after its publication in the BOE of 13 July 2022, prohibiting discrimination on listed grounds in employment, education, health, goods and services, housing and media. It creates an independent equality authority, sets administrative fines, and asks public administrations to minimise bias in algorithmic decision-making.
summary_long: Ley 15/2022 is a general anti-discrimination statute that applies to the public sector and to private persons acting in Spanish territory (art. 2). It defines direct and indirect discrimination, multiple and intersectional discrimination, harassment, retaliation and positive action (art. 6), and prohibits discriminatory treatment in employment and collective bargaining (arts. 9-11), education (art. 13), health care (art. 15), social services (art. 16), goods and services offered to the public (art. 17), housing (art. 20), venues (art. 21) and media and online services (art. 22). Article 23 asks public administrations to favour bias-minimisation, transparency and accountability mechanisms for algorithms used in public decision-making, including impact assessments. It creates the Autoridad Independiente para la Igualdad de Trato y la No Discriminación (arts. 40-45), which may mediate and bring legal actions. Administrative fines range from 300 to 500,000 euros across minor, serious and very serious infractions (arts. 47-48). Civil liability and a shifted burden of proof apply in discrimination cases (arts. 27, 30). Several provisions are declared basic State law or apply only to the State administration (Disposición final octava).

title: Ley Organica 3/2018, de 5 de diciembre, de Proteccion de Datos Personales y garantia de los derechos digitales
summary_short: Spanish organic law (LO 3/2018) adapting Spanish law to Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR) and guaranteeing digital rights. Applies to automated and filing-based processing of personal data by controllers, processors and public bodies; sets data protection officer, transfer, enforcement and workplace-privacy rules. Does not regulate AI systems as such.
summary_long: Organic Law 3/2018 supplements and implements the GDPR in Spain and adds a set of digital rights. Title I sets its object and scope (Arts. 1-3) and covers processing of deceased persons' data. Title II sets data protection principles: accuracy (Art. 4), confidentiality (Art. 5), consent, with minors able to consent from age 14 (Arts. 6-7), legal bases for public-sector and legal-obligation processing (Art. 8), and limits on special-category and criminal-offence data (Arts. 9-10). Title III covers transparency and data-subject rights (Arts. 11-18). Title IV sets rules for specific processing: credit information systems, mercantile operations, video surveillance, advertising exclusion systems, internal whistleblowing systems and statistics (Arts. 19-27). Title V sets controller and processor duties, including risk-based measures (Art. 28), records (Art. 31), blocking (Art. 32), mandatory data protection officers for listed entities (Art. 34), and codes of conduct and certification (Arts. 38-39). Title VI governs international transfers (Arts. 40-43). Title VII establishes the Spanish Data Protection Agency and regional authorities (Arts. 44-62). Title VIII sets procedures (Arts. 63-69). Title IX classifies infringements as very serious, serious or minor with limitation periods, and sets sanction rules (Arts. 70-78). Title X sets digital rights, including minors' online protection, social network rectification, workplace device, video and geolocation monitoring, and search-engine and social-network erasure rights (Arts. 79-97). Penalty amounts are cross-referenced to GDPR Art. 83 rather than stated here.The text does not define or regulate AI systems as such.(Part 1 of 2; the final provisions on entry into force are not in this part.)

title: Proyecto de Real Decreto por el que se regula la eficiencia energética y la sostenibilidad para los centros de datos
summary_short: Draft royal decree on data-centre energy efficiency. Operators with ≥500 kW IT power demand publish annual energy, water and employment indicators; owners above 1 MW must reuse waste heat; sites of 1 MW or more report best practices; grid access depends on compliance. Enters into force after BOE publication.
summary_long: Spanish draft royal decree implementing the waste-heat and reporting provisions of Directive (EU) 2023/1791 for data centres. Article 4 requires operators with IT power demand of 500 kW or more to report annually, by 15 May, the indicators under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364, plus minimisation strategies for specified indicators, employment estimates, and client and data location by country; the information is published on the ministry's website. Article 5 requires data centres above 1 MW nominal energy input to reuse waste heat, through a plan with a cost-benefit analysis (Annex I), regional assessment and municipal authorisation; a three-year voluntary period is followed by a mandatory two-year period. Article 6 requires data centres with IT demand of 1 MW or more to report how they apply EU Code of Conduct best practices; sites above 100 MW must show placement in the top 15% on specified indicators. Article 7 conditions grid access permits on compliance with Articles 4 to 6. Article 3(4) excludes facilities used exclusively for defence and civil protection. Enters into force the day after BOE publication.
text_version: Proyecto de Real Decreto por el que se regula la eficiencia energética y la sostenibilidad para los centros de datos, draft dated 2025-08-07 submitted to public hearing 8 Aug - 15 Sep 2025 (17 pp.; preamble, arts. 1-7, disposición transitoria única, two disposiciones finales, Annex I)

title: Real Decreto 729/2023, de 22 de agosto, por el que se aprueba el Estatuto de la Agencia Espanola de Supervision de Inteligencia Artificial
summary_short: Royal Decree 729/2023 approves the statute of the Spanish AI Supervision Agency (AESIA), a public-law entity under the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Digital Transformation, in force from 3 September 2023. It sets its governance and budget and empowers it to supervise AI systems, promote test environments and run voluntary certification.
summary_long: Royal Decree 729/2023 of 22 August approves the Statute of the Agencia Española de Supervisión de Inteligencia Artificial (AESIA), a public-law entity attached to the Secretariat of State for Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence. The Statute sets the agency's legal regime, seat in A Coruña, and competences. Within State competence, the agency performs supervision and, where applicable, sanction of AI systems, promotes regulated test environments, operates a voluntary certification framework for private entities, and carries out awareness and training activities. Its governing bodies are the Presidency, a Governing Board and a Control Commission; its executive bodies are a Directorate, two sub-directorates and a General Secretariat. The agency is financed by State transfers and its own revenues, and operates under a four-year management contract. The agency's sub-directorate issues impact assessments on AI systems used by public administrations. The decree also sets staffing rules and transitional provisions, including that the Governing Board is to be constituted within three months of entry into force.

title: Real Decreto 817/2023, de 8 de noviembre, que establece un entorno controlado de pruebas para el ensayo del cumplimiento de la propuesta de Reglamento europeo de inteligencia artificial
summary_short: Royal Decree creating a time-limited controlled testing environment (regulatory sandbox) in Spain for providers and users to test compliance with the proposed EU AI Regulation; open only to entities resident or with a permanent establishment in Spain; in force the day after BOE publication.
summary_long: The Decree creates a time-limited controlled testing environment (regulatory sandbox) run by the Secretaría de Estado de Digitalización e Inteligencia Artificial, to test how requirements of the proposed EU AI Regulation can be met. Eligible are AI providers and their users resident in Spain or with a permanent establishment there (Art. 5(1)). Covered systems are high-risk systems, general-purpose AI systems and foundation models; military, subliminal-manipulation, vulnerability-exploiting, social-scoring and real-time law-enforcement biometric systems are excluded (Art. 5(6)). Admission follows a public call, evaluation criteria and a resolution (Arts. 6-10); participants agree an implementation plan (Art. 11(2)). They must meet risk management, data quality, documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight and accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity requirements (Art. 11(1)), file a self-assessment declaration (Art. 13), run post-market monitoring (Art. 14) and report serious incidents (Art. 15). Personal data must follow the GDPR and LOPDGDD (Art. 16); participants are liable for damage caused by non-compliance or fault (Art. 17). The competent body may terminate individual participation (Art. 25), publishes a conclusions report (Disp. Add. 2) and may issue guides (Art. 22). The Decree lasts up to 36 months or until the EU regulation applies (Final provision 2).

title: Real Decreto-ley 24/2021, de 2 de noviembre, de transposición de directivas de la Unión Europea en las materias de bonos garantizados, distribución transfronteriza de organismos de inversión colectiva, datos abiertos y reutilización de la información del sector público, ejercicio de derechos de autor y derechos afines aplicables a determinadas transmisiones en línea y a las retransmisiones de programas de radio y televisión, exenciones temporales a determinadas importaciones y suministros, de personas consumidoras y para la promoción de vehículos de transporte por carretera limpios y energéticamente eficientes
summary_short: Spanish omnibus decree-law transposing eight EU directives: covered bonds, cross-border fund distribution, public-sector data re-use, copyright in the digital single market (including a text-and-data-mining exception with rights-holder opt-out), pandemic VAT exemptions, consumer protection and clean-vehicle procurement. In force 4 November 2021; Book One from 8 July 2022.
summary_long: Book One regulates covered bonds: issuance reserved to authorised credit institutions, programme authorisation by the Banco de España, segregated cover pools with a liquidity buffer, loan-to-value limits, a cover-pool control body, investor disclosure and Banco de España sanctions. Book Two amends the UCITS and closed-ended fund laws on pre-marketing, marketing notifications and de-notification with the CNMV. Book Three amends Law 37/2007 on re-use of public-sector information: high-value and dynamic datasets via APIs, limits on exclusive agreements and charges. Book Four transposes Directives 2019/789 and 2019/790: exceptions for text and data mining (Art. 67; general mining unless rights holders expressly reserve use by machine-readable means, and research mining with secure storage), digital teaching and cultural heritage, out-of-commerce works, press publishers' rights, liability and duties of online content-sharing service providers (Art. 73) and authors' contract rights. Book Five sets temporary VAT exemptions effective from 1 January 2021. Book Six amends consumer law (information duties for online marketplaces and personalised prices, withdrawal rights, fine bands up to 4% of turnover), in force 28 May 2022. Book Seven sets clean-vehicle public procurement targets. General entry into force is the day after BOE publication; Book One applies from 8 July 2022.

title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act)
summary_short: EU regulation setting harmonised rules for AI systems and general-purpose AI models in the Union under a risk-based approach: prohibited practices, high-risk requirements, transparency duties, GPAI obligations, sandboxes and EU governance bodies. This extract contains recitals only; operative provisions and application dates are not included.
summary_long: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act) sets out harmonised rules for placing on the market, putting into service and use of AI systems and general-purpose AI models in the Union. It applies to providers established in the Union or in a third country where outputs are used in the Union, and to deployers established in the Union. The recitals describe a risk-based approach. Certain AI practices, including manipulative or exploitative techniques, social scoring, untargeted scraping of facial images, emotion recognition in workplaces and education, and certain law-enforcement biometric uses, should be prohibited. High-risk AI systems in areas such as education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, justice and elections must meet mandatory requirements on risk management, data governance, documentation, human oversight, accuracy and cybersecurity, and undergo conformity assessment. Transparency duties apply to interaction with AI, emotion recognition, biometric categorisation and deepfakes. Providers of general-purpose AI models have documentation, copyright-policy and training-content summary duties, with further obligations for models presenting systemic risk. The text also refers to an EU database, AI regulatory sandboxes, the AI Office, a Board, a scientific panel and an advisory forum. This extract (part 1 of 3) contains recitals (1) to (153) only; the operative articles, penalties and dates of application are not in the text supplied.

title: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/454 of 7 March 2025 laying down the rules for the application of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as regards the establishment of a scientific panel of independent experts in the field of artificial intelligence
summary_short: Establishes the scientific panel of independent experts in AI provided for under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and sets its selection, composition (no more than 60 experts), independence, transparency and procedures for supporting market surveillance, qualified alerts and information requests to general-purpose AI model providers. Binding and directly applicable; enters into force on the twentieth day after publication.
summary_long: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/454 establishes the scientific panel of independent experts in AI provided for under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and sets its rules. The Commission appoints experts following a public call for expression of interest, with no more than 60 experts, aiming for gender balance and geographic representation, and with at least four-fifths of experts from EU Member States or EEA EFTA states. Experts serve a two-year term, renewable. They must be independent of AI system and general-purpose AI model providers, file declarations of interest and commitment, and keep confidential information secret. The AI Office and the Joint Research Centre provide the secretariat, which must publish the names, CVs and declarations of experts, the rules of procedure and panel opinions, except where confidential business information or trade secrets would be disclosed. The panel can support Member States' market surveillance authorities on request, and issues qualified alerts to the AI Office by at least a simple majority of its members. The panel may ask the AI Office to request documentation or information from general-purpose AI model providers, subject to necessity, proportionality, trade secret protection and data security safeguards. The regulation is binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States, and enters into force on the twentieth day following publication in the Official Journal.

title: Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing a framework of measures for strengthening Europe's cloud and AI ecosystem (Cloud and AI Development Act), COM(2026) 502
summary_short: Proposed EU regulation to expand cloud and AI capacity: Leadership Initiatives, national strategies, data centre acceleration zones with faster permits, four Union assurance levels for cloud services sold to public bodies, public-order procurement rules, a public-sector cloud federation and Commission joint procurement. Applies one year after entry into force.
summary_long: The proposal sets up Cloud and AI Leadership Initiatives with eight operational objectives implemented through grand challenges in Annex I, requires each Member State to establish Centres for AI and a national cloud and AI strategy within a year, and lets the Commission recognise frontier AI priority projects involving at least three Member States, to which the Union and Member States allocate computing resources. Member States deploying data centre capacity must designate acceleration zones within six months, issue an aggregated baseline permit per zone, designate single information points and decide permits within 12 months; the Commission may designate data centre strategic projects meeting two of five criteria. A cloud sovereignty framework defines four Union assurance levels (Annex II): level 1 by self-assessment, levels 2-4 by annual independent audit, recognised by national competent authorities with Union-wide peer review and a public repository. Criteria escalate from Union establishment and data location to Union-citizen personnel, cybersecurity certification and absence of third-country control. Public bodies must buy level 1 services, or levels 2-4 for public-order activities identified in risk assessments, with derogations. Member States set penalties; authorities may order cessation and impose fines; recipients may claim compensation.
text_version: Commission proposal COM(2026) 502 final, Brussels 3.6.2026, procedure 2026/0138(COD)

title: Regulation (EU) 2023/1781 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 September 2023 establishing a framework of measures for strengthening Europe's semiconductor ecosystem (Chips Act)
summary_short: EU semiconductor ecosystem framework: creates the Chips for Europe Initiative and a European Semiconductor Board, lets the Commission recognise first-of-a-kind integrated production facilities and open EU foundries, and sets monitoring and crisis-stage powers, including priority-rated orders. Enters into force on the third day after OJ publication; directly applicable.
summary_long: Regulation (EU) 2023/1781 sets a framework for the EU semiconductor ecosystem. It establishes the Chips for Europe Initiative, funded from Horizon Europe and the Digital Europe Programme and implemented mainly by the Chips Joint Undertaking, with five operational objectives (design platform, pilot lines, quantum chips, competence centres, Chips Fund). It lets the Commission recognise first-of-a-kind integrated production facilities and open EU foundries, which may receive Member State support and then accept priority-rated orders in a crisis. Chapter IV requires strategic mapping, monitoring and early warning indicators, and allows a Council-activated crisis stage of up to 12 months with information requests, priority-rated orders and common purchasing. It creates a European Semiconductor Board and national competent authorities. Fines reach EUR 300 000 for incorrect information, EUR 150 000 for unreported third-country obligations (EUR 50 000 for SMEs), and periodic penalty payments reach 1,5 % of daily turnover for priority-rated orders (0,5 % for SMEs).

title: Directive (EU) 2023/2225 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 October 2023 on credit agreements for consumers
summary_short: Harmonises EU rules on consumer credit agreements, covering credit information, advertising, creditworthiness assessment, database access, withdrawal, early repayment and caps, and supervision. Repeals Directive 2008/48/EC; Member States apply the measures from 20 November 2026.
summary_long: Directive (EU) 2023/2225 sets a harmonised framework for consumer credit agreements and repeals Directive 2008/48/EC. Addressed to Member States, it requires transposition by 20 November 2025 and applies from 20 November 2026. It covers most consumer credit, excluding among others mortgage-secured credit, credit above EUR 100 000 (renovation credit excepted) and certain employer or interest-free arrangements. Creditors and credit intermediaries must meet advertising standards, provide standard pre-contractual information, give adequate explanations, and assess creditworthiness before granting credit. Tying practices and unsolicited credit are prohibited. Where creditworthiness uses automated processing, consumers may obtain human intervention and an explanation. The directive also sets rules on credit databases, overdrafts and overrunning, withdrawal within 14 days, and early repayment compensation capped at 1% or 0.5% of the amount repaid. It requires forbearance measures and debt advisory referrals, staff competence, and admission or registration of non-credit creditors. Member States must introduce measures against excessive borrowing rates, such as caps, and designate competent authorities. Penalties must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive, and may include fines.

title: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2024 on horizontal cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements (Cyber Resilience Act)
summary_short: Sets horizontal cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements placed on the EU market, imposing duties on manufacturers and other economic operators covering design, vulnerability handling, support periods of at least five years and incident reporting. Reporting duties apply from 11 September 2026.
summary_long: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (Cyber Resilience Act) sets horizontal cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements (software or hardware, with remote data processing) made available on the Union market. Excluded are products under Regulations 2017/745, 2017/746 and 2019/2144, and national security products (Art. 2). Products must meet the essential requirements in Annex I, and manufacturers' vulnerability processes must comply (Art. 6). Manufacturers must assess and document cybersecurity risks, set a support period of at least five years or the expected use time, provide security updates, designate a single point of contact and exercise due diligence on third-party components (Art. 13). They must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents to a CSIRT and ENISA via a single reporting platform, with a 24-hour early warning and a 72-hour notification (Art. 14). Important products (classes I and II, Art. 7) and critical products (Art. 8) face conformity assessment, with third-party assessment for class II. Recitals give application from 11 December 2027. The text provided is part 1 of 2; enforcement and market surveillance provisions are not included.

title: Regulation (EU) 2025/38 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 laying down measures to strengthen solidarity and capacities in the Union to detect, prepare for and respond to cyber threats and incidents (Cyber Solidarity Act)
summary_short: EU regulation establishing a Cyber Solidarity framework: National and Cross-Border Cyber Hubs for threat detection, an EU Cybersecurity Reserve of trusted managed security service providers for incident response, and an ENISA-run incident review mechanism, funded through the Digital Europe Programme. Applies from the twentieth day after Official Journal publication.
summary_long: Regulation (EU) 2025/38 (Cyber Solidarity Act) amends Regulation (EU) 2021/694 and sets up three pillars funded through the Digital Europe Programme. First, a European Cybersecurity Alert System: Member States may designate National Cyber Hubs (Art. 4), and at least three Member States may form a Hosting Consortium to establish a Cross-Border Cyber Hub (Art. 5). Hubs share threat information under consortium agreements (Art. 6), participating Member States must ensure security of the network (Art. 8), and the ECCC co-procures tools with Union contributions of up to 50% or 75% of acquisition costs (Art. 9). Second, a Cybersecurity Emergency Mechanism with coordinated preparedness testing and other preparedness actions (Arts. 12-13); an EU Cybersecurity Reserve of response services from trusted managed security service providers, overseen by the Commission and possibly entrusted to ENISA, with provider selection criteria (Arts. 14-17); grants for mutual assistance (Art. 18); and support for DEP-associated third countries only under Council implementing acts (Art. 19). Third, a European Cybersecurity Incident Review Mechanism under which ENISA reviews specific significant incidents (Art. 21). The regulation also contains information, reporting and conflict-of-rules provisions (Arts. 6, 15, 16, 16a), a delegated power over reserve services (Art. 23), and an evaluation due by 5 February 2027 (Art. 25). It applies from the twentieth day after publication in the Official Journal (Art. 26).

title: Regulation (EU) 2019/881 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019 on ENISA and on information and communications technology cybersecurity certification (Cybersecurity Act)
summary_short: Regulation (EU) 2019/881 establishes ENISA as the EU Agency for Cybersecurity and creates an EU framework for voluntary cybersecurity certification of ICT products, services and processes, with basic, substantial and high assurance levels. It repeals Regulation (EU) No 526/2013 with effect from 27 June 2019.
summary_long: The Regulation sets out ENISA's objectives, tasks and organisation. ENISA advises the Union and Member States, supports capacity-building, incident response and operational cooperation (including the CSIRTs network secretariat), organises cybersecurity exercises, prepares situation reports, promotes awareness and cyber-hygiene, and analyses cybersecurity markets and standards. Its governance comprises a Management Board, an Executive Board, an Executive Director, an ENISA Advisory Group and a National Liaison Officers Network. Title III establishes the European cybersecurity certification framework. The Commission adopts certification schemes by implementing acts, based on candidate schemes prepared by ENISA. Schemes may specify assurance levels basic, substantial or high, and may allow conformity self-assessment only for basic. Certification is voluntary unless Union or Member State law provides otherwise. Manufacturers or providers of certified or self-assessed products must make supplementary cybersecurity information publicly available. Conformity assessment bodies are accredited by national accreditation bodies for a maximum of five years. Each Member State designates national cybersecurity certification authorities that supervise compliance, handle complaints and may withdraw certificates. Member States may not introduce new national schemes for products already covered by an EU scheme. Member States lay down penalties that must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.

title: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2023 on harmonised rules on fair access to and use of data (Data Act)
summary_short: Sets EU rules giving users of connected products and related services access to the data they generate, and requiring data holders to share it with users and their chosen third parties. Also governs B2B data sharing terms, public-sector emergency access and cloud switching. Applies from 12 September 2025.
summary_long: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 sets harmonised rules on fair access to and use of data.
