Article 1 covers product and related service data, data holders making data available to recipients, public-sector access in exceptional need, cloud switching and interoperability standards. This part covers Chapters I to III and only the heading of Chapter IV. Chapter II requires manufacturers and related-service providers to design products so that data are accessible to users by default (Art. 3), requires pre-contract information (Art. 3(2)-(3)), and obliges data holders to make readily available data accessible to users and, on request, to third parties (Arts. 4-5). This is subject to trade-secret safeguards (Art. 4(6)-(8)), a bar on users using data to build a competing connected product (Art. 4(10)), and exclusion of designated gatekeepers as eligible third parties (Art. 5(3)). Third parties must process data only for agreed purposes and may not profile except where strictly necessary (Art. 6). Microenterprises and small enterprises are partly exempt (Art. 7). Chapter III sets fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms for B2B data sharing (Art. 8), compensation limited to costs for SMEs (Art. 9), certified dispute settlement bodies (Art. 10), and technical protection measures and remedies (Art. 11). Personal data may be shared only where a valid GDPR legal basis exists. Enforcement in this part is limited to complaints to designated competent authorities; penalty provisions and the Chapters on public-sector access, cloud switching and interoperability are not in this part.

title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364 of 14 March 2024 on the first phase of the establishment of a common Union rating scheme for data centres
summary_short: The Regulation requires operators of data centres with at least 500 kW installed IT power demand to report defined information and sustainability indicators (energy, water, waste heat, renewables) to a European database, with first reports due 15 September 2024 and annual reporting thereafter.
summary_long: The Regulation defines the information and key performance indicators (KPIs) that operators of data centres with an installed information technology power demand of at least 500 kW must communicate to a European database, plus common measurement and calculation methods (Art. 1). Reports are due by 15 September 2024, then by 15 May 2025 and yearly, covering the preceding calendar year; they go through a national scheme where one exists, otherwise directly to the database (Art. 3(1)). In the first reporting periods, operators may omit listed KPIs for technical reasons with an explanation, and colocation operators may estimate coverage (Art. 3(2)-(3)). Annex I covers identification and redundancy; Annex II covers energy, water, waste heat, refrigerant, renewable energy, ICT capacity and traffic KPIs and requires measurement records kept for at least 10 years. Annex III defines PUE, WUE, ERF and REF. Aggregated data is published by Member State and Union level, by size category (Art. 5(2), Annex IV); individual data is kept confidential by the Commission and Member States (Art. 5(5)). It enters into force on the twentieth day after publication in the Official Journal (Art. 6).

title: Regulation (EU) 2022/868 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 May 2022 on European data governance (Data Governance Act)
summary_short: Regulation (EU) 2022/868 (Data Governance Act) sets conditions for re-use of protected public-sector data, a notification regime for data intermediation services providers, a voluntary registration framework for data altruism organisations, and a European Data Innovation Board. It applies from 24 September 2023.
summary_long: The Regulation sets a Union framework for data sharing and re-use. Chapter II covers re-use of public-sector data protected by commercial or statistical confidentiality, third-party intellectual property or personal data; conditions must be non-discriminatory, transparent, proportionate and objectively justified, and fees are limited to necessary costs. Exclusive re-use arrangements are prohibited, except where necessary for a service in the general interest, and any exclusive right may last no more than 12 months. Member States designate competent bodies and a single information point. Chapter III requires providers of data intermediation services to notify the competent authority before operating, and imposes neutrality, structural separation, security and interoperability duties; authorities may impose financial penalties, suspend services or order cessation. Chapter IV creates an optional registration for data altruism organisations, with a common logo and a rulebook to be adopted by delegated act. Chapter VI establishes the European Data Innovation Board. Chapter VII requires measures to prevent international transfer of or governmental access to non-personal data where this would conflict with Union law. Penalty rules are left to Member States. Existing intermediaries had until 24 September 2025 to comply. The Regulation does not oblige public sector bodies to allow re-use of data.

title: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 8 July 2026 amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI)
summary_short: Amends the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) and two other regulations to simplify its implementation. Adds prohibitions on AI systems generating non-consensual intimate or child sexual abuse material, sets high-risk application dates of 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028, and changes conformity assessment, sandbox and AI Office rules.
summary_long: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 amends the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), the civil aviation regulation (EU) 2018/1139 and the machinery regulation (EU) 2023/1230 to simplify AI Act implementation. It narrows the safety component definition, adds SME and small mid-cap definitions, and replaces the AI literacy duty with a duty to take measures to support AI literacy. A new Article 4a permits providers and deployers, under listed conditions, to process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction. Article 5 adds prohibitions on placing on the market, putting into service or using AI systems that generate non-consensual intimate material or child sexual abuse material, with limits for providers and deployers, applicable from 2 December 2026. High-risk rules in Chapter III, Sections 1 to 3 apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. The text changes conformity assessment and notified body designation (single application procedure), sandbox and real-world testing rules, quality management and documentation simplifications for SMEs and SMCs, and AI Office supervision, investigation, administrative fines and periodic penalty payments (Articles 75 to 75d). Machinery moves from Section A to Section B of Annex I. Article 4 sets entry into force on the third day after publication.

title: Proposal for a Regulation amending Regulations (EU) 2016/679, (EU) 2018/1724, (EU) 2018/1725, (EU) 2023/2854 and Directives 2002/58/EC, (EU) 2022/2555 and (EU) 2022/2557 as regards the simplification of the digital legislative framework (Digital Omnibus), COM(2025) 837
summary_short: Commission proposal that would amend the GDPR, EUDPR, ePrivacy Directive, Data Act, NIS2, eIDAS, DORA, CER Directive and Single Digital Gateway Regulation, move the Data Governance Act, Open Data Directive and free-flow rules into the Data Act, and repeal the P2B Regulation, mostly from entry into force.
summary_long: The proposal would fold the Data Governance Act, Regulation 2018/1807 and the Open Data Directive into the Data Act as Chapters VIIa-VIIc (voluntary registration of data intermediaries and data altruism organisations, a ban on national localisation requirements for non-personal data, re-use of public sector and protected data with charging rules and higher charges for very large enterprises), create a European Data Innovation Board, narrow business-to-government data requests to public emergencies, and exempt pre-12 September 2025 custom or SME/SMC cloud contracts from switching rules. In the GDPR it adds an entity-relative test for personal data, a definition of scientific research, legitimate interest and a special-category exception for AI development and operation, an exception for biometric verification under the data subject's sole control, limits on abusive access requests and information duties, a high-risk-only 96-hour breach notification via an ENISA single-entry point, EU-wide DPIA lists, and new rules on terminal-equipment access (consent with exceptions, single-click refusal from 6 months; machine-readable signals from 24 months; browser support from 48 months), removing personal data from ePrivacy Art. 5(3). NIS2, eIDAS, DORA and CER reporting moves to the single-entry point after 18 months. The P2B Regulation is repealed, with some provisions kept until 2032.

title: Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 September 2022 on contestable and fair markets in the digital sector (Digital Markets Act)
summary_short: EU regulation designating large online platform undertakings as gatekeepers for ten core platform services and imposing conduct obligations on them (data combination, self-preferencing, interoperability, data access, sideloading). The Commission enforces it with fines up to 10% (20% for repeat) of worldwide turnover. Applies from 2 May 2023.
summary_long: The Regulation covers core platform services gatekeepers offer to Union business or end users, wherever the gatekeeper is established. An undertaking is designated a gatekeeper if it has significant impact on the internal market, operates an important gateway and holds an entrenched position; these are presumed where it has EUR 7.5 billion annual Union turnover in each of three years or EUR 75 billion market capitalisation, serves at least three Member States, and a service has 45 million monthly active end users and 10 000 yearly active business users in each of the last three years (Annex methodology). Undertakings meeting the thresholds must notify within two months and may rebut the presumption; the Commission may also designate through market investigation. Within six months of designation gatekeepers must comply with Articles 5-7 (consent for data combination, no parity clauses, anti-steering, choice screens, sideloading, ranking neutrality, interoperability, data portability and access), report, submit audited profiling descriptions, notify concentrations and set up a compliance function. The Commission may impose fines up to 10% of worldwide turnover (20% for repeat, 1% for procedural breaches), periodic penalties up to 5% of daily turnover, and remedies for systematic non-compliance.
text_version: Consolidated text 02022R1925 — EN — 12.10.2022 — 000.002 (original act as published, incorporating Corrigendum C1, OJ L 90024, 10.1.2025); no amending acts consolidated

title: Commission decisions designating gatekeepers and core platform services under Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925
summary_short: Commission decisions designating named companies (Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta, Microsoft, later Booking) as gatekeepers and designating their core platform services under the Digital Markets Act (DMA). First designations on 6 September 2023; additions in 2024 and one undesignation in 2025.
summary_long: This portal page records European Commission decisions under the Digital Markets Act (DMA) that designate gatekeepers and their core platform services. On 6 September 2023 the Commission designated Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft as gatekeepers. On 29 April 2024 Apple was designated for iPadOS, and on 13 May 2024 Booking was designated as a gatekeeper for its online intermediation service Booking.com. On 23 April 2025 Meta was undesignated for its online intermediation service Facebook Marketplace. For each company the page lists its designated core platform services with case numbers, 23 in total, including search, video, app stores, operating systems, browsers, online advertising, social networking, messaging, marketplaces and a PC operating system. Each company entry links to its designation decision, which the page does not reproduce. The page also points to resources on submissions, the designation process, and information on acquisitions under Article 14 of the DMA.[The page describes its scope as designations made to date; it does not state the operative provisions of the decisions themselves.]

title: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/814 of 14 April 2023 on detailed arrangements for the conduct of certain proceedings by the Commission pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2022/1925
summary_short: Sets detailed procedural rules for Commission proceedings under the Digital Markets Act: form and content of gatekeeper notifications and submissions, document format and length, right to be heard, access to file, confidentiality and time limits. Enters into force on 2 May 2023.
summary_long: Adopted 14 April 2023 under Article 46(1) of the Digital Markets Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/1925), this Regulation sets detailed procedural rules for Commission proceedings under that Regulation. Chapter II governs notifications and submissions by undertakings providing core platform services, including gatekeeper notifications on the Annex I form, substantiated arguments under Article 3(5) and the duty to provide correct, complete and non-misleading information; incomplete submissions take effect only once complete. Annex II sets format and page limits, such as 50 pages per distinct core platform service for a gatekeeper notification. Chapter III allows the Commission to open proceedings up to its preliminary findings and makes the opening public. Chapter IV covers the right to be heard: time-limited written observations, business-secret protection and access to the file, including unredacted access for specified external counsel and experts under Commission-set disclosure terms. Chapter V sets time periods that begin on the working day following the triggering event (Article 9(2)) and allows extensions on reasoned request. Digital transmission is the default. The Regulation is binding in all Member States and enters into force on 2 May 2023.

title: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 December 2022 on digital operational resilience for the financial sector (DORA)
summary_short: EU Regulation establishing uniform requirements for ICT risk management, major ICT-related incident reporting, digital operational resilience testing and ICT third-party risk for listed EU financial entities, with a simplified regime for certain smaller entities.
summary_long: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 sets uniform requirements for the security of network and information systems supporting the business processes of financial entities. Article 2(1) covers listed entities, including credit institutions, payment institutions, investment firms, central counterparties, insurers and ICT third-party service providers. Chapter II requires a management-body-approved ICT risk management framework covering identification, protection, detection, response and recovery, with simplified rules for listed small entities under Article 16. Chapter III requires an ICT-related incident management process, classification of incidents, and reporting of major ICT-related incidents to competent authorities, with clients informed where their financial interests are affected. Chapter IV requires a digital operational resilience testing programme for entities other than microenterprises, and threat-led penetration testing at least every three years for entities identified by competent authorities. Chapter V sets principles for ICT third-party risk, including a register of contractual arrangements, exit strategies and contract termination circumstances. This annotation covers Articles 1 to 28 only; the application date is not in the text provided.

title: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795 of 10 July 2023 pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2016/679 on the adequate level of protection of personal data under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework
summary_short: Adequacy decision under GDPR Art. 45(3) finding that the United States ensures adequate protection for personal data transferred from the EU to US organisations on the Data Privacy Framework List, so such transfers need no further authorisation; the Commission and Member States must monitor it.
summary_long: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795 under Article 45(3) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 finds that the United States ensures an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred from the Union to organisations in the United States that are included in the Data Privacy Framework List. Such transfers may take place without further authorisation. Eligibility rests on certification to the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework Principles (Annex I), administered by the U.S. Department of Commerce, with enforcement by the FTC or DoT. Certified organisations must provide notice, honour access and choice rights, apply onward-transfer contracts, and maintain recourse mechanisms including binding arbitration. The decision also assesses U.S. government access limits for criminal law enforcement and national security, including the safeguards of Executive Order 14086 and the Data Protection Review Court. Member States must inform the Commission of relevant cases (Art. 2), and the Commission must continuously monitor the framework and evaluate it after one year from notification (Art. 3). Annexes referenced in the text are not part of the fetched document.

title: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market For Digital Services (Digital Services Act)
summary_short: EU Regulation 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act) sets harmonised due diligence and liability rules for intermediary services offered to users in the Union, regardless of provider establishment. It imposes tiered duties on hosting services, online platforms and very large online platforms, including notice-and-action, transparency, ad disclosure and risk-assessment obligations.
summary_long: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act) aims to contribute to the functioning of the internal market for intermediary services by setting harmonised rules for a safe, predictable and trusted online environment (Art. 1). Article 2 applies it to intermediary services offered to recipients in the Union, irrespective of where providers are established, and excludes services that are not intermediary services. It carries forward conditional liability exemptions for mere conduit, caching and hosting services. Due diligence duties are tiered: basic duties for all intermediary services, added duties for hosting services (notice and action, statements of reasons), further duties for online platforms (internal complaint handling, out-of-court dispute settlement, trusted flaggers, trader traceability, limits on dark patterns, and limits on profiling-based advertising using special-category data or targeting minors), and the strongest duties for very large online platforms and search engines above 45 million average monthly active recipients (systemic risk assessment and mitigation, independent audits, researcher data access, a compliance function and a supervisory fee). Member States designate Digital Services Coordinators, and the Commission holds exclusive powers over systemic-risk obligations. The recitals refer to fines and periodic penalty payments. The supplied text covers the recitals and Chapter I only; the operative provisions on these duties, and the application dates, are not in this part.

title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/436 of 20 October 2023 supplementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 by laying down rules on the performance of audits for very large online platforms and very large online search engines
summary_short: Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/436 sets rules for independent audits under DSA Article 37 of very large online platforms and search engines: auditor independence and selection, audited providers' cooperation duties, audit methodologies, risk analysis, and report templates. Binding in all Member States; in force twenty days after OJ publication.
summary_long: Sets rules for the independent audits that Article 37 of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (DSA) requires of very large online platforms and very large online search engines. Addressed to audited providers and auditing organisations. Section I defines terms and the audit period (Arts. 2-3). Section II covers selection of auditors, requiring the provider to check independence, conflict-of-interest, expertise and professional-ethics conditions (Art. 4), cooperation and access to data, systems and personnel (Art. 5), and a written agreement annexed to the audit report (Art. 7). Section III sets audit report and audit implementation report templates in Annexes I and II (Art. 6), and audit conclusions of 'positive', 'positive with comments' or 'negative', from which audit opinions are derived (Art. 8). Section IV sets methodology: audit risk analysis (Art. 9), methodologies and tests including for algorithmic systems (Art. 10), evidence quality (Art. 11), sampling (Art. 12), and specific methodologies for DSA Articles 34, 35, 36 and 37 and for codes of conduct and crisis protocols (Arts. 13-17). Binding and directly applicable in all Member States; enters into force on the twentieth day after publication in the Official Journal (Art. 18). The regulation itself sets no penalties.

title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/2050 of 1 July 2025 supplementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 by laying down the technical conditions and procedures under which providers of very large online platforms and of very large online search engines are to share data with vetted researchers
summary_short: Commission delegated regulation under the Digital Services Act setting technical conditions and procedures for vetted researchers' access to data held by very large online platforms and search engines. It requires a DSA data access portal, reasoned requests by Digital Services Coordinators, and data provider catalogues and access modalities.
summary_long: Supplements Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act) with technical conditions and procedures for vetted researchers' access to data held by very large online platform and search engine providers under Article 40(4). Requires the Commission to establish a DSA data access portal linked to AGORA, and data providers to publish points of contact, data catalogues and suggested access modalities. The Digital Services Coordinator of establishment must decide within 80 working days whether to formulate a reasoned request, assessing applicant affiliation, independence, funding, necessity, and data-protection and security risks, and determines access modalities, which may require secure processing environments. Overviews of reasoned requests are published; data providers may file amendment requests and seek mediation within five working days, with mediation capped at 40 working days and costs borne by the provider. Coordinators may consult independent experts registered in AGORA. Data providers must notify access start and termination within three working days and must not impose archiving or analytical-tool restrictions unless stated in the reasoned request. The Annex sets Commission processor duties and security measures for the portal. Enters into force on the twentieth day after OJ publication; binding in all Member States.

title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/1127 of 2 March 2023 supplementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 with the detailed methodologies and procedures regarding the supervisory fees charged by the Commission on providers of very large online platforms and very large online search engines
summary_short: Sets the methodology for annual supervisory fees the European Commission charges providers of very large online platforms and search engines under the Digital Services Act: cost estimation, per-service basic amounts, a cap of 0.05% of worldwide profit, payment rules and reporting. Applies from the twentieth day after OJ publication.
summary_long: Adopted on 2 March 2023 under Article 43(4) of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (DSA), this Regulation sets how the Commission estimates and charges annual supervisory fees on providers of designated very large online platforms and very large online search engines. The overall annual costs estimated for year n+1 (human resources, operating expenditure and other items listed in Annex I) are recovered in year n through fees. Each designated service receives a basic amount proportionate to its average monthly active recipients (coefficient U, Annex II) and its days of designation (coefficient T). Each provider's fee is capped at 0.05% of its worldwide profit in the preceding financial year, and amounts above the cap are redistributed to providers below it. Providers submit financial statements by 31 August; the Commission communicates provisional amounts by 30 September, providers may submit observations within two weeks, and implementing decisions are adopted by 30 November with payment due by 31 December. Unpaid amounts are recovered with interest, without prejudice to DSA fines. The Commission reports annually on incurred costs and fees charged and publishes the report. Article 9 allows costs from 16 November 2022 to 31 December 2023 to be added to the first estimate.

title: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2835 of 4 November 2024 laying down templates concerning the transparency reporting obligations of providers of intermediary services and of providers of online platforms under Regulation (EU) 2022/2065
summary_short: Sets harmonised templates and formats for the content-moderation transparency reports that providers of intermediary services, hosting services and online platforms must publish under the Digital Services Act. Templates apply from 1 July 2025; reports are published within two months of each period and kept five years.
summary_long: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2835 lays down the templates, format and reporting periods for the transparency reports required by Articles 15, 24 and 42 of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act). Providers of intermediary services, hosting services, online platforms, very large online platforms and very large online search engines must use the CSV or XLSX versions of the Annex I templates. The Quantitative Template covers Member State orders, notices, own-initiative content moderation, internal complaints, out-of-court dispute settlements, suspensions, use of automated means with accuracy indicators, moderator resources and monthly active recipients. The Qualitative Template requires descriptive information on content moderation and automated means. Annual reporting periods run from 1 January to 31 December for intermediary services, hosting services and online platforms, while very large online platforms and search engines report at least every six months. Reports must be made publicly available within two months after each reporting period ends, in machine-readable ODF CSV format in UTF-8, and retained publicly for at least five years. Templates apply as of 1 July 2025, with transition rules for the 2025 reporting cycles set out in Annex II. Updated versions of reports must be clearly marked.

title: Commission decisions designating very large online platforms and very large online search engines under Article 33 of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065
summary_short: Commission decisions of 25 April 2023 and 26 April 2024 designating named online platforms and search engines as very large under Article 33(4) of the Digital Services Act, each addressed to named provider entities, based on reported average monthly active recipients above 45 million in the Union.
summary_long: Bundle of Commission decisions under Article 33(4) of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act). Nineteen decisions of 25 April 2023 designate AliExpress, Bing, TikTok, App Store, Facebook, Booking.com, Google Maps, LinkedIn, Google Play, Google Shopping, Instagram, Snapchat, Amazon Store, Google Search, Twitter, Pinterest, Wikipedia, YouTube and Zalando as very large online platforms or, for Bing and Google Search, very large online search engines. A decision of 26 April 2024 designates SHEIN. Each rests on reported average monthly active recipients in the Union above 45 million. Article 1 of each decision makes the designation; Article 2 names the addressee, usually a subsidiary or main establishment in the Union, or a non-EU entity where none exists (Snapchat, Wikipedia). The SHEIN decision states that only the SHEIN Marketplace service is subject to the Regulation's obligations. A corrigendum of 13 July 2023 corrects recital numbering and a service name in the Google Search decision.
text_version: Commission designation decisions under Art. 33(4) DSA as published (non-confidential versions) via the digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu VLOP/VLOSE list

title: Directive (EU) 2019/790 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019 on copyright and related rights in the Digital Single Market and amending Directives 96/9/EC and 2001/29/EC
summary_short: EU directive harmonising copyright rules for the digital single market. Obliges Member States to provide mandatory exceptions for text and data mining, digital teaching and preservation, and rules on press publishers' rights, online content-sharing platforms and authors' remuneration. Transposition deadline 7 June 2021.
summary_long: Directive (EU) 2019/790 sets harmonised EU copyright rules and amends Directives 96/9/EC and 2001/29/EC. Title II requires Member States to provide mandatory exceptions for text and data mining for scientific research (Art. 3) and for text and data mining generally (Art. 4), for digital illustration for teaching (Art. 5) and for cultural heritage preservation (Art. 6), and makes contrary contract terms unenforceable (Art. 7). Title III covers out-of-commerce works, cross-border uses, a publicity portal, collective licensing with extended effect (Art. 12) and a negotiation mechanism for video-on-demand licensing (Art. 13). Title IV grants publishers of press publications a right over online uses by information society service providers (Art. 15). It makes online content-sharing service providers liable for unauthorised communications to the public unless they show best efforts and expeditious takedown, with a reduced regime for services available for less than three years with annual turnover below EUR 10 million (Art. 17). It sets transparency, contract adjustment and revocation rules for authors and performers (Arts 18-22). Member States transpose by 7 June 2021, and the Directive applies to works protected on or after that date (Arts 26, 29).

title: Regulation (EU) 2025/327 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 February 2025 on the European Health Data Space
summary_short: Regulation (EU) 2025/327 establishes the European Health Data Space. It grants natural persons access, download, transfer and restriction rights, requires Member States to set up access services and digital health authorities, creates the MyHealth@EU cross-border infrastructure and sets rules for secondary use. Applies from 26 March 2027.
summary_long: Regulation (EU) 2025/327 establishes the European Health Data Space (EHDS) for primary use (healthcare delivery) and secondary use (research, policymaking and related purposes) of electronic health data. The text provided covers Chapter I (general provisions and definitions) and Chapter II, Sections 1 to 3 (rights of natural persons, access by health professionals, priority data categories, digital health authorities and MyHealth@EU). Natural persons may access their priority-category data through electronic health data access services, download copies, insert information, request rectification, transmit data to providers, restrict access and obtain information on accesses. Member States must establish access services and proxy services and designate digital health authorities and national contact points for digital health. Member States may provide an opt-out from access and may delay access for patient-safety reasons. The Commission adopts implementing acts on formats and specifications and establishes MyHealth@EU. Digital health authorities publish biennial activity reports, and complaints go to digital health authorities or supervisory authorities, which may impose administrative fines under Regulation (EU) 2016/679. The recitals also describe the EHR system conformity regime, wellness application labelling, secondary use through health data access bodies and secure processing environments, HealthData@EU and penalties; these chapters are not in the text provided. The regulation applies from 26 March 2027 (Recital 115).

title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1083 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 establishing a common framework for media services in the internal market (European Media Freedom Act)
summary_short: EU regulation setting common rules for media services in the internal market. Requires Member States to safeguard editorial independence, journalistic sources and public service media; creates the European Board for Media Services; imposes ownership disclosure, state-advertising, audience-measurement and very-large-platform duties. Applies from 8 August 2025, some provisions earlier.
summary_long: Establishes a common framework for media services in the internal market to safeguard editorial independence and media pluralism. Chapter II sets recipient rights, editorial-freedom and journalistic-source protections (limiting surveillance and spyware, with narrow derogations), public service media safeguards, and ownership and state-advertising disclosure duties for media providers. Chapter III designates national regulatory authorities, creates the European Board for Media Services to replace ERGA, and sets cooperation procedures and coordination of measures against media services from outside the Union. Section 4 requires very large online platforms to offer media providers a self-declaration function (including on AI-generated content), give statements of reasons with a 24-hour reply, run a structured dialogue and let users customise device settings. Section 5 covers national measures and media market concentration assessments; Section 6 covers audience measurement transparency and allocation of state advertising funds. It requires monitoring and a 2028 evaluation and contains no penalty provisions. Application is staged from 8 November 2024 to 8 May 2027.

title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 September 2023 on energy efficiency (recast)
summary_short: Recast EU energy efficiency directive setting a framework for energy efficiency targets, the energy efficiency first principle, public-sector energy savings, energy savings obligations, energy audits, energy management systems and data-centre reporting. Binding on Member States, which must transpose it. Adopted 13 September 2023.
summary_long: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 recasts Directive 2012/27/EU and establishes a common Union framework to promote energy efficiency and meet Union energy efficiency targets. Member States must apply an energy efficiency first principle in planning, policy and major investment decisions above EUR 100 million (EUR 175 million for transport infrastructure) (Art. 3). Member States must collectively reduce final energy consumption by at least 11.7% in 2030 compared with the 2020 EU Reference Scenario and set indicative national contributions (Art. 4). Public bodies must reduce their final energy consumption by at least 1.9% each year (Art. 5), renovate at least 3% of the floor area of publicly owned buildings each year (Art. 6), and purchase high energy-efficiency products and services (Art. 7). Member States must achieve cumulative end-use energy savings through obligation schemes or alternative policy measures, with designated obligated parties (Arts 8 to 10). Enterprises above set annual energy consumption must implement a certified energy management system or undergo energy audits (Art. 11). Owners and operators of data centres with at least 500 kW of installed IT power must make energy performance information publicly available, and the Commission maintains a European database (Art. 12). Articles 13 and 14 set metering requirements for natural gas and for heating, cooling and domestic hot water. The document provided ends with Article 14; later provisions are not included in this file.

title: Directive 2002/58/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 July 2002 concerning the processing of personal data and the protection of privacy in the electronic communications sector
summary_short: EU directive on privacy in electronic communications. Requires Member States to protect confidentiality of communications, regulates traffic and location data, cookies and terminal storage, directories, and unsolicited direct marketing, and imposes security duties on electronic communications service providers. Transposition due by 31 October 2003.
summary_long: Directive addressed to Member States (Art. 21); transposition due by 31 October 2003 (Art. 17). It particularises and complements Directive 95/46/EC for publicly available electronic communications services in public networks (Arts. 1-3). Providers must take security measures and warn subscribers of particular risks (Art. 4). Member States must ensure confidentiality of communications and traffic data, prohibit interception without consent, and condition storage of or access to terminal information on clear information and a right to refuse (Art. 5). Traffic data must be erased or anonymised when no longer needed, with limited billing uses and consent-based marketing uses (Art. 6). Location data other than traffic data may be processed only if anonymised or with consent, with a temporary refusal option (Art. 9). Calling and connected line identification must be restrictable, subject to tracing and emergency exceptions (Articles 8, 10); automatic call forwarding must be stoppable (Art. 11). Subscribers must be informed of and may control directory inclusion (Art. 12). Unsolicited direct marketing by automated calls, fax or email requires prior consent, subject to an existing-customer exception; disguised senders are prohibited (Art. 13). National restrictions for security and criminal enforcement are allowed (Art. 15). It repeals Directive 97/66/EC (Art. 19).

title: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/482 of 31 January 2024 laying down rules for the application of Regulation (EU) 2019/881 as regards the adoption of the European Common Criteria-based cybersecurity certification scheme (EUCC)
summary_short: Implementing Regulation laying down the EUCC, the European Common Criteria-based cybersecurity certification scheme for ICT products and protection profiles under Regulation (EU) 2019/881. It sets assurance levels, evaluation and certification rules, monitoring, vulnerability handling and conformity-body requirements, applying from 27 February 2025.
summary_long: The Regulation sets out the European Common Criteria-based cybersecurity certification scheme (EUCC) for ICT products and protection profiles under Regulation (EU) 2019/881. Certificates are issued at assurance level 'substantial' (AVA_VAN 1 or 2) or 'high' (AVA_VAN 3, 4 or 5), evaluated under the Common Criteria and Common Evaluation Methodology (Arts 3-4). Self-assessment is not permitted (Art 6). AVA_VAN 4 or 5 certification is possible only in specified scenarios (Art 7(3)). Certificate validity generally does not exceed 5 years, with derogation subject to prior national approval (Art 12). Certification bodies operating at 'high' and ITSEF require national authorisation (Arts 21-22). Certificate holders must monitor vulnerabilities and perform vulnerability impact analyses (Arts 33-35). Certificates may be suspended for up to 42 days or withdrawn (Arts 14, 30). National authorities sample at least 4% of certificates annually (Art 25(3)), and certification bodies issuing 'high' certificates undergo peer assessment at least every five years (Art 45). Holders may affix a mark and label (Art 11). Third countries may seek mutual recognition agreements (Art 44). National certification schemes cease to produce effects 12 months after entry into force (Art 49). The Regulation applies from 27 February 2025 (Art 50).

title: Council Regulation (EU) 2024/1732 of 17 June 2024 amending Regulation (EU) 2021/1173 as regards a EuroHPC initiative for start-ups in order to boost European leadership in trustworthy artificial intelligence
summary_short: Amends Regulation (EU) 2021/1173 to give the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking a seventh objective: acquiring, owning and operating AI-optimised supercomputers and developing AI factories, with access reserved for trustworthy AI proposals. Applies from the twentieth day after publication in the Official Journal.
summary_long: Council Regulation (EU) 2024/1732 amends Regulation (EU) 2021/1173 establishing the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC). It adds a seventh objective of developing and operating AI factories, and defines 'AI-optimised supercomputer' and 'AI factory'. The Joint Undertaking may acquire and own AI-optimised supercomputers, which must be located in a EuroHPC hosting entity or a supercomputing centre in the Union. The Union contribution covers up to 50% of acquisition costs and up to 50% of operating costs, with the remainder borne by the hosting Participating States. Supplier selection must address supply-chain security, and the Governing Board may restrict supplier participation for security reasons. Existing hosting entities may apply to become AI factories through a call for expressions of interest, and hosting entities of AI-optimised supercomputers must create a one-stop shop for users. Upgrades of EuroHPC supercomputers with AI capabilities are also permitted. AI-optimised and upgraded supercomputers are to be used primarily for large-scale AI model development and testing. Access conditions reserve eligibility for trustworthy and ethical AI proposals and include dedicated access for startups and SMEs, and the Union's share of access time may not exceed 50%. The Regulation is binding and directly applicable in all Member States and enters into force on the twentieth day after publication.

title: Council Regulation (EU) 2026/150 of 16 January 2026 amending Regulation (EU) 2021/1173 on establishing the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking
summary_short: Amends Regulation (EU) 2021/1173 to give the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking legal basis to establish and operate AI gigafactories, with Union co-financing, hosting, procurement, access and governance rules. Also expands quantum provisions. Applies from the day after Official Journal publication.
summary_long: Amends Regulation (EU) 2021/1173 to give the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking a legal basis to establish and operate AI gigafactories: large AI computing facilities with supporting data centre, storage, networking and secure cloud access, located in a Member State. Each is financed by a partnership of the Joint Undertaking, a consortium and Participating States. The Union contributes up to 17% of computing CAPEX or a guaranteed access-time purchase, matched by Member States, who may channel Recovery and Resilience Facility funds through the Joint Undertaking. Selection is by joint procurement and evaluation criteria including energy efficiency. Entities from non-Participating States may be restricted from consortia. Hosting Agreements must cover governance, access, audits and liability, and certain ownership or control changes require prior approval from a public governance body. Member State-provided access time is used mainly for start-ups and SMEs. The amendment also expands the quantum pillar, sets up a Quantum Technologies Advisory Group, adjusts Governing Board voting and raises the Union contribution to EUR 4 122 300 000. It contains no sanction provisions and applies from the day after Official Journal publication.

title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data (General Data Protection Regulation)
summary_short: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR) sets rules for processing personal data by controllers and processors established in the EU and, under Article 3(2), by non-EU controllers offering goods or services to or monitoring people in the Union. Part 1 covers general provisions, principles, lawful bases, special categories and data subject rights.
summary_long: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR) sets rules on protecting natural persons in relation to personal data processing and on its free movement, repealing Directive 95/46/EC. It covers automated processing and filing systems (Art. 2), excluding among others purely household activity and criminal-law enforcement by competent authorities. It binds controllers and processors established in the Union and, for non-EU controllers, those offering goods or services to or monitoring people in the Union (Art. 3). Article 5 sets processing principles with an accountability duty; Article 6 lists six lawful bases; Article 7 sets consent conditions; Article 8 requires parental authorisation for children under 16 using information society services, which Member States may lower to 13. Article 9(1) prohibits processing of special categories of data, subject to listed exceptions. Chapter III grants transparency, information, access, rectification, erasure, restriction and notification rights (Arts. 12-19), with responses due within one month (Art. 12(3)). This annotation covers only the recitals and Articles 1-19 of the text supplied; later chapters and the application date are not described.

title: Regulation (EU) 2025/2518 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 November 2025 laying down additional procedural rules on the enforcement of Regulation (EU) 2016/679
summary_short: EU regulation setting procedural rules for supervisory authorities enforcing the GDPR in cross-border cases: complaint handling, cooperation, time limits, right to be heard, access to the file and dispute resolution before the EDPB. Applies from 2 April 2027.
summary_long: Regulation (EU) 2025/2518 lays down procedural rules for complaint handling and investigations by supervisory authorities when enforcing the GDPR in cases concerning cross-border processing. It covers complaint admissibility (required information, a two-week period to declare a complaint inadmissible), transmission to the presumed lead supervisory authority within six weeks, optional early resolution of complaints, a simple cooperation procedure, a summary of key issues and consensus-seeking between authorities, and time limits for submitting draft decisions (15 months, or 12 months under the simple cooperation procedure, with extensions). It also sets rules for full or partial rejection of complaints with complainant input, preliminary findings and the right to be heard for parties under investigation, access to the administrative file, protection of trade secrets and confidential information, a cooperation file, dispute resolution and urgency procedures before the European Data Protection Board. It enters into force on the twentieth day after publication and applies from 2 April 2027, with transitional rules for investigations opened or complaints lodged before that date.

title: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/138 of 21 December 2022 laying down a list of specific high-value datasets and the arrangements for their publication and re-use
summary_short: Lists specific high-value datasets in six thematic categories and requires public sector bodies holding them to publish them for re-use via APIs, under open licences (CC0 or CC BY 4.0), from 16 months after entry into force.
summary_long: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/138 lays down a list of specific high-value datasets under Directive (EU) 2019/1024, in six thematic categories (geospatial; earth observation and environment; meteorological; statistics; companies and company ownership; mobility), with granularity, key attributes, formats and update frequencies set in the Annex. Public sector bodies holding listed datasets must make them available for re-use in machine-readable formats via APIs, with bulk download where the Annex requires it, publish API terms of use, quality of service criteria and documentation, designate an API point of contact, and mark the datasets as high-value in their metadata (Art. 3). Art. 4 requires re-use under CC0 or CC BY 4.0 or an equivalent or less restrictive open licence, applies the obligations to existing machine-readable high-value datasets created before the date of application, and requires publication of Member State exemptions granted under Directive 2019/1024. Member States must report on implementation within two years of entry into force, then every two years on request, including the number of exempted bodies (Art. 5). Binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States, it applies 16 months after entry into force (Art. 6).

title: Directive (EU) 2022/2555 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 December 2022 on measures for a high common level of cybersecurity across the Union (NIS 2 Directive)
summary_short: Sets cybersecurity risk-management and incident-reporting duties for essential and important entities in Annex I and II sectors, and requires Member States to designate national authorities, CSIRTs and cybersecurity strategies. Repeals Directive 2016/1148.
summary_long: Directive (EU) 2022/2555 sets measures for a high common level of cybersecurity across the Union and repeals Directive (EU) 2016/1148. It applies to public and private entities of the types listed in Annexes I and II that are medium-sized enterprises or larger and operate within the Union, and, regardless of size, to listed categories including electronic communications and trust service providers, TLD registries, DNS providers and critical entities under Directive (EU) 2022/2557. Entities are classed as essential or important. Member States must adopt national cybersecurity strategies, designate competent authorities, single points of contact, cyber crisis management authorities and CSIRTs, and compile lists of essential and important entities. Essential and important entities must take cybersecurity risk-management measures, which management bodies approve and oversee, and notify changes to their registration details. The Directive also establishes a Cooperation Group, a CSIRTs network, EU-CyCLONe, peer reviews, coordinated vulnerability disclosure and a European vulnerability database. The text provided covers the provisions up to Article 22; the remaining provisions are in the second part of the document.

title: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 of 17 October 2024 laying down rules for the application of Directive (EU) 2022/2555 as regards technical and methodological requirements of cybersecurity risk-management measures and further specification of the cases in which an incident is considered to be significant
summary_short: Sets cybersecurity risk-management requirements (Annex) and significant-incident criteria for listed DNS, cloud, data centre, online platform, managed service, trust service and other relevant entities under Directive (EU) 2022/2555; binding in all Member States, in force 20 days after OJ publication.
summary_long: Implements Article 21(2) and Article 23(3) of Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS 2) for listed relevant entities: DNS service providers, TLD name registries, cloud computing, data centre and content delivery network providers, managed service and managed security service providers, online marketplaces, online search engines, social networking services platforms and trust service providers. Article 2 requires them to apply the technical and methodological cybersecurity risk-management measures in the Annex, proportionate to their risk exposure, size and incident likelihood and impact; where a requirement applies 'where appropriate', 'where applicable' or 'to the extent feasible' and is not applied, the entity must document its reasoning. The Annex covers policy, risk management, incident handling, business continuity, supply chain security, acquisition and development, security testing, cyber hygiene and training, cryptography, human resources, access control, asset management and physical security. Article 3 sets significance criteria, including direct financial loss above the lower of EUR 500 000 or 5% of turnover and severe operational disruption; Article 4 aggregates recurring incidents; Articles 5 to 14 add criteria per entity type based on outage durations and user shares. Article 15 repeals Regulation (EU) 2018/151. Binding and directly applicable in all Member States; enters into force on the twentieth day after OJ publication.

title: Directive (EU) 2019/1024 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019 on open data and the re-use of public sector information (recast)
summary_short: Recast EU directive setting minimum rules for re-use of existing documents held by public sector bodies, public undertakings and publicly funded research data. Sets free-of-charge re-use with cost-based exceptions, generally prohibits exclusive rights, and requires APIs for dynamic and high-value datasets. Member States transpose by 17 July 2021.
summary_long: Directive (EU) 2019/1024 recasts Directive 2003/98/EC on re-use of public sector information. It sets minimum rules for re-use of existing documents held by public sector bodies, by public undertakings in listed sectors, and of publicly funded research data already in public repositories (Art. 1). Re-use is free of charge, with charges limited to marginal costs; listed bodies may charge more under cost-based criteria, with return on investment capped at 5 percentage points above the ECB fixed rate (Art. 6; Art. 2(16)). Conditions must be non-discriminatory (Art. 11), and exclusive rights are generally barred, subject to exceptions (Art. 12). Dynamic data must be available via APIs immediately after collection (Art. 5). Implementing acts will designate high-value datasets from six Annex I categories, to be free of charge and provided via APIs (Art. 13-14). Member States must adopt open access policies for research data (Art. 10). Requests are processed within 20 working days, extendable (Art. 4). Transposition is due by 17 July 2021, and Directive 2003/98/EC is repealed from that date (Art. 17, 19).

title: Regulation (EU) 2019/1150 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019 on promoting fairness and transparency for business users of online intermediation services
summary_short: Regulation (EU) 2019/1150 sets transparency, fairness and redress rules for providers of online intermediation services and online search engines toward business users and corporate website users. It applies from 12 July 2020 to providers whose EU business users offer goods or services to EU consumers, wherever the providers are established.
summary_long: Regulation (EU) 2019/1150 sets transparency, fairness and redress rules for providers of online intermediation services and online search engines in relation to business users and corporate website users. Providers must draft their terms and conditions in plain and intelligible language, make them easily available, and give at least 15 days' notice of proposed changes, with termination rights for business users. They must state reasons for restricting or suspending services and, for terminating a whole service, give at least 30 days' notice, subject to listed exceptions. They must describe the main parameters determining ranking, any differentiated treatment of their own offers, ancillary goods and services, access to data, and grounds for restricting offers made through other channels. Providers must operate an internal complaint-handling system and identify at least two mediators, with exemptions for small enterprises. Organisations and designated public bodies may bring actions before national courts. Member States must ensure adequate and effective enforcement with measures that are effective, proportionate and dissuasive. The Commission monitors the regulation, must issue guidelines on ranking transparency, and must evaluate the regulation by 13 January 2022 and every three years thereafter. The regulation applies irrespective of the providers' place of establishment, provided the business users or corporate website users are established in the Union and offer goods or services to consumers located in the Union.

title: Directive (EU) 2024/2831 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2024 on improving working conditions in platform work
summary_short: Sets EU minimum rules for digital labour platforms organising platform work in the Union: a rebuttable presumption of employment, limits and transparency duties for algorithmic management, and work declarations to authorities. Member States must transpose by 2 December 2026.
summary_long: Sets minimum rules for digital labour platforms organising platform work in the Union, wherever established. Art. 5 creates a rebuttable presumption of employment where facts indicating direction and control are found, for administrative and judicial proceedings other than tax, criminal or social security; Art. 4 requires procedures to determine correct employment status; Art. 3 extends protection to workers engaged through intermediaries. Chapter III governs algorithmic management: Art. 7 bans processing of listed personal data (e.g. emotional state, private conversations, biometric identification); Art. 8 requires a data-protection impact assessment; Art. 9 imposes information duties; Art. 10 requires human oversight and impact evaluation at least every two years, and human decisions on account restriction or termination; Art. 11 grants explanation, human contact, written reasons and review. Arts. 12-14 cover safety and health risk evaluation and consultation. Art. 16 requires declaration of platform work to authorities; Art. 17 information updated every six months. Arts. 18-23 provide redress, representative actions, evidence disclosure and protection from adverse treatment. Art. 24 applies GDPR supervision and fine ceilings to Arts. 7-11 and requires effective, dissuasive, proportionate penalties. Transposition is due by 2 December 2026.

title: Regulation (EU) 2024/900 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 March 2024 on the transparency and targeting of political advertising
summary_short: EU Regulation 2024/900 harmonises transparency and due-diligence rules for political advertising. It requires labels and transparency notices on political ads, a European ad repository, and limits targeting using personal data. It restricts pre-election sponsorship to EU-linked sponsors and sets sanction maxima of 6% of turnover. Applies from 10 October 2025.
summary_long: Regulation (EU) 2024/900 sets harmonised EU rules on transparency and due diligence for political advertising services and sponsors, and on targeting and ad-delivery techniques that process personal data. Political advertising covers paid or in-house messages by, for or on behalf of political actors, or liable and designed to influence elections, referendums or legislative processes; official communication, editorial content and personal opinions are excluded. Publishers must label each political advertisement and publish a transparency notice, keep records for seven years, and very large platforms have extra repository duties and feed a public European repository. Personal-data targeting requires separate explicit consent; special-category profiling and targeting of persons known to be at least one year below voting age are prohibited. Controllers must adopt internal policies and annual risk assessments. In the three months before elections, services are limited to eligible sponsors. Non-EU providers need legal representatives. Member States set sanctions up to 6% of annual turnover or income. Applies from 10 October 2025.

title: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2024 on liability for defective products
summary_short: Replaces Council Directive 85/374/EEC with EU rules on no-fault liability for defective products, including software, for manufacturers and other economic operators. Applies to products placed on the market or put into service after 9 December 2026; Member States must transpose by that date.
summary_long: Replaces Council Directive 85/374/EEC with EU rules on no-fault liability for damage caused by defective products. 'Product' includes software, electricity, digital manufacturing files and raw materials (Art. 4(1)). Liable are manufacturers, manufacturers of defective components, importers, authorised representatives and fulfilment service providers (for non-EU manufacturers), and conditionally distributors and online platforms (Art. 8). Compensable damage: death or personal injury, property damage (not exclusively professional property) and corruption of non-professional data (Art. 6). Defectiveness is assessed by the safety the public is entitled to expect (Art. 7). Courts may order disclosure of evidence and presume defectiveness or causation (Arts 9-10). Defences are in Art. 11; liability is joint and several (Art. 12) and cannot be contractually excluded (Art. 15). Limitation period is three years; expiry period is 10 years, or 25 years for latent personal injury (Arts 16-17). Member States may keep or adopt development-risk derogations after notifying the Commission (Art. 18). Final judgments must be published and the Commission sets up a database (Art. 19). Member States transpose by 9 December 2026; rules apply to products placed on the market or put into service after that date (Arts 2, 22).

title: Laki eraiden tekoalyjarjestelmien valvonnasta (1377/2025)
summary_short: Finnish statute supplementing the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). It designates market surveillance and notifying authorities, sets up a central contact point and a sanctions board, and provides administrative fines for AI Act breaches, applying from 1 January 2026.
summary_long: Finnish statute supplementing the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). It designates national market surveillance authorities by sector for high-risk AI systems, supervises prohibited practices and transparency duties, sets up a central contact point and a sanctions board, and regulates notifying authorities and notified bodies. It provides administrative fines for AI Act breaches by providers, authorised representatives, importers, distributors, deployers and notified bodies: up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide turnover for prohibited practices, EUR 15 million or 3% for other listed breaches, and EUR 7.5 million or 1% for incorrect information; the lower amount applies to micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. Fines may be waived for minor breaches or where clearly unreasonable, and are not imposed where criminal proceedings or a final judgment exist for the same act. Parliamentary business and certain parliamentary and oversight bodies are excluded. Effective 1 January 2026.

title: Hallituksen esitys HE 156/2025 vp - laiksi sahkon ja eraiden polttoaineiden valmisteverosta annetun lain eraiden saannosten kumoamisesta (konesalien sahkovero)
summary_short: Government bill HE 156/2025 vp proposes repealing the Finnish electricity excise tax provisions (§2 points 6a–6c and §4a) that let data centres buy electricity at the lower class II rate. Data-centre electricity would move to the general class I from 1 July 2026.
summary_long: The bill repeals §2 points 6a–6c and §4a of the Electricity and Certain Fuels Excise Tax Act (1260/1996), as they stood under Act 1215/2021. Section 4a provided the reduced electricity tax class II for data centres (konesalit) with more than 0.5 MW of server capacity that met conditions on waste-heat use, ERE values or PUE values. Under the bill, electricity used in data centres would be taxed at the general class I rate of 2.24 cents per kWh instead of the class II rate of 0.05 cents per kWh, an increase of 2.19 cents per kWh. The bill proposes entry into force on 1 July 2026 and is linked to the 2026 state budget proposal. The explanatory sections also set out the background to the 2022 threshold change, the EU energy tax and state aid framework, the comparison with Sweden and Norway, and a separate bill (HE 97/2025 vp) on the mining electricity class. The operative text contains no enforcement regime of its own.},

title: Code des impositions sur les biens et services - Article L312-70 (tarif reduit d'accise sur l'electricite pour les centres de stockage de donnees numeriques)
summary_short: French excise-code article under which data-centre operators get a reduced excise rate on electricity above one gigawatt-hour per calendar year, if eight cumulative conditions are met (security, cooling, energy management, heat recovery, water use, electro-sensitivity). Amended by Law 2025-127 of 14 February 2025.
summary_long: Article L. 312-70 of the Code des impositions sur les biens et services (general excise regime) gives a reduced excise rate on electricity consumed for data-processing infrastructure, for the portion above one gigawatt-hour per calendar year. The rate applies only if eight cumulative conditions are met: data storage, processing, transport or distribution use; secured access; dedicated thermal, air-quality, power and fire-prevention controls; an energy management system; membership of a recognised good-practice programme (eco-design, efficiency, consumption reporting, cooling performance criteria); waste-heat recovery in a heat or cold network, or a multi-year power-efficiency indicator set by decree; cooling water use limited by a multi-year indicator set by decree; and electro-sensitive activities. The article itself sets no penalties. Its amendment by Law 2025-127 of 14 February 2025 is recorded in its version line.
text_version: current version of art. L312-70 as last amended by loi n° 2025-127 du 14 février 2025, art. 21 (codes.droit.org edition of 2026-10-10, generated from Légifrance API data)

title: CNIL - Deliberation de la formation restreinte n° SAN-2022-019 du 17 octobre 2022 concernant la societe CLEARVIEW AI
summary_short: CNIL restricted-committee sanction against a US-established company whose scraped-image facial-recognition search engine breached GDPR Arts 6, 12, 15, 17 and 31. Imposes a €20 million administrative fine and an injunction to stop unlawful processing of persons in France and delete their data, with a €100,000-per-day penalty after two months.
summary_long: Restricted-committee decision of the French data protection authority (CNIL) of 17 October 2022, published 20 October 2022, against a company established in the United States, named only as '[…]' in the text. The company runs a facial-recognition search engine built from images collected from publicly accessible web pages, including social networks, from which it computes biometric templates; users upload a photograph and receive matching images with their source URLs. The committee holds that the GDPR applies under Article 3(2)(b) because the processing is linked to monitoring the behaviour of people in the Union, and that the one-stop-shop mechanism does not apply because the company has no EU establishment. It finds breaches of Article 6 (no legal basis; consent absent and legitimate interests rejected on balancing), of Articles 12 and 15 (incomplete and delayed access responses), of Article 17 (no response to an erasure request) and of Article 31 (no cooperation with the CNIL). Measures: an administrative fine of 20 million euros; an injunction not to collect or process personal data of persons in France without a legal basis for the search engine and to delete such data, with a penalty of 100,000 euros per day of delay, liquidable after two months; and publication of the decision on the CNIL and Légifrance websites, not naming the company after two years.

title: Décret n° 2025-1382 relatif à la transposition de la directive (UE) 2023/1791 relative à l'efficacité énergétique (data-centre rules: code de l'énergie D. 236-1 à D. 236-7, R. 237-4 à R. 237-6)
summary_short: Transposes parts of EU Directive 2023/1791 on energy efficiency into French energy and environment codes. For data centres above a power threshold, it sets declaration, public reporting and waste-heat reuse duties. In force 1 January 2026.
summary_long: Décret no 2025-1382 transposes parts of EU Directive 2023/1791 on energy efficiency into the energy and environment codes, in force 1 January 2026. For data centres above a power threshold under Art. L. 236-1 of the energy code, operators must declare installed power and a contact to the energy minister, publish annual energy and sustainability data by 15 May, and set up data collection. The energy minister may issue formal notices and fines. Data centres are deemed to reuse waste heat if their ERF is at least 0.20, which may be raised to 0.40 by order. Heat-producing installations must file a cost-benefit analysis unless exempted, and data centres may derogate where technico-economic conditions are not met. Other provisions cover energy audits for large firms, energy performance contracts, public procurement preferences and district heating and cooling criteria.
text_version: JORF n° 305 du 30 décembre 2025, texte n° 20 (JO PDF notified to the Commission as national transposition measure)

title: LOI n° 2016-1321 du 7 octobre 2016 pour une Republique numerique
summary_short: French omnibus law (7 Oct 2016) on open public data, notice of algorithmic individual decisions by administrations, net neutrality, data portability, platform and review transparency, personal data rights and digital accessibility.
summary_long: Loi n° 2016-1321 of 7 October 2016 (in force) amends several codes. Title I (open data): administrations must communicate and publish administrative documents and data in open formats, reuse of public information is free of charge under stated conditions, and reference data, court decisions and certain concessionaire and energy-network data become available. Individual decisions taken on the basis of algorithmic processing must carry an explicit mention and, on request, the rules of the processing (Art. 4, new L. 311-3-1 CRPA). Title II (digital environment): net neutrality is written into the electronic communications code; consumers may recover their data; platform operators must inform users about ranking and referencing; hosts of consumer reviews must publish moderation rules; and the personal data act is amended (new user rights, minors' erasure right, post-mortem directives, CNIL sanctions capped at 3 million euros, criminal offences on sexual recordings). Text and data mining for research is an exception to copyright. Title III: accessibility of public and large-company websites, relay telephone services for deaf and hard-of-hearing users, maintenance of internet access for vulnerable households, and rules for esports competitions and professional player contracts. Some provisions have dated effect (e.g., 1 January 2017, 25 May 2018).
text_version: JORF text: JORF n°0235 du 8 octobre 2016 (NOR ECFI1524250L), original version as published (not consolidated); DILA JORF open data, JORFTEXT000033202746

title: LOI n° 2021-1485 du 15 novembre 2021 visant a reduire l'empreinte environnementale du numerique en France
summary_short: Sets measures to reduce the environmental footprint of digital use in France: bans on techniques restricting consumers' software installation, software-update duties on sellers, eco-design criteria and indicators for telecom operators, data-centre tax-relief conditions, public purchasing and reuse of IT equipment, and local strategies for large communes.
summary_long: Law no. 2021-1485 of 15 November 2021 seeks to reduce the environmental footprint of digital technology in France, in five chapters. Chapter I raises user awareness through education content and an observatory of digital environmental impacts and of AI's contribution to the ecological transition. Chapter II limits device renewal: it bans techniques, including software, that prevent installing chosen software after the period set by Consumer Code Art. L. 217-12, unless needed for conformity; it sets seller duties on software updates; and it adds reuse, repair and public-purchasing rules for IT equipment. Chapter III covers electronic communications and digital services: caller-identity rules for automated calls, eco-design criteria for digital services from 1 January 2024, and an audiovisual recommendation on energy information. Chapter IV covers data centres and networks: heat-recovery and water-use criteria for a data-centre tax incentive, operator environmental indicators, and mast-sharing rules. Chapter V sets local strategies: regional climate plans must address data-centre heat recovery, and communes and intercommunal bodies above 50,000 inhabitants must adopt a responsible digital strategy by 1 January 2025. Government reports are also required.

title: LOI n° 2023-380 du 19 mai 2023 relative aux jeux Olympiques et Paralympiques de 2024 et portant diverses autres dispositions (art. 10: videoprotection algorithmique)
summary_short: Olympic and Paralympic Games law (2023) setting event-specific rules. Article 10 allows experimental algorithmic analysis of event video-surveillance images until 31 March 2025, under decree and prefectoral authorisation, without biometric identification.
summary_long: Law of 19 May 2023 on the 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games and other provisions. Article 10 allows, on an experimental basis until 31 March 2025, algorithmic processing of images from authorised video-surveillance systems and aircraft cameras at sporting, recreational or cultural events, to detect predetermined events in real time and flag them to police, fire and transport security services. It excludes biometric identification, facial recognition and linking with other files, and its outputs may not by themselves ground individual decisions. Use requires a decree after CNIL opinion, with an impact assessment, prefectoral authorisation for periods of at most one month, public information, a compliance attestation for third-party developers, and CNIL oversight. Other titles cover health services and volunteer health staff for the Games, anti-doping genetic analyses and penalties, video-surveillance and stadium access rules, security inquiries, advertising and the Olympic flame relay, Sunday trading exemptions, accessible taxi permits, and overseas adaptations. Article 7 is marked as declared unconstitutional by Constitutional Council decision 2023-850 DC.
