title: LOI n° 2023-451 du 9 juin 2023 visant a encadrer l'influence commerciale et a lutter contre les derives des influenceurs sur les reseaux sociaux
summary_short: Adopted 9 June 2023: regulates paid commercial influence by electronic means. Requires disclosure labels, bans promotion of certain products (cosmetic procedures, nicotine, certain financial products, sports betting advice), sets influencer-agent, contract, joint liability and insurance duties, and platform notice duties.
summary_long: Defines commercial influence by electronic means as paid promotion of goods, services or causes to an online audience (Art. 1) and regulates it. Art. 3 applies advertising rules to influencers. Art. 4 bans promotion of cosmetic procedures, therapeutic substitutes, nicotine products, animal promotion outside listed species, certain financial products and sports betting advice, and allows gambling promotion only where under-18s can be excluded; breaches carry two years' imprisonment and a 300,000 euro fine. Art. 5 requires 'Publicité' or 'Collaboration commerciale' labels and labels for retouched and AI-generated images. Art. 6 makes sellers liable to buyers. Arts. 7-9 regulate influencer agents, require written contracts on pain of nullity, impose joint liability on advertisers and influencers, and require non-EU persons to appoint an EU legal representative and hold insurance. Title II: Arts. 10-12 add platform notice, trusted-flagger and removal-order duties under the EU Digital Services Act; Art. 13 sets Consumer Code injunction penalty limits; Art. 14 extends financial-promotion sanctions to online promoters; Art. 15 requires platform commitments; Art. 16 adds education on commercial manipulation; Art. 17 orders a report within two years. Art. 18 bars Arts. 10-12 and 15 from taking effect before EU notification clearance.
text_version: JORF text: JORF n°0133 du 10 juin 2023 (NOR ECOX2308125L); DILA JORF open data, JORFTEXT000047663185

title: LOI n° 2023-566 du 7 juillet 2023 visant a instaurer une majorite numerique et a lutter contre la haine en ligne
summary_short: Amends France's Law for Trust in the Digital Economy (LCEN): social network providers must refuse under-15 accounts without parental authorization, use age checks meeting an ARCOM framework, and display harassment-prevention messages. Entry into force is set by decree, no later than three months after EU Commission's response on notification.
summary_long: The law amends France's LCEN (Law No. 2004-575) in five respects. Art. 1 defines online social network services. Art. 2 extends the illegal-content categories hosts must address (harassment, threats, privacy, security and listed Penal Code offences). Art. 3 requires social networks to show harassment-prevention messages. Art. 4 inserts Art. 6-7: providers operating in France must refuse accounts for under-15s without parental authorization, obtain authorization for existing under-15 accounts, inform users and parents of risks, enable parental suspension and time-use controls, and verify age using technical solutions meeting an ARCOM framework. ARCOM may issue a formal notice (15 days to respond) and ask the Paris court president to order compliance; breach carries a fine up to 1% of prior-year worldwide turnover. Non-profit encyclopedias and educational or scientific directories are exempt. Art. 5 adds 10-day response deadlines (8 hours in emergencies) to LCEN Art. 6 VI. Art. 6 requires a government report on youth and platforms within one year. Art. 7 sets entry into force by decree within three months after the EU Commission's response to notification; some Art. 6-7 provisions apply later (one and two years).
text_version: JORF text: JORF n°0157 du 8 juillet 2023 (NOR JUSX2306064L); DILA JORF open data, JORFTEXT000047799533

title: LOI n° 2024-449 du 21 mai 2024 visant a securiser et a reguler l'espace numerique
summary_short: Part 1 of 2 of French Loi n° 2024-449 (SREN) covering Articles 1 to 51 as provided. It requires age verification and blocking of harmful online content under ARCOM, criminalises non-consensual algorithmic intimate deepfakes, regulates cloud switching fees and interoperability, and sets regimes for monetisable digital-object games and data intermediation.
summary_long: Part 1 of 2 of Loi n° 2024-449 of 21 May 2024 (SREN), covering Articles 1 to 51 as provided. Title I requires online publishers and video-sharing platforms to keep pornographic content from minors through age verification, enforced by notices, fines, access blocking and app-store bans, and sets a 24-hour removal duty for child sexual abuse images. Title II covers digital education, labelling of simulated crime content, criminal penalties for non-consensual algorithmic intimate images, and account-suspension penalties for certain offences. Title III regulates cloud computing: limits on switching and data-transfer fees, time-limited cloud credits barred from exclusivity conditions, ARCEP-set interoperability and portability requirements, state cloud hosting rules and transparency duties. Title IV creates a three-year experimental regime for monetisable digital-object games under the Autorité nationale des jeux. Titles V to VIII cover research data collection, DSA coordination, judicial data supervision and adaptations to the 2004 digital economy law. Articles 10, 11, 18 and 19 are marked as declared unconstitutional; Part 2 is not included.
text_version: JORF text: JORF n°0117 du 22 mai 2024 (NOR ECOI2309270L), as promulgated after CC decision n° 2024-866 DC of 17 May 2024 (censured provisions shown as bracketed notes); DILA JORF open data, JORFTEXT000049563368

title: LOI n° 2025-391 du 30 avril 2025 portant diverses dispositions d'adaptation au droit de l'Union européenne (dispositions relatives à la performance énergétique des centres de données)
summary_short: Omnibus French act adapting law to EU rules in economic, energy, transport and other fields. Its data-centre provisions (Art. 25, Code de l'énergie Art. L. 236-1 to L. 236-3) require energy-data reporting for sites of 500 kW or more, waste-heat recovery at 1 MW or more, and allow administrative fines up to 50,000 euros per data centre.
summary_long: Law n° 2025-391 of 30 April 2025 (JORF 2 May 2025) is an omnibus act adapting French law to EU rules across economic, financial, environmental, energy, transport and health fields. Article 25 adds a data-centre chapter to the Energy Code (Art. L. 236-1 to L. 236-3) that applies to all data centres, with defence-related centres excluded from the reporting duty. Centres with installed capacity of 500 kW or more must transmit administrative, environmental and energy information on an EU digital platform and make related data public. Centres of 1 MW or more must recover their waste heat, subject to decree-defined derogations. Projects of 1 MW or more require a cost-benefit analysis of energy efficiency (Art. L. 233-5). The administrative authority may issue a formal notice with a deadline of at most one year and, if it is not followed, an administrative fine of up to 50,000 euros per data centre; it may publish the sanction for two months to five years. Ministers set general rules on siting, grid availability and cooling water. Article 25 I to III enter into force on 1 October 2025, and Art. L. 236-1 from the day after publication. Other titles cover investment-service inducements, electricity aggregation, class actions and energy-efficiency duties for companies and public bodies.
text_version: JORF text: JORF n°0103 du 2 mai 2025 (NOR ECOM2415026L), as promulgated after CC decision n° 2025-879 DC of 29 April 2025; DILA JORF open data, JORFTEXT000051538879

title: LOI n° 2026-403 du 26 mai 2026 de simplification de la vie économique - article 35 (centres de données, projets d'intérêt national majeur)
summary_short: French omnibus simplification law (Loi n° 2026-403). Article 35 lets a decree qualify data centres as projets d'intérêt national majeur, lets permit authorities refuse data-centre building permits in water-stressed areas, and lets the energy minister ask the transmission operator to reserve grid capacity for electricity-intensive digital projects.
summary_long: Loi n° 2026-403 of 26 May 2026 is a broad simplification statute covering administration, business formalities, public procurement, commerce, insurance, health research and other areas. This annotation covers its AI-relevant provisions, which sit in Article 35 (Titre VII) and, for the data-protection regulator, Article 59. Article 35 I.3°b inserts a new paragraph I bis into Code de l'urbanisme L. 300-6-2: a data centre of particular importance for the digital or ecological transition or national sovereignty may be qualified by decree as a projet d'intérêt national majeur. The same paragraph allows the administrative authority to refuse a data-centre building permit where the territory faces structural water-resource tensions, and defines a data centre. Article 35 V allows the energy minister to ask the public transmission operator to reserve connection capacity for electricity-intensive industrial and digital projects, and allows the operator to charge an additional contribution to cover operating measures, with calculation principles subject to approval by the energy regulator (CRE). Article 35 IV is marked as declared unconstitutional by the Conseil constitutionnel decision cited in the text. Article 59 requires the CNIL to promote innovation in artificial intelligence when using its instruments and in its missions. The text gives no general sanction regime for these provisions.

title: Ordonnance n° 2021-1518 du 24 novembre 2021 complétant la transposition de la directive 2019/790 du Parlement européen et du Conseil du 17 avril 2019 sur le droit d'auteur et les droits voisins dans le marché unique numérique et modifiant les directives 96/9/CE et 2001/29/CE
summary_short: Ordinance 2021-1518 completes France's transposition of EU Directive 2019/790 by amending the Intellectual Property Code. It adds copyright exceptions for text and data mining, teaching illustration and unavailable works, extends collective licensing, and extends the regime to neighbouring and database rights. Published 25 November 2021 (JORF).
summary_long: The ordinance completes France's transposition of EU Directive 2019/790 by amending the Intellectual Property Code. It adds three exceptions: text and data mining (L. 122-5-3; copies of lawfully accessed works for scientific research by research bodies and heritage institutions, and for any purpose unless rightsholders have opted out appropriately; copies stored securely and destroyed after mining), teaching and vocational illustration (L. 122-5-4; flat-rate remuneration; excluded where adequate licences are offered), and unavailable works held by heritage institutions (L. 122-5-5; author opposition; notice to the EU Intellectual Property Office at least six months before publication). It creates extended collective licensing, under which ministerially approved collective management organisations may extend licences to non-members (L. 324-8-1 to L. 324-8-6, L. 137-2-1, L. 139-1, L. 134-3 to L. 134-7). It also adds a chapter on unavailable works (L. 138-1 to L. 138-5) with ministerial approval of organisations, opposition rights, and exclusions for sets of works principally first published outside the EU. Neighbouring rights (L. 211-3, L. 211-8) and database producers' rights (L. 342-3, L. 342-6) are brought into parts of the regime. Articles 10 and 13 set which exceptions the first paragraph of L. 331-8 and L. 331-28/L. 331-31 do not apply to, and which amended provisions apply under L. 811-1-1. Several chapters defer implementing conditions to Conseil d'État decrees. The text sets no fines or penalties of its own. Publication date is taken from the document header (JORF of 25 November 2021).
text_version: JORF text: JORF n°0274 du 25 novembre 2021 (NOR MICB2121839R); DILA JORF open data, JORFTEXT000044362034

title: Projet de loi portant diverses dispositions d'adaptation au droit de l'Union européenne en matière économique, financière, environnementale, énergétique, d'information, de transport, de santé, d'agriculture et de pêche (article 24 - systèmes d'intelligence artificielle)
summary_short: Article 24 of a French bill adapting national law to the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) makes AI systems subject to the regulation, designates national market-surveillance and notifying authorities across sectors, and sets their investigation, injunction and administrative-fine powers. Pending Senate-adopted text.
summary_long: Article 24 of a French bill adapting national law to the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) sets out how the regulation is applied and enforced nationally. The Senate-adopted text, pending in the Assemblée nationale, inserts a Title V bis into the 2004 digital economy law (Art. 55-1 to 55-6): AI systems are subject to the regulation, authorities may share information, agents may inspect and fine notified bodies in the toy sector, and fines follow the regulation's Art. 99 ceilings. Art. 24 bis authorises an ordinance, within six months of promulgation, on overseas adaptation and regulatory sandboxes. Art. 24 ter gives the Conseil d'État, Cour de cassation and Cour des comptes oversight of high-risk AI used in judicial functions. Further articles amend the environment, consumer, construction, defence, transport, public health, postal and electronic communications, monetary and financial, data protection (1978) and audiovisual (1986) laws, assigning market-surveillance, notification, certification and fine powers to the CNIL, Arcom, the health agency, the consumer authority, the transport minister, the radio-frequency agency and the financial supervisor. Authorities may order injunctions, suspension, withdrawal, recall and fines. The excerpt gives no entry-into-force date for Article 24.
text_version: Assemblée nationale n° 2518 (17e lég.), projet de loi adopté par le Sénat en première lecture le 18 février 2026 (Sénat T.A. n° 63, 2025-2026), transmitted 20 Feb 2026

title: Proposition de loi visant à encadrer l'intelligence artificielle par le droit d'auteur
summary_short: Proposed French bill (2023) amending the intellectual property code so that AI systems' integration and exploitation of protected works requires rights-holder authorisation, AI-generated works must be labelled and list author names, works of undetermined origin face a levy, and collective management bodies require ministerial approval.
summary_long: Private member's bill registered in the French National Assembly on 12 September 2023 and referred to the Culture and Education committee; the text is the bill as registered. Article 1 amends Article L. 131-3 of the Code de la propriété intellectuelle so that integration by AI software of protected works into its system, and their exploitation, is subject to the code's general rules and therefore to authorisation by authors or rights holders. Article 2 adds to Article L. 321-2: where a work is created by AI without direct human intervention, the rights holders are the authors or rights holders of the works used to design it; collective management of rights in AI-generated works may be carried out by collective management bodies; remuneration under Article L. 133-1 is collected by bodies approved by the minister in charge of culture, with approval weighed on membership diversity, managers' qualifications, collection means and fair representation; a Conseil d'État decree sets the conditions of grant and withdrawal. Article 3 requires the mention 'œuvre générée par IA' and the names of the authors of the works used on AI-generated works. Article 4 creates a levy on works produced by AI from works of undetermined origin, payable to the designated collective management body and imposed on the company operating the AI system; a Conseil d'État decree sets its rate and base. The text contains no penalty provisions and no entry-into-force date.

title: Proposition de loi relative à l'instauration d'une présomption d'utilisation des contenus culturels par les fournisseurs d'intelligence artificielle
summary_short: Proposed French statute adding Art. L. 331-4-1 to the Intellectual Property Code. In civil disputes, a protected work is presumed used by an AI model or system provider, unless proven otherwise, once an indicium makes that use plausible. Applies to pending proceedings at entry into force, subject to final judgments.
summary_long: Single-article bill (first reading, committee text, registered 2 June 2026). Paragraph I 1° inserts Art. L. 331-4-1 into the Intellectual Property Code: in any civil dispute, a work or protected subject matter under copyright or related rights is presumed, unless proven otherwise, to have been used by the provider of an AI model or system, once an indicium relating to the development or deployment of the system or to its generated output makes that use plausible. Paragraph I 2° replaces a reference to Law No. 2021-1382 in Art. L. 811-1-1 (1°) with a reference to the new law. Paragraph II makes the presumption in 1° applicable to proceedings pending at the date of entry into force, subject to decisions that have become final. The text sets no administrative authority, sanction or penalty.
text_version: Assemblée nationale texte de la commission des affaires culturelles n° 2864 (2 June 2026), first reading, on PPL adopted by the Senate (Sénat T.A. n° 85, AN n° 2634)

title: Proposition de loi visant à encadrer l'implantation des centres de données sur le territoire français
summary_short: Proposed French law (Senate-adopted at first reading) letting the government qualify data-centre projects as projets d'intérêt national majeur, with a local stakeholder committee and consultation steps, enabling grid-capacity reservation for energy-intensive projects, and requiring a government report within six months of promulgation.
summary_long: The bill, adopted by the Senate at first reading and transmitted to the Assemblée nationale on 26 March 2026, sets rules for data-centre siting in France. It lets the land-use master plan propose siting guidance (Art. 1) and lets the government qualify, by decree, data-centre projects of particular importance as projets d'intérêt national majeur (Art. 1 bis). Publication of such a decree requires a project committee organised by the project holder, with a presentation file sent at least one month before the first meeting, fifteen days for written observations and fifteen days for the holder's reply. The administrative authority may refuse a building permit for a data centre in an area with structural water-resource tensions. Further articles amend public-consultation rules and grid-connection derogations for such projects, and let the energy minister ask the transmission system operator to reserve connection capacity for electricity-intensive projects, subject to a possible additional connection contribution whose calculation principles the energy regulator approves. Articles 2 and 3, and Article 4 I, are deleted. Article 4 II requires a government report to Parliament within six months of promulgation on deployment conditions for data centres.
text_version: Assemblée nationale n° 2584 (26 March 2026), proposition de loi adoptée par le Sénat en première lecture le 25 mars 2026 (Sénat T.A. n° 73, 2025-2026)

title: Proposition de loi relative à l'instauration d'une présomption d'utilisation des contenus culturels par les fournisseurs d'intelligence artificielle
summary_short: Proposed French law adding Article L. 331-4-1 to the Intellectual Property Code: in civil disputes, a protected work is presumed used by an AI model or system provider once an indication makes that use plausible, unless disproved. Applies to pending cases from entry into force.
summary_long: The bill, adopted by the Senate at first reading (document dated 8 April 2026), would add Article L. 331-4-1 to the Intellectual Property Code. In any civil dispute, a work or protected object under copyright or a related right is presumed to have been used by the provider of an AI model or system, once an indication relating to the system's development or deployment, or to its output, makes that use plausible; the presumption can be rebutted by contrary proof. Article I.2° (new) updates a reference in Article L. 811-1-1 to the new law's title. Paragraph II applies the new presumption to proceedings pending on the date of entry into force, without reopening decisions that have become final. The text sets no thresholds, penalties or administrative enforcement, and does not define 'AI system' or 'model'.

title: Νόμος 5321/2026 - Μέτρα εφαρμογής του Κανονισμού (ΕΕ) 2024/1689 του Ευρωπαϊκού Κοινοβουλίου και του Συμβουλίου της 13ης Ιουνίου 2024 (Κανονισμός για την τεχνητή νοημοσύνη) - Τροποποίηση του ν. 4961/2022 (Α' 146) και άλλες διατάξεις
summary_short: Greek Law 5321/2026 sets national measures implementing the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689): designates market surveillance, notifying and single-contact authorities, creates an AI regulatory sandbox, a public-sector AI registry and an AI observatory, sets administrative sanctions, and criminalises removing deepfake labels. Takes effect on publication unless provisions say otherwise.
summary_long: Part A of Law 5321/2026 implements Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 in Greece. The Personal Data Protection Authority is designated market surveillance authority for prohibited practices, high-risk systems listed in Annex III and transparency duties under Article 50, and also acts as single point of contact. The Greek telecommunications regulator (EETT) is the notifying authority and hosts a coordination centre. A single complaints system is established. A regulatory sandbox is set up, and real-world testing of high-risk systems outside sandboxes requires prior written permission from the competent authority. Administrative measures include warnings, orders, reprimands and fines under Article 99 of the AI Regulation; periodic penalties against undertakings are capped at 2% of average daily worldwide turnover, and sanction decisions must be published. Public bodies must file a declaration before operating an AI system in a central register. Article 23 makes removing machine-readable marks on synthetic content, or the related disclosure, punishable by imprisonment and a fine where no heavier provision applies. Part B contains mostly unrelated provisions. Article 58 provides that the law enters into force on publication in the Government Gazette unless otherwise stated.
text_version: FEK A' 114/20.07.2026, Νόμος 5321/2026 as published (58 articles)

title: 2025. evi LXXV. torveny az Europai Unio mesterseges intelligenciarol szolo rendeletenek magyarorszagi vegrehajtasarol
summary_short: Hungarian implementing act for the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). Designates the notifying and market surveillance authorities, sets their powers and procedures and fine powers, creates the Hungarian AI Council and an AI regulatory sandbox. Most provisions take effect 31 days after promulgation; sec. 3(2) and sec. 10 from 2 August 2026.
summary_long: The Act provides the national framework for applying Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 in Hungary. Under sec. 3 the Government designates by decree a notifying authority and a market surveillance authority, and the market surveillance authority also operates the single point of contact. Sec. 4 governs the assessment, designation, notification and monitoring of conformity assessment bodies for high-risk AI systems, applying Act CXXXIII of 2009 with the stated deviations. Sec. 5 sets the market surveillance authority's general competence and its exclusive competence in certain proceedings, and sec. 5(4)-(5) provide for sector authorities' participation. Sec. 6 excludes summary proceedings and allows suspension in listed cases. Sec. 7 lists the authority's decision powers, including administrative fines, establishing unlawful use of an AI system and ordering cessation or restoration, and allows it to require data from providers and prospective providers and to carry out unannounced inspections and tests in real-world conditions. Sec. 8 establishes the Hungarian AI Council, a body without decision-making powers that issues recommendations and guidelines and coordinates national activities, and sec. 9 sets its membership and meeting rules. Sec. 10 requires the market surveillance authority to establish and operate an AI regulatory sandbox, with rules set by ministerial decree. Sec. 11 authorises the Government and the minister to issue implementing decrees. Sec. 12 sets entry into force 31 days after promulgation, with sec. 3(2) and sec. 10 applying from 2 August 2026.

title: Undang-Undang Nomor 27 Tahun 2022 tentang Pelindungan Data Pribadi (Law No. 27 of 2022 on Personal Data Protection)
summary_short: Indonesia's personal data protection law. Covers any person, public body and international organisation processing personal data in Indonesia, or affecting Indonesian data subjects abroad. Sets data subject rights, controller and processor duties, cross-border transfer conditions, breach notification, administrative sanctions and criminal penalties. In force on promulgation, 17 October 2022.
summary_long: Indonesia's personal data protection law, applying to individuals, corporations, public bodies and international organisations that process personal data in Indonesia, or outside Indonesia where the processing has legal effect in Indonesia or concerns Indonesian citizens (Art. 2). Distinguishes specific and general personal data (Art. 4). Grants data subject rights to information, correction, access, copies, deletion, withdrawal of consent, objection to decisions based solely on automated processing including profiling, and data portability (Arts. 5-13). Requires a lawful basis for processing, with explicit consent rules, special processing for children and persons with disabilities, impact assessments for high-risk processing (including automated decisions), security measures, record-keeping, a data protection officer in specified cases, and notice of failures of protection within 3 x 24 hours (Arts. 20-53). Restricts transfers abroad to jurisdictions with equal or higher protection, to binding safeguards, or with consent (Art. 56). Establishes an institution appointed by the President to supervise and impose sanctions (Arts. 58-60). Administrative sanctions include written warnings, temporary suspension of processing, deletion or destruction of data, and administrative fines of up to 2 percent of annual revenue (Art. 57). Criminal offences for unlawful collection, disclosure, use or falsification of personal data carry imprisonment of 4 to 6 years and fines up to Rp6 billion; corporate fines can reach ten times the maximum fine (Arts. 65-73). Controllers have two years from promulgation to comply (Art. 74).

title: Coimisiun na Mean - Online Safety Code (October 2024)
summary_short: Binding code made by Coimisiún na Meán under the Online Safety and Media Regulation Act 2022 for designated video-sharing platform services in Ireland. It requires restriction of harmful videos and commercial communications, age assurance, parental controls and complaint handling; Part B applies from a date the Commission sets.
summary_long: Code adopted under the Online Safety and Media Regulation Act 2022 and Article 28b of the Audiovisual Media Services Directive. Part A (sections 1 to 10) sets scope and general duties: it applies to video-sharing platform services designated under Irish jurisdiction, requires appropriate measures to protect children and the general public, and states that age verification based solely on self-declaration is not effective. Non-compliance is a contravention under Part 8B of the Act, and providers must maintain systems and controls to demonstrate compliance; the Commission considers size and nature of the service. Part B (sections 11 to 17), applying from a date set by the Commission, requires platforms' terms to restrict harmful video and commercial communications, adult-only content access controls and content rating, account suspension after prior warning, parental controls where users under 16 are permitted, reporting and flagging, complaint procedures, an annual media literacy action plan, a ban on commercial processing of children's personal data, and reports to the Commission every 3 months. The Code states no fine amounts.
text_version: Online Safety Code, publication date October 2024 (as adopted 10 Oct 2024)

title: CRU/2025/236 - Large Energy User Connection Policy - Decision Paper
summary_short: CRU decision, published 12 December 2025, directing Irish electricity system operators on grid connection of data centres. Data centres at or above 1 MVA must supply matching dispatchable or autoproducer generation, meet 80% of annual demand with Irish renewable electricity within a six-year glide path, and self-report annually.
summary_long: Decision paper CRU/2025/236 of the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU), published 12 December 2025, sets the connection policy for large electricity demand. It applies exclusively to data centres seeking connection to the electricity network and sets a de minimis level of 1 MVA below which its elements do not apply. Data centres at or above 1 MVA and below 10 MVA must provide an autoproducer unit in the Single Electricity Market meeting 100% of their maximum import capacity on a de-rated basis. Those at or above 10 MVA must provide separately connected dispatchable onsite or proximate generation or storage matching their capacity. Both must meet at least 80% of annual demand with renewable electricity generated in Ireland, with a six-year glide path from energisation. A connection cannot ramp up without the associated generation in place. Compliant data centres are not subject to Mandatory Demand Curtailment. System operators must publish locational information and a connection process by 31 March 2026, and data centres self-report annually. A Section 34 direction to the system operators supersedes CRU/21/124 for new applications; applications already in process continue under that direction. Gas connection rules are not changed. Non-compliance may lead to a reduction in the maximum import capacity.

title: CRU/21/124 - Direction to the System Operators related to Data Centre grid connection processing
summary_short: CRU Decision of 23 November 2021 directing EirGrid and ESB Networks to assess data centre grid connection applications against four criteria (location, onsite generation, demand flexibility), with applications terminating if no connection offer is consistent with system needs. Applies immediately to all applications except Connected or Contracted ones.
summary_long: This CRU Decision (CRU/21/124, published 23 November 2021) gives Directions under section 34(1) of the Electricity Regulation Act 1999 to the transmission system operator EirGrid and the distribution system operator ESB Networks. The system operators must assess applications for data centre grid connection against four assessment criteria: whether the applicant is in a constrained or unconstrained region of the electricity system; its ability to bring onsite dispatchable generation (and/or storage) equivalent to or greater than its demand; and its ability to provide demand flexibility by reducing consumption when requested, through onsite dispatchable generation or otherwise. The criteria are not ranked. Where a system operator is not satisfied that a connection offer can be made consistent with the needs of the electricity system, the application will not be processed further and terminates. The criteria apply to all data centre connection applications in Ireland, including those in process, with immediate effect; applications categorised as Connected or Contracted in Tables 1 and 2 are excluded. The system operators must provide bi-annual reports to the CRU, the first due 1 March 2022. The Decision considered and did not adopt a do-nothing option or a moratorium on data centre connections at this time.
text_version: CRU/21/124 Decision Paper (published 23 Nov 2021) plus the two formal Directions of 23 Nov 2021 (to EirGrid, ref D/21/25841, and to ESB Networks)

title: Data Protection Act 2018 (Number 7 of 2018)
summary_short: Establishes the Data Protection Commission and gives further effect in Ireland to the GDPR and the law-enforcement data Directive, setting national rules on children's data, automated decisions, special-category processing, law-enforcement processing and enforcement. Dated 24 May 2018; commencement by ministerial order.
summary_long: Number 7 of 2018 establishes the Data Protection Commission as supervisory authority (Part 2) and gives further effect to the GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) and to Directive (EU) 2016/680 on criminal-law processing (long title). Part 3 sets national rules within the GDPR: a child is a person under 18 (s.29); the consent age for information society services is 16 (s.31); processing a child's data for direct marketing, profiling or micro-targeting is an offence (s.30); solely automated decisions may be authorised by enactment with safeguards (s.57); and special-category processing and rights restrictions are permitted for listed purposes (ss.45-61). Part 4 deals with transfers from the 1988 Act. Part 5 sets duties for controllers and processors handling personal data for criminal-law purposes, including records, impact assessments and breach notification to the Commission (ss.69-88). Part 6 covers complaints, inquiries, corrective powers, administrative fines (s.141), offences (a maximum of EUR 50,000 on indictment under s.4(2)(b)) and judicial remedies. Parts 7 and 8 cover courts and amend other Acts. The Act comes into operation on days the Minister appoints (s.1(3)).

title: Online Safety and Media Regulation Act 2022 (Number 41 of 2022)
summary_short: Amends the Broadcasting Act 2009 and establishes Coimisiún na Meán to regulate broadcasting, on-demand audiovisual media and online safety content, with obligations on providers and administrative sanctions. Dated 10 December 2022.
summary_long: Amends the Broadcasting Act 2009 and establishes Coimisiún na Meán to regulate broadcasting, audiovisual on-demand media and certain online services. Part 2 changes definitions and the meaning of 'under the jurisdiction of the State' for media service providers, video-sharing platform services and other relevant online services. Part 3 establishes the Commission; Part 16 dissolves the Broadcasting Authority of Ireland and transfers its functions, staff, property and liabilities. Part 4 requires a register of audiovisual on-demand media providers. Part 5 imposes duties, codes and rules on media service providers and sound broadcasters; Parts 6 to 10 amend related Broadcasting Act provisions. Part 11 regulates content on relevant online services and harmful online content on designated online services. Part 12 provides investigations, sanctions and oral hearings, including administrative financial sanctions. Parts 13 and 14 cover a journalistic practices scheme and support for European works, funded partly by a levy. Part 17 amends other enactments, including the Referendum Act 1998 and the Electoral Reform Act 2022. Only the contents, long title and preamble were supplied; operative section text is not in the document.

title: Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Act 2026 (Number 31 of 2026)
summary_short: Establishes Oifig IS na hÉireann and Ireland's national framework for Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act): single point of contact, AI register, sandboxes, market surveillance, adjudication and administrative fines. Commencement by ministerial order.
summary_long: Establishes Oifig IS na hÉireann, a body corporate with a board and chief executive, to co-ordinate and supervise implementation of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 in Ireland. The Office is the single point of contact and keeps an AI register; it may create regulatory sandboxes by regulation and co-operate with foreign bodies (Parts 2 and 3). Providers may apply for real-world testing of high-risk AI systems, with review rights (Part 3). Market surveillance authorities may authorise derogations, obtain documents and source code, and receive complaints (Part 4). Authorised officers may enter premises, seize products and serve contravention, prohibition and removal notices, with District Court appeals (Part 5). Adjudicators find breaches after a notice of suspected non-compliance; administrative fines are capped by reference to the AI Regulation (€1,000,000 for public bodies) and take effect on High Court confirmation (Part 6). Offences carry fines or imprisonment of up to five years on indictment (Part 7). Part 8 applies fine powers to the Central Bank; Part 9 amends the Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2014 to add AI Regulation investigations.

title: European Union (Artificial Intelligence) (Designation) Regulations 2025 (S.I. No. 366 of 2025)
summary_short: Designates Irish bodies as national competent authorities, market surveillance authorities, notifying authorities and single point of contact under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). Made 25 July 2025 under the European Communities Act 1972; the Minister, Central Bank of Ireland, Data Protection Commission and others hold roles.
summary_long: Made 25 July 2025 by the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment under section 3 of the European Communities Act 1972 to give further effect to the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). Regulation 3 designates the Minister as a national competent authority under Article 70(1) and, through the Schedule, names market surveillance authorities as national competent authorities for specified points of Section A, Annex I, including the Health and Safety Authority, the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission, the Marine Survey Office, the Commission for Communications Regulation, the Commission for Railway Regulation and the Health Products Regulatory Authority. Regulation 4 designates the Central Bank of Ireland as market surveillance authority for Article 74(6) and the Data Protection Commission for Article 74(8). Regulation 5 designates notifying authorities under Article 28 for listed Annex I legislation: the Minister, the Minister for Transport, the Health Products Regulatory Authority and the Commission for Communications Regulation. Regulation 6 designates the Minister as single point of contact under Article 70(2). The Regulations set no obligations for private actors, no thresholds and no penalties.

title: Protection of Privacy Law, 5741-1981, as amended by Amendment No. 13 (5784-2024)
summary_short: Israel's Protection of Privacy Law 1981, as amended in 2024, binds controllers and processors of personal-information databases: purpose limits, registration, notice, access and correction, information security, data-protection officers and direct-mail rules. The Privacy Protection Authority enforces it via fines, orders, civil damages and criminal penalties.
summary_long: The Protection of Privacy Law 1981 (consolidated text with amendments marked 2024) makes privacy infringement a civil wrong (s.4) and a criminal offence (s.5, five years' imprisonment). For personal-information databases it sets purpose-limited processing (s.8), a registration duty for databases above 10,000 individuals in direct-marketing or sale activities and for public-body databases (s.8A), notice to persons asked for data (s.11), access and correction rights (ss.13-14), and security responsibility with regulations and tiered security levels (s.17, Schedule 3). It requires data-protection officers for public bodies and certain large or sensitive-data controllers (s.17B1), security officers for specified databases (s.17B), regulates direct mailing (ss.17D-17H), and restricts disclosure by public bodies (ss.23B-23D). The Privacy Protection Authority supervises through inspectors and external experts, may seek cease-violation orders and court injunctions, and imposes administrative fines (s.23K; base amount 150,000 new shekels, indexed). Courts may award statutory damages without proof of harm (ss.15A, 29A). Chapter 4A limits enforcement powers against parties and candidates during election periods.
text_version: Consolidated Hebrew text of the Protection of Privacy Law 5741-1981 incorporating amendments through Amendment No. 13 (Sefer HaChukim 5784 p. 1430), revision 3088217

title: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
summary_short: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 regulates processing of digital personal data by Data Fiduciaries, grants Data Principals rights, and establishes the Data Protection Board of India. It applies within India and to foreign processing linked to offering goods or services in India. Commencement is by Central Government notification.
summary_long: The Act governs processing of digital personal data within India, and of personal data collected in non-digital form and later digitised. It also applies to processing outside India connected with offering goods or services to Data Principals in India. Processing requires consent or a listed legitimate use, with notice to the Data Principal; personal data processed for personal or domestic purposes is excluded. Data Fiduciaries must take security safeguards, notify breaches, erase data when purposes end and provide a grievance mechanism; Data Principals hold rights of access, correction, erasure and nomination. Processing of children's data requires verifiable parental consent and bars tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children. The Central Government may designate Significant Data Fiduciaries, which must appoint a Data Protection Officer and independent data auditor and carry out periodic impact assessments and audits. The Central Government may restrict transfers of personal data to notified countries. The Data Protection Board of India can inquire into breaches, issue directions and impose monetary penalties under the Schedule, with appeals to the Appellate Tribunal. Provisions commence on dates notified by the Central Government.

title: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 (G.S.R. 846(E), 13 November 2025)
summary_short: Rules under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, published 13 November 2025, set how Data Fiduciaries must give notices, secure data, notify breaches, erase data and obtain verifiable parental consent. They also cover Consent Manager registration, Significant Data Fiduciary duties, State processing standards and Data Protection Board procedure, with staged commencement.
summary_long: Rules made under sections 40(1) and 40(2) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, published in the Gazette of India on 13 November 2025. Rules 1, 2 and 17 to 21 apply from publication; Rule 4 (Consent Managers) applies one year after publication; Rules 3, 5 to 16, 22 and 23 apply eighteen months after publication. Rule 3 sets content requirements for notices to Data Principals. Rule 4 and the First Schedule provide for Board registration of Consent Managers and their obligations. Rule 5 and the Second Schedule set standards for State processing for subsidies, benefits, licences and permits. Rule 6 requires reasonable security safeguards; Rule 7 requires breach notices to Data Principals and to the Board within seventy-two hours. Rule 8 and the Third Schedule set erasure periods for listed e-commerce, online gaming and social media intermediaries. Rules 10 and 11 require verifiable consent for children and guardian verification for persons with disability; Rule 12 and the Fourth Schedule list exempt classes. Rule 13 imposes periodic impact assessment and audit on Significant Data Fiduciaries and restricts transfer of specified data outside India. Rule 14 sets rights-request procedures and a ninety-day grievance period. Rule 15 allows transfers abroad subject to government requirements; Rule 16 exempts research, archiving and statistical processing. Rules 17 to 23 cover Board appointments, meetings, digital proceedings, appeals to the Appellate Tribunal and government information requests. The rules themselves state no penalty amounts.

title: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (G.S.R. 139(E), as amended 2022, 2023, 2025, 2026)
summary_short: Binding rules under the IT Act 2000, in force from Gazette publication, imposing due diligence, takedown and grievance duties on intermediaries, extra duties on significant social media and online real-money gaming intermediaries, labelling of synthetic content, and a Code of Ethics for digital publishers.
summary_long: The Rules, made under section 87(1) and clauses (z) and (zg) of section 87(2) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, set due diligence duties for intermediaries (rule 3), including takedown within three hours of actual knowledge, grievance handling within seven days, retention of removed information for 180 days, and technical measures and labelling for synthetically generated information (rule 3(3)). Significant social media intermediaries and online gaming intermediaries carry additional duties (rule 4), such as appointing a Chief Compliance Officer, monthly compliance reports, user declarations of synthetic content, and first-originator identification for messaging services. Online real-money games must be verified by designated online gaming self-regulatory bodies before they may be offered (rule 4A). Publishers of news and current affairs content and of online curated content must follow a Code of Ethics with age-based ratings, and are subject to a three-tier grievance and oversight structure with Ministry blocking directions (rules 13 to 16). Where an intermediary fails to observe the Rules, section 79(1) of the Act does not apply to it and it is liable for punishment under other laws (rule 7). Grievance Appellate Committees hear appeals (rule 3A).

title: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026 (G.S.R. 120(E), 10 February 2026) — synthetically generated information
summary_short: Indian IT Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code Rules, 2021, as updated 10.02.2026. Requires intermediaries offering generative tools to prevent unlawful synthetic content and label synthetically generated information, and requires intermediaries to remove unlawful information within three hours of actual knowledge.
summary_long: The Rules, as updated to 10.02.2026, set due-diligence duties for intermediaries (rule 3), additional duties for significant social media intermediaries (rule 4), and a Code of Ethics for news and current-affairs and online curated content publishers, with a three-tier grievance and oversight structure (Part III). The update adds 'synthetically generated information' (rule 2(1)(wa)). Intermediaries offering tools that create such content must deploy technical measures against unlawful outputs, such as child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery and false documents, and must label content and embed metadata. Significant social media intermediaries must require user declarations of synthetic content, verify them and label such content. Unlawful information must be removed within three hours of actual knowledge, given by court order or a reasoned authorised government intimation. Non-observance removes the section 79 protection and exposes the intermediary to punishment under other laws. Grievances must be resolved within set periods, and a Grievance Appellate Committee hears appeals. Online real-money games must be verified by designated self-regulatory bodies and are subject to identity, deposit and credit restrictions.

title: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law
summary_short: Council of Europe treaty requiring Parties to adopt or maintain measures so AI system lifecycle activities are consistent with human rights, democracy and the rule of law. Covers public authorities and, by declaration, private actors; excludes national security and defence. Opened for signature at Vilnius, 5 September 2024.
summary_long: Each Party must adopt or maintain measures so that activities within the lifecycle of AI systems are consistent with human rights, democracy and the rule of law, graduated by the severity and probability of adverse impacts (Arts. 1-2). Obligations cover public authorities and, via declarations, private actors (Art. 3(1)). Chapter II addresses human rights and democratic processes (Arts. 4-5). Chapter III covers human dignity, transparency and oversight, accountability, non-discrimination, privacy, reliability and controlled testing environments (Arts. 7-13). Chapter IV requires remedies, information allowing persons to contest decisions made or substantially informed by AI systems, complaint routes, procedural safeguards and notice of AI interaction (Arts. 14-15). Chapter V requires risk and impact management, including testing before first use, and an assessment of moratoria or bans on certain uses (Art. 16). Each Party establishes or designates oversight mechanisms (Art. 26) and reports within two years of becoming a Party (Art. 24). Excluded: national security activities, national defence and most pre-release R&D (Art. 3(2)-(4)). The text sets no fines or penalties; disputes between Parties go to negotiation or other peaceful means (Art. 29). Entry into force follows five signatories, including three member States, consenting to be bound, plus a three-month period (Art. 30(3)).

title: Decreto legislativo 9 settembre 2026, n. 160 (adeguamento della normativa nazionale al regolamento (UE) 2024/1689; schema AG 418)
summary_short: Legislative decree no. 160 of 9 September 2026 adapts Italian law to the EU AI Act for police use of AI systems and adds AI-related criminal and civil liability rules for AI systems. Police use is governed by its Title I, criminal and civil liability by its Title II.
summary_long: Legislative decree no. 160 of 9 September 2026 adapts Italian law to the EU AI Act for police use of AI systems and adds AI-related criminal and civil liability rules. Title I sets general principles and definitions (Arts 1-2), human review of automated results before use in acts affecting individuals (Art. 3), research collaborations (Art. 4), sandboxes (Art. 5) and training (Art. 6). Chapter III covers biometric uses: labelling and categorisation under conditions (Art. 7); real-time remote biometric identification authorised by a judge for up to fifteen days, with an impact assessment and notification to the Garante (Arts 8-9); post-hoc facial recognition with 48-hour judicial authorisation and a ban on untargeted use (Art. 10). Title II creates criminal offences for omitting safety or human-oversight measures for high-risk AI or altering such systems (Art. 12), allows judicial authorisation of biometric identification of suspects (Art. 13), sets entity sanctions under Decree 231 (Art. 15), and provides civil jurisdiction rules, court-ordered disclosure of evidence (Art. 17), a presumption of causation for AI Act breaches (Art. 18) and direct action against liability insurers (Art. 20). Police AI systems in use at entry into force must be made compliant within one year (Art. 21).
text_version: Decreto Legislativo 9 settembre 2026, n. 160 (GU Serie Generale n. 214 del 15-09-2026, codice redazionale 26G00179), testo originario as published; in force 30-09-2026; 22 articles

title: Decreto legislativo 7 ottobre 2026, n. 179 (adeguamento della normativa nazionale al regolamento (UE) 2024/1689; schema AG 421)
summary_short: Italian legislative decree adapting national law to the EU AI Act: names national AI and market-surveillance authorities (AgID, ACN, Banca d'Italia, CONSOB, IVASS, Garante), sets their powers and fines, creates an AI regulatory sandbox, and adds AI rules on training, employment, health and trade secrets. Dated 7 October 2026.
summary_long: Legislative decree No. 179 of 7 October 2026 adapts Italian law to the EU AI Act and to Law 132/2025 on AI. It names AgID as notifying authority and ACN as AI authority and single point of contact, and designates ACN, Banca d'Italia, CONSOB, IVASS and the Garante as market-surveillance authorities for their sectors. ACN keeps a national register of certain high-risk systems and holds inspection powers. Fines for AI Act breaches reach EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide turnover at the top tier, and warnings are possible for minor breaches. An Italian AI regulatory sandbox, run jointly by AgID and ACN, is created. Chapter III provides for AI training and literacy measures in education, professions, justice, health and public administration. Employers may not take employment decisions solely on automated processing and must inform workers; non-compliant decisions are void. Article 52 amends Article 98 of the Industrial Property Code so that AI training data and algorithms can qualify as protected trade secrets when Article 98(1) conditions are met. The text states no separate entry-into-force date beyond its adoption date. Implementation must not create new public charges (Art. 54).
text_version: Decreto Legislativo 7 ottobre 2026, n. 179 (GU Serie Generale n. 234 del 08-10-2026, codice redazionale 26G00200), testo originario as published; enters into force 23-10-2026; 54 articles

title: AGCOM Delibera n. 96/25/CONS - Modalita tecniche e di processo per l'accertamento della maggiore eta degli utenti (art. 13-bis DL 123/2023)
summary_short: AGCOM Resolution 96/25/CONS sets technical and process requirements for age verification that websites and video-sharing platforms distributing pornographic content in Italy must adopt. Access must be withheld until age is verified, using data-minimising third-party proofs, and it covers Italian and listed foreign providers.
summary_long: AGCOM Resolution 96/25/CONS, adopted under Art. 13-bis of Decree-Law 123/2023, sets technical and process requirements for age assurance that operators of websites and video-sharing platforms distributing pornographic content in Italy must adopt. It applies to listed operators, whether established in Italy or in another Member State. The requirements, which are technology-neutral, cover proportionality, data protection (no profiling, no biometric identification, no identity data collected by the site), independent third-party age-proof providers under a double-anonymity model, security and anti-circumvention, performance and accuracy (self-declaration is not considered effective), re-verification for each access session, accessibility, non-discrimination in training data, user information and complaint handling. Operators must have compliant systems within six months of publication; the provisions for foreign-established operators apply three months after the list is published. The Authority will monitor systems in real operation, cooperate with other Member States, and may revise the resolution in line with European Commission guidelines under Art. 28 of Regulation 2022/2065. The text notes that the SPID public identity system, as analysed, does not fully meet the double-anonymity requirement. Penalties are not set out in this text.

title: Delega al Governo per l'organizzazione, la realizzazione, lo sviluppo e il potenziamento dei centri di elaborazione dati (testo unificato C. 1928-A/R)
summary_short: Italian bill (unified text C. 1928-A/R, pending in the Chamber of Deputies) delegating to the Government the power to adopt legislative decrees on data centres: construction permitting, grid access, energy, security, tax and cloud oversight, within six months of entry into force.
summary_long: The bill (unified text C. 1928-A/R, pending in the Chamber of Deputies) delegates to the Government the power to adopt one or more legislative decrees on data centres (centri di elaborazione dati) within six months of entry into force (Art. 3(1)). Art. 2 defines a data centre as the physical structure and technological infrastructure for designing, producing, developing and implementing IT applications and services and for storing, processing and managing the associated data. The delegated principles cover simplified, time-limited authorisation for construction, expansion and refurbishment; a dedicated ATECO code; single procedures; qualification of such projects as works of prevailing public interest with simplified environmental assessment (VIA) and integrated environmental authorisation (AIA); urban-planning simplification; priority grid access; on-site energy self-production and storage; national rules on diesel backup generator emissions; physical and cyber security; priority for reusing existing facilities with environmental efficiency; and tax harmonisation on permanent-establishment status. They also cover digital-skills training and expand the powers of the Autorità per le garanzie nelle comunicazioni over cloud services. Draft decrees need parliamentary opinions (Art. 3(3)) and new public charges are barred unless funded (Art. 3(4)-(5)). No penalty regime is stated.
text_version: Camera stampato N. 1928-2083-2091-2152-2194-A/R (testo unificato della IX Commissione after rinvio in commissione, with committee opinions), i.e. the text taken to the floor on 24 Feb 2026

title: Decreto-legge 15 settembre 2023, n. 123 (Decreto Caivano), convertito con modificazioni dalla legge 13 novembre 2023, n. 159 - art. 13-bis (verifica della maggiore eta per l'accesso a siti pornografici)
summary_short: Italian decree-law of 15 September 2023 (Caivano), in force 16 September 2023, on youth distress, educational poverty and juvenile crime. Fetched text covers Articles 1–10-sexies: a commissioner and EUR 30 million plan for Caivano, funding and hiring measures. Digital-minors provisions (Chapter IV) are not in the fetched text.
summary_long: Decree-law on urgent measures against youth distress, educational poverty and juvenile crime, and on minors' safety in the digital environment. The fetched text (Articles 1–10-sexies) provides for a Commissioner appointed by decree of the Prime Minister within fifteen days of entry into force to prepare and implement an extraordinary infrastructure plan for the municipality of Caivano. The plan is approved by Council of Ministers resolution, with resources up to EUR 30 million from the Fondo per lo sviluppo e la coesione, and implementation may depart from non-criminal laws, subject to anti-mafia rules, general legal principles and EU constraints. The Commissioner's term runs to 31 December 2027 (Art. 3). Further articles cover works at the former Delphinia sports centre, university-funded educational projects, at least EUR 100,000 for video surveillance in Caivano for 2024, and authorised hiring of 15 municipal police officers, 3 social-service staff and 6 school educators, with budget coverage. Article 10-sexies assigns the Minister for the family a promotion role for anti-violence services in Caivano. The fetched text contains no penalties, enforcement provisions or AI-specific provisions. The digital-minors provisions of Chapter IV are not included in it.

title: Decreto legislativo 8 novembre 2021, n. 177 - Attuazione della direttiva (UE) 2019/790 del Parlamento europeo e del Consiglio, del 17 aprile 2019, sul diritto d'autore e sui diritti connessi nel mercato unico digitale e che modifica le direttive 96/9/CE e 2001/29/CE
summary_short: Italian decree implementing EU Directive 2019/790 on copyright in the Digital Single Market by amending Law 633/1941. It adds text-and-data-mining exceptions, press publisher rights, and liability and licensing rules for online content-sharing services, from 12 December 2021.
summary_long: Legislative Decree 177/2021 implements Directive (EU) 2019/790 by amending Law 633/1941; the text provided contains only Art. 1 of the decree. It adds a press publisher right for online use of journalistic publications by information society service providers, with fair remuneration set by a regulation of the Communications Authority (AGCOM) if the parties do not agree (Art. 43-bis). It adds exceptions for educational use (Art. 70-bis), research text and data extraction (Art. 70-ter), and a general text and data extraction exception that rights holders may expressly reserve (Art. 70-quater). It sets a liability regime for online content-sharing service providers, with a separate regime for services under three years old with turnover below 10 million euro (Arts 102-sexies to 102-decies), and a licensing scheme for out-of-commerce works held by cultural heritage institutions (Arts 102-undecies to 102-septiesdecies). It sets transparency duties towards authors and performers, with AGCOM dispute resolution and administrative fines of up to 1% of turnover (Arts 110-ter to 110-sexies); those duties apply from 7 June 2022. The document header lists entry into force on 12 December 2021.

title: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali - Ordinanza ingiunzione nei confronti di Clearview AI - 10 febbraio 2022 [doc. web n. 9751362]
summary_short: Italian data protection authority (Garante) decision of 10 February 2022 finding that US company Clearview AI unlawfully processed personal data, including biometric data, of persons in Italy. It orders a ban on further scraping and processing, deletion of data, designation of an EU representative, and a €20 million fine.
summary_long: The Italian data protection authority (Garante) decision of 10 February 2022 finds that Clearview AI Inc., a US company with no EU establishment, unlawfully processed personal data, including biometric data, of persons in Italy through web scraping of publicly available images and a facial-recognition search service. It holds that the GDPR applies under Article 3(2) and finds breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), (b) and (e), 6, 9, 12, 13, 14, 15 and 27; no breach of Article 22 is found. Operative orders: a prohibition on further web scraping of images and metadata of persons in Italy and on further processing of such data (Art. 58(2)(f)); deletion of that data (Art. 58(2)(g)); designation of a representative in the EU within 30 days (Art. 58(2)(d)); and a report on measures taken within 30 days. The Garante imposes an administrative fine of EUR 20 million under Article 83(5) and orders publication of the decision on its website. The decision notes the company may settle by complying and paying half the fine within 60 days; judicial opposition is available within 30 days.

title: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali - Provvedimento dell'11 aprile 2023 [doc. web n. 9874702] - ChatGPT: misure richieste a OpenAI
summary_short: Italian data protection authority (Garante) decision of 11 April 2023 ordering OpenAI L.L.C., controller of ChatGPT, to implement nine measures for people connecting from Italy: information notices, objection and erasure tools, a legal-basis change and age verification. Suspends the earlier processing limitation once measures 1 to 7 are met.
summary_long: Decision of 11 April 2023 of the Italian data protection authority (Garante) under GDPR Art. 58(2)(d), addressed to OpenAI L.L.C. as controller of personal data processed through ChatGPT. Points 1 to 9 require: a publicly posted information notice for data subjects whose data were used to train algorithms, whether or not they are users; objection, rectification or erasure tools for people connecting from Italy; a link to the user information notice in the registration flow, viewed by Italian users including registered ones; a change of the legal basis for training on users' data, removing contract and relying on consent or legitimate interest; an age gate for Italian users at reactivation; a plan by 31 May 2023 for age verification excluding under-13s and minors without parental consent, to start by 30 September 2023; and an information campaign by 15 May 2023. Measures 1 to 7 must be complied with by 30 April 2023. On compliance, the decision suspends the temporary limitation on processing adopted on 30 March 2023. The decision is without prejudice to further measures after the ongoing fact-finding and to action for infringements. The controller must report on steps taken. Failure to respond to Art. 58 requests carries the fine under Art. 83(5)(e) GDPR. Appeal lies to the ordinary court within thirty days of notification, or sixty days if the appellant resides abroad.

title: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali - Provvedimento del 30 marzo 2023 [doc. web n. 9870832] - Limitazione provvisoria del trattamento nei confronti di OpenAI L.L.C.
summary_short: Urgent order of Italy's data protection authority imposing on OpenAI an immediate temporary limitation on processing personal data of people in Italy through ChatGPT, and requiring OpenAI to report its remedial measures within 20 days.
summary_long: Acting under GDPR Article 58(2)(f), the Garante found that ChatGPT provided no information notice to users or data subjects, lacked a legal basis for collecting and processing personal data to train its algorithms, processed inaccurate data, and had no age verification although OpenAI's terms reserve the service to users aged 13 or older. It considered these breaches of GDPR Articles 5, 6, 8, 13 and 25. It ordered, with immediate effect from receipt, a provisional limitation of the processing of personal data of data subjects established in Italy, pending its investigation. OpenAI was asked to report within 20 days the measures taken and any justification. Non-compliance is subject to the criminal penalty in Article 170 of the Italian Privacy Code and to GDPR Article 83(5)(e) administrative fines. The order can be appealed to the ordinary courts within 30 days, or 60 for residents abroad.

title: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali - Provvedimento del 2 novembre 2024 [doc. web n. 10085455] - Sanzione a OpenAI (ChatGPT)
summary_short: Italian data protection authority decision of 2 November 2024 fining OpenAI OpCo LLC €15,000,000 for GDPR breaches in its ChatGPT service (conduct from 30 November 2022 to 30 March 2023). It also orders a six-month information campaign and transmits part of the file to the Irish authority.
summary_long: Decision no. 755 of 2 November 2024 by the Italian data protection authority (Garante) under the GDPR, addressed to OpenAI OpCo LLC over its ChatGPT service. The proceeding followed a 20 March 2023 data breach and an urgent provisional limitation of processing of data of persons in Italy (order 112/2023, 30 March 2023). Order 114/2023 (11 April 2023) suspended that limitation on conditions covering an information notice, opt-out and rectification tools, an age gate, an age verification plan and a public information campaign. The decision finds breaches of: notification of the breach to the authority (Art. 33); the accountability principle and the lawful-basis requirement for training data (Arts. 5(2), 6), for conduct from 30 November 2022; transparency duties (Arts. 5(1)(a), 12, 13); protection of minors through age verification (Arts. 24, 25(1)); and non-compliance with an order (Art. 83(5)(e)). The accuracy principle (Art. 5(1)(d)) was not sanctioned and the file was sent to the Irish authority. Fines total €9,000,000, €320,000 and €5,680,000 across three groupings. The accessory measure is a six-month institutional communication campaign on Italian media with content approved by the Garante. The operative part lists Art. 32, while the reasoning finds a breach of Art. 33.
text_version: Provvedimento n. 755 del 2 novembre 2024 [doc. web n. 10085455], as published on garanteprivacy.it (Wayback snapshot 23 Dec 2024)

title: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali - Provvedimento del 30 gennaio 2025 [doc. web n. 10097450] - Limitazione d'urgenza del trattamento nei confronti di Hangzhou DeepSeek / Beijing DeepSeek
summary_short: Italian data protection authority (Garante) order of 30 January 2025 declaring unlawful the processing of personal data by Hangzhou DeepSeek and Beijing DeepSeek. It orders a definitive limitation of processing of data subjects located in Italy, effective immediately on receipt of the order.
summary_long: The Garante per la protezione dei dati personali adopted this decision on 30 January 2025 concerning the DeepSeek service, which two Chinese companies run through app, website and software. The recitals record that the companies stated they had not entered and did not plan to enter the Italian market and had removed the app from local app stores. The Garante found the app no longer available in Apple and Google app stores, the website still accessible with registration limited, and existing registered users still able to log in. It applies GDPR Article 3(2)(a) because the companies offer the service to data subjects in Italy. The findings cite unanswered information requests (Art. 31), an English-only privacy policy not fully meeting Arts. 12-14, unspecified lawful bases (Art. 6), deficiencies affecting the exercise of rights (Chapter III), storage in the People's Republic of China (Art. 32), and no designated representative (Art. 27). The operative part declares the processing unlawful, orders a definitive limitation of processing of data subjects in Italy under Art. 58(2)(f) GDPR with immediate effect on receipt, and reserves further determinations pending the investigation. It orders recording in the Garante's internal register. The decision recalls that non-compliance may trigger the criminal penalty in Art. 170 of the Code and administrative fines under Art. 83(5)(e) GDPR. Appeal lies to the ordinary court within thirty days of communication, or sixty days if the applicant resides abroad.
text_version: Provvedimento del 30 gennaio 2025, Registro dei provvedimenti n. 33 [doc. web n. 10098477], Italian text followed by official English version

title: Legge 23 settembre 2025, n. 132 - Disposizioni e deleghe al Governo in materia di intelligenza artificiale
summary_short: Italian AI framework law, applied in line with the EU AI Act: principles for AI research, development and use; sectoral rules (health, work, professions, public administration, justice); AgID and ACN as national AI authorities; delegations to the Government; AI-related offences and copyright rules. In force from 10 October 2025.
summary_long: Law 132/2025 sets principles for the research, development and use of AI systems and models, to be applied in conformity with Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, and states that it creates no obligations beyond that Regulation for AI systems and general-purpose models. Intelligence, defence and national-security cyber activities are excluded. Access to AI by children under 14 requires parental consent. Patients must be informed of AI use and clinical decisions stay with physicians. Research processing of health data for AI is of significant public interest; secondary use of de-identified data is allowed after notice to the Garante. Employers must inform workers; professionals must inform clients and use AI only in support. Officials and magistrates keep decisions. AgID (notifying authority) and ACN (market surveillance, inspections, sanctions) are the national AI authorities; Banca d'Italia, CONSOB and IVASS keep market-surveillance roles. The Government is delegated to adopt decrees within 12 months on AI training data, on adapting national law to the AI Act, including its sanctions, and on unlawful AI uses. The law adds an AI aggravating circumstance and a deepfake offence, limits copyright to human works, permits text and data mining under existing exceptions, and authorises up to EUR 1 billion of venture-capital investment.
text_version: consolidated (vigente) as of 2026-10-11; Normattiva last update to the act published 26/06/2026; amended passages marked (( )) by Normattiva

title: 特定高度情報通信技術活用システムの開発供給及び導入の促進に関する法律 (Act on Promotion of Development, Supply and Introduction of Specified Advanced Information and Communication Technology Utilization Systems; Act No. 37 of 2020, as amended for semiconductor production facilities)
summary_short: Promotes development, supply and introduction of specified advanced ICT systems and production of specified semiconductors in Japan. The competent minister certifies enterprise plans; the Japan Finance Corporation, designated banks and NEDO support certified projects through loans, guarantees and subsidies. Enacted as Act No. 37 of 2020.
summary_long: Promotes the development, supply and introduction of specified advanced information and communication technology utilization systems, such as wireless and switching equipment and inspection drones used for national, local government and critical infrastructure work, and the construction and operation of production facilities for specified semiconductors. Article 3 sets basic principles and Article 6 requires competent ministers to issue guidelines. Enterprises may submit development, supply, introduction and semiconductor facility plans for certification (Arts. 7, 9, 11). Certified plans may be changed only with approval, and certification may be revoked or changes ordered for non-implementation or non-conformity (Arts. 8, 10, 12). Certified projects may obtain loans from the Japan Finance Corporation through designated financial institutions (Arts. 13-18), special rules for SME investment and credit insurance (Arts. 25-27), and NEDO grants and interest subsidies for semiconductor facilities (Art. 29). Designated institutions must keep books, report and accept supervision (Arts. 19-22). Violations of reporting, bookkeeping and inspection duties are punishable by fines of up to 300,000 yen (Art. 37). Certain officers of the Corporation face a non-penal fine of up to 1,000,000 yen for acting without required approval (Art. 38). A review clause calls for evaluation three years after enforcement.
text_version: current consolidated text on e-Gov as of 2026-10-14 (latest revision listed: enforcement 2025-04-01, by Act No. 13 of 2025)

title: 個人情報の保護に関する法律 (Act on the Protection of Personal Information; Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended)
summary_short: Japan's Act on the Protection of Personal Information regulates how personal information business operators, pseudonymized and anonymized information handlers and administrative organs handle personal data. It sets purpose limits, security, third-party and cross-border transfer rules, individual rights, and criminal penalties, and creates the Personal Information Protection Commission.
summary_long: The Act defines personal information and related categories (pseudonymously processed, anonymously processed and personal-related information) and sets basic principles and duties of the national and local governments, including a cabinet-approved basic policy. Chapter 4 imposes duties on personal information handling business operators: purpose specification and use limits, proper acquisition, notice of purposes, accuracy, security measures, supervision of employees and contractors, breach reporting, limits on third-party provision and transfers to foreign third parties, record-keeping, and rules for pseudonymized and anonymized information; accredited protection organizations are also provided for. Chapter 5 applies parallel duties to administrative organs, including registration of personal information files and rights to request disclosure, correction and suspension of use. Chapter 6 establishes the Personal Information Protection Commission, empowered to give guidance, require reports, inspect premises, and issue recommendations and orders. Chapter 8 sets criminal penalties, including up to one year's imprisonment or a 1 million yen fine for violating a Commission order, and corporate fines up to 100 million yen for certain violations. Article 171 extends the Act to foreign handling connected with goods or services offered to persons in Japan. The text includes supplementary provisions from Act No. 37 of 2021, whose provisions take effect on dates set out in that Act, including 1 September 2021.
text_version: current consolidated text on e-Gov as of 2026-10-14 (latest revision listed: enforcement 2026-10-01, by Act No. 70 of 2025)

title: 著作権法（昭和四十五年法律第四十八号）
summary_short: Japan's Copyright Act (1970) sets authors' and related rights in works, performances, records, broadcasts and wired broadcasts, with exceptions for private copying, information analysis, quotation and education, compulsory licensing with government approval, and compensation payments.
summary_long: The Act defines works (Art. 2) and sets authors' moral rights (Arts. 18-20) and economic rights of reproduction, performance, public transmission, distribution and translation (Arts. 21-28). It sets rights of performers, record producers, broadcasters and wired broadcasters (Arts. 89-100). Exceptions include private-use reproduction, with compensation duties on specified digital recording devices and media (Art. 30(3)), use for purposes not involving enjoyment of expression, including technology development and information analysis (Art. 30-4), library reproduction and transmission (Art. 31), quotation (Art. 32), school use (Arts. 33-35) and non-commercial performance (Art. 38). Certain uses require a licence or ruling from the Commissioner for Cultural Affairs, with deposits or compensation (Arts. 67-69), and compensation disputes go to court (Art. 72). Unauthorised copies made for other purposes are deemed reproductions (Art. 49). Protection depends on nationality or first publication in Japan or treaty membership (Art. 6). Terms run for 70 years after death or publication, with separate rules for related rights (Arts. 51-54, 101). The text provided is partial and covers Chapters 1 to 5 up to Art. 104-11.
text_version: current consolidated text on e-Gov as of 2026-10-14

title: 経済施策を一体的に講ずることによる安全保障の確保の推進に関する法律 (Act on the Promotion of Ensuring National Security through Integrated Implementation of Economic Measures; Act No. 43 of 2022)
summary_short: Japanese statute on ensuring national security through integrated economic measures. Sets a basic policy and creates regimes for supply security of designated critical goods, notification and review of equipment in designated social infrastructure, support for critical technology R&D, and non-disclosure of sensitive patent applications, in stages by Cabinet Order.
summary_long: The Act (Act No. 43 of 2022) sets a framework for national security through economic measures. It requires a basic policy (Art. 2) and a public-private council (Art. 3-2). Cabinet Order may designate specified critical goods (Art. 7); certified supply-security plans may receive financing and subsidies (Arts. 9, 13-34). Ministers may designate specified social infrastructure operators, such as electricity, gas, water, rail, ports, telecommunications and finance (Art. 50). Such operators must notify before introducing or outsourcing maintenance of specified critical equipment; a 30-day waiting period applies and ministers may recommend changes or order a halt (Art. 52). The Act also supports R&D in specified critical technologies (Arts. 60-63), requires secrecy review of certain patent applications and restricts their disclosure and foreign filing (Arts. 66-78), and supports specified overseas businesses (Arts. 85-2 to 85-10).
