Sets controller and processor duties (registration and audits for major data processors, DPOs, lawful bases, consent, DPIAs, 72-hour breach notice, data subject rights) and cross-border transfer rules, applying from issuance, including safeguards for AI and other emerging technologies.
summary_long: The General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID) 2025 of the Nigeria Data Protection Commission issues binding guidance under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023. From its issuance, the NDPR 2019 ceases to apply as a legal instrument for data privacy (Art. 3(3)). It covers processing of personal data of data subjects in Nigeria, including by controllers not domiciled there (Art. 1). Main provisions: compliance measures for controllers and processors (Art. 7); designation of major-importance controllers and processors in UHL, EHL and OHL tiers, with registration and annual compliance audit returns (Arts. 8-10, Schedule 7); DPO designation and duties (Arts. 11-14); principles and lawful bases, including consent and cookie consent (Arts. 15-26); information to data subjects (Art. 27); mandatory DPIAs in listed circumstances (Art. 28); security schedules and 72-hour breach notification (Arts. 29, 33); processing agreements (Art. 34); data subject rights (Arts. 36-38); complaints and investigations (Art. 39); ethics, and emerging technologies including AI (Arts. 41-44); cross-border transfers (Art. 45, Schedule 5); capacity building (Art. 46); and fees and filing charges (Schedules 7, 10). Exemptions and legal-obligation grounds are addressed in Arts. 5 and 22. Enforcement includes Commission remedial directions and temporary orders (Art. 39(12)-(13)) and an administrative penalty of 50% of the filing fee for late filing (Art. 10(9)).

title: Nigeria Data Protection Act, 2023
summary_short: Regulates personal data processing by controllers and processors operating in Nigeria, and foreign ones processing data of data subjects in Nigeria. Establishes the Nigeria Data Protection Commission; sets processing principles, consent and data subject rights (including on automated decisions), transfer limits, breach notification and penalties. Applies from commencement.
summary_long: The Act applies to personal data processing by controllers and processors operating in Nigeria, processing within Nigeria, and foreign ones processing data of data subjects in Nigeria; purely personal or household processing is exempt. It establishes the Nigeria Data Protection Commission and its Governing Council. It sets processing principles, lawful bases, consent rules (including parental consent for children), sensitive personal data limits, data privacy impact assessments, Data Protection Officers for controllers of major importance, security duties and breach notification to the Commission within 72 hours. Data subjects have rights of access, correction, erasure, objection and consent withdrawal, and a right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects. Cross-border transfers require adequacy or listed alternative bases. Controllers and processors of major importance must register. The Commission investigates complaints and issues compliance and enforcement orders; administrative penalties are capped at the greater of N10,000,000 or 2% of annual gross revenue for major importance, and N2,000,000 or 2% otherwise. Non-compliance with orders is an offence with fines or up to one year's imprisonment. Data subjects may claim civil damages.

title: Besluit van de Autoriteit Consument en Markt van 12 april 2024, kenmerk ACM/UIT/605893 tot wijziging van de voorwaarden als bedoeld in artikel 31, eerste lid, onder a, juncto artikel 32, tweede lid, van de Elektriciteitswet 1998 betreffende de prioriteringsruimte bij transportverzoeken
summary_short: ACM decision amending the Dutch electricity Netcode, effective 1 October 2024, so that grid operators give transport-capacity priority in congestion areas to listed parties (congestion mitigators, safety functions and basic-needs providers) instead of first come, first served, subject to declarations and documents.
summary_long: The ACM decision of 12 April 2024 amends the Netcode elektriciteit under the Elektriciteitswet 1998 by adding Articles 7.0a to 7.0d and Annex 22. In congestion areas, grid operators must allocate transport capacity by priority category instead of first come, first served. Category 1 covers congestion mitigators that have a contract with the operator. Category 2 covers listed safety functions (fire services, ambulance posts, police, armed forces, intelligence services, NCTV, courts, prisons, water management and acute healthcare). Category 3 covers basic needs (public drinking water, compulsory education, housing up to 3x35A, heat and gas networks). Categories 2 and 3 apply to offtake only. Applicants must submit a board declaration and documents such as a recent Chamber of Commerce extract. Operators check complete requests within twenty working days, may suspend prioritisation in agreement with the ACM when more than 25% of requests in a quarter are priority requests, withdraw capacity for breach or fraud, and report annually by 31 March. The decision takes effect on 1 October 2024, and the ACM plans an evaluation within two years.](truncated)

title: Gemeente Haarlemmermeer - Voorbereidingsbesluit Datacenters (raadsbesluit 11 juli 2019, Gemeenteblad 2019, 181101)
summary_short: Municipal moratorium (voorbereidingsbesluit) adopted by Haarlemmermeer council on 11 July 2019, in force from the day after adoption for one year. Across the whole municipality it holds data-centre building permit applications and prohibits changing land or building use while a new zoning plan is prepared.
summary_long: The Haarlemmermeer municipal council decided on 11 July 2019 to declare a preparatory decision (voorbereidingsbesluit) for the entire municipal territory, as shown on the attached map, and a new zoning plan (bestemmingsplan) is to be prepared. The decision took effect the day after the council adopted it and applies for one year. Its stated purpose is to put the existing situation regarding data centres 'on hold' pending future data-centre policy. Under the Wet algemene bepaling omgevingsrecht, building permit applications for the activity 'bouwen' must be held, and the council prohibited changing the use of land and/or buildings. The text says the same measure was adopted by Amsterdam on the same date, as most data-centre establishment and new applications occur in those two municipalities. The decision and map can be consulted on the ruimtelijkeplannen.nl and municipal websites and at the town hall in Hoofddorp. The text states that no objection or appeal is possible against the decision. No penalties, exemptions or numeric thresholds are stated.
text_version: Gemeenteblad 2019, 181101 (22 July 2019): kennisgeving (publication notice) of raadsbesluit 11 July 2019 no. 2019.0032954

title: Rechtbank Den Haag, 5 februari 2020, ECLI:NL:RBDHA:2020:865 (SyRI)
summary_short: Dutch district court judgment (5 February 2020) in a suit by civil-society plaintiffs against the State. Declares Wet SUWI art. 65 and Besluit SUWI chapter 5a, governing the SyRI data-linking and risk-report system, unenforceable toward the admitted plaintiffs as contrary to ECHR Art. 8(2).
summary_long: Judgment of the Hague District Court of 5 February 2020 in a case brought by four collective interest organisations (NJCM, Platform Bescherming Burgerrechten, Privacy First, Koepel van DBC-Vrije Praktijken), with FNV intervening, against the Dutch State. The case concerns SyRI (Systeem Risico Indicatie), a government mechanism in Wet SUWI art. 64-65 and Besluit SUWI chapter 5a, in force from 1 January 2014, under which designated public bodies link datasets in a secure environment to generate risk reports on possible social-security, tax and labour-law fraud. The court found that art. 65 Wet SUWI and chapter 5a Besluit SUWI violate ECHR Art. 8(2) for insufficient safeguards, citing limited transparency about risk indicators and the risk model, no integral prior necessity review, data-minimisation concerns and no duty to notify data subjects. It held that art. 64 Wet SUWI on its own does not violate Art. 8(2). It declared them unenforceable toward the admitted plaintiffs and those whose interests they represent. The Landelijke Cliëntenraad and two individual plaintiffs were declared inadmissible. Claims for disclosure of risk models and for destruction of data were rejected, and the data-processor claim was not reached. The State was ordered to pay costs of EUR 3,250.51.
text_version: Judgment of 5 February 2020 (published 4 Feb 2020 per metadata; record modified 2025-03-21), Rechtspraak open data XML

title: Besluit van 20 december 2023 tot wijziging van het Besluit kwaliteit leefomgeving in verband met een instructieregel voor hyperscale datacentra (Stb. 2023, 492)
summary_short: Amends the Besluit kwaliteit leefomgeving from 1 January 2024 to define hyperscale data centres (over 10 ha built area and 70 MW or more connection capacity) and bars municipal environmental plans from permitting new ones across the Netherlands, except two named areas in Het Hogeland and Hollands Kroon.
summary_long: Adds paragraph 5.1.7.7 on hyperscale data centres to the Besluit kwaliteit leefomgeving under the Omgevingswet. Article 5.161ba defines a hyperscale data centre as operating a data or computing centre with more than 10 ha built floor area and an electrical connection capacity of 70 MW or more, including functionally supporting activities on the same site. Article 5.161bb makes the whole territory of the Netherlands the exclusion area, except certain locations in Het Hogeland and Hollands Kroon whose boundaries are set by ministerial regulation. Article 5.161bc provides that an environmental plan applying to the exclusion area does not permit hyperscale data centres. Article 12.26d requires the competent authority to implement this by the time set in article 22.5(1) of the Omgevingswet. The rule is an instructieregel under article 2.24(1) of the Omgevingswet, takes effect on 1 January 2024, and does not apply to activities permitted under an environmental permit for building work. The explanatory note states that existing and already permitted hyperscale data centres are not affected and that municipalities have until 1 January 2032 to amend their plans.

title: Uitvoeringswet Algemene verordening gegevensbescherming (UAVG)
summary_short: Dutch Act implementing the GDPR: names the Autoriteit persoonsgegevens as supervisory authority, sets national exceptions for special-category, criminal-offence and automated-decision processing, and provides for administrative fines. Applies to Dutch controllers and to non-EU controllers targeting persons in the Netherlands; articles take effect by royal decree.
summary_long: The Act supplements Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR) in Dutch law. It establishes the Autoriteit persoonsgegevens (AP) as supervisory authority and sets its composition, powers and administrative fines, including fines up to 20,000,000 euro or 4% of worldwide annual turnover for certain breaches (Art. 6, 14, 17, 18, 21a). It sets national exceptions to the GDPR prohibition on processing special categories of personal data (Art. 22-30b) and rules on criminal-offence data (Art. 31-33), including for health care, insurers, employers, research and public-interest purposes. It permits automated individual decisions required by law or by a public-interest task, subject to safeguards (Art. 40), and restricts data-subject rights in listed cases (Art. 41). It sets rules for journalistic, academic, artistic and literary expression (Art. 43), research and statistics (Art. 44), archives (Art. 45), national identification numbers (Art. 46) and public registers (Art. 47). A legal representative's consent applies to persons under 16 (Art. 5). It contains transitional rules and requires an evaluation report within three years of entry into force (Art. 48, 50). Articles take effect on dates set by royal decree (Art. 53).

title: Uitvoeringswet AI-verordening
summary_short: Dutch bill implementing the EU AI Act: designates national market-surveillance and notifying authorities, grants them supervisory and fining powers, creates an AI regulatory sandbox, and amends sector laws. Entry into force is not yet set.
summary_long: Bill implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act) in Dutch law. Article 2 names the Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate as notifying authority for certain AI systems, designates market-surveillance authorities by area (the AP, AFM, De Nederlandsche Bank and others), and sets the Minister as central contact point. Chapter 3 lets designated officials enter dwellings without consent after prior judicial authorisation, access AI systems under false identity details, impose self-standing orders on online intermediaries, and levy administrative fines up to the Article 99 AI Act amounts. Chapter 4 provides an AI regulatory sandbox and conditions on approved real-world testing. Chapter 5 sets cooperation and data-sharing rules between authorities. Article 7.1 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to keep documentation available to authorities after bankruptcy or cessation. Chapter 8 amends several sector laws (telecommunications, consumer goods, cable cars, medical devices, recreational craft, judiciary, financial supervision) with AI-specific authority, fine and language rules. Article 7.2 (registration of high-risk critical-infrastructure systems) and the entry-into-force date (Article 9.2) are marked PM.

title: Forskrift om datasenter (FOR-2024-12-18-3313)
summary_short: Norwegian regulation under the Electronic Communications Act requiring data centre operators above a 0.5 MW threshold to register with the national communications authority before starting operations, and to meet customer-information, representative, security, preparedness and incident-reporting duties, with administrative fines. In force 1 January 2025.
summary_long: Regulation of 18 December 2024 under the Electronic Communications Act, in force 1 January 2025 and amended with effect from 1 July 2026. It covers data centre operators above a 0.5 MW threshold (§ 1-2). Operators must register with the national communications authority before starting operations, including public-sector customers, the share of power used for cryptocurrency mining and contracted capacity; existing operators had until 1 July 2025. Operators must keep customer information current and disclose it to police, prosecutors and security authorities on request, keep a representative in Norway and respond without undue delay. Chapter 2 requires a security management system, risk and vulnerability assessments, security and contingency plans and exercises, supplier oversight, notification of significant incidents, and customer warnings about threats and planned work. The authority may order independent security audits at the operator's cost, national operation of services in a crisis, and prioritisation of services after disruption. Administrative fines reach up to 5% of turnover for violations of § 15-12 of the Act and up to 30 day-fines for individuals.

title: Lov om elektronisk kommunikasjon (ekomloven) LOV-2024-12-13-76 - § 3-7 Datasenter
summary_short: Norway's Electronic Communications Act (ekomloven), in force from 1 January 2025, replaces the 2003 Act. It regulates communications networks and services and data centres. Data centre operators must register before operating and meet security and preparedness duties.
summary_long: The Electronic Communications Act (ekomloven) replaces the 2003 Act. Under §18-1 it applies from 1 January 2025, with the King able to set different entry dates for individual provisions. It governs electronic communications networks and services, frequencies, numbering and data centres (§§1-1, 1-2). Data centre operators must register with the ministry before starting operations (§3-7). They must provide data centre services with security and preparedness, document their security level, and may be subject to ministry orders. The state compensates certain extra national-security measures. In emergencies, operators must carry out necessary usage restrictions (§3-8), and the ministry may request police certificates for certain staff (§3-9). Network and service providers face security and incident-reporting duties (§§3-1 to 3-3), privacy and cookie-consent rules (§§3-10, 3-15), IP address retention for twelve months (§3-13), consumer information and contract rules (Chapter 4), and access obligations for providers with significant market power (Chapters 6 to 10). Enforcement includes ministry orders, coercive fines, administrative fines (§15-12) and criminal penalties of fines or up to one year's imprisonment (§15-14). The text does not state fine amounts.

title: Endringer i åndsverkloven mv. (gjennomføring av nett- og videresendingsdirektivet og digitalmarkedsdirektivet) og samtykke til godkjenning av EØS-komiteens beslutning nr. 332/2023 og 333/2023 om innlemmelse i EØS-avtalen av direktiv (EU) 2019/789 og (EU) 2019/790, og samtykke til tiltredelse til WIPO-traktatene av 20. desember 1996 om opphavsrett (WCT) og om fremføringer og fonogrammer (WPPT)
summary_short: Proposed Norwegian bill (Prop. 41 LS) amending the Copyright Act to implement EU Directives 2019/789 and 2019/790: country-of-origin rule for online broadcast services, press publishers' right, education and cultural heritage exceptions, text and data mining exceptions, platform liability, and remuneration and reporting duties. Commencement date not stated.
summary_long: Proposal (Prop. 41 LS, 2025–2026) to amend Norway's Copyright Act and related acts, implementing EU Directives 2019/789 (online broadcasting and retransmission) and 2019/790 (digital single market), and seeking consent to EEA Joint Committee Decisions 332/2023 and 333/2023 and to accession to the WIPO WCT and WPPT. Operative provisions add a press publication right for information society service providers with a two-year term (new §24a); amend education exceptions and licensing (§§43, 46, 47, 57); add out-of-commerce cultural heritage uses (§§49a, 50a–50c); create text and data mining exceptions for lawfully accessed works (§50e, with a rightholder reservation) and for research and cultural heritage institutions (§50f, with secure storage); add an annual reporting duty from acquirers of rights to authors (§69a) and a right to reasonable remuneration on transfer (§69); allow authors to revoke exclusive rights for non-use (§74); set liability and safe-harbour conditions for content-sharing service providers (§§86–86c); extend Copyright Board mediation and dispute powers (§§31a, 65–65f); and provide criminal fines or imprisonment up to one year for infringement (§79) and up to three years for gross infringement (§80). The fetched text does not state an entry-into-force date.
text_version: Prop. 41 LS (2025-2026), proposition to the Storting as submitted 27 Mar 2026 (full PDF)

title: Biometric Processing Privacy Code 2025
summary_short: The Biometric Processing Privacy Code 2025, made under the Privacy Act 2020, sets privacy rules for organisations and businesses that collect and use biometric information in biometric processing, from 3 November 2025. Agencies already using biometrics had until 3 August 2026 to comply.
summary_long: The Biometric Processing Privacy Code 2025 was issued on 21 July 2025 under the Privacy Act 2020. It sets privacy rules for organisations and businesses that collect and use people's biometric information in biometric processing, which the page describes as the use of technologies such as facial recognition to collect and process biometric information to identify people or learn more about them. Biometric information covers physical or behavioural features such as a face, fingerprints, voice, keystroke patterns, or how a person walks. The code came into force on 3 November 2025. Agencies already using biometrics had a nine-month grace period, which ended on 3 August 2026. Amendment No 1 (March 2026) reflects Information Privacy Principle 3A (IPP3A), which the page states is in force from 1 May 2026. The page lists the Privacy Act information privacy principles and the code's factsheets on collection, use, disclosure, access requests, and storage and security. The fetched page does not reproduce the code's operative provisions, penalties or enforcement terms, so these are not coded.

title: Privacy Act 2020 (Public Act 2020 No 31)
summary_short: The Privacy Act 2020 regulates how New Zealand and overseas agencies handle personal information, through information privacy principles, complaints and investigations, breach notification and compliance notices. Most provisions commenced on 1 December 2020.
summary_long: The Privacy Act 2020 sets a framework for protecting individual privacy of personal information. It applies to New Zealand agencies, overseas agencies carrying on business in New Zealand, and certain individuals not ordinarily resident there. Its core is the information privacy principles (IPPs) in s 22, plus IPP 3A, which govern collection, source and notice, storage and security, access and correction, accuracy, retention, use and disclosure, disclosure outside New Zealand, and unique identifiers. The Privacy Commissioner may issue codes of practice that modify the IPPs. Individuals may request access to and correction of their personal information, and agencies may impose charges in limited cases. Complaints go to the Commissioner, who investigates and may refer matters to the Human Rights Review Tribunal, which can grant declarations, orders and damages. Agencies must notify the Commissioner and affected individuals of notifiable privacy breaches, and failing to notify the Commissioner is an offence with a fine not exceeding $10,000. The Commissioner may issue compliance notices. Part 7 authorises approved information sharing agreements and information matching. Part 8 restricts onward transfer outside New Zealand of personal information received from overseas, with transfer prohibition notices. Commencement was 1 December 2020, with IPP 3A from 1 May 2026.
text_version: Official consolidated version as at 1 May 2026 (Privacy Act 2020 No 31), incorporating among others the Privacy Amendment Act 2025 (2025 No 53, IPP 3A), Statutes Amendment Act 2025 (2025 No 74) Part 31, Crimes (Countering Foreign Interference) Amendment Act 2025 (2025 No 71) s 17, Parliament (Repeals and Amendments) Act 2025, Customer and Product Data Act 2025 ss 150-151

title: Decreto Supremo N.° 016-2024-JUS - Reglamento de la Ley N.° 29733, Ley de Protección de Datos Personales
summary_short: Peru's implementing regulation of Law 29733 on personal data protection. Sets consent, transparency, data-subject rights, cross-border transfer, children's data, security, incident notification, data protection officer and registration duties for public and private controllers and processors, with sanctions. Applies 120 days after publication.
summary_long: Approves the Regulation of Law 29733 (Peru's personal data protection law) and repeals Supreme Decree 003-2013-JUS. It has 135 articles, six final and two transitional provisions, and applies 120 calendar days after publication in El Peruano. It sets rules for consent (free, prior, express, informed; written for sensitive data), information duties and revocation, plus special rules for children and adolescents. Cross-border transfers require an adequate level of protection or contractual guarantees and a notice to the authority. Processors and subcontractors have specific duties. Controllers must notify security incidents within 48 hours and keep security documents and access controls. A data protection officer is required for public entities and for large-volume or sensitive-data processing, with staggered deadlines by company sales. Data subjects have access, rectification, cancellation, opposition and portability rights, and a right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The Dirección General de Transparencia supervises and sanctions; infractions are minor, serious or very serious, with coercive fines and corrective measures.

title: Decreto Supremo N.° 115-2025-PCM - Reglamento de la Ley N.° 31814, Ley que promueve el uso de la inteligencia artificial en favor del desarrollo económico y social del país
summary_short: Regulation of Peru's AI Law 31814. Classifies AI uses as prohibited ('uso indebido'), high-risk or acceptable-risk, and sets transparency, human-oversight, record-keeping, impact-assessment and security duties for public entities and private developers and implementers, phased in from 1 to 4 years after September 2025 by entity type, sector and firm size.
summary_long: The Reglamento applies to public administration entities, state-owned companies and private-sector, civil-society and academic actors in the National Digital Transformation System; personal use is excluded, and defence and national-security uses are excluded if they meet listed principles. The PCM, through the SGTD, is the national technical-normative authority: it issues guidelines and binding interpretive opinions, monitors prohibited and high-risk uses, supervises compliance and refers breaches to competent authorities. Six uses are prohibited, including manipulative influence, autonomous lethal capability in the civil sphere, mass surveillance without legal basis, biometric inference of sensitive traits, real-time biometric identification in public spaces (with exceptions for authentication and serious-crime investigation) and predictive profiling of individuals for crime. High-risk uses (critical infrastructure, education, employment, social programmes, credit, health) trigger algorithmic transparency and human oversight. Public entities must also adopt an AI policy, use NTP-ISO/IEC 42001:2025, run security audits and mandatory impact assessments, and publish publicly funded source code; for private actors impact assessments are voluntary, with three-year retention of documentation. The text sets no penalties of its own; it refers to the Comptroller, data-protection law and other authorities. It enters into force 90 business days after publication on 9 September 2025.
text_version: original as published in El Peruano, 2025-09-09 (no consolidated version used)

title: Decreto Supremo N.° 126-2025-PCM - Decreto Supremo que aprueba el Reglamento del Decreto de Urgencia N.° 007-2020, Decreto de Urgencia que aprueba el marco de confianza digital y dispone medidas para su fortalecimiento
summary_short: Implements Emergency Decree 007-2020 on Peru's digital trust framework. Requires public entities and digital service providers to manage digital security risks, report incidents to the national security centre, and, for listed providers, evaluate algorithms and inform people of automated decisions. Enters into force 90 calendar days after publication.
summary_long: Supreme Decree 126-2025-PCM approves the regulation of Emergency Decree 007-2020 on Peru's digital trust framework, covering digital security, personal data, transparency and consumer protection. The Secretaría de Gobierno y Transformación Digital (SGTD-PCM) is the governing body. Public entities and listed digital service providers (PSD), including financial, basic-service (electricity, water, gas), health, passenger transport, internet, critical-activity and education providers, must manage digital security risks, implement security controls and notify digital security incidents to the National Digital Security Centre (CNSD). Critical incidents must be notified within 48 hours of the provider becoming aware of them. Listed PSD must evaluate their algorithms for privacy, ethical use and human rights, and provide a channel to inform people of automated algorithm-based decisions and a way to contest them. The regulation sets up or governs the CNSD, a national incident registry, a national data centre, a digital talent platform and trust networks, and provides for monitoring and supervision by the SGTD-PCM. It does not itself set fines; Article 21(k) refers non-compliance to the competent supervisory authority. Entry into force is 90 calendar days after publication.

title: Ley N.° 29733 - Ley de Protección de Datos Personales
summary_short: Peru's general personal data protection law. It applies to personal data in public and private databanks processed in national territory. It sets processing principles, consent and data-subject rights, security and cross-border transfer rules, and administrative fines enforced by the national data protection authority.
summary_long: Establishes the rules for processing personal data held in public and private databanks in Peru, with the stated object of guaranteeing the constitutional right to personal data protection (Art. 1). It applies to data processed in national territory and excludes purely personal or family databanks and certain public-sector databanks used for defence, public security and criminal matters (Art. 3). It sets principles including legality, consent, purpose, proportionality, quality, security and an adequate-protection standard for cross-border flows (Arts. 4-11). Processing requires prior, informed, express and unequivocal consent, subject to listed exceptions (Arts. 5, 13, 14); sensitive data requires written consent. Cross-border transfers are allowed only to countries with adequate protection, subject to listed exceptions (Art. 15). Data subjects hold information, access, update, opposition and objective-treatment rights, the latter against decisions with significant legal effects based solely on automated evaluation of personality (Arts. 18-23), and a right to compensation (Art. 25). Controllers and processors must ensure security and confidentiality (Arts. 9, 16, 17, 28). Databanks must be registered in a National Registry (Art. 34). The Ministry of Justice's National Directorate of Justice is the national authority, with sanctioning power (Art. 32). Infractions are classed as minor, serious or very serious (Art. 38); fines range from 0.5 to 100 UIT and may not exceed 10% of the offender's gross revenue of the prior year (Art. 39).
text_version: Text as originally published (El Peruano, 2011-07-03); SPIJ export dated 2016, before the DL 1353 (2017) amendments

title: Ley N.° 30096 - Ley de Delitos Informáticos
summary_short: Peru's 2013 Cybercrime Law (Ley 30096) criminalises offences against computer systems and data, computer fraud, identity theft, illicit data trafficking, interception, and child-related offences committed via ICT. It also requires telecom concessionaires and other companies to provide data or geolocation under judicial orders.
summary_long: Law 30096, published 22 October 2013, criminalises computer-related offences and sets prison terms and day-fines. Arts. 2-4 cover unlawful access and data and system integrity. Art. 5 penalises contact with minors for sexual purposes via ICT. Art. 6 covers illegal data trafficking and Art. 7 interception of non-public data transmissions, with heavier terms for classified information or national defence and security. Art. 8 covers computer fraud, Art. 9 identity theft and Art. 10 making or distributing devices, programmes or passwords designed for these offences. Art. 11 allows sentences to be raised by up to one third for criminal-organisation membership, abuse of access positions, economic gain, or harm to social aid, defence or security. Final provisions authorise undercover agents, order police-prosecutor protocols, and direct the banking and telecom regulators to set fine scales for supervised firms that fail to meet judicial information orders. Amendments to the Criminal Procedure Code require telecom concessionaires to provide geolocation and call data within 30 working days and keep equipment compatible with the police interception system; cybercrime is added to wiretap and organised-crime lists, and Penal Code provisions on telephone interference, child pornography and discrimination are amended.

title: Ley N.° 32314 - Ley que modifica el Código Penal, Decreto Legislativo 635, y la Ley 30096, Ley de Delitos Informáticos, para incluir el uso de la inteligencia artificial en la comisión de delitos
summary_short: Amends Peru's Penal Code and Law 30096 on computer crimes so that use of artificial intelligence, including deepfakes, aggravates or defines offences such as child pornography, defamation, aggravated fraud and copyright crimes. Binding criminal law; implementing regulations due within 60 days of entry into force.
summary_long: Law No. 32314 amends Peru's Penal Code (Decreto Legislativo 635) and Law 30096 on computer crimes to cover the use of artificial intelligence in offences. Article 1 adds AI or similar technologies as an aggravating circumstance (art. 46); extends child pornography (art. 129-M) to AI-based tools and deepfakes; adds a defamation penalty band for content spread through AI or deepfakes (art. 132); creates aggravated fraud for AI manipulation of a third party's voice, image, audio or body movement causing economic loss (art. 196-A(7)); limits copyright offences (arts. 217-219) to works of human authorship; and adds an aggravating case for profit from exploiting a plagiarised work (art. 220(f)). Article 2 adds a fifth aggravating circumstance to art. 11 of Law 30096, letting judges raise penalties by up to one third above the legal maximum for computer crimes committed with AI. The single final provision requires the Executive to issue implementing regulations within sixty calendar days of entry into force. The law imposes no AI-specific licensing, registration or transparency duties; its effects are criminal penalties imposed by courts, in prison terms and day-fines.

title: Proyecto de Ley N.° 10756/2024-CR - Ley que modifica el Código Penal, Decreto Legislativo 635 y la Ley de Delitos Informáticos, Ley 30096, para sancionar el uso indebido de la inteligencia artificial en la comisión de delitos
summary_short: Peru Congress committee majority report (20 May 2026) recommending a substitute text for 7 bills. It amends Penal Code arts. 196-A and 438-A: new aggravated fraud for abuse of professional trust and fraud by phone or mass electronic media; penalises buying or selling scientific research to claim authorship.
summary_long: Majority committee report (dictamen) of the Justice and Human Rights Committee of Peru's Congress, dated 20 May 2026, on seven bills, including bill 10756/2024-CR on AI misuse. It recommends a substitute text amending Penal Code (Decreto Legislativo 635) arts. 196-A and 438-A. Art. 196-A would add numeral 8 (fraud committed with abuse of trust arising from professional or business activity) and numeral 9 (fraud committed by telephone calls, text messages or electronic mass media). The formula legal also restates numeral 7 (fraud by AI-based manipulation of a person's voice, image, audio or body movement, enacted by Law 32314) without its economic-harm clause. New Art. 438-A(2) would punish buying, selling or claiming authorship of scientific research without having participated in it, with 3 to 6 years' imprisonment and 60 to 150 day-fines. The AI provisions of bill 10756/2024-CR (Penal Code Arts. 46 and 129-M; Law 30096 Art. 11(5)) are not in the substitute text; the committee states that Law 32314, published 29 April 2025, already enacted them. The formula legal contains no entry-into-force clause.
text_version: Majority dictamen of the Comisión de Justicia y Derechos Humanos (2026-06-04) on PL 4097 y otros incl. 10756/2024-CR, with texto sustitutorio (fórmula legal)

title: Resolución SBS N.° 504-2021 - Reglamento para la Gestión de la Seguridad de la Información y la Ciberseguridad
summary_short: Peruvian SBS rule (Resolución 504-2021, in force 1 July 2021) requiring supervised financial, insurance and pension firms to run an information security and cybersecurity management system, with tiered regimes, incident reporting, digital-channel authentication and prior authorization for certain foreign data-processing services.
summary_long: Resolución SBS N° 504-2021 approves the Reglamento para la Gestión de la Seguridad de la Información y la Ciberseguridad for the entities in Articles 16 and 17 of the General Law, AFPs and named public financial bodies (Art. 1). Firms must maintain an information security and cybersecurity management system (SGSI-C) proportionate to their size and complexity, sorted into General, Simplified and Reinforced regimes (Arts. 3-4, 26-27). Duties include board and management responsibilities, a security function, minimum controls, a cybersecurity programme, reporting significant incidents to the Superintendencia and a forensic analysis (Arts. 5-15). Digital-channel transactions require strong authentication, with exemptions for low-risk payments, and the company is responsible for unrecognised operations made under an exemption (Arts. 17-20). Significant outsourced data processing, including cloud services, requires notice 30 days before start (Art. 24.3) and prior authorization for foreign providers where legal limits apply (Art. 25). The rule also amends the internal audit, external audit, corporate governance, operational risk, credit card and e-money regulations (Arts. Second to Eighth). It takes effect 1 July 2021 (Art. Tenth), with an adaptation plan due within 60 days (Art. Ninth).

title: Ustawa z dnia 3 lipca 2026 r. o systemach sztucznej inteligencji (Dz.U. 2026 poz. 1003)
summary_short: Polish statute on AI systems that sets up national supervision of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. It creates the Commission for the Development and Security of Artificial Intelligence as market surveillance authority, with inspections, enforcement decisions, notified-body rules, regulatory sandboxes and administrative fines. General entry into force is 14 days after publication.
summary_long: Polish Act of 3 July 2026 on AI systems (Dz.U. 2026 poz. 1003). It applies to the entities in Art. 2(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and excludes defence, national security and certain research activities (Art. 2(1), Art. 3). It creates the Commission for the Development and Security of Artificial Intelligence as market surveillance authority and single point of contact, and sets its composition, appointment, independence and procedure (Art. 5, Art. 19-47). The Commission may run inspections, issue warnings, and order an operator to cease use or withdraw a system where there is a direct risk to life, health, safety or fundamental rights, and it may impose administrative fines (Art. 48-66, Art. 104). Individual opinions and clarifications are available (Art. 8-17). The minister for informatisation accredits and notifies conformity assessment bodies (Art. 86-90). Regulatory sandboxes last 6 to 12 months and carry participation fees (Art. 91-101). Obstructing inspections or not complying with a Commission decision is a criminal offence (Art. 112-113). Other Acts are amended (Art. 115-124), and a state budget spending ceiling for 2026-2035 is set (Art. 126). General entry into force is 14 days after publication, with listed provisions 3 months after (Art. 127).

title: Law No. (13) of 2016 on Protecting Personal Data Privacy
summary_short: Qatar's Law No. 13 of 2016 governs personal data processed electronically. It requires controllers to obtain consent, give notice, limit use, secure data and restrict cross-border transfers, with stricter rules for sensitive data and children's websites. It sets fines and gave existing processing six months to conform.
summary_long: The law applies to personal data processed electronically or collected for electronic processing, and excludes purely personal or family use and processing for official statistics (Art. 2). Individuals may withdraw consent, object, request deletion and correction (Art. 5), and receive access, notice and a copy of their data for a fee not exceeding the service cost (Art. 6). Controllers must obtain consent unless processing serves a legitimate purpose (Art. 4), give prior notice of purposes and processing (Art. 9), keep data relevant and no longer than necessary (Art. 10), and adopt internal measures including data protection officers, training, complaint systems and audits (Art. 11). Controllers and processors must protect personal data (Art. 13), and controllers must notify the competent administration and individuals of serious breaches (Art. 14). Controllers may not take decisions that restrict cross-border data flows, except where processing violates the law or would cause serious harm (Art. 15). Sensitive data, including racial origin, children, health, religion, marital status and criminal offences, may be processed only with a permit from the competent administration (Art. 16). Operators of websites directed at children must give notice, obtain parental consent and meet further conditions (Art. 17). Exemptions apply for national security, public interest and certain legal duties (Arts. 18 to 21). Direct marketing by electronic communication requires prior consent and an opt-out (Art. 22). Violations are punishable by fines (Arts. 23 to 25). Individuals may complain, and the competent administration may order a remedy, with appeal to the Minister (Art. 26). Contracts made in breach of the law are void (Art. 28). Existing data handlers had six months from the effective date to conform (Art. 30).},
text_version: Original Arabic text as published in the Official Gazette No. 15 of 2016 (Al Meezan portal, MOJ Qatar)

title: Personal Data Protection Law, Royal Decree No. M/19 of 9/2/1443H (amended by Royal Decree No. M/148 of 5/9/1444H)
summary_short: Sets rules for collecting, processing, disclosing and transferring personal data, granting data subjects rights and imposing duties on controllers and processors. Applies in the Kingdom and to residents' data processed abroad. Enforced by a Competent Authority with fines and criminal penalties. Effective 720 days after publication.
summary_long: The Law regulates collecting, processing, disclosing, transferring and destroying personal data in the Kingdom and residents' data processed abroad, excluding purely personal or family use. Data subjects gain rights to be informed, access and obtain their data, correct it and request its destruction. Processing generally requires consent, subject to listed exceptions including legitimate interest, which does not cover sensitive data. Controllers must limit purpose and content, provide a privacy policy and notice at collection, restrict disclosure, implement security measures and notify breaches. Health data, credit data, marketing communications and research uses have specific conditions. Controllers must carry out impact assessments for products or services and keep processing records. Cross-border transfers require a listed purpose and an adequacy assessment by the Competent Authority. The Competent Authority supervises compliance, may keep a national register of controllers, and may license accreditation and audit bodies. Intentional disclosure of sensitive data for harm or personal benefit carries up to two years' imprisonment and/or a three-million-riyal fine; other violations carry warnings or fines up to five million riyals. Courts may order confiscation and publication of judgments, and individuals may claim compensation. The Law takes effect 720 days after publication.

title: Implementing Regulation of the Personal Data Protection Law (SDAIA, 2023)
summary_short: Implementing regulation of Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law, plus a regulation on transferring personal data outside the Kingdom. Sets controller duties on data subject rights, consent, notices, security, breach notice within 72 hours, impact assessments and cross-border transfer safeguards; applies from the Law's enforcement date.
summary_long: The Implementing Regulation supplements the Personal Data Protection Law (Royal Decree M/19, as amended by M/148). A second part regulates transfers of personal data outside the Kingdom. It applies to Controllers and Processors and excludes personal or family use (Art. 2). Controllers must act on data subject requests within 30 days, extendable by 30 days (Art. 3), inform data subjects at or before collection (Art. 4), and obtain explicit consent for sensitive data, credit data and solely automated decisions (Art. 11). They must notify the Competent Authority of personal data breaches within 72 hours (Art. 24). Impact assessments are required for sensitive data, data linking, continuous monitoring, new technologies and automated decisions (Art. 25). A data protection officer must be appointed in listed cases (Art. 32). Transfers outside the Kingdom must not affect national security, vital interests or data subject rights (Transfer Reg. Art. 2). They rely on adequacy decisions or safeguards such as standard contractual clauses, certifications or approved binding codes, with listed exemptions (Transfer Reg. Arts. 3-8). Data subjects may complain to the Competent Authority within 90 days (Art. 37). The text does not set penalty amounts.

title: Lag (2025:570) om offentliggörande av information om datacenters energiprestanda
summary_short: Requires owners or operators of data centres with at least 500 kW installed IT power to publish annual energy performance data by reporting it to the EU database under Directive (EU) 2023/1791 Art. 12. Excludes security-sensitive, defence and crisis-preparedness uses. Supervised by a government-designated authority. Issued 28 May 2025.
summary_long: Lag (2025:570) requires the owner or manager of a data centre with an installed IT power demand of at least 500 kilowatts to publish information on the data centre's energy performance each year, by reporting it to the database referred to in Article 12 of Directive (EU) 2023/1791 in its original wording. The reporting duty does not apply to information covered by secrecy under the Public Access to Information and Secrecy Act (2009:400), or to data centres used for security-sensitive activities, for defence or crisis-preparedness purposes, or exclusively for such services. Reporting rules are set in Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364. A supervisory authority designated by the government may request information and documents, access premises other than dwellings, and issue orders needed to ensure compliance, which may be combined with a conditional fine (vite). Its decisions may be appealed to the general administrative court, and leave to appeal is required for appeals to the administrative court of appeal.

title: Lag (2026:806) om användning av AI-system för ansiktsigenkänning i realtid för brottsbekämpande ändamål
summary_short: Sets conditions under which the Swedish Police Authority and Säkerhetspolisen may use real-time facial or remote biometric identification AI systems in public places for law enforcement. Requires prior permission from a prosecutor or court, with urgent exceptions and notification duties; applies from a date set by government.
summary_long: The Act governs use by the Swedish Police Authority (Polismyndigheten) and Säkerhetspolisen of AI systems for real-time facial recognition or other real-time remote biometric identification in public places, where personal data processing falls under the Criminal Data Act (2018:1177). Use is allowed only when absolutely necessary to locate or identify a specified person in listed situations, including suspected trafficking, a missing person suspected of a crime, imminent risk of a serious crime endangering life or physical safety, and suspected crimes carrying four years' imprisonment or more; the benefit must outweigh the intrusion (5 §). Use requires prior permission: from a prosecutor for crime prevention and enforcement of sentences (6 §), and from a court on a prosecutor's application for investigation or prosecution (7 §). Permits state the person, purpose, time and area, last at most one month, and cover no more than absolutely necessary (10 §). Use may start without permission in urgent cases, with an application within 24 hours (13–14 §). Section 3 requires a fundamental-rights impact assessment under AI Act Article 27 and registration under Article 49 before first use; it exists in two versions tied to dates set by government. Identified persons must be notified, subject to secrecy exceptions (17–18 §). The Act contains no penalty provisions.

title: Lag (2022:1781) om andring i lagen (1994:1776) om skatt pa energi
summary_short: Amends the Swedish Energy Tax Act (1994:1776) from 1 July 2023. It repeals 1 kap. 14 §, 9 kap. 5 a § and 11 kap. 15 §, and gives new wording to rules on state-aid exemptions, electricity tax deductions and refunds, and approval of voluntary taxpayers consuming more than 10 GWh a year.
summary_long: The Act amends the Energy Tax Act. Section 1 kap. 11 a § lists energy and carbon tax exemptions treated as state aid under Article 107(1) TFEU. Section 9 kap. 5 b § sets how electricity and fuels used jointly for heat or cooling are apportioned for refunds. Section 9 kap. 8 § sets minimum refund amounts per calendar quarter and a 2,000 kronor threshold for certain refunds. Section 11 kap. 6 § allows approval as a voluntary taxpayer for persons expected to consume more than 10 GWh of electricity per calendar year in listed uses, with approval revoked if conditions lapse. Section 11 kap. 9 § sets deductions of the difference from the prevailing tax rate minus 0.6 öre per kWh for listed industrial uses and 9.6 öre per kWh for listed municipal uses. Section 11 kap. 16 § requires annual refund applications, allows monthly applications where consumption is at least 150,000 kWh per year, sets a three-year filing limit, and requires electronic filing except for certain refunds. Section 11 kap. 17 § conditions deductions and refunds on the recipient not being a company without a right to state aid and on disclosure of recipient information where amounts exceed 50,000 euro (15,000 euro for certain deductions and refunds). The Act repeals 1 kap. 14 §, 9 kap. 5 a § and 11 kap. 15 §. The new wording of 11 kap. 9 § has no item 7 and the list in 1 kap. 11 a § has no item 10; the text does not state what the removed items covered. Earlier rules continue for periods before entry into force. The text states no penalties.

title: Copyright Act 2021
summary_short: Division 8 of Singapore's Copyright Act 2021 (ss 243-244) makes it a permitted use for a person to copy works or recordings for computational data analysis, including training computer programs, if conditions on lawful access, copy status and supply are met.
summary_long: Section 243 defines 'computational data analysis' for a work or a protected-performance recording to include using a computer program to identify, extract and analyse information or data from it, and using it as an example to improve a program's functioning on that type of data; the illustration gives training an image-recognition program. Section 244(1) makes it a permitted use for a person (X) to make a copy of a work or recording for that analysis or for preparing it for analysis. The conditions in s 244(2) are: the copy is used for no other purpose; it is supplied to others only to verify X's results or for collaborative research or study; X has lawful access to the first copy; and either the first copy is not an infringing copy, or it is an infringing copy and X does not know this (with a further knowledge condition for flagrantly infringing online locations), or it is an infringing copy, a prescribed purpose requires its use, and X uses it for no other purpose. Storing or retaining the copy counts as making it (s 244(3)). Section 244(4) permits communication to the public of such a copy under the same supply limits. Section 244(5) provides that such supply is not publishing and is disregarded in determining copyright duration. The excerpt contains no enforcement, penalty or commencement provisions.
text_version: current version as at 14 Oct 2026 (Singapore Statutes Online)

title: Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act 34 of 2024)
summary_short: Amends Singapore's Parliamentary and Presidential Elections Acts to ban publishing online election advertising with realistic but false audio, visual or audiovisual depictions of candidates made with digitally generated or manipulated content during election periods. Commencement date: 22 January 2025.
summary_long: The Act amends the Parliamentary Elections Act 1954 and the Presidential Elections Act 1991 (sections 2 and 3). It creates an offence (new sections 61MA and 42LA) for a person who publishes, or causes to be published, in Singapore online election advertising during an election period that contains a representation of a candidate saying or doing something the candidate did not do, where the representation is realistic enough that some members of the public would likely believe it and was created wholly or partly with digitally generated or manipulated content. The offence requires that the person knows or ought reasonably to have known the content is election advertising. It is a defence to prove that the person did not know and had no reason to believe the candidate did not say or do the thing. Private communications, news published by authorised news agencies and other excluded circumstances are exempt. Offenders face a fine up to $1,000, imprisonment up to 12 months, or both. After a writ is issued, the Returning Officer must publish and maintain a public list of candidates who have deposited the required sum and consented to publication. Candidates may request Returning Officer directions in respect of these offences. Failure to comply with a direction is an offence, with a fine up to $1,000,000 for social media service providers and otherwise a fine up to $1,000 or imprisonment up to 12 months. Knowingly false or misleading requests are an illegal practice. The Act was passed on 15 October 2024 and assented on 8 November 2024; the document gives a date of commencement of 22 January 2025.
text_version: Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act 2024 (No. 34 of 2024), as published in the Government Gazette Acts Supplement No. 37 (22 Nov 2024; SSO status 'Published in Acts Supplement on 21 Nov 2024'); passed 15 Oct 2024, assented 8 Nov 2024, commencement 22 Jan 2025

title: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025
summary_short: Creates offences and civil torts for twelve online harmful activities, including harassment, doxxing, intimate image abuse and inauthentic (possibly AI-generated) material. Sets up a Commissioner of Online Safety with power to issue directions and orders to individuals, administrators and online services, plus reconsideration and appeal. Commencement is set by Ministerial notification.
summary_long: The Act defines twelve online harmful activities (Part 3), including online harassment, doxxing, intimate image abuse, image-based child abuse, online impersonation and inauthentic material abuse, which covers audio, visual or audiovisual material altered or generated by digital means such as generative AI. Eligible victims may report to a Commissioner of Online Safety (Part 4). The Commissioner may give Part 5 directions to communicators, administrators and online service providers, such as stop-communication, access-disabling, right-of-reply, labelling and account-restriction directions, and may issue orders following non-compliance, including access blocking orders to internet access providers and app removal orders. Part 6 gives information-gathering powers and allows end-user identity collection notices to prescribed online service providers. Part 7 provides reconsideration and appeal to an Online Safety Appeal Panel. Part 8 creates offences for non-compliance and for false information. Parts 10 to 12 create civil torts and administrator and online service provider duties to respond to online harm notices. Part 13 governs damages and remedies, and Part 15 amends the Defamation Act 1957, the Protection from Harassment Act 2014, the Family Justice Act 2014 and the Info-communications Media Development Authority Act 2016.

title: Personal Data Protection Act 2012 (as amended by the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2020)
summary_short: Singapore's general data protection statute. It governs organisations' collection, use and disclosure of personal data (consent, purpose, access, protection, retention, cross-border transfer, breach notification), creates the Do Not Call Registry, and provides for Commission directions, financial penalties and private action. Commenced in phases from 2 January 2013.
summary_long: The Act governs collection, use and disclosure of personal data by organisations, balancing individuals' right to protect their data with organisations' need to use it for appropriate purposes. Parts 3 to 6B bind organisations, not individuals acting personally or domestically, employees acting in employment, or public agencies; records at least 100 years old are outside the Act. Parts 2 and 3 establish the Personal Data Protection Commission and accountability duties. Part 4 covers consent, deemed consent, withdrawal, collection without consent and purpose limitation. Parts 5 and 6 cover access, correction, accuracy, protection, retention and transfers outside Singapore. Part 6A requires breach assessment and notification. Part 9 creates the Do Not Call Registry; Part 9A prohibits dictionary attacks and address-harvesting software; Part 9B creates offences for unauthorised disclosure, improper use and re-identification of anonymised information. Part 9C provides directions, financial penalties, voluntary undertakings and a right of private action; Part 9D provides appeals. Part 10 covers guidelines, investigation powers, offences and penalties, employer liability and regulations. Only Part 1 and the outline are reproduced in the supplied text; penalty amounts and the operative wording of later Parts are absent.

title: Zakon o izvajanju uredbe (EU) o določitvi harmoniziranih pravil o umetni inteligenci (ZIUDHPUI)
summary_short: Slovenian statute implementing the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689). Designates market surveillance and notifying authorities, creates a national AI ethics council and regulatory sandboxes, requires public-sector AI systems to be published, and sets misdemeanour fines for providers, deployers, importers, distributors, representatives and notified bodies. In force 15 days after publication.
summary_long: The Act implements Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act) in Slovenia and sets national enforcement arrangements. The ministry for the information society is notifying authority for certain high-risk systems, and market surveillance is shared among the communications agency, the Information Commissioner, the Bank of Slovenia, the insurance supervision agency and the market inspectorate, each for defined areas. The communications agency is the single point of contact, coordinates a market surveillance council and must set up the first AI regulatory sandbox by 2 August 2026. It keeps a register of certain critical-infrastructure high-risk systems and requires public bodies to publish data on AI systems in use through a single information point. A five-member National Council for Ethics in AI is created. Misdemeanour fines apply to providers, deployers, importers, distributors, authorised representatives and notified bodies: base fines of EUR 25,000 to 250,000 (EUR 100,000 to 450,000 for large companies), with maxima of EUR 35 million or 7% of turnover for prohibited practices and lower tiers for other breaches. The Act enters into force fifteen days after publication.

title: Artificial Intelligence Law Proposal (Grand National Assembly of Turkey)
summary_short: Turkish bill on artificial intelligence. It sets principles (safety, transparency, fairness, accountability, privacy) for AI operators, requires risk assessment, registration and conformity assessment for high-risk systems, and provides administrative fines of up to 35 million TL or 7% of turnover for prohibited applications.
summary_long: The bill's purpose is to ensure safe, ethical and fair use of AI systems, to protect personal data and privacy, and to establish a regulatory framework for developing and using AI systems. It applies to providers, deployers, users, importers and distributors of AI systems and to persons affected by them. Article 3 lists five principles: safety, transparency, fairness, accountability and privacy. Article 4 requires risk assessments during development and use, special measures for high-risk systems, registration of high-risk systems with the relevant supervisory authorities, and a conformity assessment. Article 5 obliges operators to comply with the law and related regulations and gives supervisory authorities monitoring and detection powers. Article 6 sets fines of up to 35 million Turkish Liras or 7% of annual turnover for prohibited AI applications, up to 15 million Turkish Liras or 3% for breaches of obligations, and up to 7.5 million Turkish Liras or 1.5% for providing false information. The text refers to prohibited applications but does not set them out. The law enters into force on publication (Article 7) and is executed by the President (Article 8). The document is an introduced proposal and has not been enacted.

title: Kişisel Verilerin Korunması Kanunu, Kanun No. 6698 (Law on the Protection of Personal Data)
summary_short: Turkey's Law No. 6698 on the Protection of Personal Data governs processing of personal data by natural and legal persons, setting consent and other processing conditions, data-subject rights, transfer rules, security duties, a controllers' registry and a Personal Data Protection Authority, with most provisions in force from 7 April 2016.
summary_long: Law No. 6698 applies to natural and legal persons who process personal data, whether by automated means or as part of a data recording system (Art. 2). It sets processing principles (Art. 4), requires explicit consent unless a listed condition applies (Art. 5), restricts special-category data (Art. 6) and governs deletion and anonymisation (Art. 7). Transfers abroad are permitted on an adequacy decision or listed safeguards, with Board authorisation in some cases (Arts. 8-9). Controllers must inform data subjects (Art. 10), take data security measures (Art. 12) and register in the public Data Controllers Registry (Art. 16). Data subjects have rights including objection to results from exclusively automated analysis (Art. 11). Complaints go to the Board after a request to the controller (Arts. 13-15). Crimes and administrative fines from 5,000 to 1,000,000 Turkish lira apply (Arts. 17-18). The law establishes the Personal Data Protection Authority, comprising the Board and the Presidency (Arts. 19-27). Most provisions took effect on publication on 7 April 2016; Arts. 8, 9, 11 and 13-18 took effect six months later (Art. 32).

title: İnternet Ortamında Yapılan Yayınların Düzenlenmesi ve Bu Yayınlar Yoluyla İşlenen Suçlarla Mücadele Edilmesi Hakkında Kanunda Değişiklik Yapılmasına Dair Kanun, Kanun No. 7253
summary_short: Amends Law No. 5651 on internet publications. For social network providers with over one million daily accesses from Turkey, requires a Turkish representative, reporting, 48-hour replies to applications and local data hosting, enforced by escalating fines, advertising bans and bandwidth throttling. Articles 6-7 apply from 1 October 2020.
summary_long: Amends Law No. 5651 on internet publications. Defines social network providers. Lets administrative fines be notified directly to addressees abroad. Raises a fine under Article 5(6) from 100,000 to 1,000,000 Turkish lira. Adds content removal to access-blocking rules and sets four-hour compliance for Union orders. Additional Article 4 covers social network providers with over one million daily accesses from Turkey: they must appoint a Turkish representative and notify the Authority, answer applications within 48 hours, publish six-monthly reports, and take steps to store Turkish users' data in Turkey. Non-compliance draws administrative fines, a ban on new advertising by Turkish-resident taxpayers, and, on application to a criminal judgeship of peace, bandwidth reduction of up to 90%. Providers are liable for damages if unlawful content identified by a court is not removed within 24 hours of notice. A transitional provision allows three months to prepare for application duties and sets June 2021 for the first report. Articles 6 and 7 apply from 1 October 2020; other provisions from publication.

title: 人工智慧基本法 (Artificial Intelligence Basic Act)
summary_short: Taiwan's Artificial Intelligence Basic Act, promulgated 14 January ROC year 115 and in force from promulgation, sets principles for AI research, development and application and directs central and local governments to promote AI, support industry and manage high-risk uses under risk-based rules.
summary_long: The Act sets seven principles for AI research, development and application (Art. 4): sustainability and welfare, human autonomy, privacy and data governance, security, transparency and explainability, fairness and non-discrimination, and accountability. It requires the government to avoid harmful or discriminatory AI uses (Art. 5) and to designate high-risk AI applications, which must carry warnings (Art. 5(2)). It creates a National AI Strategy Special Committee under the Executive Yuan (Art. 6), and directs the government to promote education, budgets, subsidies, tax and financial incentives, with an annual performance reporting system (Arts. 7–10). It allows innovation experimental environments (Art. 11), calls for data sharing and reuse and minimisation of personal data by sectoral agencies (Arts. 13–14), and sets labour-related duties (Art. 15). The Ministry of Digital Development is to build a risk classification framework and sectoral agencies are to issue risk-based management rules (Art. 16). The government is to define liability and relief mechanisms for high-risk applications (Art. 17), review existing laws within two years (Art. 18), and assess risks of its own AI use (Art. 19). The text contains no private-sector penalty provisions.

title: Artificial Intelligence (Regulation) Bill [HL] (HL Bill 76)
summary_short: Bill requiring regulations to create an AI Authority to coordinate regulators, support sandboxes and accredit AI auditors, and to impose AI officer, training-data record, consent, labelling and third-party audit duties on AI businesses across the UK. The Act comes into force on the day it is passed.
summary_long: Requires the Secretary of State, by regulations, to create an AI Authority to coordinate regulators, assess AI risks, support sandboxes and accredit independent AI auditors (s.1). The Authority must have regard to principles including safety, transparency, fairness and proportionality of burdens (s.2). It must work with regulators to construct regulatory sandboxes in which firms test innovative propositions with real consumers (s.3). Regulations must require businesses that develop, deploy or use AI to have a designated AI officer (s.4). Further regulations must require persons training AI to supply the Authority a record of third-party data and intellectual property used and to assure informed consent and copyright compliance; require suppliers of AI products or services to give customers health warnings, labelling and opportunities to consent; and require businesses using AI to allow accredited independent auditors to audit their processes and systems (s.5). The Authority must run a public engagement programme (s.6). Regulations are made by statutory instrument and may create offences and require fees, penalties and fines, with no amounts stated in the Bill (s.8). The Act extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland and comes into force on the day it is passed (s.9).

title: Artificial Intelligence (Regulation) Act 2024
summary_short: A bill that, once enacted, would create an AI Authority, set AI regulatory principles, and provide by regulations for sandboxes, AI officers, training-data records, labelling and independent audits; the Act comes into force on the day it is passed.
summary_long: As introduced, the bill has the Secretary of State make regulations creating an AI Authority (s.1), with functions including coordinating regulators, reviewing legislation, monitoring AI risks, supporting sandboxes and accrediting independent AI auditors. Section 2 sets regulatory principles the Authority must have regard to. Section 3 requires it to construct regulatory sandboxes in which firms test innovative propositions with real consumers on a small scale. Section 4 requires, by regulations, that businesses developing, deploying or using AI designate an AI officer. Section 5 provides for regulations requiring persons training AI to record third-party data and IP used and to assure informed consent and copyright compliance; for AI product or service suppliers to give health warnings, labelling and consent opportunities; and for businesses to allow accredited independent auditors to audit their systems. Section 7 defines AI, including generative AI. Section 8 allows regulations to create offences, fees, penalties and fines. The Act extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland and comes into force on the day it is passed.

title: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 (c. 48)
summary_short: Section 29A of the UK Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988, in force from 1 June 2014, lets a person with lawful access copy a work for non-commercial computational analysis research without infringing copyright, subject to acknowledgement and transfer limits; contract terms blocking such copying are unenforceable.
summary_long: Section 29A, inserted by the Copyright and Rights in Performances (Research, Education, Libraries and Archives) Regulations 2014 with effect from 1 June 2014, is a text and data analysis exception. Under subsection (1), copying a work by a person with lawful access does not infringe copyright if the copy is made so that a person with lawful access can carry out computational analysis of anything recorded in the work for the sole purpose of non-commercial research, and the copy is accompanied by a sufficient acknowledgement unless that is impossible for reasons of practicality or otherwise. Subsection (2) makes copyright infringed if the copy is transferred to another person without the copyright owner's authorisation, or is used for any other purpose without authorisation. Subsection (3) treats a dealt-with copy as an infringing copy for that dealing and, if that dealing infringes, for all later purposes. Subsection (4) defines dealt with as sold or let for hire, or offered or exposed for sale or hire. Subsection (5) makes unenforceable any contract term that purports to prevent or restrict copying that the section permits. The provided text sets no penalties; the section operates within the Act's general copyright infringement rules.

title: CMA decision: strategic market status investigation into Apple's mobile platform
summary_short: The UK Competition and Markets Authority designates Apple as having strategic market status in its Mobile Platform (iOS, iPadOS, App Store, Safari, WebKit) under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, effective 22 October 2025 for five years. No conduct requirements are imposed.
summary_long: The CMA decides under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 that Apple has strategic market status (SMS) in a single grouped digital activity, the Mobile Platform. It covers the Smartphone and Tablet Operating Systems (iOS, iPadOS), Native App Distribution (the App Store) and the Mobile Browser and Browser Engine (Safari and WebKit), linked to the UK. The designated undertaking comprises Apple Inc. and Apple Distribution International Limited. The decision finds that the turnover condition is met (global turnover above £25 billion or UK turnover above £1 billion, either sufficing) and that Apple has substantial and entrenched market power and a position of strategic significance. Designation takes effect from the decision date and lasts five years, subject to review or revocation. The decision imposes no conduct requirements; any such measures would require separate processes and further public consultation. It states that it does not find wrongdoing. Pre-installation, sideloading and web apps are excluded from the activity descriptions, and developer tools fall within Native App Distribution only where they fit its description.

title: CMA decision: strategic market status investigation into Google's mobile platform
summary_short: The CMA's decision designates Google as having strategic market status (SMS) in the provision of its Mobile Platform (Android operating system, Play Store and Chrome/Blink browser engine) under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, effective from 22 October 2025 for five years. It imposes no conduct requirements.
summary_long: This CMA decision designates Google as having strategic market status (SMS) in the provision of its Mobile Platform under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (the Act). The CMA finds that the Google undertaking (Alphabet Inc., Google LLC, Google Ireland Limited and Google UK Limited) meets the turnover condition, has substantial and entrenched market power, and holds a position of strategic significance. The Mobile Platform is one grouped digital activity comprising the Mobile Operating System (Android), Native App Distribution (Google Play Store) and the Mobile Browser and Browser Engine (Chrome and Blink), linked to the UK. Mobile devices themselves, third-party native apps and sideloading are outside the defined activities. The designation takes effect on the date of the decision and lasts five years, subject to review or revocation. The Act imposes no automatic rules; any conduct requirements or pro-competition interventions require further public consultation. The decision makes no finding of wrongdoing.

title: CMA decision: strategic market status investigation into Google's general search and search advertising services
summary_short: CMA final decision designating Google as having strategic market status in general search and search advertising under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, effective from 10 October 2025 for five years. Includes AI Overviews and AI Mode in scope; excludes the Gemini AI assistant for now.
summary_long: Under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, the Competition and Markets Authority designates Google as having strategic market status (SMS) in general search services, defined as general search and search advertising, for five years from the date of the decision. The designated undertaking comprises Alphabet Inc., Google LLC, Google Ireland Limited, Google UK Limited and Google Commerce Limited. General search covers Google Search however accessed, including AI Overviews and AI Mode, the News tab, Top Stories and Google Discover; organic search syndication products and AdSense for Search are in scope only in the configurations the decision describes. Google News, standalone specialised search, display advertising and the Gemini AI assistant are currently excluded. The decision finds substantial and entrenched market power and a position of strategic significance, and states that designation imposes no rules by itself: any conduct requirements or other measures require further public consultation before they are introduced.

title: Crime and Policing Act 2026 (c. 20)
summary_short: Crime and Policing Act 2026 (UK, dated 29 April 2026) makes provision on anti-social behaviour, offensive weapons, retail crime, child criminal exploitation, cuckooing and police powers across the United Kingdom, with some measures specific to England, Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland.
summary_long: The Act makes provision on anti-social behaviour, offensive weapons, retail crime, child criminal exploitation and cuckooing, and police powers. Respect orders may be made against persons aged 18 or over; youth injunctions are confined to those aged 10 to 17. Some police directions and closure notices may last longer, and some fixed penalty notice amounts rise from £100 to £500. Part 2 provides for removal of unlawful weapons content from user-to-user and search services, with penalties up to £60,000 for providers and £10,000 for content managers. It creates offences of possessing a bladed article or offensive weapon with intent to use unlawful violence, regulates remote sale and delivery of knives and crossbows, and raises weapons sentences. Part 3 creates an offence of assaulting a retail worker, requires a criminal behaviour order in certain convictions, and makes theft from shops triable either way. Part 4 creates child criminal exploitation and cuckooing offences and CCE prevention orders against persons aged 18 or over. The long title also covers sexual offences, stalking, police and border powers, terrorism and corporate liability; those provisions are not in the text reviewed.

title: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
summary_short: Amends the Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018 and confers Secretary of State powers on the security and resilience of network and information systems used in essential activities. Extends duties to data centres, load controllers, managed service providers and critical suppliers, adds incident reporting, penalties and national-security directions.
summary_long: The Bill amends the Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018 (NIS Regulations) and gives the Secretary of State powers over the security and resilience of network and information systems used in essential activities. Part 2 extends the NIS Regulations to data centre services (a rated IT load of at least 1 megawatt, or 10 megawatts on an enterprise basis), to load controllers (potential electrical control of at least 300 megawatts) and to managed service providers. It adds registration, representative and incident-notification duties, customer notification, designation of critical suppliers, periodic cost-recovery charges, information-sharing rules, information notices and financial penalties. Part 3 lets the Secretary of State designate a statement of strategic priorities, make regulations on security and resilience (including requirements, enforcement, penalties and appeals), issue a code of practice, and report to Parliament at least every five years. Part 4 allows the Secretary of State to give national-security directions to regulated persons, with monitoring, information gathering, inspections, penalties and non-disclosure requirements. Part 5 sets the extent (England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland), the commencement (some provisions on the day of Royal Assent, some two months later, the rest by regulations) and the short title.

title: Data Protection Act 2018 (c. 12)
summary_short: Supplements the UK GDPR and regulates personal data processing by controllers, law enforcement competent authorities and intelligence services, with data subject rights, automated decision-making limits, transfer rules and the Information Commission. Enacted 23 May 2018.
