summary_long: The Act supplements the UK GDPR, which governs most personal data processing (ss.1-4), and regulates processing by law enforcement competent authorities (Part 3) and intelligence services (Part 4). Part 2 covers general processing, special category data (s.10), exemptions (ss.15-16), certification providers (s.17) and significant decisions based solely on automated processing (ss.50A-50D). Part 3 sets six principles (ss.35-40), data subject rights (ss.44-54), controller and processor duties (ss.56-71) and third-country transfer conditions (ss.73-78). Part 4 applies parallel principles and rights (ss.86-100), designation notices for qualifying competent authorities (ss.82A-82E) and transfer limits (s.109). Part 5 establishes the Information Commission (s.114A), which may issue standard data protection clauses (s.119A) and enforcement and penalty notices, including administrative fines (s.115(8)-(9)). Parts 6 and 7 are listed in s.1 but their text is not in the extract, which ends at s.120. The Act is dated 23 May 2018.

title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c. 18)
summary_short: Creates powers for customer and business data access regulations (Part 1), a trust framework and register for digital verification services (Part 2), a national underground asset register (Part 3), changes to registers of births and deaths (Part 4), and UK GDPR and privacy amendments (Part 5).
summary_long: The text provided has five Parts. Part 1 confers powers on the Secretary of State and the Treasury to make regulations requiring data holders to provide customer data and business data to customers or authorised third-party recipients, with supplementary provision on interfaces, decision-makers, enforcement, financial penalties, fees and levies, and review duties. Part 2 requires the Secretary of State to publish a DVS trust framework and maintain a register of digital verification services, with registration tied to certification by accredited conformity assessment bodies, and powers to refuse, remove or amend entries. Part 3 requires a National Underground Asset Register, with duties on undertakers to enter and correct apparatus information and offences for non-compliance. Part 4 changes how registers of births and deaths are kept. Part 5, Chapter 1 amends the UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018, including recognised legitimate interests, purpose limitation and consent provisions. The long title also refers to copyright and the development of artificial intelligence systems, but the text provided ends within Part 5 and contains no operative AI or copyright provisions. The outline supplied with the document is empty.

title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (c. 13)
summary_short: Gives the UK Competition and Markets Authority powers over digital markets: designating firms with strategic market status, imposing conduct requirements and pro-competition orders, and enforcing them with penalties. It also amends UK competition and merger law. Dated 24 May 2024 in the text.
summary_long: Part 1 (digital markets) lets the CMA designate undertakings with strategic market status in a digital activity linked to the UK, where substantial and entrenched market power, strategic significance and a turnover condition (global turnover over £25 billion or UK turnover over £1 billion) are met; designations last five years (ss 2, 7, 18). Designated undertakings may face conduct requirements, enforcement orders, commitments, a final offer mechanism and pro-competition interventions (ss 19–56), must report certain mergers before completion (ss 57–68), and must name a nominated officer and file compliance reports (ss 83–84). Investigatory powers apply (ss 69–82). Penalties reach 10% of turnover for breaches of orders, conduct requirements and merger duties, 1% of turnover for undertakings failing investigative requirements, and up to £30,000 for individuals; offences carry up to two years' imprisonment (ss 85–98). Part 2 (competition) amends Competition Act 1998 prohibitions, investigation and penalty powers, and Enterprise Act 2002 merger, market study and market investigation rules (ss 119–146). The outline also lists Part 3 (enforcement of consumer protection law) and Chapter 1 of Part 4 and Chapter 2 of Part 5, whose text is not in this part of the document.

title: The Data Protection Act 2018 (Code of Practice on Artificial Intelligence and Automated Decision-Making) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/425)
summary_short: Requires the Information Commissioner to prepare a code of practice giving good-practice guidance on processing personal data when developing and using AI and automated decision-making under the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 (except Part 4), including children's data. In force from 12 May 2026, UK-wide.
summary_long: These Regulations, made 16 April 2026 under sections 124A and 124B of the Data Protection Act 2018, require the Information Commissioner to prepare an appropriate code of practice. The code gives guidance on good practice in processing personal data under the relevant data protection legislation when developing and using artificial intelligence and when making automated decisions. It must also include guidance on processing children's personal data. Automated decision-making is defined by reference to Article 22C(1) of the UK GDPR and section 50C(1) of the 2018 Act. Relevant data protection legislation means the UK GDPR and the 2018 Act, except Part 4. Regulation 3 modifies section 124B so that the panel considering the code must not consider or report on any aspect of the code relating to national security. The Regulations come into force 21 days after being laid (stated as 12 May 2026) and extend to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. The Explanatory Note states that no full impact assessment was produced for the instrument, and that the Commissioner must produce one when preparing the code.

title: The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 6 and Transitional and Saving Provisions) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/82)
summary_short: Commencement regulations bringing into force specified provisions of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 on 5 February 2026 and 19 June 2026, with transitional and saving rules for data subject requests, automated decision-making, penalty notices, complaints handling and PEC Regulations enforcement. Addressed to controllers and the Information Commissioner.
summary_long: The Regulations (SI 2026/82), made on 29 January 2026 by the Secretary of State, bring into force on 5 February 2026 provisions of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 listed in regulation 2, including provisions on research and statistical purposes, consent for scientific research, lawfulness of processing, purpose limitation, responses to data subjects' requests, automated decision-making, children's higher protection, third-country transfers, and the Information Commissioner's enforcement powers under the PEC Regulations. Section 103 and Schedule 10 (complaints by data subjects) come into force on 19 June 2026. Savings provide that the amended time limits for responding to requests (section 76) do not apply to requests received before 5 February 2026, the automated decision-making amendments (section 80 and Schedule 6) do not apply to decisions taken before that date, and the penalty-notice amendments (section 101) do not apply where a notice of intent was given before that date. Complaint-handling duties apply only to complaints received on or after 19 June 2026. Regulations 8 to 11 set transitional rules for PEC Regulations enforcement, under which pre-commencement breaches are governed by the earlier regime. Regulation 12 updates commencement references in the Data Protection Act 2018.

title: The Export Control (Amendment) Regulations 2024 (SI 2024/346)
summary_short: Amends the UK Export Control Order 2008 and the assimilated Dual-Use Regulation (EC) 428/2009 control lists from 1 April 2024. Adds export and electronic-transfer prohibitions for emerging technologies, including advanced integrated circuits, cryogenic CMOS and quantum computers, and updates existing military and dual-use entries.
summary_long: The Export Control (Amendment) Regulations 2024 (SI 2024/346) were made on 7 March 2024 under sections 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7 of the Export Control Act 2002 and Article 15(1) of Council Regulation (EC) No 428/2009. They come into force on 1 April 2024. Regulation 2 amends Schedule 2 (military goods) and Schedule 3 (UK controlled dual-use goods) of the Export Control Order 2008. It inserts new entries PL9013, PL9014 and PL9015. PL9013 covers cryogenic CMOS integrated circuits, dry-etching and SEM equipment, integrated circuits with a total processing performance of 6000 or more (including GPUs, TPUs and neural processors), parametric amplifiers, cryogenic cooling, EUV masks, and related software and technology. PL9014 covers quantum computers and computers containing PL9013.a.4 circuits. PL9015 covers metal additive manufacturing equipment and certain coating technology. For these items the export or transfer by electronic means is prohibited to any destination. Regulation 3 amends Annex I of Regulation 428/2009, changing definitions and control entries across the categories 1 to 9, including cryptography controls in 5A002. Regulations 1 and 2 extend to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland; Regulation 3 extends to England and Wales and Scotland. The text itself does not set penalties.}},

title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation) as retained in UK law (UK GDPR)
summary_short: UK-retained version of EU Regulation 2016/679 (UK GDPR). Sets rules for controllers and processors processing personal data in the UK or offering goods or services to, or monitoring, people in the UK, covering principles, lawful bases, consent, children's consent, special-category data and transparency. This extract covers Articles 1 to 12A only.
summary_long: This extract of the UK GDPR (part 1 of 2) covers Articles 1 to 12A, with recitals as context. It applies to processing of personal data in the context of an establishment of a controller or processor in the UK (Art. 3(1)), and to controllers or processors not established in the UK that offer goods or services to, or monitor, data subjects in the UK (Art. 3(2)). Article 5 sets principles of lawfulness, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation and integrity. Article 6 permits processing only on listed lawful bases, including consent, contract, legal obligation, public task and legitimate interests; a recognised legitimate interest basis requires a condition in Annex 1, which the Secretary of State may amend by regulations. Article 7 sets consent conditions. Article 8 makes processing of a child's data for information society services lawful from age 13, and below 13 only with parental consent or authorisation; the Secretary of State may vary the age between 13 and 16. Article 9 prohibits processing of special categories of data, subject to listed exceptions; Article 10 governs criminal conviction data. Article 12 requires transparent communication and responses to data subject requests, generally within one month (Art. 12A), extendable by two further months. Enforcement, supervisory authorities, international transfers and impact assessments are not in this extract. The application date is not stated in this extract.

title: JSP 936 V1.1 Dependable Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Defence (part 1: directive)
summary_short: UK Ministry of Defence directive (JSP 936 Part 1) setting mandatory requirements for dependable AI in Defence: ethical principles, governance, human-AI teaming, lifecycle controls, safety, security and supplier assurance. Applies to all MOD staff and AI across the system lifecycle; the extract states no commencement date.
summary_long: JSP 936 Part 1 is a UK Ministry of Defence directive on dependable artificial intelligence. It adopts a broad characterisation of AI and covers AI in Robotic and Autonomous Systems and digital systems across all lifecycle phases, from pre-concept to disposal. Tailoring of its requirements is permitted only after a risk assessment. It requires an AI ethical risk assessment at project outset, structured around five MOD ethical principles: human-centricity, responsibility, understanding, bias and harm mitigation, and reliability. Each TLB must appoint a Responsible AI Senior Officer (RAISO) and provide annual Statements of AI Ethical Assurance. Overall risk ratings determine approval levels, and special-attention uses such as AI in kinetic effects are referred to the DAU. Operative requirements cover human-centred design, allocation of functions between humans and AI, data correctness and provenance, model documentation, verification and validation, safety and security analysis, disclosure of AI use in products, and supplier competence. The extract contains no penalties and no commencement date. Its requirements are expressed as 'must' provisions addressed to MOD staff and suppliers, and Part 2 guidance is stated to follow.

title: The Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018 (SI 2018/506)
summary_short: Implements EU Directive 2016/1148 (NIS) in the UK from 10 May 2018: sets security and incident-notification duties for operators of essential services and relevant digital service providers, with designated authorities and penalties up to £17,000,000.
summary_long: Implements Directive (EU) 2016/1148 (the NIS Directive) in the UK, in force 10 May 2018. Requires a national NIS strategy and designates sector competent authorities; GCHQ is the single point of contact and CSIRT (regs 2–5). Persons providing essential services above Schedule 2 thresholds are deemed operators of essential services (OES), or may be designated by a competent authority (reg. 8). OES must take appropriate security measures and notify significant incidents within 72 hours (regs 10–11). Relevant digital service providers (online marketplaces, online search engines, cloud computing services), other than micro or small enterprises, must manage security risks, notify substantial incidents within 72 hours and register with the Information Commission (regs 12–14). Non-UK providers offering digital services in the UK must nominate a UK representative (reg. 14A). Enforcement tools include information notices, inspections, enforcement notices and penalty notices (regs 15–18). Penalties are capped at £1,000,000 for non-material contraventions and £8,500,000 or £17,000,000 for material ones. Appeals lie to the First-tier Tribunal (regs 19A–19B); penalties are recoverable as court orders (reg. 20). Fees and periodic review reports are also covered (regs 21, 25).

title: National Security and Investment Act 2021 (c. 25)
summary_short: The National Security and Investment Act 2021 lets the Secretary of State review acquisitions of control over UK entities and assets that may raise national security risks. It requires mandatory notification of notifiable acquisitions, which are void without approval, and allows call-in notices, interim and final orders, and monetary penalties and offences.
summary_long: The Act creates a national security review regime for acquisitions of control over UK qualifying entities (any non-individual entity) and qualifying assets (including land, ideas and information such as databases, source code and algorithms). The Secretary of State may give a call-in notice where a trigger event (gaining control under ss.8-9) may give rise to a national security risk, within 6 months of becoming aware of it and 5 years of the event (s.2). Notifiable acquisitions require a mandatory notice before completion and are void without approval (ss.13-14), with a 30-working-day review period; voluntary notices are also possible (s.18). The assessment period has an initial 30 working days, extendable by 45 working days (s.23). Information and attendance notices (ss.19-20), interim orders (s.25) and final orders (s.26) may be made, and final orders can reach persons outside the UK in defined cases. The Act also provides financial assistance (s.30), CMA coordination (s.31), offences with imprisonment up to 5 years on indictment (s.39), civil monetary penalties capped at the higher of 5% of turnover and £10 million (s.41), cost recovery, appeals within 28 days (ss.49-51), information-sharing gateways (ss.54-55) and an annual report (s.61).

title: The National Security and Investment Act 2021 (Notifiable Acquisition) (Specification of Qualifying Entities) Regulations 2021 (SI 2021/1264)
summary_short: Specifies, in 17 Schedules, the descriptions of qualifying entities and UK activities whose acquisitions are notifiable under section 6(2) of the National Security and Investment Act 2021. In force from 4 January 2022 across the UK. Schedule 3 covers artificial intelligence.
summary_long: These Regulations specify, for section 6(2) of the National Security and Investment Act 2021, the descriptions of qualifying entities whose acquisition of control is notifiable. Regulation 2 provides that the Schedules 1 to 17 descriptions apply, and that an entity falls within a description only if it carries on the specified activity in the United Kingdom. Regulation 3 defines development and production. Regulation 4 requires the Secretary of State to review the regulations and publish reports at intervals not exceeding three years, the first before the end of three years from commencement. The Schedules cover advanced materials, advanced robotics, artificial intelligence (research into AI, or developing or producing goods using AI, for identification or tracking of objects, people or events, advanced robotics, or cyber security), civil nuclear, communications (including a turnover condition of at least GBP 50,000,000), computing hardware, critical suppliers to government, cryptographic authentication, data infrastructure, defence, energy (including generating-asset capacity and throughput conditions), military and dual-use, quantum technologies, satellite and space technology, suppliers to emergency services, synthetic biology, and transport (ports and airports). The instrument does not itself set out enforcement penalties or the notification procedure, which sit in the Act.

title: The Infrastructure Planning (Business or Commercial Projects) (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/13)
summary_short: Amends the Infrastructure Planning (Business or Commercial Projects) Regulations 2013 to add data centres to the prescribed description of business or commercial projects under the Planning Act 2008 regime in England and Wales, in force from 8 January 2026.
summary_long: The Regulations were made on 7 January 2026 and came into force on 8 January 2026. Regulation 2 inserts a new paragraph 10, 'Data centres', into the Schedule to the 2013 Regulations after paragraph 9 (Tourism), so that data centre projects fall within the prescribed description of business or commercial projects for the purposes of section 35(2)(a)(ii) of the Planning Act 2008. According to the Explanatory Note, development forming part of such a project can be authorised under the planning regime if other section 35 requirements are met and the Secretary of State gives a direction, which may be given only where the project is of national significance. The Regulations extend to England and Wales. They contain no other operative provisions, and no full impact assessment was produced.

title: Online Safety Act 2023 (c. 50)
summary_short: Sets duties of care for providers of UK-linked user-to-user and search services to assess and mitigate risks of illegal content and content harmful to children, and gives OFCOM regulatory functions, codes of practice and enforcement powers.
summary_long: The Act imposes duties of care on providers of UK-linked user-to-user and search services to assess and mitigate risks of illegal content and content harmful to children (ss. 9-12, 26-29). Category 1 services face further duties on user empowerment, democratic and journalistic content and impact assessments (ss. 14-19, 22). Services must run complaints procedures, keep records and publish terms of service and transparency reports (ss. 20-23, 71-72, 77). Services likely to be accessed by children must carry out access assessments (ss. 35-37); pornographic internet services must ensure children are not normally able to encounter such content (s. 81). Fraudulent advertising duties apply to Category 1 and 2A services (ss. 38-40). CSEA content must be reported to the NCA; knowingly false reports are an offence punishable by up to 2 years' imprisonment on indictment or a fine (ss. 66, 69). OFCOM issues codes of practice recommending compliance measures (ss. 41-50), and regulated services must notify OFCOM for fee-paying years (s. 83). The fetched text covers Parts 1-6 to s. 83(4); Parts 7-12 are not included.

title: The Online Safety Act 2023 (Category 1, Category 2A and Category 2B Threshold Conditions) Regulations 2025 (SI 2025/226)
summary_short: Sets the user-number and functionality thresholds that place online services in Category 1, 2A or 2B under the UK Online Safety Act 2023, which triggers additional duties under the Act. In force 27 February 2025.
summary_long: These regulations, made by the Secretary of State on Ofcom's advice and approved by both Houses of Parliament, define when regulated online services meet the threshold conditions for the Online Safety Act 2023 categories. Category 1 covers user-to-user services with more than 34 million average monthly active UK users and a content recommender system, or more than 7 million with a recommender system and a forward or share function. Category 2A covers search engines with more than 7 million users, except vertical search engines that search selected sources through API-based arrangements. Category 2B covers user-to-user services with more than 3 million users and a direct-messaging function. User numbers are the monthly mean over the six months before the month in which Ofcom's assessment begins. The duties attached to each category, and the assessment and register process, are set in the parent Act (sections 95-97), not in this instrument.

title: The Online Safety Act 2023 (Fees) (Threshold Figure) Regulations 2025 (SI 2025/1204)
summary_short: Sets the £250 million threshold figure for qualifying worldwide revenue, at or above which providers of regulated services must notify OFCOM and pay fees under sections 83 and 84 of the Online Safety Act 2023, from the charging year beginning 1 April 2026.
summary_long: Made under section 86(2) of the Online Safety Act 2023 as the first regulations under section 86, and in force from 11 December 2025 in England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Regulation 2(1) specifies a threshold figure of £250 million for the purposes of section 83 (duty to notify OFCOM) and section 84 (duty to pay fees). Regulation 2(2) provides that the figure takes effect from the beginning of the charging year beginning 1 April 2026. The explanatory note (not part of the Regulations) states that providers whose qualifying worldwide revenue is at or above the figure must notify OFCOM unless they meet an exemption published by OFCOM and approved by the Secretary of State, and that OFCOM's fees are determined by reference to qualifying worldwide revenue for the qualifying period as defined in S.I. 2025/1032. It also notes that the initial notification falls within four months of the Regulations coming into force. The instrument contains no sanctions and no other thresholds. The figure follows an OFCOM consultation and advice, and the Secretary of State must keep it under review under section 86(3).

title: The Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003 (SI 2003/2426)
summary_short: Sets privacy and confidentiality rules for public electronic communications in the UK from 11 December 2003: consent for storing information on terminal equipment, traffic and location data limits, calling line identification, directories, unsolicited direct marketing by calls, fax and email, breach notification and security duties for communications providers.
summary_long: These Regulations, made under the European Communities Act 1972 to implement parts of Directive 2002/58/EC, come into force on 11 December 2003 and revoke the Telecommunications (Data Protection and Privacy) Regulations 1999. Providers of public electronic communications services must take appropriate security measures (reg. 5), notify personal data breaches to the Information Commission and, where likely to adversely affect a subscriber or user, to that subscriber or user (reg. 5A). Regulation 6 prohibits storing information in, or accessing information in, a subscriber's or user's terminal equipment unless an exception in Schedule A1 applies, including consent. Regulations 7 and 8 restrict the processing of traffic data, and regulation 14 restricts location data. Regulations 10 to 13 require calling and connected line identification facilities, and regulation 15 to 16A cover malicious calls, emergency calls and emergency alerts. Regulation 18 governs directories of subscribers, and regulation 19 to 24 restrict direct marketing by automated calling systems, fax, calls and email, subject to consent, opt-out and register rules. Regulations 25 and 26 require the Information Commission to keep registers of numbers. Regulation 27 voids inconsistent contract terms, and regulations 28 and 29 exempt national security and legal-requirement cases. Regulation 30 allows damages claims, and regulation 31 and Schedule 1 apply Data Protection Act 2018 enforcement powers, including a fixed monetary penalty of £1,000 for breach-notification failures (reg. 5C). Regulations 32A to 32C provide for codes of conduct and accreditation of monitoring bodies, and regulation 37 requires periodic reviews by the Secretary of State.</think>

title: Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025 (c. 34)
summary_short: The Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025 changes UK rules on nationally significant infrastructure consent, electricity connections and benefits, transport and harbour orders, EV charge point accessibility, and English planning fees and decisions, with some provisions applying only in Scotland or Wales.
summary_long: Dated 18 December 2025, this Act amends the Planning Act 2008 to change national policy statement review duties, remove pre-application consultation duties, and let the Secretary of State disapply development consent by direction. It allows electricity licence and connection-agreement modifications for three years, requires the Independent System Operator and Planner and electricity distributors to have regard to designated strategic plans, and directs the Authority to run a long duration electricity storage scheme. It enables regulations for benefits to homes near new transmission infrastructure, with pass-through to end-users, civil enforcement, monetary penalties and information disclosure. It amends the Electricity Act 1989 for Scottish consent procedures, the Highways Act 1980 and Transport and Works Act 1992 (deadlines, fees, deemed consents, publication), and the Automated and Electric Vehicles Act 2018 (charge point accessibility). For English planning authorities it lets fees be set locally within cost limits, allows Secretary of State review directions, permits a planning fee surcharge, requires certified training for relevant members, sets delegation and committee rules, and extends implementation periods after legal challenges. Natural England may decline certain non-ministerial advice requests. Scottish and Welsh provisions apply to their own ministers.

title: Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act 2022 (c. 46)
summary_short: Sets security requirements for internet- and network-connectable consumer products sold in the UK, with duties for manufacturers, importers and distributors enforced by the Secretary of State. Part 2 amends electronic communications infrastructure rules. Most provisions commence by regulations.
summary_long: The Act sets security requirements for internet-connectable and network-connectable consumer products made available in the UK (Part 1). The Secretary of State may specify requirements by regulations, and manufacturers, importers and distributors must comply with them, provide a statement of compliance before supply, investigate and remedy compliance failures, notify the enforcement authority and customers, and keep records for 10 years. Importers and distributors may not supply products known to have a compliance failure, and non-UK manufacturers may appoint UK authorised representatives. Enforcement uses compliance, stop and recall notices, forfeiture orders, and monetary penalty notices up to the greater of £10 million or 4% of qualifying worldwide revenue; failing to comply with an enforcement notice is an offence. Part 2 amends the electronic communications code on infrastructure sharing, upgrades, code rights for unresponsive occupiers, alternative dispute resolution and compensation, and tenancy rent rules in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and gives the Secretary of State regulation-making powers for network access rights. Most provisions commence by regulations.

title: The Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure (Security Requirements for Relevant Connectable Products) Regulations 2023 (SI 2023/1007)
summary_short: Sets security requirements for manufacturers of UK consumer connectable products, covering passwords, vulnerability reporting and minimum security update periods. It also sets deemed-compliance routes through ETSI EN 303 645, ISO/IEC 29147 and labelling schemes, excepted product categories, and statement-of-compliance content and retention rules, in force 29 April 2024 across the UK.
summary_long: Made under the Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act 2022 and in force 29 April 2024 in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, these Regulations set security requirements for manufacturers of relevant connectable products. Schedule 1 requires unique or user-defined passwords, a published point of contact for security reports with acknowledgement and status updates, and a published defined support period for security updates. Regulation 5 applies these requirements to each manufacturer where there is more than one. Schedule 2 deems compliance where ETSI EN 303 645 or ISO/IEC 29147 provisions are met, or where a Japan JC-STAR STAR-1 or Singapore Cybersecurity Labelling Scheme label is held; Schedule 2A applies similar deemed compliance to statements of compliance. Schedule 3 lists excepted products, such as certain medical devices, computers, smart meters, electric vehicle charge points and vehicles. Schedule 4 sets statement-of-compliance content, and regulations 8 and 9 require manufacturers and importers to keep statements for the longer of ten years or the defined support period. Regulation 10 requires review at least every five years. This text itself contains no penalty provisions.

title: Advancing Artificial Intelligence Education for American Youth
summary_short: Executive order directing federal agencies to promote AI literacy through education and workforce programs. Establishes a White House AI Education Task Force, a Presidential AI Challenge, K-12 AI resources, educator training priorities and AI-related Registered Apprenticeships, with 90-, 120- and 180-day deadlines from the order's date.
summary_long: Directs federal agencies to promote AI literacy and an AI-ready workforce through education programs. Establishes the White House Task Force on AI Education, chaired by the OSTP Director, to coordinate federal efforts (Sec. 4). Within 90 days the Task Force plans a Presidential AI Challenge, to be held within 12 months of the plan's submission (Sec. 5). Agencies seek public-private partnerships for K-12 AI resources, prioritize related funding where consistent with law, and within 180 days of the first partnership announcement aim to have resources ready (Sec. 6). Within 120 days the Education Secretary is to prioritize AI in teacher-training grants and NSF is to prioritize AI-in-education research (Sec. 7). Within 120 days the Labor Secretary is to increase AI-related Registered Apprenticeships, set goals and performance targets, and prioritize grants for high school AI courses (Sec. 8). The order is subject to applicable law and appropriations and creates no enforceable rights (Sec. 9).

title: Alabama House Bill 172
summary_short: Alabama HB 172 makes it a crime to distribute materially deceptive media, meaning AI-produced images, audio or video that falsely depict an individual, within 90 days before an election when the distributor knows the media is false and intends to influence the election. It also lets specified parties seek permanent injunctions. Effective October 1, 2024.
summary_long: Alabama HB 172 makes it a crime to distribute materially deceptive media, meaning AI-produced images, audio or video that falsely depict an individual saying or doing something they did not, when a reasonable viewer would incorrectly believe it. Distribution is prohibited within 90 days before an election when the distributor knows the media falsely represents the depicted individual and intends, with reasonable likelihood, to harm a candidate's reputation or prospects or to change voters' patterns by deception. A disclaimer stating the media was manipulated by technical means and depicts speech or conduct that did not occur avoids the prohibition, with specific placement and language rules for video, audio, image and edited media. A violation is a Class A misdemeanor, but a second or subsequent conviction within five years is a Class D felony. Websites, interactive services, broadcasters and publishers are excluded absent actual knowledge and intent to injure or influence, and satire, qualifying news coverage and rights under federal law are carved out. Distributors may not intentionally remove a disclaimer. The Attorney General, depicted individuals, injured candidates and entities representing likely-deceived voters may seek permanent injunctive relief, must prove knowledge by clear and convincing evidence, and face dismissal and possible fees for frivolous complaints; non-Attorney General plaintiffs may recover costs and fees. The act takes effect October 1, 2024.

title: Alabama (2019) SB 47
summary_short: Alabama 2019 act allowing automated commercial motor vehicles to operate in the state without a conventional driver when listed criteria are met, and allowing commercial vehicles with teleoperation systems to run with a remote driver. Effective on passage and Governor approval.
summary_long: SB 47 (2019) defines automated driving and teleoperation terms and authorizes automated commercial motor vehicles to operate in Alabama without a conventional driver physically present, provided the vehicle can comply with federal and state traffic laws, is registered and titled in Alabama, is certified under 49 C.F.R. Part 567, can reach a minimal risk condition, and carries at least $2,000,000 motor vehicle liability coverage. The owner or lessee is treated as the operator for traffic-law compliance, and the automated driving system is considered licensed to operate the vehicle. Section 6 permits commercial vehicles with teleoperation systems to run without a conventional driver when a remote driver operates them. The remote driver is treated as the operator for traffic and criminal-charge purposes, must hold the required license class, is subject to alcohol and drug testing provisions regardless of location, and the vehicle must meet the Section 7 requirements, including achieving a reasonably safe state if teleoperation fails. The Department of Transportation is the sole state agency with jurisdiction over these vehicles, and political subdivisions may not impose additional requirements specific to them. Accident-reporting duties are deemed satisfied if specified steps are taken, and existing liability under common or statutory law is preserved. The Act takes effect immediately following passage and Governor approval, or on becoming law.

title: Arkansas HB 1876 (Ownership of Model Training and Content Generated by a Generative Artificial Intelligence Tool 2025)
summary_short: Adds Ark. Code § 18-4-101 allocating ownership of content generated by, and models trained with, a generative AI tool: to the person giving input or training data, or to the employer where an employee acts within employment under direction. Does not override existing copyright or IP rights.
summary_long: The section, added to Arkansas Code Title 18, Chapter 4, Subchapter 1 (Sec. 1), addresses ownership rather than regulating AI systems. Under subsection (a)(1), when a person uses a generative AI tool to generate content, the person who provides the input or directive owns the generated content, provided it does not infringe existing copyrights or intellectual property rights. Under subsection (a)(2), when a person uses such a tool to conduct model training, the person who provides data or input owns the resulting trained model, provided the training data was lawfully acquired and the person has not transferred ownership rights by contract or agreement. Subsection (b) gives the employer ownership of training data and generated content where an employee is directed to use the tool as part of employment duties, within the scope of employment and under the employer's direction and control. Subsection (c) states that the section grants no ownership over content infringing pre-existing copyrights or other IP rights, regardless of tool use. The text contains no penalty or enforcement provisions and states no effective date.

title: Arizona Revised Statutes § 41-1519 -- Computer data center certification; tax relief (with A.R.S. 42-5061 TPT exemption)
summary_short: Arizona statute allowing tax relief (deductions on sales, use and related transactions in computer data center equipment) for owners, operators and qualified colocation tenants of data centers certified by the state authority, from August 31, 2013, subject to investment thresholds and a qualification period.
summary_long: From August 31, 2013, the owner or operator of a computer data center certified by the state authority, and its qualified colocation tenants, may claim tax relief. The relief is the deduction of gross proceeds or gross income from sales, use, installation, assembly, repair or maintenance of computer data center equipment under listed sections of Title 42. Applicants file a form with the authority, which must approve or deny within sixty days or the application is deemed approved; the certification then runs for a qualification period of ten full calendar years, or twenty for sustainable redevelopment projects. A new data center must invest at least $25,000,000 (county population of 800,000 or fewer) or $50,000,000 (larger counties) within five years of certification, with notice to the authority and records kept until the requirement is met; an existing data center needs $250,000,000 invested in the 72 months before September 1, 2013. Owners must list qualified colocation tenants. The center may not generate electricity for resale or sell electricity outside the center. The authority revokes certification for non-compliance with the investment requirements (permitting recapture of relief by the department of revenue) or for violation of the electricity restriction. Proprietary business information in applications is confidential.

title: City of Chandler Ordinance No. 5033 (PLH22-0053) -- Zoning Code amendment for data centers (Chapter 35, Section 2214)
summary_short: Amends Chandler City Code Chapter 35 to define data center and add Section 35-2214 regulating data centers. Data centers are not permitted unless approved in a Planned Area Development district or as limited ancillary uses, with neighbor notice, meetings, noise studies, and backup-generator notice duties. Adopted December 2022.
summary_long: Ordinance No. 5033 amends the City of Chandler, Arizona zoning code (Chapter 35) relating to data centers. Section 1 adds a definition of Data Center as a facility or portion of a facility housing networked computer systems and telecommunications equipment used for remote storage, processing, and distribution of data. Section 2 adds Section 35-2214. Data centers are not permitted to operate in the city unless explicitly approved as part of a Planned Area Development zoning district. Data centers ancillary to another primary use are permitted if they occupy no more than ten percent of the building footprint, serve the enterprise functions of the on-site property owner rather than leasing storage or processing to third parties, and are not in a separate stand-alone structure. Before a data center is built in a Planned Area Development district, the property owner must notify residents and homeowners associations within a half-mile radius by mail, and the operator must hold two neighborhood meetings with posted signs. A third-party acoustic engineer must document baseline sound levels before the first meeting, and the building must include sound mitigation so that emitted sound does not exceed baseline ambient levels. After occupancy, noise studies are required at completion and annually for five years, with results sent to the city. On request, the operator must provide an on-site neighborhood liaison from 8:00 am to 10:00 pm to respond to noise complaints. Backup generator testing and routine operation must be announced on a public website at least 24 hours in advance and notified to the city, generally limited to 9:00 am to 5:00 pm on weekdays except during outages. Sections 3 and 4 repeal conflicting ordinances and provide for severability. The ordinance was adopted by the City Council in December 2022.

title: Arizona HB 2311 (Artificial Intelligence Service, Disclosures, Requirements 2026)
summary_short: Introduced Arizona bill adding chapter 8 on conversational AI services. Operators must disclose AI interaction to minor account holders, prevent sexual and human-simulating statements to minors, offer privacy tools, adopt suicide-response protocols, and not represent services as mental health care. Attorney General enforces civil penalties; effective September 30, 2027.
summary_long: HB 2311 would add chapter 8 to Title 18 of the Arizona Revised Statutes, regulating operators that develop and make available to the public a conversational AI service: AI software or web interfaces that primarily simulate human conversation, excluding developer-, research-, narrow-topic-, business-only, embedded and voice-assistant products. Operators must clearly disclose AI interaction to minor account holders (as a persistent disclaimer, or at session start and at least every three hours) and where a reasonable person would be misled. They must not give minors unpredictable reward incentives to increase engagement, must take reasonable measures to prevent sexual visual material, sexual statements and human-simulating or romantic statements to minors, must offer privacy and account tools to minor account holders and, for those under thirteen, their parents or guardians, must adopt a protocol for suicidal ideation or self-harm prompts including referral to crisis services, and must not knowingly represent that the service is designed to provide professional mental or behavioral health care. A violation is subject to injunction and liability for the greater of actual damages or civil penalties of $1,000 per violation, not exceeding $500,000 per operator. Civil penalties are sought only by the Attorney General, and the section creates no private right of action. The chapter is effective from and after September 30, 2027.

title: Arizona 2024 House Bill 2394
summary_short: Creates a civil cause of action in Arizona for 'digital impersonation': deceptive AI-generated synthetic media that replaces or simulates a person's likeness or voice without consent. Plaintiffs may seek declaratory relief and, in limited cases, injunctive relief and damages. Applies fourteen days after the section's effective date.
summary_long: Adds A.R.S. § 16-1023 creating a civil action for 'digital impersonation': deceptive AI-generated synthetic media that replaces or simulates a person's likeness or voice without consent. Ballot candidates for public or party office and any Arizona citizen may sue within two years of knowing of publication, proving non-consensual publication and either no reasonable conveyance of inauthenticity or non-obviousness to a reasonable person. Paid-advertisement claims lie only against the originator, orderer, placer or payer; interactive computer service providers are shielded for third-party content. Preliminary declaratory relief requires clear and convincing evidence plus one additional element, such as an election within 180 days, a sexual or criminal depiction, or significant personal, financial or reputational harm; court rules within two days, excluding weekends and court holidays. Injunctive relief and damages require further proof, including a sexual depiction, non-public-figure status and actual knowledge or failure to take corrective action within 21 days. Unserved defendants are dismissed after 90 days. Parents or guardians may sue for minors or incapacitated persons. The section must be narrowly construed to protect public discourse and artistic expression, and contested actions for permanent relief or damages carry a jury right. It applies fourteen days after the section's effective date.

title: Arizona 2024 Senate Bill 1359
summary_short: Adds Arizona Revised Statutes section 16-1023. Within ninety days before an election with a candidate on the ballot, creators may not distribute a deceptive, fraudulent deepfake of that candidate unless it carries a clear and conspicuous AI-generated disclosure. Satire, parody and interactive computer services are excluded.
summary_long: SB 1359 adds section 16-1023 to Title 16, chapter 7, article 1 of the Arizona Revised Statutes, concerning election communications. Within ninety days before an election at which a candidate for elected office will appear on the ballot, a person who acts as a creator may not create and distribute a synthetic media message that the person knows is a deceptive and fraudulent deepfake of that candidate on that ballot, unless the message includes a clear and conspicuous disclosure that it includes content generated by artificial intelligence. A creator is a person who uses artificial intelligence or other digital technology to generate synthetic media, and the term excludes providers of the technology used. The prohibition does not apply to media that constitutes satire or parody, or to an interactive computer service as defined in 47 United States Code section 230. A person who fails to make the required disclosure is liable for the civil penalty prescribed by section 16-937, subsection B, for each day the deceptive and fraudulent deepfake is distributed without disclosure. The act defines a deceptive and fraudulent deepfake as synthetic media that depicts a candidate with knowledge of its falsity and intent to injure the candidate's reputation, and that is intentionally calculated to mislead a reasonable person. It contains a severability clause. The text states no effective date.

title: State of Arizona Senate Bill 1565, An Act Amending Sections 16-442, 16-552 and 16-621, Arizona Revised Statutes; Relating to Conduct of Elections.
summary_short: Would amend Arizona election statutes to bar artificial intelligence or learning hardware, firmware and software from voting machines and devices used in federal, state and county elections, from early ballot processing, and from electronic vote adjudication. No effective date appears in the text; registry metadata lists the bill as failed.
summary_long: Senate Bill 1565 would amend three Arizona Revised Statutes provisions on election administration. Section 1 amends A.R.S. 16-442: machines, devices, firmware or software used in the state may not include artificial intelligence or learning components; the secretary of state must adopt standards for loss of certification after consulting a committee; the secretary of state may revoke certification or prohibit for up to five years the purchase, lease or use of a voting system in connection with federal, state or county elections; and emergency certification of an upgrade is limited to six months. Section 2 amends A.R.S. 16-552: artificial intelligence or learning software or firmware may not be used in processing early ballots or by the early election board in verifying the voter's affidavit. Section 3 amends A.R.S. 16-621: any electronic vote adjudication feature may not include artificial intelligence or learning software or firmware; the county officer must provide live video recording of ballot custody in tabulation rooms for statewide, county and legislative elections, contingent on legislative appropriation; and chain-of-custody records must be kept from early voting through provisional tabulation. The text states no effective date. Registry metadata records the bill as failed.](string-placeholder)}]}</br>{

title: City of Tucson Ordinance No. 12188 -- Tucson Code Ch. 27, Secs. 27-20 and 27-21: Large Quantity Water Users
summary_short: From 19 August 2025, Tucson Code Secs. 27-20 and 27-21 govern large quantity water users (10,000+ ccf monthly). Users need Mayor and Council approval of a conservation plan before new connections or meter upsizing, stay within 120% of approved use, and face civil sanctions up to 2000% of monthly charges.
summary_long: Ordinance No. 12188, adopted and effective 19 August 2025, adds Tucson Code Sections 27-20 and 27-21 on large quantity water users. Large quantity water users may not connect to City water except under Section 27-20. Applicants projecting or reaching 10,000 ccf per month, or upsizing meters to that level, must submit a water service application and conservation plan. The Director reviews applications against criteria including efficiency, water availability, economic benefit, a 30 percent reclaimed-water offset (unless the Director sets another figure), and assured water supply; the Mayor and Council approve, deny or return them. Approved applications become binding water service contracts. Users must submit updated plans every five years. Use above 120 percent of the approved amount is prohibited, and the Director may suspend service for violations. Section 27-21 sets civil sanctions of up to 200, 500, 1000 or 2000 percent of monthly charges, rising with repeat violations or duration. After a second violation, Tucson Water may install a flow-restricting device at the user's expense. Users must repay civil penalties and costs the City incurs from their violations. Section 6 declares an emergency. The text does not mention artificial intelligence or computing facilities.
text_version: Ordinance No. 12188 as adopted by Mayor and Council, 19 August 2025

title: Implementation of Additional Export Controls: Certain Advanced Computing and Semiconductor Manufacturing Items; Supercomputer and Semiconductor End Use; Entity List Modification
summary_short: Interim final rule amending the Export Administration Regulations to license exports, reexports and in-country transfers of advanced computing chips, related computers and semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China; adds supercomputer and chip-fab end-use controls, Entity List foreign-direct-product rules and a temporary supply-chain general license, effective 7–21 October 2022.
summary_long: Interim final rule of the Bureau of Industry and Security amending the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Adds ECCNs 3A090, 4A090 and related software and technology, and 3B090 for certain semiconductor manufacturing equipment, to the Commerce Control List with regional stability (RS) license requirements for exports, reexports and in-country transfers to China, subject to a presumption of denial. Adds Advanced computing and Supercomputer foreign direct product rules (§ 734.9(h), (i)) and a footnote 4 Entity List FDP rule. Adds § 744.23 end-use prohibitions for supercomputers and certain PRC chip fabrication facilities, with no license exceptions and a BIS 'is informed' mechanism. Amends § 744.6 to inform U.S. persons that certain support activities require a license. Expands license requirements for 28 Entity List entities in China. Creates a temporary general license for supply-chain activities from 21 October 2022 to 7 April 2023 and a model certification in supplement no. 1 to part 734. Most provisions take effect 7, 12 or 21 October 2022; comments were due 12 December 2022.

title: Implementation of Additional Export Controls: Certain Advanced Computing Items; Supercomputer and Semiconductor End Use; Updates and Corrections
summary_short: Interim final rule amending the Export Administration Regulations to revise export controls on advanced computing integrated circuits, computer commodities containing them, and supercomputers, plus related end-use and U.S.-person rules. Binds exporters and foreign manufacturers; effective November 17, 2023.
summary_long: Interim final rule, published October 25, 2023 in the Federal Register, amending the Export Administration Regulations (15 CFR parts 732 to 774) to revise the October 7, 2022 controls on advanced computing integrated circuits, computer commodities containing them, and supercomputers. It replaces the 3A090 parameters with total processing performance and performance density thresholds, adds License Exception Notified Advanced Computing (NAC) with prior notification for exports to Macau and Country Group D:5, and adds .z items paragraphs to nine ECCNs. Regional stability license requirements are extended to destinations in Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5 not also in A:5 or A:6, with presumption-of-approval or presumption-of-denial license review policies. The rule broadens the advanced computing foreign direct product rule and the section 744.23 end-use controls to entities headquartered in Macau or Country Group D:5, expands the section 744.6 U.S.-person activity controls, requires .z classification in export filings and commercial invoices, and adds five red flags. It is effective November 17, 2023, except one amendatory instruction effective through January 1, 2026; comments are due December 18, 2023.

title: Expansion of End-User Controls To Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
summary_short: Interim final rule extending Export Administration Regulations end-user license requirements to foreign entities at least 50 percent owned by Entity List, Military End-User List or designated SDN parties. Effective 29 September 2025, it applies to exporters, reexporters and transferors dealing with those affiliates.
summary_long: Interim final rule by the Bureau of Industry and Security amending parts 732, 734, 736, 744 and 748 of the Export Administration Regulations, effective 29 September 2025. It replaces the prior 'legally distinct' standard with a 50 percent ownership rule (the Affiliates rule): foreign entities owned 50 percent or more, directly or indirectly and in aggregate, by Entity List, MEU List or SDN parties are subject to the same license requirements as those parties, and the most restrictive owner's requirements apply. Where an exporter cannot determine the ownership percentage, it must resolve new Red Flag 29, obtain a license or identify a license exception before proceeding. Further provisions cover license application content (supplement no. 2 to part 748, marking 'Affiliates rule'), requests by affiliates to modify owners' listings (sections 744.16(e) and 744.21(b)(2)), and supplement no. 8 guidelines. A temporary general license (General Order No. 7) authorizes certain transactions involving non-listed affiliates; the preamble summary gives its expiry as November 28, 2025, while the regulatory text says December 1, 2025. A savings clause covers shipments en route on 29 September 2025 until 29 October 2025. The End-User Review Committee may grant case-by-case exceptions.

title: Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion
summary_short: BIS interim final rule, effective 13 January 2025 (compliance from 15 May 2025), amending the Export Administration Regulations to require licences worldwide for advanced computing chips and for weights of closed AI models trained on 10^26 or more operations, with country compute allocations, new license exceptions and data-center VEU authorizations.
summary_long: The rule extends licensing of advanced computing chips (ECCN 3A090.a, 4A090.a and corresponding .z items) to all destinations and creates ECCN 4E091 for the parameters (weights) of AI models trained with 10^26 or more operations, excluding published weights and models less capable than the most advanced published model; foreign-direct-product rules reach foreign-produced items. License review is tiered by destination and headquarters: presumption of approval for 18 listed destinations plus the United States (Supplement No. 5 to part 740), presumption of denial for Country Group D:5 and Macau, and for all other destinations approval up to a per-country allocation of 790,000,000 TPP for 2025-2027 (raisable up to 100% with government assurances). New license exceptions: AIA (listed destinations, including model weights stored in secure facilities), ACM (development and production by private end users) and LPP (up to 26,900,000 TPP per consignee per year). Universal and National Data Center VEU authorizations carry compute caps (quarterly NVEU allocations; UVEU limits of 25%, 7% and 50% of compute outside listed countries) and conditions on ownership, supply chains, training location, model-weight storage, NIST 800-53/FedRAMP High security, personnel vetting and semi-annual reporting. Breaches may lead to revocation of VEU status and denial of licences.
text_version: original interim final rule as published in the Federal Register (2025-01-15), effective 2025-01-13; no consolidated (eCFR) version used

title: Establishment of Reporting Requirements for the Development of Advanced Artificial Intelligence Models and Computing Clusters
summary_short: Proposed BIS rule adding 15 CFR 702.7 to require covered U.S. persons to notify the Department quarterly of planned AI model training runs above 10^26 operations or qualifying computing clusters, and to answer BIS questions on model security and safety.
summary_long: The proposed rule amends 15 CFR part 702 by adding section 702.7 on on-going reporting for advanced AI development. Covered U.S. persons, defined to include U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, entities organized under U.S. law (including foreign branches), and persons located in the United States, must email BIS each quarter (April 15, July 15, October 15, January 15) if they conduct or plan within six months an AI training run above 10^26 computational operations, or acquire or develop a computing cluster with data center networking above 300 Gbit/s and a theoretical maximum above 10^20 OP/s for AI training without sparsity. Each notification identifies planned activities for the following six months. Covered persons must answer BIS questions within 30 calendar days, correct incomplete filings within 14 calendar days of BIS notice, answer clarification questions within seven calendar days, and submit quarterly affirmations of no applicable activities for up to seven quarters. BIS questions may address training, ownership and protection of model weights, red-team results, and safety and reliability of dual-use foundation models. Section 702.7(c) defines terms including AI model, AI system, AI red-teaming, dual-use foundation model, model weights and training run. The text states no effective date and no penalties.

title: Expansion of Validated End User Authorization: Data Center Validated End User Authorization
summary_short: Amends the Export Administration Regulations to add a Data Center Validated End User (VEU) authorization allowing exports and reexports of controlled items for data centers to preapproved end users in destinations requiring a license, excluding D:5 countries and 600 series items. Effective 2 October 2024.
summary_long: The rule adds a Data Center Validated End User (VEU) Authorization to the Export Administration Regulations, effective 2 October 2024, alongside the existing General VEU Authorization for China and India. It permits exports and reexports of Commerce Control List items that require a license to destinations other than Country Group D:5 (excluding 600 series items) for use in data centers, to end users approved by the End-User Review Committee and listed in Supplement No. 7 to part 748. Applicants submit an advisory opinion request with the information in Supplement No. 8, including security and information-security plans, a supply-chain risk plan and a list of current and potential customers; the committee's evaluation includes whether the host country has given assurances on safe and secure use. Exporters must obtain end-use certifications before a first export. Reexporters and Data Center VEU end users file semiannual reports with BIS, and records are subject to review and on-site inspection. Items may be used at the end user's own facility in an authorized destination, consumed, or reexported only as BIS authorizes; in-country transfers are restricted, and part 744 activities are barred. Authorizations may be revised, suspended or revoked.

title: Additions and Modifications to the Entity List; Removals From the Validated End-User (VEU) Program
summary_short: Final rule adding 140 entities to the US Entity List (China, Japan, Singapore, South Korea), modifying 14 existing entries, and removing three entities from the Validated End-User program. Listed parties face export license requirements, generally with a presumption of denial, effective 2 December 2024.
summary_long: The rule amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to add 140 entities to the Entity List, under China, Japan, Singapore and South Korea, and to modify 14 existing China entries. Listed entities face a license requirement for all items subject to the EAR, generally with a presumption of denial. Nine added entries and seven modified entries carry a Footnote 5 designation, which also covers foreign-produced items subject to the EAR under § 734.9(e)(3). Wuhan Xinxin Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited is eligible for License Exception RFF. The rule removes CSMC Technologies Corporation, Shanghai Huahong Grace Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation and Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment, Inc., China from the Validated End-User program (supplement no. 7 to part 748). Shipments en route may proceed under prior eligibility until January 2, 2025 (January 31, 2025 for Footnote 5-related changes). The rule is effective December 2, 2024; Footnote 5-related Entity List requirements have a compliance date of December 31, 2024. Authority cited is Export Control Reform Act of 2018 sections 1753 and 1754. BIS estimates 200 additional annual license applications.

title: Foreign-Produced Direct Product Rule Additions, and Refinements to Controls for Advanced Computing and Semiconductor Manufacturing Items
summary_short: Interim final rule amending the Export Administration Regulations (EAR), effective 2 December 2024, adding foreign direct product rules, license requirements and exceptions for advanced-node chip manufacturing equipment, high-bandwidth memory and software keys. Obligations fall on exporters, reexporters and transferors.
summary_long: Interim final rule amending the Export Administration Regulations (EAR), effective 2 December 2024. It adds two foreign direct product (FDP) rules in § 734.9 covering foreign-produced semiconductor manufacturing equipment and items for Entity List Footnote 5 entities, with de minimis provisions and license requirements in § 744.11. It adds ECCN 3A090.c, controlling high-bandwidth memory above a stated memory bandwidth density, together with a License Exception HBM that requires reporting of discrepancies. It adds a License Exception Restricted Fabrication Facility (RFF) with 45-day pre-shipment notifications, installation reports and annual end-use confirmations. It adds eight Red Flags to supplement no. 3 to part 732, redefines advanced-node DRAM integrated circuits, extends § 744.23 end-use controls, and provides that software license keys follow the controls of the software or hardware they unlock. Some changes have compliance dates of 2 or 31 December 2024, and comments were due 31 January 2025.

title: Implementation of Additional Due Diligence Measures for Advanced Computing Integrated Circuits; Amendments and Clarifications; and Extension of Comment Period
summary_short: Interim final rule amending the Export Administration Regulations, effective 16 January 2025, for front-end fabricators and OSAT companies exporting advanced logic ICs under ECCN 3A090.a. Adds a worldwide license requirement, a presumption rebuttable through approved IC designer or OSAT lists or attestations, quarterly reporting, and a KYC form.
summary_long: Interim final rule amending the Export Administration Regulations, effective 16 January 2025; compliance with revised text from 31 January 2025. Front-end fabricators and OSAT companies exporting applicable advanced logic ICs under ECCN 3A090.a need a license for any destination worldwide, and such ICs are presumed to be 3A090.a items designed or marketed for datacenters. The presumption can be overcome through an approved or authorized IC designer, a front-end fabricator attestation on aggregated approximated transistor count, or an approved OSAT attestation. Supplements no. 6 and 7 to part 740 list named approved IC designers and approved OSAT companies. License Exceptions AIA and ACM cover 3A090.a items only when designed by an approved or authorized designer. Section 743.9 requires front-end fabricators to file quarterly reports to BIS, first due 31 May 2025, with a KYC vetting form (supplement no. 2 to part 743). Section 748.16 sets an advisory-opinion process for list changes. The rule adds definitions in §772.1, revises the advanced-node DRAM definition, amends the December 2024 FDP IFR, and extends its comment period to 14 March 2025.

title: Revision to License Review Policy for Advanced Computing Commodities
summary_short: BIS final rule, effective 15 January 2026, moves licence review for exports to China or Macau of certain advanced AI chips (TPP below 21,000, total DRAM bandwidth below 6,500 GB/s) from a presumption of denial to case-by-case review, conditional on exporter certifications and independent third-party testing.
summary_long: Final rule by the Bureau of Industry and Security amending the Export Administration Regulations (15 CFR parts 742, 744 and 748), effective 15 January 2026. For exports from the United States of advanced computing commodities with a TPP below 21,000 and total DRAM bandwidth below 6,500 GB/s destined to end-users in China or Macau, § 742.6(b)(10)(iii)(A)(1) replaces the presumption of denial with case-by-case review, if the applicant submits the certifications in Supplement No. 2 to Part 748, paragraph (dd). Certifications cover units shipped in the United States, sufficient US supply, no diversion of foundry capacity, aggregate shipments to China and Macau no more than 50 percent of US end-use shipments, exclusion of military and WMD end uses, Know Your Customer procedures, a list of IaaS remote end users in listed countries, physical security, and review of each shipment by a US-based independent third-party testing lab. BIS may revoke a lab's qualification, which suspends the policy for exporters using it. The presumption of denial continues for Macau, Country Group D:5 destinations, entities headquartered there, reexports and in-country transfers, and applications lacking the certification. Section 744.23(d) and section 748.8 receive conforming changes. Notice-and-comment is waived under ECRA section 1762.

title: Export Controls on Semiconductor Manufacturing Items
summary_short: Interim final rule, effective 17 November 2023, amending the EAR to control semiconductor manufacturing equipment and related technology: adds license requirements for Macau and Country Group D:5 destinations, removes ECCN 3B090, narrows end-use and U.S.-person controls, and adds a temporary general license.
summary_long: Interim final rule published 25 October 2023 by the Bureau of Industry and Security, amending the Export Administration Regulations on semiconductor manufacturing equipment (SME). It removes ECCN 3B090 and places its items in revised ECCNs 3B001 and 3B002. National Security and Regional Stability license requirements apply to exports, reexports and in-country transfers of these items and related software and technology to Macau and Country Group D:5 destinations. A 0% de minimis rule covers certain lithography equipment used for advanced-node integrated circuits, unless the origin country controls it equivalently. License exceptions are restricted. Section 744.23 end-use controls are restructured and the SME control is narrowed to front-end production equipment in specified ECCNs, with exclusions for back-end steps and masks. Section 744.6 U.S.-person restrictions are revised, with exclusions for U.S. persons working for U.S. or Country Group A:5 or A:6-headquartered companies. A temporary general license covers certain SME parts and components through 31 December 2025, and its paragraph (d) is removed effective 1 January 2026. New section 772.1 definitions cover advanced-node integrated circuits and extreme ultraviolet. Most provisions take effect 17 November 2023.

title: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
summary_short: Final rule amending the Export Administration Regulations, effective 10 July 2026, to move the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 to Country Group A:5. License Exception STA becomes available for approved UAE government and commercial entities, and license requirements for advanced computing items to the UAE are kept except for approved recipients.
summary_long: Final rule of the Bureau of Industry and Security, effective 10 July 2026, amending the Export Administration Regulations (15 CFR parts 740, 742 and 774) for the United Arab Emirates. It removes the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4, which lifts certain license-exception limits and missile-related end-use restrictions, and adds it to Country Group A:5. Under new § 740.2(a)(26), License Exception STA is available for UAE exports only to ultimate consignees and end users listed in new Supplement no. 8 to part 740. That supplement lists UAE government agencies (from 10 July 2026), two UAE-based AI companies, and named U.S.-headquartered AI companies and their UAE subsidiaries, which may receive advanced computing items license-free. The license requirement for advanced computing items to or within the UAE (§ 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(B)) is retained, except for these approved recipients. Other UAE entities may request an advisory opinion under § 748.3(c). The authorization for G42 and Core42 expires on 6 April 2027 absent notice by BIS. The rule also covers recordkeeping and Paperwork Reduction Act burden estimates and states that it is exempt from notice-and-comment requirements.

title: Revocation of Validated End-User Authorizations in the People's Republic of China
summary_short: US Bureau of Industry and Security final rule removing Intel Semiconductor (Dalian) Ltd, Samsung China Semiconductor Co. Ltd and SK hynix Semiconductor (China) Ltd from the Validated End-User authorization list in Supplement No. 7 to part 748 of the EAR. Effective December 31, 2025. Affects exports to those facilities.
summary_long: A final rule of the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), U.S. Department of Commerce, amends the Export Administration Regulations (15 CFR Part 748) to revise the Validated End-User (VEU) Authorizations list for the People's Republic of China. It removes three facilities, Intel Semiconductor (Dalian) Ltd, Samsung China Semiconductor Co. Ltd and SK hynix Semiconductor (China) Ltd, by deleting their entries under China from Supplement No. 7 to part 748. The rule states that the End-User Review Committee determined the removals under § 748.15 and supplement no. 9 to part 748. It is effective December 31, 2025. BIS cites Section 1762(a) of the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 as allowing the change to be imposed in a final rule without prior notice and comment, and estimates an additional 1,000 license applications annually as a result of the removals. The document as fetched also contains unrelated Federal Register rules (a Syria rule under § 746.9 and a Department of Labor rescission), which are outside this annotation.

title: AB 1043, Digital Age Assurance Act
summary_short: California AB 1043 (Digital Age Assurance Act), operative January 1, 2027, requires operating system providers to obtain account-holder age information and send age-bracket signals to app developers, requires developers to request and apply those signals, and provides Attorney General civil penalties for violations.
summary_long: AB 1043 (Statutes of 2025, ch. 675) adds the Digital Age Assurance Act, Civil Code Sections 1798.500 to 1798.505, operative January 1, 2027. Operating system providers must offer an account-setup interface for an account holder to indicate the user's birth date or age, and a real-time interface giving developers a signal of one of four age brackets (under 13, 13 to under 16, 16 to under 18, 18 and over), limiting data sharing to purposes required by the title. Developers must request a signal when an application is downloaded and launched, are deemed to have actual knowledge of the user's age range, and treat the signal as the primary age indicator unless they hold clear and convincing contrary information. Existing devices and applications have a July 1, 2027 compliance date. Operating system providers and covered application stores must not treat their own apps more favorably than third-party apps and must not use third-party data collected under the title to compete against those third parties. Broadband, telecommunications and physical products are excluded. The Attorney General may seek an injunction and civil penalties of up to $2,500 per affected child for negligent violations or $7,500 for intentional violations.

title: Leading Ethical AI Development (LEAD) for Kids Act
summary_short: Establishes a LEAD for Kids Standards Board and imposes risk-based duties on developers and deployers of AI systems used by or applied to Californian children: registration, assessments, labels, incident reports, audits and limits on child data use, from 1 July 2028. Enforced through Attorney General civil penalties and child lawsuits.
summary_long: Adds Chapter 25.1 (the LEAD for Kids Act) to the Business and Professions Code. It creates the LEAD for Kids Standards Board, which must adopt regulations by January 1, 2028 on risk levels (prohibited, high, moderate, low), assessments, information labels, audit standards, incident reporting and a public registry. By July 1, 2028, developers of covered AI products must register them, submit risk assessments, issue labels and report incidents within 30 days. Covered products are subject to independent third-party audits from July 1, 2028. Prohibited-risk products require reasonable steps to keep children from accessing them. Developers may not knowingly or recklessly use a child's personal information for training without consent of the child (aged 13 to under 16) or parent or guardian (under 13). Developers, deployers and contractors may not retaliate against employees who report violations to the Attorney General. The Attorney General may seek $25,000 civil penalties per violation after board referral, and children harmed by a covered product, or their parents, may bring civil actions for damages. Registration fees may not exceed regulatory costs. Duplicative requirements under other state risk-assessment laws need not be met.

title: California AB-1170
summary_short: Amends the California Consumer Privacy Act's definitions and rulemaking directions, including on automated decisionmaking, and requires developers of generative AI systems made available to Californians to post training-data documentation by 1 January 2026. Also convenes an education AI working group reporting by 1 January 2027.
summary_long: Sec. 27 and Sec. 28 amend the California Consumer Privacy Act (Civil Code 1798.140 and 1798.185). They revise definitions, including profiling, personal information (which covers inferences and AI systems capable of outputting personal information) and sensitive personal information. They direct the California Privacy Protection Agency to adopt regulations on access and opt-out rights for automated decisionmaking, annual cybersecurity audits and risk assessments for processing presenting significant risk, and opt-out preference signals. Civil and administrative enforcement of the amended provisions may not commence before 1 July 2023. Sec. 46 (Education Code 33328.5) requires the Superintendent to convene an artificial intelligence working group that develops guidance by 1 January 2026, a model policy by 1 July 2026 and a report by 1 January 2027; the section is repealed on 1 January 2031. Sec. 35 (Civil Code 3111) requires developers of generative AI systems released on or after 1 January 2022 and made publicly available to Californians to post training-data documentation on their websites by 1 January 2026 and before each later release or substantial modification. The documentation covers data sources, copyright status, personal and aggregate consumer information, cleaning and synthetic data use. Exemptions cover systems whose sole purpose is security and integrity, aircraft operation in national airspace, and federal national-security or defense uses.

title: California (2017) AB 1444
summary_short: Authorizes the Livermore Amador Valley Transit Authority, with or without a private entity, to test shared autonomous vehicles without a driver seat, steering wheel or pedals within the City of Dublin. Testing requires insurance of $5,000,000, a Department of Motor Vehicles submission, and speeds under 35 mph. Inoperative May 1, 2018; repealed January 1, 2019.
summary_long: Adds Vehicle Code Section 38756, which authorizes the Livermore Amador Valley Transit Authority to conduct a shared autonomous vehicle (SAV) demonstration project for vehicles without a driver seat, steering wheel, brake pedal or accelerator. Testing is limited to the City of Dublin and the vehicles must operate at speeds of less than 35 miles per hour. Before testing on public roads, the authority or a private entity must obtain insurance, surety bond or proof of self-insurance of $5,000,000 and provide evidence to the Department of Motor Vehicles, and must submit a detailed testing program. The program must cover controlled-condition testing, local authority approval of the area and conditions, operation only in the authorized area, compliance with federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards or an NHTSA exemption, a communication link to a remote operator, and a law enforcement interaction plan. The operator must disclose to participants what personal information the vehicle collects.
