The department may require data collection, including accident reports within 10 days and an annual report on unplanned technology disengagements. The demonstration project may not be conducted if the department adopts regulations under Section 38750 by December 31, 2017. The section becomes inoperative on May 1, 2018 and is repealed as of January 1, 2019.

title: California AB 1777 (Autonomous vehicles)
summary_short: California statute amending the Vehicle Code so that autonomous vehicles may be tested and deployed on public roads only under Department of Motor Vehicles approval, insurance and certification requirements, with emergency-response duties for manufacturers from July 1, 2026.
summary_long: Amends Vehicle Code section 38750 and adds sections 38751, 38752 and 38753. Defines autonomous technology, autonomous vehicles (SAE Level 3, 4 or 5), manufacturer and operator. Testing on public roads is allowed by designated personnel with a licensed driver seated in the driver's seat, provided the manufacturer holds 5 million dollars in insurance, surety bond or self-insurance. Other operation requires the department's approval of the manufacturer's application, which must include certifications on engagement mechanisms, visual indicators, failure alerts, operator takeover, federal safety standards, and at least 30 seconds of read-only sensor data retained for three years after a collision. The department adopts regulations, may impose additional requirements (including for vehicles without a driver), and must post public notice 30 days before approvals under the regulations. Federal NHTSA regulations prevail in conflict. Manufacturers must give purchasers a written disclosure of collected information and the department may assess a cost-recovery fee. From January 1, 2030, light vehicles of model year 2031 or later may operate only under a deployment permit if zero-emission. Section 38751 (operative July 1, 2026) requires an emergency telephone line answered within 30 seconds, two-way communication devices, remote operators able to immobilize vehicles, law enforcement override access with training, and direction to leave an area within two minutes of an emergency geofencing message. Section 38752 lets peace officers issue notices of autonomous vehicle noncompliance, which manufacturers must provide to the department within 72 hours; it is inoperative until regulations are adopted.

title: California Assembly Bill 1831 (2024)
summary_short: Amends California Penal Code §§ 311–311.12 so child sexual abuse material and obscenity offenses also cover digitally altered or AI-generated depictions of what appears to be a person under 18; adds an AI definition. Operative only if SB 1381 is enacted and takes effect on or before January 1, 2025.
summary_long: Adds legislative findings on AI-generated child sexual abuse material (Sec. 1) and amends Penal Code §§ 311, 311.2, 311.11 and 311.12. Section 311 adds a definition of artificial intelligence. Section 311.2 covers matter containing digitally altered or AI-generated content that depicts, or appears to depict, a person under 18 in sexual conduct: subdivision (b) makes commercial sending, distribution or exhibition of obscene matter a felony (two, three or six years in state prison, a fine up to $100,000, or both); subdivision (c) covers distribution to adults (misdemeanor, up to one year in county jail, fine up to $2,000, or state prison; felony after a prior conviction); subdivision (d) covers distribution to persons under 18 (felony). Section 311.11 penalizes possession or control of such matter (felony; fine up to $2,500), with enhanced penalties for prior convictions and listed aggravating factors. Section 311.12 adds a fine up to $2,000 for offenses involving government-owned computers or property. Exemptions cover law enforcement, certain medical, scientific or educational activities, and emancipated minors (§ 311.2(e)–(f)). Section 7 makes the act operative only if SB 1381 (2023–24) is enacted and takes effect on or before January 1, 2025.

title: California AB 1836
summary_short: Amends California Civil Code § 3344.1 to impose liability on persons who produce, distribute or make available a deceased personality's digital replica in expressive audiovisual works or sound recordings without consent, with listed exemptions. Effective date not stated in the provided text.
summary_long: Section 1 states legislative intent to protect intellectual property from exploitation. Section 2 amends Civil Code § 3344.1 on use of a deceased personality's name, voice, signature, photograph or likeness. Subdivision (a)(1) makes unconsented use on products, merchandise, goods, advertising or solicitation liable for the greater of $750 or actual damages, plus profits not counted in actual damages; punitive damages and attorney's fees are available. Subdivision (a)(2) makes a person who produces, distributes or makes available a digital replica of a deceased personality's voice or likeness in an expressive audiovisual work or sound recording without consent liable for the greater of $10,000 or actual damages, unless an exception applies: news, public affairs or sports broadcasts; comment, criticism, scholarship, satire or parody; certain documentary or biographical representations; fleeting or incidental use; or advertisements for such works. A digital replica is defined as a computer-generated, highly realistic, readily identifiable representation. Other subdivisions cover transferability and succession of rights, a 70-year post-death limit, claims registration with the Secretary of State, cumulative remedies, application to acts occurring directly in California, and retroactivity for personalities who died before January 1, 1985. The document reproduces the amended section in full and does not mark which text is new.

title: AB 2013, Generative artificial intelligence: training data transparency
summary_short: Requires developers of generative AI systems made publicly available to Californians to post on their websites documentation of their training data, on or before January 1, 2026 and before each later release or substantial modification. Exempts certain security, aviation and defense systems.
summary_long: Adds Title 15.2 (Sections 3110 and 3111) to the Civil Code. Section 3110 defines artificial intelligence, developer, generative artificial intelligence, substantial modification, synthetic data generation and training of a generative AI system. Section 3111 requires a developer of a generative AI system or service released on or after January 1, 2022 that is made publicly available to Californians for use to post on its website documentation of the data used to train it. The posting duty applies on or before January 1, 2026 and before each later release or substantial modification. The documentation must include a high-level summary of the datasets: sources or owners, how they further the intended purpose, approximate number of data points, types of data points, whether they include copyright, trademark or patent protected data or are entirely public domain, whether they were purchased or licensed, whether they include personal information or aggregate consumer information, any cleaning or modification, the collection period, first-use dates, and any use of synthetic data generation. Exempt are systems whose sole purpose is security and integrity, systems whose sole purpose is operating aircraft in the national airspace, and systems developed for national security, military or defense purposes and made available only to a federal entity. The provided text contains no penalty or enforcement provision.

title: AB 2355, Political Reform Act of 1974: political advertisements: artificial intelligence
summary_short: Adds Gov. Code § 84514: committees that create, originally publish or distribute a qualified political advertisement containing AI-generated or substantially altered image, audio or video must include a prescribed AI disclosure. The Commission may seek injunctive relief or pursue administrative or civil remedies for non-compliance.
summary_long: Adds Government Code section 84514 to the Political Reform Act of 1974. Under subdivision (a), a committee, as defined in Section 82013, that creates, originally publishes or originally distributes a qualified political advertisement must include the disclosure “Ad generated or substantially altered using artificial intelligence” in a clear and conspicuous manner, displayed or spoken as prescribed in Sections 84504 to 84504.5, as applicable. A qualified political advertisement is one containing any image, audio or video generated or substantially altered using artificial intelligence. Media is entirely created by AI if it would falsely appear authentic to a reasonable person, or materially altered if the alteration would give a reasonable person a fundamentally different understanding; immaterial alterations such as cosmetic adjustments, colour edits, cropping or resizing are excluded. If a committee does not comply, the Commission may seek injunctive relief under Section 90009 or pursue administrative or civil remedies under Chapter 3 or Chapter 11, but a violation is not a misdemeanor. The section does not alter rights, obligations or immunities of interactive service providers under 47 U.S.C. Section 230. The text states no effective date of its own.

title: AB 2655, Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act of 2024
summary_short: Requires large online platforms to remove or label materially deceptive election deepfakes and to run a reporting process for Californians, during periods before and after California elections. Allows candidates, officials and prosecutors to seek injunctive relief against platforms.
summary_long: Adds Chapter 7 (Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act of 2024) to the Elections Code and amends Code of Civil Procedure § 35 to give precedence to actions under it. Covers large online platforms (public-facing websites, apps or search engines with at least 1,000,000 California users in the preceding 12 months) and audio or visual materially deceptive content, including deepfakes and chatbot output. Platforms must use state-of-the-art techniques to remove, within 72 hours of a report, deceptive content depicting candidates, elections officials or elected officials, from 120 days before a California election through election day (60 days after for elections-official content). A candidate may avoid removal of self-portrayals by including a 'manipulated' disclosure. Platforms must label other deceptive election content, within 72 hours of a report, from six months before an election. They must provide a reporting channel for California residents and respond within 36 hours. Candidates, elected and elections officials, the Attorney General, and district or city attorneys may seek injunctive relief. Newspapers, broadcasting stations and satire or parody are exempt. The text sets no fines.

title: AB 2839, Elections: deceptive media in advertisements
summary_short: Adds Elections Code § 20012 barring knowing, malicious distribution of materially deceptive audio or visual content (deepfakes) about California candidates, election officials and voting equipment within set periods before elections, unless labelled; allows injunctions and damages. Urgency statute, immediate effect.
summary_long: Adds Elections Code § 20012 (Sec. 3). From 120 days before a California election, and for content about elections officials and voting equipment through 60 days after, a person, committee or other entity may not knowingly and with malice distribute an advertisement or other election communication with materially deceptive audio or visual content depicting a candidate, elections official, elected official, or voting equipment. Exceptions apply where a 'This ____ has been manipulated' disclosure is included, for satire or parody with a labelled disclosure, and for certain broadcasting stations, newspapers and interactive computer services. Removing required disclosures is prohibited. Recipients, candidates, committees and elections officials may seek injunctions with attorney's fees, or damages, on clear and convincing evidence. Sections 1, 1.5, 2 and 2.5 amend Code of Civil Procedure § 35 to give election-related actions precedence, in versions that depend on Assembly Bill 2655. Sec. 6 declares an urgency statute effective immediately.

title: California Assembly Bill 2876 (2024)
summary_short: Amends California Education Code § 33548 so the commission shall consider adding AI literacy, media literacy and related content to curriculum frameworks and instructional-material criteria, with timing keyed to revisions after January 1, 2024 or 2025.
summary_long: Amends Education Code § 33548, which defines 'Artificial Intelligence (AI) literacy', 'digital citizenship' and 'media literacy' (subd. (a)). For the English language arts/English language development framework, the commission shall consider, when next revised after January 1, 2024, incorporating the Model Library Standards and media literacy content at each grade level (subd. (b)). For the mathematics, science and history-social science frameworks and related instructional-material criteria, the commission shall consider incorporating media literacy content when those frameworks are next revised or materials next adopted after January 1, 2024 or 2025 (subd. (c)). Subdivision (d) provides that the commission shall consider incorporating AI literacy content into the mathematics, science and history-social science frameworks when those frameworks are next revised after January 1, 2025, and shall consider including AI literacy in its criteria for evaluating instructional materials when those materials are next adopted after January 1, 2025. The operative duties are phrased as 'consider', not as a requirement to adopt. The text states no penalties, enforcement mechanism or private right of action.

title: California Assembly Bill 2905 (2024)
summary_short: Amends California Public Utilities Code § 2874 so that automated calls using an automatic dialing-announcing device must, after a natural voice announcement, inform the person called if the prerecorded message uses an artificial voice, and defines artificial intelligence and artificial voice. Effective date not stated in text.
summary_long: AB 2905 amends Section 2874 of the California Public Utilities Code, which governs telephone calls placed with an automatic dialing-announcing device. Under the amended section, such a device may be operated only after an unrecorded, natural voice announcement by the calling person. The announcement must state the nature of the call and the name, address and telephone number of the business or organization represented, if any, and ask whether the called person consents to hear the prerecorded message. It must also inform the called person if the prerecorded message uses an artificial voice. The calling person must disconnect the device when the call terminates. Subdivision (c) defines artificial intelligence as an engineered or machine-based system that varies in its level of autonomy and can infer from its input how to generate outputs that influence physical or virtual environments, and defines an artificial voice as a voice generated or significantly altered using artificial intelligence. The text states no penalty, enforcement authority or private right of action. Section 2 states that no state reimbursement is required under Article XIII B, Section 6 of the California Constitution, because any local agency or school district costs arise from creating, eliminating or changing the penalty for a crime or infraction. The effective date is not stated in the text.

title: California AB 2930 (Automated decision systems)
summary_short: Bill adding Business and Professions Code Chapter 25 on automated decision systems used in consequential decisions such as employment and government benefits. Requires developers and deployers to perform impact assessments, give notice and explanations, and mitigate algorithmic discrimination risk; Civil Rights Department enforces via civil action.
summary_long: AB 2930 adds Business and Professions Code Chapter 25 on automated decision systems (ADS) used to make, or be a substantial factor in, consequential decisions about government benefits or services, government penalties, or employment (pay, promotion, hiring, termination, task allocation). Deployers must perform impact assessments before first deployment and annually; developers must do so before making a system available and give deployers results and documentation. Deployers must notify affected persons, explain the system and its outputs, allow an alternative selection process where feasible, and let persons correct personal data. Both must maintain a governance program against algorithmic discrimination, publish a summary policy, and keep assessments for five years. A system with an identified unmitigated risk of algorithmic discrimination may not be used or made available. Retaliation is unlawful. The Civil Rights Department may investigate and sue for injunctive and declaratory relief, and for algorithmic discrimination violations a $25,000 civil penalty per violation, after 45 days' notice and a cure opportunity. Cybersecurity technology is excluded. The registry lists the bill as failed.

title: An act to add Section 11546.45.5 to the Government Code, relating to automated decision systems
summary_short: Adds Government Code § 11546.45.5, requiring the Department of Technology to inventory high-risk automated decision systems used, developed or procured by California state agencies by September 1, 2024, and to report the inventory annually to legislative committees from January 1, 2025.
summary_long: Adds Government Code section 11546.45.5. It defines automated decision system, high-risk automated decision system, state agency and board, and excludes the University of California, the Legislature, the judicial branch and boards except as provided. By September 1, 2024, the Department of Technology must conduct, in coordination with other interagency bodies as it deems appropriate, an inventory of high-risk automated decision systems proposed for, or in use, development or procurement by state agencies. The inventory must describe each system's decisions and intended benefits, alternatives, research results on efficacy, categories of data and personal information used, and measures in place, if any, to mitigate risks such as cybersecurity risk and biased decisions. From January 1, 2025 and annually thereafter, the department must submit a report of the inventory to the Assembly Committee on Privacy and Consumer Protection and the Senate Committee on Governmental Organization. The reporting requirement becomes inoperative on January 1, 2029. The text sets no penalties and creates no private right of action.

title: AB 3030, Health care services: artificial intelligence
summary_short: Adds Health and Safety Code §1339.75. Health facilities, clinics, physician offices and group practices that use generative AI to generate written or verbal patient communications about clinical information must include an AI disclaimer and instructions for reaching a human provider. Communications reviewed by a licensed provider are exempt.
summary_long: Section 1 adds Chapter 2.13 to Division 2 of the Health and Safety Code. Subdivision (a) applies to health facilities, clinics, physician offices and offices of group practices that use generative artificial intelligence to generate written or verbal patient communications pertaining to patient clinical information. Such communications must include a disclaimer that they were generated by generative AI, placed by medium: at the beginning for letters and emails, throughout for continuous online interactions and video, and at the start and end for audio. They must also give clear instructions on how a patient may contact a human health care provider or other appropriate person. Subdivision (b) exempts communications that a licensed or certified health care provider reads and reviews. Subdivision (c) defines terms including artificial intelligence, generative artificial intelligence, health care provider and patient clinical information, which excludes administrative matters such as scheduling and billing. Subdivision (d) makes violations by licensed health facilities and clinics subject to enforcement mechanisms in the Health and Safety Code chapters cited, and places physicians under the jurisdiction of the Medical Board of California or the Osteopathic Medical Board of California. The text states no effective date.

title: California AB 316 (Artificial intelligence: Defenses 2025)
summary_short: Adds Civil Code § 1714.46: in civil actions against a defendant who developed, modified or used AI alleged to have caused harm, it is not a defense that the AI autonomously caused the harm. Effective date not stated in the text.
summary_long: AB 316 adds Section 1714.46 to the California Civil Code. Subdivision (a) defines "artificial intelligence" as an engineered or machine-based system that varies in its level of autonomy and can, for explicit or implicit objectives, infer from its input how to generate outputs that can influence physical or virtual environments. Subdivision (b) provides that, in an action against a defendant who developed, modified, or used artificial intelligence that is alleged to have caused harm to the plaintiff, it is not a defense, and the defendant may not assert, that the artificial intelligence autonomously caused the harm. Subdivision (c) states that the section does not limit or preclude the defendant from presenting any other affirmative defense, including evidence relevant to causation or foreseeability, or other evidence relevant to the comparative fault of any other person or entity. The text sets no penalties, thresholds or effective date, and operates through civil actions.

title: An act to add Chapter 25 (commencing with Section 22756) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code, relating to artificial intelligence.
summary_short: Would require deployers and developers of automated decision tools, AI used for consequential decisions such as employment, housing, health care, financial services and criminal justice, to document impact assessments by 1 January 2025, give affected persons notice, and not use tools that result in algorithmic discrimination.
summary_long: The bill would add Chapter 25 to the Business and Professions Code on automated decision tools: AI systems developed or marketed to be a controlling factor in consequential decisions such as employment, housing, health care, financial services and criminal justice. Deployers must perform, and developers must document, impact assessments by 1 January 2025 and annually, and assessments go to the Civil Rights Department within 60 days. Deployers must notify affected persons and, where a decision rests solely on the tool, accommodate requests not to be subject to it if technically feasible. Developers must give deployers documentation on known limitations and training data. Both must maintain governance programs and publish policy summaries. Deployers may not use tools that result in algorithmic discrimination; from 1 January 2026 a person may sue a deployer for compensatory damages, declaratory relief and fees, and public attorneys may seek injunctive relief after 45 days' written notice, which may be cured. The Civil Rights Department may impose administrative fines of up to $10,000 per violation. Deployers with fewer than 25 employees are excluded from assessment and governance duties unless the tool impacted more than 999 people per year.

title: California AB 412
summary_short: Proposed California bill AB 412 would require developers of generative AI models offered or used commercially in California to document copyrighted training materials, answer rights-owner requests, and face civil actions of $1,000 per violation for non-compliance. The text states no operative date.
summary_long: AB 412 would add Title 15.3 to Part 4 of Division 3 of the Civil Code on copyrighted materials used for AI training. It defines artificial intelligence, generative AI, covered materials (works registered or indexed with the US Copyright Office), rights owners, developers and approximate content fingerprints. A developer of a GenAI model must document covered materials it knows were used in training, make reasonable efforts to identify others, document rights owners, publish information enabling fingerprint generation, and provide a website mechanism for rights-owner information requests. It must document those requests and retain records for the model's use period plus five years. Within 30 days of a request, the developer must assess fingerprints received and provide lists of covered materials held by the rights owner that it documented or that appear likely in its dataset; each further day of non-compliance is a discrete violation. Rights owners may submit one request per calendar quarter per model. A rights owner that complied in good faith may sue for $1,000 per violation or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus injunctive or declaratory relief and attorney's fees. Models trained only on publicly available data, used only for noncommercial academic or governmental research, not trained on covered materials, or trained only on materials the developer owns are excluded. The text names no enforcing agency and states no operative date.

title: California AB 489 (Health Care Professions: Deceptive Terms or Letters: Artificial Intelligence 2025)
summary_short: Adds Business and Professions Code Chapter 15.5, which prohibits using health-profession license terms in the advertising or functionality of AI or GenAI systems where they imply care is given by a licensed person. Enforced by health care licensing boards; each use is a separate violation.
summary_long: Adds Chapter 15.5 (Health Advice From Artificial Intelligence) to Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code. Section 4999.8 defines AI and GenAI by reference to Government Code Sections 11546.45.5 and 11549.64, and defines health care profession as any profession subject to licensure or regulation under the Division or an initiative act referred to in it. Section 4999.9(c) prohibits using a term, letter or phrase in the advertising or functionality of an AI or GenAI system that indicates or implies that the care, advice, reports or assessments offered are provided by a licensed natural person. Section 4999.9(b) makes existing Division provisions that bar specified license-indicating terms enforceable against a person or entity that develops or deploys such a system. Section 4999.9(a) places violations under the jurisdiction of the appropriate licensing board or enforcement agency, which may seek an injunction or restraining order under Section 125.5, and preserves other remedies. Section 4999.9(d) treats each use of a prohibited term as a separate violation. Section 2 is a state-mandate clause stating that no reimbursement is required for local agencies or school districts. The text states no effective date and sets no fines or penalty amounts.

title: California AB 723 (Real Estate: Digitally Altered Images: Disclosure 2025)
summary_short: California adds Business and Professions Code §10140.8: real estate brokers, salespersons and persons acting for them must disclose, with a link to the unaltered original, any digitally altered image in sale advertising. Common photo edits are excluded. The text states no effective date.
summary_long: AB 723 adds Business and Professions Code §10140.8. A real estate broker or salesperson, or person acting on their behalf, who includes a digitally altered image in an advertisement or other promotional material for the sale of real property must include a reasonably conspicuous statement that the image has been altered, placed on or adjacent to the image, together with a link, URL or QR code to a publicly accessible website showing the original, unaltered image. Where such material is posted on a website the person controls, the unaltered version must be included in the posting or linked to. A digitally altered image is one created by or at the direction of the broker, salesperson or person acting for them and altered through photo editing software or artificial intelligence to add, remove or change elements, including fixtures, furniture, walls, landscape, floor plans, streetlights, utility poles, views through windows and neighboring properties. Adjustments that do not change the representation of the property, such as lighting, cropping, white balance, straightening and exposure, are excluded. Section 2 is a state-mandate clause stating that local agency and school district costs arise because the act creates, eliminates or changes a crime or infraction. The text states no effective date, enforcing authority or penalty amount.

title: AB 730, Elections: deceptive audio or visual media
summary_short: Prohibits distributing, with actual malice, materially deceptive audio or visual media of a candidate within 60 days of an election, unless it carries a manipulation disclosure; gives candidates injunctive relief and damages; the new provision is repealed 1 January 2023 unless extended.
summary_long: Adds Elections Code Sec. 20010 (subds. a-g). Within 60 days of an election in which a candidate for elective office appears on the ballot, a person, committee or other entity may not distribute, with actual malice and intent to injure the candidate's reputation or deceive a voter, materially deceptive audio or visual media of the candidate. Such media are intentionally manipulated so as to falsely appear authentic and to convey a fundamentally different impression of their expressive content. The ban does not apply if the media carries a 'has been manipulated' disclosure meeting size, duration or audio-reading rules. A candidate may seek injunctive relief, with precedence under Code of Civil Procedure Sec. 35, and sue for general or special damages and fees, proving violation by clear and convincing evidence. Exemptions cover paid broadcasts, bona fide news coverage acknowledging authenticity questions, websites or periodicals stating the media does not accurately represent the candidate, and satire or parody. Rights, obligations and immunities of interactive service providers under 47 U.S.C. Sec. 230 are not altered. Other sections amend Sec. 20010 on superimposed candidate images, operative 1 January 2023, and Code of Civil Procedure Sec. 35 on election-case precedence. The new Sec. 20010 text is in effect only until 1 January 2023, unless a later statute extends it.

title: AB 853, California AI Transparency Act amendments
summary_short: Amends Business and Professions Code Chapter 22757: from 1 January 2027, large online platforms must detect and display provenance data and GenAI hosting platforms may not offer systems lacking disclosures; from 1 January 2028, capture device makers must offer and default latent disclosures; $5,000 civil penalty per violation.
summary_long: Amends Business and Professions Code chapter 22757 (sections 22757.1 to 22757.4) and adds sections 22757.3.1 to 22757.3.3. Large online platforms (public-facing social media, file-sharing, mass messaging or stand-alone search engines exceeding 2,000,000 unique monthly users) must, from 1 January 2027, detect standards-compliant provenance data, provide a user interface disclosing system provenance data, let users inspect it, and not knowingly strip it or digital signatures. GenAI hosting platforms may not knowingly make available a GenAI system that lacks disclosures under Section 22757.3, a section not reproduced in this document. From 1 January 2028, capture device manufacturers must offer users an option to embed latent disclosures (manufacturer name, device name and version, time and date) and embed them by default, where technically feasible and standards-compliant. Violators are liable for a $5,000 civil penalty per violation, with each day a discrete violation, in actions by the Attorney General, a city attorney or a county counsel, plus prevailing-plaintiff fees; injunctive relief applies to violations by third-party licensees under Section 22757.3(c)(3). The chapter is operative 2 August 2026 (Section 6). Covered providers are generative AI creators with over 1,000,000 monthly visitors or users publicly accessible in California.

title: California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act of 2020 (Civil Code 1798.100-1798.199.100)
summary_short: California statute giving consumers rights to know, delete, correct and opt out of the sale or sharing of their personal information, and to limit use of sensitive data and minors' data. Binds businesses above revenue or volume thresholds and their service providers. Enforced by the California Privacy Protection Agency and the Attorney General.
summary_long: Gives California consumers rights to know, delete, correct and opt out of sale or sharing of their personal information, and to limit use of sensitive personal information (§§1798.105–1798.121). Affirmative authorization is required before selling data of consumers under 16. Businesses must give notice at collection, provide request methods, and not discriminate against consumers exercising rights (§§1798.100, 1798.125, 1798.130, 1798.135). Duties apply to businesses doing business in California that meet revenue, volume or data-sale thresholds (§1798.140(d)); service providers and contractors must act under written contracts. Exemptions cover certain medical, credit, financial and deidentified data (§§1798.145–1798.146). Consumers may sue for statutory damages of USD 100 to 750 per incident after certain security breaches (§1798.150). The California Privacy Protection Agency enforces through administrative fines of up to USD 2,500 per violation, or 7,500 for intentional violations; the Attorney General may seek civil penalties (§§1798.155, 1798.199.90). The Agency's regulations cover opt-out signals, risk assessments, cybersecurity audits and automated decisionmaking (§1798.185). Local laws are preempted (§1798.180).

title: CCPA Updates, Cybersecurity Audits, Risk Assessments, Automated Decisionmaking Technology (ADMT), and Insurance Regulations (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, §7000 et seq.)
summary_short: California Privacy Protection Agency regulations implementing the CCPA: privacy policy, notice, consumer request, opt-out, service provider contract, non-discrimination, minors and cybersecurity audit duties for covered businesses, plus automated decisionmaking technology (ADMT) rules; timing varies by provision.
summary_long: Regulations issued by the California Privacy Protection Agency (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7000 et seq.) under the California Consumer Privacy Act. Article 1 defines terms, including automated decisionmaking technology (ADMT) and significant decisions, and limits collection and use of personal information to reasonably necessary and proportionate purposes. Articles 2 to 4 require privacy policies, notices at collection, opt-out and limit notices, handling of consumer requests (confirmation within 10 business days; response within 45 calendar days, extendable to 90), opt-out preference signals, and contract terms for service providers and third parties. Article 5 sets identity verification rules; Article 6 sets parental consent rules for consumers under 13; Article 7 restricts discriminatory price or service differences; Article 8 requires request metrics from businesses handling personal information of 10,000,000 or more consumers. Article 9 requires cybersecurity audits for businesses above processing thresholds, with first reports due by April 1, 2028 for businesses with 2026 gross revenue above $100,000,000. The table of contents also lists sections on risk assessments, ADMT pre-use notices, opt-out and access rights, insurance companies and sworn complaints; their operative text is not in the part of the document provided here.

title: City of San Jose Artificial Intelligence Policy 1.7.12
summary_short: City of San José internal policy governing how City departments and their staff, contractors and vendors purchase, develop, use and maintain AI systems. It sets guiding principles, AI risk review, vendor disclosure duties, prohibited AI uses, 24-hour harm reporting and sunset procedures.
summary_long: The City of San José's internal AI Policy governs how City departments purchase, configure, develop, operate and maintain AI systems. It applies to all systems the City deploys and to staff, interns, consultants, contractors, partners and volunteers acting as users. It sets eight guiding principles (effectiveness, transparency, equity, accountability, human-centered design, privacy, security and safety, workforce empowerment) and requires users to uphold them, conduct an AI Review of potential risk, and follow the AI Incident Response Plan. The CIO designates a City Information Security Officer and a City Digital Privacy Officer. Finance must require vendors to disclose AI use and provide technical documentation, including an AI Fact Sheet, and procurement solicitations must ask about AI use. Prohibited uses include real-time and covert biometric identification, emotion analysis, fully automated decisions substantially affecting rights or safety without meaningful human oversight, social scoring and cognitive behavioral manipulation. Staff must report AI-caused harm within 24 hours of discovery. Systems that cease to provide a positive outcome must be halted unless the CIO grants an exception; disruptive systems follow a CIO-approved phased shutdown. Violations may result in discipline, breach-of-contract remedies or damages. Detailed requirements sit in the AI Handbook, which is referenced but not included in the text provided.

title: SB 1047, Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act
summary_short: Adds Business and Professions Code Chapter 22.6 requiring developers of covered AI models to maintain safety and security protocols, assess critical-harm risk, undergo annual audits and report incidents to the Attorney General; also imposes customer checks on compute clusters. Several duties apply from January 1, 2026.
summary_long: Adds Business and Professions Code Chapter 22.6 for developers of 'covered models': models trained with over 10^26 operations costing over $100 million (fine-tuning: 3×10^25 operations and $10 million), with later thresholds set by a state agency from 2027. Before training, developers must implement cybersecurity protections, a full-shutdown capability and a written safety and security protocol. Before use or release, they must assess whether the model can cause a 'critical harm' (such as mass-casualty CBRN weapons or large cyberattacks on critical infrastructure), safeguard against it, and not release it if the risk is unreasonable. Developers publish redacted protocols, file annual compliance statements with the Attorney General, report safety incidents within 72 hours, and obtain annual independent audits from 2026. Computing-cluster operators must verify customers and keep records. The Attorney General may sue for civil penalties (10% of training compute cost for a first violation, 30% thereafter, for violations causing harm or imminent risk), injunctions and damages; whistleblower protections apply. A nine-member Board of Frontier Models is created, and a CalCompute public cloud framework is to be developed, subject to appropriation.

title: California SB-1119 Companion chatbots: children’s safety.
summary_short: Introduced bill that would add Business and Professions Code Chapter 22.6.1 on companion chatbots and children's safety. It would apply to operators that make companion chatbots available to users in California, with child-safety duties, advertising and data limits, independent audits and civil enforcement.
summary_long: Introduced bill adding Chapter 22.6.1 (Companion Chatbots: Children's Safety) to the Business and Professions Code. It covers operators that make companion chatbots available to users in California. Operators must verify user age or apply child protections to all users. On or before July 1, 2027, operators must annually assess and mitigate child safety risks, publish a child safety policy, run a crisis response protocol, set parent-controlled defaults (including ephemeral mode and time limits), give AI notices to children, restrict specified outputs, provide parental controls, and offer an incident reporting mechanism. Operators may not target advertising at children using their data or sell or share children's personal information beyond authorized uses. Operators must undergo annual independent audits, reported confidentially to the Attorney General. By January 1, 2028 the Attorney General must adopt auditor regulations, a complaint mechanism and annual public reports. Public prosecutors may seek civil penalties up to $5,000 (negligent) or $15,000 (intentional) per affected child; children or parents may sue for actual damages.

title: California Senate Bill 1120 (2024)
summary_short: Amends California Health and Safety Code §1367.01 and Insurance Code §10123.135 to regulate health plans and disability insurers using AI or algorithms in utilization review. Such tools may not deny, delay or modify care based on medical necessity; a licensed physician or health care professional must decide.
summary_long: Section 1 amends Health and Safety Code §1367.01 for health care service plans, including specialized plans, and entities that use AI, algorithm or software tools for utilization review based on medical necessity. The plan must ensure the tool bases determinations on the enrollee's clinical history and individual circumstances, does not rely solely on a group dataset, does not supplant provider decisionmaking, does not discriminate, is fairly applied, is open to department inspection, and does not directly or indirectly harm enrollees. The tool may not deny, delay or modify services; only a licensed physician or qualified health professional may make that determination. Plans must document AI use in written policies, periodically review performance, and limit patient data use. The department may issue guidance within one year of federal rules. Section 2 adds parallel requirements for disability insurers in Insurance Code §10123.135, including annual review of criteria. The director or commissioner may assess administrative penalties by order for each failure to meet timeframes or other requirements; amounts are not stated. Section 3 states that no state reimbursement is required for local agencies. No effective date is stated in the text.},

title: California Senate Bill 1381 (2024)
summary_short: Amends four California Penal Code sections to cover child sexual-abuse matter that is digitally altered or AI-generated and depicts a person under 18. Applies to any person; operative only if AB 1831 is enacted and takes effect by January 1, 2025.
summary_long: SB 1381 amends four California Penal Code sections on child sexual-abuse material to cover matter that is digitally altered or generated by artificial intelligence. Section 311.1 (obscene matter depicting a person under 18) and Section 311.3 (sexual exploitation of a child) now reach such matter, including data depicting what appears to be a minor engaged in or simulating sexual conduct. Section 311.1 carries up to one year in county jail and a $1,000 fine, or state prison and a $10,000 fine. Section 311.3(e) carries a fine up to $2,000, up to one year in county jail, or both, with state prison after a prior conviction. Section 311.4 extends its minor-employment and minor-use offences to such matter; subdivision (b) is a felony with three, six or eight years in state prison where commercial purposes are shown. Section 312.3 adds such matter to the definition of matter subject to forfeiture and destruction. Existing exemptions for law enforcement, legitimate medical, scientific or educational activities, lawful conduct between spouses and legally emancipated minors are retained. Section 5 provides that no state reimbursement is required for local agencies. Section 6 makes the act operative only if AB 1831 of the 2023–24 Regular Session is enacted and takes effect on or before January 1, 2025.

title: California (2021-2022) SB 1398
summary_short: Adds Vehicle Code §24011.5: manufacturers and dealers must give buyers a distinct notice naming and describing the functions and limitations of any SAE Level 2 partial driving automation feature, and may not market such features as implying autonomous capability. The text states no start date.
summary_long: Adds Vehicle Code §24011.5. Subdivision (a) bars dealers and manufacturers from selling a new passenger vehicle equipped with a partial driving automation feature, or providing an update that adds one, unless the buyer or owner receives a distinct notice at delivery or upgrade naming the feature and describing its functions and limitations. Subdivision (b) bars naming or marketing such features in ways that imply autonomous capability or functions not actually included; a violation is a misleading advertisement under Vehicle Code §11713. Subdivision (c) defines the covered features by reference to SAE Level 2 in J3016 (April 2021). Subdivision (d) preserves existing duties of care and civil liability. Subdivision (e) requires manufacturers to give dealers information, including recommended notice language, before delivery, on which dealers may rely; subdivision (f) shields manufacturers that provide it when a dealer fails to give notice. Section 2 states no state reimbursement is required for local agencies or school districts. The text gives no effective date and no penalty amounts beyond the §11713 cross-reference.

title: SB 243, Companion chatbots
summary_short: Adds Chapter 22.6 on companion chatbot platforms available to users in California, under the Business and Professions Code. Requires operators to give AI disclosures, maintain suicide-prevention protocols, protect known minors, and report annually to the Office of Suicide Prevention from July 1, 2027, with a private right of action.
summary_long: Adds Chapter 22.6 to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code, regulating operators that make companion chatbot platforms available to users in California. A companion chatbot is an AI system with a natural-language interface that gives adaptive, human-like responses, can meet social needs and sustains relationships across interactions; customer-service bots and limited video-game bots are excluded. Operators must issue a clear and conspicuous notice that a chatbot is artificial and not human where a reasonable person would be misled. They must maintain and publish a protocol against suicidal ideation and self-harm content, including referrals to crisis services, before letting chatbots engage users. For users known to be minors, operators must disclose AI interaction, give default reminders at least every three hours to take a break, and take reasonable measures against sexually explicit visual material. From July 1, 2027, operators must annually report to the Office of Suicide Prevention referral counts and protocols, without personal identifiers. Operators must also disclose that companion chatbots may not be suitable for some minors. Injured persons may sue for injunctive relief, the greater of actual damages or $1,000 per violation, and attorney's fees.

title: California SB-300 (Companion chatbots).
summary_short: Bill amending California Business and Professions Code §22602 on companion chatbots. Operators must disclose non-human status where users may be misled, maintain and publish a suicide-prevention protocol, and for known minors disclose AI status, give break reminders every three hours and prevent sexually explicit material.
summary_long: Senate Bill 300 (introduced; status pending) amends Section 22602 of the California Business and Professions Code, as added by Chapter 677 of the Statutes of 2025, which governs companion chatbots. Under subdivision (a), an operator must issue a clear and conspicuous notification that a companion chatbot is artificially generated and not human where a reasonable person would be misled into believing it is human. Under subdivision (b), an operator must prevent a companion chatbot on its platform from engaging with users unless it maintains a protocol for preventing the production of suicidal ideation, suicide or self-harm content, including referral to crisis services, and must publish details of that protocol on its website. Under subdivision (c), where an operator has actual knowledge that a user is a minor, it must disclose that the user is interacting with artificial intelligence, provide by default a notification at least every three hours reminding the user to take a break and that the chatbot is not human, and prevent the chatbot from producing or facilitating sexually explicit material. The excerpt contains no penalty or enforcement provision.

title: SB 362, Data broker registration: accessible deletion mechanism (Delete Act)
summary_short: Requires data brokers to register with the California Privacy Protection Agency and honor consumer deletion requests through an accessible deletion mechanism the agency must establish by January 1, 2026; broker deletion duties apply from August 1, 2026, with triennial audits from 2028 and administrative fines.
summary_long: Amends Civil Code Sections 1798.99.80 to 1798.99.89 on data brokers, defined as businesses that knowingly sell to third parties personal information of consumers with whom they have no direct relationship. Data brokers must register with the California Privacy Protection Agency by January 31 each year, pay a fee, and disclose specified information, including whether they collect minors' data, precise geolocation or reproductive health care data. The agency must establish by January 1, 2026 an accessible deletion mechanism through which a consumer can, with one verifiable request, ask all registered brokers to delete their personal information. From August 1, 2026, brokers must access the mechanism at least every 45 days, delete the consumer's data within 45 days, and not sell or share new personal information of requesting consumers. Brokers must undergo an independent audit every three years from January 1, 2028. Failure to register carries fines of $200 per day; failure to comply with deletion duties carries $200 per deletion request per day, plus fees and agency costs. Penalties and fees go to the Data Brokers' Registry Fund, administered by the agency.

title: California SB 384 (Preventing Algorithmic Price Fixing Act: Prohibition on Certain Price-Setting Algorithm Uses 2025)
summary_short: California SB 384 proposed bill would prohibit selling, licensing, providing or using a price-setting algorithm that processes competitors' nonpublic input data to set prices, supply levels or rents, if two or more competitors are expected to use it. Enforced by civil actions. No effective date is stated.
summary_long: Proposed Business and Professions Code § 22949.85 (SB 384) would prohibit selling, licensing, providing or using a price-setting algorithm, with intent or reasonable expectation that two or more competitors in the same market use it, if the person knows or should know it processes nonpublic input data to set a price or supply level for goods or services, or a rent or occupancy level for rental property. Users have an affirmative defense if they exercise reasonable due diligence, including written assurances from the provider that the algorithm does not process nonpublic input data. Providers face a separate violation per authorized user or licensee; users face a separate violation for each calendar month of use. The Attorney General, a district attorney, or a city attorney or county counsel may sue for actual damages, injunctive relief, restitution or civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation, with attorney's fees for prevailing public plaintiffs. Conflicting contracts are void to that extent, and the section does not limit antitrust laws. Definitions cover artificial intelligence, nonpublic input data, price-setting algorithms and competitors. No effective date is stated.

title: California SB 420 (Automated decision systems)
summary_short: Introduced California bill adding Business and Professions Code Chapter 24.6: developers and deployers of high-risk automated decision systems must perform impact assessments, give notices, and maintain governance programs against algorithmic discrimination, and state agencies may not contract for such systems without anti-discrimination certification.
summary_long: Adds Business and Professions Code Chapter 24.6 on automated decision systems (ADS). High-risk ADS assist or replace discretionary decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, such as on education, employment, housing, health care, lending or essential services. Developers must complete impact assessments before making a high-risk ADS publicly available, and deployers within two years of deploying systems first deployed after 1 January 2026. Deployers must notify affected persons, publish a website statement and offer human review of decisions where technically feasible; developers and deployers must maintain governance programs. Deploying or making available a system that the assessment finds likely to cause algorithmic discrimination is prohibited unless safeguards are implemented. Entities with 50 or fewer employees are excluded. The Attorney General or Civil Rights Department may sue for civil penalties (tiered from $2,500 to $10,000 for failed assessments; $25,000 per algorithmic-discrimination violation), injunctions and fees, after 45 days' notice, with possible cure. Public Contract Code Section 10285.8 bars state agencies from awarding high-risk ADS contracts unless the vendor certifies compliance with anti-discrimination laws and the chapter.

title: California SB 480 (Autonomous vehicles 2025)
summary_short: Amends the California Vehicle Code so autonomous vehicles may not run on public roads until the DMV approves a manufacturer application; adds testing conditions, a $5 million insurance requirement, ADS marker lamp and lamp-color rules, and from 2030 a deployment permit for certain zero-emission vehicles.
summary_long: Sec. 1 amends Vehicle Code § 25950 on lamp and reflector colors, adding exceptions for ADS marker lamps on autonomous vehicles. Sec. 2 amends § 38750, defining autonomous technology, autonomous vehicle (SAE Level 3, 4 or 5), operator and manufacturer. It allows testing on public roads by a licensed driver when the vehicle is operated solely by employees, contractors or persons designated by the manufacturer, with a driver seated and a $5,000,000 insurance, surety bond or self-insurance requirement. Otherwise an autonomous vehicle may not operate on public roads until the DMV approves the manufacturer's application, which must include certifications on safety systems, data recording, federal motor vehicle safety standards, testing and insurance. The DMV must adopt implementing regulations and may impose additional requirements for vehicles without a driver; it must post public notice and wait 30 days before approving applications. Manufacturers must give purchasers a written disclosure of collected information. NHTSA federal rules supersede conflicting state provisions. From January 1, 2026, ADS marker lamps are permitted; from January 1, 2030, certain zero-emission autonomous vehicles of model year 2031 or later must operate under a deployment permit, with DMV rulemaking not before January 1, 2027.

title: California SB 500 (Autonomous Vehicles: Zero Emissions 2021)
summary_short: Amends California Vehicle Code § 38750 to govern autonomous vehicles on public roads: testing conditions and $5,000,000 insurance for manufacturers, Department of Motor Vehicles application approval, required safety certifications and data recording, and from January 1, 2030, deployment permits for certain zero-emission vehicles.
summary_long: SB 500 amends Vehicle Code § 38750 on autonomous vehicles (SAE Level 3-5 vehicles; driver-assistance systems excluded). Testing on public roads is allowed by licensed drivers if vehicles are operated solely by employees, contractors or designated persons, a driver is seated, and the manufacturer holds $5,000,000 in insurance, surety bond or self-insurance. Other operation requires Department of Motor Vehicles approval of a manufacturer application with certifications covering engagement controls, cabin indicator, failure alerts and stopping capability, manual override, federal safety compliance, and a read-only sensor recorder retaining 30 seconds before collisions for three years. The department must adopt regulations, may add requirements, must hold hearings for driverless operation, and must give 30 days' public notice before approving applications. Manufacturers must give purchasers written disclosure of collected information. Federal NHTSA rules prevail in conflict. From January 1, 2030, to the extent federal law allows, certain autonomous vehicles of model year 2031 or later under 8,501 pounds may operate only under a deployment permit if zero-emission. The section sets no penalties.

title: California SB 524 (Law enforcement agencies: artificial intelligence.)
summary_short: Requires California law enforcement agencies to adopt a policy on AI-generated official police reports, including an AI-use statement, officer signature, retained first drafts and an audit trail, and limits contracted AI vendors' use of agency data. Adds Penal Code § 13663.
summary_long: Adds Penal Code § 13663, which requires each law enforcement agency to maintain a policy under which an official report generated fully or partly by artificial intelligence must identify each AI program used, carry the statement that the report was written either fully or in part using artificial intelligence, and be signed by the officer attesting to review and accuracy. The first AI-produced draft must be retained for as long as the official report, and such drafts are not officer statements. The agency must keep an audit trail identifying the person who used AI and any video or audio footage used. Contracted vendors, defined as third parties that make AI available to law enforcement for drafting police reports, may not share, sell or otherwise use agency-provided information except for the agency's purposes or under a court order, but may access processed data for troubleshooting, bias mitigation, accuracy improvement or system refinement. The definition of artificial intelligence covers systems that automatically draft report narratives from in-car, dash-mounted or body-worn camera footage or audio, and systems that generate narratives from an officer's dictated report. Section 2 provides for reimbursement of local agencies and school districts if the Commission on State Mandates finds state-mandated costs. The text states no penalties, enforcement authority or effective date.

title: SB 53, Artificial intelligence models: large developers (Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act)
summary_short: Requires developers that train foundation models with more than 10^26 operations to publish transparency reports and report critical safety incidents to California's Office of Emergency Services; those with over $500 million revenue must also publish and follow frontier AI frameworks. Adds whistleblower protections, preempts later local rules and plans CalCompute.
summary_long: SB 53 enacts the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act. A frontier model is a foundation model trained with more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, counting fine-tuning and later modifications; a large frontier developer also has, with affiliates, annual gross revenues above $500 million. Large frontier developers must write, implement, follow and publish a frontier AI framework on catastrophic risk, review it yearly, and send the Office of Emergency Services (OES) quarterly summaries of internal-use risk assessments. All frontier developers must publish a transparency report when deploying a new or substantially modified frontier model, report critical safety incidents to OES within 15 days (24 hours to an appropriate authority for imminent risk), and avoid materially false or misleading statements. Meeting an OES-designated federal standard can count as incident-reporting compliance. Large frontier developers face civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, recoverable only by the Attorney General. Labor Code Chapter 5.1 protects covered employees who report catastrophic risks or violations, with injunctive relief and attorney's fees. A Government Operations Agency consortium is to design CalCompute, a public cloud computing cluster, once funds are appropriated. Local frontier-AI rules adopted from 2025 are preempted.
