title: California SB 7 (Employment: Automated Decision Systems 2025)
summary_short: Adds Labor Code Part 5.5.5 on employers' use of automated decision systems (ADS): written pre-use and post-use notices to workers, bar on relying solely on ADS for discipline, termination or deactivation, worker data access, and Labor Commissioner and prosecutor enforcement.
summary_long: Adds Labor Code Part 5.5.5 (§§1520–1539) on automated decision systems (ADS) used in employment. Employers must give written notice to affected workers at least 30 days before first deploying an ADS for employment-related decisions other than hiring (existing users by April 1, 2026; new workers within 30 days of hiring), notify job applicants of hiring-related ADS use, and maintain a list of ADS in use. Employers may not use ADS to violate labor or civil rights laws, infer protected status, take adverse action for exercising legal rights, or collect worker data for undisclosed purposes. Discipline, termination or deactivation may not rest solely on ADS; where ADS output is primarily relied on, a human reviewer must review it and a post-decision notice is required. Customer ratings may not be the only or primary ADS input. Workers may request a copy of their own data from the most recent 12 months primarily used by an ADS in such decisions, once every 12 months. The Labor Commissioner and public prosecutors enforce the part; violators face a $500 civil penalty. Carve-outs: collective bargaining agreements that explicitly waive the part; federal contract compliance; CCPA rules.

title: California SB 892 (Public contracts: automated decision systems: procurement standards)
summary_short: Would add Public Contract Code § 12100.1, directing the Department of Technology to adopt regulations creating an automated decision system (ADS) procurement standard. From January 1, 2027, state agencies could contract for ADS only after those regulations exist and only with specified contract clauses.
summary_long: The bill would add Public Contract Code § 12100.1 and define 'artificial intelligence' and 'automated decision system' (ADS), excluding listed low-risk tools such as spam filters and calculators. It directs the Department of Technology to adopt regulations creating an ADS procurement standard, considering listed frameworks and consulting the California Privacy Protection Agency. The standard must include a detailed risk assessment, risk-control methods between agency and vendor, adverse incident monitoring, identification of prohibited use cases, an equity assessment, a human-oversight assessment, and data minimization, including a bar on vendors using agency-provided data to train proprietary or third-party systems. The department must review the standard and regulations annually from January 1, 2026. Commencing January 1, 2027, a state agency may not procure an ADS or contract for an ADS-using service before the regulations are adopted. Afterwards, it may contract only if the contract includes clauses on a completed risk assessment, procurement standards, adverse incident monitoring, authorization before ADS upgrades, notice to affected individuals with appeal or opt-out information, and a termination right for significant breach. Projects approved before January 1, 2027 through the annual budget process are exempt. The text contains no penalty or enforcement provisions.]

title: SB 942, California AI Transparency Act
summary_short: California statute, operative 1 January 2026, requiring covered providers of publicly accessible generative AI systems with over 1,000,000 monthly visitors or users to offer a no-cost AI detection tool and to include latent disclosures in AI-generated image, video or audio content, with civil penalties of $5,000 per violation.
summary_long: Adds the California AI Transparency Act (Business and Professions Code Chapter 25). Covered providers, meaning persons producing generative AI systems with over 1,000,000 monthly visitors or users publicly accessible in California, must offer a free AI detection tool that outputs system provenance data but not personal provenance data, and collect feedback on its efficacy. Tool users' personal information and submitted content face collection and retention limits. They must offer users an optional manifest disclosure of AI-generated content and include latent disclosures (provider name, system name and version, creation time and date, unique identifier) in AI-generated image, video or audio content, detectable by the tool. Licenses must require maintenance of that capability; providers must revoke a license within 96 hours of learning a licensee removed it, and licensees must then stop using the system. Violations carry a $5,000 civil penalty per violation, recoverable in civil actions by the Attorney General, a city attorney or a county counsel; each day is a discrete violation and prevailing plaintiffs recover fees. Licensees failing to cease use may be sued for injunctive relief and fees. Exempt: services offering exclusively non-user-generated video game, television, streaming, movie or interactive experiences. Operative 1 January 2026.

title: Required Rulemaking on Personal Financial Data Rights (12 CFR Part 1033)
summary_short: CFPB final rule under CFPA section 1033 requires banks, credit unions and other financial data providers to make covered consumer financial data available, without fees, to consumers and authorized third parties. Third parties must limit collection and use of that data. Compliance is phased in from 2026 to 2030.
summary_long: The CFPB final rule, effective January 17, 2025, implements CFPA section 1033 by requiring data providers to make covered consumer financial data available to consumers and authorized third parties in electronic form. Covered data concerns Regulation E accounts, Regulation Z credit cards and payment facilitation products; depository institutions at or below the $850 million SBA size standard are excluded, while nondepository providers are covered. Providers must use standardized, machine-readable formats, meet minimum response rates, avoid credential-based screen scraping, and charge no access fees. Third parties must obtain express informed consent, certify limits on collection, use and retention, limit collection duration to one year, provide revocation, and retain records for at least three years. Data aggregators may perform authorization for third parties. CFPB-recognized consensus standards serve as indicia of compliance. Part 1001 treats financial data processing as a financial product or service under the CFPA. Compliance dates are tiered from April 1, 2026 to April 1, 2030 by asset size or receipts.

title: Preventing the Improper Use of CHIPS Act Funding (15 CFR Part 231)
summary_short: Final NIST rule (15 CFR Part 231) setting conditions on CHIPS Act funding recipients: bars significant semiconductor manufacturing capacity expansions and certain joint research or technology licensing with foreign entities of concern, subject to exceptions; requires notification and records; effective November 24, 2023.
summary_long: Final rule of the National Institute of Standards and Technology implementing CHIPS Act conditions that keep CHIPS Incentives Program funding from benefiting foreign countries of concern. Subpart A defines key terms, including foreign entity of concern, legacy semiconductor and semiconductors critical to national security. Sec. 231.202 bars covered entities and affiliated group members, for 10 years after the award, significant transactions involving material expansion of semiconductor manufacturing capacity in a foreign country of concern, except for existing legacy facilities and legacy capacity that predominately serves that country's market. Sec. 231.203 bars knowingly engaging in joint research or technology licensing with a foreign entity of concern on technologies or products raising national security concerns; ongoing activities may be grandfathered if memorialized in the required agreement. Sec. 231.204 permits additional conditions against circumvention by related entities, and Sec. 231.205 requires record retention. Subpart C requires notification of planned significant transactions, sets review and reconsideration timelines, and allows mitigation agreements. Violations can lead to recovery of the full federal financial assistance as a debt owed to the government. Subpart D covers periodic legacy-semiconductor notices, liability for false information under 18 U.S.C. 1001, and severability. Effective November 24, 2023.

title: CHIPS Act of 2022 and Research and Science (CHIPS and Science Act), Pub. L. 117-167
summary_short: Authorizes and directs Department of Energy Office of Science and NIST research programs, with fiscal 2023-2027 funding authorizations. Bars entities of concern from receiving federal research support. Includes AI-related research and biometric performance standards.
summary_long: Headed Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act, the text authorizes research programs and fiscal 2023-2027 appropriations. Title I amends the Department of Energy Research and Innovation Act for Office of Science programs (basic energy sciences, biological and environmental research, advanced computing, fusion, high energy and nuclear physics, isotopes, accelerators, laboratory upgrades) with start-of-operations deadlines. It adds AI-related research, including autonomous chemistry facilities and bias-mitigation guidance for high-performance computing. Section 10114 bars entities of concern and linked individuals from covered research support, subject to a Secretary waiver and exclusions of one to ten years. Title II directs NIST measurement research on engineering biology, greenhouse gas measurement and biometrics, including a biometrics test program, performance standards for high-risk biometric identification systems, and AI-enabled cybersecurity research, plus voluntary standards for software, cloud, privacy and identity management. Later sections listed in the outline cover NSF education and workforce programs, foreign funding, and microelectronics and DOE RD&D; their text is not in this part.

title: Colorado HB 1263 (Conversational Artificial Intelligence Service Operator Requirements)
summary_short: Adds definitions to C.R.S. 6-1-1701 and section 6-1-1708 on operators of conversational AI services, requiring AI-status disclosure, suicide and self-harm referral protocols, and no false professional claims, with minor protections and annual Attorney General reporting from 2027.
summary_long: Adds definitions to C.R.S. 6-1-1701 and section 6-1-1708 on operators of conversational artificial intelligence services, meaning publicly accessible AI systems that primarily simulate human conversation, with carve-outs. Operators develop or offer such services to consumers; app stores and search engines are excluded. Operators must estimate user age by commercially reasonable or generally accepted methods and may not willfully disregard clear and convincing evidence of minority. From January 1, 2027, where an operator knows a user is a minor, it must disclose AI status, avoid unpredictable engagement rewards, prevent sexual content and emotional-dependence simulation, comply with Part 13 privacy duties, and offer privacy tools to minors and parents. From January 1, 2027, for all users, operators must disclose AI status at the start of daily use and at least every three hours, implement a suicide and self-harm referral protocol, and not claim outputs come from licensed health, legal or mental health professionals. From July 1, 2027, operators must report crisis-referral and safeguard metrics annually to the Attorney General without user identifiers, and the Attorney General posts report data publicly. The section does not limit information access, require trade-secret disclosure or authorize unconstitutional moderation. The act takes effect after the 90-day post-adjournment period, subject to referendum.

title: House Bill 24-1130, Privacy of Biometric Identifiers & Data
summary_short: Amends the Colorado Privacy Act to regulate controllers and processors that collect, use, retain, disclose or protect biometric identifiers and data, including written policies, consent, sale and disclosure limits, and employer consent rules. Takes effect July 1, 2025, subject to a referendum petition.
summary_long: Adds C.R.S. 6-1-1314 to the Colorado Privacy Act, with new biometric definitions in 6-1-1303 and an applicability rule in 6-1-1304. Controllers must adopt a public written policy with a retention schedule and deletion dates and a security-incident protocol; processors need an incident protocol. Before collecting biometric identifiers, controllers must give notice and obtain consent. They may not sell, lease or trade identifiers, disclose them except in listed cases, or refuse service or vary prices for consumers who decline or exercise rights. Consumers may request free access to their biometric data details. Employers may require consent only for listed security, timekeeping and safety purposes, and may not retaliate. The Department of Law may adopt rules. The act reaches controllers handling any amount of biometric identifiers and takes effect July 1, 2025, subject to a referendum petition. The text contains no penalty provisions; its title refers to remedies and civil actions, which do not appear in this document.

title: House Bill 24-1147, Candidate Election Deepfake Disclosures
summary_short: Prohibits knowingly or recklessly distributing communications that include a candidate deepfake within 60 days before a primary or 90 days before a general election, unless a clear and conspicuous disclosure is included. Effective July 1, 2024; enforced by complaint, hearing, civil penalties and candidate lawsuits.
summary_long: Amends Colorado law to add Article 46 on deepfakes concerning candidates for elective office. Section 1-46-103(1) prohibits distributing a communication that includes a deepfake depicting a candidate, to an electorate audience, within 60 days before a primary or 90 days before a general election, if the person knows or recklessly disregards that the depicted candidate did not say or do it. Section 1-46-103(2) exempts communications with a clear and conspicuous disclosure, with requirements for visual, audio and metadata disclosure and permanence. Section 1-46-103(3) excludes certain broadcasters, websites and periodicals, satire or parody, technology providers and interactive computer services. Violations are adjudicated by complaint and administrative hearing (1-46-104); candidates may seek injunctions, compensatory and punitive damages and fees, requiring clear and convincing evidence (1-46-105). Section 1-45-111.5(1.5)(c.5) sets civil penalty minimums, including at least 100 dollars per violation for missing disclosures without paid advertising and at least 10 percent of amounts spent on undisclosed prohibited communications. Section 1-46-106 preserves other legal actions and criminal liability. Effective July 1, 2024, applying to communications distributed on or after that date.

title: Senate Bill 21-169, Restrict Insurers' Use of External Consumer Data
summary_short: Colorado SB 21-169 bars insurers from unfairly discriminating on protected characteristics, including through external consumer data, algorithms and predictive models. It requires the insurance commissioner to adopt rules, after a stakeholder process, under which insurers must test and demonstrate non-discrimination.
summary_long: SB 21-169 adds Colorado Revised Statutes section 10-3-1104.9. It prohibits insurers, for any insurance practice, from unfairly discriminating based on race, color, national or ethnic origin, religion, sex, sexual orientation, disability, gender identity or gender expression. It also prohibits using external consumer data and information sources, or algorithms and predictive models that use them, in a way that unfairly discriminates on those grounds, as the commissioner's rules permit. The commissioner must hold a stakeholder process and then adopt rules by insurance type and practice. The rules must require insurers to report the external data sources they use, explain their use, maintain a risk management framework, assess results, and provide an officer attestation. The rules must also allow a reasonable period to remedy discriminatory impacts. Rule-making documents are treated as confidential trade secrets. The commissioner may examine and investigate insurers' use of these tools under section 10-3-1106. The section excludes title insurance and surety bonds, and commercial policies except business owners' and general liability policies with annual premiums of $10,000 or less. It does not require insurers to collect protected characteristics. The act takes effect 90 days after final adjournment, subject to referendum.

title: Senate Bill 21-190, Protect Personal Data Privacy (Colorado Privacy Act)
summary_short: SB 21-190 (Colorado Privacy Act) gives Colorado consumers rights over their personal data and imposes duties on controllers and processors that do business in Colorado or target residents, enforced by the Attorney General and district attorneys, from July 1, 2023.
summary_long: SB 21-190 enacts the Colorado Privacy Act as Part 13 of Article 1 of Title 6, effective July 1, 2023. It covers controllers that conduct business in Colorado or target products to Colorado residents and process personal data of 100,000 or more consumers a year, or 25,000 or more while deriving revenue from selling data. Exemptions include HIPAA-covered health information, Gramm-Leach-Bliley financial institutions, FCRA-regulated activity and employment records. Consumers may access, correct, delete, port and opt out of targeted advertising, data sales and certain profiling; controllers must respond within 45 days, provide appeals, and honor universal opt-out mechanisms meeting Attorney General specifications from July 1, 2024. Controllers must give privacy notices, specify purposes, minimize data, avoid secondary use without consent, secure data, avoid unlawful discrimination, and obtain consent before processing sensitive data, including a known child's data with parental consent. Processing that presents a heightened risk of harm requires documented data protection assessments, available to the Attorney General on request. Processors must follow controller instructions under binding contracts. The Attorney General and district attorneys enforce the Act, with no private right of action; violations are deceptive trade practices, and penalty amounts are not stated here.

title: Senate Bill 24-205, Concerning Consumer Protections in Interactions with Artificial Intelligence Systems
summary_short: Colorado statute adding Part 17 on artificial intelligence to Article 1 of Title 6, C.R.S. From 1 February 2026, developers and deployers of high-risk AI systems making consequential decisions about Colorado consumers must use reasonable care against algorithmic discrimination, with documentation, disclosure and risk-management duties. The Attorney General enforces it.
summary_long: Adds Part 17 (sections 6-1-1701 to 6-1-1707) to Article 1 of Title 6, Colorado Revised Statutes, on artificial intelligence systems. High-risk AI systems are those that make, or are a substantial factor in making, consequential decisions about Colorado consumers in education, employment, financial or lending services, essential government services, health care, housing, insurance or legal services. From 1 February 2026, developers must use reasonable care against known or foreseeable algorithmic discrimination, provide deployers with documentation and publish a statement; deployers must use reasonable care, adopt a risk management program, complete impact assessments at least annually, notify consumers before consequential decisions, give explanations for adverse decisions, correction and appeal rights, and report discovered discrimination within 90 days. Deployers with fewer than 50 full-time equivalent employees that do not use their own data to train the system are exempt from several duties under conditions. Consumer-facing AI systems must disclose AI interaction unless obvious. Exemptions cover certain federally approved systems, insurers, banks and credit unions. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority; violations are unfair trade practices, with an affirmative defense for cured violations and a rebuttable presumption of reasonable care. No private right of action is created. The Attorney General may adopt rules.

title: Senate Bill 25B-004, Increase Transparency for Algorithmic Systems (delay of SB24-205)
summary_short: Colorado Senate Bill 25B-004 moves from February 1, 2026 to June 30, 2026 the start date of duties for developers and deployers of high-risk artificial intelligence systems under Colorado Revised Statutes sections 6-1-1702 to 6-1-1704, which cover algorithmic discrimination, impact assessments and AI-interaction disclosure.
summary_long: Senate Bill 25B-004 moves from February 1, 2026 to June 30, 2026 the start date of duties for developers and deployers of high-risk artificial intelligence systems in Colorado Revised Statutes sections 6-1-1702 to 6-1-1704. Developers must use reasonable care against known or reasonably foreseeable algorithmic discrimination, give deployers documentation for impact assessments, publish a website statement on their systems, and disclose such risks to the attorney general and known deployers. Deployers must use reasonable care, implement a risk management policy and program, complete impact assessments at least annually and within ninety days after an intentional and substantial modification, and report discovered algorithmic discrimination within ninety days. Deployers must also inform consumers of adverse consequential decisions, and deployers and other developers must disclose to consumers that they are interacting with an AI system. A rebuttable presumption of reasonable care applies in attorney general enforcement actions where the entity complied with these sections and any rules adopted under section 6-1-1707. Section 4 sets the effective date at 12:01 a.m. the day after the ninety-day period following final adjournment, unless a referendum petition delays it to the November 2026 general election.

title: Senate Bill 26-189, Automated Decision-Making Technology (repeal and reenactment of Colorado AI Act)
summary_short: Repeals and reenacts C.R.S. title 6, article 1, part 17 as a law on automated decision-making technology (ADMT) used in consequential decisions about consumers. Developers must document covered ADMT for deployers; deployers must give notices, adverse-outcome disclosures, data correction and human review. Attorney General enforcement; mainly from 1 January 2027.
summary_long: SB 26-189 repeals and reenacts, with amendments, C.R.S. title 6, article 1, part 17. It covers ADMT that processes personal data and materially influences consequential decisions in education, employment, residential housing, financial or lending services, insurance, health care and essential government services; listed technologies and low-stakes uses are excluded. From 1 January 2027, developers must document intended uses, training-data categories, limitations and use instructions for deployers, notify material updates and keep records for three years. Deployers must keep records for three years, give consumers prior notice of ADMT use and, within 30 days of an adverse outcome, a plain-language description, an information-request process and an explanation of rights. Affected consumers may request data correction and meaningful human review, to the extent commercially reasonable. The Attorney General must adopt rules by 1 January 2027. Violations are deceptive trade practices enforced only by the Attorney General, with a 60-day cure notice until 2030 and no new private right of action. Developers and deployers may be liable under anti-discrimination law by relative fault; indemnification for own acts is void. Insurers under C.R.S. 10-3-1104.9, HIPAA covered entities, FDA-regulated devices, FERPA and ECOA processes get exemptions or alternative compliance.
