title: Colorado SB 25-288 (Intimate Digital Depictions Criminal & Civil Actions)
summary_short: Creates a civil cause of action against persons who disclose or threaten to disclose intimate digital depictions without consent, and amends Colorado criminal and juvenile provisions on such depictions and on sexually exploitative material. Applies to offenses committed on or after the effective date, subject to referendum.
summary_long: New Part 15 (CRS 13-21-1501 to 13-21-1507) gives a depicted individual a civil action against a person who discloses or threatens to disclose an intimate digital depiction without consent, if the person knew or recklessly disregarded that lack of consent, that severe emotional distress would result, and that the individual was identifiable. Consent to disclosure requires a signed, plain-language written agreement with listed contents; disclaimers are no defense. Exceptions cover good-faith reporting, legal proceedings, public-interest matters, satire, technology providers, interactive computer services and broadcasters meeting listed conditions. Remedies include the greater of actual damages or $150,000 liquidated damages, the defendant's monetary gain, exemplary damages, costs and fees, and injunctions. Sections 2 to 8 amend criminal, juvenile and related provisions: disclosure for harassment or pecuniary gain (CRS 18-7-107, 18-7-108) with a court fine of up to $10,000; sexually exploitative material extended to realistic digital depictions of identifiable children (18-6-403); and juvenile offenses (18-7-109). Sections 2 to 8 apply to offenses committed on or after the effective date, subject to a referendum petition.

title: Colorado SB 25-318 (Artificial Intelligence Consumer Protections)
summary_short: Bill text that would amend Colorado Revised Statutes 6-1-1701 to 6-1-1707 to govern developers and deployers of high-risk artificial intelligence systems making consequential decisions, mainly to avoid algorithmic discrimination. Most duties apply from January 1, 2027; the attorney general enforces them.
summary_long: Amends Part 17 of Article 1 of Title 6, Colorado Revised Statutes (sections 6-1-1701 to 6-1-1707), on high-risk artificial intelligence systems used in consequential decisions about consumers, such as employment, lending, housing, health care and insurance. From January 1, 2027, developers must give deployers documentation and statements of intended and known harmful uses, and keep records for at least three years. Deployers must adopt a risk management policy and program, complete impact assessments before first deployment and annually, and review systems yearly for algorithmic discrimination. From May 1, 2026, deployers must give consumers a pre-decision statement and, after an adverse decision, a notice within thirty days with an opportunity to correct data and appeal. AI systems interacting with consumers must be disclosed as AI from January 1, 2027. Exemptions cover small deployers, recruitment-only uses and systems that are not the principal basis of decisions. The attorney general has exclusive enforcement authority from January 1, 2027; violations are unfair trade practices, and an affirmative defense is available for curable violations cured within seven days. The act takes effect ninety days after adjournment, subject to referendum.

title: Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 (15 U.S.C. 6501-6506)
summary_short: US federal statute requiring operators of child-directed online services, or those with actual knowledge of child users, to give notice and obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from children under 13. It directs FTC rulemaking and enforcement.
summary_long: This statute (15 U.S.C. 6501-6506) defines a child as an individual under 13 and an operator as a commercial website or online service operator that collects personal information online. Section 6502(a) makes it unlawful for such an operator, or one with actual knowledge of collecting from a child, to collect personal information from a child in violation of FTC regulations. Section 6502(b) requires the FTC, within one year of 21 October 1998, to issue rules requiring website notice of collection and use practices, verifiable parental consent, parental access and refusal rights, no conditioning of a child's participation on excess disclosure, and reasonable confidentiality and security procedures. The rules must set out exceptions for certain online contact information. Section 6502(c) treats a rule violation as an unfair or deceptive practice under the FTC Act. Section 6503 allows self-regulatory guidelines approved by the Commission to serve as deemed compliance, with action on requests within 180 days. Section 6504 lets state attorneys general sue in federal court for injunctions, enforcement, or damages on behalf of residents, after notice to the FTC. Section 6505 assigns enforcement to the FTC and to listed federal banking, transport and agricultural agencies. Section 6502(d) bars inconsistent state liability. Section 6506 requires an FTC review and a report to Congress within five years after the initial regulations take effect. Under the statutory notes, subsection (a) takes effect on the later of 18 months after enactment or the Commission's ruling on the first safe harbor application, and no later than 30 months after enactment.}},
text_version: 15 U.S.C. ch. 91 (6501-6506), United States Code 2023 edition (GPO)

title: An Act Concerning Artificial Intelligence, Automated Decision-Making and Personal Data Privacy
summary_short: Requires Connecticut state agencies and the Judicial Department to inventory their AI systems and to assess them for unlawful discrimination or disparate impact before implementation, and requires state contracts with businesses to include privacy-act compliance clauses. Sections 1-3 take effect July 1, 2023.
summary_long: Substitute Senate Bill 1103 (approved June 7, 2023) governs artificial intelligence use in Connecticut state government. Section 1 requires the Department of Administrative Services to inventory state agencies' AI systems annually, first by December 31, 2023, publish the inventory, and assess the systems from February 1, 2024 for unlawful discrimination or disparate impact. Section 2 requires the Office of Policy and Management to set procurement, implementation and assessment policies by February 1, 2024, and bars state agencies from implementing AI systems without a prior impact assessment or where the agency head determines discrimination or disparate impact would result. Section 3 imposes parallel duties on the Judicial Department. Section 4, from October 1, 2023, requires state contracts with businesses to require compliance with sections 42-515 to 42-525 of the general statutes. Section 5, effective on passage, creates a working group to make recommendations on AI use in state government and private-sector regulation, reporting by February 1, 2024. The sections state no penalties.

title: Public Act 22-15 (SB 6), An Act Concerning Personal Data Privacy and Online Monitoring
summary_short: Connecticut's Public Act 22-15 gives state residents rights over their personal data, including opt-out rights for targeted advertising, data sales and certain profiling. It imposes controller and processor duties on businesses above volume thresholds, effective 1 July 2023, enforced exclusively by the Attorney General.
summary_long: Public Act 22-15 (SB 6) applies to persons that conduct business in Connecticut or target products or services to its residents and that, in the preceding calendar year, controlled or processed personal data of at least 100,000 consumers, or of at least 25,000 consumers while deriving more than 25 per cent of gross revenue from selling personal data. It exempts state bodies, nonprofits, higher-education institutions, Gramm-Leach-Bliley financial institutions, HIPAA covered entities and business associates, and listed categories of data. Consumers may confirm, access, correct, delete and port their personal data, and opt out of targeted advertising, data sales and certain solely automated profiling. Controllers must limit collection, secure data, obtain consent for sensitive data, avoid unlawful discrimination, provide a privacy notice, and from 1 January 2025 honour opt-out preference signals. Processors must follow controller instructions under a binding contract. Controllers must conduct data protection assessments for targeted advertising, data sales, certain profiling and sensitive data processing. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority; from 1 July 2023 to 31 December 2024 it must issue notice and allow a sixty-day cure period, and the Act creates no private right of action. A task force is convened to study related topics and report.

title: Connecticut Substitute Senate Bill 1103
summary_short: Connecticut Public Act 23-16 requires state agencies and the Judicial Department to inventory and assess AI systems for unlawful discrimination, bars agencies from deploying AI without a prior impact assessment from February 1, 2024, requires state contracts to include data privacy compliance clauses, and creates an AI working group.
summary_long: Public Act No. 23-16 (Substitute Senate Bill 1103) governs artificial intelligence (AI) systems used by Connecticut state agencies and the Judicial Department. Sections 1 and 3 require the Department of Administrative Services and the Judicial Department to inventory their AI systems annually, publish the inventories, and assess the systems for unlawful discrimination or disparate impact. Section 2 requires the Office of Policy and Management to establish policies and procedures for state agency AI systems, including a pre-implementation impact assessment, and bars state agencies from implementing such a system without that assessment or where the agency head determines it will cause unlawful discrimination or disparate impact, from February 1, 2024. Section 3(d) applies similar limits to the Judicial Department. Section 4, effective October 1, 2023, requires state contracting agencies to include in business contracts a clause requiring compliance with sections 42-515 to 42-525 of the general statutes. Section 5 creates a legislative working group on AI in state government, which must report by February 1, 2024. The text states no penalties or enforcement mechanism.

title: Public Act 25-113 (SB 1295), amending the Connecticut Data Privacy Act and related online safety provisions
summary_short: Connecticut Public Act 25-113 amends the state's Data Privacy Act and adds minors' online protections, social media safety duties, affordable broadband and related consumer rules, mostly applying from 1 July 2026.
summary_long: Public Act 25-113 (SB 1295), approved 24 June 2025, amends the Connecticut Data Privacy Act and adds unrelated provisions. Sec. 1 (from 1 July 2025) creates a Net Equality Program: qualified broadband providers must offer eligible households affordable service capped at $40 monthly, and state agencies must prefer such providers. Sec. 4 requires social media owners to add online safety centers and cyberbullying policies. Secs. 5-12 (effective 1 July 2026) amend the privacy act: applicability at 35,000 consumers or sensitive data, rights including opt-out of legal-effect profiling, minimization and consent duties, privacy notices disclosing large-language-model training, opt-out signals, processor contracts, and data protection and profiling impact assessments. Secs. 13-18 add minors' rules on account deletion, targeted advertising, sale, profiling, geolocation, design features and direct messaging. Sec. 19 requires vehicle providers to act on survivors' requests within two business days. Secs. 2-3 (lottery licensing, sports wagering voids) and 20-22 (automatic renewal, dealer fees, home-improvement advertising) add further consumer and gaming rules.

title: Connecticut (2017) SB 260
summary_short: Connecticut 2017 act creating a pilot program in which autonomous vehicle testers may test fully autonomous vehicles on highways of up to four municipalities under registration, insurance and operating conditions, plus a task force to study their regulation. Effective from passage.
summary_long: Section 1 defines fully autonomous vehicles (SAE J3016 levels four or five), operators, testers, fleet service providers and manufacturers. The Office of Policy and Management must establish a pilot program for up to four municipalities, selected by the Secretary using 2010 census population ranges, in which autonomous vehicle testers may test fully autonomous vehicles on highways. Each municipality signs a written agreement fixing locations, routes, vehicles and hours. Testing requires an operator seated at the wheel, able to take manual control and holding an operator's license; registration of each vehicle with the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles; liability insurance, self-insurance or a surety bond of at least five million dollars; and compliance with traffic law and NHTSA standards. Testing on limited access highways is prohibited. The Secretary may immediately prohibit an operator or tester posing a risk to public safety or not complying, and testers must provide performance information, withholding commercially valuable or proprietary data. The Secretary reports to the transportation committee by January 1, 2019 and annually thereafter. Section 2 creates a 14-member task force to study state regulation of fully autonomous vehicles, with interim reports due January 1 and July 1, 2018 and a final report by January 1, 2019; it terminates on the final report or January 1, 2019, whichever is later. Sections 1 and 2 take effect from passage; the act was approved June 27, 2017.

title: A Bill in the District of Columbia to prohibit users of algorithmic decision-making from utilizing algorithmic eligibility determinations in a discriminatory manner, to require corresponding notices to individuals whose personal information is used, and to provide for appropriate means of civil enforcement.
summary_short: The Stop Discrimination by Algorithms Act of 2023, a pending District of Columbia bill, would bar covered entities from making algorithmic eligibility or information-availability determinations based on protected traits in discriminatory ways. It would also require notices, adverse-action disclosures, annual audits, reports to the Attorney General, and civil enforcement. It would take effect after approval, congressional review and publication.
summary_long: The bill, introduced in the Council of the District of Columbia, prohibits covered entities from making algorithmic eligibility or algorithmic information availability determinations on the basis of protected traits in a manner that segregates, discriminates against, or makes important life opportunities unavailable (Sec. 4(a)). Practices with that effect are deemed unlawful discriminatory practices. Covered entities include those with personal information on more than 25,000 District residents, more than $15 million in average annualized gross receipts, data brokers meeting a revenue test, and service providers. Important life opportunities cover credit, education, employment, housing, public accommodations and insurance. Sec. 4(b) preserves Human Rights Act exemptions and affirmative action plans. Sec. 5 requires written agreements with service providers. Sec. 6 requires a public notice on personal information use, posting and pre-use delivery, and a disclosure to individuals after adverse actions based on eligibility determinations. Sec. 7 requires annual audits, an audit trail kept at least five years, annual impact assessments, and an annual report to the Attorney General. Sec. 8 authorizes Attorney General civil actions and investigations with civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation, and private civil actions with damages of $100 to $10,000 per violation or actual damages, plus punitive damages and attorney's fees. Under Sec. 10 the act takes effect after mayoral approval or veto override, a 30-day congressional review period, and publication in the District of Columbia Register.

title: House Bill 154 (152nd GA), Delaware Personal Data Privacy Act (6 Del. C. ch. 12D; 84 Del. Laws c. 197)
summary_short: Creates the Delaware Personal Data Privacy Act (6 Del. C. ch. 12D). It gives Delaware residents rights to access, correct, delete and obtain a portable copy of personal data, and imposes duties on controllers and processors. Takes effect 1 January 2025 or 2026, depending on enactment date.
summary_long: Creates the Delaware Personal Data Privacy Act (6 Del. C. ch. 12D). Residents gain rights to confirm and access, correct, delete and obtain a portable copy of their personal data, to learn recipients, and to opt out of targeted advertising, sale, and solely automated profiling with legal or similarly significant effects. Controllers must respond within 45 days (extendable by 45), provide an appeal, honor authorized agents and opt-out preference signals, limit collection and purposes, obtain consent for sensitive data and for certain minors' data, post a privacy notice, and not discriminate against consumers who exercise rights. Processors must follow controller instructions and meet contract terms. Controllers handling data of 100,000 or more consumers must document data protection assessments for high-risk processing. Coverage: persons doing business in Delaware or targeting residents that process data of 35,000 or more consumers (or 10,000 plus over 20 percent of gross revenue from data sales); excludes state bodies, GLBA financial institutions, HIPAA data and other listed categories. The Department of Justice alone enforces, after a notice of violation with at least 60 days to cure; no private right of action is created. Takes effect 1 January 2025 if enacted on or before 1 January 2024, otherwise 1 January 2026.

title: Department of Defense Directive 3000.09 ("Autonomy in weapon systems")
summary_short: DoD Directive 3000.09 sets DoD policy for the design, testing, approval, fielding and employment of autonomous and semi-autonomous weapon systems. It requires senior review and approval of certain autonomous weapon systems before formal development and again before fielding, and sets verification and testing requirements. Effective January 25, 2023.
summary_long: DoD Directive 3000.09, effective January 25, 2023, applies to DoD organizations and to the design, development, acquisition, testing, fielding and employment of autonomous and semi-autonomous weapon systems. It excludes cyberspace capabilities, unarmed platforms, unguided and manually guided munitions, mines, unexploded ordnance and non-weapon systems. It requires that systems allow commanders and operators to exercise appropriate levels of human judgment over the use of force, and sets verification, validation and test-and-evaluation requirements, including for AI capabilities. Certain autonomous weapon systems require senior review and approval by named DoD officials before formal development and again before fielding. Certain semi-autonomous, defensive and non-lethal systems are exempt from that review. International sales or transfers follow existing technology security processes. The directive assigns responsibilities to the Under Secretaries, the Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, DOT&E, the CDAO, the CJCS, the Military Departments and Combatant Commanders, and establishes an Autonomous Weapon System Working Group. A Deputy Secretary of Defense waiver is available for urgent military need. The excerpt sets out no penalty provisions. It reissues and cancels the November 21, 2012 directive of the same title.

title: Preventing Access to U.S. Sensitive Personal Data and Government-Related Data by Countries of Concern or Covered Persons (28 CFR Part 202)
summary_short: US Department of Justice final rule (28 CFR Part 202), effective April 8, 2025, implementing Executive Order 14117. It prohibits or restricts U.S. persons' data brokerage, vendor, employment and investment transactions giving countries of concern or covered persons access to bulk sensitive personal or government-related data.
summary_long: Final rule of the U.S. Department of Justice, National Security Division, 28 CFR Part 202, effective April 8, 2025, implementing Executive Order 14117 of February 28, 2024. It concerns U.S. persons' covered data transactions that give countries of concern or covered persons access to government-related data or bulk U.S. sensitive personal data. Subpart C prohibits data brokerage and related transactions, including certain human 'omic data transactions and evasions. Subpart D authorizes restricted transactions (vendor, employment and investment agreements) only if CISA-based security requirements are met. Definitions cover sensitive personal data categories (covered personal identifiers, precise geolocation, biometric identifiers, human 'omic, personal health and personal financial data), bulk thresholds (for example 100 U.S. persons for human genomic data), countries of concern (subpart F) and covered persons, including designation (subpart G). Subpart E sets exemptions, such as official U.S. Government business, financial services and regulatory approval data. Subpart H provides for licenses, subpart I for advisory opinions, subpart J for due diligence and audits (certain provisions applicable from October 6, 2025), subpart K for recordkeeping and reporting, and subpart M for penalties and findings of violation.

title: Executive Order 14110 of October 30, 2023: Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence
summary_short: Executive Order of October 30, 2023 directs federal agencies on safe, secure and trustworthy AI development and use. It requires developers of potential dual-use foundation models and owners of large computing clusters to report specified information to the Commerce Secretary, and sets compute thresholds for that reporting. It also directs guidance, standards, studies, and rules on federal AI use, privacy, workers, civil rights and sectors.
summary_long: Executive Order of October 30, 2023 directs executive departments and agencies to govern AI development and use under eight stated principles. Section 4 requires the Commerce Secretary to require companies developing potential dual-use foundation models, and entities possessing large-scale computing clusters, to report specified information, using compute thresholds above 10^26 integer or floating-point operations (and 10^23 for primarily biological sequence data). It also directs proposed rules requiring US infrastructure-as-a-service providers to report foreign training runs and to verify foreign resellers' customers. NIST is to develop AI safety guidance, including red-teaming, and Section 4.4 directs biosecurity measures for synthetic nucleic acids. Section 4.5 addresses labeling and provenance of synthetic content. Other sections cover innovation and talent (5), workers (6), equity and civil rights, including criminal justice and benefits (7), sector guidance for health, transportation, education and communications (8), privacy (9), and federal government AI use through OMB guidance, Chief AI Officers, minimum risk-management practices and procurement (10). Most deadlines run from 30 to 540 days after the order's date. Section 13 states that the order creates no enforceable rights and is subject to applicable law and appropriations.

title: Executive Order 14117 of February 28, 2024: Preventing Access to Americans' Bulk Sensitive Personal Data and United States Government-Related Data by Countries of Concern
summary_short: Executive Order 14117 directs the Attorney General to issue regulations restricting U.S. persons' transactions that give countries of concern or covered persons access to Americans' bulk sensitive personal data or US Government-related data. DHS/CISA must publish security requirements for restricted transactions. Signed 28 February 2024.
summary_long: Sets national-security restrictions on access by countries of concern to Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and US Government-related data, under IEEPA and the national emergency in EO 13873. Section 2 directs the Attorney General, with DHS, to issue regulations that prohibit or restrict U.S. persons' transactions involving such data or classes of transactions posing unacceptable risk. Regulations must define terms, identify countries of concern and covered persons, create licensing, and address recordkeeping; they may not impose generalized data localization. A proposed rule is due within 180 days. DHS/CISA must publish security requirements for restricted transactions based on NIST frameworks. Evasion, conspiracy and knowingly directing prohibited transactions are also prohibited. Section 3 directs the Committee for the Assessment of Foreign Participation in the US Telecommunications Services Sector to prioritise reviews of submarine cable licences linked to countries of concern; agencies are to consider limiting federal healthcare and research assistance that enables such access; the CFPB is encouraged to address data brokers. Sections 4 to 6 require recommendations on prior transfers, reports to the President, and an assessment of other human 'omic data. Section 8 creates no enforceable rights. The order states no penalty amounts; enforcement terms are left to implementing regulations.

title: Executive Order 14141 of January 14, 2025: Advancing United States Leadership in Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure
summary_short: Directs federal agencies to enable AI data centers and supporting power infrastructure on Federal land, using competitive lease solicitations, clean-power, security and labor conditions, accelerated permitting and grid measures, effective from 14 January 2025.
summary_long: This order sets federal policy to enable AI infrastructure, including data centers, under five principles: national security, competitiveness, clean power, consumer electricity costs, and labor and community benefits. Sec. 3 defines AI data center and related terms. Sec. 4 directs the Defense and Energy Secretaries to identify Federal sites and run competitive solicitations for private leases, with winners subject to conditions on new clean power, hourly matching, cybersecurity and lab security, a memorandum of understanding with the AI Safety Institute, investment reporting and limits, and national-security access to models. Sec. 4(i) requires Defense Department regulations on heightened safeguards for computing hardware at sites it manages, with penalties; Interior must identify BLM sites and designate at least five Priority Geothermal Zones. Secs. 5 to 9 direct reports on electricity prices, transmission and interconnection reporting, expedited NEPA, Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act permitting, endangered-species consultation, transformer supply measures, nationwide permit review, nuclear deployment sites, distributed-energy model contracts and a voluntary power-usage target below 1.1. Sec. 10 directs a State Department plan for allied AI infrastructure; Sec. 11 creates no enforceable rights. Deadlines run from 14 January 2025 to 2027.

title: Executive Order 14299 of May 23, 2025: Deploying Advanced Nuclear Reactor Technologies for National Security
summary_short: Executive Order 14299 directs federal agencies, chiefly the Departments of Defense and Energy, to accelerate advanced nuclear reactor deployment for national security, including reactors powering military installations and AI data centers at DOE facilities, fuel supply, nuclear exports and prioritized nuclear security clearances.
summary_long: Executive Order 14299 directs agencies, chiefly the Departments of Defense and Energy, to accelerate advanced nuclear reactor deployment, fuel supply and exports for national security. Sec. 3 requires a Defense program of record and a reactor operating at a domestic military base by September 30, 2028. Sec. 4 directs DOE to initiate designating AI data centers located at or operated in coordination with DOE facilities as critical defense facilities, treats their electrical infrastructure as defense critical electric infrastructure, and requires DOE to authorize privately funded reactors at DOE sites, targeting operation within 30 months. Sec. 5 requires at least 20 metric tons of HALEU to be released to a fuel bank for authorized private projects. Sec. 7 directs NEPA consultation on categorical exclusions. Sec. 8 has State pursue at least 20 new 123 Agreements and DOE decide technology export authorizations within 30 days of a complete application, subject to concurrence. Sec. 9 prioritizes nuclear security clearances. The order is subject to appropriations, creates no enforceable rights and states no penalties.

title: Executive Order 14318 of July 23, 2025: Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure
summary_short: Executive Order of July 23, 2025 directs federal agencies to speed permitting, NEPA and ESA review, financial support and federal-land access for AI data centers above 100 MW and related covered components such as energy infrastructure and semiconductors.
summary_long: Directs federal agencies to speed permitting and support for Qualifying Projects: AI data centers over 100 MW of new load and related Covered Components, including energy infrastructure, natural gas turbines, semiconductors and data storage. Sec. 2 defines Qualifying Projects by capital expenditure of at least $500 million, incremental load above 100 MW, national-security status, or designation by a named Secretary. Sec. 3 directs Commerce to launch a financial support initiative (loans, guarantees, grants, tax incentives, offtake agreements). Sec. 4 revokes Executive Order 14141. Sec. 5 has agencies identify categorical exclusions under NEPA and CEQ coordinate new ones; federal financial assistance below 50% of project cost is presumed not substantial federal control. Sec. 6 lets the FPISC Executive Director designate transparency projects and publish them on the Permitting Dashboard. Sec. 7 directs EPA to expedite permitting and identify Brownfield and Superfund sites, with guidance within 180 days. Sec. 8 requires programmatic ESA consultation and an Army review of nationwide permits within 180 days. Sec. 9 directs Interior and Energy to offer authorizations on federal sites and Defense to identify and lease military-installation sites. Sec. 10 disclaims enforceable rights and makes implementation subject to law and appropriations.

title: Executive Order 14319 of July 23, 2025: Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government
summary_short: Directs federal agency heads to procure only large language models that meet two Unbiased AI Principles (truth-seeking and ideological neutrality), with OMB guidance due within 120 days of the order dated July 23, 2025.
summary_long: The order requires federal agency heads, consistent with applicable law, to procure only large language models (LLMs) developed under two Unbiased AI Principles: truth-seeking (truthful responses to factual prompts, prioritising historical accuracy and acknowledging uncertainty) and ideological neutrality (no manipulation of responses in favour of ideological dogmas such as DEI, and no intentional encoding of partisan or ideological judgments unless prompted or readily accessible to end users). Within 120 days the Director of OMB must issue implementing guidance, which must account for technical limitations, allow vendors to show transparency through system prompts, specifications, evaluations or other documentation, and make exceptions for national security systems. Agency heads must include contract terms requiring compliance in new LLM contracts, charge decommissioning costs to vendors terminated for noncompliance after a reasonable cure period, revise existing contracts where practicable, and within 90 days of the OMB guidance adopt compliance procedures. The order does not impair existing agency authority, is subject to appropriations, and creates no enforceable rights.

title: Executive Order 14320 of July 23, 2025: Promoting the Export of the American AI Technology Stack
summary_short: Directs the Secretary of Commerce, within 90 days, to establish the American AI Exports Program for full-stack American AI export packages, soliciting industry-led consortia proposals. Directs the Secretary of State to coordinate Federal financing tools through the EDAG for priority packages. Dated July 23, 2025.
summary_long: Executive Order 14320 of July 23, 2025 directs the Secretary of Commerce, within 90 days, to establish the American AI Exports Program to support United States full-stack AI export packages. The Secretary must issue a public call for industry-led consortium proposals. Each proposal must include a full-stack package (AI-optimized hardware, data pipelines, AI models and systems, cybersecurity measures and use-case applications), target countries or regional blocs, a high-level data-center business model, requested Federal incentives, and compliance with export control and outbound investment rules. Proposals are due within 90 days of the call and considered on a rolling basis. Selected proposals are designated priority AI export packages with priority access to Federal financing tools. Section 4 makes the Secretary of State responsible for a unified export strategy and for coordinating the Economic Diplomacy Action Group (EDAG), whose members the SBA and OSTP may appoint. Listed financing tools, used to the maximum extent permitted by law, include direct and guaranteed loans, equity investments, political risk insurance and technical assistance. Implementation is subject to applicable law and appropriations, and the order creates no enforceable rights. The order sets no penalties.

title: Executive Order 14409 of June 2, 2026: Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security
summary_short: Directs federal agencies to prioritize cyber defense of national security and federal information systems, creates a Treasury-led AI cybersecurity clearinghouse, and sets up a voluntary government-access framework for frontier models before release. Bars mandatory model licensing. Directs DOJ to prioritize prosecution of AI-enabled computer crime.
summary_long: Executive order on AI-related cybersecurity and frontier-model security. Within 30 days, the Committee on National Security Systems, the Secretary of War, and DHS (through CISA) must prioritize cyber defense of national security and federal systems; DHS must issue binding operational directives and other guidance. Treasury must form an AI cybersecurity clearinghouse in voluntary collaboration with industry and critical-infrastructure operators, and OMB must assess whether federal grant funds can support AI vulnerability detection. Within 60 days, OPM must expand cybersecurity hiring pathways; Treasury, the Secretary of War, NSA, CISA, NIST and Commerce must develop a classified benchmark for designating 'covered frontier models' and a voluntary framework giving government up to 30 days' pre-release access. The order states that it authorizes no mandatory licensing, preclearance or permitting for AI model development or release. The Attorney General must prioritize enforcement of existing federal computer-crime statutes against AI-enabled unauthorized access. The order creates no enforceable rights and is subject to applicable law and appropriations.

title: Declaratory Ruling, Implications of Artificial Intelligence Technologies on Protecting Consumers from Unwanted Robocalls and Robotexts (FCC 24-17, CG Docket No. 23-362)
summary_short: FCC declaratory ruling applying the TCPA's restrictions on artificial or prerecorded voice calls to AI technologies that generate or simulate human voices, including voice cloning. Callers need prior express consent absent an emergency purpose or exemption, and must give caller identification and disclosure. Effective upon release, 8 February 2024.
summary_long: Declaratory ruling of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC 24-17, CG Docket No. 23-362), adopted 2 February 2024 and released 8 February 2024. It confirms that the Telephone Consumer Protection Act's restrictions on calls using an 'artificial or prerecorded voice' cover current AI technologies that resemble human voices or generate call content using a prerecorded voice, including voice cloning (paras. 1-5). Under the ruling, callers using such technologies must obtain the called party's prior express consent before initiating the call, absent an emergency purpose or exemption, and the presence of a live agent on the call does not change this (paras. 5, 8-9). Calls must state the identity of the entity responsible for initiating them, and advertising or telemarketing calls must offer specified opt-out methods, under existing 47 CFR 64.1200(b) rules (para. 9). The ruling is effective upon release (para. 11) and follows a November 2023 Notice of Inquiry (paras. 4, 8). The ruling itself sets no penalties. The separate commissioner statements refer to enforcement by State Attorneys General and the FCC's authority, but those statements are not operative provisions.

title: Order Instituting Proceeding (show cause) on Large Load Interconnection, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,211, Docket No. EL26-67 (and parallel orders to CAISO, ISO-NE, MISO, NYISO, SPP)
summary_short: FERC order under FPA section 206 instituting a proceeding against PJM Interconnection and its listed Transmission Owners on transmission service, cost recovery and interconnection for large loads. PJM and the Transmission Owners must show cause or propose Tariff revisions within 60 days. Issued June 18, 2026.
summary_long: Order under Federal Power Act section 206 instituting a proceeding in Docket No. EL26-67-000 against PJM Interconnection and its listed Transmission Owners. It makes preliminary findings that PJM's Tariff appears unjust and unreasonable for lacking provisions on large loads. It proposes a large-load definition: a new commercial or industrial customer at a single site with a peak load of 50 MW or greater, interconnecting above 69 kV, and not part of a co-location arrangement. Preliminary findings cover the study process and application process for transmission service on behalf of large loads, including a non-refundable application fee and readiness requirements; ongoing operational requirements such as telemetry, remote disconnection and ramp-rate rules; public posting of Network Upgrade cost data; a pro forma cost recovery agreement with minimum contribution and credit support; new transmission services for flexible large loads; evaluation of alternative transmission technologies; and generator interconnection processes for electrically proximate large load and co-located load. Within 60 days PJM and the Transmission Owners must either show cause or propose replacement Tariff changes. Within 30 days PJM must file an informational report on resource adequacy. Interventions are due within 21 days, and abeyance requests may cover up to 90 days. The refund effective date is the Federal Register publication date of the notice of initiation. The order states that it does not intrude on state retail authority.

title: PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Order Directing PJM to Establish Rules for Co-Located Load (193 FERC ¶ 61,217) and Order on Rehearing, Clarification, Compliance Filing (195 FERC ¶ 61,209), Docket No. EL25-49
summary_short: FERC order (Docket EL25-49) on rehearing and PJM compliance. Sustains finding that PJM's Tariff lacks clear co-location rules; sets replacement transmission services (Interim NITS, firm and non-firm contract demand) for Eligible Customers serving Co-Located Load or load with BTMG; directs further PJM compliance filings within 60 days.
summary_long: Order of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, issued June 18, 2026, on rehearing, clarification, PJM's second compliance filing and the paper hearing that followed the December 18, 2025 show-cause order (193 FERC ¶ 61,217). It sustains the finding that PJM's Tariff is unjust and unreasonable for lacking clear provisions on Co-Location Arrangements, where a generator and load share a site, and for not offering transmission services that reflect a load's willingness to limit its withdrawals. It sets as just and reasonable three new transmission services for Eligible Customers serving Co-Located Load or load with behind-the-meter generation (BTMG): Interim NITS, Firm Contract Demand (FCD) and Non-Firm Contract Demand (NFCD) service, charged on contract demand. It finds PJM's retail BTMG netting rules remain unjust and unreasonable and directs revisions, including a transition period, grandfathering, and an exemption for certain cogeneration Qualifying Facilities integrated with load. It states that states keep authority over generator siting and retail cost allocation, while wholesale sales and transmission charges fall under FERC jurisdiction. It denies or dismisses most rehearing and clarification requests and directs PJM and PJM transmission owners to file further compliance filings within 60 days of the order's date.

title: CS/HB 919 (2024), Artificial Intelligence Use in Political Advertising (Ch. 2024-126, Laws of Florida)
summary_short: From 1 July 2024, Florida requires political advertisements that use generative AI to depict a real person doing something that did not occur, made with intent to injure a candidate or deceive on a ballot issue, to carry a specified AI disclaimer. Omission is a first-degree misdemeanor.
summary_long: Section 1 creates s. 106.145, Florida Statutes, and defines generative artificial intelligence. Political advertisements, electioneering communications and other miscellaneous advertisements of a political nature must prominently state the disclaimer "Created in whole or in part with the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI)" where they contain generative AI content that appears to depict a real person performing an action that did not occur, created with intent to injure a candidate or deceive regarding a ballot issue. The disclaimer is additional to other chapter 106 disclaimers. Subsection (3) sets size, font and audibility requirements by medium. A person identified under another chapter 106 disclaimer as paying for, sponsoring or approving such an advertisement who omits the disclaimer commits a first-degree misdemeanor, in addition to civil penalties provided by law. Any person may file a complaint with the Florida Elections Commission under s. 106.25, and expedited hearings apply. Section 2 sets the effective date as July 1, 2024.

title: Florida Senate Bill 1680
summary_short: Florida SB 1680 (2024) creates a Government Technology Modernization Council to study and recommend on AI and government technology, and makes knowingly possessing or intentionally creating generated child pornography a third-degree felony. Effective July 1, 2024.
summary_long: SB 1680 (2024) makes three changes to Florida law. Section 1 creates s. 282.802, F.S., establishing the Government Technology Modernization Council as an advisory council within the Department of Management Services, with state officials, appointed experts and legislators as members. The council meets at least quarterly to study new technologies, including automated decision systems, AI safety standards, digital provenance disclosure for generated images and audio, and bad-actor uses of AI, and must submit legislative recommendations to the Governor and legislative leaders by December 31, 2024 and each December 31 thereafter. Section 2 creates s. 827.072, F.S., defining generated child pornography as computer-generated images of a fictitious person a reasonable person would regard as a real person under 18 in sexual conduct. Knowingly possessing, controlling or intentionally viewing such material, and intentionally creating it, are third-degree felonies, each item possessed is a separate offense, and possession during a law enforcement investigation is excluded. Section 3 amends s. 92.561, F.S., requiring such material in criminal proceedings to stay secured with law enforcement, the state attorney or the court, and requiring courts to deny defendants' requests to reproduce it where the state attorney makes it reasonably available for inspection. The act takes effect July 1, 2024.

title: Florida CS/SB 482 (Artificial Intelligence Bill of Rights 2025)
summary_short: This bill text would amend Fla. Stat. s. 287.138 to bar governmental entities from knowingly contracting for AI technology with entities owned by, controlled by, or based in a foreign country of concern. It would create the Artificial Intelligence Bill of Rights (part IX of chapter 501), listing resident rights without creating new ones. Companion chatbot platforms would need parental consent for minor account holders, offer parents monitoring and time-limit controls, disclose AI status and remind minors hourly to take breaks. Bot operators must display hourly non-human notices, and AI technology companies may not sell or disclose personal information unless deidentified. The Department of Legal Affairs would enforce these as deceptive trade practices, with civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation and 45-day cure periods; minor account holders may recover damages of up to $10,000. The bill also amends s. 540.08 to require consent for commercial use of generative-AI likenesses and creates s. 1006.1495 limiting student access to AI instructional tools before grade 6 and requiring parental notice and opt-out. Effective July 1, 2026.
summary_long: This bill text would amend Fla. Stat. s. 287.138 to bar governmental entities from knowingly contracting for AI technology with entities owned by, controlled by, or based in a foreign country of concern. It would create the Artificial Intelligence Bill of Rights (part IX of chapter 501), listing resident rights without creating new ones. Companion chatbot platforms would need parental consent for minor account holders, offer parents monitoring and time-limit controls, disclose AI status and remind minors hourly to take breaks. Bot operators must display hourly non-human notices, and AI technology companies may not sell or disclose personal information unless deidentified. The Department of Legal Affairs would enforce these as deceptive trade practices, with civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation and 45-day cure periods; minor account holders may recover damages of up to $10,000. The bill also amends s. 540.08 to require consent for commercial use of generative-AI likenesses and creates s. 1006.1495 limiting student access to AI instructional tools before grade 6 and requiring parental notice and opt-out. Effective July 1, 2026.

title: 21 CFR § 892.2070 ("Medical image analyzer")
summary_short: Classifies medical image analyzers, including computer-assisted detection (CADe) devices for mammography, ultrasound, radiograph lung nodule and dental caries detection, as Class II prescription devices under special controls. Sets design verification, validation and labeling requirements for these devices; the text states no effective date.
summary_long: 21 CFR § 892.2070 describes medical image analyzers, including CADe devices for mammography breast cancer, ultrasound breast lesions, radiograph lung nodules and radiograph dental caries, as prescription devices that mark or direct clinicians' attention to portions of previously acquired radiology images that may reveal abnormalities. The device uses pattern recognition and data analysis, is not intended to replace review by a qualified radiologist, and is not intended for triage or to recommend diagnosis. Paragraph (b) classifies the device as Class II (special controls). Design verification and validation must include a description of the algorithms, pre-specified performance testing and results showing reader performance improvement with diagnostic accuracy measures, and software documentation including cybersecurity. Labeling must describe the patient population, reading protocol, intended user and training, inputs and outputs, compatible imaging hardware, warnings and limitations including failure situations, operating instructions and a summary of performance testing. The text contains no penalty, effective-date or enforcement provisions.

title: 21 CFR § 892.2060 ("Radiological computer-assisted diagnostic software for lesions suspicious of cancer")
summary_short: FDA regulation classifying radiological computer-assisted diagnostic software that characterizes lesions suspicious for cancer as Class II (special controls) image-processing devices. It sets design verification, validation and labeling requirements for manufacturers, with the clinical user making diagnostic decisions.
summary_long: The section identifies radiological computer-assisted diagnostic software for lesions suspicious of cancer as an image processing prescription device. It aids in characterizing lesions on images such as magnetic resonance, mammography, radiography or computed tomography, extracting features from the images and giving information about the lesions to the user. Diagnostic and patient management decisions remain with the clinical user. Paragraph (b) classifies the device as Class II (special controls). Design verification and validation must include a detailed description of the image analysis algorithms, pre-specified performance testing protocols, results showing the device improves reader performance in the intended use population, test datasets with sufficient cases from important cohorts, standalone performance testing, and software documentation including cybersecurity. Labeling must include the patient population, reading protocol, intended user and training, device inputs and outputs, compatible imaging hardware and protocols, warnings and limitations (including situations where the device may fail), instructions for use, and a detailed summary of performance testing with sub-analyses. The text states no numeric thresholds, enforcement measures or penalties.

title: 21 CFR § 870.2345 ("Electrocardiograph software for over-the-counter use")
summary_short: 21 CFR § 870.2345 classifies over-the-counter electrocardiograph software devices, which create, analyze and display ECG data and can provide information for identifying cardiac arrhythmias, as Class II (special controls). The special controls require clinical, software, non-clinical and human-factors testing, and labeling for such devices.
summary_long: Section 870.2345 identifies an over-the-counter electrocardiograph software device as one that creates, analyzes and displays electrocardiograph data and can provide information for identifying cardiac arrhythmias, and states that it is not intended to provide a diagnosis. It classifies the device as Class II (special controls). The special controls require: (1) clinical performance testing under anticipated conditions of use, showing the ability to obtain an ECG of sufficient quality and the detection algorithm's sensitivity and either specificity or positive predictive value; (2) software verification, validation and hazard analysis, with documentation characterizing the software's technical specifications, detection algorithm and its inputs and outputs; (3) non-clinical performance testing of the detection algorithm against a previously adjudicated data set; (4) human factors and usability testing showing that users can use the device from its labeling alone, interpret its output and understand when to seek medical care; and (5) labeling covering hardware and operating system requirements, situations where the device may not perform at an expected level, a summary of clinical performance testing, a description of what the device measures and outputs, and guidance on interpreting results. The text states no effective date and contains no enforcement or penalty provisions. It does not use the terms artificial intelligence or machine learning.

title: 21 CFR § 870.2790 ("Photoplethysmograph analysis software for over-the-counter use")
summary_short: FDA regulation classifying over-the-counter photoplethysmograph analysis software that identifies irregular heart rhythms as Class II (special controls). It requires clinical, software, non-clinical and human factors testing and specified labeling. The text states no effective date.
summary_long: Section 870.2790 identifies a photoplethysmograph analysis software device for over-the-counter use. The device analyzes photoplethysmograph data and provides information for identifying irregular heart rhythms, and is not intended to provide a diagnosis. The device is classified as Class II (special controls). The special controls require clinical performance testing of the detection algorithm under anticipated conditions of use; software verification, validation and hazard analysis, with documentation of the software's technical specifications; non-clinical testing of signal-quality detection; and human factors and usability testing showing that users can correctly use the device from the labeling alone and interpret its output. Labeling must include hardware platform and operating system requirements, situations in which the device may not perform at an expected level, a summary of clinical performance testing, a description of what the device measures and outputs, and guidance on interpreting results. The provision sets no enforcement regime and states no effective date.

title: 21 CFR § 870.2210 ("Adjunctive predictive cardiovascular indicator")
summary_short: Classifies the adjunctive predictive cardiovascular indicator, a prescription software device that predicts future cardiovascular status or events, as Class II (special controls) and sets software, validation, clinical data, human factors and labeling requirements for it.
summary_long: 21 CFR § 870.2210 defines an adjunctive predictive cardiovascular indicator as a prescription device that uses software algorithms to analyze cardiovascular vital signs and predict future cardiovascular status or events. The device is intended for adjunctive use with other physical vital sign parameters and patient information and is not intended to independently direct therapy. Paragraph (b) classifies the device as Class II (special controls). The special controls require a software description and verification and validation results based on a hazard analysis and risk assessment, a scientific justification for the algorithm validated on an independent data set, a human factors and usability assessment of the risk of misinterpreting output, and a clinical data assessment covering representativeness and the correlation of output with the predicted event. Labeling must describe what the device measures, warn about sensor factors, give interpretation guidance stating that the output is adjunctive, state the time before the predicted status or event, list key calculation assumptions, identify sensor data types and compatible sensors, state expected performance, and report the characteristics of the patients studied and validation results. The section contains no enforcement provisions and states no effective date.

title: 21 CFR § 870.1420 ("Coronary artery disease risk indicator using acoustic heart signals")
summary_short: Classifies coronary artery disease risk indicators using acoustic heart signals as Class II devices subject to special controls on testing, algorithm validation, biocompatibility, software, usability, electrical safety and labeling. Addressed to device makers; the text states no effective date.
summary_long: 21 CFR § 870.1420 defines a coronary artery disease risk indicator using acoustic heart signals as a device that records heart sounds including murmurs and vibrations to calculate a patient-specific risk of presence of coronary artery disease, as an aid in cardiac analysis and diagnosis. Paragraph (b) classifies the device as Class II (special controls) and sets out the special controls: clinical performance testing covering the patient population and representativeness of the intended use population; acoustic performance testing of microphone sensitivity, sound acquisition bandwidth and amplitude accuracy; a scientific justification for the algorithm, including verification and validation on an independent data set; biocompatibility of patient-contacting components; software verification, validation and hazard analysis; human factors and usability testing; electromagnetic compatibility and electrical safety data; and labeling that describes the device outputs, placement instructions, care and cleaning, sensor acquisition warnings and expected performance for all intended use populations and environments. The text contains no effective date, penalty or enforcement provision.

title: 21 CFR § 870.1345 ("Intravascular bleed monitor")
summary_short: 21 CFR § 870.1345 classifies intravascular bleed monitors, which use bioimpedance and an algorithm to detect internal bleeding, as Class II devices subject to special controls. The controls require specified performance, software, biocompatibility, sterility, shelf-life and labeling data. The text states no effective date.
summary_long: Section 870.1345 of Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations defines an intravascular bleed monitor as a probe, catheter or catheter introducer that measures changes in bioimpedance and uses an algorithm to detect or monitor progression of potential internal bleeding complications. Paragraph (b) classifies the device as Class II (special controls) and lists the special controls. These require in vivo animal performance testing, non-clinical testing of eleven listed characteristics (including tensile, leakage, insertion force and corrosion testing), data supporting sterility, pyrogenicity and shelf life, biocompatibility of patient-contacting components, software verification, validation and hazard analysis, and EMC, electrical, thermal and mechanical safety data. A human factors evaluation must show correct use from the directions for use alone. Labeling must include instructions for use, shelf life and storage conditions, compatible procedures, a sizing table and quantification of blood detected. The text sets out no penalties, enforcement measures or effective date, and does not use the term artificial intelligence.

title: 21 CFR § 864.3750 ("Adjunctive hemodynamic indicator with decision point")
summary_short: 21 CFR § 870.2220 classifies an adjunctive hemodynamic indicator with decision point as a Class II (special controls) device. It sets special controls on software validation, algorithm justification, usability, clinical data and labeling for devices that monitor hemodynamic conditions and give notifications at a decision point.
summary_long: Section 870.2220 defines an adjunctive hemodynamic indicator with decision point as a device that identifies and monitors hemodynamic condition(s) of interest and provides notifications at a clinically meaningful decision point, intended for use alongside other monitoring and patient information. Paragraph (b) classifies the device as Class II (special controls) and lists the special controls: (1) software description, verification and validation based on hazard analysis and risk assessment, covering algorithm characterization, sensor hardware impact, sensor data quality controls, mitigation of user error or subsystem failure, and sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values for pre-specified time windows; (2) scientific justification of the algorithm, validated on an independent data set; (3) a usability assessment of misinterpretation risk; (4) clinical data representative of the intended population, compared with an acceptable reference method, with agreement assessed across the measurement range; and (5) labeling covering sensor data types, warnings, interpretation guidance, key assumptions and a clinical validation summary. The text sets no numeric thresholds, penalties or effective date.

title: 21 CFR § 882.1491 ("Pediatric Autism Spectrum Disorder diagnosis aid")
summary_short: 21 CFR § 882.1491 defines a pediatric Autism Spectrum Disorder diagnosis aid as a prescription device and classifies it as Class II (special controls). The special controls require clinical performance testing, software and cybersecurity documentation, usability assessment, and specified labeling. No effective date is stated.
summary_long: The rule is an administrative classification under 21 CFR § 882.1491 for a device intended as an aid in diagnosing Autism Spectrum Disorder in pediatric patients. It is placed in Class II (special controls). Under paragraph (b), the special controls require: clinical performance testing against a reference method of diagnosis, including sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values; software verification, validation and hazard analysis, with a technical description of the algorithms and a cybersecurity assessment; a usability assessment showing intended users can safely and correctly use the device; and labeling with instructions for use, a summary of clinical testing, and a statement that the device is not intended as a stand-alone diagnostic. The text states no effective date and contains no enforcement provisions or penalties.

title: 21 CFR § 876.1520 ("Gastrointestinal lesion software detection system")
summary_short: 21 CFR § 876.1520 adds a classification for gastrointestinal lesion software detection systems, computer-assisted detection devices used with endoscopy, as Class II (special controls). It sets clinical and non-clinical performance testing, usability, safety, software and labeling requirements. Dated 27 December 2022; no effective date is stated in the text.
summary_long: The FDA rule amends 21 CFR Part 876 (Gastroenterology-Urology Devices) by adding § 876.1520 to subpart B. It identifies a gastrointestinal lesion software detection system as a computer-assisted detection device used with endoscopy to detect abnormal gastrointestinal lesions, which may include hardware that interfaces with an endoscope. The device is classified as Class II (special controls). The special controls require clinical performance testing covering detection of lesions and evaluation of adverse events; non-clinical performance testing, including standalone algorithm performance, pixel-level image-quality degradation, marker-annotation video delay and real-time endoscopic video delay; usability assessment; electromagnetic compatibility, electrical, mechanical and thermal safety testing for hardware; and software verification, validation and hazard analysis with a detailed technical software description. Labeling must include instructions for use, warnings against overreliance and against diagnostic use, and summaries of clinical and standalone performance testing. The text cites 21 U.S.C. provisions as its authority. It contains no penalty or enforcement provisions and no numeric thresholds.](truncated)

title: 21 CFR § 870.2785 ("Software for optical camera-based measurement of pulse rate, heart rate, breathing rate, and/or respiratory rate")
summary_short: Classifies software that estimates pulse, heart, breathing or respiratory rate from video as a Class II (special controls) device. Requires software documentation, a cybersecurity process, clinical data, a human factors assessment and labeling. The text states no effective date.
summary_long: 21 CFR 870.2785 covers software that uses algorithms to analyze a video signal and estimate pulse rate, heart rate, breathing rate, and/or respiratory rate. The device is not intended to independently direct therapy. The device is classified as Class II (special controls). The special controls require: (1) a software description and verification and validation testing based on a hazard analysis and risk assessment, including a characterization of software parameters and algorithms, specifications for any image acquisition hardware not included with the device, mitigations for user error and subsystem failure, and a cybersecurity vulnerability and management process; (2) clinical data representative of the intended use population, showing output consistency and comparison with a clinically accurate patient-contacting comparator device; (3) a human factors and usability assessment of the risk of improper measurement; and (4) labeling that describes what the device measures, warns about sensor and subject factors, gives interpretation guidance stating the output is adjunctive to other vital sign parameters and patient information, states expected performance for all intended populations and environments, and gives setup instructions. The text sets no enforcement penalties and states no effective date.

title: 21 CFR § 864.3750 ("Software algorithm device to assist users in digital pathology")
summary_short: FDA classification rule placing software algorithm devices that assist pathology diagnosis from scanned whole slide images in Class II, subject to special controls on labeling, design verification, performance testing and cybersecurity. The text states no effective date.
summary_long: 21 CFR § 864.3750 classifies a software algorithm device to assist users in digital pathology, an in vitro diagnostic device that uses software algorithms on scanned whole slide images to flag areas with clinical implications, as Class II (special controls). The special controls require that the intended use and labeling state the specimen type, device inputs and outputs, intended users, necessary input/output devices, and limiting statements on adjunct use and on use with complete standard of care evaluation. Labeling must include a detailed device description, a summary of performance testing with stratified sub-analyses, and limiting statements on situations where the device may fail and on interpretation by intended users. Design verification and validation must include a software description with training, tuning and test datasets, emergency recovery functions, a system architecture diagram, and a risk management plan covering cybersecurity. Analytical and clinical studies must document study details, and clinical studies must compare intended users' performance with and without the device using diagnostic accuracy measures. The text states no effective date and contains no penalty or enforcement provisions. Paragraph (b)(3)(iii)(B) is marked [Reserved].

title: Federal Register Doc. No. 2024-01580. Taking Additional Steps To Address the National Emergency With Respect to Significant Malicious Cyber-Enabled Activities
summary_short: Subpart D rule (§§ 7.300–7.310) requiring U.S. infrastructure-as-a-service providers to run customer identification programs for foreign accounts, certify them to the Department, report foreign training of large AI models with potential malicious cyber-enabled capabilities, and accept special measures and penalties.
summary_long: Subpart D (§§ 7.300–7.310) of a Department of Commerce rule implementing Executive Orders 13984 and 14110 requires U.S. infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) providers to run a written Customer Identification Program (CIP) that verifies the identity of foreign customers and beneficial owners, and to ensure foreign resellers maintain equivalent CIPs (§§ 7.302–7.303). Providers must submit CIP certification forms and annual certifications, notify material changes, and keep records for at least two years (§ 7.304). The Department may conduct compliance assessments (§ 7.305). The Secretary may exempt providers with a finding under an Abuse of IaaS Products Deterrence Program (§ 7.306), and may impose special measures, such as prohibitions or conditions on accounts, on foreign jurisdictions or persons found to use IaaS products for malicious cyber-enabled activity (§ 7.307). Providers must report covered transactions that could train a large AI model with potential malicious cyber-enabled capabilities within 15 calendar days (§ 7.308). Violations carry civil penalties under IEEPA (the greater of $250,000 per violation or twice the transaction amount) and criminal fines up to $1,000,000 or imprisonment up to 20 years for willful violations (§ 7.309).

title: Train Crew Size Safety Requirements (New Technology and Automated Operations)
summary_short: Train crew size rule of the US Federal Railroad Administration, as adopted. This excerpt is the agency's preamble discussion of automated operations. It states that the rule requires a description of crew-substituting technology in special approval petitions and does not regulate autonomous operations.
summary_long: Excerpt from section c, 'New Technology and Automated Operations', of the Federal Railroad Administration's final rule on train crew size. The section responds to commenters on the proposed rule, which would have required a two-person train crew with exceptions. The excerpt states that the rule requires a petition for special approval to describe any technology used to perform or support second-crewmember tasks, or to prevent or mitigate accidents, so FRA can check whether that technology has gone through the proper waiver or regulatory processes. It says the rule is not intended to impede rail innovation and does not regulate autonomous operations. A railroad seeking autonomous operation without at least a one-person train crew would also need a waiver from this rule, specifically the requirements in 218.123. The text states that the rule addresses rail operations nationwide. The excerpt is preamble discussion; it contains no operative provisions, and the rule's effective date is not in the excerpt.

title: Section 106.11 Application: Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Sex in Education Programs or Activities Receiving Federal Financial Assistance
summary_short: Final Title IX rule § 106.11 requires recipients of federal financial assistance to address sex-based harassment occurring under their education program or activity, including off-campus conduct they control or discipline. The excerpt is the preamble discussion, not the full regulatory text.
summary_long: Section 106.11 of the Title IX final regulations, as discussed in this excerpt, requires a recipient to address sex-based harassment under its education program or activity. The provision covers conduct in off-campus settings operated or overseen by the recipient, conduct subject to the recipient's disciplinary authority, conduct on school-sponsored devices, networks and digital platforms (including AI technologies), and training programs sponsored at other locations. The Department states that a recipient is responsible for conduct over which it has disciplinary authority or substantial control, and that the list of covered conduct is not exhaustive. The changed text extends the duty to a sex-based hostile environment in the United States even where contributing conduct occurred outside the program or outside the United States. The Department states that Title IX does not apply to sex-based harassment outside a recipient's education program or activity. The excerpt also records commenters' support and opposition and the Department's responses; these are context, not operative text.

title: Federal Register Doc. No. 2024-28335 (Securing the Information and Communications Technology and Services Supply Chain)
summary_short: Amends 15 CFR Part 791 to set procedures for the Secretary of Commerce to review and prohibit or mitigate ICTS transactions involving foreign adversary-linked persons, for parties to such transactions. Binding prohibitions, recordkeeping duties and civil and criminal penalties apply.
summary_long: Federal Register rule amending 15 CFR Part 791 under E.O. 13873 and IEEPA, governing Commerce review of information and communications technology and services (ICTS) transactions involving persons owned by, controlled by, or subject to the jurisdiction of foreign adversaries. Revises definitions (including Covered ICTS Transaction, Dealing in, Importation and foreign-adversary persons), the scope in § 791.3 (ICTS integral to listed categories including connected software applications, data hosting and critical and emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence), and review criteria in § 791.103. Procedure: interagency notification with 21 days to comment (§ 791.104); Initial Determination (§ 791.105); response within 30 days (§ 791.107); interagency consultation (§ 791.108); Final Determination within 180 days of service (§ 791.109), classifying a transaction as prohibited, not prohibited or permitted with mitigation. Notified persons must retain records for at least ten years (§ 791.106). Prohibited transactions and related conduct are set out in § 791.200(a). Civil penalties follow IEEPA (greater of $250,000 per violation, inflation-adjusted, or twice the transaction amount); criminal fines up to $1,000,000 and imprisonment up to 20 years apply on conviction.

title: Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule (16 CFR Part 312), final rule amendments
summary_short: Amends the COPPA Rule (16 CFR Part 312), governing operators of child-directed and actual-knowledge services collecting personal information from children under 13. Effective June 23, 2025; regulated entities have until April 22, 2026 to comply, except specified provisions.
summary_long: The amended Rule updates the Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule (16 CFR Part 312), which governs operators of websites and online services directed to, or with actual knowledge of collecting personal information from, children under 13. It adds mobile telephone numbers to 'online contact information' for limited use to send text messages to parents to obtain parental consent, and adds government-issued identifiers and biometric identifiers that can be used for automated recognition of an individual to 'personal information'. It defines 'mixed audience website or online service', clarifies that persistent identifiers used for support for internal operations may be used for those activities, and modifies operators' direct and online notice, information security, deletion and retention obligations, and the annual assessment, disclosure and reporting duties of FTC-approved Safe Harbor programs. A 'text plus' verifiable parental consent method is added. The Commission declined to adopt proposed changes on ed tech and school authorization, removal of 'directly' from the third-party provision, screen and user names, engagement prompts, and an audience-analysis exemption. Effective June 23, 2025; compliance by April 22, 2026, except § 312.11(d)(1), (d)(4) and (g).

title: Trade Regulation Rule on Impersonation of Government and Businesses (16 CFR Part 461)
summary_short: Final FTC trade regulation rule, effective April 1, 2024, that makes it an unfair or deceptive act or practice to materially and falsely pose as, or misrepresent affiliation with, a government or business or its officers in or affecting commerce. Proposed §461.4 (means and instrumentalities) is not finalized.
summary_long: Final rule of the Federal Trade Commission (16 CFR Part 461), issued under section 18 of the FTC Act and effective April 1, 2024. Section 461.1 defines 'business' (including not-for-profit entities), 'government', 'materially' and 'officer'. Section 461.2 makes it an unfair or deceptive act or practice to materially and falsely pose as, or materially misrepresent affiliation or endorsement with, a government entity or officer, in or affecting commerce. Section 461.3 applies the same prohibition to businesses. The final text replaces 'unlawful' with 'unfair or deceptive act or practice' and adds 'materially' and 'in or affecting commerce' to track section 5 of the FTC Act. The proposed means-and-instrumentalities provision (proposed § 461.4) is not finalized and is addressed in a separate supplemental proposal. The rule contains no reporting or recordkeeping requirements. The preamble says the rule lets the Commission seek monetary relief and civil penalties more efficiently; the regulatory text sets no penalty amounts.

title: Trade Regulation Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials (16 CFR Part 465)
summary_short: FTC final rule (16 CFR Part 465), effective 21 October 2024, prohibits businesses from creating, selling or buying fake or false consumer reviews and testimonials, buying sentiment-conditioned reviews, undisclosed insider reviews, company-controlled review sites, review suppression and fake social media indicators.
summary_long: FTC final trade regulation rule (16 CFR Part 465), effective 21 October 2024, defines terms and bars specified unfair or deceptive practices involving consumer reviews and testimonials. Section 465.2 prohibits businesses from writing, creating or selling fake or false reviews and testimonials, and from purchasing reviews or disseminating testimonials they knew or should have known were fake or false; it exempts generalized solicitations and mere consumer review hosting. Section 465.3 (review reuse) was not finalized. Section 465.4 prohibits incentives conditioned, expressly or by implication, on reviews expressing a particular sentiment. Section 465.5 requires clear and conspicuous disclosure of material insider relationships and bars officers and managers from soliciting reviews from employees or agents. Sections 465.6 to 465.8 address company-controlled review websites, review suppression, and misuse of fake indicators of social media influence; section 465.9 is a severability clause. Civil penalties for violations require the knowledge standard of section 5(m)(1)(A) of the FTC Act.

title: O.C.G.A. § 48-8-3(68.1) -- High-technology data center equipment sales and use tax exemption
summary_short: Exempts high-technology data center equipment from Georgia sales and use tax during July 1, 2018 to December 31, 2031, for qualifying data centers that meet a county-tiered minimum investment threshold and hold a commissioner's certificate.
summary_long: Paragraph 68.1 exempts high-technology data center equipment from Georgia sales and use tax for the period July 1, 2018 to December 31, 2031. The exemption covers computer equipment and related materials, such as backup generators, cooling equipment and power distribution units, used in a data center that meets a minimum investment threshold. The threshold is 25 new quality jobs and $250 million in expenditures in counties over 50,000 population, 10 jobs and $75 million in counties of 30,000 to 50,001, and 5 jobs and $25 million in other counties, measured over any consecutive seven-year period. Sellers must collect the tax unless the buyer holds a commissioner's certificate. The commissioner may issue a certificate only if the data center will more likely than not meet the threshold, may require a bond of up to $20 million, and may revoke the certificate. Data centers must file a final report within 60 days after the end of the seventh year, report annual exempted taxes and jobs, and list their customers. If the threshold is missed, taxes and interest must be repaid within 90 days. Exempt data centers may not claim listed income tax credits. The commissioner must issue implementing rules and an annual report to legislative finance chairs. The paragraph is repealed by operation of law on January 1, 2032.

title: Coweta County data center ordinance (Zoning and Development Ordinance amendment) following 2025 moratoria
