summary_short: Zoning ordinance excerpts for Coweta County, Georgia: defines data centers and permits them as conditional uses in the LM light industrial district and as permitted uses in the M industrial district, subject to siting, buffer, noise, lighting, generator, water, sewer, power and emergency-response requirements. Effective date not stated.
summary_long: Zoning ordinance excerpts (Article 3 definitions; Article 18 LM Light Industrial and Article 19 M Industrial districts) for Coweta County, Georgia. Defines data center (up to 500,000 sq ft GFA), excludes cryptocurrency data centers, and defines data center campus and cryptocurrency mining. In the LM district, data centers are a conditional use requiring a conditional use permit from the board of commissioners after a board of zoning appeals recommendation; in the M district they are a permitted use. Both are subject to the same requirements: minimum 25-acre lot, height and setback limits, public water and sewer, a community meeting with mailed, newspaper and sign notice, building design standards, a 300-foot buffer from residential property, fencing, a pre-construction noise survey, daytime and nighttime noise limits, an environmental impact assessment, full-cutoff lighting, backup generator testing limits, a construction traffic plan, an annual waste report, equipment screening, a ban on open-loop cooling, a ban on primary onsite power generation, Tier 4 Final generator standards, substation setbacks, and emergency-response training with cost reimbursement. Violations are addressed by the county authority through written notice and other compliance action, including legal remedies; no penalty amounts are stated. The effective date is not stated in the excerpt.
text_version: Data Center Ordinance (amendments to the Zoning and Development Ordinance) as adopted by the Board of Commissioners on 16 December 2025

title: Georgia Technology Authority Artificial Intelligence Responsible Use (SS-23-002)
summary_short: Sets responsible-use rules for AI, generative AI, deep learning and machine learning tools used by Georgia state agencies, and duties for contractors and vendors supplying AI to the state, covering reporting, bias, accuracy, data protection, training and audit. No effective date is stated.
summary_long: This Georgia Technology Authority standard (SS-23-002) sets rules for state agencies' use of artificial intelligence, including generative AI, deep learning and machine learning tools. Agencies must use AI tools only for their intended purpose, check AI outputs for bias, inaccuracy and inappropriate content, keep records of AI tool usage, report AI tools to GTA, and designate a responsible staff member. Before procuring a new AI tool, agencies must submit a Business Solutions Review request to GTA. Service and technology contracts must require contractors and subcontractors to follow GTA policies and NIST guidance, provide their responsible AI policies, and allow agency verification. Non-agency entities must disclose testing, agree to ethical review and submit an AI development plan. Agencies must protect sensitive data used with AI, report breaches, and ensure users complete training. The State CIO or GTA OIS may order termination of use of an AI tool. Violations are subject to disciplinary action, and GTA audits AI tools found out of compliance. No effective date is stated.

title: Georgia HB 1192 (2023-2024 Session) -- suspension of new high-technology data center sales tax exemption certificates; Special Commission on Data Center Energy Planning
summary_short: Suspends new sales and use tax exemption certificates for high-technology data center equipment from July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2026, with a contract exception; revises the new quality jobs definition; creates a 14-member Special Commission on Data Center Energy Planning, abolished June 30, 2026.
summary_long: As passed by both chambers, the bill amends Code Section 48-8-3 so the commissioner must suspend new sales and use tax exemption certificates under paragraph (68.1) from July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2026, unless a later Act based on the commission's findings provides otherwise. An exception covers high-technology data center customers under ongoing contracts entered before July 1, 2024, with data centers that applied for certificates before that date. The bill also revises the 'new quality jobs' definition: located in Georgia, a regular work week of 30 hours or more, not a job that is or was already located in Georgia regardless of employer, and pay at or above 150 percent of the county average wage. It creates a 14-member Special Commission on Data Center Energy Planning to review grid and energy supply, recommend data center locations and grid expansion, examine trends including artificial intelligence, survey corporate employers and propose legislation. The commission reports in writing within three months after its last meeting, may hold hearings and obtain agency information, and is abolished and its article repealed on June 30, 2026. No penalties are stated; the Act takes effect on approval or on becoming law without signature and repeals conflicting laws.
text_version: HB 1192/AP (LC 50 0792S/AP), as passed House and Senate; vetoed 2024-05-07 (Veto No. 7)

title: An act to amend Chapter 12 of Title 31 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to the control of hazardous conditions, preventable diseases, and metabolic disorders [...]
summary_short: Amends Georgia Code Section 31-12-12 on the sale, dispensing and prescribing of contact lenses and spectacles. Allows licensed prescribers to use AI or other 'assessment mechanisms' for eye assessments under listed conditions, and sets penalties for violations. Applies within Georgia; the document states no effective date.
summary_long: Amends Code Section 31-12-12 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated on the sale, dispensing and prescribing of contact lenses and spectacles. Defines 'assessment mechanism', including artificial intelligence devices, and 'eye assessment'. Only persons licensed under specified Title 43 chapters may sell or dispense these products, and only a prescriber (a licensed optometrist or ophthalmologist) may write a prescription. A prescription requires an eye examination or, under stated conditions, an eye assessment. A prescriber using an assessment mechanism must meet listed conditions: the standard of care, no sole reliance on assessment data, a medical record kept for seven years, verification that the patient is 21 to 50 years old, specified exclusions, a recent eye examination, liability insurance, and disclosure to the patient with acceptance as a term of use. An assessment cannot generate an initial contact lens prescription. Assessment mechanisms must comply with telehealth, HIPAA and ADA requirements. Violations are misdemeanors or felonies depending on repetition, and a civil penalty of up to $11,000 per violation is payable to the Office of the Attorney General. Licensing boards may promulgate rules and may bring civil proceedings. Section 2 repeals conflicting laws. The text states no effective date.

title: Georgia HB 986 (Elections; election interference with a deep fake; establish criminal offense)
summary_short: Georgia bill HB 986 would make knowingly publishing materially deceptive audiovisual media within 90 days of an election, intended to deceive electors, a felony, and would require disclosure of AI-generated content in campaign advertisements. It would take effect on the Governor's approval. Registry status: failed.
summary_long: The bill would add Code Section 21-2-605 to Georgia's election code. Materially deceptive media means video, audio or still images that appear to depict a real individual's speech or conduct that did not occur and would appear authentic to a reasonable observer. Knowingly publishing, broadcasting, streaming or uploading such media within 90 days of an election, intending to deceive electors, would be a felony punishable by two to five years' imprisonment and a fine up to $50,000; soliciting such conduct would also be an offense. Satire, parody, artistic expression and bona fide journalism are excluded. The Attorney General would have concurrent prosecution jurisdiction, but prosecution would start only on a State Election Board recommendation. The depicted individual, the Attorney General or an injured candidate could seek injunctive relief. The State Election Board would publish findings of completed investigations. A new Article 21-5-90 et seq. would allow AI-generated content in campaign advertisements only if disclosed, with prescribed size and duration requirements; violations would carry a fine of at least $10,000. The Act would take effect on the Governor's approval or on becoming law without approval.

title: Georgia PSC approval of Georgia Power rule on terms of service for new customers > 100 MW (large load rule)
summary_short: Georgia Public Service Commission order (Docket 44280) approving revisions to Georgia Power's Rules and Regulations for electric service. Allows the company to impose minimum billing requirements and longer contract terms on new customers with 100 MW or more of load, with conditions protecting existing customers. Effective from 1 February 2025 for the added paragraphs.
summary_long: Order of 23 January 2025 approving revisions that Georgia Power Company filed on 11 December 2024 under O.C.G.A. § 46-2-25(a). The revisions, in Section A (General Rules) and Section D (Transmission or Wholesale Distribution Line Extension and Service Connection Regulations), apply to customers with an expected peak demand of 100 MW or greater at one or more premises on one tract or contiguous tracts of land. For these customers the company may require additional terms and conditions, including minimum billing requirements and a longer contract term, to recover costs of serving or preparing to serve them. Section D also allows the company to require performance and credit provisions, and, on contract termination, payment of costs including distribution, transmission and generation costs. The Commission adopted Staff's modifications: the company must exercise its discretion so as to protect existing customers from bearing any costs of adding these large customers; provide Staff with the terms, conditions and criteria before using them for contracting; file complete contracts within 30 days of execution; and make compliance filings of the relevant tariffs. The Commission retains jurisdiction to modify the rules. The order states no penalties.
text_version: Docket 44280 Order Approving Revisions to Georgia Power's Rules and Regulations (Word text of the order, filed 2025-01-28) + approved Rules and Regulations Sections A (p. 1.10) and D (p. 1.40), clean versions filed 2024-12-11

title: Georgia SB 9 ("Ensuring Accountability for Illegal AI Activities Act")
summary_short: The bill would criminalize knowingly publishing materially deceptive media within 90 days of an election to deceive electors, and require disclosure of AI-generated content in campaign advertisements. It would take effect on gubernatorial approval or becoming law.
summary_long: SB 9 would add Code Section 21-2-605 to Georgia's election code, creating the offenses of fraudulent election interference and solicitation of fraudulent election interference. A person commits the first offense by knowingly publishing, broadcasting, streaming or uploading materially deceptive media (video, audio or still images depicting a real individual's speech or conduct that did not occur and would appear authentic to a reasonable observer) within 90 days of an election, with intent to deceive electors. A first offense is a misdemeanor; a second or subsequent offense is a felony punishable by two to five years' imprisonment and a fine not to exceed $50,000. Activity protected by the First Amendment, including satire, parody and bona fide journalism, is excluded. New Article 5 of Chapter 5 allows campaign advertisements to use AI-generated content if they disclose the sponsoring candidate or committee, any impersonated person, that events may not have occurred, and that artificial intelligence was used. Violations carry a fine of at least $10,000, and AI-generated fundraising solicitations also require disgorgement of funds raised. Injunctive relief may be sought by the depicted individual, the Attorney General or an injured candidate. Prosecution requires a recommendation from the State Election Board. The Act takes effect upon approval by the Governor or upon becoming law without such approval.

title: Nondiscrimination in Health Programs and Activities (Section 1557 final rule; 45 CFR 92.210 patient care decision support tools)
summary_short: Requires covered entities, in their health programs and activities, not to discriminate on the basis of race, color, national origin, sex, age or disability through patient care decision support tools, and to make reasonable efforts to identify and mitigate such risk from tools using those input variables.
summary_long: This excerpt of 45 CFR § 92.210 (the registry title describes it as part of the Section 1557 final rule) has three paragraphs. Paragraph (a) provides that a covered entity must not discriminate on the basis of race, color, national origin, sex, age, or disability in its health programs or activities through the use of patient care decision support tools. Paragraph (b) imposes an ongoing duty to make reasonable efforts to identify uses of such tools that employ input variables or factors measuring those characteristics. Paragraph (c) requires reasonable efforts to mitigate the risk of discrimination resulting from the use of each tool identified under paragraph (b). The provisions address covered entities. The excerpt does not define covered entity or patient care decision support tool, does not state an effective date or compliance deadline, and contains no enforcement, penalty or private right of action provisions.

title: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability: Certification Program Updates, Algorithm Transparency, and Information Sharing (HTI-1)
summary_short: HHS final rule amending 45 CFR Part 170 on certified health IT. It updates interoperability, vocabulary and API standards and certification criteria, defines Predictive Decision Support Interventions, and requires developers of such tools in certified Health IT Modules to provide source-attribute information and risk management.
summary_long: HTI-1 is a federal health IT rule that amends Part 170 of Title 45 of the Code of Federal Regulations for developers of health IT seeking ONC certification. It adds definitions, including 'Predictive Decision Support Intervention' and 'Provide', and revises or adds standards in § 170.205 (content exchange, including electronic case reporting), § 170.207 (vocabularies such as SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm, and sex, gender identity and sexual orientation codes), § 170.210 (NTP-synchronized clocks), § 170.213 (USCDI v1 and v3) and § 170.215 (FHIR, US Core, SMART and bulk export APIs), with incorporation by reference in § 170.299. It amends the certification criteria in § 170.315, including patient demographics, family health history and decision support interventions. For Predictive DSIs supplied in a certified Health IT Module, § 170.315(b)(11) requires source-attribute information (such as training-data inclusion criteria and fairness and performance measures), access and modification functions, and intervention risk management covering risk analysis, mitigation and governance. Some standard adoptions expire, and some criteria require conformance, on January 1, 2025 or January 1, 2026. The provided text contains no enforcement provisions.

title: Hawaii HB 1782 (Relating to Artificial Intelligence for the Protection of Minors) 2026
summary_short: HB 1782 would add a part to Hawaii Revised Statutes Chapter 481B requiring providers of conversational AI and companion systems available to Hawaii residents to disclose AI status to known minors, restrict specified engagement practices, adopt a minor protection plan, and offer parental tools. Effective January 1, 2077.
summary_long: As introduced, HB 1782 would add a part to Hawaii Revised Statutes Chapter 481B on AI companion system safety for minors. It defines key terms and excludes narrow task, customer-service, developer and internal-only systems. Providers that know or have reasonable certainty a user is a minor must disclose AI status at session start and at least every three hours, and must not allow representations that the system is human, capable of a romantic or sexual relationship, has independent emotions, or provides professional mental health services, nor personalized outputs discouraging disengagement. Providers must take reasonable measures against sexually explicit or self-harm content for minors and direct at-risk users to crisis resources. Each provider must adopt and publish a minor protection plan, review it annually, and submit risk assessment summaries to the office of consumer protection before deploying new or substantially modified services. Providers must offer parental tools and apply age assurance. Enforcement is by the attorney general or the executive director of the office of consumer protection; private actions are barred; violations may draw injunctive relief and civil penalties up to $15,000 per violation, per day; good-faith compliance is a defense. Effective January 1, 2077.

title: Hawaii Senate Bill 2687
summary_short: Bans persons from recklessly distributing materially deceptive AI or deepfake media that risks harming election candidates or voter behavior, from February of each even-numbered year through the next general election, unless a prescribed disclaimer is included. Sets graded criminal penalties and civil remedies; effective on approval.
summary_long: Adds HRS §11-A barring any person from recklessly distributing, or agreeing to distribute, materially deceptive media between the first working day of February in each even-numbered year and the next general election, in reckless disregard of risks to candidates or voters. Covered media are advertisements depicting someone in speech or conduct they did not engage in, that a reasonable viewer would believe, made with AI, GAN or digital technology. Broadcasters, cable and satellite providers, and online, cloud, streaming and technology providers are largely excluded unless they helped create the media or, for online services, knew it was deceptive and intended to deceive a state resident. A prescribed disclaimer exempts media, with detailed size, placement, language and citation rules. Violations are a petty misdemeanor, a misdemeanor if repeated within five years, or a class C felony with intent to cause violence or bodily harm; the commission may assess a fine or refer cases for prosecution. Adds HRS §11-B allowing damages suits by depicted individuals, candidates and voter organizations, and injunctions sought by officials and those parties; civil fines up to $1,000 per day apply for violating injunctions. Takes effect upon approval.

title: Hawaii SB 3001 (Artificial Intelligence Disclosure and Safety Act) 2026
summary_short: Amends Hawaii Revised Statutes chapter 481B to regulate operators of public conversational AI services: AI-status disclosure, minor protections, suicide and self-harm response protocols, and an annual report. Enforced by the attorney general and office of consumer protection; no private right of action. Section 2 takes effect July 1, 2027.
summary_long: Adds a section to Hawaii Revised Statutes chapter 481B on operators of conversational artificial intelligence services offered to the public; app stores and search engines merely providing access are excluded. Operators must tell users when a reasonable person could think they are talking to a human, and must disclose AI status to known minors, by persistent disclaimer or at session start and at least every three hours. They must adopt self-harm and suicide response protocols with crisis referrals and not present the service as professional mental health care. For known minors they must restrict sexually explicit material, romantic or sexual representations and manipulative engagement, and offer privacy tools. From 1 January 2028, operators must file annual reports on crisis referrals and protocols with the department of commerce and consumer affairs. Violations are unfair or deceptive practices enforced by the attorney general and office of consumer protection: injunctions, damages or a $1,000 civil penalty per violation, capped at $1,000,000 per operator. Private actions are barred; developers are not liable for third-party systems. Section 2 takes effect 1 July 2027; the other sections take effect 1 July 3000.

title: China Technology Transfer Control Act of 2025
summary_short: Directs the President to control exports and transfers to China of covered national interest technology or intellectual property, starting 180 days after enactment. Authorises IEEPA blocking of foreign persons who knowingly sell, provide or buy such technology with China, and requires a USTR list of Chinese products.
summary_long: Directs the President to control exports, re-exports and transfers to the People's Republic of China of covered national interest technology or intellectual property, starting 180 days after enactment, with regulations due within 180 days and a joint State-Commerce report due within 90 days assessing whether ITAR or EAR controls should apply. Covered technology includes items contributing to PRC military potential detrimental to US national security, components of listed products, and technology used for human rights violations; 'technology' expressly includes artificial intelligence, computing and robotics. Section 5 directs blocking of property under IEEPA of foreign persons who knowingly sell, provide or purchase such technology with the PRC, and of Chinese persons who knowingly use it in violation of section 4 or other US export controls, subject to a national security waiver and an exclusion for importation of goods. Section 6 adds Trade Act section 183, requiring the USTR to list, within 120 days and annually, PRC products receiving Made in China 2025 support or used for human rights violations, including products in artificial intelligence, high-capacity computing, semiconductors, quantum computing and robotics. Section 3 is a sense-of-Congress statement.

title: Protecting Our Children in an AI World Act of 2025
summary_short: Amends federal criminal law (18 U.S.C. 2252A, 2256) to remove the affirmative defense for AI-produced child pornography and add simulated obscene exhibition of genitals, pubic area, buttocks or female nipple to sexually explicit conduct. Includes a severability clause. No effective date is stated.
summary_long: The bill amends title 18 of the United States Code, the federal criminal code, in two places. Section 2(a) strikes paragraph (2) of section 2252A(c) and the sentence that barred the affirmative defense for child pornography described in section 2256(8)(C). Section 2(b) amends the definition of sexually explicit conduct in section 2256(2)(B) to add a clause (iv) covering actual or simulated obscene exhibition of the clothed or unclothed genitals, pubic area, buttocks, or female nipple. The text does not itself set penalties and states no effective date or compliance period. Section 2(c) is a severability clause preserving the remaining provisions if any part is held unconstitutional. The short title is the Protecting Our Children in an AI World Act of 2025. In this text the bill is at the introduced stage.

title: Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021
summary_short: Federal AI provisions from several excerpted acts: creates an AI Center of Excellence in GSA, directs OMB to issue agency AI-use guidance and OPM to update AI occupational series, authorizes AI, microelectronics, grid and health research programs, and orders recurring AI-related studies and reports. Most deadlines run from enactment.
summary_long: Excerpts from several acts, each under an AGORA heading: the AI in Government Act of 2020 (Secs. 101-105), Secs. 502 and 604 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021, Energy Act of 2020 provisions (Secs. 3002(g), 6006, 8002, 9008) and American COMPETE Act study provisions (Sec. 1501). Sec. 103 creates an AI Center of Excellence in the General Services Administration, sunsetting five years after enactment. Sec. 104 directs the OMB Director to issue a federal AI use memorandum within 270 days, covering bias mitigation, and agency plans within 180 days after it. Sec. 105 directs OPM to update AI occupational series within 18 months. Sec. 502 allows awards of up to $15,000,000 for AI microelectronics research; Sec. 604 requires a DNI assessment of AI, chip and supply-chain trends within 180 days. Energy Act provisions authorize DOE research on geothermal computing, grid modeling and a veterans health AI program, and direct a smart manufacturing plan within three years. Sec. 1501 directs Commerce and FTC studies with reports six months after completion, including an FTC study of AI against online harms.

title: Supporting Innovation in Agriculture Act of 2025
summary_short: Adds a 30% federal income tax credit (new IRC §48F) for qualified investment in agricultural technology projects producing specialty crops with precision or controlled environment agriculture, placed in service before 31 December 2035. Allows elective payment and transfer of the credit.
summary_long: Adds Internal Revenue Code section 48F, a credit of 30% of qualified investment in an innovative agricultural technology project for each taxable year. Qualified investment is the basis of depreciable tangible property or software used integrally in a project, placed in service during the year. A project is an agricultural technology or system placed in service before 31 December 2035 whose primary purpose is producing, storing, processing or packaging specialty crops using precision or controlled environment agriculture. Definitions include sensors, robotics, and software with machine learning or artificial intelligence; the Secretary may add technologies. Process-expenditure rules and a bar on double benefit for certain grants and EQIP payments apply. Section 2(b) and (c) allow taxpayers other than entities already covered to elect payment (IRC §6417) for property placed in service after 31 December 2023, and make the credit transferable (§6418). Section 2(d) makes conforming amendments to §§46, 49 and 50 and the table of sections. The amendments apply to property whose construction began after 1 January 2025. The bill contains no penalty or enforcement provisions.

title: Fair Grocery Pricing Act
summary_short: Prohibits food producers from exchanging value for the services of a 'coordinator' that runs algorithmic price or supply coordination, and bars coordinators from facilitating non-competition agreements among food producers. Enforced by the FTC, the Attorney General and state attorneys general, with treble-damages private suits. No effective date is stated.
summary_long: The bill defines 'coordinating function' as collecting price or supply data from two or more food producers, analysing it with software or algorithms (including to train an algorithm), and recommending food prices, supply, output or other commercial terms to a food producer. Sec. 3(a)(1) makes it unlawful for a food producer, in or affecting commerce, to subscribe to, contract with, or otherwise exchange value for a coordinator's services, and deems this a per se violation of the Sherman Act. Sec. 3(a)(2) makes it unlawful for a coordinator to facilitate an agreement among food producers not to compete on prices, supply, output or other commercial terms. Sec. 4(a) assigns enforcement to the FTC (including civil penalties in its own name), the Attorney General and state attorneys general, and treats a violation as an unfair method of competition. Sec. 4(a)(4) lets a complaint plausibly plead a violation by alleging consciously parallel pricing coordination. Sec. 4(b) allows any aggrieved person to sue for threefold damages and litigation costs, and lets the plaintiff void pre-dispute arbitration agreements and joint action waivers. Sec. 5 preserves the antitrust laws, Sec. 6 does not preempt state laws that supplement the Act, and Sec. 7 is a severability clause. The text states no effective date.},

title: Foreign Investment Guardrails to Help Thwart (FIGHT) China Act
summary_short: As introduced, amends the Defense Production Act so the Treasury Secretary can prohibit, or require notification of, US-person investments in China involving listed technologies such as chips and AI. Also authorizes IEEPA sanctions on designated Chinese covered foreign persons; regulations due within 450 days of enactment.
summary_long: As introduced, the bill has three titles. Title I authorizes the President to block property of foreign persons that the Secretary, in consultation with the Secretary of State, determines to be covered foreign persons (entities incorporated in or controlled from China, Chinese Communist Party Central Committee members, and persons knowingly engaged in significant defense or surveillance operations), using IEEPA powers and penalties. Title II adds Title VIII to the Defense Production Act: the Secretary may prohibit US persons from knowingly engaging in covered national security transactions in prohibited technologies (including listed chip, AI, quantum and hypersonic items) and, within 450 days of enactment, must issue rules requiring notification within 30 days of completion for transactions in prohibited and notifiable technologies. Civil penalties are the greater of $250,000 or twice the transaction amount, and divestment may be compelled. Exemptions cover de minimis transactions, listed securities and certain fund interests. Title III requires reports within 365 days on the Non-SDN Chinese Military-Industrial Complex Companies List and directs rules barring US persons from knowingly holding listed securities after 365 days, subject to waiver. The Act ends when Commerce removes the PRC from 15 CFR 791.4. $150,000,000 is authorized for the first two fiscal years.

title: Healthy Technology Act of 2025
summary_short: Amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to let AI and machine learning technology qualify as a practitioner licensed to administer drugs, if a State statute authorizes it to prescribe the drug and FDA approves, clears or authorizes it under sections 510(k), 513, 515 or 564.
summary_long: The Healthy Technology Act of 2025 (bill as introduced) adds a new paragraph (6) to section 503(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. The paragraph provides that the term 'practitioner licensed by law to administer such drug' includes artificial intelligence and machine learning technology that meets two conditions: (A) it is authorized under a statute of the State involved to prescribe the drug involved, and (B) it is approved, cleared or authorized under section 510(k), 513, 515 or 564 of that Act. The bill addresses the prescription-drug provisions of federal law and applies nationally. It contains no effective date, no enforcement provisions and no reporting duties. The bill has the status of introduced and is pending.

title: Protect Victims of Digital Exploitation and Manipulation Act of 2025
summary_short: Amends Title 18 to create a federal offense of producing or distributing, with reckless disregard and without consent, software- or AI-generated intimate depictions of identifiable individuals that use interstate commerce. Penalties: fine, up to 5 years' imprisonment, or both. No effective date is stated.
summary_long: The bill adds section 1802 to chapter 88 of Title 18 of the United States Code, titled Protect Victims of Digital Exploitation and Manipulation Act of 2025. It makes it an offense for whoever, in circumstances involving interstate or foreign commerce, acts with reckless disregard to produce or distribute, or causes to be produced or distributed, a digital forgery of an identifiable individual without the individual's consent. The offense is punishable by fine, imprisonment for not more than 5 years, or both. A digital forgery is an intimate visual depiction created through software, machine learning, artificial intelligence or other computer-generated means that appears to a reasonable person to be authentic. Intimate depictions cover uncovered genitals, pubic area, anus or female nipple, bodily sexual fluids, and sexually explicit conduct. Consent must be affirmative, conscious, competent and voluntary, free from force, fraud, misrepresentation or coercion. Exceptions cover good-faith distributions to law enforcement, as part of legal proceedings, in medical education, diagnosis or treatment, and in reporting or investigating unlawful content or unsolicited conduct. Communications service providers are excluded for content provided by another information content provider, unless the provider recklessly distributes content in violation of the section. The section applies extraterritorially where the offender or the victim is a United States national. Section 2(b) adds a clerical table-of-sections entry, and section 3 provides a severability clause. The text states no effective date.

title: Next Generation Pipelines Research and Development Act
summary_short: Proposed federal bill authorizing Department of Energy grants for demonstration projects on next-generation pipeline technologies, a joint DOE, DOT and NIST research program, a National Pipeline Modernization Center and NIST pipeline metrology funding, with appropriations authorized for fiscal years 2026 to 2030.
summary_long: The bill would add section 40344 to the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, authorizing the Secretary of Energy to award financial assistance to eligible entities for low- to mid-technology-readiness demonstration projects on pipelines, LNG facilities and gas and liquid fuel storage. Eligible entities include universities, nonprofit research organizations, National Laboratories and private commercial entities. Listed focus areas include leak detection, sensors, machine learning models and cybersecurity. Section 40344 authorizes $45,000,000 for fiscal year 2026 and $50,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2027 through 2030, drawn from section 10771 funds, and terminates five years after enactment. Section 5 directs a joint DOE, DOT and NIST research program, subject to appropriations. Section 6 directs a National Pipeline Modernization Center, run with a competitively selected eligible entity for up to five years. Section 7 directs NIST pipeline measurement research with up to $2,500,000 per fiscal year for 2026 through 2030. Section 8 authorizes appropriations for Sections 5 and 6 and amends section 10771 funding amounts. The bill is pending.

title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024
summary_short: Selected sections of the FY2024 US National Defense Authorization Act: directs Defense, State and intelligence agencies to run AI pilots, studies, reports, bug-bounty and prize competitions and create AI governance bodies; also sets AUKUS export exemptions and submarine transfers.
summary_long: Selected sections of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, mostly on defense and intelligence use of AI. Defense: the Chief Digital and AI Officer must run a pilot on AI-driven aerial refueling logistics (Sec. 346) and the Secretary of the Navy a shipyard AI strategy (Sec. 350); DoD must set up a bug bounty program for foundational AI models (Sec. 1542), a generative AI detection and watermarking prize competition (Sec. 1543), and AI plans, guidance and a responsible-AI compliance process (Sec. 1544); Sec. 1545 requires a vulnerability study; Sec. 1521 creates a CDAO Governing Council and CDAO data control; Sec. 1524 requires a content provenance course and pilot for DoD media. Intelligence: DNI AI policies (Sec. 7513) and AI-oriented microelectronics research (Sec. 7507). Other: a State Department Chief AI Officer (Sec. 6303) and an Office of Strategic Capital making loans for critical technologies (Sec. 903). AUKUS provisions add oversight offices, an AECA section 38(l) licensing exemption for certified partners that ends after 15 years, expedited export licence review and submarine transfers. Most duties start on enactment with deadlines from 30 days to one year; several pilots and prize authorities terminate between 2025 and 2028.

title: NO FAKES Act of 2025
summary_short: Proposes a federal intellectual property right in an individual's voice and visual likeness, enforceable through civil action against unauthorized digital replicas and products designed to produce them, with notice-and-takedown safe harbors for online services; applies from 180 days after enactment.
summary_long: The bill would create a federal right to authorize use of an individual's voice or visual likeness in a digital replica (a highly realistic computer-generated representation of that individual) or in a product or service requiring such authorization. The right is licensable, not assignable during life, and survives death for 10 years, extendable in 5-year periods on active authorized use, ending no later than 70 years after death. Lifetime licences last up to 10 years and must be written, signed and specific; licences involving minors last up to 5 years, end at age 18 and require court approval. Liability attaches to unauthorized digital replicas made available to the public and to products or services primarily designed to produce them. Online services with a designated agent, a repeat-violator policy and prompt removal after compliant notice are shielded for user-uploaded material. Knowingly false notices incur liability of the greater of $25,000 per notification or actual damages. Civil actions allow statutory damages (individuals: $5,000 per work), injunctions and a three-year limitations period. Exceptions include news, documentary, commentary and parody uses. State-law claims are preempted, except those existing on 2 January 2025. Liability covers only post-enactment conduct; the Act takes effect 180 days after enactment.

title: HR 3303 America—Israel AI Cooperation Act 2025 (Exception to export  license requirements for certain advanced integrated circuits to Israel)
summary_short: Directs the Secretary of Commerce, when finalizing the 'Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion' interim rule, to add Israel to the country list in Supplement No. 5 to part 740 of the CFR and apply the same export requirements and exceptions to Israel as to listed countries.
summary_long: H.R. 3303, the America–Israel AI Cooperation Act, was introduced in the House on May 8, 2025 and referred to the Committee on Foreign Affairs. Its operative section, Sec. 2, applies notwithstanding any other provision of law. When finalizing the interim rule 'Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion' (90 Fed. Reg. 4544), the Secretary of Commerce, acting through the Undersecretary of Commerce for Industry and Security, must modify the rule. The modification must include Israel in the list of countries in the amendment to Supplement No. 5 to part 740 of title 15, Code of Federal Regulations. It must also ensure that exports to Israel of items controlled under that rule are subject to the same requirements and exceptions as exports to other listed countries. The bill states no penalties, thresholds or separate effective date. Its practical content depends on the terms of the final rule.

title: H.R. 3447 Chip Security Act
summary_short: As introduced, H.R. 3447 would require the Secretary of Commerce to make covered integrated circuit products carry chip security mechanisms such as location verification before export, reexport or in-country transfer, and would require licensees to report diversion or tampering.
summary_long: The bill, titled the Chip Security Act, directs the Secretary of Commerce to require covered integrated circuit products (ECCN 3A090, 3A001.z, 4A090, 4A003.z and successors) to carry chip security mechanisms implementing location verification before export, reexport or in-country transfer to a foreign country, not later than 180 days after enactment. Licensees must promptly report credible information of unauthorized location, diversion or tampering to the Under Secretary of Industry and Security. Within one year the Secretary must assess additional mechanisms and report to the appropriate congressional committees; any secondary mechanisms must then be required within two years of that assessment, prioritizing confidentiality. The Secretary may verify ownership and location of exported products and keep a record of their location and end-user. Starting two years after enactment and annually for three years, the Secretary must assess new mechanisms and report, including on export-control flexibility. Section 2 findings are not operative. The bill sets no penalties of its own.

title: AI Whistleblower Protection Act
summary_short: Bill barring employers from retaliating against covered employees and independent contractors who report AI security vulnerabilities or AI violations to regulators, law enforcement, Congress or supervisors. Enforced by Labor Department complaint or district court action, with reinstatement, double back pay and damages.
summary_long: The bill would prohibit any employer engaged in commerce from discharging, demoting, suspending, threatening, blacklisting, harassing or otherwise discriminating against a covered individual (employees, former employees, independent contractors and former independent contractors) because of protected disclosures about an AI security vulnerability or AI violation. Protected disclosures include information given to the appropriate regulatory official or the Attorney General, a regulatory or law enforcement agency, any Member of Congress or congressional committee, or a supervisor, and assistance in related investigations or proceedings. AI security vulnerability means a security failure that could allow emerging AI technology to be acquired by theft or other means. AI violation covers violations of federal law relating to AI and failures to respond to a substantial and specific danger to public safety, health or national security. A covered individual may file a complaint with the Secretary of Labor under the procedures of 49 U.S.C. 42121(b), or, if no final decision issues within 180 days, sue in federal district court with a jury trial, subject to limitation periods of 6 years, 3 years from knowledge of the facts, and an outer limit of 10 years. Prevailing individuals may receive reinstatement, two times back pay with interest, compensatory damages including litigation costs and attorneys' fees, and other remedies. These rights may not be waived or altered by contract, including mandatory arbitration. The text states no effective date and no civil penalty amounts.

title: Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act
summary_short: Selected sections of the US Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act: federal grants, pilots and reports on AI-relevant sectors (critical minerals, smart manufacturing, automated and connected transport), directed at federal agencies, research institutions, states and grantees. Binding statute; obligations run from enactment or stated deadlines.
summary_long: Selected sections (not the full Act) of the US Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. Sec. 40210 directs the Secretary, with the NSF Director, to make competitive basic-research awards on critical minerals mining and recycling, including AI for geological exploration, and creates a grant program for pilot processing projects capped at $10,000,000 per grant, barring export of processed minerals to foreign entities of concern. Sec. 40433 requires a one-year report on digital tools, including AI, as climate solutions. Secs. 40531-40535 define smart manufacturing (including AI), expand industrial assessment centers, study national-laboratory computing access for small and medium manufacturers, and authorize state grants up to $2,000,000 with a 30 percent match. Sec. 11401 amends 23 U.S.C. 151 to fund charging and fuelling infrastructure with an 80 percent federal share. Sec. 13005 sets a $5,000,000 annual pilot on automated-vehicle effects on pavement. Sec. 25005 funds SMART grants for smart-city and transport technologies, including automated vehicles, with shares by community size and a GAO review. Sec. 25017 amends 49 U.S.C. 5505 to add cybersecurity of connected and autonomous vehicles to university transportation centre research. Duties bind federal agencies and grant recipients; the excerpt contains no penalty provisions.

title: Securing Growth and Robust Leadership in American Aviation Act
summary_short: Directs the FAA Administrator to review AI and machine learning applications for airport efficiency and safety, research AI-enabled controller training, and direct use of big data analytics and machine learning in Part 107 waiver processing. Applies to the FAA; reports to Congress are due within one year of enactment.
summary_long: Sections 1024, 1028 and 908 direct the FAA Administrator; they impose no duties on private parties and set no thresholds or penalties. Section 1024 requires a review of current and planned AI and machine learning technologies for airport efficiency and safety, including jet bridges, airport service vehicles, aircraft taxi and air traffic control, and a report to Congress within one year of enactment. Section 1028 requires, subject to appropriations, a research program on AI, machine learning and other technologies for air traffic controller training, with collaboration with labor organizations and a report within one year. Section 908 directs a performance- and risk-based review of Part 107 drone waivers under 14 CFR 107.200, including a standardized application format, use of prior waiver data and big data analytics and machine learning, consideration of applicant property-access control, online publication of waivers, streamlined approval of similar applications and expedited modification review.

title: Medicare Transaction Fraud Prevention Act
summary_short: Amends Social Security Act §1128K to require the HHS Secretary to run a two-year pilot, beginning by January 1, 2026, using a predictive risk-scoring algorithm to oversee Medicare payments for durable medical equipment and clinical diagnostic laboratory tests. Participation by beneficiaries is voluntary.
summary_long: The bill, the Medicare Transaction Fraud Prevention Act, adds subsection (d) to Social Security Act §1128K. It requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to run a two-year pilot, beginning no later than January 1, 2026, that tests a predictive risk-scoring algorithm to oversee Medicare claims for durable medical equipment and clinical diagnostic laboratory tests. Only beneficiaries who opt in to electronic Medicare Summary Notices and the pilot participate, and they may withdraw at any time. The algorithm learns from beneficiary data and scores relevant transactions from 1 (least risky) to 99 (most risky), considering listed factors such as the absence of a prior provider relationship, aberrant billing patterns, electronic fund transfer changes and ownership changes. Before implementation the Secretary must require testing, evaluation and review, establish notice methods for affected beneficiaries, providers and suppliers, and set up communication with the HHS Office of Inspector General. For transactions scoring above a risk level set by the Secretary, the Secretary reviews whether to suspend the transaction; beneficiaries may seek to cure inaccurate data or confirm the transaction by email or phone. Suspended transactions trigger electronic Medicare Summary Notices, sent at two-week intervals for three months. Any suspension must be based on human review. The Secretary may also decide when Medicare cards are terminated or reissued to prevent fraud and abuse.

title: HR 4419 Autonomous Vehicle Accessibility Act 2025
summary_short: Would bar States from issuing motor vehicle operator's licenses for Level 4 or 5 ADS-equipped vehicles operated in a manner that discriminates on disability. Directs the Secretary of Transportation to seek a National Academies study on accessible ride-hail vehicle access.
summary_long: H.R. 4419, the Autonomous Vehicle Accessibility Act, was introduced in the House on 15 July 2025 and referred to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure. Section 3 provides that, in accordance with title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act, a State shall not issue a motor vehicle operator's license for the operation or use of an ADS-equipped vehicle at SAE Level 4 or Level 5 in a manner that discriminates on the basis of disability against a qualified individual with a disability. Section 2 defines disability by reference to 42 U.S.C. 12102, public transportation by reference to 49 U.S.C. 5302, a ride-hail ADS-equipped vehicle as an ADS-equipped vehicle offered for compensated pre-arranged transportation through an online platform and dispatched in driverless operation, and SAE terms by reference to SAE J3016. Section 4 directs the Secretary of Transportation to seek an agreement with the National Academies for a study on public transportation infrastructure changes and access options for ride-hail ADS-equipped vehicles. Section 5 authorizes $5,000,000 to carry out Section 4, available until expended. The text states no penalties, enforcement procedure or effective date.

title: HR 4518 Cooper Davis and Devin Norring Act 2025 (Requires communication service and remote computing providers to report certain controlled substances violations)
summary_short: Proposed federal law adding Controlled Substances Act Sec. 521, requiring electronic communication service and remote computing service providers to report to the Attorney General facts indicating certain fentanyl, methamphetamine, counterfeit or unauthorized prescription drug crimes, within 60 days of actual knowledge.
summary_long: The bill would add Section 521 to the Controlled Substances Act. Providers of electronic communication services and remote computing services would have to submit reports to the Attorney General as soon as reasonably possible, and no later than 60 days after obtaining actual knowledge, of facts or circumstances establishing crimes involving fentanyl or methamphetamine, counterfeit substances, or unauthorized prescription pain medication or stimulants. Reports must include provider contact details and, to the extent reasonably available, account identifying information, but not the contents of wire or electronic communications except as provided. Providers may also report on a reasonable belief. The Attorney General must conduct a preliminary review, may investigate or close reports, must limit storage and delete reports after use, and must publish an annual report. Knowingly failing to report is unlawful and carries a fine of not more than $190,000 for an initial violation and $380,000 for subsequent violations. Knowingly submitting materially false reports carries a civil penalty of $50,000 to $100,000. Law enforcement officers may not submit reports, and broadband and text messaging providers are exempt. The bill also adds disclosure exceptions to the Stored Communications Act and states that no monitoring duty is created. The text states no separate effective date for these provisions.

title: H.R.4640 Stop AI Price Gouging and Wage Fixing Act of 2025
summary_short: Bars persons from surveillance-based price setting and surveillance-based wage setting using automated decision systems, subject to exceptions for price setting. Requires publishing accuracy and correction procedures 180 days before use. Enforced by the FTC, state attorneys general and private suits.
summary_long: Introduced bill that would prohibit a person from engaging in surveillance-based price setting: using an automated decision system to offer or inform a customized price based in whole or part on surveillance data, subject to exceptions for cost-based differences, broadly defined group discounts and affirmatively enrolled loyalty programs with conditions. It would prohibit surveillance-based wage setting, except where the system uses only data on the worker's city or state and its cost of living. Persons using such systems for price or wage setting must publish, at least 180 days in advance, procedures on data accuracy, correction and disclosure. Violations are treated as FTC rule violations; state attorneys general may sue for injunctions and the greater of actual damages or $3,000 per violation; the EEOC may sue for wage violations; injured persons have a private right of action, with awards of up to three times the amount for willful violations, fee-shifting, a five-year limitation period, and pre-dispute arbitration agreements and joint action waivers made unenforceable for such claims. The Act preempts only directly conflicting state laws and preserves collective bargaining, where employers must give advance notice and a bargaining opportunity before using such systems to set compensation.

title: HR 4661 Autonomous Mobility Ensuring Regulation, Innovation, Commerce, and Advancement Driving Reliability in Vehicle Efficiency and Safety Act 2025
summary_short: H.R. 4661 would add 49 U.S.C. § 31140 allowing Level 4 or 5 automated-driving-system commercial motor vehicles to operate in interstate commerce without an on-board or remote human driver. It directs the Secretary of Transportation to issue regulations and address motor carrier rules for such vehicles by September 30, 2027.
summary_long: H.R. 4661, introduced 23 July 2025, would amend title 49, United States Code. Section 2 adds section 31140, under which a commercial motor vehicle equipped with a Level 4 or Level 5 automated driving system (ADS) may operate in interstate commerce without a human driver on board or a remote human driver, and directs the Secretary of Transportation to issue implementing regulations. Section 2 also defines ADS terms by reference to SAE J3016 and states that nothing requires a vehicle to be equipped with an ADS. Section 3 directs the Secretary, by September 30, 2027, to address the applicability of 49 CFR sections 350 through 399 to ADS-equipped commercial motor vehicles, including rules that apply to human drivers. It bars regulations that unduly burden motor carriers operating such vehicles or discriminate against them, and excludes ADS technologies from width calculations under section 31113. Section 4 treats cab-mounted warning beacons as a permissible warning device under 49 CFR 392.22 and 393.95(f). The bill contains no penalty or enforcement provisions. Its title refers to preemption of State laws requiring a human occupant, but the operative text contains no express preemption clause.

title: Servicemember Quality of Life Improvement and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2025
summary_short: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2025 (selected AI-related sections). Directs the Department of Defense and the NSA to set up AI initiatives, centers and pilots, requires related reports, and conditionally bars DoD procurement of certain foreign-made unmanned ground vehicles. Deadlines generally run from enactment.
summary_long: Extract of selected sections of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2025 on artificial intelligence (AI) and related defense technology. Section 6504 requires the National Security Agency to establish an AI Security Center within 90 days of enactment, with disestablishment possible after three years. Sections 1531-1534 and 1087 direct the Department of Defense (DoD) to set up an AI human factors initiative, expand high-performance computing infrastructure with a roadmap, plan AI training-data budgeting, evaluate an AI-enabled weapon systems center of excellence, and establish a multilateral AI working group ending 30 September 2028. Sections 221, 222 and 232-237 and 1007 set AI workforce, education, maintenance-data, target-recognition, biotechnology and audit pilot requirements, mostly as plans, briefings and reports. Section 1078(b) bars DoD from procuring or operating unmanned ground vehicles made by covered foreign entities one year after a required report, unless a national-interest exception applies. Sections 1066, 1514 and 1515 require reports on lethal autonomous weapons, multi-cloud cybersecurity and mobile-device protections. Section 1031 requires Navy maritime autonomy standards within 180 days. Section 6506 adds AI to intelligence-community talent-exchange focus areas. The extract sets no fines or penalties.

title: HR 5022 No Advanced Chips for the CCP Act 2025 (Congressional approval for the export of advanced artificial intelligence semiconductors to China)
summary_short: Bars any person from exporting, reexporting or transferring an advanced AI semiconductor to the People's Republic of China unless the Secretary of Commerce approves the transfer and Congress enacts a joint resolution approving it. The Act sunsets three years after enactment.
summary_long: The bill would prohibit any person from exporting, reexporting or transferring an advanced AI semiconductor to the People's Republic of China unless the Secretary of Commerce has approved the transfer after an interagency review and Congress has enacted a joint resolution specifically approving it. An advanced AI semiconductor is one that exceeds any of four thresholds: total processing performance of 2,400 or performance density of 1.6, DRAM bandwidth above 4,100 GB/s, interconnect bandwidth above 1,100 GB/s, or combined DRAM and interconnect bandwidth above 5,100 GB/s. The People's Republic of China includes Hong Kong, Macau and entities owned or controlled by its government or the Chinese Communist Party. The Secretary must submit a report to Congress within 30 days of a determination. Exceptions cover humanitarian exports, exports needed for U.S. diplomatic or consular facilities in China, and returns for repair or replacement of chips lawfully exported before enactment. The Act ceases to be effective three years after enactment. The text contains no penalty provisions and no separate enforcement authority.

title: HR 5272 Protect Elections from Deceptive AI Act
summary_short: Amends the Federal Election Campaign Act to bar knowingly distributing materially deceptive AI-generated audio or visual media of federal candidates, or in federal election activity, to influence an election or solicit funds. Candidates may seek injunctions and damages. Exempts bona fide news and satire. No effective date is stated.
summary_long: Section 2(a) adds new section 325 to Title III of the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971. It defines a covered individual as a candidate for Federal office, and defines deceptive AI-generated audio or visual media as AI or machine-learning output that merges, replaces or superimposes content, or generates inauthentic content, and that a reasonable person would find to show a fundamentally different appearance or speech, or a person who did not actually exhibit it. Subsection (b) prohibits a person, political committee or other entity from knowingly distributing such media of a covered individual, or in Federal election activity, with intent to influence an election or solicit funds. Subsection (c) exempts licensed broadcasters and streaming services carrying such media in bona fide news coverage with a clear acknowledgement of authenticity questions, regularly published periodicals that clearly state the media does not accurately represent the covered individual, and satire or parody. Subsection (d) gives covered individuals a civil action for injunctive or equitable relief, and for general or special damages and attorney's fees, with a clear and convincing evidence burden on the plaintiff. Subsection (b) of the Act makes a violation of section 325 defamation per se for defamation actions. Subsection (c) contains a severability clause. The bill creates no public enforcement body or government fine, and states no effective date.

title: American Artificial Intelligence Leadership and Uniformity Act
summary_short: Proposed federal bill that would require the President to produce a National Artificial Intelligence Action Plan within 30 days of enactment and would bar states and political subdivisions from enforcing laws regulating AI models, systems or automated decision systems in interstate commerce for five years.
summary_long: As introduced, the bill defines 'artificial intelligence', 'artificial intelligence model', 'artificial intelligence system' and 'automated decision system' (Sec. 2). Sec. 5(a) requires the President, acting through specified officials, to develop and submit to Congress a National Artificial Intelligence Action Plan within 30 days after enactment. Sec. 5(b) requires annual updates. Sec. 5(c) lists minimum contents, including identifying barriers to AI innovation, aligning federal risk management with NIST standards and frameworks, critical-infrastructure security, and measures to reduce small-business compliance burdens. Sec. 5(d) directs review of actions under Executive Orders 14110 and 14179 and suspension, revision or rescission of inconsistent actions. Sec. 6(a)(1) bars States and political subdivisions from enforcing, for five years from enactment, laws limiting, restricting or otherwise regulating AI models, systems or automated decision systems entered into interstate commerce. Sec. 6(a)(2) excludes laws whose primary purpose is to facilitate deployment or streamline procedures, certain laws imposing no substantive requirements, and provisions carrying criminal penalties. Sec. 6(b) and (c) preserve generally applicable criminal law and state procurement requirements. Sec. 7 limits federal agencies' authority to impose substantive requirements on AI beyond existing law.

title: GUARD Act
summary_short: The bill would authorize the Secretary of Defense to establish at least one National Security and Defense Artificial Intelligence Institute at a senior military college and award it competitive, five-year financial assistance, renewable once, for AI research, testbeds, data sets and workforce development. Recipients must be US-based.
summary_long: The bill, titled the GUARD Act, would authorize the Secretary of Defense to establish at least one National Security and Defense Artificial Intelligence Institute at an eligible host institution, defined as a senior military college under 10 U.S.C. 2111a(f). An Institute would be an AI research institute focused on cross-cutting or foundational science for national security and defense, building partnerships among public and private organizations and supporting interdisciplinary research and workforce development. The Secretary may seek to award financial assistance to a host institution or consortia for uses including curated data sets for training and testing AI systems, testbeds for evaluation before deployment, computing and data access, technical assistance and outreach. Awards run for five years, may be renewed once for up to five more, require an application, and follow a competitive merit-based review. Recipients and subgrantees must be based in the United States. The bill contains no separate penalties or enforcement provisions and states no effective date; it is at the introduced stage.

title: HR 5511 Algorithmic Accountability Act 2025 (Impact assessments of certain algorithms)
summary_short: As introduced, this bill would direct the Federal Trade Commission to require covered entities deploying machine-learning or AI-based algorithms for consequential decisions to perform impact assessments and submit summary reports, and would make violations unlawful. Regulations due two years after enactment.
summary_long: As introduced, the bill would direct the Federal Trade Commission to promulgate regulations, within two years after enactment, requiring covered entities to perform impact assessments of covered algorithms before and after deployment and to submit summary reports to the Commission. A covered algorithm is a computational process derived from machine learning, natural language processing, AI or similar techniques that, for a consequential action, creates content, affects information delivery, makes a decision or facilitates human decision making. Covered entities are persons under Commission jurisdiction that deploy such algorithms and meet receipts, equity-value or identifying-information thresholds. Assessments must address listed matters, including stakeholder consultation, privacy risks, differential performance, input data and consumer rights. Covered entities must disclose their status to persons that sell, license or otherwise provide the algorithm, and the Commission must publish annual reports and a public repository of summary report information. Violations, and knowing substantial assistance to them, are unlawful and treated as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act; state attorneys general may bring civil actions. The bill creates a Bureau of Technology within the Commission and does not preempt state, tribal, city or local law.

title: Securing Reliable Power for Advanced Technologies Act
summary_short: Adds Sec. 306 to the Defense Production Act of 1950 on critical AI infrastructure (data centers of 50 MW or more, dispatchable power plants, transmission, fuel supply). Lets the President designate covered projects as priority national defense projects, coordinate federal permits, and authorize financial assistance for baseload power facilities.
summary_long: The bill, introduced and pending, amends Title III of the Defense Production Act of 1950 by adding Sec. 306. Critical AI infrastructure includes data centers or high-performance computing facilities with at least 50 MW of connected load dedicated primarily to AI, dispatchable baseload generation of at least 100 MW, associated high-voltage transmission, and essential fuel supply infrastructure. The President may designate covered projects as priority national defense projects. For designated projects the President must require federal agencies to review permits concurrently under a consolidated schedule, with federal authorizations to be completed within 2 years of a complete application unless extraordinary circumstances require more time. Agency failure to follow the schedule is treated as a failure to act under 5 U.S.C. 706(1). The President resolves inter-agency disputes, and a single lead agency prepares environmental reviews. Civil actions have a 60-day filing window, with Circuit-court venue and limits on injunctions and vacatur. The President may exempt designated projects from new emissions limitations by executive order if defense necessity is determined and published. The United States must compensate owners or operators for federal changes that prohibit or materially impair a designated facility for at least 180 days, subject to claim deadlines and exclusions. Eligible facilities may receive Title III financial assistance covering up to 90 percent of project costs, and guidance is due within 180 days of enactment. A conforming amendment adds the designated infrastructure to Sec. 702(14). The text states no enactment date for the new provisions.

title: HR 5932 Claims Legitimacy and Evaluation Accountability Nationwide for VA Act 2025 (Utilizing AI for VA Disability rating schedule)
summary_short: Would expedite disciplinary actions against VA employees, raise criminal penalties for fraud and misconduct involving veterans' benefits, set whistleblower investigation and incentive rules, mandate annual ethics training, and require the VA Secretary to review the disability rating schedule and build AI tools to flag claims subject to human review.
summary_long: As introduced, the CLEAN VA Act amends titles 38, 18 and 5 of the U.S. Code. Section 2 sets factors for removal, demotion or suspension of VA covered individuals, requires review for substantial evidence, limits administrative judge, Merit Systems Protection Board and court review of penalties, and sets 15-business-day and 7-business-day timing limits. Section 3 adds penalties for VA-employee offenses under 18 U.S.C. 641, 1001, 201 and 1920, including imprisonment terms and fines stated in the text, forfeiture of federal annuity benefits under 5 U.S.C. 8312, a 60-day deadline for whistleblower retaliation investigations, annual settlement reporting, and incentive awards of up to $10,000. Section 4 directs the VA Secretary to review the disability rating schedule and develop data analytics and AI systems to flag claim irregularities, with human review required before administrative or disciplinary action; a report is due within 180 days. Section 6 repeats that text. Section 5 requires annual ethics and fraud training under new 38 U.S.C. 7735, overseen by the Inspector General.

title: Healthcare Education in AI Literacy Act
summary_short: The bill adds a competitive HRSA grant program in the Public Health Service Act for AI education and training of medical students, residents and faculty at qualified medical schools and residency sponsoring institutions. It authorizes $1,000,000 per fiscal year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030.
summary_long: The bill amends Part C of title VII of the Public Health Service Act by adding subpart III (Secs. 749C to 749G). The Secretary of Health and Human Services, acting through the Health Resources and Services Administration, must establish a competitive grant program for qualified medical schools or residency sponsoring institutions to educate and train medical students, medical residents and medical faculty in deploying artificial intelligence in the medical profession. Individual grants may not exceed $100,000, and a recipient may receive no more than $100,000 per fiscal year. Permitted uses include AI for diagnostics and treatment recommendations, integration into clinical decision-making, instruction on ethical issues such as bias and patient data privacy, and practical demonstrations. Administrative costs are capped at 10 percent, and grant funds may not support publication in predatory journals. Recipients must submit annual reports starting within 180 days of receiving a grant, and must make funded educational materials publicly available within 30 days of each report. The Secretary gives priority to schools serving medically underserved communities and may award no more than two grants within the same 2020 Census Division. The authorization of $1,000,000 per fiscal year covers fiscal years 2026 through 2030.](placeholder)

title: Algorithmic Transparency and Choice Act
summary_short: Would require providers of online platforms using personalized recommendation systems, from one year after enactment, to give minor users notices about those systems and options to switch to or limit them, with an input-transparent algorithm as default. Violations are treated as FTC unfair or deceptive practices.
summary_long: The bill would apply to providers of covered online platforms, meaning public-facing online platforms that use a personalized recommendation system and primarily provide a forum for user-generated content. Beginning one year after enactment, a provider must give covered users, meaning minors who register an account or create a profile, a clear and conspicuous notice the first time they interact with such a system. The terms and conditions must include a description of the system's essential features, inputs and parameters, the user-specific data collected or inferred, the opt-out and profile options available, and the quantities the system is designed to optimize. Providers must offer an option to switch to an input-transparent algorithm and an option to limit the type or category of recommendations, and must set an input-transparent algorithm as the default for covered users. A violation is treated as a violation of an FTC rule defining unfair or deceptive acts or practices, and the Federal Trade Commission enforces the section under the FTC Act. The bill does not require disclosure of trade secrets, confidential business information or privileged information, and it bars states from enforcing laws that cover the same requirements.

title: HR 6306 AI Fraud Deterrence Act 2025 (AI for the commission of financial crimes)
summary_short: Amends federal criminal statutes in title 18 (mail, wire and bank fraud, money laundering, and impersonation of federal officials) to set higher fines and prison terms where the offence is committed with AI assistance. Introduced bill, pending.
summary_long: The AI Fraud Deterrence Act amends federal criminal law in title 18 of the United States Code. Its findings (Sec. 2) cite 2025 incidents in which AI was used to impersonate senior US officials. Mail fraud (Sec. 3(a)) and wire fraud (Sec. 3(b)): the general fine rises from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000, and an AI-assisted violation is subject to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or imprisonment of not more than 20 years, or both. Bank fraud (Sec. 3(c)) gets a new subsection (b): AI-assisted violations carry a fine of not more than $2,000,000 or imprisonment of not more than 30 years, or both. Money laundering (Sec. 3(e)) carries, for AI-assisted violations, a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or thrice the value involved, whichever is greater, or imprisonment of not more than 20 years. Sec. 3(d) and 3(e)(2) define 'artificial intelligence' by reference to section 5002 of the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020. Impersonation of federal officials (Sec. 4, amending 18 U.S.C. 912) adds an AI-assisted penalty of not more than $1,000,000 or 3 years, and a rule of construction that does not limit AI use in satire or parody if the content clearly discloses that it is not authentic. The bill states no effective date.

title: Deepfake Liability Act
summary_short: Amends Section 230 of the Communications Act to condition its liability shield on providers' reasonable process for cyberstalking and intimate privacy violations, requires covered platforms to remove reported violations within 48 hours, and revises criminal prohibitions on sexually explicit digital forgeries. Introduced; not enacted.
summary_long: Amends Section 230 of the Communications Act of 1934 so that its general liability protection for interactive computer service providers applies only if the provider runs a reasonable process for cyberstalking and intimate privacy violations, including prevention measures, the TAKE IT DOWN Act notice process, minimum data logging and removal of court-determined unlawful content. Adds generative-model use to content creation under Section 230(f)(3). Revises TAKE IT DOWN Act definitions and criminal prohibitions on sexually explicit digital forgeries. Covered public platforms, excluding broadband, email, messaging and data storage services, must provide a notice-and-removal process and remove reported violations within 48 hours of a valid request; good-faith removal carries liability protection. The FTC, consulting the FCC and as appropriate the Attorney General, must issue implementing regulations within 180 days of enactment. The amendments apply to information made available on or after enactment. The bill is introduced and not enacted.

title: HR 6356 Artificial Intelligence Civil Rights Act of 2025
summary_short: Proposed federal bill, introduced 2 December 2025 and pending, that would bar developers and deployers from using covered algorithms in consequential actions in ways causing disparate impact or discrimination, require evaluations, impact assessments and disclosures, and allow FTC and state enforcement and private suits.
summary_long: H.R. 6356 (Artificial Intelligence Civil Rights Act of 2025), introduced 2 December 2025 and pending, applies to developers and deployers of 'covered algorithms' used in 'consequential actions' such as employment, education, housing, credit, health care and criminal justice. Section 101 bars uses causing disparate impact or discrimination on protected characteristics. Section 102 requires pre-deployment evaluations, annual deployer impact assessments, developer reviews, reports to the Federal Trade Commission and ten-year retention. Title II adds mitigation, certification, deceptive-marketing and off-label use limits, developer-deployer contracts, human alternatives, appeal rights and anti-retaliation rules. Title III requires public disclosures, short-form notices and a reporting mechanism, and an FTC study. Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act. State attorneys general and state data protection authorities may sue for civil penalties of $15,000 per violation or 4 percent of average gross annual revenue; individuals may sue for treble damages or $15,000 per violation. Pre-dispute arbitration agreements are unenforceable for disputes under the Act. No general effective date is stated; several rules are due within two years of enactment.

title: HR 6361 Ban AI Denials in Medicare Act 2025
summary_short: Bill that bars the HHS Secretary from implementing the WISeR prior-authorization payment model described at 90 Fed. Reg. 28749 or any substantially similar model, and bars selecting future CMI model tests that would apply prior authorization, including through AI, to traditional Medicare services.
summary_long: The Ban AI Denials in Medicare Act is an introduced bill. Section 2(a) provides that the Secretary of Health and Human Services may not implement the WISeR model described in a notice dated July 1, 2025 (90 Fed. Reg. 28749), or any substantially similar model. Section 2(b) amends section 1115A(b)(2) of the Social Security Act to add a limitation on model selection: beginning on the date of enactment, the Secretary may not select a model to be tested if the model would provide for prior authorization, including through artificial intelligence, for items or services payable under Part A or Part B of title XVIII. The operative provisions bind only the Secretary. The bill sets out no penalties, enforcement mechanisms, definitions of artificial intelligence, or exceptions, and it cites the WISeR notice by reference without restating its contents.

title: Safeguarding Adolescents From Exploitative BOTs Act
summary_short: Bill requiring chatbot providers to disclose to minor users that chatbots are AI systems, bar chatbots from falsely claiming licensed-professional status, require crisis resources and break reminders, and address harmful content. Enforced by the FTC and state attorneys general; applies one year after enactment.
summary_long: Bill applying to chatbot providers and covered users, meaning users the provider knows, or would know but for willful disregard, are minors under 17. Providers may not give covered users a chatbot that claims to be a licensed professional unless true. They must disclose in plain, age-appropriate language that the chatbot is an artificial intelligence system and not a natural person, at the first interaction and when asked, and must provide suicide and crisis hotline resources when suicide is raised. They must maintain reasonable policies prompting a break after three hours of continuous interaction and addressing sexual material harmful to minors, gambling, and illegal drugs, tobacco and alcohol.
