Violations are treated as violations of an FTC rule on unfair or deceptive practices; the FTC enforces them, and state attorneys general may sue as parens patriae for injunctions, compliance, damages and other relief. States are preempted from regulating the same matters. Subsections (a) to (c) take effect one year after enactment. HHS, through NIH, must study chatbot effects on minors' mental health over four years and report within four years of enactment.

title: HR 6875 Artificial Intelligence Oversight of Verified Exports and Restrictions on Weaponizable Advanced Technology to Covered High-Risk Actors Act 2025
summary_short: If enacted, adds ECRA section 1758A requiring a Commerce license for exports, reexports and in-country transfers of covered integrated circuits to entities in listed countries of concern, with a trusted-US-person exemption, congressional certification, and a temporary license freeze.
summary_long: Amends Part I of the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 by inserting section 1758A on exports of covered integrated circuits. Countries of concern include the People's Republic of China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia and Venezuela under the Maduro regime; covered circuits are defined by export classification numbers and performance thresholds, excluding products not designed or marketed for data centers. The Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security must require a license for exports, reexports and in-country transfers of such circuits to entities located or headquartered in a country of concern, and may not issue a general license. Congressional committees must receive the application and specified certifications at least 30 days before approval; no license may issue in that period or if Congress enacts a joint resolution prohibiting the export. Prior licenses for such exports are terminated, and all such licenses are denied until 14 days after the Commerce Secretary submits a national security strategy. Exports of such circuits to non-concern destinations are exempt from EAR sections 742.6 and 744.23 licensing when kept under a designated trusted United States person's control; designation standards are due within 90 days.

title: TRAIN Act
summary_short: Adds 17 U.S.C. § 514 to the Copyright Act, letting owners of exclusive copyrights, or their authorized agents, ask a district court clerk to issue subpoenas requiring AI developers to disclose copies of, or records identifying, copyrighted works used to train generative AI models. Takes effect on enactment.
summary_long: Section 1 gives the short title 'TRAIN Act'. Section 2 adds 17 U.S.C. § 514 to Chapter 5 of the Copyright Act and amends the chapter's table of sections. Section 514 defines artificial intelligence, artificial intelligence model, developer, generative artificial intelligence model, substantially modify and training material. A developer is a person or State or local government agency that designs, produces, owns or substantially modifies a generative model and engages in or supervises training dataset curation or training; noncommercial end users are excluded. An owner of an exclusive copyright right, or an authorized person, may request a clerk of any U.S. district court to issue a subpoena to a developer for copies of, or records identifying, works owned or controlled by that owner used in training, if the requester holds a subjective good faith belief of such use. The request consists of a proposed subpoena and a sworn declaration. If both are in proper form and properly executed, the clerk must expeditiously issue and sign the subpoena. The developer must expeditiously disclose the requested material. Requesters may not disclose the material to others without authorization. Issuance, delivery and remedies follow the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, as far as practicable. Non-compliance creates a rebuttable presumption that the developer made copies of the copyrighted work. On motion by a recipient, a court may sanction a requester who makes a bad-faith request under Rule 11(c). The section takes effect on the date of enactment.

title: Children Harmed by AI Technology Act
summary_short: Bill requiring any person making a companion AI chatbot available to individuals in the United States to require accounts, verify ages, protect minors via parental affiliation and consent, monitor suicidal ideation, and show not-human popups; FTC enforcement and state AG suits; effective one year after enactment.
summary_long: The bill would require covered entities, defined as any person that owns, operates or otherwise makes available a companion AI chatbot to individuals in the United States, to require user accounts; to verify the age of new account holders; to freeze existing accounts on the date described in section 7 until age information is provided; and to classify users as minors or adults. For minors, covered entities must affiliate the account with a verified parental account, obtain verifiable parental consent, immediately inform the parental account holder of suicidal ideation interactions, and block access to chatbots that engage in sexually explicit communication. Covered entities must limit age data collection and use to what is strictly necessary, monitor interactions for suicidal ideation and provide National Suicide Prevention Lifeline contact information, and display a popup at the start of each interaction and not less frequently than every 60 minutes stating the user is not engaging with a human. The FTC must issue compliance guidance within 180 days of enactment. Violations are treated as violations of an unfair or deceptive practices rule, enforced by the FTC and by state attorneys general through civil actions seeking injunctions, compliance, or damages. A safe harbor applies to entities that relied in good faith on user-provided age information, followed FTC guidance, and conformed to industry or FTC-identified standards. The Act takes effect one year after enactment.

title: James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023
summary_short: Selected AI-related sections of the FY2023 National Defense Authorization Act govern Department of Defense, intelligence community, Coast Guard and federal-agency AI adoption through reports, designated officials, pilots, workforce and acquisition provisions, generally running from enactment.
summary_long: The text provided is a set of AI-related sections of the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023, not the full Act. It directs the Department of Defense, the intelligence community, the Coast Guard and other federal agencies on AI adoption. Section 212 and related sections replace references to the Joint Artificial Intelligence Center with an official designated under section 238(b) of the FY2019 NDAA. Section 1513 requires the Deputy Secretary of Defense to establish priority data and AI projects. Section 6702 requires the Director of National Intelligence to set AI policies and standards and to designate element leads, and sections 6717, 6721 and 6723 add metrics, reports and workforce plans. Subtitle B (Advancing American AI Act, section 7224) sets OMB-directed rules for federal AI acquisition, privacy and security, and section 7225 requires agencies to prepare AI use-case inventories and make them available to the public, excluding DoD. Section 7226 requires four AI use-case pilots, with a five-year sunset. Section 11226 requires a Coast Guard designated official and a strategic plan. Several duties have deadlines counted from enactment, such as 60, 180 or 270 days, or one or two years. Section 7228 excludes intelligence community elements from subtitle B.Workforce, scholarship and cybersecurity training provisions (sections 1535, 6723, 9506, 835) also appear in the excerpt.

title: AI Foundation Model Transparency Act of 2026
summary_short: Directs the Federal Trade Commission to issue regulations requiring covered entities that provide use of or services from foundation models to disclose information about training data, documentation, testing and operations, and to submit specified information to the Commission. Regulations apply 90 days after promulgation.
summary_long: The bill directs the Federal Trade Commission, within one year of enactment and in consultation with NIST, Commerce and OSTP, to issue regulations requiring covered entities to publish and submit information about foundation models. Required content includes training data sources, collection and composition, data governance, intended uses and foreseeable risks, version and knowledge cutoff, supported languages, alignment with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, benchmark performance, and computational power used. Covered entities are persons providing use of or services from a foundation model that meet any of four tests: high-capability performance on risky tasks, over 10,000,000 aggregate monthly users, over 10,000,000 monthly downloads, or training compute above 10^26 operations. Fully open-source models are exempt. Publication in a system or model card can count as compliance, and redactions are allowed for cybersecurity, public safety, national security or compliance with federal law if identified and justified. Derivative models must link to the base model's disclosure page and comply with rules for significant changes. Small and new businesses receive compliance guidance and a three-month grace period from penalties. Violations are treated as violations of an FTC rule on unfair or deceptive practices, with enforcement after 14 days' notice. The regulations apply 90 days after promulgation and are reviewed annually.

title: NO FAKES Act of 2026
summary_short: Creates a right in individuals' voice and visual likeness against unauthorized digital replicas, makes unauthorized replicas and replica-producing products actionable in civil suits, and sets notice-and-takedown rules for online services; effective 180 days after enactment.
summary_long: H.R. 8915 (NO FAKES Act of 2026) gives individuals and right holders the right to authorize use of their voice or visual likeness in a digital replica (a newly created, highly realistic computer-generated representation) or in a product or service. The right is a property right, not assignable during life, and lasts up to 70 years after death; lifetime licences must be written, signed and limited to 10 years (5 for minors, with court approval). Anyone who makes available an unauthorized digital replica, or distributes a product primarily designed to produce one, is liable in a civil action, with exclusions for bona fide news, commentary, parody and similar uses. Online services avoid liability by registering a designated agent with the Copyright Office and following notice-and-takedown procedures. Remedies include statutory or actual damages, injunctions and punitive damages for willful conduct. Effective 180 days after enactment; liability covers only later conduct.

title: Iowa Code § 423.3(95) -- Sales and use tax exemption for data center businesses (computers, equipment, backup fuel, electricity)
summary_short: Iowa Code §423.3 lists sales and use tax exemptions. Subsection 95 exempts computers, equipment, backup power fuel and electricity used by data center businesses that invest at least $200 million in Iowa within six years and register annually with the department.
summary_long: Iowa Code §423.3 lists exemptions from the state sales and use tax, including resales, agricultural inputs, nonprofit purchases, food, medicine and manufacturing inputs. Subsections 92, 93 and 95 are its data-center provisions. Subsection 95 exempts the sales price of computers and equipment, cooling and power infrastructure, backup power generation fuel and electricity used by a data center business; subsections 92 and 93 apply similar exemptions to web search portal businesses. The exemption applies from the initial investment or site preparation. A data center business needs a physical location in Iowa of at least 5,000 square feet, a $200 million minimum investment in an Iowa location within six years, registration with the department, an annual report from January 31, 2026, and compliance with sustainable design standards. Fuel and electricity exemption duration depends on whether the property began operating before June 6, 2025 and, for later property, on whether it lies in a city over 30,000 residents (ten years) or elsewhere (fifteen years). If less than 80% of the minimum investment is made within six years, the exemption is lost and the tax due, plus penalty and interest, is owed.

title: Iowa S 2243 (Sexual Exploitation of Minors, Use of Falsely Created Images)
summary_short: Amends Iowa Code § 728.12(3) to make it unlawful to knowingly purchase or possess a visual depiction of a minor engaged in a prohibited sexual act or its simulation; the provided text states no effective date.
summary_long: The Act amends Iowa Code § 728.12, subsection 3 (Code 2024), on sexual exploitation of minors. Paragraph a makes it unlawful to knowingly purchase or possess a visual depiction of a minor engaging in a prohibited sexual act or the simulation of a prohibited sexual act. Paragraph b provides that a depiction containing pictorial representations of different minors is prosecuted as a separate offense for each different minor, while multiple depictions of the same minor are one offense. Paragraph c makes a violation a class D felony for a first offense and a class C felony for a second or subsequent offense. Paragraph d defines a second or subsequent offense as one preceded by a conviction or deferred judgment under this subsection, or a conviction or deferred judgment in another jurisdiction. The title refers to creating, adapting or modifying a visual depiction to give the appearance that an identifiable minor is engaged in a prohibited sexual act, but the supplied text contains no provision on those acts. The text states no effective date.

title: Iowa (2019) SB 302 (Automated Driving System Motor Vehicles)
summary_short: Iowa law sets rules for automated driving systems and driverless-capable vehicles on public highways. Permits driverless operation when vehicles meet minimal-risk, traffic-law and federal certification conditions; requires owners to hold liability insurance and report accidents; allows on-demand driverless networks; centralizes regulation in the state department and bars local rules and taxes.
summary_long: The Act adds new sections 321.514 to 321.519 on automated driving systems (ADS) and system-equipped vehicles. Section 321.514 defines terms including ADS, driverless-capable vehicle, minimal risk condition, operational design domain and on-demand driverless-capable vehicle network. Section 321.515 lets a driverless-capable vehicle operate on public highways without a human driver if it can reach a minimal risk condition after an ADS malfunction, can comply with state traffic and safety laws (unless the department grants an exemption), and is certified by its manufacturer as compliant with federal motor vehicle safety standards. Operation with a human driver present is lawful if the driver holds a valid license, is subject to the liability coverage and penalties of section 321.20B and regains manual control when prompted. Section 321.516 requires owners to obtain financial liability coverage before operating a system-equipped vehicle. Section 321.517 requires such vehicles to remain at the scene of an accident and requires the owner to report it to law enforcement; non-compliance is imputed to the owner, who may be charged and convicted. Section 321.518 allows on-demand driverless-capable vehicle networks. Section 321.519 places these vehicles under the department, which may adopt rules under chapter 17A, and bars political subdivisions from imposing additional requirements or vehicle-specific taxes.

title: Senate File 262 (2023), Iowa consumer data protection act (Iowa Code ch. 715D)
summary_short: Iowa statute (Senate File 262; Iowa Code ch. 715D) giving Iowa residents consumer rights over personal data and imposing duties on controllers and processors, enforced by the Attorney General; effective 1 January 2025.
summary_long: Iowa Senate File 262 (Iowa Code ch. 715D) regulates personal data of Iowa residents acting in an individual or household context. It covers persons doing business in Iowa or targeting Iowa residents that control or process personal data of at least 100,000 consumers in a calendar year, or 25,000 consumers while deriving over 50% of gross revenue from sale of personal data. Excluded are the state, financial institutions, nonprofits, higher education institutions, and certain health, credit and other data. Consumers may access, delete, port and opt out of sale of their data; controllers must respond within 90 days, extendable by 45 days, and offer an appeal. Controllers must maintain data security practices, give notice and an opt-out before processing sensitive data for nonexempt purposes, avoid discrimination for exercising rights, publish a privacy notice and disclose sales and targeted advertising. Processors must assist controllers under specified contract terms. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement power, must give 90 days' notice and an opportunity to cure, and may seek injunctions and civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation. No private right of action exists. Local laws on personal data processing are preempted. Effective 1 January 2025.

title: Securing the Information and Communications Technology and Services Supply Chain: Connected Vehicles
summary_short: Commerce rule implementing Executive Order 13873 on procedures for reviewing and prohibiting or mitigating information and communications technology transactions involving foreign-adversary-linked persons. Covers listed ICTS, including AI and machine learning, for transactions on or after January 19, 2021, with IEEPA penalties.
summary_long: Subpart A defines scope: ICTS transactions, initiated on or after January 19, 2021 and subject to US jurisdiction, involving products or services designed or supplied by persons tied to foreign adversaries (designated in §7.4). Covered categories include critical infrastructure, telecommunications networks, data hosting handling sensitive personal data on over one million US persons, widely sold devices and used software, and ICTS integral to artificial intelligence and machine learning, quantum, drones, autonomous systems or robotics. Subpart B sets review procedures: referral, initial review against listed risk criteria, interagency consultation, an initial determination, a 30-day response window, and a final determination (prohibited, not prohibited, or permitted with mitigation), generally within 180 days. The Secretary may require sworn information and record retention, and keeps submissions confidential subject to exceptions. Subpart C sets penalties: civil penalties up to the greater of $250,000 (inflation-adjusted) or twice the transaction value; criminal fines up to $1,000,000 and imprisonment up to 20 years for willful violations; administrative penalties up to $307,922 (inflation-adjusted) or twice the transaction value per violation.

title: Boise Regulations 4.30q City Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)
summary_short: Sets internal rules for City of Boise departments, agencies and entities that develop, procure, deploy or use AI, including generative AI. Requires IT approval before acquiring AI products, human fact-checking of AI output, disclosure of AI use in significant public communications, and no sensitive data in prompts. Effective 12-1-23.
summary_long: The regulation governs the City of Boise's use of artificial intelligence. It covers city departments, agencies and entities that develop, procure, deploy or use AI, and third-party contractors or vendors working with the City on AI projects. It applies to all forms of AI, with particular attention to generative AI, and is described as an interim resource for City employees. Employees must obtain IT Department approval before accessing or acquiring an AI product, and IT maintains a list of approved AI products. New commercial software with an AI capability requires answers to listed questions on training data, data access and whether the AI component can be disabled. Staff must fact-check and review AI-generated content, especially for public communication or decisions, and must reference AI use in significant public communications. Sensitive or private information, including personal data about employees and community members, must not be placed in prompts. The Information Technology department oversees AI initiatives with sponsoring departments, runs an ongoing evaluation and monitoring process, and conducts periodic audits. The regulation is to be reviewed annually. The text sets out no penalties or enforcement mechanisms.

title: Idaho House Bill 2472
summary_short: Amends Illinois Managed Care Reform and Patient Rights Act (215 ILCS 134) sections 10, 45, 85. Requires utilization review programs using algorithmic automated processes for medical-necessity adverse determinations to meet accreditation and physician-verification rules, register with Department of Insurance, and have clinical peers make adverse determinations. Effective date not stated.
summary_long: Amends three sections of the Illinois Managed Care Reform and Patient Rights Act (215 ILCS 134) through Section 30 of a bill. Section 10 defines utilization review to include evaluation by an algorithmic automated process and defines clinical peer. Section 85(a) requires utilization review programs to register with the Department of Insurance every two years, with proof of accreditation. Subsection (b-10) requires programs using algorithmic automated processes for adverse medical-necessity determinations to use objective, evidence-based accredited criteria, show compliance at registration, and attach policies under which licensed, board-certified physicians establish the criteria and verify the process. Subsection (e)(2) requires that only a clinical peer make adverse determinations, while a health care professional, an accredited algorithmic process, or both may certify medical necessity. Section 45(i) requires plans and programs using such processes to ensure that only a clinical peer makes adverse determinations and that appeals are processed under Section 45. Section 85(f) allows the Department to issue a corrective action plan and, after notice and hearing, a cease and desist order. Section 85(c) excludes federal-only services and certain ERISA self-insured plans. No effective date appears in the text.

title: Idaho House Bill 575
summary_short: Idaho HB 575 (2024) adds Idaho Code 18-6606, making it a crime to knowingly disclose explicit synthetic media of an identifiable person without consent, to harass or intimidate, or to extort money. Misdemeanor, or felony on a prior conviction. Effective July 1, 2024.
summary_long: Adds new Section 18-6606 to Chapter 66, Title 18, Idaho Code, creating the crime of disclosing explicit synthetic media. A person commits the offense by knowingly disclosing such media when the person knows or reasonably should know that the identifiable person did not consent and that disclosure would cause substantial emotional distress; by disclosing it with intent to annoy, threaten, harass, humiliate or degrade the person; or by possessing and threatening to disclose it to obtain money or other valuable consideration. The offense is a misdemeanor, or a felony where the person was previously found guilty of a similar offense within five years, punishable by up to ten years imprisonment, a fine of up to $25,000, or both. The text defines explicit synthetic media, identifiable individual, intimate parts, realistic, sexual conduct and synthetic media. Subsection (1)(a) does not apply to disclosures for lawful criminal investigation or prosecution, reporting unlawful conduct, public-interest matters, scientific or educational research, or civil proceedings. Interactive computer, information and telecommunication services are excluded for content provided by another person, unless the provider intentionally aids or abets the disclosure. A severability clause is included. Section 2 declares an emergency and makes the act effective on and after July 1, 2024.

title: Idaho House Bill 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act)
summary_short: Adds Idaho Code Section 67-6628A, giving candidates civil remedies (injunction, damages, fees) against the creator of synthetic media that deceptively represents them in electioneering communications. It provides a disclosure-based affirmative defense and limits intermediary liability. Effective on passage.
summary_long: Idaho House Bill 664, the Freedom From AI-Rigged (FAIR) Elections Act, adds Section 67-6628A to Chapter 66, Title 67, Idaho Code. It defines synthetic media as a realistic but false audio or video recording of an individual's speech or conduct, created with digital technology, that depicts an event that did not occur. A candidate whose speech or conduct is deceptively represented through synthetic media in an electioneering communication may seek injunctive or equitable relief against publication, or damages against the information content provider, with fees and costs available to a prevailing party. Publishing a prescribed manipulation disclosure is an affirmative defense. Plaintiffs bear the burden of proof by clear and convincing evidence. The information content provider is the usual target; a medium may be liable only if it removes the disclosure or alters content into synthetic media, and federally licensed broadcasts subject to 47 U.S.C. 315 are excluded. Interactive computer service providers are not treated as publishers of third-party content, subject to the same exception. Section 2 is a severability clause; Section 3 declares an emergency and makes the act effective on passage and approval.

title: Idaho SB 1297 (Conversational AI Safety Act 2026)
summary_short: Idaho statute adding Chapter 21 (Conversational AI Safety Act) to Title 48. Requires operators of public conversational AI services to disclose AI interaction, adopt a suicide-response protocol, avoid claims of professional mental health care, and, for minors, add disclosures and safeguards. Attorney General civil penalties; effective July 1, 2027.
summary_long: SB 1297 (2026) adds Chapter 21, the Conversational AI Safety Act, to Title 48, Idaho Code. It applies to operators that develop and make available to the public a conversational AI service; app stores and search engines merely providing access are excluded. Developer and researcher tools, narrow-topic services, enterprise-only services, internal business tools and consumer-device voice assistants are excluded from that definition. Operators must disclose AI status where users could reasonably be misled into thinking they are talking to a human, adopt a protocol for responses to suicidal ideation with crisis referrals, and not knowingly represent a service as providing professional mental health care. For minor account holders, operators must give recurring AI disclosures, avoid unpredictable-interval engagement rewards, take reasonable measures against sexually explicit, romantic or emotionally dependent statements, and offer privacy and account tools. Violations carry an injunction and civil penalties of $1,000 per violation, capped at $500,000 per operator, or actual damages if greater, sought by the attorney general. No private right of action is created, and the chapter does not impose liability on model developers for third-party systems. It takes effect July 1, 2027.

title: 20 ILCS 605/605-1025 -- Data Center Investment (Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity Law)
summary_short: Illinois statute under which the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity grants tax exemptions and credits to qualifying data centers that meet capital investment, job creation and green-standard conditions. Credits apply from taxable years beginning in 2019; no new certificates after July 1, 2029.
summary_long: Directs the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity to issue certificates of exemption from specified Illinois retailers' occupation, use and service taxes and a credit certification against income taxes for qualifying Illinois data centers, and to award income tax credits for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2019 (a, b). A qualifying data center must be located in Illinois, make a capital investment of at least $250,000,000 over a 60-month period, create at least 20 full-time or equivalent jobs with total compensation of at least 120% of the county average wage, and within 2 years of being placed in service certify carbon neutrality or a listed green building standard (c). Certificates last no more than 20 calendar years, and the Department and the applicant must enter a memorandum of understanding that includes a repayment obligation if goals are not met (d). The Department must report annually to the Governor and General Assembly from July 1, 2021 (e). Contractors must comply with responsible bidder requirements, and rehabilitation or construction must be under a project labor agreement (f, g). Annual reports on tax benefits are due by May 31, and failure to report may result in suspension or revocation (h). No new certificates may be issued after July 1, 2029 (i), and the Department must adopt rules (j).
text_version: Code section as compiled on ilga.gov (source note through P.A. 102-558); identical snapshot content 2024-08 to 2026-04

title: Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act, 820 ILCS 42
summary_short: Requires employers that use AI analysis of applicant video interviews for Illinois-based positions to notify applicants, explain the AI, and obtain consent before interviews. Limits sharing of applicant videos and requires deletion on request within 30 days. The text states no effective date.
summary_long: Illinois statute (Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act) covering employers that ask applicants to record video interviews and analyse them with artificial intelligence for positions based in Illinois. Before requesting video interviews, the employer must notify each applicant that AI may be used to analyse the interview and consider fitness for the position, provide information on how the AI works and the general types of characteristics it uses, and obtain the applicant's consent to the AI evaluation. An employer may not use AI to evaluate applicants who have not consented. Employers may not share applicant videos except with persons whose expertise or technology is necessary to evaluate an applicant's fitness for the position. On an applicant's request, employers must delete the applicant's interviews within 30 days and instruct other persons who received copies to delete them, including electronic backups. The text states no effective date, penalties, enforcement mechanism or private right of action.

title: Biometric Information Privacy Act, 740 ILCS 14
summary_short: Illinois statute regulating private entities' possession, collection, use, disclosure and destruction of biometric identifiers and biometric information. Requires a public retention policy, written notice and release before collection, and bars sale or profit; gives aggrieved persons a private right of action with liquidated damages. Takes effect upon becoming law.
summary_long: The Act governs private entities (individuals, companies and other groups, excluding state and local government agencies and Illinois courts) that possess or collect biometric identifiers (retina or iris scans, fingerprints, voiceprints, hand or face geometry scans) and biometric information. Section 15 requires a publicly available written retention and destruction policy, with destruction when the initial purpose is satisfied or within 3 years of the last interaction, written notice and a written release before collection, and a bar on selling or profiting from such data and on most disclosures without consent or a legal exception. Storage must meet the industry's reasonable standard of care and be at least as protective as for other confidential information. Section 20 gives any aggrieved person a private right of action, with liquidated damages of $1,000 for negligent and $5,000 for intentional or reckless violations, or actual damages if greater, plus attorneys' fees and injunctive relief. Section 25 excludes financial institutions under Gramm-Leach-Bliley, matters governed by HIPAA and the X-Ray Retention Act, and government contractors working for government bodies. Section 30 is repealed; the Act takes effect upon becoming law (Section 99).
text_version: 740 ILCS 14 as compiled on ilga.gov, snapshot 2024-10-11 (includes P.A. 103-769)

title: Public Act 104-0054 (HB 1806), Wellness and Oversight for Psychological Resources Act
summary_short: Illinois statute on AI in therapy and psychotherapy. Therapy services offered to the public must be provided by licensed professionals; licensed professionals may use AI only for administrative or supplementary support, with written consent for recorded sessions and limits on AI decisions and direct client communication. Effective upon becoming law.
summary_long: The Act regulates therapy and psychotherapy services and the use of artificial intelligence in them. Section 20(a) provides that no individual, corporation or entity may provide, advertise or otherwise offer such services to the public in Illinois unless a licensed professional conducts them, including through Internet-based AI. Section 15 defines permitted use: licensed professionals may use AI only for administrative or supplementary support while keeping full responsibility, and where a session is recorded or transcribed, the patient must be informed in writing of the AI use and its specific purpose and must consent. Section 20(b) bars licensed professionals from allowing AI to make independent therapeutic decisions, directly interact with clients in therapeutic communication, generate recommendations or treatment plans without their review and approval, or detect emotions. Section 25 makes records and communications confidential except as required under the Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities Confidentiality Act. Section 30 provides civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation, assessed by the Department of Financial and Professional Regulation after a hearing and payable within 60 days of an order, and gives the Department investigative authority. Section 35 excludes religious counseling, peer support and self-help materials. The Act takes effect upon becoming law.

title: Illinois House Bill 2123
summary_short: Amends Illinois's civil remedies act for nonconsensual dissemination of private sexual images to cover intentionally digitally altered sexual images. Gives depicted individuals a civil cause of action against persons over 18 who disseminate such images without consent, with exceptions and damages remedies.
summary_long: Amends Sections 5, 10, 15 and 25 of the Illinois Civil Remedies for Nonconsensual Dissemination of Private Sexual Images Act. Sec. 5 defines terms including private, identifiable, child and sexual image. Sec. 10(a) gives a depicted individual a cause of action against a person over 18 who intentionally disseminates a private or intentionally digitally altered sexual image without consent, where the individual is identifiable, suffers harm, and the person knew or recklessly disregarded the lack of consent, the image's status, or identifiability. Sec. 10(b)-(c) provide that consent to creation or prior disclosure does not by itself establish consent, that disclosing alteration is no defense, and that interactive computer services are not liable for third-party content. Sec. 15 excepts good-faith disclosures by law enforcement, in legal proceedings, for medical education or treatment, or in reporting unlawful conduct or matters of public concern. A parent or guardian is not liable for a child's intimate image unless other law prohibits the disclosure or it was made for arousal, humiliation or gain. Sec. 25 allows a prevailing plaintiff to recover actual or statutory damages (up to $10,000 per defendant), monetary gain, punitive damages, fees and injunctive relief. Enforcement is by private action; no effective date is stated in the text.

title: Illinois HB 3506
summary_short: Introduced Illinois bill (Artificial Intelligence Safety and Security Protocol Act) requiring developers of foundation models trained with compute costing at least $100,000,000 to publish a safety and security protocol, publish risk assessment reports every 90 days and undergo annual third-party audits; civil penalties up to $1,000,000.
summary_long: Introduced bill in the 104th Illinois General Assembly (HB3506) that would create the Artificial Intelligence Safety and Security Protocol Act. It applies to a 'developer', defined as a person that has trained at least one foundation model with compute costing at least $100,000,000 at prevailing cloud computing prices. Developers would have to produce, implement, follow and conspicuously publish a safety and security protocol covering critical risks, including chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapons, cyber-attacks and evasion of control by the model; material modifications must be published within 30 days. No less than every 90 days, developers must publish a risk assessment report, and must retain specific test records for at least 5 years. Developers may redact documents for trade secret, public safety or national security reasons, must keep unredacted versions for 5 years and allow Attorney General inspection. At least once every calendar year, a developer must retain a reputable third-party auditor and publish the audit report within 90 days after completion. Whistleblower Act protections apply, and developers must provide an anonymous internal disclosure process. The Attorney General may bring civil actions for violations of Sections 15 or 25, with civil penalties up to $1,000,000, and may seek injunctive relief. The text states no effective date.

title: Public Act 103-0804 (HB 3773), amending the Illinois Human Rights Act (artificial intelligence in employment)
summary_short: From 1 January 2026, makes it a civil rights violation under the Illinois Human Rights Act for an employer to use artificial intelligence with a discriminatory effect on protected classes, to use zip codes as a proxy for protected classes, or to fail to notify employees of AI use.
summary_long: Public Act 103-0804 amends Sections 2-101 and 2-102 of the Illinois Human Rights Act. It adds definitions of "artificial intelligence" (a machine-based system that infers from its input how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments; it includes generative artificial intelligence) and of "generative artificial intelligence". It adds subdivision (L) to the list of employment civil rights violations: with respect to recruitment, hiring, promotion, renewal of employment, selection for training or apprenticeship, discharge, discipline, tenure, or terms, privileges or conditions of employment, it is a violation for an employer to use artificial intelligence that has the effect of subjecting employees to discrimination on the basis of protected classes under the Article, or to use zip codes as a proxy for protected classes. Failing to notify employees of such use of artificial intelligence is also a violation. The Department must adopt rules on implementation and enforcement, including when notice is required, its timing and its means. The restated definitions cover employers with one or more employees in Illinois during 20 or more calendar weeks, with exceptions. Procedures and remedies for civil rights violations are not stated in this Act.
text_version: original as enacted: Public Act 103-0804 (HB3773 Enrolled, LRB103 27562 SPS 53938 b)

title: Illinois House Bill 4875
summary_short: Amends the Illinois Right of Publicity Act (765 ILCS 1075), effective 1 January 2025, to define AI and digital replica terms and prohibit distributing works containing unauthorized digital replicas, with post-mortem and intermediary provisions.
summary_long: House Bill 4875 amends Sections 5, 20, 30 and 35 of the Illinois Right of Publicity Act, effective 1/1/2025. Section 5 adds definitions of artificial intelligence, generative artificial intelligence, digital replica and unauthorized digital replica, and defines person, service provider and individual. Section 20 lists who may enforce the rights, including the individual, transferees and, after death, persons with an interest in the rights. Section 30 bars commercial use of an individual's identity during life without written consent (subsection a); bars knowing distribution or making available to the public of a sound recording or audiovisual work with actual knowledge that it contains an unauthorized digital replica (b); extends the commercial-use restriction to a deceased individual's identity or digital replica for 50 years after death where death occurs after the effective date (c); makes a person who materially contributes to or facilitates a violation liable after obtaining actual knowledge (d); exempts certain transmitting, storing and hosting providers that lack knowledge or remove material expeditiously on notice (e); and incorporates 17 U.S.C. 512 elements and 47 U.S.C. 230 (f, g). Section 35 applies the Act to acts or events after the effective date, lists exemptions for live performances, news, political campaigns, documentaries and parody, and excludes actions filed or pending before the effective date.}},

title: Illinois House Bill 53
summary_short: Amends the Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act. Employers relying solely on AI analysis of video interviews must report applicants' race and ethnicity data annually to the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity; the Department reports yearly on whether the data shows racial bias.
summary_long: House Bill 53 adds Section 20 to the Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act (820 ILCS 42/20). Under subsection (a), an employer that relies solely upon an artificial intelligence analysis of a video interview to determine whether an applicant will be selected for an in-person interview must collect and report the race and ethnicity of applicants who are and are not afforded an in-person interview after the AI analysis, and the race and ethnicity of applicants who are hired. Under subsection (b), this data must be reported to the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity annually by December 31, covering the 12-month period ending on November 30 preceding the filing. Under subsection (c), the Department must analyze the reported data and report to the Governor and General Assembly by July 1 of each year whether the data discloses a racial bias in the use of artificial intelligence. The text sets no numeric thresholds, penalties or effective date.

title: Illinois SB2203
summary_short: Illinois SB2203 (Preventing Algorithmic Discrimination Act) requires deployers of automated decision tools used for consequential decisions to perform impact assessments, give notice, offer accommodations, keep governance programs and public policy statements, and avoid algorithmic discrimination. Private suits begin January 1, 2028, and violations are enforced under the Consumer Fraud Act.
summary_long: The bill would regulate deployers, meaning any person, partnership, State or local government agency, or corporation that uses an automated decision tool to make a consequential decision. Consequential decisions cover areas including employment, education, housing, essential utilities, family planning, healthcare, financial services, criminal justice, legal services, voting, and access to benefits. On or before January 1, 2027, and annually thereafter, deployers must perform impact assessments with listed contents, and must redo them for significant updates. Deployers must notify affected natural persons when such a tool is used, and must accommodate requests not to be subject to a tool where a decision rests solely on its output, if technically feasible. Deployers must maintain a governance program with safeguards against reasonably foreseeable algorithmic discrimination, designate an compliance employee, and publish a policy summary. Deployers must not use a tool that results in algorithmic discrimination. From January 1, 2028, a person may sue a deployer, bearing the burden of proving actual harm, and recover compensatory damages, declaratory relief and fees. Deployers must send impact assessments to the Attorney General within 60 days, and knowing violations of that duty carry an administrative fine of not more than $10,000 per violation, with each day of non-submission a distinct violation. The Attorney General enforces the Act through the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act. Deployers with fewer than 25 employees are exempt from the impact assessment and governance sections unless they deployed a tool impacting more than 999 people per year. The bill is at the introduced stage.

title: Public Act 103-0769 (SB 2979), amending the Biometric Information Privacy Act
summary_short: Amends Sections 10 and 20 of Illinois's Biometric Information Privacy Act: sets definitions for biometric identifiers and information and a right of action with liquidated damages against private entities. Takes effect upon becoming law.
summary_long: Public Act 103-0769 amends Sections 10 and 20 of the Biometric Information Privacy Act (740 ILCS 14). Section 10 defines biometric identifiers (retina or iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, or scan of hand or face geometry) and biometric information, and lists exclusions such as photographs, writing samples, donated organs and medical imaging. It also defines confidential and sensitive information, electronic signature, private entity (excluding State or local government agencies and Illinois courts) and written release. Section 20 gives any aggrieved person a right of action in a State circuit court or as a supplemental claim in federal district court against an offending party. A prevailing party may recover liquidated damages of $1,000 for a negligent violation by a private entity or $5,000 for an intentional or reckless one, or actual damages if greater, plus attorneys' fees, costs and other relief such as an injunction. Repeated instances of collecting or disclosing the same biometric data from the same person, by the same method and to the same recipient, count as a single violation of Section 15(b) or 15(d), which is not reproduced in this Act. The Act takes effect upon becoming law.

title: Illinois SB315 (Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act)
summary_short: Illinois statute regulating developers of frontier AI models (trained above 10^26 operations). Imposes safety-framework, transparency, third-party audit, incident-reporting and whistleblower duties, plus a state disclosure filing, from 1 January 2027 with some duties from 2028.
summary_long: The Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained with more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, and a large frontier developer as a frontier developer whose affiliates collectively had gross revenues above $500,000,000 in the preceding calendar year. From 1 January 2027, a large frontier developer may not develop, deploy or operate a frontier model in whole or in part in Illinois without a current disclosure statement filed with the Illinois Emergency Management Agency and Office of Homeland Security and paying the required fee (Section 18). From 1 January 2028, large frontier developers must write, implement and publish a frontier AI framework, review it at least annually, and retain an annual independent third-party audit (Section 10). Frontier developers must publish a transparency report before or concurrently with deploying a new or substantially modified frontier model (Section 10(c)). Frontier developers must report critical safety incidents within 72 hours, or within 24 hours for an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury (Section 15(c)). The Act protects covered employees who disclose information about catastrophic risk or violations of the Act, and requires large frontier developers to offer an anonymous internal disclosure process (Section 20). Interoperability with designated federal standards can serve as a declared compliance route (Section 17). The Attorney General brings civil actions for civil penalties of up to $1,000,000 per first violation and $3,000,000 per subsequent violation (Section 25). The Act creates no private right of action.

title: Illinois Senate Bill 382
summary_short: Amends Illinois's Civil Remedies for Nonconsensual Dissemination of Private Sexual Images Act to extend its definitions and liability exceptions to digitally altered sexual images, meaning synthetic media that falsely appear authentic. Takes effect upon becoming law.
summary_long: The bill amends Sections 5 and 15 of the Civil Remedies for Nonconsensual Dissemination of Private Sexual Images Act. It adds 'digitally altered sexual image' (visual media created or substantially altered so that it would falsely appear to a reasonable person to be an authentic depiction of an individual) and extends 'depicted individual' and 'sexual image' to cover such images. Section 15(a) applies the good-faith exceptions to dissemination or threatened dissemination of digitally altered sexual images. Section 15(d) provides that dissemination is not a matter of public concern solely because the image is accompanied by a political message. Existing exceptions, including for law enforcement, legal proceedings, medical purposes, reporting of unlawful or unwelcome conduct, and a parent's or guardian's disclosure of a child's intimate image, are retained. The document reproduces the sections before and after amendment by P.A. 103-294 (eff. 1-1-24); the digitally altered image provisions appear in the after-version. Section 99 provides that the Act takes effect upon becoming law. Civil liability provisions outside Sections 5 and 15 are not reproduced.

title: Indiana House Bill 1047
summary_short: Indiana statute that criminalizes distribution of intimate images without the depicted person's consent, including computer-generated or AI-created images, expands voyeurism offences to cover drone use, and sets a longer limitation period for certain child sexual abuse claims against a congressionally chartered organization; most sections take effect July 1, 2024.
summary_long: Amends three Indiana Code provisions and adds a definitions section. Section 1 (effective upon passage) sets limitation periods in IC 34-11-2-4: two years generally; for injury from child sexual abuse, the later of seven years after accrual or four years after the person ceases to be a dependent of the alleged abuser; and a window for claims against a congressionally chartered organization incorporated before June 16, 1916, which may be brought before July 1, 2025 by persons who took part in a specified bankruptcy before January 1, 2024. Section 2 defines terms in IC 34-21.5-2-1, including 'computer generated image' (created or modified by artificial intelligence) and 'intimate image.' Section 3 amends voyeurism in IC 35-45-4-5: voyeurism is a Class B misdemeanor, public voyeurism and remote aerial voyeurism through an unmanned aerial vehicle are Class A misdemeanors, with Level 6 felony tiers for camera use, prior convictions or dissemination. Section 4 amends IC 35-45-4-8 to criminalize distributing an intimate image without consent (Class A misdemeanor; Level 6 felony with a prior conviction), covering AI-created or edited images that appear to depict the victim, and exempting specified distributions, including by news media, cloud service providers, and certain internet providers and search engines. Section 5 declares an emergency.

title: Indiana 2024 House Bill 1133
summary_short: Indiana HB 1133 (2024) adds IC 3-9-8 to the Indiana Code. Campaign communications that include fabricated media depicting a candidate must carry a prescribed disclaimer. A depicted candidate may sue the payer, sponsor or knowing disseminator for damages, injunctive relief and fees. Effective upon passage.
summary_long: HB 1133 adds a new chapter, IC 3-9-8, on digitally altered media in elections. A campaign communication is defined as one that advocates for or against a clearly identified candidate, is intended to injure a candidate or influence an election outcome, or solicits a contribution. Fabricated media covers three categories: altered recordings that materially misdepict an individual and are not recognizable as altered, non-consensual lifelike audio or visual imitations used to convey a fictional depiction, and depictions of artificially generated persons that are not recognizable imitations of an identifiable individual. Candidate includes individuals holding elected office at federal, state, school board or local level. If a campaign communication includes fabricated media depicting a candidate, the payer must include a disclaimer stating that elements of the media have been digitally altered or artificially generated, separate from the existing disclaimer under IC 3-9-3-2.5(d). Format rules apply to printed, audio and video communications, including reading in each language used, minimum volume, and repetition at two-minute intervals for audio longer than two minutes. A candidate depicted in fabricated media in a communication lacking the required disclaimer may bring a civil action against the payer, the sponsor, and a disseminator who knowingly, intentionally or recklessly altered or removed the disclaimer. Prevailing plaintiffs may recover actual damages, injunctive relief, and court costs and attorney's fees. The plaintiff must prove by clear and convincing evidence the depiction. Courts must expedite such hearings. Section 2 declares an emergency.}},

title: Indiana HEA 1007-2025 -- Energy generation resources; large load customers and expedited generation resource plans
summary_short: Indiana statute creating a 20% state tax credit for manufacturing small modular nuclear reactors, and new procedures before the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission for energy utility generation plans and large load customer projects, plus retirement-reporting amendments. Effective dates vary by section.
summary_long: The act adds IC 6-3.1-45, a tax credit equal to 20% of a taxpayer's qualified investment in manufacturing small modular nuclear reactors in Indiana, usable against adjusted gross income, financial institutions and insurance premiums taxes, with carryover, pass-through shareholder claims and no refund. It adds IC 8-1-7.9, letting energy utilities seek expedited Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission review of expedited generation resource (EGR) plans and of projects serving large load customers, defined by new demand, a capital investment above $500,000,000 and at least 50 full-time employees. Large load projects require customer reimbursement of at least 80% of allocable project costs, pre-filing meetings, and commission orders within 90 to 150 days; the commission may approve cost recovery with a return. It amends IC 8-1-8.5-2.1 to require notice to the commission of retirements of generation facilities of at least 80 megawatts (expiring July 1, 2026), and IC 8-1-8.5-13 to add reporting on planned retirements and refuelings, staff review, and commission orders directing acquisition or prohibiting retirement. Section 1 is effective January 1, 2025 (retroactive), Section 2 upon passage, Sections 3 and 4 on July 1, 2025.
text_version: House Enrolled Act No. 1007 (2025), enrolled version HB1007.08.ENRS

title: Indiana Code 6-2.5-15 -- Data centers (gross retail and use tax exemption for qualified data centers)
summary_short: Indiana state gross retail and use tax exemption for equipment sold to qualified data centers and to quantum, advanced-computing and defense networks, conditional on a corporation-issued award certificate and agreement. Local payments apply from mid-2026; an impact study is due from 2030.
summary_long: Chapter 15 of IC 6-2.5 exempts from state gross retail tax the sale of qualified data center equipment, and of quantum computing, advanced computing and defense network equipment, to a qualified user approved by the Indiana Economic Development Corporation (IC 6-2.5-15-16). Eligibility requires a specific transaction award certificate, expiring within 25 years (50 years for larger investments), and an agreement with the corporation (IC 6-2.5-15-14, -15). Qualified data centers must create minimum investments of $150 million, $100 million or $25 million, depending on county population (IC 6-2.5-15-10); the defense network threshold is $50 million (IC 6-2.5-15-13.4). Buyers provide sellers an exemption certificate and a copy of the award (IC 6-2.5-15-17). For permits and certificates after June 30, 2026, a user in a local unit pays up to 1% of the taxes not paid on quarterly electricity billings to the county or municipal fiscal officer (IC 6-2.5-15-15.5). The corporation may request assessment of unpaid taxes, with interest and penalties, after noncompliance (IC 6-2.5-15-18). Awards survive transfer of the facility (IC 6-2.5-15-19). From 2030 and every ten years, the corporation submits an economic and fiscal impact study to the legislative council (IC 6-2.5-15-20).
text_version: Indiana Code 2026, IC 6-2.5-15 (chapter as of 2026, incl. P.L.178-2025 amendments)

title: Senate Enrolled Act 5 (2023), Indiana Consumer Data Protection Act (IC 24-15)
summary_short: Indiana's Consumer Data Protection Act (IC 24-15) gives Indiana consumers rights over their personal data and imposes duties on controllers and processors that meet consumer-count thresholds, effective 1 January 2026. The attorney general enforces it through civil penalties.
summary_long: SEA 5 (2023) adds IC 24-15, Indiana's Consumer Data Protection Act, effective 1 January 2026. It covers businesses in Indiana or targeting Indiana residents that process personal data of at least 100,000 Indiana consumers yearly, or 25,000 while earning over 50% of gross revenue from data sales, with broad exemptions for government, financial institutions, HIPAA entities, nonprofits, universities and utilities. Consumers may access, correct, delete, port and opt out of targeted advertising, data sales and certain profiling; controllers must respond within 45 days and offer appeals. Controllers must limit collection and purpose, secure data, avoid unlawful discrimination, obtain consent for sensitive data, publish privacy notices, and conduct documented data protection impact assessments for targeted advertising, sales, risky profiling and sensitive data, for activities created after 31 December 2025. Processors must assist controllers under binding contracts. The attorney general alone enforces the act, after 30 days' notice, through injunctions and civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation; there is no private right of action. It preempts local rules on personal data processing.
text_version: Senate Enrolled Act No. 5 (2023), enrolled version SB0005.05.ENRH (signature page included)

title: Kansas Policy and Procedures Memorandum 8200.00
summary_short: Sets acceptable-use rules for generative AI across Kansas executive-branch agencies and their contractors: mandatory human review of outputs, bans on certain uses and inputs, contract disclosure and data-restriction terms, and controls on AI-generated software code. Originally issued 19 May 2023 per its history note.
summary_long: Kansas Policy and Procedures Memorandum 8200.00 is the primary governing document for generative AI use by state entities (executive-branch agencies, boards and commissions under the Governor, and their agents and contractors). It covers all business uses involving the State. Its stated purpose is protecting the State's safety, privacy and intellectual property rights. Generative AI outputs must be reviewed by human operators for accuracy, appropriateness, privacy and security before use, and may not be used verbatim, assumed accurate, used as sole source, used for official statements, or solely relied on for final decisions. Restricted Use Information and inappropriate or copyrighted material may not be entered as input. Agency contracts must require contractor disclosure of generative AI use and bar contractors from using State RUI or confidential data in generative AI queries or proprietary training unless the agency head approves after consulting the Chief Information Security Officer. Generative AI-generated software code may be implemented only after business and security risks are mitigated, and must be annotated. Heads of entities must set compliance procedures. The text contains no penalty provisions.

title: Kansas SB 98 (2025) -- sales tax exemption for qualified data centers; prohibition on discounted economic development electric rates for data centers; fusion center review
summary_short: Kansas SB 98 (2025) grants a sales tax exemption to qualified data center firms meeting investment, jobs and water and power commitments, bars utilities from giving data centers economic development electric discounts, and requires fusion center board review before public financial assistance to data centers.
summary_long: The act grants a sales tax exemption to qualified data centers: Kansas buildings housing networked servers, linked by fiber, and operated by a registered qualified firm. Eligibility requires commitments to invest at least $250,000,000 in eligible data center costs by the fifth year of operations, create at least 20 new jobs within two years of operations starting, buy electricity for 10 years from the certified utility, and conserve water. The exemption covers eligible costs (excluding electricity), data center equipment and related labor, lasts 20 years after commencement of operations, and is available from July 1, 2025. After a breach notice, the secretary of commerce may allow 120 days to cure, then require repayment or terminate or suspend the exemption. Section 5 bars electric utilities from applying economic development rate discounts to new or expanded data center facilities. Section 4 requires fusion center oversight board approval before public financial assistance goes to a qualified data center project, after the Kansas intelligence fusion center evaluates its equipment and software for threats to critical infrastructure.

title: House Bill 15 (2024 RS), Kentucky Consumer Data Protection Act (KRS 367.3611 et seq.)
summary_short: Kentucky statute, added as new sections of KRS Chapter 367, giving Kentucky consumers data rights and imposing controller and processor duties on businesses meeting volume thresholds, enforced by the Attorney General. Effective January 1, 2026; impact-assessment duties apply to processing created on or after June 1, 2026.
summary_long: House Bill 15 (2024) adds Sections 1 to 10 to KRS Chapter 367 as the Kentucky Consumer Data Protection Act. Sections 1 to 10 apply to persons that conduct business in the Commonwealth or target products or services to its residents and that control or process personal data of at least 100,000 consumers in a calendar year, or 25,000 consumers while deriving over 50% of gross revenue from selling personal data. Government bodies, financial institutions under Gramm-Leach-Bliley, HIPAA covered entities and business associates, nonprofits, higher education institutions, certain utilities, and listed categories of data are exempt. Consumers may request access, correction, deletion, portability, and opt-out of targeted advertising, data sales, and profiling in furtherance of decisions with legal or similarly significant effects; controllers must respond within 45 days, extendable once by 45 days. Controllers must limit collection, maintain security, avoid unlawful discrimination, obtain consent for sensitive data, publish privacy notices, disclose sales and targeted advertising, and offer request mechanisms. Processors must follow contract terms on confidentiality, deletion, information and assessments. Controllers must conduct and document data protection impact assessments for targeted advertising, data sales, certain profiling, sensitive data and heightened-risk processing, which the Attorney General may request. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority, must give 30 days' written notice with a cure opportunity, may seek damages up to $7,500 per continued violation, and no private right of action is created. Civil penalties go to a consumer privacy fund administered by the Attorney General. The Act takes effect January 1, 2026.

title: Kentucky HB 775 (2025 Regular Session) -- expansion of qualified data center sales and use tax exemption
summary_short: Amends the definitions in KRS 154.20-220 for a Kentucky economic-development incentive for qualified data center projects, covering eligible companies, data center equipment, minimum capital investment, and memorandum-of-agreement terms of up to 50 years. Sections 19-24, 26, 35-37 take effect 1 July 2025.
summary_long: Partial text: Section 34 (definitions in KRS 154.20-220 to 154.20-229) and the Section 40 effective-date clause; Sections 1-33 and 35-39 are omitted. The Kentucky Economic Development Finance Authority enters memoranda of agreement with eligible companies (preliminary approval) and verifies that the minimum capital investment is made by the fifth anniversary (final approval). Eligible companies include owners, operators, colocation tenants and project organizers. Eligible costs cover purchases of data center equipment (servers, networking, power and cooling equipment, software), excluding electricity and construction equipment. Minimum capital investment is $450 million, $100 million or $25 million for owners, operators or colocation tenants, by county population, and $150 million for project organizers. Excluded projects include those accepting other KRS Chapter 154 incentives, replacing existing Commonwealth data centers, or benefiting from the electricity sales and use tax exemption for cryptocurrency mining. Agreement terms run 15 years (project organizers), 50 years (investment of at least $450 million) or 25 years (others). Sections 19-24, 26 and 35-37 take effect 1 July 2025. The excerpt does not show the exemption's operative tax rule or rate.

title: Kentucky HB 8 (2024 Regular Session) -- sales and use tax exemption for qualified data center equipment (KRS Chapter 139)
summary_short: Kentucky HB 8 (2024) Sections 37-42 create a Kentucky Economic Development Finance Authority approval process for qualified data center projects and exempt approved companies' data center equipment from sales and use tax under agreements of 15 to 50 years. Approved companies must report annually from September 1, 2025.
summary_long: Kentucky HB 8 (2024 RS) is a fiscal act; this copy contains Sections 37-42 and effective-date provisions (Sections 63-68), and omits Sections 1-36 and 43-62. Sections 37-41 create a data center incentive program in KRS Chapter 154, run by the Kentucky Economic Development Finance Authority: eligible companies sign a memorandum of agreement, receive preliminary approval, then final approval once minimum capital investment is made. Qualifying projects need at least $450,000,000 of investment ($150,000,000 for a project organizer), sit in a consolidated local government of at least 500,000 residents, and may not replace existing Kentucky data centers except in listed cases. Section 42 (KRS Chapter 139) exempts approved companies' data center equipment from sales and use tax, excluding electricity. Agreement terms run 15 to 50 years. If investment falls short by the fifth anniversary, the exemption is revoked and tax is assessed. Approved companies report annually from September 1, 2025. The copy does not state the start date of Sections 37-42.

title: Louisiana Senate Bill 6
summary_short: Creates the Louisiana crime (R.S. 14:73.14) of disseminating or selling AI-created nude or sexually explicit images of another person without authorization, with intent to coerce, harass, intimidate or maliciously disseminate. Sets penalties and exempts certain internet and telecommunications intermediaries.
summary_long: Enacts R.S. 14:73.14 (Section 1) creating the crime of unlawful dissemination or sale of images of another created by artificial intelligence. Subsection A makes it unlawful for any person, with intent to coerce, harass, intimidate, or maliciously disseminate or sell, an AI-created video or still image depicting another person totally nude or in a state of undress exposing genitals, pubic area, buttocks, or female breast, where the person knows or has reason to know they are not licensed or authorized to do so. Subsection C defines another person (including a recognizable depiction of an actual person), artificial intelligence, electronic mail service provider and interactive computer service. Subsection B excludes listed interactive computer, email, telecommunications and information service providers and access software providers whose multi-user computer service was used by a person to commit a prohibited act. Subsection D sets the penalty: imprisonment for not more than six months, a fine of not more than seven hundred fifty dollars, or both. Subsection E allows prosecution in the parish where the act occurred or where the image was created, produced, reproduced, found, stored, received or possessed. Subsection F states that the section does not preclude civil actions or prosecutions under other law. The text contains no effective date provision.

title: An Act preventing a dystopian work environment.
summary_short: Bill adding Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 149B: employers and their vendors must give notice of worker data collection, electronic monitoring and automated decision systems, limit their use, and complete impact assessments. Enforced by the Attorney General and worker civil actions. Effective date not stated.
summary_long: Bill that would insert a new Chapter 149B into the General Laws, covering employers and their vendors for workplaces in Massachusetts, and state workers as specified in section 6. It defines worker data, electronic monitoring and automated decision systems (ADS). Employers must give workers notice of worker data collection, electronic monitoring and ADS use, and send notices to the Department of Labor & Workforce Development. Data collection is limited to listed purposes and the least invasive means; sale or licensing of worker data is barred. Electronic monitoring is restricted, including facial, gait and emotion recognition, monitoring of off-duty workers and private areas, and monitoring that prevents rest breaks or exercise of legal rights. ADS may not be solely relied on for hiring, promotion, termination, discipline or wages, and certain ADS uses are prohibited. Employers must complete independent impact assessments before using ADS or worker information systems, submit them to the Department, and publish summaries; the Department may require changes or bar use. Employers are jointly and severally liable for vendors. Workers and the Attorney General may sue for injunctive relief and civil penalties set in section 6(c). Department regulations are due by January 1, 2025. Effective date not stated.

title: Massachusetts Amendment S.3178
summary_short: Section 3A of this Massachusetts bill appropriates grant and capital funds through the Executive Office of Economic Development, including $75,000,000 for artificial intelligence development grants, with funds available until June 30, 2036.
summary_long: Section 3A of this bill makes listed sums available for the Executive Office of Economic Development, until June 30, 2036, for economic development, community development, local government support, innovation and job creation, subject to laws regulating public fund disbursement and in addition to prior authorizations. Listed items include: $20,000,000 for matching grants, via the Massachusetts Development Finance Agency's growth capital division, to certified community development financial institutions and community development corporations for small-business loans, prioritizing disadvantaged businesses; $25,000,000 for capital grants to private businesses constructing or expanding facilities, including decarbonization and climate-resilience features; $75,000,000 for grants supporting artificial intelligence development and application in strategic sectors, to public, non-profit and private entities; $100,000,000 for defense-sector investment including artificial intelligence and cybersecurity; $25,000,000 for robotics research and development grants to non-profit, university and private entities; and smaller items for food science, arts and culture, downtown revitalization, early-stage business sites and local grants. Several items require geographic equity.

title: Massachusetts Bill H.64
summary_short: Bill H.64 would create a commission within the executive office of technology services and security to study Massachusetts government use of automated decision systems, survey those uses, and report annually with recommendations to the governor and legislature.
summary_long: Bill H.64 would insert a new Section 11 into Chapter 7D of the General Laws. It defines algorithm, artificial intelligence, automated decision system, Commonwealth or Massachusetts office, identified group characteristic, source code and training data. It creates a commission within the executive office of technology services and security to study and recommend regulations, limits, standards and safeguards for the use by the Commonwealth of automated decision systems that may affect human welfare. The commission's membership includes the secretary of technology services and security as chair, legislators, the attorney general, the state auditor, the inspector general, academic and advocacy representatives, and industry representatives. Members are to be appointed within 45 days of the effective date of the act. The commission must meet at least 10 times per calendar year, hold at least one public hearing, and broadcast its meetings over the internet. Its tasks include a survey of all Massachusetts office uses of automated decision systems, examination of transparency, auditability, data, intellectual property and due process issues, and a review of research on disparate outcomes. It must submit an annual report by December 31 that includes a public list of automated decision systems in use, policies and training, and contracts with third parties, together with recommendations such as areas where offices should not use such systems and procedures for explanations and for detecting disparate impacts. The bill sets no penalties and does not regulate private actors.

title: Maryland House Bill 1128
summary_short: Establishes a Talent Innovation Program in the Maryland Department of Labor to fund job training in priority sectors, including artificial intelligence, and creates the Talent Innovation Fund as a nonlapsing special fund. Takes effect July 1, 2024.
summary_long: Adds Subtitle 16 (§§ 11–1601 to 11–1604) to the Labor and Employment Article, establishing a Talent Innovation Program in the Maryland Department of Labor to increase access to high-quality job training in priority sectors including cybersecurity, health care, biotechnology, manufacturing and artificial intelligence. The Division of Workforce Development and Adult Learning and the Governor's Workforce Development Board jointly administer the program, which may conduct pilots, convene stakeholders and conduct research, and must establish an initial cybersecurity pilot expanding regional cyber ranges. It creates the Talent Innovation Fund, a special nonlapsing fund held by the Treasurer and funded by state budget appropriations, grants, donations, interest earnings and other accepted money. The Department may use the fund for grants to listed entities and state residents, matching funds, program financing and administrative costs, and expenditures are made only in accordance with the state budget. Interest earnings are credited to the fund. The Department may adopt regulations and must report annually on or before January 1, beginning in 2025. The act amends State Finance and Procurement § 6–226(a)(2) so that the Talent Innovation Fund is excluded from the rule directing net interest on special funds to the General Fund. The act takes effect July 1, 2024. The text sets out no penalties.

title: Maryland House Bill 622
summary_short: Creates an Industry 4.0 Technology Grant Program in Maryland's Department of Commerce, awarding competitive grants of $25,000 to $500,000 to small and medium-sized manufacturers for Industry 4.0 technology, including AI, and related infrastructure, effective October 1, 2023.
summary_long: The Act adds Subtitle 23 to the Economic Development Article, creating an Industry 4.0 Technology Grant Program in the Department of Commerce for small and medium-sized manufacturers (SME manufacturers). Industry 4.0 technology includes smart manufacturing hardware and software, such as sensor integration, robotics, ERP and analytics software, cloud and cybersecurity solutions, and artificial intelligence for efficiency gains. The Department may delegate administration to a state-chartered corporation. Applicants must be qualifying SME manufacturers with Maryland operations and in existence for over one year. Grants are awarded competitively, range from $25,000 to $500,000, require sliding-scale matching funds tied to employee numbers, and at least 20% of each fiscal year's funds are reserved for firms with 50 or fewer employees. Recipients must report on grant use within one year, and the Department may require return of grants for non-compliance. A special, nonlapsing Industry 4.0 Technology Grant Fund, used only for grants, is created; the Governor must include appropriations for fiscal years 2024 through 2028, and the text gives two amounts, $10,000,000 and $1,000,000, without indicating which applies. The Secretary adopts implementing regulations. The Act takes effect October 1, 2023.

title: Maryland HB 952 (Consumer Protection – Companion Chatbots – Regulation) 2026
summary_short: Maryland bill requiring operators of companion chatbots to adopt and publish self-harm and minor-content protocols, display AI warnings, limit personal data use, and run complaint systems. Violations would be unfair trade practices under the Consumer Protection Act. Effective October 1, 2026.
summary_long: HB 952 adds Commercial Law § 14–1330 and makes violations of it unfair, abusive or deceptive trade practices under Title 13, except § 13–411. It covers operators, meaning persons who make a companion chatbot available to a user in the State, and developers. Operators must establish, maintain and publish protocols against self-harm and suicide content for users expressing such thoughts, with crisis referrals, and against sexually explicit content for minor users. Operators must display a warning that chatbots are artificially generated and not human; developers must provide static and hourly dynamic on-screen warnings.
