Controllers must limit personal data collection to what is reasonably necessary, may not use emotional or mental health vulnerability data to increase use, and must run a complaint system with review and removal within 3 calendar days. Operators report annually to the Office of Suicide Prevention from March 1, 2027; the Office publishes compiled data by July 1 each year. A chatbot is treated as a product for product liability actions, and operators or developers may be held strictly liable. The Act takes effect October 1, 2026.

title: Maryland Online Data Privacy Act of 2024 (SB 541/HB 567, Chapter 455)
summary_short: Maryland statute creating consumer personal-data rights and duties for controllers and processors, including notice, consent for sensitive data, opt-outs, processor contracts and data protection assessments, enforced as unfair trade practices. Applies to businesses above volume thresholds; assessment duties apply from 1 October 2025.
summary_long: Maryland's Online Data Privacy Act adds Commercial Law Subtitle 46 (§§ 14-4601 to 14-4614). It covers businesses that conduct business in Maryland or target products or services to residents and that, in the preceding calendar year, processed data of at least 35,000 consumers, or of 10,000 consumers while deriving over 20% of gross revenue from data sales. Controllers must obtain consent for sensitive data, publish privacy notices, honor consumer rights requests within 45 days, and recognize opt-out preference signals. Targeted advertising and sales without consent involving known minors aged 13 to 17 are restricted. Processors must sign binding contracts. Controllers must conduct and document data protection assessments for heightened-risk processing, including each algorithm used. Sale of consumer health data without consent and geofencing near mental or reproductive health facilities are prohibited. Violations are unfair, abusive or deceptive trade practices under Commercial Law Title 13; the Division may issue a notice allowing at least 60 days to cure for violations on or before April 1, 2027. The effective-date clause in Section 4 is marked with both 2024 and 2025. Assessment duties apply to processing from October 1, 2025.

title: Michigan House Bill 4668 (Artificial Intelligence Safety and Security Transparency Act)
summary_short: A bill that would require large developers of foundation models to publish and follow safety and security protocols for critical risks, publish transparency reports, undergo annual third-party audits, and protect employees who report risks, from January 1, 2026, with attorney general civil enforcement.
summary_long: Introduced June 24, 2025 and referred to the Judiciary Committee, the bill would require 'large developers' of foundation models to produce, publish and follow safety and security protocols for critical risks from January 1, 2026. A large developer has developed a foundation model with computing power costing at least $5,000,000 and, within the preceding 12 months, models costing at least $100,000,000 in computing power. Critical risks include death or serious injury to more than 100 people, or over $1,000,000,000 in damages, from incidents such as weapons of mass destruction or cyberattacks. Developers must publish transparency reports at least every 90 days, keep test records for 5 years, and undergo an annual third-party audit published within 90 days. Employees who report critical risks are protected from retaliation. The attorney general may seek fines of up to $1,000,000 per violation of the publication or audit sections, plus injunctive relief; employees may sue for retaliation.

title: Public Act 263 of 2023 (Enrolled House Bill 5141), AI disclosure in political advertisements (Michigan Campaign Finance Act amendments)
summary_short: Amends Michigan Campaign Finance Act section 47 and adds section 59, requiring that political advertisements and prerecorded telephone messages generated in whole or substantially by artificial intelligence carry a disclosure statement. Covers Michigan candidates, elections and ballot questions; violations carry civil fines or misdemeanor penalties.
summary_long: Amends section 47 of the Michigan Campaign Finance Act and adds section 59. Section 59 requires a person, committee or other entity that creates, originally publishes or originally distributes a qualified political advertisement (a paid advertisement relating to a federal, state or local candidate or election in Michigan, or a ballot question, containing AI-generated image, audio or video) to state that it was generated in whole or substantially by artificial intelligence, with minimum size, duration and language rules for graphic, audio and video formats. A first violation is a state civil infraction with a fine of up to $250; later violations carry up to $1,000 each, and each distribution is a separate violation. Exemptions cover bona fide news coverage, paid broadcasts, satire or parody, businesses regulated by the Michigan Public Service Commission or the FCC, and distribution platforms with a written disclosure policy; platforms are not liable for missing disclosures if they gave notice of their prohibitions. Section 47 requires AI-generated prerecorded telephone messages advocating for or against a candidate or ballot question to carry a specified statement. Knowing violations of section 47 are misdemeanors punishable by a fine of up to $1,000, imprisonment for up to 93 days, or both. The amendments do not take effect unless House Bill 5143 of the 102nd Legislature is enacted into law.

title: Michigan House Bill 5144 of 2023 (Election Law)
summary_short: Adds section 932f to Michigan's Election Law. Bars any person from distributing AI-produced media that falsely depicts an individual within 90 days before an election, with intent to harm a candidate or deceive electors, unless a disclaimer is included. Sets misdemeanor and felony penalties and allows injunctive relief.
summary_long: Adds section 932f to the Michigan Election Law (1954 PA 116). Prohibits knowingly distributing, or agreeing to distribute, AI-produced image, audio or video that falsely depicts an individual, within 90 days before an election, when intended to harm a candidate or deceive electors and reasonably likely to do so. A disclaimer stating that the media was manipulated by technical means, with placement and size rules by media type, takes the media outside the prohibition; edited media must cite the original source. A first violation is a misdemeanor (up to 90 days' imprisonment or a $500 fine, or both); a violation within five years of a previous conviction is a felony (up to 5 years or a $1,000 fine, or both). The attorney general, depicted individuals, injured candidates and organizations representing likely-deceived voters may seek permanent injunctive relief in specified circuit courts. The plaintiff must prove knowledge by clear and convincing evidence, frivolous complaints are dismissed, and preliminary injunctions are barred. The act takes effect only if House Bill 5143 of the 102nd Legislature is enacted.

title: Michigan Public Acts 207 and 181 of 2024 (HB 4906 / SB 237) -- General Sales Tax Act and Use Tax Act exemptions for qualified data center equipment
summary_short: Exempts sales and use of data center equipment to qualified and enterprise data centers in Michigan from 2016 through 2050 (2065 for some sites), subject to job, investment, energy, water and certification conditions; amends 1933 PA 167 and 1937 PA 94.
summary_long: Public Acts 207 and 208 of 2024 amend the tax exemptions for data center equipment (1933 PA 167, Sec. 4ee; 1937 PA 94, Sec. 4cc). Qualified data center exemptions run from January 1, 2016 through December 31, 2050, continuing after 2022 and 2026 only if certified job counts of 400 and 1,000 are met. Enterprise data center exemptions, granted by Michigan strategic fund certificate, run to 2050 or 2065 for certain brownfield or former power-plant sites. Certificate criteria include at least $250,000,000 capital investment, 30 qualified new jobs at 150% or more of the prosperity region median wage, municipal water, green building certification, and clean energy procurement equal to 90% of forecasted electricity use. Electric rate limits, a bar on property tax benefits absent local approval, annual reporting, revocation with repayment, and a December 31, 2029 cutoff for new certificates also apply. Act 207 takes effect April 17, 2025.

title: Laws of Minnesota 2025, 1st Special Session, Chapter 12 (HF 16) -- data center regulation: permitting, water appropriation, energy, annual fee, sales tax changes
summary_short: Minnesota session law (2025 1st Special Session, ch. 12) regulating data centers: permitting coordination, water-appropriation conditions for large data centers, utility tariffs and energy-standard treatment, an annual fee on qualified large-scale data centers, and sales tax exemption changes. Most sections take effect the day following final enactment.
summary_long: Chapter 12 (HF 16) of the Laws of Minnesota 2025, 1st Special Session, regulates data centers. Sections 1, 2, 5 and 6 state that data-center permitting inquiries are referred to the Minnesota Business First Stop Program and direct agency permitting staff to be made aware of this policy. Sections 3-4 set water-appropriation rules for data centers with consumptive use above 100,000,000 gallons per year, covering preapplication information requests, evaluation of water availability, permit conditions on public health and water conservation, and possible aquifer tests. Section 7 defines a data center as a facility designed to have a load of 100 megawatts or more. Sections 9-10 require the commission to define a very large customer class by December 15, 2026, allow it to approve or reject tariffs for such customers, and require utilities to offer a clean energy and capacity tariff. Sections 11-15 exclude qualified large-scale data centers from solar-standard calculations and energy-conservation contributions, and direct fee revenue to the energy and conservation account. Section 16 imposes an annual fee on qualified large-scale data centers by peak demand, in four tiers from $2,000,000 to $5,000,000. Section 17 extends sales and use tax exemptions to qualified large-scale data centers (at least $250,000,000 invested within 60 months after June 30, 2025), conditioned on prevailing wages and green-building certification within three years of service, with repayment if certification is not met. Most sections take effect the day following final enactment; the sales tax changes apply to purchases made after June 30, 2025.

title: Minnesota Statutes § 297A.68, subd. 42 -- Qualified data center and qualified refurbished data center equipment exemption
summary_short: Exempts from Minnesota sales and use tax purchases of enterprise IT equipment and computer software by qualified data centers, qualified refurbished data centers and qualified large-scale data centers that meet square-footage and investment thresholds. Refunds follow certification by the Commissioner of Employment and Economic Development.
summary_long: Subdivision 42 of Minnesota Statutes section 297A.68 exempts from the taxes of Chapter 297A purchases of enterprise information technology equipment and computer software for use in a qualified data center, a qualified refurbished data center or a qualified large-scale data center (para. a). A qualified data center is a Minnesota facility of at least 25,000 square feet with total construction or refurbishment, equipment and software costs of at least $30,000,000 within a 48-month period, and with specified power, fire suppression and security features (para. b). A qualified refurbished data center requires $50,000,000 within a 24-month period (para. c). A qualified large-scale data center requires at least 25,000 square feet connected by fiber and $250,000,000 collectively within a 60-month period beginning after June 30, 2025 (para. e). The exempt tax is collected and then refunded, and no refund issues until the Commissioner of Employment and Economic Development certifies the facility (paras. h, i). Exemption claims are limited to purchases within 35 years of the first qualifying purchase (para. f). Construction work on qualified large-scale data centers must pay prevailing wages and follow specified enforcement provisions (para. k). Those centers must certify a sustainable design or green building standard within three years after being placed in service, and the exemption must be repaid if the Commissioner of Commerce determines non-compliance (paras. l, m).

title: Minn. Stat. 609.771, Use of deep fake technology to influence an election (Laws 2023, ch. 58, HF 1370; amended 2024)
summary_short: Makes it a crime to disseminate a deep fake, or agree to disseminate one, knowing or recklessly disregarding that it is one, without the depicted individual's consent, to injure a candidate or influence an election, within 90 days before a party nominating convention or after absentee voting starts before specified primaries and elections. Enacted 2023 (Laws 2023, c 58, s 2); amended 2024.
summary_long: Subd. 2 criminalizes disseminating a deep fake, or entering a contract or agreement to do so, knowing or recklessly disregarding that it is one, without the depicted individual's consent, with intent to injure a candidate or influence an election, and within the periods stated in Subd. 2(a)(3). A deep fake is a realistic recording or representation, substantially dependent on technical means, of speech or conduct the depicted individual did not engage in. Penalties under Subd. 3(a): up to five years and/or $10,000 for violations within five years of prior convictions; up to 364 days and/or $3,000 with intent to cause violence or bodily harm; otherwise up to 90 days and/or $1,000. A convicted candidate for state or local office forfeits the nomination or office by supplemental judgment, and convicted individuals are disqualified from appointment to office (Subd. 3(b)-(c)). Subd. 2(b) exempts a broadcaster or cable system disseminating a candidate's deep fake where federal law requires it. Subd. 4 allows injunctive or equitable relief against persons reasonably believed about to violate the section, sought by the attorney general, a county or city attorney, the depicted individual, or an injured candidate.

The dissemination must also fall within stated periods: within 90 days before an election, within 90 days before a political party nominating convention, or after the start of the absentee voting period before a presidential nomination primary or a regular or special state or local primary or general election. title: Minnesota HF 1370 (Deepfake Accountability and Public Safety)
summary_short: Minnesota HF 1370 (2023) creates a civil cause of action and two crimes concerning deep fakes: nonconsensual dissemination of sexual deep fakes (Secs. 1 and 3) and dissemination of deep fakes to influence elections within 90 days before an election (Sec. 2), effective August 1, 2023.
summary_long: HF 1370 adds three sections to Minnesota Statutes. Section 1 (Minn. Stat. 604.32) creates a civil cause of action against a person who disseminates a deep fake depicting intimate parts or sexual acts knowing the depicted individual did not consent to public dissemination. A court may award general and special damages, an amount equal to profits, a civil penalty up to $100,000 to the plaintiff, and fees, and may issue injunctions and a civil fine up to $1,000 per day for violating a court order; listed exceptions apply. Section 2 (Minn. Stat. 609.771) makes it a crime to disseminate a deep fake within 90 days before an election without consent, with intent to injure a candidate or influence the result. Penalties are up to five years or a $10,000 fine for repeat violations, up to one year or $3,000 with intent to cause violence or bodily harm, and up to 90 days or $1,000 otherwise. Section 3 (Minn. Stat. 617.262) makes nonconsensual dissemination of a sexual deep fake a gross misdemeanor, or punishable by up to three years' imprisonment or a $5,000 fine where a listed factor is present, with exemptions and immunity for interactive computer services and telecommunications providers solely for third-party content. Effective August 1, 2023.

title: Minnesota HF 4452 (Chatbot Prohibitions, Liability 2026)
summary_short: Proposed Minnesota bill HF 4452 would add Minn. Stat. 604.115 on AI chatbots. Proprietors must give AI notice to Minnesota users, may not let chatbots give licensed mental health, medical or legal advice, and must take self-harm and minor-protection steps for companion chatbots, with civil liability. Effective August 1, 2026.
summary_long: Proposed Minnesota bill (introduced; HF 4452) adding Minn. Stat. 604.115 on chatbots. It applies to proprietors, meaning persons that own, operate or deploy a chatbot used to interact with users, with respect to users located in Minnesota. Proprietors must give clear, conspicuous and explicit notice that users are interacting with an AI chatbot, in the chatbot's language and a readable size. A proprietor may not permit a chatbot to give substantive responses, information, advice or actions that would require a professional license for mental health or medical care (chapters 147 and 148E) or for legal advice (section 481.02). Violations give users a civil action for general and special damages, with fees if willful; liability cannot be waived by notice. For companion chatbots, meaning chatbots designed to simulate an interpersonal relationship as their primary function, proprietors must make a good-faith effort to prevent promotion of self-harm and to identify covered users expressing self-harm thoughts. On such determinations they must prohibit continued use for at least 72 hours and display suicide crisis contact information. They must also make a good-faith effort to determine whether a user is a minor, with strict liability for minor self-harm resulting from non-compliance. Effective August 1, 2026, for actions taken on or after that date.

title: Minnesota Consumer Data Privacy Act (Laws 2024, ch. 121, art. 5; Minn. Stat. ch. 325O)
summary_short: Minnesota's Consumer Data Privacy Act (Minn. Stat. ch. 325O) gives Minnesota consumers rights over personal data and imposes controller and processor duties on entities that do business in Minnesota or target Minnesota residents above specified consumer-count or revenue thresholds. Effective July 31, 2025, with a later date for certain postsecondary institutions.
summary_long: The Act gives Minnesota consumers rights to access, correct, delete and port personal data, and to opt out of targeted advertising, sale and certain profiling, including through opt-out preference signals. Consumers may appeal refusals. Controllers must provide a privacy notice, limit collection and retention, secure personal data, and obtain consent before processing sensitive data, and before targeted advertising or sale for consumers aged 13 to 16. Consent obtained through dark patterns is invalid. Controllers may not discriminate against consumers for exercising rights, though loyalty programs are excepted. Controllers must conduct and document data privacy and protection assessments for targeted advertising, sales, sensitive data and risky profiling. Processors must follow written contracts. The Act applies to entities doing business in Minnesota or targeting residents that meet consumer-count or revenue thresholds, and excludes government entities, Indian tribes, and many health, financial and credit-reporting regimes. Small businesses may not sell sensitive data without prior consent. The Attorney General enforces the Act after a 30-day warning letter (a cure provision expiring January 31, 2026), with civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation. The Act creates no private right of action and preempts local laws on processing personal data. It is effective July 31, 2025, and postsecondary institutions regulated by the Office of Higher Education have until July 31, 2029.

title: Minnesota SF 1857 (Minor Access to Chatbots 2025)
summary_short: Minnesota bill SF 1857 (2025, introduced) would make it unlawful for operators of websites, applications or programs to let minors access chatbots for recreational purposes, require age proof, and allow individual damages suits and attorney general civil penalties.
summary_long: Minnesota SF 1857 (Section 1, Minn. Stat. § 325M.40 as proposed) defines a chatbot as a computer program designed to simulate conversation with human users and a minor as an individual under 18. Subdivision 2 makes it unlawful for a person who owns or controls a website, application, software or program to allow a minor to access chatbots for recreational purposes. Subdivision 3 requires a person offering chatbot services for recreational purposes to require proof of age before allowing access. Subdivision 4 allows an individual injured by a violation to bring a civil action for damages, statutory damages not to exceed $1,000, injunctive relief, and costs and reasonable attorney fees. The attorney general may enforce the section under section 8.31, and a violating person is liable for a civil penalty not to exceed $5,000,000. The text states no effective date. The instrument is at the introduced stage.

title: Mississippi Senate Bill 2577
summary_short: Makes it a crime to knowingly disseminate a non-consensual deepfake ('digitization') of a person within 90 days of an election, intending to injure a candidate, influence results or deter voting. Penalties up to 1 year or $5,000, or up to 5 years or $10,000. Effective July 1, 2024.
summary_long: The act adds a section to Title 97, Chapter 13 of the Mississippi Code. Section 1(1) defines 'candidate', 'digitization' (altered or computer-generated images or audio, including those made with software or machine learning artificial intelligence, that a reasonable person would believe depict conduct the depicted individual did not engage in), 'depicted individual' and 'disseminates'. Section 1(2) makes it a crime to disseminate, or contract to disseminate, a digitization with knowledge that it is one, if it is disseminated within 90 days of an election, without the depicted individual's consent, and with intent to injure a candidate, influence the results of an election or deter voting. Section 1(3) sets penalties: up to 5 years or a fine up to $10,000, or both, where there is intent to incite violence, cause bodily harm or deter voting, or a prior conviction within 5 years; otherwise up to 1 year or a fine up to $5,000, or both. Section 1(4) allows injunctive relief against a person reasonably believed to be about to violate or violating the section, sought by the Attorney General, a district attorney, the depicted individual, an injured candidate, or an injured political party whose nominee is on the ballot; the court may order removal of disseminated digitizations. Section 1(5) makes clear and prominent on-screen disclaimers that the depicted individual did not engage in the depicted conduct a defense to prosecution. Section 1(6) excludes interactive computer and information service providers, broadcasters in bona fide news coverage or paid broadcasts, certain news publishers that clearly state content does not accurately represent a ballot issue or candidate, satire or parody, and security, fraud or investigative uses. Section 2 sets the effective date as July 1, 2024.

title: Montana Consumer Data Privacy Act (SB 384, 2023), MCA 30-14-2801 et seq.
summary_short: Governs controllers and processors above consumer-count thresholds. Grants Montana residents rights to access, correct, delete, port and opt out of personal data processing, and imposes notice, security, assessment and minor-protection duties. The attorney general enforces it through civil penalties.
summary_long: Applies to persons doing business in Montana or targeting its residents that control or process personal data of at least 25,000 consumers, or 15,000 consumers while deriving over 25% of gross revenue from selling personal data. Consumers may access, correct, delete and port personal data and opt out of targeted advertising, sales and certain profiling; controllers must respond within 45 days, extendable by 45, and offer an appeal. Controllers must limit collection, secure data, obtain consent for sensitive data, avoid discrimination for exercising rights and publish a privacy notice; processors act under contract terms. Data protection assessments are required for heightened-risk processing of activities created after January 1, 2025. Controllers offering online services to known minors must use reasonable care, obtain consent before targeted advertising, sale or certain profiling of minors, and assess heightened risks to minors from October 1, 2025. Exemptions include state and local government bodies, certain banks, insurers and HIPAA covered entities, and institutions of higher education. The attorney general has exclusive enforcement authority and may seek civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation; the Act creates no private right of action.

title: National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020 (Division E of the William M. (Mac) Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021, Pub. L. 116-283)
summary_short: Establishes a federal National Artificial Intelligence Initiative with coordinating offices, committees, a NIST standards mandate, research institutes and agency R&D programs. Its duties fall mainly on federal agencies and grant recipients; the NIST risk management framework is voluntary.
summary_long: Division E of the FY2021 National Defense Authorization Act (Pub. L. 116-283) establishes a National Artificial Intelligence Initiative, defines artificial intelligence and machine learning, and directs federal agencies to coordinate AI research, development, education and workforce activities. It creates a National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Office under the Office of Science and Technology Policy, an Interagency Committee to prepare a strategic plan within two years, and a National Artificial Intelligence Advisory Committee under the Secretary of Commerce. It establishes a workforce study by the National Academies, a National AI Research Resource Task Force, and an NSF-led program of financial assistance for AI research institutes limited to US-based awardees. Section 22A of the NIST Act directs NIST to develop a voluntary risk management framework within two years, support standards, and issue dataset documentation and data-sharing guidance. It also sets up a NOAA AI Center, NSF research and education grants with an ethics-statement report, and a DOE AI research program, with authorized appropriations for each. The Initiative terminates ten years after enactment; the text contains no penalties or private-sector mandates.

title: North Carolina House Bill 591
summary_short: North Carolina HB 591 (2024) creates sexual extortion offenses under G.S. 14-202.7: a Class F felony for adults and, for minors, a Class 1 misdemeanor (first offense) or Class F felony (repeat). Aggravated sexual extortion against a minor or a person with a disability by an adult is a Class E felony. The act extends the material and image definitions to algorithm- or AI-created or altered depictions of identifiable individuals and adds identifiable-minor material to sexual exploitation offenses. It adds G.S. 14-190.17C, extends registrant premises restrictions, requires entities receiving certain reports to forward them to the Cyber Tip Line, and gives private-image disclosure victims a civil action with liquidated damages of $1,000 per day or $10,000 plus punitive damages and fees. Effective 1 December 2024 for offenses committed on or after that date.
summary_long: HB 591 (2024) creates sexual extortion offenses under G.S. 14-202.7: a Class F felony for adults and, for minors, a Class 1 misdemeanor (first offense) or Class F felony (repeat). Aggravated sexual extortion against a minor or a person with a disability by an adult is a Class E felony. title: N.D.C.C. § 57-39.2-04.17 -- Sales and use tax exemption for enterprise information technology equipment and computer software used in a qualified data center
summary_short: North Dakota sales and use tax exemption for enterprise information technology equipment and computer software bought for use in a certified qualified data center. Covers owners, operators and tenants, with a certification step and annual reporting to the tax commissioner.
summary_long: Exempts from North Dakota sales and use tax the gross receipts from sales of enterprise information technology equipment and computer software purchased for use by a qualifying business in a qualified data center, including upgraded or replacement equipment. A future owner must apply to the tax commissioner for certification and answer information requests within thirty days. The exemption requires a commissioner certificate at purchase; otherwise the business pays the tax and applies for a refund, and contractor-installed purchases may be refunded. A qualified data center is a newly constructed or substantially refurbished facility of at least 15,000 square feet, at least half used for data processing, on one or contiguous parcels, with construction completed after December 31, 2020, sophisticated fire suppression, enhanced security features, and commissioner certification. Owners must give collocated operators or tenants documentation of certification. By January 31 each year the owner files a report of the exemption claimed, jobs created or retained, and local incentives. The commissioner may disclose these report details to legislative management chairs on written request, excluding the owner's name and identifiers. Heading notes retroactive application.

title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, Pub. L. 119-60 (incl. Title LXXXV, Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act of 2025)
summary_short: Selected FY2026 NDAA sections on defense AI: DoD AI institutes, AI cybersecurity and procurement security rules, bans on DeepSeek and certain Chinese-linked AI for DoD and contractors, outbound investment controls covering AI, and AI governance bodies. Most dates run from enactment or fixed deadlines.
summary_long: Selected sections of the FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act govern artificial intelligence in defense and national security. The Secretary of Defense may fund National Security and Defense AI Institutes at eligible U.S. host institutions (Sec. 224). Sections 1512 and 1513 require a Department-wide AI cybersecurity policy and a risk-based security framework for covered AI systems, with contract requirements to implement it. Sections 1533 and 1535 create an AI model assessment team and an AI Futures Steering Committee. Section 1532 requires removal of covered AI, including DeepSeek and High Flyer products, from Department systems and bars contractors from using it in contract performance, subject to waivers. Section 8521 adds Title VIII to the Defense Production Act: the Treasury Secretary may prohibit U.S. person investments in covered national security transactions in prohibited technologies, including AI systems; regulations are to require notification of certain transactions, and civil penalties apply. Other sections set up sandboxes and pilots and require reports to Congress. Deadlines are mostly keyed to enactment or fixed calendar dates.

title: Legislative Bill 1074 (108th Legislature), Nebraska Data Privacy Act
summary_short: LB1074, approved April 17, 2024, enacts the Nebraska Data Privacy Act, giving Nebraska consumers rights over personal data and imposing controller and processor duties on non-small businesses, enforced by the Attorney General through civil penalties.
summary_long: LB1074, approved April 17, 2024, adopts the Nebraska Data Privacy Act (Secs. 1–30) and conforming changes to other banking and finance statutes. It applies to persons doing business in Nebraska or serving its residents that process or sell personal data and are not small businesses; state agencies, financial institutions, HIPAA covered entities, nonprofits, higher education and certain utilities are excluded. Consumers may access, correct, delete and port personal data and opt out of targeted advertising, sales and certain profiling. Controllers must respond within 45 days, give privacy notices, limit collection, secure data, obtain consent for sensitive data, conduct data protection assessments for defined high-risk processing, and avoid discrimination against consumers exercising rights; processors act under contract. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority, must give 30 days' notice and an opportunity to cure, and may seek civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation. No private right of action is created; local ordinances on personal data processing are preempted.

title: Nebraska L 1284 (Teacher Incentive Programs)
summary_short: Creates a Dyslexia Research Grant Program run by the State Department of Education, awarding grants to Nebraska-based private businesses researching AI-based writing assistance for individuals with dyslexia, capped at $500,000 in total. Grant money must be used only for that research; misuse leads to Attorney General civil recovery.
summary_long: Section 2 of the Nebraska act creates a Dyslexia Research Grant Program administered by the State Department of Education. Eligible applicants are privately owned businesses based in Nebraska that are researching AI-based writing assistance for individuals with dyslexia (subsection 1). Applicants apply to the department on a prescribed form, and grants are conditioned on compliance with the section; the department may award grants to any eligible applicant (subsection 3). Total grants may not exceed $500,000, and the Legislature intends funding from the Education Future Fund. Grant money may be used only to research AI-based writing assistance by individuals with dyslexia, focused on aggregate writing analytics that teachers can use to develop comprehensive literacy plans for students with dyslexia (subsection 4). If grant money is used in violation, the department notifies the Attorney General, who must bring a civil action to recoup the money; recovered funds are remitted to the State Treasurer for the Education Future Fund (subsection 5). The State Board of Education may adopt rules to carry out the section (subsection 6). The provided document contains only this section, and no effective date appears in it.

title: New Hampshire House Bill 1432
summary_short: Adds to New Hampshire law a class B felony for knowingly creating, distributing or presenting deepfakes to embarrass, harass, defame, extort or cause financial or reputational harm, plus a private civil action for such use and a lobbyist-registration bar. Effective January 1, 2025.
summary_long: Adds RSA 638:26-a, defining 'artificial intelligence' and 'deepfake' (digitally altered media of a person appearing to say or do what they never said or did), and making it a class B felony to knowingly create, distribute or present a deepfake of an identifiable individual to embarrass, harass, entrap, defame, extort or otherwise cause financial or reputational harm. Paragraph III creates a separate class B felony where the deepfake results in the person's arrest, with liability for the victim's legal expenses. Paragraph IV exempts interactive computer services for third-party content, bona fide news reports acknowledging authenticity questions, paid election communications that keep the sponsor's disclaimer, and satire or parody not dependent on AI. Adds RSA 507:8-j, a parallel civil action for damages against anyone who knowingly uses a person's likeness to create such a deepfake, with the same exemptions. Section 3 bars the secretary of state from accepting lobbyist registration of anyone convicted under RSA 638:26-a or found liable under RSA 507:8-j relating to lobbying. Severability clauses apply to both new sections. Effective January 1, 2025; approved July 19, 2024.

title: New Hampshire House Bill 1596
summary_short: New Hampshire statute adding RSA 664:14-c. Effective 1 August 2024, it prohibits persons and entities from distributing AI-created deepfakes of candidates, election officials, or parties within 90 days of an election, unless the media carries a prescribed AI-manipulation disclosure. It gives candidates and election officials injunctive relief and damages actions.
summary_long: Section 345:1 adds RSA 664:14-c, defining synthetic media, AI, generative AI and deepfake. Paragraph II bars any person, corporation, committee or other entity from distributing, within 90 days of an election with a candidate on the ballot, an AI-generated deepfake of a candidate, election official or party on the state or local ballot that it knows or should have known is a deepfake. Paragraph III exempts media carrying a prescribed disclosure that it was manipulated or generated by AI, with size, duration and audio-repetition rules. Paragraph IV allows a depicted candidate or election official to seek injunctive or equitable relief and to sue the sponsor for general or special damages, with prevailing-party attorneys' fees. Paragraph V exempts interactive computer service providers for third-party content, persons without knowledge, bona fide news reports, paid broadcast or platform election communications that keep disclaimers, and satire or parody. Paragraph VI provides severability. Section 345:2 sets the effective date as August 1, 2024. The text states no agency penalty or criminal sanction.

title: SB 255 (2024), Expectation of Privacy (RSA 507-H, Consumer Data Privacy)
summary_short: Chapter 507-H, enacted by SB 255 (2024), gives New Hampshire consumers rights over their personal data and imposes duties on controllers and processors that meet volume thresholds. It applies from 1 January 2025.
summary_long: Chapter 507-H applies from 1 January 2025 to persons doing business in New Hampshire, or targeting products to its residents, that control or process personal data of at least 35,000 unique consumers in a year, or 10,000 consumers with more than 25 percent of gross revenue from data sales. It excludes state bodies, nonprofits, higher education institutions, and certain financial and health-care entities. Consumers may access, correct, delete and port personal data and opt out of targeted advertising, data sales and certain profiling. Controllers must respond within 45 days, provide appeals, and honour opt-out preference signals from 1 January 2025. Controllers must limit collection, obtain consent for sensitive data, document data protection assessments for heightened-risk processing, and publish privacy notices. Processors act under written contracts. From 1 January 2027 controllers may not sell a child's personal data. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority, with a 60-day cure period during 2025 and discretionary cure afterward. Violations are unfair or deceptive trade practices, and the chapter creates no private right of action.
text_version: RSA chapter 507-H as codified (enacted by 2024, 5:1 = SB 255), snapshot 2026-09-29

title: New Jersey A 4732 (Notification Requirements for Artificial Intelligence Companion Models 2026)
summary_short: Would require operators of AI companion systems to notify users that they are not communicating with a human, at the start of each interaction and at least every three hours thereafter. Violations would carry a $15,000 civil penalty per violation. Would take effect immediately on enactment.
summary_long: As introduced, the bill would apply to operators of 'artificial intelligence companion' systems: systems using generative AI designed to simulate a sustained human or human-like relationship with a user by retaining information from prior interactions, asking unprompted emotion-based questions, and sustaining personal dialogue. Operators, defined to include members, affiliates, subsidiaries and beneficial owners of firms that operate or provide such a system, would have to give clear and conspicuous notice to a user, verbally or in writing, at the beginning of any AI companion interaction that the user is not communicating with a human. The notice would repeat at least every three hours during continued interaction. 'User' means an individual using an AI companion for personal use within New Jersey who is not an operator, agent or affiliate. Operators that violate the act would be subject to a civil penalty of $15,000 per violation, collected in a civil action by summary proceeding under the Penalty Enforcement Law of 1999; the Superior Court and municipal court would have jurisdiction. The act would take effect immediately.

title: An Act concerning the use of automated tools to assist with hiring decisions and supplementing Title 34 of the Revised Statutes.
summary_short: Pending New Jersey bill making it unlawful to sell or offer for sale in the State an automated employment decision tool without a bias audit in the past year, an annual audit service and a notice. Users must notify candidates within 30 days; the act takes effect immediately.
summary_long: Pending New Jersey bill that supplements Title 34 and defines an automated employment decision tool as a system that automatically filters candidates for hire or for any term, condition or privilege of employment in a way that establishes a preferred candidate. It makes it unlawful to sell or offer for sale in the State such a tool unless it has been the subject of a bias audit conducted in the past year, the sale includes at no additional cost an annual bias audit service that provides the results to the purchaser, and the tool is sold with a notice that it is subject to the act. Any person who uses such a tool to screen a candidate for an employment decision must notify each candidate within 30 days that the tool was used and that it assessed the candidate's job qualifications or characteristics. Violations carry a civil penalty of not more than $500 for a first violation and each additional violation on the same day, and not less than $500 nor more than $1,500 for each subsequent violation, accruing daily for each tool; each 30-day notice failure is a separate violation. Penalties are payable to the State Treasurer and may be recovered in a summary proceeding brought by the commissioner. The Department of Labor and Workforce Development, in consultation with the Division on Civil Rights, must promulgate rules. The act affirms candidates' rights without limiting other rights or enforcement authority, and takes effect immediately.

title: An Act concerning discrimination and automated decision systems and supplementing P.L.1945, c.169 (C.10:5-1 et seq.).
summary_short: Prohibits financial institutions and lenders, insurers, and health care providers from discriminating against members of protected classes through use of automated decision systems, deeming a system discriminatory if it selects protected-class members at a disproportionate rate. Takes effect on the first day of the third month after enactment.
summary_long: As introduced, the bill would supplement the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (P.L.1945, c.169). Section 1 defines 'automated decision system' as a computational process, including one derived from machine learning, statistics, or other data processing or artificial intelligence techniques, that makes a decision or facilitates human decision making, and defines 'health care provider' and 'member of a protected class' by reference to listed characteristics. Sections 2 to 4 bar a person, bank, banking organization, credit reporting agency, mortgage company or other financial institution, lender or credit institution involved in making or purchasing loans; an insurance company licensed, registered or authorized under New Jersey law; and a health care provider from discriminating through the use of an automated decision system against members of a protected class. Each section deems a system discriminatory where it selects protected-class members for participation or eligibility, or in setting rates, terms or conditions, at a rate disproportionate to the rate for non-members. Section 5 makes a violation unlawful discrimination and a violation of section 11 of P.L.1945, c.169 (C.10:5-12). Section 6 sets the effective date as the first day of the third month next following enactment. The bill does not set out separate penalties or an enforcing authority.},

title: P.L.2023, c.266 (S332), New Jersey Data Privacy Act
summary_short: New Jersey statute giving consumers rights over their personal data and imposing duties on controllers and processors, enforced by the Attorney General, effective on the 365th day after enactment.
summary_long: P.L.2023, c.266 applies to controllers doing business in New Jersey or targeting its residents that control or process personal data of at least 100,000 consumers a year, or 25,000 consumers while selling personal data for revenue or a price discount. It gives consumers rights to access, correct, delete and obtain copies of their personal data and to opt out of targeted advertising, sale and certain profiling. Controllers must provide a privacy notice, limit collection and purposes, obtain consent for sensitive data and for targeted advertising or profiling of consumers aged 13 to 17, answer verified requests within 45 days with an appeal process, and document data protection assessments for heightened-risk processing. Controllers must honour a user-selected universal opt-out mechanism from six months after the effective date. Exemptions cover protected health information, certain financial institutions, consumer reporting agencies and state agencies. The Attorney General has sole enforcement authority, with a 30-day cure notice before enforcement until the 18th month after the effective date, and no private right of action. The act takes effect on the 365th day after enactment.

title: New Jersey P.L.2026, c.75 (S3379/A4096) -- data center energy and water use reporting
summary_short: Requires owners and operators of New Jersey data centers to submit semi-annual water and energy usage reports to the Board of Public Utilities, which publishes the submitted usage information. Reporting runs for three years from first submission; performance and sustainability data stay confidential. Effective immediately.
summary_long: Requires owners and operators of New Jersey data centers to report water and energy usage to the Board of Public Utilities (BPU), first within six months after the act takes effect (three months for facilities operating a year or more), then semi-annually. Reports cover facility details, energy consumption, the serving electric public utility and its agreements, on-site power, and water input and sources. Data centers receiving a State financial incentive must also report performance and sustainability indicators, which are confidential; others may submit them voluntarily. The Board publishes submitted usage information within 30 days, excluding confidential data. Operators must notify the Board at least 60 days before substantial operational or technology changes. The reporting duty runs for three years from first submission, after which the Board decides whether to continue it and adopts rules under the Administrative Procedure Act if so. Excludes data centers primarily used for internal operations of licensed health care providers, unless operated as commercial colocation. The Board consults the Department of Environmental Protection. The act takes effect immediately.
text_version: Senate No. 3379, Second Reprint (S3379 2R), latest reprint before enactment (signed 2026-08-27)

title: New Jersey S731/A796 (2026) -- Data Center Fair Share: data center rate class and large load tariff
summary_short: Requires New Jersey electric public utilities to seek Board of Public Utilities approval of a rate class and tariff for large data center customers, so that other customers do not subsidize their costs. Customers must post financial guarantees and accept curtailment and flexibility duties. Takes effect immediately.
summary_long: Supplements Title 48 to regulate retail electricity service to large data centers in New Jersey. Within 12 months, the Board of Public Utilities must set by order standards for each electric public utility, including defining characteristics of a large data center (minimum size not greater than 50 megawatts, with commonly owned or co-located facilities aggregated). The standards aim to keep other customers from subsidizing data center costs and from bearing stranded costs. They also cover co-located generation, capacity valuation, load-forecast submissions, a voluntary demand-reduction program, interconnection and curtailment priority (data centers before residential customers, excluding designated critical load), and anti-evasion measures. Within 180 days after that order, each utility must petition for a rate class and tariff, which the Board approves if it meets the Act. Large data center customers must provide financial guarantees for at least 85 percent of their electricity supply over 10 years, post deposits or security, accept demand-flexibility commitments, report flexibility performance annually, and pay interconnection study costs. Facilities approved before enactment are exempt from some of these duties for their already approved megawatts. Rate and service agreements must meet the Act's protections, and FERC jurisdiction over wholesale sales and transmission is preserved. The Act takes effect immediately.
text_version: P.L.2026, c.32 (Assembly No. 796, Fourth Reprint), approved July 7, 2026; advance law (chaptered) text, C.48:7-6.2; effective immediately

title: New Jersey Senate Bill 3432
summary_short: Creates the Next New Jersey Program under the New Jersey Economic Development Authority, offering tax credits to businesses primarily engaged in artificial intelligence or large-scale AI data centers that meet investment and job thresholds, for applications before March 1, 2029.
summary_long: Establishes the Next New Jersey Program under the New Jersey Economic Development Authority, which may award tax credits to businesses primarily engaged in artificial intelligence or large-scale AI data center activities. Applications are accepted before March 1, 2029, and require at least $100,000,000 in capital investment at a qualified business facility, at least 100 new full-time jobs, a collaboration with New Jersey research universities or technology startups, minimum environmental standards, and prevailing wages for construction work. The Authority board approves projects; the business signs a project agreement with recapture, reporting and annual certification duties. Credits equal the lesser of 0.1 percent of capital investment times new jobs, 25 percent of capital investment, or $250,000,000, usable over the eligibility period, carried forward ten years, or sold as transfer certificates at no less than 85 percent of value. Section 98 of P.L.2020, c.156 is amended to add the program to an $11.5 billion overall cap and to allot up to $500,000,000 of Aspire and Emerge credits to it from fiscal year 2025. The authority's chief executive officer may adopt rules immediately, effective up to 365 days. Effective immediately upon approval on July 25, 2024.

title: New Mexico House Bill 182 of 2024(Campaign Reporting Act)
summary_short: Amends New Mexico's Campaign Reporting Act to require AI disclaimers on ads containing materially deceptive media and to bar distributing such media within ninety days before an election with intent to mislead voters; violations carry civil penalties or crimes. The text states no effective date.
summary_long: The act amends the Campaign Reporting Act and adds §1-19-26.8. It defines artificial intelligence and materially deceptive media (an image, video or audio depicting an individual in conduct or speech they did not engage in, published without consent and produced in whole or part using AI). Section 2 requires advertisements with expenditures above $1,000 to name the candidate, committee or person who authorized and paid for them. Advertisements containing materially deceptive media must carry a disclaimer that the media has been manipulated or generated by artificial intelligence, with prominence and duration rules; each non-compliant occurrence is a separate violation subject to civil penalties under §1-19-34.6. Exemptions cover certain broadcasters, satire, and distribution platforms with consistent disclaimer requirements. Section 3 prohibits distributing, or agreeing with another person to distribute, materially deceptive media within ninety days before an election, where the person knows it falsely represents a depicted individual and intends to mislead electors, unless a disclaimer is included. Willful and knowing violations are a misdemeanor for a first conviction and a fourth-degree felony for a second. Enforcement may be sought by the attorney general, a district attorney, a depicted individual, an injured candidate or an organization representing voters.

title: New Mexico Senate Bill 192
summary_short: Section 9 appropriates general fund money to the public education department for fiscal years 2023 and 2024 for listed projects. Item Q provides $290,000 for artificial intelligence equipment and consultants at ASK academy charter school in Sandoval county.
summary_long: Section 9 of New Mexico Senate Bill 192 (2023) makes appropriations from the general fund to the public education department for expenditure in fiscal years 2023 and 2024, for named statewide projects and for purposes tied to specific school districts and schools. Unless otherwise indicated, any unexpended or unencumbered balance at the end of fiscal year 2024 reverts to the general fund. Item Q appropriates two hundred ninety thousand dollars for the purchase of artificial intelligence equipment and to contract with consultants at ASK academy charter school in Sandoval county. The section contains no regulatory provisions on artificial intelligence; its other items cover education programs, equipment, vehicles and facilities. One item (Albuquerque, item C(1)) requires a report to the legislative education study committee by October 1, 2024 on program effects.

title: NRS 360.754 -- Partial abatement of taxes for new or expanded data centers
summary_short: Nevada statute letting the Office of Economic Development approve partial abatements of taxes under NRS chapters 361 or 374 for data centers that locate or expand in the State, if they meet jobs, investment, wage and health-benefit conditions and operate at least 10 years. Effective through 2056.
summary_long: The statute lets a person who intends to locate or expand a data center in Nevada apply to the Office of Economic Development (OED) for a partial abatement of taxes under NRS chapters 361 or 374. OED must approve if the application fits the State Plan for Economic Development, a binding agreement is executed within one year (operation for at least 10 years), the applicant is registered or commits to licensing, and the employment, investment, wage, health-insurance and construction-workforce conditions in subsection 2(d) (up to 10 years) or 2(e) (10 to 20 years) are met. Thresholds include 10 or 50 full-time Nevada-resident employees, $25 million or $100 million capital investment within five years, and wages of at least 100 percent of the statewide average. OED may impose stricter or additional requirements (subsection 3) and may approve colocated businesses (subsection 5). Data centers must keep resident-employee records, furnish records on request, and repay abated amounts with interest on non-compliance (subsections 6, 8, 11). Affected local bodies must be asked for acknowledgment letters (subsection 3). OED may not approve applications received on or after 1 January 2036 (subsection 13).
text_version: NRS 360.754 as codified (source note through 2021 amendments), snapshot 2026-10-12

title: New York Bill A5309
summary_short: Amends New York State Finance Law §165 to require state units purchasing algorithmic decision systems to buy products that adhere to responsible AI standards (harm avoidance, transparency, fairness, impact evaluation). Amends Executive Law §292 so that unlawful discriminatory practices include those performed through an algorithmic decision system. Takes effect January 1 after enactment.
summary_long: The bill adds subdivision 9 to State Finance Law §165. It defines an algorithmic decision system as a computational process that makes or facilitates decisions impacting individuals, and defines a state unit as the state, its agencies, political subdivisions and public benefit corporations. When a state unit purchases a product or service that is or contains such a system for state use, it must buy one that adheres to responsible AI standards: minimizing risks of physical or mental injury, unjustified deletion or disclosure of information, and unwarranted damage; full disclosure to the state unit of the system's capabilities, limitations and potential problems; fairness, including eliminating discrimination and providing a feedback avenue to redress harms; and a comprehensive evaluation of impact and risks. The commissioner of taxation and finance must adopt regulations to carry out the subdivision. The bill also amends Executive Law §292(4) so that the term unlawful discriminatory practice includes an act prohibited under the listed provisions that is performed through an algorithmic decision system. The act takes effect on the first of January next succeeding its enactment. The bill is at the introduced stage and was referred to the Committee on Governmental Operations.

title: New York A 6767 (AI Companion Models)
summary_short: The bill would bar operators from offering AI companion models to New York users without a protocol for suicidal ideation, self-harm and harm to others, require recurring notices that the system is not human, and allow harmed persons to sue; effective 180 days after enactment.
summary_long: The bill adds Article 47 to New York's General Business Law on AI companion models. An AI companion is a system using AI, generative AI and/or emotional recognition to simulate social human interaction, retaining prior interactions and user preferences and conversing on personal well-being; business information-only systems are excluded. Operators may not operate or provide an AI companion to a user unless it has a protocol addressing possible suicidal ideation or self-harm, and possible physical or financial harm to others, including referral to crisis services (§ 1701). Operators must notify users at the start of each interaction and at least every three hours thereafter that the companion is a computer program, not a human, unable to feel human emotion (§ 1702). Users physically injured through self-harm, or physically or financially harmed by another, due to a violation of §§ 1701 or 1702 may sue for damages and equitable relief (§ 1703). The bill sets no agency enforcement or penalty amounts and takes effect on the 180th day after becoming law.

title: New York 2025-A768
summary_short: Bill adding GBL Article 45-A. From 1 January 2027, developers and deployers of high-risk AI decision systems used for consequential decisions about New York consumers must use reasonable care against algorithmic discrimination, with documentation, impact assessment and notice duties; the attorney general enforces it.
summary_long: The bill adds GBL Article 45-A, the AI Consumer Protection Act. It covers high-risk AI decision systems that make or substantially assist consequential decisions about New York consumers in listed areas such as education, employment, lending, housing, insurance, health care and essential government services. From 1 January 2027, developers must use reasonable care against known algorithmic discrimination risks, supply documentation to deployers and publish system statements; an independent audit creates a rebuttable presumption of reasonable care. Deployers must keep a risk management program, complete impact assessments annually and within 90 days of substantial modifications, notify consumers of consequential decisions, explain adverse decisions, allow correction and appeal, and publish a statement. Developers of general-purpose AI models must keep technical documentation. Persons must disclose AI interaction to consumers unless obvious. Exemptions cover certain federal approvals, insurers and banks deemed compliant, and specified research and security activities. The attorney general has exclusive enforcement authority, with a notice-and-cure period in 2027 and discretionary cure from 2028; violations are unfair trade practices under GBL § 349, and there is no private right of action.

title: New York Assembly Bill A8808A
summary_short: Amends New York civil rights, penal and election laws on images, audio and records altered by digitization (including AI). Adds civil false-light action, crimes for intimate and fabricated records, and disclosure of deceptive political media within sixty days of elections. Subpart A effective immediately; B and C on ninetieth day.
summary_long: Part MM has three subparts on images, audio and records altered by 'digitization' (software, machine learning, artificial intelligence or other computer-generated means that realistically alter a depiction). Subpart A amends Civil Rights Law §§ 50, 51, 52-b and 52-c to cover likeness, voice and digitized images, and adds § 50-h, a private false-light action against actors who disseminate digitally-altered material containing false statements; remedies include injunctions, punitive and compensatory damages and fees, with three-year or one-year limitation periods. Subpart B amends the Penal Law so digitization does not relieve criminal liability and extends intimate-image, coercion, impersonation, identity theft and sexual-performance offenses to digitized material; new § 245.20 criminalizes disseminating fabricated records intended to cause harm, subject to listed exemptions such as satire, news reporting and initial platform dissemination. Subpart C amends Election Law § 14-106(5): political communications containing digitized deceptive media distributed within sixty days of an election must carry a prescribed disclosure, with exemptions for satire, parody and news, and injunctive relief for registered voters and candidates. Subpart A takes effect immediately; Subparts B and C on the ninetieth day after enactment.

title: An Act to amend the general business law, the executive law, the state finance law and the education law, in relation to enacting the "digital fairness act" - Sections 7-9 ("AUTOMATED DECISION SYSTEM IMPACT ASSESSMENTS," etc.)
summary_short: Amends New York State Finance Law § 165 and § 8 so that the State, its agencies, political subdivisions and public benefit corporations must commission neutral impact assessments and publish use policies before acquiring or using automated decision systems, give notice, provide explanations and human review, and face payment bars and a private right of action. Covers only Sections 7 to 9 of the bill.
summary_long: Sections 7 to 9 of the bill add subdivisions 9 and 10 to State Finance Law § 165 and subdivisions 21 to 25 to State Finance Law § 8. The rules apply to the State and any governmental agency, political subdivision or public benefit corporation of the State that purchases, obtains, uses or accesses information from an automated decision system (ADS). Before doing so, such bodies must engage a neutral third party to conduct an ADS impact assessment and publish it; existing systems are covered within one year of the subdivision's effective date and every two years thereafter, and new systems before acquisition. Use policies must be published at least ninety days before acquisition or deployment of new systems and within 180 days for existing ones. Changes require an addendum, and certain acquisitions or new uses require approval by a city or county council or the state legislature after a public hearing. The Committee on Open Government conducts annual audits; the Office of Information Technology Services must complete a statistical impact study within two years. Bodies must give plain-language notice when an ADS affects decisions, be able to explain decisions, and develop a human review process. Individuals may sue, and the court must award injunctive relief, actual damages or ten thousand dollars per violation (whichever is greater), fees and costs. Section 8 bars payment for such systems unless they use only open source software and the impact assessment and use policy requirements were met, where contracts impair these duties, where they discriminate on enumerated protected factors, or where they make final decisions without human intervention affecting legal rights or deploy or trigger a weapon. The effective date is referenced but not stated in the excerpt.

title:
An Act to amend the general business law, in relation to the management
 and oversight of personal data
summary_short: Proposed New York bill amending the General Business Law. Requires controllers using solely automated decisions that materially contribute to denials of key services (finance, housing, insurance, health care, education, employment, necessities) to disclose this, offer appeals with 45-day responses, and conduct annual impact assessments by independent auditors.
summary_long: Proposed bill amending New York's General Business Law on the management and oversight of personal data. Under subdivision (A), a controller making an automated decision involving solely automated processing that materially contributes to denial of financial or lending services, housing, public accommodation, insurance, health care services, or access to basic necessities must disclose that the decision was made by a solely automated process, offer an appeal allowing the consumer to contest the decision, provide supporting information and obtain meaningful human review, and explain the appeal process. Controllers must respond to appeals within forty-five days, extendable once by forty-five days with notice and reasons. Under subdivision (C), controllers or processors engaged in automated decision-making in those fields, including those assisting others, must conduct an annual impact assessment describing objectives, design, training data, accuracy, fairness and bias testing, and assessing discriminatory results across protected characteristics. Assessments must use an external independent auditor or researcher, be publicly available online, be retained for at least six years, and be available to state, federal or local authorities on request. The excerpt states no effective date, penalties or enforcement authority, and it disapplies the jurisdictional limits of another section for these paragraphs.

title: New York Senate Bill S3008C
summary_short: New York S3008C adds consumer rules for personalized algorithmic pricing (disclosure of algorithm use, personal data and prices) and AI companion models (suicide-detection protocols and not-human notices), enforced by the attorney general with civil penalties. Part X takes effect on the sixtieth day after enactment.
summary_long: Part X adds General Business Law § 349-a on personalized algorithmic pricing, defining algorithm, personal data, dynamic pricing and personalized algorithmic pricing. Providers must disclose that they use such pricing, disclose the personal data used to set it, and give a clear and conspicuous disclosure of the price. After a consumer report, the attorney general may send a cease and desist letter and then seek an injunction; courts may impose civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation. Part U adds General Business Law Article 47 on AI companion models, defining AI companions as systems that retain personal information, ask unprompted emotion-based questions and sustain ongoing personal dialogue, and excluding customer-service, efficiency or research tools and internal business systems. Operators must maintain a protocol to detect suicidal ideation or self-harm and refer users to crisis services, and must tell users at the start of an interaction that they are not communicating with a human; such notices need not exceed once per day and must recur at least every three hours in continuing interactions. The attorney general may seek injunctions and civil penalties of up to $15,000 per day; fines are deposited in a suicide prevention fund created by State Finance Law § 99-ss. The excerpt gives no effective date for Part U.

title: DCWP Rules on Automated Employment Decision Tools (6 RCNY 5-300 et seq.)
summary_short: City rules (6 RCNY Subchapter T) under which employers and employment agencies using automated employment decision tools must obtain a bias audit within one year before use, publish audit results and the distribution date, and give candidates and employees notice before use.
summary_long: Subchapter T of Title 6 of the Rules of the City of New York implements Local Law 144 of 2021 on automated employment decision tools (AEDTs). It covers employers and employment agencies that use an AEDT to screen candidates or employees considered for promotion in New York City. An AEDT may not be used or continued in use if more than one year has passed since its most recent bias audit (§ 5-301(a)). The bias audit, conducted by an independent auditor, must calculate selection rates, or scoring rates for scoring tools, and impact ratios for sex, race/ethnicity and intersectional categories, and report individuals in unknown categories. An auditor may exclude categories under 2% of the data, with justification (§ 5-301(b)-(d)). Audits must use historical data, with test data allowed only where historical data is insufficient (§ 5-302). Before use, employers must publish the audit date, a results summary and the distribution date on their website, and keep them posted for at least six months after last use (§ 5-303). Notice must go to city residents at least 10 business days before use, with instructions for requesting an alternative process or accommodation where available, though no alternative process is required (§ 5-304(a)-(c)). Employers must also publish data retention and data source information and answer written requests within 30 days (§ 5-304(d)). The excerpt contains no penalty provisions and gives no effective date.

title: New York City Local Law 144 of 2021 (Int. 1894-2020), Automated Employment Decision Tools
summary_short: NYC law barring employers and employment agencies from using automated employment decision tools to screen candidates or employees for city employment decisions unless a bias audit within one year, public results summary, and candidate notices are provided. Civil penalties apply; effective 1 January 2023.
summary_long: Local Law 144 of 2021 adds Subchapter 25 to the New York City administrative code, regulating automated employment decision tools (AEDTs): computational processes derived from AI, machine learning, statistical modeling or data analytics that substantially assist or replace discretionary screening of candidates or employees for promotion within the city. Employers and employment agencies may not use an AEDT unless an independent bias audit occurred within one year before use and a summary of results is publicly posted. Candidates and employees residing in the city must receive notice at least ten business days before use, covering the tool and assessed job qualifications, and data information on written request within 30 days. Section 20-872 sets civil penalties of up to $500 for a first violation and $500 to $1,500 for later violations, each day of use a separate violation. Section 20-873 authorizes the corporation counsel to sue to correct violations; § 20-874 preserves private civil actions and Commission on Human Rights enforcement. Effective 1 January 2023.

title: New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection Amendment to Rules of NY City (Use of Automated Employment Decisionmaking Tools)
summary_short: Adds Subchapter T to New York City's rules requiring employers and employment agencies using automated employment decision tools (AEDTs) in hiring or promotion to obtain a bias audit within one year before use, publish audit results and distribution date, and give candidates and employees notice and data-related information.
summary_long: Adds Subchapter T (§§ 5-300 to 5-304) to Chapter 5 of Title 6 of the Rules of the City of New York, governing automated employment decision tools (AEDTs). Section 5-300 defines AEDT by reference to § 20-870 of the Administrative Code and defines bias audit, independent auditor, impact ratio, selection rate, scoring rate, historical data and test data. Section 5-301 bars an employer or employment agency from using or continuing to use an AEDT if more than one year has passed since its most recent bias audit, and sets minimum audit calculations by sex, race/ethnicity and intersectional categories, with an optional exclusion for categories under 2% of the data. Section 5-302 sets data requirements, allowing historical data from one or more employers and test data where historical data is insufficient. Section 5-303 requires publication before use of the audit date, a summary of results and the distribution date on the employment website, kept for at least six months after last use. Section 5-304 sets notice methods for city candidates and employees at least 10 business days before use, and requires data retention, data type and data source disclosures with written requests answered within 30 days. The text states no effective date and contains no penalty provisions.

title: Responsible AI Safety and Education Act (RAISE Act), S.6953-B / A.6453-B, Chapter 699 of the Laws of 2025
summary_short: Adds Article 44-B (RAISE Act) to New York's General Business Law, requiring large developers of frontier AI models to implement and publish safety and security protocols, report safety incidents within 72 hours, and not deploy models posing unreasonable risk of critical harm. Effective 90 days after enactment.
summary_long: Adds Article 44-B, the Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act, to New York's General Business Law. The article applies to frontier AI models developed, deployed or operating in whole or in part in New York. A frontier model is defined by training computation exceeding a stated number of operations and compute cost above $100 million, or a distilled model with compute cost above $5 million. A large developer is a person that has trained at least one frontier model and spent over $100 million in compute costs in aggregate on frontier models. Before deploying a frontier model, a large developer must implement a written safety and security protocol, retain an unredacted copy, publish a redacted copy, record and retain test information, and implement safeguards against unreasonable risk of critical harm. It must not deploy a frontier model where doing so would create an unreasonable risk of critical harm. It must review the protocol annually, disclose safety incidents to the attorney general and the division of homeland security and emergency services within 72 hours, and not knowingly make false or materially misleading statements. The attorney general may bring a civil action for civil penalties of up to $10 million for a first violation and $30 million for a subsequent violation, or for injunctive or declaratory relief. The article creates no private right of action. The act takes effect on the ninetieth day after it becomes law.

title: A.9449 / S.8828, chapter amendment to the RAISE Act (Chapter 96 of the Laws of 2026)
summary_short: Replaces Article 44-B of the New York General Business Law (RAISE Act) on frontier AI models. Requires frontier developers to publish safety frameworks and transparency reports and report critical safety incidents to a new DFS office; large developers file disclosure statements. Effective January 1, 2027, with the 2025 chapter.
summary_long: Repeals and replaces Article 44-B of the New York General Business Law, added by a 2025 chapter on frontier AI models, with the Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act (bill A.9449/S.8828, recorded as signed Chapter 96 of 2026). It covers frontier models trained with more than 10^26 operations that are developed, deployed or operating in whole or in part in New York, excluding certain academic research (§§ 1420, 1425–1426). Large frontier developers (affiliates' prior-year revenue above $500 million) must publish and annually review a frontier AI framework and publish transparency reports before or concurrently with deploying new models; developers must avoid materially false or misleading statements about catastrophic risk (§ 1421). Developers must report critical safety incidents to a new DFS office within 72 hours, and disclose imminent-risk incidents to an authority within 24 hours (§ 1422). Large developers must file a disclosure statement and pay pro rata assessments (§ 1428). The attorney general may seek civil penalties of up to $1 million for a first violation and $3 million for subsequent violations; no private right of action (§ 1427). Section 3 sets the 2025 chapter's effective date at January 1, 2027.

title: New York S 1169 (New York AI Act)
summary_short: Pending New York bill (print S1169-B) adding Civil Rights Law article 10-A: developers and deployers of high-risk AI used for consequential decisions must prevent algorithmic discrimination, notify people, offer appeals with human review, commission audits, report to DFS and keep risk programs. Bans social scoring. Effective one year after enactment.
summary_long: S1169-B, the New York artificial intelligence act, would add article 10-A to the Civil Rights Law. It covers developers and deployers that do business in New York or target New York residents; state agencies, local governments and public universities are excluded. Failing to take reasonable care against foreseeable algorithmic discrimination from a high-risk AI system becomes an unlawful discriminatory practice, also added to Executive Law section 296. High-risk systems are a substantial factor in consequential decisions on employment, education, housing, family planning, health care, financial or legal services, or materially affect rights or safety. Covered deployers must notify people before and within ten days after such decisions, offer an appeal with meaningful human review answered within 45 days, and have a human review each decision. Covered developers and deployers must commission recurring independent audits (ISO 42001 audits count; in-house auditors allowed if a compliant audit costs over 1% of fair market value), file periodic reports with the Department of Financial Services, keep a risk management program and protect whistleblowers. Social scoring is banned; the Attorney General can seek injunctions and civil penalties up to $25,000 per violation for developers and $10,000 for deployers. Audits start two years after enactment.
