title: New York S7422
summary_short: Amends New York Tax Law § 24 to exclude from the qualified-film definition, and so from the Empire State film production credit, any production using AI in a manner that displaces employees whose salaries are qualified expenses, unless a current collective bargaining agreement permits the replacement. Effective immediately.
summary_long: Bill S7422-A (2023-2024 session) amends paragraph 3 of subdivision (b) of section 24 of the New York Tax Law, which defines 'qualified film' for the Empire State film production credit. The amendment adds a new clause (iii) to the list of exclusions from that definition: a production that uses artificial intelligence in a manner resulting in the displacement of employees whose salaries are qualified expenses, unless the replacement is permitted by a current collective bargaining agreement covering those employees. The other exclusions (documentaries, productions requiring 18 U.S.C. § 2257 records, and certain variety series) and the minimum-budget rule are restated unchanged. Section 2 provides that the act takes effect immediately. The bill was introduced in May 2023 and committed to the Senate Committee on Investigations and Government Operations. The text states no penalty, enforcement authority or definition of artificial intelligence; its only operative provision concerns eligibility for the tax credit.

title: New York S 7599 (Relates to automated decision-making by government agencies)
summary_short: Requires New York State government agencies to publish lists of automated decision-making tools, complete impact assessments for tools used with meaningful human review, and submit them to the governor and legislature before implementation. Article V takes effect one year after enactment.
summary_long: Adds Article V to the State Technology Law. Government agencies (state and local bodies, school districts, SUNY, CUNY, public authorities) using automated decision-making tools must publish a list of them by 30 December after section one takes effect, then annually. Where a tool is used with ongoing meaningful human review, agencies must complete signed impact assessments at least every two years and before material changes, and submit them to the governor and legislative leaders at least 30 days before implementation; assessments are published with permitted redactions. If an assessment finds discriminatory or biased outcomes, use must cease. A state office maintains an inventory on the open data website, and agencies must report existing tools to the legislature within one year. Education Law sections 115, 2510, 2585, 2588 and 3013 and Civil Service Law section 80(10) provide that use of such tools shall not affect collective bargaining rights or result in employee discharge, displacement or transfer of duties. Section one takes effect one year after enactment; the other sections take effect immediately. The text sets no penalties.

title: New York S8391 (Relates to the right of publicity)
summary_short: Amends New York Civil Rights Law §50-f on post-mortem publicity rights. Defines digital replicas and makes unauthorized knowing use of a deceased performer's digital replica in audiovisual works, sound recordings or live musical performances actionable for damages, subject to exceptions. Takes effect immediately.
summary_long: The bill amends subdivisions 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 10 of Civil Rights Law §50-f on rights in deceased personalities' name, voice, signature, photograph or likeness. Its amended definitions cover deceased performers and personalities domiciled in New York at death, and describe a digital replica as a highly realistic, readily identifiable computer-generated representation of an individual's voice or visual likeness. Subdivision 2(b) makes a person liable for damages for knowingly using a deceased performer's digital replica without authorization or prior consent in an audiovisual work, sound recording or live musical performance. Subdivision 2(c) sets liability at the greater of $2,000 or compensatory damages plus unauthorized profits, and allows punitive damages. Subdivision 2(d) revises exemptions, including for docudramas and self-portrayals with some fictionalization, except in live musical performances. Subdivision 9 adds streaming services to the advertising media whose owners and employees are exempt absent actual knowledge by prior notification. Subdivision 10 keeps the exemption for services selling visual works unless the person received a successor's notice of an unauthorized digital replica and did not promptly remove it. The act takes effect immediately.

title: New York S 8420 (Relates to requiring advertisements to disclose the use of a synthetic performer)
summary_short: Requires persons who create or produce commercial advertisements for property or services to conspicuously disclose a synthetic performer's presence where they have actual knowledge. Civil penalty: one thousand dollars for a first violation, five thousand dollars for subsequent violations. Takes effect 180 days after becoming law.
summary_long: Amends General Business Law section 396-b, which governs advertisements, by adding definitions and new subdivisions. Subdivision 1 defines artificial intelligence, generative artificial intelligence and synthetic performer; a synthetic performer is a digitally created asset intended to create the impression of a human performer who is not recognizable as any identifiable natural performer. Subdivision 3 applies to persons engaged in dealing in any property or service who, for any commercial purpose, produce or create an advertisement in any medium, and requires them to conspicuously disclose that a synthetic performer is in the advertisement where they have actual knowledge. A violation carries a civil penalty of one thousand dollars for a first violation and five thousand dollars for any subsequent violation. Subdivision 4 excludes advertisements and promotional materials for expressive works, provided use of a synthetic performer is consistent with its use in the work. Subdivision 7 excludes audio advertisements and uses of artificial intelligence solely for language translation of a human performer. Subdivisions 5 and 6 preserve rights under Civil Rights Law sections 50, 50-f and 51 and other law, and the protections of 47 U.S.C. section 230. Subdivision 8 states that the section does not apply to advertising media by whom an advertisement is published or disseminated. Section 2 is a severability clause. The act takes effect on the 180th day after it becomes law.

title: New York S 8828 (RAISE Act, Article 44-B)
summary_short: Replaces New York General Business Law Article 44-B (RAISE Act) with rules for frontier AI developers: publish safety frameworks and transparency reports, report critical safety incidents to a new DFS office, file disclosure statements, and face Attorney General civil penalties. Effective January 1, 2027.
summary_long: Replaces Article 44-B of the New York General Business Law, as added by a 2025 chapter, with the Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act. It covers frontier developers that trained a foundation model using more than 10^26 operations, and 'large frontier developers' that, with affiliates, had over $500 million in prior-year gross revenues. Large developers must publish and annually review a frontier AI framework, publish transparency reports before deploying new or substantially modified models, and make no materially false statements on catastrophic risk. All frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to a new office within the Department of Financial Services within 72 hours, or 24 hours where there is imminent risk of death or serious injury. Large developers must file a disclosure statement, renewed every two years, and pay assessments. The Attorney General may seek civil penalties of up to $1 million for a first violation and $3 million for later violations. The text creates no private right of action. Exemptions cover accredited New York colleges and universities doing academic research and the Empire AI consortium and institute. Effective January 1, 2027.

title: New York S 934 (Requires warnings on generative artificial intelligence systems)
summary_short: Proposed New York bill S 934 would add section 399-zzzzzz to the General Business Law, requiring owners, licensees and operators of generative artificial intelligence systems to display a conspicuous notice that outputs may be inaccurate. Failure carries a civil penalty of up to one thousand dollars per violation, and the act takes effect on the ninetieth day after it becomes law.
summary_long: The bill adds section 399-zzzzzz to the New York General Business Law. It defines a generative artificial intelligence system as a class of self-supervised AI models that emulate the structure and characteristics of input data to generate derived synthetic content, such as images, videos, audio and text. It also defines artificial intelligence broadly as machine-based systems that make predictions, recommendations or decisions for human-defined objectives. Under subdivision 2, the owner, licensee or operator of a generative AI system must clearly and conspicuously display a notice on the system's user interface that the system's outputs may be inaccurate. Under subdivision 3, an owner, licensee or operator that fails to provide this notice is assessed a civil penalty of up to one thousand dollars for each violation, and each user to whom the notice is not provided constitutes a separate violation. The text does not name the authority that assesses the penalty and does not address a private right of action or a cure period. Section 2 provides that the act takes effect on the ninetieth day after it becomes law. The document is bill text and states no legislative history.

title: New York Senate Bill 1042
summary_short: Amends New York Penal Law § 245.15 so that unlawful dissemination or publication of an intimate image covers images created or altered by digitization, defined as altering an image in a realistic manner using images of another person or computer-generated images. Also repeals subdivision 2-a. Takes effect on the sixtieth day after enactment.
summary_long: Section 1 amends penal law section 245.15 subdivisions 1 and 2, added by chapter 109 of the laws of 2019. Subdivision 1(a) keeps the offence of intentionally disseminating or publishing a still or video image showing another person with intimate parts exposed or engaging in sexual conduct, with intent to cause harm to emotional, financial or physical welfare, and now expressly includes an image created or altered by digitization where the person is reasonably identifiable. Subdivision 1(b) requires that the actor knew or reasonably should have known the person did not consent, including for an image first taken with consent where the depicted person had a reasonable expectation that it would remain private. Subdivision 2 adds a definition of digitization and keeps definitions of intimate part, and refers to other provisions for disseminate, publish and sexual conduct. Section 2 repeals subdivision 2-a, whose content the bill does not reproduce. Section 3 sets the effective date as the sixtieth day after the act becomes law. The bill states no penalty; the offence sits within the penal law.

title: New York SB5959 (2020)
summary_short: Creates a New York right of publicity for deceased performers and personalities, covering unauthorized commercial use of likenesses and digital replicas, and a private right of action for disseminating sexually explicit digitized depictions of individuals. Applies from the 180th day after enactment.
summary_long: Adds Civil Rights Law § 50-f, which recognizes property rights in the name, voice, signature, photograph or likeness of deceased personalities domiciled in New York. Users who exploit these without prior consent are liable for damages, including the greater of $2,000 or compensatory damages plus attributable profits, and punitive damages may be awarded. Digital replicas of deceased performers in scripted audiovisual works or live musical performances are covered where the use is likely to deceive the public. Exemptions include news, public affairs, parody, documentaries and other listed works. The rights are transferable and descendible, last no longer than forty years after death, and successors may register claims with the Secretary of State; advertising media owners are liable only with prior notice. Adds Civil Rights Law § 52-c, a private cause of action against a person who discloses, disseminates or publishes sexually explicit material depicting a digitized individual where the person knew or should have known there was no consent. Written consent must be in plain language, and the individual may rescind within three business days in specified cases. Available remedies include injunctive relief, punitive and compensatory damages, and fees and costs. Actions must be brought within the later of three years from dissemination or one year from discovery. The act takes effect on the 180th day after it becomes law and applies to living individuals and to deceased individuals who died on or after that date.

title: New York Senate Bill 9678
summary_short: Amends New York Election Law § 14-106 so that persons who distribute political communications containing materially deceptive media, with actual knowledge of that, must disclose it using a prescribed label, subject to exemptions. Candidates depicted without consent may seek injunctive relief and costs. Takes effect immediately.
summary_long: Amends Election Law § 14-106 to require disclosure when a person, campaign, committee or organization distributes a political communication containing materially deceptive media that it knows to be materially deceptive. Visual media must carry the statement 'This (image, video, or audio) has been manipulated' in a font no smaller than other text; audio must state it at the start and end and, if longer than two minutes, at intervals of no more than two minutes. Exemptions cover satire or parody, news reporting that acknowledges questions about authenticity, paid broadcasts by stations with consistent disclaimer requirements, and initial dissemination by platforms of content from other providers. A candidate whose voice or likeness appears without consent may seek injunctive relief, court costs and attorneys' fees in the supreme court, with expedited proceedings. Preliminary relief is available where plaintiffs are more likely than not to succeed and a remedy is possible in the upcoming election. The plaintiff must prove use by clear and convincing evidence. Nothing requires cancelling, editing or labelling content where inconsistent with federal law. Takes effect immediately.

title: An Act to provide for reconciliation pursuant to title II of H. Con. Res. 14 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act), Pub. L. 119-21
summary_short: Reconciliation statute (Pub. L. 119-21, dated July 4, 2025) with mainly fiscal provisions across tax, nutrition, agriculture, health, education, immigration fees, energy leasing, transportation and defense; includes appropriations for defense AI programs.
summary_long: Public Law 119-21, an Act to provide for reconciliation pursuant to title II of H. Con. Res. 14, dated July 4, 2025, is a fiscal statute organized by House committee title. It appropriates or rescinds funds, and extends, modifies or terminates programs and tax provisions. Title I (agriculture) amends the Food and Nutrition Act and the Agricultural Act of 2014 and sets crop insurance and conservation funding. Title II appropriates defense funds. Title III changes the CFPB funding cap and the SEC reserve fund. Title IV covers the Coast Guard, spectrum auctions, air traffic control, space launch fees, NASA, fuel economy penalties and airport lease payments. Title V repeals energy provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act and sets oil, gas and coal leasing duties. Title VI rescinds environmental funds. Title VII covers tax rates, credits and deductions, terminates clean energy credits, and sets Medicaid, ACA premium credit and Medicare eligibility rules. Title VIII covers student loans and Pell grants; Title IX covers border security and homeland funding; Title X covers immigration fees and appropriations. AI-related provisions are defense and government appropriations.

title: State of Ohio Administrative Policy on AI
summary_short: Ohio policy binding state agencies, boards and commissions under the Governor on AI use planning, procurement, security, privacy and governance. Requires use-case approval, human verification of consequential AI outputs, supplier and generative AI controls, and an AI Council. No effective date stated.
summary_long: Sets statewide requirements for planning, procurement, security, privacy and governance of AI use by Ohio state agencies, boards and commissions under the Governor, citing ORC 125.18 as authority. Agencies must approve AI use cases, document testing, and keep human review for AI outputs and for decisions with legal or financial impact. Procurement rules cover supplier disclosure of generative AI, documentation of AI systems, a bar on supplier use of state data in generative AI absent approval, and licensing due diligence for training data. Workforce rules require approval for generative AI use, disclosure of generative AI-created deliverables, and entry of only public-record data into such tools. Security and privacy controls include risk assessment, a bar on sensitive data in unconstrained generative AI tools, consent before AI systems collect PII, and disclosure to users that they are interacting with a state AI solution. A multi-agency AI Council under DAS oversees a statewide sandbox and auditing of AI solutions. The policy is to be reviewed at least every two years. The text states no penalties and no effective date.

title: Ohio Revised Code § 122.175 -- Data center equipment sales and use tax exemption (Tax Credit Authority)
summary_short: Ohio statute letting the Tax Credit Authority exempt, by agreement, computer data center equipment at eligible data centers from state sales and use taxes, subject to investment and payroll tests. In force from September 30, 2025.
summary_long: Section 122.175 lets the Ohio Tax Credit Authority, under agreements with taxpayers proposing data center projects, fully or partly exempt from state sales and use tax the computer data center equipment used at eligible facilities. Eligibility requires project payments of at least one hundred million dollars over three to six consecutive calendar years and annual compensation of at least 1.5 million dollars subject to withholding. The Tax Commissioner and Director of Development review applications for economic impact. Approval requires increased payroll, economic soundness, ability to maintain operations, and that the exemption be a major factor in the investment decision. Agreements fix the exemption percentage (up to 100 percent), term, annual reporting, a limit on relocating employment without notice, and a waiver of limitations periods. Taxpayers use a direct payment permit and file returns. For noncompliance the authority may reduce the exemption or terminate the agreement and recover prior taxes. The Director adopts rules, reports annually by 1 August, and the statute is effective September 30, 2025.
text_version: Code section as of 2026 (effective 2025-09-30, as amended by H.B. 96, 136th GA)

title: The City of Tulsa Municipal Court Rules 2024
summary_short: Tulsa Municipal Criminal Court rule requiring any attorney, pro se defendant, victim or other party who uses generative AI in preparing a filing to disclose that use in the filing and name the specific tool. Filings remain subject to 12 O.S. §2011 certification.
summary_long: The rule applies to documents filed with the Tulsa Municipal Criminal Court. Any attorney, pro se defendant, victim or other party that uses a generative AI tool in preparing or drafting a filing must disclose in that filing that generative AI was used, and must state the name of the specific tool. Generative AI is stated to include, but not be limited to, ChatGPT, Bing AI and Google Bard. The rule states that 12 O.S. §2011 continues to apply to all filings. The court will construe filings, as certified by the person signing them, to comply with 12 O.S. §2011(B)(2). The text gives no effective date and states no penalty or other enforcement measure for non-disclosure.

title: Oklahoma H 3642
summary_short: Amends Oklahoma child pornography statutes (21 O.S. §§ 1021.2, 1024.1, 1040.12a) to criminalize knowing possession, viewing, sharing and other conduct, and to cover computer-generated and altered images appearing to be children. Effective November 1, 2024.
summary_long: Amends three sections of Title 21 of the Oklahoma Statutes on child pornography. Section 1021.2 makes it a felony to procure or cause the participation of a minor in child pornography or obscene material, or knowingly to possess, view, access, share, stream, download, procure, sell, distribute or manufacture child pornography. The penalty is imprisonment of up to 20 years and a fine of up to $25,000, with no deferred sentence and mandatory post-imprisonment supervision for sentences of two years or more. The minor's consent is not a defense. Section 1024.1 extends the definition of child pornography to altered depictions of children and to computer-generated or altered images that appear to be a child and are obscene, defines the related terms, and treats each image as a separate item. Section 1040.12a creates aggravated possession of 100 or more separate visual depictions of child pornography, punishable by imprisonment up to life and a fine of up to $10,000, with registration as a sex offender upon conviction. The act takes effect November 1, 2024.

title: Oklahoma House Bill 1916
summary_short: Oklahoma HB 1916 (introduced) would require public and private deployers of AI systems affecting Oklahomans to classify systems by risk, prohibit unacceptable-risk systems, assess and audit high-risk systems, and create an AI Council, sandbox and workforce grant program, effective November 1, 2025.
summary_long: Oklahoma HB 1916, as introduced, would enact the Responsible Deployment of AI Systems Act (Title 25, Sections 501-511), effective November 1, 2025. It covers public agencies and private entities deploying AI systems affecting individuals in Oklahoma. Deployers must classify systems into four risk categories before deployment, assess them for bias and risks to safety and civil liberties, and notify individuals when high-risk systems influence decisions. High-risk systems require qualified human overseers, ongoing performance evaluations and annual independent audits; deployers must keep governance groups, system inventories and feedback channels. Unacceptable-risk systems are prohibited. A nine-member AI Council, appointed by the Governor and legislative leaders, would run an AI Regulatory Sandbox and a workforce grant program for small businesses and educational institutions. The Council may impose financial penalties, suspend or prohibit noncompliant systems, or require external oversight, and deployers must publicly disclose noncompliance incidents.

title: OMB Memorandum M-25-22: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government
summary_short: Sets requirements and recommendations for US federal agencies acquiring AI systems and services, covering market research, solicitation disclosures, contract terms on IP, data, privacy, vendor lock-in and testing. Applies to contracts from solicitations issued 180 days after issuance onward.
summary_long: Issued under Executive Order 13960 and the Advancing American AI Act, and consistent with OMB Memorandum M-25-21, this memorandum guides agencies in acquiring AI systems or services and rescinds and replaces M-24-18. It applies to agencies defined in 44 U.S.C. 3502(1), with CFO Act agencies covered by some requirements, and excludes the Intelligence Community, national security systems, and AI used incidentally by contractors, among other exclusions. Agencies must update acquisition procedures within 270 days. Where practicable, they must disclose in solicitations whether a planned use meets the high-impact use case threshold. Contracts must include terms on IP rights and government data, including a permanent bar on using nonpublic agency data to train publicly or commercially available AI absent explicit agency consent, and on privacy, vendor lock-in protections and ongoing testing. Agencies must test proposed solutions to the greatest extent practicable and obtain an authorization to operate before deployment. GSA must develop acquisition guides within 100 days and a shared repository within 200 days. The memorandum does not specify penalties.

title: OMB Memorandum M-26-04: Increasing Public Trust in Artificial Intelligence Through Unbiased AI Principles
summary_short: OMB Memorandum M-26-04 requires US federal agencies to include contractual requirements addressing the Unbiased AI Principles in new LLM procurements, requires vendor transparency documentation, and mandates updated agency procurement policies by March 11, 2026. It excludes national security systems and sunsets two years after issuance.
summary_long: OMB Memorandum M-26-04, dated December 11, 2025, implements a directive in a July 2025 executive order on Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government. The executive order sets two Unbiased AI Principles for large language models (LLMs): truth-seeking and ideological neutrality. The memorandum applies to each executive department, military department, independent establishment and wholly owned Government corporation, and not to national security systems. Agencies must include contractual requirements addressing compliance with the principles in any LLM solicitation or order issued after the memorandum's date, and should modify existing LLM contracts where practicable before any option extends performance. By March 11, 2026, agencies must update procurement policies, including processes for agency users to report outputs that violate the principles. Appendix A sets a minimum vendor disclosure set (acceptable use policy, model, system or data cards, end-user resources, and a feedback mechanism), a further set of enhanced disclosures an agency may request, and states that compliance may be designated material to contract eligibility and payment. The memorandum does not govern regulatory actions on non-agency AI uses, assessments of AI providers that are targets of enforcement, or incidental contractor AI use. It ceases to have effect two years after issuance unless the OMB Director provides otherwise.

title: Oregon HB 3546 (2025) -- POWER Act: separate rate class for large energy use facilities
summary_short: Oregon HB 3546 (2025) adds ORS chapter 757 provisions requiring the Public Utility Commission to set a separate rate class and tariff for large energy use facilities (20 MW or more) and requiring electric companies to contract with them for 10 years or longer. Effective on passage.
summary_long: Oregon HB 3546 (2025) adds Sections 2 and 5 to ORS chapter 757. A large energy use facility is a facility, under common ownership or control, that uses or can use 20 megawatts or more and is primarily engaged in a service under NAICS code 518210 (2022). The Public Utility Commission must create a separate classification of service and tariff schedule for these retail electricity consumers. The tariff must allocate or directly assign the costs of serving the class and mitigate the risk of unwarranted cost shifts to other consumers; the Commission must weigh listed criteria when approving tariffs. Electric companies must contract with these consumers for 10 years or longer, with a minimum payment obligation and a possible excess-demand charge, and must notify consumers of delays within their reasonable control. Section 6 applies the contract rules to contracts made on or after the effective date and to earlier contracts that require significant new investment. Section 3 provides that neither party must use the classification until a tariff is approved; Section 3 is repealed January 2, 2028. Section 7 requires a Commission report to interim energy committees by September 1 of each even-numbered year; Section 7 is repealed January 2, 2035. Direct access, green power rates and special contracts are preserved. The Act takes effect on passage as an emergency measure.

title: ORS Chapter 285C -- Enterprise zones, long-term rural enterprise zones (ORS 285C.400-.420), strategic investment program
summary_short: Oregon statute (ORS Chapter 285C, 2023 Edition) setting up enterprise zones and tax-incentive programs. Authorized firms can receive property tax exemptions conditioned on employment, wage and investment requirements, administered by the Oregon Business Development Department, zone sponsors and county assessors. Not AI-specific.
summary_long: ORS Chapter 285C (2023 Edition; this part covers ORS 285C.045 to 285C.547 in part, with the remainder in part 2) provides for enterprise zones designated by cities, counties and ports, with designation made final by a positive determination of the Oregon Business Development Department. Eligible business firms that are authorized may receive a 100 percent property tax exemption on qualified property for three tax years, extendable by up to two years by agreement. Exemption depends on employment levels, minimum compensation, first-source hiring agreements and a school support fee, and non-compliance can lead to disqualification and additional taxes. Reservation enterprise zones are available to listed tribes. Rural renewable energy development zones and long-term rural enterprise zone certifications provide property tax exemptions for 7 to 15 years. The chapter also covers a business development income tax exemption through preliminary and annual certification and renewable energy equipment manufacturing tax credits with annual cost limits. Under ORS 285C.255, no area may be designated as an enterprise zone, and no authorization may be obtained under ORS 285C.140, after June 30, 2032. The table of contents also lists a Strategic Investment Program and a Low Income Community Jobs Initiative, whose text is not in this part. The instrument contains no AI-specific provisions.
text_version: ORS chapter 285C, 2023 edition (with 2024 session notes), snapshot 2025-10-10

title: Oregon Senate Bill 1571
summary_short: Oregon SB 1571 (2024) requires any campaign communication that includes synthetic media of an individual, meaning a realistic but false AI-manipulated depiction, to carry a disclosure that it has been manipulated. Certain providers and publishers are exempt. The act takes effect on passage.
summary_long: SB 1571 (2024) adds a section to Oregon's election chapter (ORS chapter 260) on AI-manipulated media in campaign communications. Synthetic media is an image, audio or video recording of an individual, intentionally manipulated with artificial intelligence or similar digital technology, that creates a realistic but false depiction materially different from the original. A campaign communication supporting or opposing a clearly identified candidate or measure that includes any synthetic media must include a disclosure stating the recording has been manipulated. Exemptions cover interactive computer and information service providers; broadcasters and publishers carrying bona fide news coverage with authenticity acknowledgments or non-representation statements; paid broadcasts or publications under stated conditions; and satire or parody. The Secretary of State or Attorney General may seek injunctions in circuit court without proof of injury, and the prevailing party recovers reasonable attorney fees. On proof of a violation, the court imposes a civil penalty of up to $10,000, paid to the General Fund. This remedy is exclusive. ORS 260.345 is amended to route complaints and enforcement for these violations, with a 90-day filing limit for electors. The Secretary of State may adopt implementing rules. The act takes effect on passage under an emergency declaration.

title: Senate Bill 619 (2023), Oregon Consumer Privacy Act
summary_short: Oregon Senate Bill 619 (2023) enacts the Oregon Consumer Privacy Act, operative July 1, 2024. It imposes consumer data rights and controller and processor duties on businesses serving Oregon above volume thresholds, enforced by the Attorney General.
summary_long: Oregon Senate Bill 619 (2023) enacts the Oregon Consumer Privacy Act, operative July 1, 2024. It applies to businesses serving Oregon that process personal data of 100,000 or more consumers a year, or 25,000 or more while earning 25 percent of gross revenue from data sales. Consumers may access, correct, delete and port their personal data and opt out of targeted advertising, data sales and certain profiling. Controllers must give a privacy notice, limit collection and use to disclosed purposes, obtain consent for sensitive data, avoid discriminating against consumers who exercise rights, and conduct data protection assessments for heightened-risk processing; responses are due within 45 days. Processors must follow controller instructions under contract. The Attorney General enforces with investigative demands and civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation after a 30-day cure notice; no private right of action exists. Many exemptions apply, including HIPAA and financial institutions. From January 1, 2026, the cure notice is removed and controllers must allow universal opt-out signals.

title: An Act amending Title 18 (Crimes and Offenses) of the Pennsylvania Consolidated Statutes, in sexual offenses, providing for the offense of unlawful dissemination of artificially generated depiction; and, in minors, further providing for the offense of sexual abuse of children and for the offense of transmission of sexually explicit images by minor.
summary_short: Pennsylvania House Bill 1063 (2023, introduced) would create a misdemeanor offense of unlawfully disseminating an artificially generated depiction of an individual with intent to harass, annoy or alarm, and extend child sexual abuse and minor image offenses to such depictions. Takes effect in 60 days.
summary_long: As introduced on 28 April 2023 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, the bill amends Title 18 (Crimes and Offenses) of the Pennsylvania Consolidated Statutes. Section 1 adds 18 Pa.C.S. § 3131.1, which makes it an offense to disseminate an artificially generated depiction of an individual with intent to harass, annoy or alarm that individual. An artificially generated depiction is a visual depiction that appears to authentically show an individual in nudity or sexual conduct that did not occur, produced substantially through technical means such as artificial intelligence or photoshop software. Consent of the depicted individual is a defense. Grading is a first-degree misdemeanor when the depicted individual is a minor and a second-degree misdemeanor otherwise. A person may be convicted if the victim or offender is located in Pennsylvania. The Attorney General receives concurrent authority to investigate and prosecute violations involving more than one county or another state. Law enforcement officers acting in official duties are excluded. Sections 2 and 3 extend the child sexual abuse offense (§ 6312) and the offense of transmission of sexually explicit images by a minor (§ 6321) to artificially generated depictions of minors and add related definitions. Section 4 provides that the act takes effect in 60 days.

title: Pennsylvania Senate Bill 1090 (Safeguarding Adolescents from Exploitative Chatbots and Harmful AI Technology Act 2025)
summary_short: Pennsylvania bill requiring operators of AI companion platforms to disclose AI status, maintain suicide and self-harm safeguards, and add minor protections (reminders every three hours, sexual-content measures, notice of unsuitability), enforced by the Attorney General with civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation; takes effect in 120 days.
summary_long: The bill, introduced in the Pennsylvania General Assembly, regulates operators of AI companion platforms made available to users in the Commonwealth. An AI companion is defined as an AI system designed to simulate a sustained human or human-like relationship through retained personal information, unprompted emotion-based questions or ongoing personal dialogue, with listed exclusions for customer-service, productivity, research, video-game bots and certain speaker devices. Operators must issue a clear and conspicuous notice that the companion is artificially generated and not human where a reasonable person would be misled (Sec. 3(a)). They must maintain and implement, to the extent technologically feasible, a protocol to prevent suicidal ideation, suicide or self-harm content and content directly encouraging violence, including crisis referrals, and publish its details online (Sec. 3(b)). For users the operator knows or should have known are minors, operators must disclose AI interaction, give default break-and-reminder notices at least every three hours, and institute reasonable measures against sexually explicit visual material; where a service is offered to known minors, operators must disclose on the platform that AI companions may not be suitable for some minors (Sec. 3(c)-(d)). Section 4 excludes the underlying AI model unless it is directly offered, configured or deployed as an AI companion. The Attorney General enforces the act; an operator that violates it is liable, in addition to other remedies, for a civil penalty not to exceed $10,000 per violation, collected in a civil action (Sec. 5). The act takes effect in 120 days (Sec. 6). The text contains no private right of action.

title: Protecting Americans' Data from Foreign Adversaries Act of 2024 (Division I of Pub. L. 118-50)
summary_short: Bans data brokers from selling, licensing, transferring or otherwise making available personally identifiable sensitive data of United States individuals to foreign adversary countries or entities they control. The FTC enforces it as an unfair or deceptive practice violation. Effective 60 days after enactment.
summary_long: Division I of Public Law 118-50 prohibits data brokers from selling, licensing, renting, trading, transferring, releasing, disclosing, providing access to or otherwise making available personally identifiable sensitive data of United States individuals to a foreign adversary country or an entity controlled by one. 'Data broker' excludes service providers and some other entities, such as those transmitting data at the individual's direction or publishing news. 'Sensitive data' is a defined list, including government identifiers, health and financial data, biometric and genetic information, precise geolocation, private communications, data on minors under 17 and online activity over time. Foreign adversary countries are those in 10 U.S.C. 4872(d)(2); control includes foreign ownership of at least 20 percent. The Federal Trade Commission enforces the prohibition as a violation of an unfair or deceptive practices rule under FTC Act section 18(a)(1)(B), with that Act's powers and penalties. The prohibition takes effect 60 days after enactment. No AI-specific provisions appear in this excerpt.

title: Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act (Division H of Pub. L. 118-50)
summary_short: Makes it unlawful for entities to distribute, maintain or update a foreign adversary controlled application in the United States through app marketplaces or internet hosting, starting 270 days after enactment or after a presidential determination. Requires data portability for users and sets civil penalties enforced by the Attorney General.
summary_long: Sets out a prohibition on entities distributing, maintaining or updating a foreign adversary controlled application in the United States through app marketplaces or internet hosting services. Named applications (ByteDance, TikTok and related entities) are covered from 270 days after enactment; other covered companies from 270 days after a presidential determination. The President may grant one extension of up to 90 days on certified divestiture conditions. Before a prohibition applies, the owner or controller must give users, on request, their account data in machine-readable format. Qualified divestitures and services needed for compliance are exempt. Civil penalties reach $5,000 per affected US user for prohibited conduct and $500 per user for data violations, sought by the Attorney General; individual users are excluded from enforcement. Judicial review lies only in the D.C. Circuit: within 165 days of enactment for challenges to the division, 90 days for challenges to later actions or determinations.

title: William M. (Mac) Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021
summary_short: FY2021 NDAA sections on AI in the Department of Defense and federal government: JAIC acquisition authority (sunset 1 October 2025), JAIC advisory board, AI workforce hiring and pay, pilots, studies and reports, and deepfake-forgery reporting. Addressed to the Secretary of Defense and federal agencies.
summary_long: Selected AI-related sections of the FY2021 National Defense Authorization Act. Sec. 808 gives the Director of the Joint Artificial Intelligence Center (JAIC) acquisition authority of an agency head, a JAIC acquisition executive, at least 10 full-time staff, and a $75,000,000 cap per fiscal year on new contracts, with the authority sunsetting on 1 October 2025. Secs. 231-233 amend JAIC reporting and create a board of advisors. Secs. 234 and 235 require AI use-case identification, prototyping, and an assessment of ethically developed AI acquisition. Sec. 236 permits a steering committee on emerging technology until 1 October 2024. Sec. 1751 directs the Secretary of Defense to review and issue hiring guidance for AI professionals. Secs. 241 and 247-249 set proficiency tests, incentive pay, electronic-portfolio and self-directed training pilots, and part-time faculty and student employment. Sec. 513 authorizes STEM grants covering AI for JROTC units. Secs. 9004 and 589F require reports or studies on digital content forgery and deepfakes. Secs. 9407, 9412 and 9414 address national cybersecurity challenges, an industries-of-the-future council, and a study of Chinese influence on international standards. Other sections cover spectrum IT modernization, unmanned systems, and AI use by FinCEN.

title: Proclamation 11002 of January 14, 2026: Adjusting Imports of Semiconductors, Semiconductor Manufacturing Equipment, and Their Derivative Products Into the United States
summary_short: Proclamation 11002 (January 14, 2026) imposes a 25 percent Section 232 tariff, effective January 15, 2026, on imports of defined advanced computing chips ('Covered Products'), exempting listed uses such as U.S. data centers, R&D and startups, and directs trade negotiations and reports to the President.
summary_long: Proclamation 11002 under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, signed January 14, 2026, finds that imports of semiconductors, semiconductor manufacturing equipment and derivative products threaten national security. It directs the Secretary of Commerce and the U.S. Trade Representative to pursue trade agreements and to report within 90 days. It imposes a 25 percent ad valorem duty, effective January 15, 2026, on imports of 'Covered Products' (advanced computing chips and certain derivatives meeting the Annex parameters), with no duty for listed uses including U.S. data centers, R&D, repairs, startups, and non-data-center consumer, civil industrial and public sector applications. Annex U.S. note 39 defines covered semiconductor articles by total processing performance and total DRAM bandwidth, and defines a 'U.S. data center' as a facility requiring more than 100 MW of new AI load; new HTSUS headings 9903.79.01 to 9903.79.09 implement the duty and exemptions. Agencies may modify the HTSUS and customs procedures, drawback is unavailable, and the Secretary must provide a data-center market update by July 1, 2026. Broader tariffs may be considered after negotiations conclude.

title: Rhode Island Data Transparency and Privacy Protection Act (2024 H 7787 Sub A / S 2500 Sub A; R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 6-48.1)
summary_short: Rhode Island act (H 7787 Sub A, adding R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 6-48.1) requiring for-profit controllers of personal data above customer-count thresholds to disclose data practices, honour customer rights and assess heightened-risk processing, enforced by the attorney general as a deceptive trade practice. Takes effect 1 January 2026.
summary_long: Adds R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 6-48.1. Applies to for-profit entities doing business in Rhode Island or targeting residents that, in the preceding calendar year, processed personal data of at least 35,000 customers, or of 10,000 customers while deriving over 20% of gross revenue from data sales. Excludes state bodies, nonprofits, higher-education institutions, GLBA financial institutions, HIPAA covered entities and several other data categories. Controllers must disclose data categories, third parties receiving sold data and a contact mechanism, maintain data security, and obtain consent for sensitive data, including data of known children. Customers may confirm, access, correct, delete, port and opt out of targeted advertising, sales and certain profiling; controllers may not discriminate for exercising rights, and consent revocation takes effect within 15 days. Requests are answered within 45 days, extendable by 45, with 60-day appeals. Processors are bound by contract terms. Data protection assessments are required for targeted advertising, sales, risky profiling and sensitive data processing. The attorney general has sole enforcement authority; violations are deceptive trade practices, and intentional unlawful disclosures carry fines of $100 to $500 per disclosure. No private right of action. Effective 1 January 2026.

title: Rhode Island HB 6654 (2022)
summary_short: Adds Rhode Island chapter 97 (Consumer Protection in Eye Care Act) to Title 23. It sets conditions for eye assessments and contact lens or eyeglass prescriptions made through assessment mechanisms, including AI devices, and imposes civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation. Takes effect upon passage.
summary_long: Adds chapter 97, the Consumer Protection in Eye Care Act, to Title 23 (Health and Safety). It defines 'assessment mechanism' as automated or virtual equipment, applications or technologies used for eye assessments, expressly including artificial intelligence devices. Assessment mechanisms used to conduct an eye assessment or generate a prescription for contact lenses or visual aid glasses in Rhode Island must provide patient-provider interaction, collect medical history, and disclose as a term of use that the assessment does not replace an in-person examination and has limits on use. Providers using them must be actively licensed, meet in-person standards of care, not rely solely on assessment data for a prescription, verify patient identity and age (18 or older), and confirm recent in-person examinations. Violations carry a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per violation, with administrative hearings and appeal to superior court. The Department of Health must adopt rules. The act takes effect upon passage.

title: Rhode Island SB 2083 (2022)
summary_short: Rhode Island statute regulating eye assessments and prescriptions for contact lenses and visual aid glasses made through assessment mechanisms, including AI devices. Requires licensed providers to meet in-person examination and disclosure conditions, sets a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per violation, and takes effect upon passage.
summary_long: The Consumer Protection in Eye Care Act regulates assessment mechanisms, defined to include artificial intelligence devices, used to conduct eye assessments or generate prescriptions for contact lenses or visual aid glasses in Rhode Island. Mechanisms must allow synchronous or asynchronous provider-patient interaction, collect medical history and prior prescription data, and disclose to patients, as a term of use, that the assessment does not replace an in-person comprehensive eye examination and cannot generate an initial contact lens prescription. An assessment may be used for visual aid glasses only if the patient had an in-person comprehensive eye examination within the previous twenty-four months. Providers must be actively licensed, meet in-person standards of care, not rely on assessment data as the sole basis for a prescription, verify patient identity and that the patient is at least eighteen, keep medical records, and certify with their state license number. Any person violating the chapter or Department of Health rules faces a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per violation, with an administrative hearing and appeal of final orders to superior court. The Department of Health must adopt implementing rules. The act takes effect upon passage.

title: S 1213 Protect Elections from Deceptive AI Act
summary_short: Amends the Federal Election Campaign Act to bar persons, political committees and other entities from knowingly distributing materially deceptive AI-generated audio or visual media in federal election activity or depicting covered candidates, to influence elections or solicit funds. Exempts certain news outlets and satire. Candidates may seek injunctions and damages.
summary_long: Adds new section 325 to the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971. Section 325(b) bars a person, political committee or other entity from knowingly distributing materially deceptive AI-generated audio or visual media in a Federal election activity, or of a covered individual (a candidate for Federal office), to influence an election or solicit funds. Such media is AI-generated content that merges or replaces content, or generates inauthentic content, appearing authentic, and that a reasonable person would perceive as differing from the original or as showing conduct that did not occur. Section 325(c) exempts broadcasters and streaming services airing it in bona fide news coverage with a clear acknowledgment of authenticity questions, periodicals that clearly state it does not accurately represent the covered individual, and satire or parody. Section 325(d) lets a covered individual whose likeness appears in such media seek injunctions, with precedence under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, and damages from the distributor, plus attorney's fees at the court's discretion; the plaintiff must prove the violation by clear and convincing evidence. The text provides no government enforcement mechanism and states no effective date. A severability clause applies.

title: NO FAKES Act of 2025
summary_short: Creates a federal property-type right in an individual's voice and visual likeness, making unauthorized digital replicas and products designed to produce them actionable in civil suits, with notice-and-takedown and safe-harbor rules for online services. Effective 180 days after enactment.
summary_long: The bill creates a federal intellectual property right in the voice and visual likeness of individuals. The right is not assignable during life, is licensable, and does not expire on death; it is exclusive to the individual and to a right holder for 10 years after death, extendable by 5-year periods subject to public use, and terminates at the earlier of non-renewal or 70 years after death. Lifetime licenses are limited to 10 years (5 years for a living minor, court approval required for minors) and must be written, signed and describe intended uses; collective bargaining agreements are excepted. Anyone who, affecting interstate commerce, makes available an unauthorized digital replica, or distributes, imports or markets a product primarily designed to produce digital replicas of identified individuals, is liable in a civil action. Remedies are the greater of statutory amounts (from 5,000 dollars per work for individuals, up to 750,000 dollars per work or product for online providers that have not made a good faith compliance effort) or actual damages and profits; punitive damages are available for willful conduct. Online services that adopt a repeat-violator termination policy, designate an agent with the Copyright Office, and remove material on valid notice receive safe harbor. Knowingly false notices incur liability of at least 25,000 dollars per notification. Bona fide news, documentary, commentary, parody and fleeting uses are excluded, except sexually explicit depictions. Actions must be brought within 3 years of discovery, and state-law claims are preempted with stated exceptions. Liability applies to conduct after enactment.

title: Content Origin Protection and Integrity from Edited and Deepfaked Media Act of 2025
summary_short: Would require providers of tools creating synthetic or covered content to let users attach provenance information from two years after enactment; bar removing it deceptively or by covered platforms; bar unconsented AI training or generation with marked covered content; enforced by FTC, attorneys general and private suits.
summary_long: As introduced in the Senate (S. 1396, 9 April 2025), the bill would require persons who, for a commercial purpose, make available in interstate commerce a tool primarily used to create synthetic or covered content to let users include content provenance information, from two years after enactment, with security measures to keep it machine-readable and not easily removed. Knowingly removing or tampering with provenance information in an unfair or deceptive practice is unlawful, as is removal by covered platforms (with a security-research exception). Knowingly using covered content bearing provenance information to train AI or generate synthetic content is unlawful without express, informed consent and compliance with usage terms. The Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology would facilitate standards and detection research and a public education campaign within one year. Violations are treated as FTC rule violations; state attorneys general and content owners may sue, with a four-year limitation period for private actions.

title: Health Tech Investment Act
summary_short: Amends Social Security Act §1833(t) so that FDA-cleared algorithm-based healthcare services furnished in hospital outpatient departments from January 1, 2026 are assigned to new technology ambulatory payment classifications based on manufacturer-submitted costs, and directs HHS to apply a software-as-a-service payment policy from January 1, 2023.
summary_long: The Health Tech Investment Act amends Section 1833(t) of the Social Security Act to add a special rule for algorithm-based healthcare services, defined as services delivered through an FDA-cleared or approved device that uses artificial intelligence, machine learning or similar software to yield clinical outputs for use by a physician or practitioner in screening, detection, diagnosis or treatment. For covered outpatient department services furnished on or after January 1, 2026, the Secretary must ensure that qualifying services are assigned to a new technology ambulatory payment classification based on costs submitted by the manufacturer, must adjust that classification as necessary, and may not remove a service from it until adequate claims data exists, and in no case before the service has received payment under the classification for at least five years. The Secretary must also adjust eligibility criteria so that distinct adjunctive algorithm-based services can qualify. Section 2(b) directs the Secretary to apply the outpatient payment policy for software as a service, described in a November 23, 2022 final rule, to services provided on or after January 1, 2023. The text contains no enforcement or penalty provisions.

title: TAKE IT DOWN Act
summary_short: Federal US statute criminalising knowing publication of nonconsensual intimate depictions, including AI-generated digital forgeries, and requiring covered online platforms to run notice-and-removal processes and remove reported depictions within 48 hours, enforced by the FTC; process set-up is due within one year of enactment.
summary_long: Amends Section 223 of the Communications Act of 1934 by inserting a new subsection (h). It makes unlawful the knowing publication, by any person using an interactive computer service in interstate or foreign commerce, of an authentic intimate visual depiction or a digital forgery (computer-generated, indistinguishable from an authentic depiction) of an identifiable individual without consent, where listed harm or intent conditions and exceptions apply. Publication involving adults is punishable by fine, up to 2 years' imprisonment, or both; involving minors, up to 3 years; threats to commit these offenses are also punishable. Courts must order forfeiture and restitution. Section 3 requires covered platforms to set up a notice-and-removal process within 1 year of enactment, post a plain-language notice, and remove a reported nonconsensual intimate depiction within 48 hours of a valid request, making reasonable efforts to remove known identical copies; good-faith removal is shielded from liability. The FTC enforces these duties as violations of a rule against unfair or deceptive practices. Section 4 defines covered platforms as public-facing websites or apps primarily hosting user-generated content or regularly publishing such depictions, excluding broadband access, email and preselected-content services.

title: Protection Against Foreign Adversarial Artificial Intelligence Act of 2025
summary_short: Bars federal contractors with active contracts from using DeepSeek or successor applications developed or provided by High Flyer to perform those contracts, subject to a Commerce Secretary waiver. Requires a Commerce Secretary report to Congress within one year on national security threats from AI platforms linked to countries of concern.
summary_long: The Protection Against Foreign Adversarial Artificial Intelligence Act of 2025 is a bill in introduced form. Section 2 prohibits any Federal contractor with an active Federal contract from using the DeepSeek application, or any successor application or service developed or provided by High Flyer or any entity it owns, to fulfil or support a contract with a Federal agency. The Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of Defense, may waive this prohibition case by case where use is required for a national security-related objective of a contract or for research purposes. Section 3 defines 'country of concern' by reference to 'covered nation' in 10 U.S.C. 4872(f). It requires the Secretary of Commerce, within one year after enactment, to submit to specified congressional committees an unclassified report, which may include a classified annex, on national security threats from AI platforms based in or affiliated with countries of concern. The report must cover censorship laws, state-sponsored propaganda, circumvention of United States GPU export controls, and privacy and data security threats to United States user data, and may include recommendations for administrative and legislative action. The bill states no penalties or private right of action.

title: Protecting AI and Cloud Competition in Defense Act of 2025
summary_short: If enacted, requires the Secretary of Defense to use competitive awards, retain government data rights and prioritize multi-cloud technology in contracts with cloud, data infrastructure and foundation model providers, and to bar training commercial AI products on Defense data without authorization.
summary_long: The bill would direct the Secretary of Defense, in contracts with cloud, data infrastructure and foundation model providers, to require a competitive award for each procurement of cloud computing, data infrastructure or foundation model solutions, to keep exclusive Government rights to Government data, and to prioritize multi-cloud technology unless infeasible or a substantial danger to national security. It defines covered providers as those with Department of Defense contracts totaling at least $50,000,000 in the five previous fiscal years. It directs the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office to update the DFARS so that Government-furnished data for AI development is not used to train or improve commercial products of covered providers without express Department authorization, and it provides that violations are subject to specific penalties, including fines and contract termination. Component acquisition executives may grant exemptions for national security, with notice to the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer. The Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff must report annually for four years, beginning by January 15, 2027, on AI competition and market concentration, listing exemptions granted, and the report must be publicly posted on a Department of Defense website.

title: DEFIANCE Act of 2025
summary_short: Amends the federal civil remedy for intimate images (15 U.S.C. 6851) so that identifiable individuals can sue persons who knowingly produce, possess, disclose or solicit non-consensual intimate digital forgeries in U.S. district courts. The text ends with a Senate passage date of January 13, 2026.
summary_long: The bill amends Section 1309 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2022 (15 U.S.C. 6851). It defines an intimate digital forgery as an intimate visual depiction of an identifiable individual that falsely represents the individual or the intimate conduct, is created by software, machine learning, artificial intelligence or other computer-generated means, and is indistinguishable from an authentic depiction to a reasonable person; labels or disclosure do not change this status. Identifiable individuals may sue in federal district court persons who knowingly produce or possess a forgery with intent to disclose it, disclose it, or solicit or receive it without consent, and persons who knowingly produce a forgery where the individual was harmed or reasonably likely to be harmed, where the conduct affects interstate or foreign commerce. Relief includes liquidated damages of $150,000, or $250,000 in specified aggravated cases, or actual damages including defendant profits; punitive damages; injunctions; and privacy-protective orders. Actions must be filed within 10 years of the later of discovery or age 18. Sec. 3(c) preserves other federal, state and tribal law and allows at-least-as-protective state laws; Sec. 4 provides severability and states the Act does not limit or expand intellectual property law. No effective date is stated.

title: Responsible Innovation and Safe Expertise Act of 2025
summary_short: Would give AI developers conditional immunity from state-law civil liability for errors by their AI products when used by learned professionals in professional services, if they publicly release model cards and model specifications and document limitations. Applies to acts or omissions on or after 1 December 2025.
summary_long: The bill, the Responsible Innovation and Safe Expertise Act of 2025 (RISE Act of 2025), defines developers, learned professionals, clients, errors, model cards and model specifications for AI products. Section 4 makes a developer immune from civil liability for errors generated by an AI product when used by a learned professional in providing professional services to a client, if the developer publicly releases and continuously maintains a model card and a model specification before deployment and provides documentation of known limitations, failure modes and appropriate domains of use. Model specifications may be redacted only for trade-secret information unrelated to safety, with a written justification for each redaction. Immunity is conferred only for acts or omissions that do not constitute recklessness or willful misconduct. Immunity does not apply to a developer that fails to update the model card, model specification and documentation within 30 days of deploying a new version or discovering a new and material failure mode, where that failure proximately causes a later harm. Section 4(d) applies the section to State-law claims against developers for errors arising from professional use, but not to claims based on fraud, knowing misrepresentation, or conduct outside professional use. Section 5 preserves other immunities. The Act takes effect on 1 December 2025 and applies to acts or omissions on or after that date.

title: S2367 AI Accountability and Personal Data Protection Act 2025
summary_short: Proposed federal private tort: any person who uses or otherwise exploits an individual's covered data without express, prior consent is liable to that individual, including via generative AI training. Provides a consent defense and makes predispute arbitration agreements unenforceable for such claims. No effective date stated.
summary_long: The bill, the AI Accountability and Personal Data Protection Act, would create a federal civil tort. Under Section 3, any person who, in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce, appropriates, uses, collects, processes, sells or otherwise exploits an individual's covered data without express, prior consent is liable to that individual in civil action; aiders and abettors are also liable. Covered data includes personally identifiable information, identifiers, geolocation, biometric, behavioral and inferred data; exploitation includes training a generative AI system used by its provider and generating covered data about an individual. Remedies include the greater of actual damages, treble profits or $1,000, punitive damages, injunctive relief and attorney's fees. Consent is an affirmative defense but is invalid if obtained through coercion, deception, or as a condition of a product or service beyond what is reasonably necessary; third-party consent requires separate, specific and affirmatively presented disclosure. Predispute arbitration agreements and joint-action waivers are unenforceable for such claims, and courts decide applicability; Section 4 preserves state laws and sets a minimum standard. The text states no effective date and no public enforcement authority.

title: S.2455 Transparency and Responsibility for Artificial Intelligence Networks Act 2025
summary_short: Creates a 17 U.S.C. § 514 process letting copyright owners request a clerk-issued subpoena compelling generative AI developers to disclose copies or records identifying copyrighted works used to train their models. Developers must comply expeditiously; non-compliance creates a rebuttable presumption of copying; bad-faith requests may be sanctioned. Effective on enactment.
summary_long: As introduced, the bill adds § 514 to Chapter 5 of title 17, United States Code. The legal or beneficial owner of an exclusive copyright right, or an authorized person, may file with a U.S. district court clerk a proposed subpoena and a sworn declaration stating a subjective good-faith belief that a developer used the owner's works to train a generative AI model. If the filing is in proper form, the clerk issues the subpoena. A developer receiving it must expeditiously disclose copies of, or records sufficient to identify with certainty, the training material. Requests are limited to the requester's own works. Recipients of disclosed material may not disclose it to others without authorization. Issuance, service and enforcement follow the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, and noncompliance creates a rebuttable presumption that the developer made copies of the work. Courts may impose Rule 11(c)-style sanctions for bad-faith requests on motion of the recipient. The section takes effect on enactment.

title: S.2528 Unleashing AI Innovation in Financial Services Act 2025
summary_short: Creates AI Innovation Labs at US financial regulatory agencies. Regulated entities may apply to run AI test projects under alternative compliance strategies approved by the agency, with enforcement limited to the approved terms. Agencies must issue implementing rules within 180 days of enactment.
summary_long: S.2528 (Unleashing AI Innovation in Financial Services Act) would require each financial regulatory agency to establish, or designate, an AI Innovation Lab where regulated entities may run AI test projects under alternative compliance strategies that waive or modify specified agency regulations. Applications must describe the project, the regulation to be waived or modified, an assessment of public interest, systemic risk, anti-money laundering consistency and national security risk, a termination date, limits on size and growth, a business plan and an economic impact estimate. Agencies must decide within 120 days, extendable once by 120 days; an application still undecided after the extension is deemed approved. During an approved project, the agency may enforce the waived regulation only as set out in the strategy, but fraud and unsafe or unsound practices remain enforceable. Denied applicants may resubmit no more than two substantially similar applications, and agencies may sue to enjoin projects that present an immediate danger or specified risks. Agencies must issue regulations within 180 days of enactment after a 60-day comment period, and must submit annual reports on project outcomes beginning two years after enactment and continuing for seven years thereafter.

title: Children Harmed by AI Technology Act
summary_short: The CHAT Act would require operators of companion AI chatbots to create user accounts, verify ages, link minors' accounts to verified parental accounts, and display non-human notices every 60 minutes. The FTC enforces it, and it takes effect one year after enactment.
summary_long: The CHAT Act applies to any person that owns, operates or otherwise makes available a companion AI chatbot (software whose primary purpose is simulating interpersonal, emotional, friendship or therapeutic interaction) to individuals in the United States. Covered entities must require user accounts, verify users' ages (freezing existing accounts until age information is provided) and classify users as minors or adults. For minors they must link the account to a verified parental account, obtain verifiable parental consent, inform the parent of suicidal-ideation interactions and block access to chatbots that engage in sexually explicit communication. They must limit age-data use to what is strictly necessary, monitor for suicidal ideation and present National Suicide Prevention Lifeline contact information, and show a popup at the start of each interaction and at least every 60 minutes stating the user is not engaging with a human. The FTC must issue compliance guidance within 180 days; violations are treated as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act, and state attorneys general may bring civil actions for injunctions, compliance, damages or other relief after notice to the FTC. A safe harbor covers good-faith reliance on user-provided age information, compliance with the guidance and conformity with industry standards. The Act takes effect one year after enactment.

title: Identifying Outputs of Generative Adversarial Networks Act
summary_short: Directs the National Science Foundation to fund research on manipulated or synthesized content, including GAN-generated deepfakes, and the National Institute of Standards and Technology to support measurement research and voluntary standards for GANs. Requires a joint NSF-NIST report on public-private detection partnerships within one year of enactment.
summary_long: The Identifying Outputs of Generative Adversarial Networks Act (IOGAN Act), approved December 23, 2020, addresses research on generative adversarial networks (GANs) and comparable techniques that create or manipulate content. Section 3 directs the National Science Foundation, in consultation with other relevant Federal agencies, to support merit-reviewed, competitively awarded research on manipulated or synthesized content and information authenticity, covering digital forensic tools, watermarking, social and behavioral research, public awareness research, and awards coordinated with DARPA and IARPA. Section 4 directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology to support research on measurements and standards for GANs and other content-synthesizing technologies, to conduct outreach to stakeholders, and to consider the feasibility of ongoing public and private engagement on voluntary standards. Section 5 requires NSF and NIST to jointly submit, within one year of enactment, a report to specified congressional committees on the feasibility of research with the private sector, including digital media companies, and on policy recommendations for coordination. Section 6 defines generative adversarial network. The operative provisions impose duties on federal agencies; they do not set obligations, thresholds or penalties for private parties.

title: Deceptive Practices and Voter Intimidation Prevention Act of 2025
summary_short: Amends federal law to prohibit materially false information about time, place, manner or voter eligibility for federal elections, including AI-generated content, within 60 days before those elections, and voter intimidation or hindrance. Adds a private civil action, criminal penalties including up to 1 year's imprisonment, and Attorney General corrective communications.
summary_long: The bill, the Deceptive Practices and Voter Intimidation Prevention Act of 2025, amends the Revised Statutes (52 U.S.C. 10101) and Title 18 of the United States Code. Section 3 prohibits any person, whether acting under color of law or otherwise, from communicating or producing materially false information about the time, place or manner of federal elections, or about voter eligibility or registration status, within 60 days before such an election, with intent to impede voting. A separate provision bars using an artificial intelligence system, including a generative system, to produce such information with intent to use it for that purpose. Intentionally hindering or interfering with voting, including by operating a falsely labelled polling place, is also prohibited. Violations of the criminal provisions carry a fine or imprisonment for not more than 1 year, or both. A person aggrieved by a violation may bring a civil action for preventive relief, and the court may award attorney's fees. Section 4 directs the Attorney General, after a credible report and where state and local officials have not corrected the information, to communicate accurate corrective information, and to publish procedures within 180 days of enactment. Section 3 also directs the Sentencing Commission to review sentencing guidelines within 180 days and amends the Voting Rights Act to cover payments for not voting. Section 5 requires reports to Congress after each federal general election, made public. Section 6 gives election officials a civil action, and Section 7 makes intimidation of ballot tabulation, canvass and certification efforts a crime under the National Voter Registration Act. The bill is at the introduction stage.

title: S 2937 Act Aligning Incentives for Leadership, Excellence, and Advancement in Development Act 2025
summary_short: Creates federal civil liability for developers and deployers of artificial intelligence systems ('covered products') for harm caused by them; makes unenforceable contract and terms language that waives liability; requires foreign developers to designate a US agent before making covered products available; applies to actions commenced after enactment.
summary_long: Introduced in the Senate on 29 September 2025 and referred to the Judiciary Committee, the bill makes developers and deployers of artificial intelligence systems ('covered products') civilly liable for harm to persons, property, finances or reputation caused by those products. Developers are liable for failure to exercise reasonable care in design or warnings, breach of express warranty, or a defective condition unreasonably dangerous at sale, with strict liability for defective condition (Sec. 101). Deployers are liable as developers for substantial modification or intentional misuse (Sec. 102). Contract and terms-of-service language that waives rights or unreasonably limits liability is unenforceable (Sec. 201). Suits may be brought in federal district court by the Attorney General, state attorneys general, individuals or classes; limitations period is four years from discovery (Secs. 301, 303). State law is superseded only where it conflicts with the Act (Sec. 304). Foreign developers must designate a US agent for service of process before making covered products available in the United States and notify the Attorney General of changes within 15 days; deploying without designation is prohibited (Title IV). The Act applies to liability actions commenced on or after enactment (Sec. 501).

title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Evaluation Act of 2025
summary_short: If enacted, requires the Secretary of Energy to establish an Advanced AI Evaluation Program within 90 days; developers of AI systems trained with over 10^26 operations must participate and provide materials on request, and may not deploy without compliance, subject to fines of at least $1,000,000 per day.
summary_long: S. 2938, the Artificial Intelligence Risk Evaluation Act of 2025, introduced in the Senate on 29 September 2025 and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, would direct the Secretary of Energy to establish, within 90 days of enactment, an Advanced Artificial Intelligence Evaluation Program within the Department of Energy. The program would offer standardized and classified testing of advanced AI systems, including adversarial testing by red teams, to collect data on the likelihood of adverse AI incidents, and would provide participating entities with formal reports and recommended containment protocols. An advanced AI system is one trained with more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations. The Secretary may propose a replacement definition by rule, which takes effect only after Congress enacts a joint resolution approving it. Covered advanced AI system developers must participate in the program and, on request, provide the Secretary with code, training data, model weights, and implementation and training information. No person may deploy such a system for use in interstate or foreign commerce unless compliant. Violators are fined not less than $1,000,000 per day of violation. The Secretary must submit a plan for a permanent federal oversight framework within 360 days and update it annually. The program terminates seven years after enactment unless renewed by Congress.

title: Right to Override Act
summary_short: Requires covered health care entities using AI/CDSS to adopt override policies, bars adverse employment actions against health care professionals who override AI/CDSS outputs, and creates whistleblower protections and enforcement. Introduced bill text.
