summary_long: The Right to Override Act would require covered entities (employers, health care facilities and health plans engaged in commerce, including government) that use AI/CDSS to adopt a policy ensuring AI/CDSS outputs are not substituted for a health care professional's independent judgment and allowing timely override. Entities must inform and train staff, establish an AI/CDSS committee convening at the later of AI/CDSS adoption or 120 days after enactment, and bar sharing of override data identifying a specific professional or an inferable group, subject to exceptions. Covered entities may not take adverse employment actions against professionals who override outputs consistent with the policy requirements, or retaliate against whistleblowers. The Department of Labor may investigate and impose civil monetary penalties of up to $76,987 per violation ($769,870 for repeat violations, inflation-indexed). Individuals may file complaints and commence civil actions for damages, and state attorneys general may bring civil actions. HHS's Office for Civil Rights handles Title I complaints, including civil monetary penalties. Pre-dispute arbitration and class-action waivers are unenforceable for alleged violations. Section 303 does not protect professionals from malpractice or negligence claims, and Section 304 preserves state law and collective bargaining agreements.

title: S.305 Small Business Technological Act of 2025
summary_short: Amends Section 7(a) of the Small Business Act so the Administration may make loans for business software or cloud computing services, including AI-based business tools, covering functions such as payroll, sales, billing and accounting. Introduced bill; the text states no effective date.
summary_long: The Small Business Technological Act of 2025 (S.305, introduced) amends Section 7(a) of the Small Business Act (15 U.S.C. 636(a)) by adding a new paragraph (38). Under the new paragraph, the Administration may provide 7(a) loans, in whole or in part, to finance business software or cloud computing services, or any technology that facilitates business operations, product or service delivery, payroll processing, payment or tracking, human resources, sales and billing, or accounting, inventory, records and expenses. The paragraph expressly includes business tools that utilize artificial intelligence. A rule of construction provides that the amendment does not make earlier 7(a) loans for these purposes impermissible, does not authorize using 7(a) loans for research and development, and does not limit the definition of working capital under the Small Business Act. The bill's text sets no eligibility thresholds, penalties or effective date. The registry records its status as pending, at the introduced stage.

title: S3062 Guidelines for User Age-verification and Responsible Dialogue Act of 2025
summary_short: S. 3062 (GUARD Act, introduced 28 October 2025) would require any person who owns, operates or makes available an AI chatbot to individuals in the United States to verify users' ages, bar identified minors from AI companions, and make AI and non-professional disclosures. It also creates criminal offenses and civil penalties for chatbots that solicit minors or promote violence.
summary_long: S. 3062, the GUARD Act (introduced 28 October 2025), applies to any person who owns, operates or makes available an AI chatbot to individuals in the United States. Covered entities must require user accounts, verify users' ages with a reasonable age verification process (self-declaration and birth-date entry excluded), review verified accounts periodically, and limit, secure and delete age-verification data. Chatbots must disclose at each conversation start and every 30 minutes that they are AI, must not claim to be human when asked, must not represent themselves as licensed professionals, and must disclose they do not provide medical, legal, financial or psychological services. Covered entities must bar minors identified by age verification from AI companions. Section 4 makes it unlawful to design, develop or make available a chatbot knowing or with reckless disregard that it poses a risk of soliciting minors into sexually explicit conduct or of encouraging suicide, self-injury or violence; each offense carries a fine of up to $100,000. The Attorney General may seek injunctions and civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation, and state attorneys general may bring injunctive actions. The Act takes effect 180 days after enactment.

title: S3193 Algorithm Accountability Act 2025
summary_short: Amends Section 230 of the Communications Act of 1934 to remove liability protection for social media platforms that fail to use reasonable care in designing and operating recommendation-based algorithms causing bodily injury or death, and allows private damages suits. No commencement date is stated.
summary_long: The bill adds a new subsection (f) to Section 230 of the Communications Act of 1934 (47 U.S.C. 230) for providers of social media platforms. A provider must exercise reasonable care in the design, training, testing, deployment, operation and maintenance of a recommendation-based algorithm to prevent bodily injury or death that a reasonable and prudent person would agree was reasonably foreseeable and attributable in whole or in part to the algorithm's design characteristics or performance. Ranking by chronological order, or in response to an individual user search, is excepted, except after a user navigates beyond the initially populated search results. The duty may not be enforced by the Commission based on viewpoint protected by the First Amendment. A provider that violates the duty loses the protection of subsection (c)(1). A injured person, or a legal representative, may bring a civil action in federal district court for compensatory and punitive damages. Predispute arbitration agreements and joint-action waivers are invalid for disputes under the subsection, and courts decide their applicability. Federal and State laws at least as protective of users are not affected, and a severability clause applies. For-profit interactive computer services are covered if they meet a profile test, and services with fewer than 1,000,000 registered users, email, direct messaging, internal enterprise, certain video conferencing, and certain review, commerce, music and news platforms are excluded. Conforming amendments replace references to Section 230(f) in the Trademark Act of 1946, title 18 section 2421A, the Webb-Kenyon Act and title 31 section 5362(6). The text states no commencement date.

title: Decoupling America's Artificial Intelligence Capabilities from China Act of 2025
summary_short: Bill prohibiting US persons from advancing AI capabilities in China: bars AI technology imports from China and exports to China from 180 days after enactment, bars certain AI research and development linked to Chinese entities of concern with criminal and civil penalties, and bars certain investments in such entities from one year after enactment.
summary_long: The bill would amend title 18 to bar US persons from advancing AI capabilities within China. Sec. 3 bars importing AI or generative AI technology or intellectual property developed or produced in China, and exporting, reexporting or transferring it to or within China, from 180 days after enactment; Commerce must issue regulations within 90 days. Sec. 4 adds 18 U.S.C. §§ 2741-2743, barring US persons from intentionally conducting or aiding AI or generative AI research and development in China, for or with entities of concern, or for certain Chinese nationals, and from transferring related research information. Penalties include fines up to $100,000,000 for entities and $1,000,000 for individuals and officers, forfeiture of federal licenses, contracts and grants, five years' ineligibility for federal financial assistance, and civil suits with treble damages. Sec. 5, from one year after enactment, bars US persons from knowingly holding or managing interests in, or lending money to, Chinese entities of concern that conduct AI R&D and assist military-civil fusion, surveillance or human rights abuses, under IEEPA powers and penalties.

title: S 3275 Humanoid Robotics Oversight and Blocking of Obtainment from Totalitarians Act of 2025
summary_short: Bill would bar federal executive agencies and their contractors from buying or using humanoid robots made by covered entities tied to countries of concern, subject covered-nation investments in US humanoid-robot businesses to CFIUS review and mandatory declarations, and require a Defense Department threat report. Procurement bans apply 180 days after enactment.
summary_long: As introduced, the bill covers humanoid robots made by covered entities, including governments and political parties of countries of concern, certain foreign entities, Chinese military companies listed under NDAA section 1260H, and entities headquartered in or subject to such countries' jurisdiction. Section 3 bars executive agencies from procuring such robots and bars contractors from using them to perform awarded contracts, with a Secretary of Defense waiver for national security or research; the bans apply 180 days after enactment, and the Federal Acquisition Regulatory Council must amend the FAR within 180 days, including prime-contractor flow-down. Section 4 amends the Defense Production Act's CFIUS provisions to cover, subject to regulations, covered-nation investments in US businesses that design, test, develop or manufacture humanoid robots, and requires declarations for such covered transactions; these amendments apply to transactions proposed or pending on or after enactment. Section 5 requires the Secretary of Defense, within one year, to report to specified committees on national security threats from humanoid robots in countries of concern, including export controls, intellectual property, data privacy and security, with recommendations. The text sets no penalties.

title: S 3308 Artificial Intelligence Civil Rights Act of 2025 (Establish protections for individual rights with respect to computational algorithms)
summary_short: Proposed bill that would bar developers and deployers from offering or using covered algorithms in ways causing disparate impact on protected characteristics in consequential actions such as employment, housing and credit, and require pre-deployment evaluations, annual impact assessments and disclosures, enforced by the FTC, state attorneys general and private suits.
summary_long: Introduced federal bill that would regulate developers and deployers of covered algorithms (computational processes used for consequential actions such as employment, education, housing, health care, credit, insurance and criminal justice). It bars use or offering of such algorithms in ways causing disparate impact or discrimination on protected characteristics, subject to exceptions such as self-testing. Developers and deployers must conduct pre-deployment evaluations, with an independent auditor where harm is plausible, and deployers must conduct annual impact assessments, filing them with the FTC. Other duties include harm mitigation, certifications, written developer-deployer contracts, public disclosures, notice, a reporting mechanism and an anti-retaliation rule. Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive acts under the FTC Act. States may seek civil penalties of $15,000 per violation or 4 percent of average gross annual revenue, and individuals may sue for treble damages or $15,000 per violation. Pre-dispute arbitration agreements are unenforceable for disputes arising under the Act. The FTC must issue rules on human alternatives and appeals within two years.

title: S 3374 Secure and Feasible Exports of Chips Act of 2025
summary_short: Bill to add section 1758A to the Export Control Reform Act of 2018, requiring a license for exports, reexports and in-country transfers of advanced integrated circuits to foreign adversary countries or to entities headquartered there, and denying such license applications, from enactment.
summary_long: The bill adds new section 1758A to the Export Control Reform Act of 2018. From the date of enactment, the Secretary must require a license for the export, reexport or in-country transfer of an advanced integrated circuit to a foreign adversary country, or to an entity located in any country if the entity or its ultimate parent company is headquartered in a foreign adversary country, and must deny any application for such a license. Subsection (b) excludes circuits, and products containing them, that are not designed or marketed for data centers. Subsection (c) defines advanced integrated circuit by reference to Export Control Classification Numbers 3A090 or 4A090 or by specified total processing performance, performance density, DRAM bandwidth and interconnect bandwidth thresholds. Beginning 30 months after enactment, the Secretary may modify these technical parameters by Federal Register notice, after a majority vote of the End-User Review Committee and a briefing to specified congressional committees at least 30 days before publication. Foreign adversary country is defined by reference to 10 U.S.C. 4872(f)(2) and includes the Macau and Hong Kong Special Administrative Regions. The bill sets out no penalties.

title: An act to include certain computer-related projects in the Federal permitting program under title XLI of the FAST Act, and for other purposes
summary_short: Amends paragraph (6)(A) of Section 41001 of the FAST Act to add semiconductors, artificial intelligence and machine learning, high-performance computing, advanced computer hardware and software, quantum information science, data storage and management, and cybersecurity to a list of project types. Approved August 16, 2022.
summary_long: This Act has one operative section. Section 1 amends paragraph (6)(A) of Section 41001 of the FAST Act (42 U.S.C. 4370m(6)(A)), in the matter preceding clause (i), by inserting after 'manufacturing' a list of computer-related fields: semiconductors, artificial intelligence and machine learning, high-performance computing and advanced computer hardware and software, quantum information science and technology, data storage and data management, and cybersecurity. The title states that the purpose is to include these computer-related projects in the Federal permitting program under title XLI of the FAST Act. The text does not contain separate obligations, thresholds, enforcement provisions or definitions. The Act was approved August 16, 2022.

title: Artificial Intelligence Scam Prevention Act
summary_short: Proposed federal bill making AI-enabled impersonation fraud, including voice or image replication, unlawful; requires disclosure when AI emulating a human is used in calls or texts; extends telemarketing and robocall rules to text messages; directs FTC and FCC reports and an advisory group.
summary_long: As introduced, the bill would make it unlawful under Sec. 3(a)(1) for any person to engage in deceptive impersonation of a government, business or official, to replicate an individual's image or voice, including with artificial intelligence and with intent to defraud, or to knowingly provide substantial assistance to such conduct. Sec. 3(a)(2) treats violations as violations of an FTC unfair or deceptive practices rule, enforced by the Federal Trade Commission with its FTC Act powers. Sec. 3(b) amends the Seniors Fraud Prevention Act to add information about AI-enabled scams to an advisory office's remit. Sec. 4 extends the Telemarketing Act to text messages and video conference calls, requires disclosure when AI emulating a human is used in calls or texts, and adds a parallel disclosure duty to Communications Act section 227. Sec. 5 authorizes FTC web portal updates and complaint procedures, establishes a joint FTC-FCC AI Scam Prevention Advisory Group that terminates five years after enactment, requires FTC reports within 180 days and FCC regulations within 270 days. The bill states no penalty amounts of its own.

title: S 3555 Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act of 2025
summary_short: Would amend the Defense Production Act to let the Treasury Secretary prohibit, and require notification of, US persons' covered investments in prohibited and notifiable technologies (including AI systems) in countries of concern; also authorizes IEEPA sanctions on covered foreign persons. Sunsets seven years after enactment.
summary_long: Introduced bill (S. 3555, 119th Congress) with five titles. Title II lets the President use IEEPA powers to prohibit US persons from investing in or buying significant equity or debt of covered foreign persons, a term tied to the People's Republic of China (including Hong Kong and Macau). Title III adds Title VIII to the Defense Production Act: the Treasury Secretary may prohibit covered national security transactions by US persons, including controlled foreign entities, in prohibited technologies, which include artificial intelligence systems. Notification of such transactions, and of transactions in notifiable technologies such as AI systems, is required within 30 days after completion, with regulations due within 450 days of enactment. Exemptions cover national-interest and intelligence activities, de minimis values and listed securities. Civil penalties follow IEEPA amounts, and the Secretary may compel divestment. Title VIII also requires reports and testimony to Congress, allows a non-exhaustive public database of covered foreign persons, and protects filed information from disclosure. Title IV requires presidential reports on the Non-SDN Chinese Military-Industrial Complex Companies List. The Act ceases to have effect seven years after enactment.

title: Copyright Labeling and Ethical AI Reporting Act
summary_short: Requires persons who use training datasets of registered copyrighted works to train or release generative AI models to file a notice with the Register of Copyrights 30 days before commercial use or release. Copyright owners may sue for civil penalties.
summary_long: The bill, titled the CLEAR Act, requires any person that uses a training dataset in connection with training or release of a generative AI model to submit to the Register of Copyrights a notice containing a sufficiently detailed summary of each copyrighted work in the dataset, and the dataset's URL if it is publicly available. For models first used or released on or after the effective date, notice is due 30 days before commercial use (including internal use) or release; for earlier models, notice is due 30 days after the Register issues implementing regulations, which must be issued within 180 days of the effective date. A copyright owner may sue in a United States district court for failure to file; the court may impose a civil penalty of at least $5,000 per instance, capped at $2,500,000 in total per person per year, may enjoin use until notice is submitted, and may award attorney's fees. The Register must maintain a publicly available online database of notices. The Act takes effect 180 days after enactment.

title: NO FAKES Act of 2026
summary_short: Bill (S. 4591, reported in Senate June 24, 2026) creating a federal property right in individuals' voice and visual likeness, enforceable by civil action against unauthorized digital replicas and related products, with notice-and-takedown safe harbors for online services. Effective 180 days after enactment.
summary_long: S. 4591, reported with an amendment on June 24, 2026, would give each individual and right holder a licensable property right to authorize use of the individual's voice or visual likeness in a 'digital replica' (a newly created, highly realistic computer-generated representation) or in a product or service requiring such authorization. The post-mortem right lasts 10 years, extendable in 5-year periods on proof of active public use, and terminates no later than 70 years after death. Living-person licenses are limited to 10 years and must be written, signed and specific as to uses; minors' licenses are limited to 5 years and need court approval. Anyone who makes available an unauthorized digital replica, or a product primarily designed to produce one, is liable in a civil action, subject to exclusions for news, documentary, commentary, parody and similar uses. Remedies include statutory damages, actual damages and profits, and injunctions. Online services that register a designated agent with the Copyright Office and follow a notice-and-takedown process get a safe harbor. The bill also adds subpoenas to identify violators and preempts most state causes of action with exceptions. It applies to post-enactment conduct and takes effect 180 days after enactment.

title: Flood Level Observation, Operations, and Decision Support Act
summary_short: Section 14 directs the NOAA Administrator to establish a hydrologic research fellowship program for U.S. citizens in graduate programs, with research priorities that include applying AI and machine learning to hydrologic modeling. It also gives federal agencies direct-hire authority for fellowship graduates from fiscal year 2022 onward.
summary_long: Section 14 requires the Administrator to establish a hydrologic research fellowship program for qualified individuals: U.S. citizens enrolled in research-based graduate programs at institutions of higher education in listed fields such as hydrology, computer sciences and engineering. Selection must give preference to historically Black colleges and universities and minority-serving institutions, and fellowships last up to 2 years. Fellows are placed in executive-branch positions. The Assistant Administrator for Weather Services sets award guidelines and, with NOAA line offices, USGS, FEMA and the Army Corps of Engineers, publishes research priorities that may include applying artificial intelligence and machine learning to hydrologic modeling. From fiscal year 2022, any federal agency head may directly appoint graduates who completed a qualifying degree and the fellowship, meeting Office of Personnel Management standards, within 2 years of completing the fellowship. The section contains no enforcement provisions.

title: S.C. Code § 12-36-2120(79) -- Sales tax exemption for datacenter computer equipment and electricity
summary_short: Exempts from South Carolina sales and use tax the purchase of computer equipment used within a qualifying datacenter and the electricity used by it, for facilities certified by the Department of Commerce that meet investment and job thresholds. Applies to datacenters certified before January 1, 2032.
summary_long: Item (79) of Section 12-36-2120 exempts from the state sales and use tax (A)(1) original or replacement computers, computer equipment, and computer hardware and software purchases used within a datacenter, and (A)(2) electricity used by a datacenter and eligible business property located there; other electricity sales remain taxable. Subitem (B) defines a datacenter as a facility at a single location in South Carolina with concurrently maintainable power and cooling, a capital investment of at least fifty million dollars by a taxpayer over five years (or seventy-five million aggregate by one or more taxpayers), at least twenty-five full-time jobs at average cash compensation of 150% of per capita income (State or county, whichever is lower), and those jobs maintained for three consecutive years. Under subitems (C) and (D), the taxpayer notifies the Department of Revenue and the Department of Commerce, and may claim the exemption on eligible purchases once Commerce certifies the facility; limitation periods are suspended. Subitem (E) extends the exemption to later purchases and investments. Subitem (F) allows assessment of tax if requirements are not met and reduces the electricity exemption in proportion to qualifying jobs below twenty-five. Subitem (G) applies to datacenters certified before January 1, 2032, continues for ten years for those certified by December 31, 2031, and is then repealed.

title: South Carolina 2023 H 4754
summary_short: Adds S.C. Code § 40-57-820 to Chapter 57, Title 40. A licensee under the chapter is responsible for all work product produced by or with AI, machine learning or similar programs. Violations committed through such programs are treated as the licensee's own violations.
summary_long: The excerpt contains only Section 4 of the bill, which adds Section 40-57-820 to Article 7, Chapter 57, Title 40 of the South Carolina Code. The new section makes a licensee under the chapter responsible for any and all work product produced by the licensee or with the assistance of artificial intelligence, machine learning, or similar programs. It further provides that a violation of the chapter committed through the use of these programs is treated as if committed directly by the licensee. The excerpt states no effective date, and the text does not describe any separate enforcement procedure, penalty or definition of the programs covered.

title: South Carolina S 1037 (Protecting Children From Chatbots Act 2026)
summary_short: Adds Chapter 81 to South Carolina Code Title 39 on chatbots. Covered operators (500,000+ monthly users) must offer a limited-access mode, verify ages before enabling restricted features, add safeguards for minors, and report covered incidents to the Attorney General. Effective upon Governor's approval.
summary_long: It adds Chapter 81 to Title 39 on chatbot operators. A covered entity is an operator with 500,000 or more worldwide monthly active users, aggregated across affiliates, excluding internal, clinical, research and customer-service tools. Unverified users may access chatbots only in limited-access mode. Before enabling restricted features (personalization, proactive outreach, extended sessions, relationship simulation, explicit content), covered entities must verify age, classify users, and delete age verification data within 24 hours. Minors may use restricted features only with verifiable parental consent and parental controls. Covered entities may not design features to prioritize engagement at the expense of wellbeing, must address emotional dependence, must not falsely claim to be human, and must provide crisis messages. They must make reasonable efforts to notify emergency services about imminent risks and report covered incidents to the Attorney General within fifteen days. The Attorney General may seek injunctions and civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation, with each day a separate violation. Harmed persons and parents of harmed minors may sue for damages, fees, and punitive damages for wilful, reckless or grossly negligent violations. Waivers of these rights are void. The act takes effect upon the Governor's approval.

title: A bill to amend the South Carolina Code of Laws by adding Section 63-5-380 so as to prohibit operators of internet-based applications from using "automated decision systems" to place content on social media platforms for users under the age of eighteen who are residents of the State of South Carolina, to require operators to perform age-verification practices for certain users, to establish that a violation is an unfair or deceptive act or practice under the South Carolina Unfair Trade Practices Act, and for other purposes.
summary_short: Bill adding S.C. Code § 63-5-380. Bars operators of websites, online services and apps, including social media, from using automated decision systems for content placement for South Carolina residents under 18. Requires age verification for adult residents using such systems. Violations are unfair or deceptive trade practices.
summary_long: The bill would add Section 63-5-380 to the South Carolina Code. Under subsection (A)(1), it is unlawful for any operator of a website, online service, or online or mobile application, including any social media platform, to use an automated decision system for content placement, including feeds, posts, advertisements, or product offerings, for a user under eighteen who is a South Carolina resident. Under (A)(2), an operator that uses such a system for South Carolina residents eighteen or older must verify age through an independent third-party service that compares public records with the personal information the user entered, unless the operator uses one of two alternatives: verification of an account profile against publicly available records, or a required upload of a government-issued identification with a current photograph. Relying on such verification is a defense to an action under the section. Under (A)(3), failure to perform required age verification is prima facie evidence of a violation. Under (B)(1), a violation is an unfair or deceptive act or practice under the South Carolina Unfair Trade Practices Act, enforceable by the Attorney General through an injunction or civil penalties. Under (B)(2), a user who suffers damages may sue individually for actual damages. Under (B)(3), each use of an automated decision system in violation counts as a separate violation for each minor user who is a South Carolina resident. Subsection (C) defines an automated decision system as a computational process, including one derived from machine learning, statistics, or other data processing or artificial intelligence techniques, that makes or facilitates decisions and impacts consumers. Under Section 2, the act takes effect upon the Governor's approval. The registry lists the bill as introduced and pending.

title: South Dakota 2024 Senate Bill 79
summary_short: Revises South Dakota child pornography offenses: creates felony crimes of possessing, distributing and manufacturing child pornography, including computer-generated depictions made with artificial intelligence, with mandatory minimum prison terms for first and repeat offenses; also amends related sex-offense, sentencing and juvenile sexting provisions. The text states no effective date.
summary_long: Amends South Dakota's child pornography statutes. Section 1 revises definitions in § 22-24A-2, adding 'computer-generated child pornography', which includes an individual indistinguishable from an actual minor created by artificial intelligence or other computer technology, and a 'child-like sex doll' definition. Sections 2 to 4 create offenses of possessing (Class 4 felony), distributing (Class 3) and manufacturing (Class 2) child pornography, each with mandatory minimum prison terms for first and subsequent offenses. Section 5 counts out-of-state convictions toward second-offense status. Section 6 requires a § 22-22-1.3 assessment after conviction. Section 7 makes minor consent and mistake of age no defense. Section 8 gives an affirmative defense where the depiction is of the accused alone. Section 9 allows a departure from mandatory sentences on written findings of mitigating circumstances. Related amendments cover sentencing (§ 22-6-11), indecent exposure (§ 22-24-1.2; a prior felony conviction under sections 2 to 4 makes it a Class 6 felony), a nudity exemption (§ 22-24A-20), the sex-crime list (§ 22-24B-1) and juvenile sexting (§ 26-10-33; a Class 1 misdemeanor for minors). Section 15 repeals § 22-24A-3.

title: Cybersecurity Risk Management, Strategy, Governance, and Incident Disclosure
summary_short: SEC final rule requiring public companies subject to Exchange Act reporting to file a Form 8-K Item 1.05 within four business days of determining a cybersecurity incident is material, and to describe cybersecurity risk management, strategy and governance in annual reports. Effective September 5, 2023.
summary_long: Adopted by the SEC (Release Nos. 33-11216; 34-97989), this rule amends Regulation S-K, Regulation S-T, and Securities Act and Exchange Act forms and rules for public companies subject to Exchange Act reporting. It adds Form 8-K Item 1.05, requiring disclosure of the material aspects of the nature, scope and timing of a material cybersecurity incident and its material or reasonably likely material impact, within four business days of the materiality determination; information not determined or unavailable at filing may be added by Form 8-K amendment. The Attorney General may, by written notice to the Commission, delay disclosure that poses a substantial risk to national security or public safety, for up to 30 days, extendable by a further 30 days and, in extraordinary circumstances, a final 60 days. Item 106 of Regulation S-K requires annual-report descriptions of processes for assessing, identifying and managing material cybersecurity risks, whether risks have materially affected the registrant, and board and management oversight of those risks. Foreign private issuers furnish incident information on Form 6-K and report under Form 20-F. An untimely Item 1.05 filing does not cause loss of Form S-3 eligibility, and Item 1.05 is added to the safe-harbor list in Rules 13a-11(c) and 15d-11(c). Cybersecurity disclosures are to be presented in Inline XBRL. Asset-backed issuers are exempted from the new rules.

title: Regulation S-P: Privacy of Consumer Financial Information and Safeguarding Customer Information (amendments)
summary_short: SEC rule amending Regulation S-P requires covered financial institutions (broker-dealers, investment companies, registered investment advisers, funding portals, transfer agents) to adopt incident response programs, notify affected individuals of sensitive customer information breaches, and keep compliance records. Effective 2 August 2024.
summary_long: The amendments to Regulation S-P, adopted by the SEC, require covered institutions (broker-dealers, investment companies, registered investment advisers, funding portals and transfer agents) to adopt written policies and procedures for an incident response program covering unauthorized access to or use of customer information. The program must assess incidents, contain and control them, and notify each affected individual whose sensitive customer information was, or is reasonably likely to have been, accessed or used without authorization, as soon as practicable and no later than 30 days after becoming aware of the incident. Notice is not required if a reasonable investigation determines that sensitive customer information has not been and is not reasonably likely to be used in a manner that would result in substantial harm or inconvenience. Covered institutions must oversee their service providers, which must notify them as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of a breach affecting a customer information system. The Attorney General may, by written notice to the Commission, allow delay of notice for national security or public safety reasons. The amendments extend the safeguards and disposal rules to transfer agents, broaden the customer information covered, and require written records documenting compliance. The annual privacy notice delivery provisions are conformed to a statutory exception. The rule is effective 2 August 2024.

title: Tools to Address Known Exploitation by Immobilizing Technological Deepfakes on Websites and Networks Act (TAKE IT DOWN Act), Pub. L. 119-12
summary_short: Makes knowingly publishing nonconsensual intimate visual depictions, including deepfakes, a federal crime and requires covered online platforms to create notice-and-removal processes and remove flagged depictions within 48 hours of a valid request; the FTC enforces the platform duties.
summary_long: Adds section 223(h) to the Communications Act of 1934, making it a federal offence to knowingly publish, via an interactive computer service in interstate or foreign commerce, a nonconsensual intimate visual depiction of an identifiable individual; deepfakes are covered. Publication of depictions of adults requires harm or intent to harm; depictions of minors require intent to abuse, humiliate, harass, degrade or sexually gratify. Penalties are up to 2 years' imprisonment for adult offences and 3 years for minor offences, plus fines; threats are punished alike, and courts must order forfeiture and restitution. Law-enforcement, good-faith reporting and medical or educational disclosures are excepted. Covered platforms (public services primarily hosting user-generated content, excluding broadband, email and mainly preselected content) must, within one year of enactment, set up a removal-request process with clear notice, and remove reported depictions and identical copies within 48 hours of a valid request. Platforms are not liable for claims arising from good-faith removal of apparently unlawful material. The FTC enforces platform duties as violations of a rule on unfair or deceptive practices.

title: Ensuring Likeness, Voice, and Image Security Act of 2024 (Public Chapter No. 588, HB 2091/SB 2096)
summary_short: Tennessee statute that recognizes a property right in an individual's name, photograph, voice or likeness and creates civil liability for unauthorized commercial use. It also reaches anyone who distributes a technology whose primary purpose is producing an identifiable individual's likeness or voice. Effective July 1, 2024.
summary_long: The Act amends the Tennessee Personal Rights Protection Act (Tenn. Code Ann. Title 47, Chapter 25, Part 11) and renames it the Ensuring Likeness, Voice, and Image Security Act of 2024. It adds 'voice' as a protected attribute with a definition that covers both actual and simulated voices, and it states that every individual has a property right in the use of their name, photograph, voice or likeness. Section 6 makes a person liable to a civil action for knowingly using an individual's name, photograph, voice or likeness for advertising, fundraising or sales without prior consent, with parental or guardian consent required for minors and executor, heirs or devisees for deceased individuals. Liability also attaches to knowingly making an individual's voice or likeness publicly available without authorization, and to distributing an algorithm, software, tool or other technology whose primary purpose is producing a particular identifiable individual's photograph, voice or likeness. Section 5 sets a post-death non-use termination period. Section 10 provides fair-use exceptions for news, commentary, scholarship, satire, parody, certain audiovisual representations and fleeting or incidental uses, and Section 11 extends a knowledge element to what a defendant reasonably should have known. Section 8 allows a contracting person to bring enforcement actions for recording-artist contracts. The Act specifies civil actions only and states no damages amounts. It takes effect July 1, 2024.

title: Tennessee House Bill 2163 (Sexual Exploitation of Children)
summary_short: Amends Tennessee Code Annotated Section 39-17-1002 on the sexual exploitation of children so that covered images include computer-generated images, including images created, adapted or modified by artificial intelligence, and adds definitions of 'artificial intelligence' and 'generative artificial intelligence'. Takes effect July 1, 2024.
summary_long: Amends Tennessee Code Annotated Section 39-17-1002 (Title 39), which concerns the sexual exploitation of children. Section 1 replaces subdivision (2)(E) so that covered images include any computer image or computer-generated image, expressly including an image created, adapted or modified by artificial intelligence, whatever the means of making or producing it. Section 2 adds two definitions to the same section. 'Artificial intelligence' means a machine-based system that, for human-defined objectives, makes predictions, recommendations or decisions, influences real and virtual environments, or learns and improves from data sets, or that solves tasks requiring human-like perception, cognition, planning, learning, communication or physical action; it includes generative artificial intelligence. 'Generative artificial intelligence' means an AI system capable of creating new content or data, including text, images, audio or video, when prompted by an individual. Section 3 sets the effective date as July 1, 2024. The document states no penalty amounts, enforcement authority, private right of action or exceptions. It adds to existing offense provisions and does not set separate AI-specific duties on developers or deployers.

title: Tennessee Information Protection Act (Public Chapter No. 408, HB 1181/SB 73)
summary_short: Tennessee's consumer data privacy statute gives state residents access, correction, deletion, portability and opt-out rights and imposes controller and processor duties on large businesses meeting revenue and consumer-count thresholds; the attorney general enforces it. Effective 1 July 2025.
summary_long: Adds a Tennessee consumer personal-information part (Title 47, Ch. 18). Covers businesses producing products or services targeting Tennessee residents that exceed $25 million in revenue and meet a consumer-count or data-sale test; excludes state bodies, financial institutions, HIPAA-covered entities, nonprofits and higher-education institutions. Consumers gain access, correction, deletion, portability and opt-out rights (sale, targeted advertising, certain profiling); controllers must respond within 45 days, limit collection, secure data, obtain consent for sensitive data, publish privacy notices and conduct data protection assessments for targeted advertising, sales, certain profiling and sensitive data. Processors act under binding contracts. The attorney general enforces exclusively after a 60-day cure notice, with civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation and treble damages for willful or knowing violations; no private right of action. A NIST-conforming privacy program is an affirmative defense. Preempts conflicting local ordinances; effective July 1, 2025.

title: Advanced Manufacturing Investment Credit Rules Under Sections 48D and 50(a)
summary_short: IRS final regulations implementing 25% advanced manufacturing investment tax credit (section 48D) for U.S. semiconductor facilities, setting eligibility, qualified property and construction-start rules, and a 10-year recapture rule for material expansion of semiconductor capacity in foreign countries of concern. Applies to property placed in service after December 31, 2022.
summary_long: Final Treasury/IRS regulations (TD 10009, published 23 October 2024) under sections 48D and 50 of the Internal Revenue Code, implementing the advanced manufacturing investment credit added by section 107 of the CHIPS Act of 2022. The credit equals 25 percent of the qualified investment in an advanced manufacturing facility of an eligible taxpayer, for qualified property placed in service after 31 December 2022. No credit is allowed for property whose construction begins after 31 December 2026. Qualified property is tangible depreciable property integral to the operation of the facility, constructed or reconstructed by the taxpayer or acquired with original use commencing with the taxpayer; buildings used for offices and administrative functions are excluded. A facility qualifies if its primary purpose, measured by more than 50 percent of potential output, is manufacturing semiconductors or semiconductor manufacturing equipment. An eligible taxpayer is not a foreign entity of concern and has made no applicable transaction in the taxable year. The rules define semiconductor, semiconductor manufacturing and semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and set beginning-of-construction tests (physical work test, five percent safe harbor, continuity requirement). Under section 50(a), an applicable transaction, including a significant transaction involving material expansion of semiconductor capacity in a foreign country of concern, made before the end of the 10-year period after placing property in service triggers recapture of the credit; legacy semiconductors are excepted. The regulations cross-reference elective payment rules in section 1.48D-6.

title: Provisions Pertaining to U.S. Investments in Certain National Security Technologies and Products in Countries of Concern (31 CFR Part 850)
summary_short: Treasury rule (31 CFR part 850), effective 2 January 2025, requiring U.S. persons to notify Treasury of, or barring them from, investments in Chinese, Hong Kong or Macau entities active in semiconductors, quantum technologies and AI, according to technology-specific criteria and compute thresholds.
summary_long: Part 850 implements Executive Order 14105 under IEEPA. It covers U.S. persons' acquisitions of equity or contingent equity, equity-like loans, conversions, greenfield and brownfield projects, joint ventures and limited-partner stakes in non-U.S. funds involving a 'covered foreign person': a person of a country of concern (as listed in the Order's Annex) engaged in a covered activity, or a person that derives more than 50% of its revenue, net income, capital expenditure or operating expenses from such persons. Prohibited transactions involve EDA software, front-end, advanced-packaging and EUV equipment, advanced chip design and fabrication (non-planar or 16/14 nm logic, 128-layer NAND, 18 nm DRAM), advanced packaging, supercomputers, quantum computers and components, military or surveillance AI, AI trained with more than 10^25 operations (10^24 using primarily biological sequence data), and listed entities. Other chip activities and AI for military, cyber or robotic uses, or trained with more than 10^23 operations, are notifiable within 30 days. Exceptions cover publicly traded securities, registered funds, LP commitments of $2 million or less, buyouts of country-of-concern interests and pre-2025 binding commitments; Treasury may grant national interest exemptions. Violations carry IEEPA civil penalties (greater of $250,000, inflation-adjusted, or twice the transaction value), criminal penalties and divestment orders.

title: Texas Business & Commerce Code ch. 503, Capture or Use of Biometric Identifier (CUBI), sec. 503.001
summary_short: Texas statute prohibiting capture of biometric identifiers (retina or iris scans, fingerprints, voiceprints, hand or face geometry) for a commercial purpose without notice and consent. Also limits disclosure, requires reasonable-care storage and destruction, and imposes civil penalties up to $25,000 per violation. Originally effective April 1, 2009.
summary_long: Prohibits a person from capturing a biometric identifier (retina or iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, or record of hand or face geometry) for a commercial purpose unless the person first informs the individual and receives consent. Images found on the internet or other public sources do not count as notice or consent unless the individual made them public. A person possessing such an identifier may not sell, lease or otherwise disclose it, subject to listed exceptions (disappearance or death, financial transactions, federal or state statute, warrants), and must store and protect it with at least the care applied to other confidential information. Destruction is due within a reasonable time and no later than the first anniversary of the purpose expiring; the period extends where another law requires longer retention, and is presumed to expire on termination of employment for identifiers an employer collected for security. The Attorney General may sue for a civil penalty of up to $25,000 per violation. Exclusions cover voiceprints held by financial institutions, AI training, processing and storage (unless used to uniquely identify a person), and security or fraud purposes. Identifiers captured to train an AI system and later used commercially fall under the section's possession and destruction duties and penalties. Amended in 2009, 2017 and 2025 (2025 amendment effective January 1, 2026).
text_version: Business & Commerce Code ch. 503 as of 2026 (incl. H.B. 149, 89th Leg., eff. 2026-01-01)

title: H.B. 149, Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (89th Legislature, R.S.)
summary_short: Texas H.B. 149 creates Business & Commerce Code Subtitle D on artificial intelligence: prohibited AI uses, a consumer disclosure duty, Attorney General enforcement with civil penalties, a regulatory sandbox and an AI council, and amends biometric and processor rules. Effective January 1, 2026.
summary_long: The Act adds Business & Commerce Code Subtitle D. Chapter 551 defines AI system and applicability to persons who do business in Texas, produce products used by Texas residents, or develop or deploy AI in Texas. Chapter 552 requires governmental agencies and health care providers to disclose AI interaction to consumers and bars AI developed or deployed to incite self-harm or crime, government social scoring, government biometric identification without consent, intentional unlawful discrimination, and listed deepfake and child-sexual material. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement, with a 60-day cure notice, civil penalties of $10,000 to $12,000 for curable violations, $80,000 to $200,000 for uncurable ones, and $2,000 to $40,000 per day for continued violations, and no private right of action. Chapter 553 creates a sandbox for up to 36 months of testing with waivers of certain laws, except Subchapter B of Chapter 552. Chapter 554 creates a seven-member Texas Artificial Intelligence Council with advisory powers and no power to adopt binding rules. The Act amends Business & Commerce Code Sections 503.001 (biometric identifiers, including AI training exemptions) and 541.104 (processor duties), and state agency review and IT reporting rules. Section 9 conditions certain agency duties on appropriations. Effective January 1, 2026.

title: Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (HB 1709)
summary_short: Texas Responsible AI Governance Act (HB 1709, bill text): duties for developers, distributors and deployers of high-risk AI systems used in consequential decisions; prohibited AI uses; consumer disclosures; attorney general enforcement with civil penalties. Takes effect September 1, 2025.
summary_long: HB 1709 would add Chapter 551 to the Business & Commerce Code for non-small businesses operating in or serving Texas and for developers, distributors and deployers of high-risk AI systems. High-risk systems are substantial factors in consequential decisions, such as employment, education, financial, housing, insurance, health-care or criminal-case decisions. Developers must use reasonable care against algorithmic discrimination and give deployers a High-Risk Report; developers and distributors must correct or withdraw non-compliant systems. Deployers must use reasonable care, maintain a risk management policy, complete annual and post-modification impact assessments, and notify authorities and affected consumers of discrimination. Consumers must be told when they interact with such a system and may appeal certain consequential decisions. It bans AI uses for manipulation, social scoring, certain biometric identification, sensitive-attribute inference and unlawful deepfakes. It creates a sandbox program of up to 36 months, an Artificial Intelligence Council and an AI workforce grant program. The attorney general enforces the chapter after a 30-day cure notice, with fines of $50,000 to $100,000 per uncured violation and $80,000 to $200,000 for prohibited uses. The Act takes effect September 1, 2025.

title: Texas HB 3512 (Relating to artificial intelligence training programs for certain employees and officials of state agencies and local governments.)
summary_short: Requires Texas state agencies and local governments to have covered employees and officials complete annual artificial intelligence training alongside cybersecurity training, and directs the Department of Information Resources to certify AI training programs. Effective 1 September 2025.
summary_long: Amends Texas Government Code Chapter 2054 and related provisions. State agencies must identify employees who use a computer for at least 25 percent of their duties, and those employees and elected or appointed officers must complete an annual cybersecurity training program and an annual artificial intelligence training program. Local governments must identify employees and officials with access to a local government computer system and require the same two trainings annually. Local governing bodies must verify and report completion to the department and require periodic audits. The Department of Information Resources must annually certify at least five AI training programs for state and local government employees, update certification standards, ensure AI programs are equal in length to the cybersecurity programs, and publish the certified list annually. Local governments applying for grants under Chapter 772 must certify compliance; a local government determined non-compliant must repay the grant award and is ineligible for another grant until the second anniversary of the ineligibility determination. School district cybersecurity coordinators are covered under Education Code Section 11.175(h-1). The department must adopt implementing rules as soon as practicable after the effective date. The Act takes effect September 1, 2025.

title: H.B. 4, Texas Data Privacy and Security Act (88th Legislature, R.S.)
summary_short: Texas Data Privacy and Security Act: adds Chapter 541 to the Business & Commerce Code, giving Texas consumers rights over their personal data and imposing duties on controllers and processors that conduct business in Texas or produce products consumed by its residents. Enforced by the attorney general; in force from July 1, 2024.
summary_long: Adds Chapter 541 (Consumer Data Protection) to the Business & Commerce Code. It applies to persons that conduct business in Texas or produce products or services consumed by Texas residents, excluding state agencies, financial institutions, HIPAA-covered entities, nonprofits, higher education institutions and certain electric utilities; small businesses are excluded except for a consent rule on sales of sensitive data. Consumers may confirm, access, correct, delete, port and opt out of targeted advertising, data sales and certain profiling. Controllers must respond to requests within 45 days, provide an appeal process, offer two or more request methods, limit collection, secure data, and obtain consent for sensitive data, and must post privacy notices, with sale notices for sensitive or biometric data. Processors act under controller contracts. Controllers must assess processing for targeted advertising, sales, risky profiling and sensitive data. The attorney general has exclusive enforcement authority and may issue civil investigative demands; a written notice and 30-day opportunity to cure apply before action, and violations carry civil penalties of up to $7,500 each. No private right of action is created, and local ordinances are preempted. Chapter 541 takes effect July 1, 2024, with one provision effective January 1, 2025.

title: Texas SB 1188 (AI in Electronic Health Records 2025)
summary_short: Texas SB 1188 adds Health and Safety Code Chapter 183 on electronic health records. It requires U.S. storage, limits access and amendments, mandates record fields including biological sex, gives minors' parents access, permits practitioners' AI diagnostic use with disclosure, and sets agency and attorney general enforcement, effective September 1, 2025.
summary_long: SB 1188 adds Chapter 183 to the Texas Health and Safety Code. Section 183.001 defines terms, including covered entity, which includes health care practitioners but excludes listed facilities and waiver providers. Section 183.002 requires covered entities to keep electronic health records physically in the United States or a U.S. territory, limits access to staff with employment-related need, and requires reasonable safeguards. Section 183.003 requires records to include an option to record metabolic health and diet communications between covered entities. Section 183.004 bars collecting, storing or sharing credit score or voter registration status in records. Section 183.005 permits practitioners to use AI for diagnostic purposes under listed conditions, including review of AI-created records, and requires disclosure of that use to patients. Section 183.006 requires systems for minors' records to allow parents or guardians complete access, subject to legal restrictions. Section 183.007 requires a separate space recording biological sex and sexual development disorders, and requires decision tools to use the recorded biological sex. Section 183.008 limits amendments to biological sex. Sections 183.009 and 183.010 require investigations and allow disciplinary action after three or more violations. Section 183.011 allows attorney general injunctions and civil penalties of up to $5,000, $25,000 or $250,000 depending on culpability. Section 183.012 requires an memorandum of understanding and rules. Section 2 applies the chapter to records prepared on or after the effective date, and the storage rule to storage from January 1, 2026. Section 4 sets the effective date as September 1, 2025.

title: Texas SB 6 (89th Legislature, R.S., 2025) -- relating to electric service for large loads (Utilities Code amendments)
summary_short: Texas SB 6 (2025) amends the Utilities Code and Water Code on electric service to large loads, mainly in the ERCOT power region. It covers interconnection standards, cost and financial commitment rules, disclosure, curtailment, and water-corporation power generation, effective immediately or September 1, 2025.
summary_long: Texas SB 6 amends the Utilities Code and Water Code on electric service for large loads. It directs the Public Utility Commission (PUC) to set interconnection standards for new or expanded loads above a demand threshold, set by default at 75 megawatts in the ERCOT power region. The standards cover disclosure of competing requests, a flat study fee of at least $100,000, site control, uniform financial commitments with conditional refunds, and cost contribution by large load customers. Large loads with on-site backup generation that can serve at least 50 percent of on-site demand must disclose it, and ERCOT may direct them to deploy it or curtail load. Power generation companies must notify ERCOT before netting an existing stand-alone generation resource with a new large load; the PUC may approve, deny or condition such arrangements after an ERCOT study. Loads interconnected after December 31, 2025 must have curtailment protocols, and ERCOT must procure demand reductions from large loads of at least 75 megawatts. Water or sewer corporations may generate power for their own water uses and, if they meet conditions and register, sell excess power. The PUC must evaluate transmission cost allocation and amend rules by December 31, 2026. The Act takes effect immediately if passed by two-thirds of each house, otherwise on September 1, 2025.

title: S.B. 751, relating to the creation of a criminal offense for fabricating a deceptive video with intent to influence the outcome of an election
summary_short: Texas Election Code amendment creating a criminal offense for a person who, intending to injure a candidate or influence an election result, creates a deep fake video and causes it to be published or distributed within 30 days of an election. Takes effect September 1, 2019.
summary_long: S.B. 751 (86(R) session) amends Section 255.004 of the Texas Election Code by adding Subsections (d) and (e). Subsection (d) makes it an offense for a person, with intent to injure a candidate or influence the result of an election, to create a deep fake video and cause it to be published or distributed within 30 days of an election. Subsection (e) defines 'deep fake video' as a video, created with the intent to deceive, that appears to depict a real person performing an action that did not occur in reality. Section 2 provides that the Act takes effect September 1, 2019. The text states no penalty amount, exceptions or enforcing authority. The Senate passed the bill 31-0, the House passed it with amendment 141-3 with two present not voting, and the Senate concurred in the House amendment 30-0 on May 25, 2019. The governor's approval date line is blank in this document.

title: Texas SB 815 (Use of AI systems in Utilization Reviews 2025)
summary_short: Texas SB 815 bars utilization review agents from using automated decision systems to make, wholly or partly, adverse health care determinations, exempting administrative and fraud-detection uses, and expands the content of adverse-determination notices. Applies to plans delivered or renewed from January 1, 2026.
summary_long: SB 815 amends Chapter 4201 of the Texas Insurance Code on utilization review. Section 1 adds definitions of 'algorithm', 'artificial intelligence system' and 'automated decision system'. Section 2 provides that a utilization review agent may not use an automated decision system to make, wholly or partly, an adverse determination; lets the commissioner audit and inspect such use at any time; and exempts use for administrative support or fraud-detection functions. Section 3 expands the required contents of notices of adverse determinations to include principal reasons, the clinical basis, the source and description of screening criteria and review procedures, and the complaint and appeal process, including appeal to an independent review organization. Section 4 applies the amended chapter to utilization review for health benefit plans delivered, issued for delivery, or renewed on or after January 1, 2026; earlier review remains under prior law. Section 5 sets the effective date as September 1, 2025. The text states no penalties.

title: Texas Tax Code § 151.359 -- Property used in certain data centers; temporary exemption
summary_short: Exempts electricity, equipment and software used in large single-occupant Texas data centers from state sales and use tax for 10 or 15 years, if the Comptroller certifies the center and it creates 20 well-paid jobs and invests at least $200 million.
summary_long: Section 151.359 of the Texas Tax Code exempts from state sales and use tax the tangible personal property necessary to operate a qualifying data center: electricity, electrical and cooling systems, generators, servers, storage, network equipment, racks, software and related components. A data center must occupy at least 100,000 square feet in a single building used by a single qualifying occupant. Certification by the Comptroller requires that, on or after 1 September 2013, the occupant, owner or operator create at least 20 qualifying jobs in the county, paying at least 120% of the county average weekly wage, and invest at least $200 million over five years. The exemption runs from certification for 10 years, or 15 years if investment reaches $250 million. Office supplies, short leases, taxable services and local sales taxes are excluded, as are centers with former Chapter 313 value-limitation agreements. Registration numbers are revoked if requirements are not met, and the taxes become due with penalty and interest.

title: Utah Code § 59-12-104 -- Sales and use tax exemptions (machinery, equipment, and normal operating repair parts for a new or expanding data center)
summary_short: Utah Code 59-12-104 lists sales and use tax exemptions. Item (84) exempts purchases or leases of machinery, equipment and repair parts by a qualifying data center or its occupant, when used in its operation and with an economic life of one or more years. Effective 7/1/2026, superseded 1/1/2027.
summary_long: Utah Code 59-12-104 is the exemptions section of the Sales and Use Tax Act (Chapter 12). Exemptions from the taxes imposed by the chapter are listed in numbered items (1) to (103), covering, among others, government purchases, vending, airline in-flight sales, farming, prescription and medical items, manufacturing, mining and refining equipment, semiconductor materials, industrial energy, school and fundraising sales, and disaster-related imports. Item (84) exempts amounts paid or charged for a purchase or lease, by a qualifying data center or an occupant of a qualifying data center, of machinery, equipment, or normal operating repair or replacement parts that are used in the operation of the data center or the occupant's operations there and have an economic life of one or more years. The excerpt does not define qualifying data center. The header states the text is effective 7/1/2026 and superseded 1/1/2027, and the text notes it was amended by Chapter 433, 2026 General Session. The excerpt contains no enforcement provisions and no thresholds for item (84) beyond the economic-life test.
