title: Utah House Bill 148
summary_short: Utah HB 148 (2024) amends Utah's criminal code on sexual images: it redefines child and vulnerable-adult sexual abuse material, criminalizes distributing intimate images without consent, and adds an offense for distributing counterfeit (edited) intimate images, effective May 1, 2024.
summary_long: HB 148 (2024) amends Utah's criminal code on sexual images. Section 1 amends the definitions in 76-5b-103, including child sexual abuse material, which covers images created, adapted or modified to appear that an identifiable minor is engaging in sexually explicit conduct, and vulnerable adult sexual abuse material. Section 2 amends 76-5b-203 to make it an offense to knowingly distribute an intimate image of an adult without consent where the distribution causes or would cause emotional distress or harm, subject to listed exceptions; the base offense is a class A misdemeanor, and a third degree felony on a second or subsequent conviction. Section 3 amends 76-5b-204 on sexual extortion, with penalties for adult actors ranging from third degree to first degree felonies depending on the victim and aggravating circumstances. Section 4 adds 76-5b-205, unlawful distribution of a counterfeit intimate image (an edited or altered depiction of an identifiable individual's likeness), a class A misdemeanor, with an aggravated offense where the depicted individual is a child. Sections 2 and 4 exempt internet service providers, interactive computer services and hosting companies under stated conditions; hosting companies must remove counterfeit images immediately upon notice to keep that exemption. The text does not mention artificial intelligence. Effective date: May 1, 2024.

title: Utah H.B. 366 (Criminal Justice Amendments 2024
summary_short: Amends Utah criminal justice provisions so that courts, magistrates and the Board of Pardons and Parole may not rely solely on an algorithm or risk assessment tool score in diversion, sentencing, pretrial release, probation and parole decisions. Effective May 1, 2024.
summary_long: House Bill 366 (2024) amends several Utah criminal justice statutes in Sections 9 to 14 of the bill and takes effect May 1, 2024 (Section 15). In each amended section, the court, magistrate or board may not rely solely on an algorithm or risk assessment tool score: in approving a diversion agreement (77-2-5(11)), in determining the appropriate sentence (77-18-103(9)), in determining pretrial release (77-20-205(9)(b)), in deciding whether parole should be granted or terminated (77-27-5(8)), and in probation decisions (77-18-105(9)(b)). Other amendments require a presentence investigation report to include findings from any screening and assessment of the defendant (77-18-103(2)(c)), cap a diversion program at two years (77-2-5(10)), and require the court to consider a defendant's ability to pay a diversion fee on request, with the fee not to exceed the suggested fine in the Uniform Fine Schedule (77-2-5(7), (9)). Section 14 requires the Administrative Office of the Courts to submit case data to the Commission on Criminal and Juvenile Justice every six months, including a convicted defendant's total pretrial risk assessment score (78A-2-109.5(2)(i), (3)). The bill text provided contains no separate penalty or enforcement provisions.

title: H.B. 418 Data Sharing Amendments (Digital Choice Act)
summary_short: H.B. 418 (Utah Digital Choice Act, new ch. 75) covers social media services, meaning public sites or apps with account-holder content, for users located in Utah. On request, a service must provide a consumer's personal data, including the social graph, in portable, usable form. Social media companies must offer a transparent, third-party-accessible interoperability interface that lets users share personal data across designated services. Most provisions take effect 1 July 2026.
summary_long: H.B. 418 (Utah Digital Choice Act, new ch. 75) covers social media services, meaning public sites or apps with account-holder content, for users located in Utah. On request, a service must provide a consumer's personal data, including the social graph, in portable, usable form. Social media companies must offer a transparent, third-party-accessible interoperability interface that lets users share personal data across designated services. The interface must use an open protocol, be offered on non-discriminatory terms, be documented, and may carry a reasonable fee for requests above company-set thresholds. Shared data requires user consent and reasonable security. Inferences, proprietary algorithms and certain proprietary-format data need not be provided. The Division of Consumer Protection enforces the chapter, may impose administrative fines and seek civil penalties of up to $2,500 per violation, and may identify open protocols that give companies a rebuttable presumption of non-discriminatory access. Violating an order carries a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation. Most provisions take effect 1 July 2026; section 13-75-301 takes effect 7 May 2025.

title: H.B. 452 Artificial Intelligence Amendments (mental health chatbots)
summary_short: Enacts Utah Code 13-72a and 58-60-118 regulating mental health chatbots that use generative AI. Suppliers may not sell or share Utah users' health information or chat input, must restrict and disclose advertising and disclose AI status, and may file a policy for an affirmative defense. Takes effect May 7, 2025.
summary_long: H.B. 452 amends Utah Code 13-2-1 to add a new Chapter 72a to the chapters administered by the Division of Consumer Protection, and enacts Chapter 72a and 58-60-118. It defines mental health chatbot, generative artificial intelligence and Utah user, the last by location in the state. Suppliers may not sell or share individually identifiable health information or user input of a Utah user with third parties, subject to exceptions for disclosures to a health care provider with consent, to a health plan on request, and to associated third parties under HIPAA-referenced security provisions. A supplier may not use a mental health chatbot to advertise unless the advertisement is clearly identified and sponsorships and affiliations are disclosed, and may not use user input to select or customize advertising, except for advertising the chatbot itself. The chatbot must disclose that it is artificial intelligence and not a human before access, at the start of an interaction after seven days of non-use, and when asked. The Division of Consumer Protection enforces the chapter, with administrative fines of up to $2,500 per violation; courts may grant injunctions, disgorgement and fines of up to $2,500 per violation, and impose civil penalties of up to $5,000 for violating an order. Under 58-60-118, a supplier has an affirmative defense to liability under 58-1-501 if it created, maintained and implemented a written policy covering listed matters such as therapist involvement, testing, harm reporting and risk response, keeps related documentation, files the policy with the division for a fee, and complies with it. The defense does not bar division actions and does not recognize a chatbot as a therapist. The chapter contains a severability clause. The bill takes effect May 7, 2025.

title: Utah HB 464 (Social Media Amendments)
summary_short: Utah HB 464 amends the state's electronic communication harassment offense (Sec. 1) and enacts a civil action by minor account holders or their parents against social media companies for adverse mental health outcomes linked to excessive use of algorithmically curated services (Secs. 2-7), effective May 1 and October 1, 2024.
summary_long: Amends Utah Code 76-9-201 (electronic communication harassment). Defines terms and makes it an offense, with intent to intimidate, abuse, threaten, harass, frighten or disrupt, to repeatedly contact a person, insult or threaten them, overload an electronic communication system, or publish or misuse personal identifying information; violations are class B or class A misdemeanors. An adult who publicly discloses a minor's personal identifying information while consciously disregarding a substantial risk of resulting harm commits a class A misdemeanor, and a minor victim has a civil right of action for damages, attorney fees and costs. Enacts 78B-3-1101 to 78B-3-1106 creating a civil action by a Utah minor account holder or parent against a social media company for an adverse mental health outcome diagnosed by a licensed provider and caused by excessive use of an algorithmically curated social media service. Claimants receive a rebuttable presumption of causation. A company that limits minors' use to three hours per 24 hours, blocks access from 10:30 p.m. to 6:30 a.m., requires parental consent and disables engagement driven design elements is entitled to a rebuttable presumption of no causation. Recovery is the greater of $10,000 per outcome or actual damages, plus fees and costs. Waivers of these protections are void. Section 8 repeals Sections 13-63-101 to 13-63-701. Part 11 takes effect October 1, 2024; other provisions take effect May 1, 2024.

title: Utah House Bill 534
summary_short: Amends Sections 53B-26-301 and 53B-26-302 to establish a deep technology talent initiative, under which the board may fund employer-partnered deep technology programs at named Utah institutions of higher education, subject to appropriations and advisory council review. Effective 05/01/24.
summary_long: The instrument amends the definitions in Section 53B-26-301 and the deep technology initiative in Section 53B-26-302. Deep technology means technology leading to new products and innovations based on scientific discovery or meaningful engineering innovation; artificial intelligence is one of several listed fields it may include. Subject to appropriations, the board develops and oversees a talent initiative that funds expanded undergraduate and graduate programs and stackable credentials. An institution of higher education partnering with employers submits a proposal listing specified elements, such as enrollment estimates, employer commitments and requested funding. The advisory council reviews proposals against listed criteria and recommends funding; the board may fund programs on or before September 1 of each fiscal year. Funded institutions report annually to the board, which reports by November 1 each year to two legislative committees. The provisions set no sanctions. The advisory council is created in Section 53B-26-303, which is not in the text provided.

title: S.B. 131 Information Technology Act Amendments (synthetic media in political advertising)
summary_short: Amends Utah election code to require disclosure labels and tamper-evident provenance for paid political audio or visual communications containing AI-generated synthetic media, with court-imposed civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation; adds an AI-use aggravating factor to criminal sentencing. Effective May 1, 2024; sentencing provision July 1, 2024.
summary_long: Section 1 creates Section 20A-11-1104, effective May 1, 2024. It applies to audio or visual communications that are paid for by a candidate campaign committee, political action committee, political issues committee, political party, or a person using a contribution; that are intended to influence voting for or against a candidate or ballot proposition in an election or primary in the state; and that contain synthetic media. Audio containing synthetic audio media must include spoken statements of the words 'Contains content generated by AI' at the beginning and end. Visual communications must display specified wording throughout each portion containing synthetic media, varying by whether the content is video, image, or both. Creators or sponsors who publish such online communications viewable, audible, or accessible in the state must ensure embedded tamper-evident digital content provenance disclosing the initial author and creator, subsequent editors, and any use of generative artificial intelligence. In a civil action to enforce the section, a court may impose a civil penalty not to exceed $1,000 per violation. A creator excludes a person that solely provides the technology used. Compliance does not exempt a person from other applicable civil or criminal liability. Section 2 creates Section 76-3-203.18, effective July 1, 2024, under which the sentencing judge or the Board of Pardons and Parole may consider intentional or knowing use and material assistance of an artificial intelligence system as an aggravating factor in criminal offenses.

title: Utah SB 132 (2025) -- Electrical Power Amendments (large load service outside Rocky Mountain Power)
summary_short: Utah SB 132 (2025) creates Utah Code chapter 54-26 on electric service to large load customers. Qualified electric utilities must process service requests; large load contracts require Public Service Commission approval; large-scale generation providers may serve large loads; large loads bear incremental costs. Effective May 7, 2025.
summary_long: The Act enacts Utah Code Chapter 54-26 on large-scale electric service. Large-scale service requests cover new or added service of 100 megawatts or more within five years. Utilities must acknowledge requests, complete evaluations within set deadlines, issue written service proposals, and may charge fees. Large load service must be provided under contracts approved by the Public Service Commission, which approves a contract if the customer bears incremental costs and existing ratepayers do not. Qualified electric utilities have the sole right to serve large loads, except that customers may take alternative service from registered large-scale generation providers if a utility misses deadlines or no agreement is reached within 90 days. Closed private generation and connected generation systems are established, with some exemptions from public utility regulation. Chapter service is exempt from specified rate regulation, and large load costs are excluded from rates. The commission must investigate a large load flexible tariff, set transmission cost-allocation rules for contracts executed on or after January 1, 2026, and review the chapter before October 31, 2027 and every three years. The chapter applies to contracts with service commencing on or before December 31, 2034. The bill takes effect May 7, 2025.

title: S.B. 149 Artificial Intelligence Amendments (Artificial Intelligence Policy Act)
summary_short: Utah S.B. 149 creates an Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy in the Department of Commerce to run an AI learning laboratory, where approved participants may receive temporary regulatory mitigation. It also lets an actor be found guilty of an offense committed with generative AI's aid. Effective May 1, 2024.
summary_long: S.B. 149 creates the Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy in the Department of Commerce, headed by a director appointed by the executive director. The Office must create and administer an AI learning laboratory program, consult stakeholders, make rules on participation fees, criteria, data usage limits, cybersecurity and disclosures, and report annually before November 30 to the Business and Labor Interim Committee. Participants may receive temporary regulatory mitigation through agreements that limit scope (users, geography) and set safeguards; they remain subject to requirements not expressly waived and may be removed at any time. Participants must report required information, retain records, and immediately report incidents of consumer harm, privacy breach or unauthorized data usage. Initial agreements run up to 12 months, with one 12-month extension. The text also repeals Chapter 70 on May 1, 2025 and adds Section 76-2-107, under which a person may be found guilty of an offense committed with the aid of generative AI or by prompting it to commit the offense. The bill takes effect May 1, 2024.

title: Utah S.B. 166 (Aviation Amendments
summary_short: Amends Utah Code 72-14 on unmanned aircraft and advanced air mobility. Section 5 revises definitions, including advanced air mobility system and unmanned aircraft. Section 6 bars political subdivisions from regulating private use of such aircraft, except as authorized or by airport operators, and supersedes earlier local laws.
summary_long: This excerpt contains two sections of Utah's aviation amendments to Title 72, Chapter 14, which governs unmanned aircraft and advanced air mobility systems. Section 5 amends the chapter's definitions. It defines advanced air mobility system as a system that transports individuals and property using piloted and unpiloted aircraft, including electric and vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, and includes components such as remote and autonomous functions. It defines unmanned aircraft as an aircraft capable of sustaining flight with no possible direct human intervention, and unmanned aircraft system as the entire system used to operate one. Section 6 amends 72-14-103. A political subdivision or an entity within one may not enact a law, ordinance or rule governing private use of unmanned aircraft or advanced air mobility systems, unless the chapter authorizes it or an airport operator enacts it to govern operations within the airport or takeoff and landing there. Subsection (2) states that the chapter supersedes local laws or rules enacted before July 1, 2017. The excerpt sets out no penalties and gives no effective date.

title: S.B. 226 Artificial Intelligence Amendments (2025)
summary_short: S.B. 226 (2025) adds Utah Code 13-75 on generative artificial intelligence in consumer transactions and regulated services. Suppliers must disclose AI use when asked, and regulated-occupation providers must disclose high-risk AI interactions. Violations are enforced by the Division of Consumer Protection with fines and court remedies, effective 05/07/25.
summary_long: S.B. 226 (2025) creates Utah Code 13-75 on generative artificial intelligence (AI) in consumer transactions and regulated services, effective 05/07/25. It defines generative AI and high-risk AI interactions. A supplier using generative AI must disclose that the individual is interacting with AI and not a human when the individual asks. Individuals in regulated occupations must prominently disclose generative AI use in high-risk interactions, verbally or in writing, and must comply with occupational requirements. A violation of the chapter is a violation of the consumer protection provision in Subsection 13-11-4(1), and it is no defense that generative AI made, undertook or furthered the violative act. A safe harbor protects a person from enforcement under the disclosure section if the generative AI clearly and conspicuously discloses its nature, and the Division of Consumer Protection may make rules on disclosure forms. The Division director may impose an administrative fine of up to $2,500 per violation. The Division may sue for injunctions, disgorgement and fines of up to $2,500 per violation. A person who violates an administrative or court order faces a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation. The bill also extends the repeal date of the Artificial Intelligence Policy Act to July 1, 2027 and repeals Section 13-2-12.

title: S.B. 227 Consumer Privacy Act (Utah Consumer Privacy Act)
summary_short: Utah Consumer Privacy Act, effective December 31, 2023. Applies to controllers and processors above revenue and consumer-count thresholds that do business in Utah or target its residents. Gives consumers access, deletion, portability and opt-out rights; imposes controller duties; enforced by the Attorney General with no private right of action.
summary_long: Enacts the Utah Consumer Privacy Act, effective December 31, 2023, for controllers and processors doing business in Utah or targeting Utah residents, with annual revenue of $25,000,000 or more and personal data of 100,000 or more consumers controlled or processed in a calendar year (or 25,000 or more consumers where over 50% of gross revenue comes from selling personal data). Excludes governmental entities, covered entities, nonprofits, higher education institutions and certain financial institutions. Consumers may confirm processing, access, delete, port and opt out of targeted advertising and sale of their personal data. Controllers must respond within 45 days (extendable once by 45 days), provide a privacy notice, maintain reasonable data security, give notice and an opt-out opportunity before processing sensitive data, not discriminate against consumers exercising rights, and bind processors by contract. The Division of Consumer Protection takes complaints and refers them to the Attorney General, who has exclusive enforcement authority after a 30-day cure notice and may recover actual damages and up to $7,500 per violation. No private right of action is created. A report on enforcement is due before July 1, 2025.

title: Utah S.B. 271 (Unauthorized Artificial Intelligence Impersonation Amendments)
summary_short: Amends Utah's personal identity abuse statute to reach AI-generated or simulated likenesses, voices and personas. Bars using an individual's personal identity in advertising, fundraising or solicitation without consent, and knowingly distributing tools whose primary purpose is unauthorized creation of such content; gives individuals civil remedies. Effective May 7, 2025.
summary_long: Amends Utah's personal identity abuse provisions (Sections 45-3-2 to 45-3-7). Section 45-3-2 defines advertisement, consent, content, generative artificial intelligence, personal identity (including simulations or recreations made by generative AI, computer animation or digital manipulation), publish and voice. Section 45-3-3 makes personal identity abused when content containing it is used to advertise products or services, fundraise, solicit donations or promote purchases, where it expresses or implies endorsement, creates confusion about participation, or creates a false impression, and consent has not been obtained. It also prohibits knowingly distributing, selling or licensing technology whose intended primary purpose is unauthorized creation or modification of such content for commercial purposes. Consent cannot be inferred from failure to object. Individuals may sue the person who caused publication for injunctive relief, damages, exemplary damages and attorney fees (45-3-4). Publishers may be sued if the content on its face signals non-consent and the publisher took no reasonable steps to assure consent (45-3-5). Section 45-3-7 exempts news, public affairs, entertainment, parody and similar works, and excludes interactive computer services for content provided by others. Prosecution under Section 76-9-407 is preserved. The act takes effect May 7, 2025.

title: S.B. 332 Artificial Intelligence Policy Act Amendments (2025)
summary_short: Sets a July 1, 2027 repeal date for the Artificial Intelligence Policy Act (Title 13, Chapter 72) in the repeal-date list of Section 63I-2-213, and lists repeal dates for other Title 13 provisions. Applies to Utah; effective May 7, 2025, except as Section 2(2) provides.
summary_long: S.B. 332 amends Section 63I-2-213, the Title 13 repeal-date list, and sets the bill's effective date. Subsection (5) of the amended list provides that Title 13, Chapter 72, Artificial Intelligence Policy Act, is repealed July 1, 2027. The other subsections set repeal dates for Section 13-1-16 (Latino Community Support Restricted Account) on July 1, 2024; Sections 13-14-103 and 13-35-103 (motor vehicle and powersport vehicle franchise advisory boards) on October 1, 2024; and Title 13, Chapter 47 (Private Employer Verification Act) on the program start date defined in Section 63G-12-102. The bill text does not mark which entries are new, and it does not set out the Artificial Intelligence Policy Act's substantive duties. Under Section 2, the bill takes effect May 7, 2025, except as provided in subsection (2). Subsection (2) applies if approved by two-thirds of all members elected to each house, and then takes effect on governor approval, on the day after the constitutional time limit without signature, or on the date of a veto override.

title: Utah SB 34 (Governmental Use of Facial Recognition Technology)
summary_short: Restricts Utah government entities' use of facial recognition systems on image databases to specified law enforcement purposes, bans use for civil immigration violations, requires trained-employee verification, public notice and data-use limits, and annual reporting. Effective date not stated in the provided text.
summary_long: The chapter covers the government entities defined in Section 77-23e-102(5), including state agencies, the Legislature, courts and political subdivisions. Section 77-23e-103 bars government entities from using a facial recognition system on an image database, subject to exceptions in Sections 77-23e-103 to 105. Only law enforcement agencies may request comparisons, in writing; a trained employee may complete them only for listed purposes such as investigating a felony, a violent crime or a threat to human life, with a case number and, for crime investigations, a statement supporting a fair probability of connection. Civil immigration violations are excluded. The Department of Public Safety alone may run comparisons on images it maintains or shares (Section 77-23e-104). Trained employees must use an algorithm comparing only facial biometric data, verify possible matches visually and obtain a second opinion. Entities must notify individuals when capturing images, publish notice at least 30 days before new use, accept public comment for 15 days and post the final decision. Comparison data may not be used or shared beyond the chapter's purposes. Entities release statistics on request and report annually to the Government Operations Interim Committee between August 1 and October 15. The text contains no penalty provisions and no effective date.

title: Utah Senate Bill 84
summary_short: Creates the Innovation in Artificial Intelligence Grant Pilot Program, administered by the office subject to available funds. Business entities may receive grants to develop a practical AI course with a public or private school for kindergarten-through-twelfth-grade students and prepare them for technology careers. No start date stated.
summary_long: Part 13 of Utah Senate Bill 84 enacts Sections 63N-3-1301 and 63N-3-1302. It defines business entity (a for-profit or nonprofit organization), pilot program, and student (a child enrolled in a public or private school, grades kindergarten through twelfth grade). It creates the Innovation in Artificial Intelligence Grant Pilot Program, administered by the office subject to the availability of funds. The purpose is to award a grant to a business entity to develop a program, material, and curriculum that teaches an AI course to students with an emphasis on practical training and prepares students for technology careers. A grantee must work in partnership with a public or private school. Applications must describe the proposal, the school partnership, and any partnerships with other entities. The office considers the likelihood the proposal achieves the purpose and its overall viability. Before receiving funds, a grantee must enter a written agreement with the office specifying the grant amount and the distribution period and structure. The office may make rules under the Utah Administrative Rulemaking Act on application criteria, awards, and grantee reporting. The office must include an annual written update on the pilot in the report under Section 63N-1a-306. The excerpt contains no penalties, enforcement provisions, or start date.

title: Code of Virginia § 58.1-609.3 (Commercial and industrial exemptions), subdivisions 17-19 (data center computer equipment)
summary_short: Virginia sales and use tax exemptions for commercial and industrial goods, including subdivisions 18–19 exempting data center computer equipment and software for operators meeting investment and job thresholds, from July 1, 2010 to June 30, 2035, with conditional extensions to 2040 or 2050.
summary_long: Section 58.1-609.3 of the Code of Virginia lists 21 commercial and industrial exemptions from the retail sales and use tax. Subdivisions 1 to 11, 16, 20 and 21 cover industrial materials, machinery, vessels, research, rail and airline property, meals, textiles, taxicab parts, beer brewing and advanced recycling; subdivision 2 excludes most electric power generation. Subdivisions 12 and 13 cover oil, gas and spaceport activities, and subdivisions 14 and 15 cover semiconductor manufacturing property. Subdivision 17 covers data center computer equipment bought by June 30, 2011, subject to a $75 million investment and 100 jobs. Subdivision 18 covers computer equipment, enabling software and related hardware for data centers in Virginia localities from July 1, 2010 to June 30, 2035, if investment and job thresholds are met (lower in distressed localities) under a memorandum of understanding with the Virginia Economic Development Partnership Authority; operators must file annual reports. Subdivision 19 extends subdivision 18 to June 30, 2040 or 2050 for operators meeting larger investment and job levels, including $35 billion and $100 billion investment thresholds. The Department publishes a biennial report on the data center exemption.

title: Fairfax County Zoning Ordinance Amendment ZO 112.1-2024-9 / 112.2-2024-8 -- Data centers
summary_short: Amends Fairfax County zoning chapters 112.1 and 112.2 for data centers, effective September II, 2024 (as printed): removes or conditions data center use permissions in several districts and adds siting, noise, and design standards for data center owners and operators.
summary_long: Amends the Fairfax County Zoning Ordinance (Chapters 112.1 and 112.2) on data centers, adopted 10 September 2024 and effective September II, 2024 (as printed). Changes use permissions: data centers become special exceptions (SE) or permitted-or-SE in the 1-4, 1-5 and 1-6 Districts, are removed from the PRC District, and become SE in the PDC and PTC Districts. Revised Sec. 4102.6.A sets siting and design standards: equipment must be fully enclosed or screened; building size is capped at 40,000 sq ft in C-3 and C-4 and 80,000 sq ft in the 1-2 to 1-4 Districts, exceedable by special exception; buildings must be at least 200 feet from R-district or residential lots; equipment must be 300 feet away or separated by the building; buildings must be at least one mile from a Metro station entrance; noise studies are required before site plan approval and after construction; by-right facades must meet entrance and fenestration rules. Rezoning and special exception applications for data centers must include noise studies and architectural depictions. Site plans accepted by July 16, 2024 may be reviewed under prior rules if approved by July 16, 2025, and other earlier approvals may continue.

title: HB 2094, High-Risk Artificial Intelligence Developer and Deployer Act (2025)
summary_short: Bill adding Virginia Code Chapter 58 (§§ 59.1-607 to 59.1-612) on high-risk AI systems used in consequential decisions. Imposes duties of care, documentation, impact assessments, consumer notice and appeal on developers and deployers, enforced by the Attorney General; effective July 1, 2026 if enacted.
summary_long: The bill would add Chapter 58, the High-Risk Artificial Intelligence Developer and Deployer Act, to Title 59.1 of the Code of Virginia. It covers developers and deployers doing business in the Commonwealth whose high-risk AI systems make, or are a substantial factor in making, consequential decisions such as education, employment, financial or lending services, health care, housing, insurance, legal services and parole. Developers must use a reasonable duty of care against algorithmic discrimination, provide documentation to deployers, and make outputs of high-risk generative AI systems identifiable, subject to exceptions. Deployers must maintain a risk management policy and program, complete impact assessments before initial deployment and before significant updates, retain records for three years, disclose AI use, give adverse-decision explanations, correction and appeal rights, and publish a statement on managing algorithmic discrimination risk. Exemptions cover, among others, certain federal, banking, insurance and health care actors. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority, with a 45-day cure opportunity, civil penalties of up to $1,000 for violations and $1,000 to $10,000 for willful violations, and no private right of action. The provisions take effect July 1, 2026.

title: Virginia HB 2154
summary_short: Amends Virginia Code § 32.1-127 so that hospitals, nursing homes and certified nursing facilities must establish and implement policies on patient access to and use of intelligent personal assistants during inpatient services, with health information protected under HIPAA. Approved March 18, 2021.
summary_long: Chapter 219 (2021) amends and reenacts § 32.1-127 of the Code of Virginia, which governs regulations of the Board for hospitals, nursing homes and certified nursing facilities. The AI-relevant addition is a subdivision requiring each hospital, nursing home and certified nursing facility to establish and implement policies ensuring the permissible access to and use of an intelligent personal assistant provided by a patient, in accordance with the Board's regulations, while the patient receives inpatient services. These policies must ensure protection of health information under the federal Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996. The subdivision defines an intelligent personal assistant as a combination of an electronic device and a specialized software application that assists users with basic tasks using natural language processing and artificial intelligence, including digital or virtual assistants. The provision states no penalty of its own; the other subdivisions of § 32.1-127 concern hospital and nursing-home standards and are outside the scope of this annotation. The document as provided does not mark which text is newly added, so the annotation rests on the intelligent personal assistant subdivision only.},

title: West Virginia HB 2760 (2021)
summary_short: West Virginia code section 11-13Q-1Oa grants a 20-year credit of 100 percent of tax attributable to qualified investment in new or expanded high technology manufacturing businesses, covering electronics, semiconductors and, from 2022, drone, autonomous vehicle, robot, AI-operated machine, biotechnology and medical-device manufacturing, conditioned on 20 new jobs.
summary_long: West Virginia code section 11-13Q-1Oa allows an eligible high technology manufacturing business taxpayer a credit against state taxes equal to 100 percent of the tax attributable to its qualified investment in a new or expanded high technology manufacturing business in this state that creates at least 20 new jobs within 12 months after the investment is placed in service. The credit runs for a 20-year period, may be taken without carryover, and cannot be combined with other credits in the code for the same investment. Eligible activities are six-digit NAICS manufacturing codes for computers, electronic components and semiconductors; from tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2022, also drones, autonomous motor vehicles, robots, machines operated by and incorporating artificial intelligence, biotechnology products and medical devices. New jobs must pay a median compensation above $45,000 a year, adjusted annually by a consumer price index formula based on 2007. The commissioner may prescribe rules to determine and verify the credit and may require a notice of intent before estimated tax payments are reduced. The text defines artificial intelligence, autonomous, robot, drone and medical device.},

title: 2026 Appropriation Act, HB 30 (2026 Special Session I), 2026-2028 biennium -- data center electricity consumption tax and related provisions
summary_short: Virginia's 2026 Special Session I appropriation act (HB 30) levies, from July 1, 2026 to July 1, 2028, an electricity consumption tax on data center operators, with refunds of excess revenue, and adds data center cooling-water, noise, grid and reporting provisions.
summary_long: Virginia's 2026 Special Session I appropriation act (HB 30), covering fiscal years 2027 and 2028, amends the Code and adds data center provisions. From July 1, 2026 to July 1, 2028 it levies an electricity consumption tax of $0.011/kWh per month on each data center operator; revenue above $600,000,000 per fiscal year goes to a non-reverting fund used for refunds from fiscal 2027, administered by the State Corporation Commission. The Department of Environmental Quality must set cooling-water scarcity criteria by July 1, 2027; in designated areas data centers must certify water-saving cooling before July 1, 2032, and new air-permit applicants in the Eastern Virginia Groundwater Management Area after January 1, 2027 must use air, recycled-water, stormwater or closed-loop cooling. DEQ noise regulations apply from December 31, 2029, with civil penalties of up to $32,500 per day from January 1, 2030. The Corporation Commission may weigh economic benefits to disadvantaged communities in large-load interconnection requests, and Phase II utilities' annual incremental strategic undergrounding investment increases are limited to three percent of distribution rate base. Utilities, water providers and agencies report data center contracts, water use and generators by October 1, 2026, and a Joint Subcommittee on Tax Policy studies data center incentives, reporting by December 15, 2026. The act takes effect July 1, 2026; the first enactment expires June 30, 2028.

title: Loudoun County CPAM-2024-0001 / ZOAM-2024-0001 -- Data Center Standards and Locations (Phase 1): data centers moved from by-right to special exception
summary_short: Loudoun County, Virginia zoning amendments (ZOAM-2024-0001), adopted March 18, 2025, move data center use from by-right to special exception (SPEX) approval in the Industrial Park, General Industry and Mineral Resource-Heavy Industry districts. A grandfathering resolution covers applications accepted on or before February 12, 2025.
summary_long: The Loudoun County Board of Supervisors adopted the Phase 1 Zoning Ordinance text amendments (ZOAM-2024-0001) on March 18, 2025. They amend Table 3.02.05-1 so that data center use requires a special exception (SPEX) in the Industrial Park (IP), General Industry (GI) and Mineral Resource-Heavy Industry (MR-HI) districts, where it was previously permitted by-right. Table footnote 3 allows minor site plan changes for approved data center uses without SPEX, applying Section 10.11.01.H. Footnote 4 deems certain rezoning approvals made on or before March 18, 2025 that detail a specific data center use to include a SPEX approval. A companion Grandfathering Resolution lets legislative applications, and administrative applications for by-right data center uses, officially accepted on or before February 12, 2025 proceed without SPEX. Administrative applications must show that proposed structures and external mechanical equipment are more than 500 feet from existing residential structures. Grandfathered status is lost after a substantial modification, six months of non-response to project-manager requests, or, for administrative applications, failure to meet Zoning Ordinance and related standards within three years. The document also contains companion 2019 General Plan amendments (CPAM-2024-0001) to place-type text and maps, which this record does not code.

title: Prince William County PW Digital Gateway -- Comprehensive Plan Amendment and rezonings (approved 2023-12-13) and judicial voiding (Circuit Court 2025; Court of Appeals 2026-03-31)
jurisdiction: United States - Virginia - Prince William County
summary_short: Prince William County Board of Supervisors adopted Comprehensive Plan Amendment CPA2021-00004 (PW Digital Gateway) on 1 November 2022, creating a technology corridor along Pageland Lane for data center uses. Board rezoning approvals for the area were later declared void by court order, while the plan amendment remains in place.
summary_long: Prince William County's Board of County Supervisors initiated Comprehensive Plan Amendment CPA2021-00004 on 20 July 2021 (Res. No. 21-445) and adopted it on 1 November 2022 (Res. No. 22-508). The amendment, described as a request to create a technology corridor along Pageland Lane for data center uses that would use existing transmission and fiber optic infrastructure, initially proposed changing Long Range Land Use from AE and ER to Technology/Flex with a T-3 transect. The study area was expanded to 194 parcels and 2,139 acres between Route 234 and Route 29. Three rezoning applications for the area (REZ2022-00032, REZ2022-00033, REZ2022-00036) carry proffers dated December 2023. A Court of Appeals decision of 31 March 2026 was stayed; by order of 29 July 2026 the Board's rezoning approvals were declared void and zoning reverts to the district in place before approval. The Comprehensive Plan Amendment remains in place. Any future rezoning must follow the normal application process, with Planning Commission and Board public hearings. The page also lists related data center overlay review materials and process tasks. The source is a county project webpage summarizing the process, not the adopted plan text.

title: Virginia 2024 SB 731
summary_short: Amends Virginia Code § 18.2-374.1 on child pornography. Defines the offense, covers depictions where the minor need not actually exist, allows age to be inferred from appearance, sets prison terms and mandatory minimums by victim age, and sets venue. The provided text states no effective date.
summary_long: The act amends and reenacts § 18.2-374.1 of the Code of Virginia on child pornography. Subsection A defines child pornography as sexually explicit visual material that utilizes or has as a subject an identifiable minor, or that depicts a minor in nudity or sexual conduct where obscene; for the second limb the minor depicted need not actually exist. Sexually explicit visual material includes digital images and cached images when three or more are present. Subsection B lists production-related offenses (enticing a person under 18, producing, knowingly participating in production, and knowingly financing), with subsections B1 and B5 repealed. Subsections C1 and C2 set prison terms by the age of the subject (under 15: five to 30 years; 15 to under 18: one to 20 years), with higher mandatory minimums where the offender is at least seven years older and longer terms for second or subsequent violations. C3 requires mandatory minimum terms to run consecutively with any other sentence. Subsection D allows inference of minority from text, title or appearance. Subsection E sets venue. Section 2 states that the act may increase periods of imprisonment and that the Virginia Criminal Sentencing Commission must assign a minimum fiscal impact of $50,000.

title: Virginia SCC Final Order, Case No. PUR-2025-00058 -- Biennial review of Virginia Electric and Power Company (Dominion) rates; new GS-5 rate class
summary_short: Final order of Virginia's State Corporation Commission setting Dominion's base rates for 2026 and 2027 and approving a new GS-5 rate class for large-load customers, including data centers, with contract, collateral and minimum-demand terms effective from January 1, 2027.

title: Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act (Code of Virginia Title 59.1, Chapter 53; SB 1392/HB 2307, 2021)
summary_short: Virginia's Consumer Data Protection Act regulates businesses that control or process personal data of Virginia residents above volume thresholds: consumer rights of access, correction, deletion, portability and opt-out; controller and processor duties, including data protection assessments and children's protections; exclusive Attorney General enforcement. Effective 1 January 2023.
summary_long: The Act (Code of Virginia §§ 59.1-575 to 59.1-584) applies to persons conducting business in Virginia or targeting its residents that, in a calendar year, control or process personal data of at least 100,000 consumers, or of at least 25,000 consumers while deriving over 50 percent of gross revenue from selling personal data. Public bodies, GLBA financial institutions, HIPAA covered entities and business associates, nonprofits and higher-education institutions are excluded, as are listed health, credit-reporting, FERPA, employment and other data. Consumers may confirm and access, correct, delete and port their data and opt out of targeted advertising, sale and profiling for significant decisions; controllers answer within 45 days and run an appeal process. Controllers must limit collection, secure data, obtain consent for sensitive data, not sell precise geolocation data, give privacy notices, restrict processing of known children's data and conduct data protection assessments for high-risk processing. Processors act under binding contracts. Social media platforms must screen for users under 16 and limit their use to one hour a day unless a parent consents. The Attorney General enforces exclusively, after a 30-day cure notice, with injunctions and civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation; there is no private right of action.
