title: Washington House Bill 1999
summary_short: Amends Washington criminal and civil law on intimate and sexual images of minors and adults to cover fabricated depictions, including those made by artificial intelligence. Creates a crime and a civil cause of action for disclosing fabricated intimate images without consent. The text states no effective date.
summary_long: HB 1999 (2024) amends Washington's child sexual exploitation provisions (RCW 9.68A), the intimate-image crime (RCW 9A.86.010) and civil remedies (RCW 7.110). 'Digitization' is defined to include artificial intelligence (Sec. 1), and lacking knowledge that an image was digitized is no defense (Sec. 3(7)). Section 7 creates the crime of disclosing fabricated intimate images: knowing disclosure, without consent and with knowledge of likely harm, is a gross misdemeanor on a first offense and a class C felony after a prior conviction. Minors are liable only if they acted intentionally and maliciously. Exemptions cover public-interest disclosures and interactive computer, mobile and network providers acting on content from others. Section 12 creates a civil cause of action for identifiable depicted individuals harmed by intentional disclosure or threatened disclosure without consent; consent to creation alone does not establish consent to disclosure. Section 14 allows a prevailing plaintiff to recover the greater of actual damages or statutory damages up to $10,000 per defendant, plus monetary gain, punitive damages up to three times actual damages, fees and injunctive relief. Section 15 sets a four-year limitation period, tolled for minors until majority. Sections 4 to 6 adjust evidence handling for minor depictions, including fabricated ones.

title: Washington HB 2157 (Regulating high-risk artificial intelligence system development, deployment, and use.)
summary_short: Washington bill regulating high-risk artificial intelligence systems used to make consequential decisions about consumers. It imposes reasonable-care, documentation, impact assessment, risk management, disclosure and synthetic-content labelling duties on developers and deployers, enforceable through civil actions, from 1 January 2027 if enacted.
summary_long: As introduced, the bill adds a chapter to Title 19 RCW on high-risk artificial intelligence systems, meaning systems intended to make, or be a substantial factor in making, consequential decisions on parole, education, employment, financial or lending services, health care, housing, insurance, marital status or legal services. Developers must use reasonable care against known or foreseeable algorithmic discrimination, give deployers documentation of intended uses, limitations and evaluations, and make high-risk generative outputs identifiable. Deployers must maintain a risk management policy and program, complete impact assessments before initial deployment and before significant updates, keep records for three years, disclose AI use and the principal reasons for adverse decisions to consumers, and publish a statement on managing discrimination risk. Compliance with listed risk frameworks such as NIST AI RMF or ISO/IEC 42001 creates a rebuttable presumption of conformity. Certain insurers, financial institutions, health-care uses and federal acquisitions are excluded or treated as compliant. Consumers may bring civil actions, where courts may enjoin violations and award attorneys' fees; a violation cured within 45 days is an affirmative defense. The act takes effect 1 January 2027.

title: Washington HB 2225 (Artificial Intelligence Companion Chatbots 2026)
summary_short: Washington HB 2225 (2026) regulates operators of AI companion chatbots available to Washington users. It requires recurring disclosure that chatbots are artificial, minor protections, self-harm detection protocols and violations treated as consumer protection act violations. Effective January 1, 2027.
summary_long: HB 2225 adds a new chapter to Title 19 RCW regulating AI companion chatbots: AI systems with a natural language interface that give adaptive, human-like responses and sustain relationships across interactions, excluding certain business, video game, voice assistant and curriculum-aligned educational bots. Operators (persons making available or controlling access to such chatbots for users in Washington) must give clear notice that the chatbot is artificial and not human at the start of an interaction and at least every three hours, and must take reasonable measures to stop chatbots claiming to be human. Where an operator knows a user is a minor, or the chatbot is directed to minors, it must repeat the notice hourly, prevent sexually explicit or suggestive dialogue, and prohibit listed manipulative engagement techniques. Before making a chatbot available, operators must maintain a protocol to detect suicidal ideation or self-harm, refer users to crisis resources and prevent self-harm content, and must publicly disclose the protocol and the annual number of crisis referrals. Violations are deemed unfair or deceptive acts under the consumer protection act, chapter 19.86 RCW; the text sets no separate penalty. Effective January 1, 2027.

title: Washington HB 2481 (Prohibiting surveillance-based price discrimination and surge pricing for retail goods.)
summary_short: Introduced Washington bill that would require retail grocery sellers to post prices clearly, prohibit surveillance-based price discrimination and surge pricing, and bar electronic shelf label systems in retail locations of 15,000 square feet or larger until January 1, 2030, with a state study due June 30, 2029.
summary_long: State bill (introduced, pending) covering algorithmic and AI-based pricing of retail goods. Section 3 requires a person engaged in retail sale of goods to clearly post prices in a retail location, and prohibits surveillance-based price discrimination (setting or modifying a consumer's price from monitoring, tracking or automated analysis of behavior, location, demographics or personal information) and surge pricing (price increases based on demand, consumer behavior or willingness to pay rather than actual costs). Uniform price reductions for eligible consumers and certain loyalty programs are excepted where personal information is not used to modify prices. Section 4 bars use of electronic shelf label systems in retail locations of 15,000 square feet or larger until January 1, 2030, and expires June 30, 2031. Section 5 declares violations an unfair or deceptive act and unfair method of competition under the Consumer Protection Act, chapter 19.86 RCW. Section 2 defines key terms, including Consumer (a Washington resident) and Person (a business in retail sale of goods, excluding small businesses under RCW 19.85.020). Section 8 directs the department to study electronic shelf label systems and their impact on pricing transparency and employee job security, with a report due by June 30, 2029; that section also expires June 30, 2031.

title: Engrossed Substitute House Bill 1155, My Health My Data Act (RCW 19.373)
summary_short: Washington statute regulating collection, sharing and sale of consumer health data by regulated entities and small businesses. Requires privacy policies, consent, consumer rights and signed authorization for sales; prohibits certain geofences around health care facilities. Most duties apply from March 31, 2024; small businesses from June 30, 2024.
summary_long: Washington's My Health My Data Act (Laws of 2023, ch. 191) regulates consumer health data collected, shared or sold in Washington. Regulated entities and small businesses must publish a consumer health data privacy policy, obtain consent before collecting or sharing such data, and avoid unlawful discrimination against consumers exercising rights. Access must be restricted, data secured, and processors bound by contracts. Consumers may access, delete and withdraw consent over their data, with a 45-day response period and appeal rights. Selling consumer health data requires a signed valid authorization meeting listed requirements, expiring after one year. Sellers and purchasers keep authorizations for six years. Geofencing around in-person health care services to track consumers or send them health-related messages is unlawful. Violations are unfair or deceptive acts under the Consumer Protection Act. HIPAA-protected and other specified information is exempt. A joint legislative committee reviews enforcement actions; that section expires June 30, 2031. Most duties apply from March 31, 2024; small businesses from June 30, 2024.

title: RCW 82.08.986 -- Exemptions: eligible server equipment, eligible power infrastructure, computer data centers
summary_short: Washington sales tax exemption for server equipment, eligible power infrastructure and installation labor at eligible computer data centers, subject to certificate, job and certification conditions; expires July 1, 2048.
summary_long: Exempts from the Washington sales tax imposed under RCW 82.08.020 sales to qualifying businesses and tenants of eligible server equipment and eligible power infrastructure installed at an eligible computer data center, plus related installation and construction labor. Eligible centers must be in a rural county, have at least 20,000 square feet housing working servers, and meet construction-start windows. Exemption certificates are issued by the Department of Revenue; no new certificates issue on or after July 1, 2036 (refurbished centers: July 1, 2026, capped at six per year). Holders must establish and maintain a net increase of family-wage jobs (35, or three per 20,000 square feet), with health insurance, within six years. Newly constructed centers must certify a recognized green building or energy standard within three years. Non-compliance cancels the certificate and makes exempted taxes due, with a 10 percent penalty for green-standard failure. Annual tax performance reports are required, and environmental practices are encouraged. The exemption expires July 1, 2048.

title: RCW 19.375, Biometric Identifiers (EHB 1493, 2017)
summary_short: Washington statute (RCW 19.375, enacted 2017) requiring a person who enrolls a biometric identifier for a commercial purpose to give notice or obtain consent, limiting its sale, disclosure and retention, and enforceable solely by the attorney general under the Consumer Protection Act.
summary_long: Chapter 19.375 RCW applies to persons (individuals, partnerships, corporations, LLCs, organizations and other entities, excluding government agencies) that enroll a biometric identifier in a database for a commercial purpose. Before enrollment, the person must give notice, obtain consent, or provide a mechanism to prevent later commercial use. A person who knowingly possesses enrolled identifiers must take reasonable care against unauthorized access and may retain them only as long as reasonably necessary for listed purposes. Selling, leasing or disclosing an enrolled identifier for a commercial purpose requires consent unless a listed exception applies, such as a product or service the individual requested, a statute or court order, or a contractually bound third party. Use materially inconsistent with the original terms requires new consent. Disclosure and retention limits do not apply to unenrolled identifiers, and notice and consent are not required for collection for a security purpose. The chapter does not apply to financial institutions subject to GLBA Title V or to activities subject to HIPAA Title V, and it does not limit law enforcement authority. Violations are unfair or deceptive acts under the Consumer Protection Act, and the attorney general alone may enforce the chapter. The document states no effective date beyond the 2017 session law reference.},

title: Substitute Senate Bill 5152, Synthetic media in campaigns for elective office (RCW 42.62)
summary_short: Creates a civil remedy for candidates whose appearance, speech or conduct is altered by synthetic media in an electioneering communication: injunctions and damages against the sponsor, with limited liability for media, and a disclosure-based affirmative defense. Directs the Public Disclosure Commission to adopt rules.
summary_long: The act adds a new chapter to Title 42 RCW. Synthetic media is an intentionally manipulated image, audio or video recording of an individual, made with generative adversarial network or other digital technology, that is realistic but false and gives a fundamentally different impression than the original. A candidate whose appearance, action or speech is altered by synthetic media in an electioneering communication may seek injunctive or equitable relief against its publication, or general or special damages against the sponsor, and a prevailing party may recover reasonable attorneys' fees and costs. The plaintiff must prove use of synthetic media by clear and convincing evidence. It is an affirmative defense that the communication carries a disclosure that the media has been manipulated, placed as prescribed for visual or audio media. Sponsors may be held liable; a medium is liable only if it removes the disclosure or changes content to create synthetic media, and federally licensed broadcasters subject to 47 U.S.C. 315 are excluded. Interactive computer service providers and users are not treated as publishers of third-party information, subject to the same exception. The public disclosure commission must adopt rules; the chapter does not create a violation under chapter 42.17A RCW or authorize commission action under RCW 42.17A.755. The text states no effective date.

title: Washington (2022) SB 5460
summary_short: Amends Washington rules for the department's autonomous vehicle self-certification testing pilot (RCW 46.92.010). Testing entities must provide information, report collisions and moving violations, and give advance notice to law enforcement. Also amends RCW 46.37.480 on headsets while driving. Section 1 takes effect October 1, 2022.
summary_long: Amends RCW 46.92.010 for the department's autonomous vehicle self-certification testing pilot program. Before testing on public roadways, a self-certifying entity must provide contact information, planned local jurisdictions, vehicle identification numbers where required, and proof of insurance under RCW 46.30.050. Vehicles without a required identification number must be assigned and display a unique number. The entity must notify the department of reportable collisions and of moving violations involving the vehicle during testing, state whether the autonomous driving system was operating, and submit an annual report by February 1. It must give written notice to local and state law enforcement 14 to 60 days before testing. The department may adopt a fee to offset program administration, must make submitted information publicly accessible, and must report annually to the house and senate transportation committees. Autonomous vehicles may not be operated for testing until the information is provided. Autonomous is defined as SAE J3016 level four or five. Section 2 amends RCW 46.37.480, which bars operating a motor vehicle while wearing headsets or earphones that exclude other sounds, subject to listed exceptions. Section 1 takes effect October 1, 2022, and the Section 2 effective date is set in Section 4. The text states no penalty amounts.

title: Washington Senate Bill 5950
summary_short: Appropriates $300,000 (FY2024) and $500,000 (FY2025) of Washington's general fund-state, provided solely for the city of Seattle to lease space for nonprofit and academic institutions that incubate AI-focused technology startups and to develop and teach AI workforce curricula.
summary_long: This partial text, subsection (50) of Senate Bill 5950, makes appropriations of $300,000 of the general fund-state for fiscal year 2024 and $500,000 for fiscal year 2025. The funds are provided solely for the city of Seattle to lease space for nonprofit and academic institutions to incubate technology business startups, especially those focusing on artificial intelligence. The same provision states that the funds are also to develop and teach curricula that skill up workers to use artificial intelligence as a business resource. The excerpt contains no other operative provisions, no eligibility criteria, selection procedures, reporting duties or enforcement terms.

title: City of Seattle Generative Artificial Intelligence Policy
summary_short: Seattle policy POL-209, effective 11/1/2023, sets requirements for City departments, employees, and vendors or contractors acting for the City when acquiring and using generative AI. It requires pre-approval of tools, human review of outputs, attribution, equity review, data-privacy limits and records retention.
summary_long: Seattle policy POL-209 applies to all City departments, and to vendors, contractors and volunteers operating on behalf of the City. It covers software meeting its definition of generative artificial intelligence. It sets general AI principles (innovation, transparency, reliability, bias reduction, privacy, explainability, security) and states policy requirements for generative AI only. Acquisition of generative AI tools follows the City's technology acquisition standard, with pre-approved tools or exception requests reviewed by Seattle IT, which may approve, deny or revoke authorization. Outputs must be reviewed by humans before each official use, with documented review processes. Images, videos, substantive text and significant source code generated by AI must be attributed to the AI system, with a human review assertion. Departments must conduct a Racial Equity Toolkit before using generative AI tools. Confidential data may not be submitted unless enterprise controls are in place, and City data may not be used to train externally controlled models; tools that cannot prevent this may not be used. Prompts, outputs and inputs are treated as potentially public records, and vendors must support their retrieval and export. Exceptions require advance approval. The Chief Technology Officer is responsible for compliance, and non-compliance may lead to discipline, access restriction, or termination of employment or vendor contracts. The policy is effective 11/1/2023 and is to be reviewed annually.

title: Washington Executive Order 24-01
summary_short: Executive Order 24-01 directs executive and small cabinet agencies to govern state use and procurement of generative AI. It sets deadlines from September 2024 to January 2025 for reports, guidelines, risk assessments, vendor governance certification, workforce assessment and training, and research partnerships. Effective on signature, 30 January 2024.
summary_long: The order applies to executive and small cabinet agencies and sets rules for state government use and procurement of generative AI. Section 1 defines generative AI technology and high-risk generative AI systems. Deadlines run from September 2024 to January 2025: a WaTech report on generative AI initiatives and pilot infrastructure (section 2); WaTech and DES guidelines on procurement, use and monitoring, requiring vendors of high-risk systems to certify an AI governance program consistent with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (section 3); a DES training plan for state workers (section 4); guidelines on impact on vulnerable communities and criteria for high-risk use cases (section 5); updated procurement templates (section 6); an Office of Equity accountability framework (section 7); WaTech risk-assessment guidance (section 8); an assessment of generative AI's impact on the state workforce (section 9). The Workforce Training and Education Coordinating Board is encouraged to form research partnerships by January 2025 (section 10). Agencies act consistent with federal and state law, federal law supersedes inconsistent provisions, and the order creates no enforceable rights (sections 11-12). The order states no penalties.

title: 2023 Wisconsin Act 123 (Assembly Bill 664), disclosures regarding content generated by artificial intelligence in political advertisements
summary_short: Wisconsin amends its statute s. 11.1303 to require that audio and video political communications containing AI-generated synthetic media carry specified 'generated by AI' labels, with a forfeiture of up to $1,000 per intentional violation. It applies to communications created on the subsection's effective date.
summary_long: The Act amends Wisconsin statute s. 11.1303 by creating subsection (2m) on synthetic media in political communications. 'Synthetic media' means audio or video content substantially produced in whole or in part by generative artificial intelligence. The labelling duties cover communications described in s. 11.1303(2)(a) or (b) that contain express advocacy, issue advocacy, or support or opposition to a referendum. Audio communications must include the words 'Contains content generated by AI.' at the beginning and at the end. Video communications must display, throughout each portion containing synthetic media, readable text stating one of three specified phrases depending on whether the synthetic media is video, audio or both. The commission may promulgate implementing rules, which may include limited exceptions. Compliance does not exempt a person from civil or criminal liability, including under s. 12.05. Intentional violations of the labelling duties carry a forfeiture of up to $1,000 per violation, enforced under s. 11.1400(5). Broadcasters and other hosts or carriers are not liable unless they are the committee responsible for the communication, and the subsection does not alter rights under 47 USC 230. Initial applicability covers communications created on the subsection's effective date.

title: Proyecto de ley: modificación del artículo 92 de la Ley N° 19.580 (violencia hacia las mujeres basada en género) para incluir imágenes o grabaciones reales o simuladas de contenido íntimo o sexual (Carpeta N° 691/2025, Cámara de Representantes)
summary_short: Proposed bill amending Article 92 of Uruguay's Law No. 19.580 to penalise unauthorised disclosure of real or AI-simulated intimate images or recordings, with six months to two years' imprisonment. Website, portal and search-engine administrators must remove such content immediately once notified, under the same penalty; no start date stated.
summary_long: Single-article bill (Carpeta 691/2025, July 2025) replacing Article 92 of Law No. 19.580. Paragraph 1 criminalises whoever disseminates, discloses, exhibits or transfers to third parties real or simulated images or recordings of a person with intimate or sexual content without authorisation, punishable by six months to two years' imprisonment ('prisión' to 'penitenciaría'). Paragraph 2 defines simulated images as those created by artificial intelligence, digital editing or other technology producing a false but credible representation of a person's appearance, voice or conduct. Paragraph 3 states that authorisation given by a person under eighteen is never valid, and that the offence applies even if the disseminator took part in the recordings. Paragraph 4 applies the same penalty to administrators of websites, portals, search engines or similar services who, once notified of the lack of authorisation, do not remove the images immediately. The explanatory memorandum cites deepfake abuse mainly affecting women and minors and foreign measures; it says the bill would also penalise creation and modification, which the operative wording does not expressly cover. No entry-into-force date is stated.
text_version: Bill as introduced: Carpeta Nº 691 de 2025, Repartido Nº 346 (July 2025), with exposición de motivos

title: Decreto N° 64/020 - Reglamentación de los arts. 37 a 40 de la Ley 19.670 y art. 12 de la Ley 18.331, referente a protección de datos personales
summary_short: Implements Uruguay's personal data protection law (Laws 19.670 and 18.331): extends duties to controllers abroad in listed cases, sets security and breach-notification rules, requires impact assessments and data protection officers for specified entities. Published 21/02/2020.
summary_long: Regulates Articles 37 to 40 of Law 19.670 and Article 12 of Law 18.331 on personal data protection. Articles 1-2 extend Law 18.331, including its database registration duties, to controllers or processors not established in Uruguay where they offer goods or services to inhabitants, analyse inhabitants' behaviour, use means located in the country, or are bound by international law or contract. Article 3 requires technical and organisational security measures and initial containment steps within 24 hours of a security incident. Article 4 requires notice to the Unidad Reguladora y de Control de Datos Personales within 72 hours of a breach, notice to affected data subjects in clear language where their rights are significantly affected, and a final report. Articles 5-9 require documented, periodically reviewed proactive measures; impact assessments before processing in listed cases (including sensitive data as core business, profiling, vulnerable groups, and large volumes); and privacy by design and by default. Articles 10-15 require a data protection officer for public entities, private entities mainly processing sensitive data, and private entities processing data of more than 35,000 persons; designation must be notified within 90 days. Article 16 empowers the Unidad to set criteria, and its Consejo Ejecutivo to impose sanctions under Law 18.331 Art. 35. Article 17 repeals Articles 7 and 8 of Decree 414/009. Processing already under way that falls within Article 6 must be assessed within one year of publication in the Diario Oficial.

title: Decreto N° 66/025 - Reglamentación de los arts. 55 de la Ley N° 18.046, 119 de la Ley N° 18.172, 73 de la Ley N° 18.362, 149 de la Ley N° 18.719 y 78 a 84 de la Ley N° 20.212 (seguridad de la información y ciberseguridad)
summary_short: Sets cybersecurity duties for Uruguayan public entities and private entities linked to critical services: 24-hour incident reporting, a national cybersecurity framework with maturity levels, audits and transparency. Implements Laws 18.046, 18.172, 18.362, 18.719 and 20.212 (Arts. 78-84) and was published on 14/03/2025.
summary_long: Decree 66/025 implements Laws 18.046 (Art. 55), 18.172 (Art. 119), 18.362 (Art. 73), 18.719 (Art. 149) and 20.212 (Arts. 78-84) on information security and cybersecurity. It applies to all public entities and to private entities linked to critical services (Art. 2). It assigns functions to the Directorate of Information Security of AGESIC, including issuing regulations, auditing compliance and advising the Executive (Arts. 1, 4, 5). The CERTuy response centre coordinates incident response and handles the national incident register (Arts. 7-9). Covered entities must adopt safeguards, designate an information security officer, keep audit logs for at least 12 months, report incidents to CERTuy within 24 hours, adopt the Cybersecurity Framework at a minimum maturity level, audit it, and send audit summaries within 30 days (Arts. 10-17). Outsourced services must meet the Framework (Art. 18). AGESIC publishes maturity indicators (Art. 19) and sets security criteria for public procurement (Art. 20). Art. 20-BIS, added by Decree 168/026 of 17/07/2026, sets incident procedures for central administration bodies. AGESIC may issue reprimands and reports non-compliant entities semi-annually to the General Assembly (Art. 21); the text states no fines. Decrees 451/009 and 452/009 are repealed (Art. 22).

title: Ley N° 15.921 - Aprobación de la Ley de Zonas Francas
summary_short: Uruguay's free zones law (zonas francas; promulgation 17/12/1987 per document header) lets the Executive designate free zones run by the State or authorized developers, admits user companies under approved contracts, grants national tax and trade exemptions, and sets local-hiring and sanction rules.
summary_long: Ley 15.921 sets the regime for free zones (zonas francas) in Uruguay. Chapter I declares their promotion a national interest, lets the Executive determine zone areas, and allows expropriation for siting. Chapter II assigns administration and control to the Ministry of Economy and Finance through the Dirección Nacional de Zonas Francas, and provides for exploitation by the State or authorized private developers under paid authorization, with possible revocation. Chapter III governs users: contracts need prior approval and registration; authorizations run up to 15 years for industrial and 10 years for commercial or service activities, and 5 years for indirect users; users must employ at least 75% Uruguayan personnel (50% for services); teleworking is allowed under conditions; sworn declarations are due every two years. Chapter IV exempts users from national taxes on their activities, excludes social security contributions, exempts certain intellectual property income, and exempts imports and exports of goods; public utilities may set promotional tariffs. Chapters V and VI cover buildings, goods in zones, retail sales (generally prohibited, with exceptions) and free movement of securities. Chapter VII sets fines up to UI 10,000,000, prohibitions on operations, and loss of benefits. Chapter VIII allows thematic audiovisual and entertainment zones outside the Metropolitan Area, defined as 40 km from central Montevideo.

title: Ley N° 18.331 - Ley de Protección de Datos Personales y Acción de Habeas Data
summary_short: Uruguay's 2008 personal data protection law governs personal data in public and private databases and processing. It sets processing principles and consent rules, data subject rights, limits on sensitive, biometric and cross-border data, registration duties, and administrative sanctions enforced by the Unidad Reguladora.
summary_long: The law treats personal data protection as a human right (Art. 1) and covers personal data in any medium used by public or private actors, excluding purely personal databases, public security and defence files, and databases created by special laws (Art. 3). It sets principles of legality, accuracy, purpose limitation, prior informed consent, security and confidentiality (Arts. 5-11). Data subjects have rights to information, access, rectification and deletion (Arts. 13-15), and a right not to be subject to significant decisions based solely on automated processing (Art. 16). Sensitive data require express written consent or a legal mandate (Art. 18), and biometric data require a prior impact assessment (Art. 18-BIS). Transfers to countries without adequate protection are prohibited, with listed exceptions (Art. 23). Databases must be registered (Art. 29), and controllers must adopt proactive measures such as privacy by design (Art. 12). The Unidad Reguladora y de Control de Datos Personales, within AGESIC, may inspect (Art. 34) and impose warnings, fines up to 500,000 indexed units, five-day database suspension or court-ordered closure (Art. 35). Habeas data proceedings are available (Arts. 37-45).

title: Ley N° 19.670 - Aprobación de Rendición de Cuentas y Balance de Ejecución Presupuestal. Ejercicio 2017
summary_short: Budget accountability statute approving the 2017 Rendición de Cuentas. Its few data and labour provisions apply Law 18.331 to certain foreign controllers, require breach notices, data protection officers, and an annual report on automation and jobs. Generally in force from 1 January 2019.
summary_long: Approves the 2017 Rendición de Cuentas and budget execution balance (Art. 1). Most of the provided text reallocates budget credits and creates or suppresses posts across ministries. Its data-related provisions are operative. Art. 37 extends the personal data law (Ley 18.331) to controllers not established in Uruguay where processing relates to offering goods or services to inhabitants or analysing their behaviour, or uses means located in the country. Art. 38 requires controllers to notify data subjects and the Unidad Reguladora y de Control de Datos Personales of security breaches. Art. 40 requires data protection officers in public entities and some private entities. Art. 41 requires an annual executive report on the employment impact of automation, supported by a risk and opportunity matrix of jobs over five-year periods. Arts. 81 and 97 impose device-identification and location-data duties on mobile and telecom operators. Art. 194 creates an electronic clinical history with a patient right to oppose access. Unless a provision states otherwise, the law applies from 1 January 2019. The text sets no separate sanctions for the data provisions.

title: Ley N° 20.327 - Regulación para la prevención y represión de la ciberdelincuencia
summary_short: Uruguayan statute on cybercrime: adds offences to the Penal Code, requires the Executive to promote a national educational campaign on cybersecurity and personal finance, and lets financial institutions and e-money issuers share fraud registries and freeze funds in disputed transfers. Promulgated 23/08/2024.
summary_long: Statute on the prevention and repression of cybercrime. Chapter I adds offences to the Penal Code (arts. 277-TER, 288-BIS to 288-TER, 297-BIS to 297-QUATER, 347-BIS, 347-TER, 348-BIS, 348-TER, 358-QUATER, 358-QUINQUIES, 359-TER) and amends Ley 19.574 art. 34 numeral 34; the reproduced text gives only these amendment notes, not the text of the added articles. Chapter II requires the Executive Power to promote a national educational campaign on personal finance and cybersecurity in specified secondary and technical education centres and for beneficiaries of listed public programmes, covering payment means, bank accounts, credit, phishing, vishing, smishing, malware, trojans and social engineering. Chapter III authorises financial intermediation institutions and electronic-money issuers to create inter-institutional registries of data on unauthorised transactions, and disapplies the limits of Decree-Law 15.322 for sharing those records among themselves and with judicial authorities. Chapter IV authorises these institutions not to execute withdrawal or transfer orders on accounts receiving funds from disputed transactions, up to the disputed amount; requires notice to the Banco Central del Uruguay within one business day; and lists cases in which the freeze must be lifted, including no complaint filed within 48 hours or no court order within 30 days. Penalties for the added offences are not stated in the reproduced text.

title: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013
summary_short: Protection of Personal Information Act 2013, assented 19 November 2013, regulates processing of personal information by responsible parties domiciled in or using means in South Africa. It sets eight processing conditions, limits on special and child information, automated decisions and transborder transfers, and Information Regulator enforcement with offences and fines.
summary_long: The Act regulates the processing of personal information by responsible parties domiciled in South Africa or using automated or non-automated means in it, and excludes purely personal or household activity, fully de-identified data, and certain journalistic, national security and judicial processing. Chapter 3 sets eight conditions: accountability, lawfulness and minimality with consent or other grounds, purpose specification, further processing limits, information quality, openness and notice, security safeguards with breach notification, and data subject participation. Part B prohibits processing special personal information and Part C prohibits processing children's personal information, each subject to listed authorisations or exceptions. Chapter 6 requires prior authorisation from the Regulator for listed processing. Chapter 8 regulates unsolicited electronic direct marketing and section 71 limits decisions based solely on automated profiling. Section 72 limits transfers outside the Republic. Chapter 5 establishes the Information Regulator, which may investigate, issue information and enforcement notices, and refer matters to an Enforcement Committee. Chapter 10 provides civil damages actions. Chapter 11 sets offences punishable by fines or imprisonment of up to 10 years or 12 months, and administrative fines not exceeding R10 million, which the Minister may adjust under section 109(10). The annotated part ends at section 109.
